# Christian Questions Rewind — 2026

## Episode 1418 — How Do I Know if I Am REALLY Following Jesus? (Part II)
Published: 2026-01-05
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1418-follow-jesus-part-ii/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/03100458/CQ_Rewind_01-05-2026_How_Do_I_Know_if_I_Am_Really_Following_Jesus_Part_II.pdf

Romans 12:2: And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect.

In Part I of this two-part series, we focused on the magnificent gift we receive as Christians when we accept the redemption for our sins available through Jesus’ sacrifice. We talked about the magnitude of this gift and how, as true disciples of Jesus, we are also required to give back as a result of receiving it. According to Scripture, the action of “giving back” is accomplished through our responsibility to care for it reverently. This care is clearly identified by how we choose to live our lives as genuine followers of Christ. Fortunately, we have clear and concise instructions waiting for us in the Scriptures!

Part I focused on Romans 12:1 to help us define what it REALLY means to follow Jesus:

Romans 12:1: Therefore I urge you, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living and holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.

In Part I, I mentioned polishing silver for one of my clients, which required a great deal of care to do it properly. Similarly, our gift of being called to follow in Jesus' footsteps also demands tremendous care and maintenance.

This serves as a great analogy for what it means to follow Jesus, as it requires specific areas of focus and care.

Required Care for the Gift of Discipleship:

The end of Romans 11 sets up chapter 12, showing the great privilege we have been given:

Romans 11:33: (KJV) O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God!

How unsearchable are His judgments, and His ways past finding out!

We have been given incredible, undeserved gifts—redemption for our sins and the opportunity of discipleship. As followers of Jesus, it is important we recognize and receive these.

REQUIRED CARE FOCUS (OUR MAINTENANCE FOCUS) IS THREE PIECES

o Awe

o Gratitude

o Humility

Awe: 1 Peter 2:10: For you once were NOT A PEOPLE, but now you are THE PEOPLE OF GOD; you had NOT RECEIVED MERCY, but now you have RECEIVED MERCY.

We have been given something beyond our comprehension. We look at it with awe.

Gratitude: Ephesians 2:8: For by grace you have been saved through faith; and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God.

We say thank you when we receive a gift. When that gift is truly unmerited, we might struggle with how to properly thank God.

Humility: 1 Corinthians 1:27: But God has chosen the foolish things of the world to shame the wise, and God has chosen the weak things of the world to shame the things which are strong.

Realizing how small we are helps us keep proper perspective.

All of these REQUIRED CARE FOCUSES bring us now to the action required as a result of these reactions to our receiving this incredible gift, as found in Romans 12:1.

REQUIRED CARE FOCUS: (ACTIONS)

o Intentional self-denial

o Adopting a NEW mindset

o Full engagement

Intentional self-denial: Luke 9:23: And he was saying to them all, If anyone wishes to come after me, he must deny himself, and take up his cross daily and follow me.

Adopting a NEW mindset: 1 Corinthians 3:16-17: 16 Do you not know that you are a temple of God and that the spirit of God dwells in you? 17 …for the temple of God is holy, and that is what you are.

Jesus’ true followers are likened to a temple of God where His spirit (His power and influence) dwells. This realization should inspire us in an entirely different way of thinking.

Full engagement: Philippians 3:13-14: 13 Brethren, I do not regard myself as having laid hold of it yet; but one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead, 14 I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.

Forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward is what full engagement with the God’s plan looks like for us.

Our summary of Romans 12:1: recognition, awe, gratitude, humility, intentional self-denial, adopting a new mindset and full engagement.

In this episode, we will focus on Romans 12:2 and the transformation discipleship brings:

Romans 12:2: And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect.

There is so much to learn about being a Christian from this verse!

What does it actually mean to be transformed by the renewing of our minds? Here is a glimpse:

Philippians 1:21: For to me, to live is Christ and to die is gain.

Why would dying be considered gain?

To die is gain because it is a big change in who we are. Dying means the old is put aside, put away from us. We do not need it anymore because something new has come.

This may sound sad; however, once we see what this death ultimately leads to, the whole picture changes:

Revelation 19:7-8: 7 Let us rejoice and be glad and give the glory to him, for the marriage of the lamb has come and his bride has made herself ready. 8 It was given to her to clothe herself in fine linen, bright and clean; for the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints.

If you are part of the bride of Christ, a faithful follower, then you have “made yourself ready.” But ready for what? Many people don't see a future purpose for a Christian other than being saved and going to heaven. This gives us a glimpse of what being saved and going to heaven are all about; what going to heaven produces.

Getting to heaven is not the end; it is actually a beginning!

His bride—all the faithful followers of Christ. They have many descriptions, including a temple of God as we discussed, and the body of Christ of which Christ is the head.

What are they ready for? What will this marriage accomplish?

Revelation 21:1-4: 1 Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth… 2 And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, made ready as a bride adorned for her husband. 3 And I heard a loud voice from the throne, saying, Behold, the tabernacle of God is among men...

This picture intentionally describes the new Jerusalem as a bride adorned for her husband. The governing power over the world—the bride of Christ—comes down from heaven. This is not an end; this is a beginning.

...and He will dwell among them, and they shall be His people, and God Himself will be among them, 4 and He will wipe away every tear from their eyes; and there will no longer be any death; there will no longer be any mourning, or crying, or pain; the first things have passed away.

We can now see how dying is gain because it brings about the promise there will no longer be any death. The death of the faithful followers, the heavenly bride, is part of the process to remove death forever, for everyone! We can’t wish for a better gain than this!

The transformation we are called to engage in is bigger, broader and far more powerful and focused than anything our feeble human minds can comprehend.

THE TRANSFORMATIONAL WALK OF TRUE DISCIPLESHIP

We have already established the concepts surrounding self-denial and full engagement. Seeing this lofty prophetic view of the future of Jesus’ disciples, we now need to clearly understand the two main points of Romans 12:2:

NOT CONFORMING, AND INSTEAD TRANSFORMING.

These hold the key to what a REAL CHRISTIAN LIFE looks like!

It’s great to love Jesus, but we are now seeing that there certainly is more to living a true Christian life than that wonderful beginning.

How do we understand what this nonconformity and transformation are, and how do we engage in all they require?

These ARE two absolutely fundamental foundations for living in a Christlike fashion. Understanding them comes in steps, and applying them is no different.

To begin, we need to start where the Apostle Paul started—not conforming.

As usual with biblical teachings, there is far more to this than we might imagine:

Romans 12:2: And do not be conformed <4964> to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind…

Conformed: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4964 suschematizo; to fashion alike, i.e. conform to the same pattern (figuratively)

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to conform one’s self (i.e. one’s mind and character) to another’s pattern, (fashion one’s self according to)

We are not to fashion ourselves in the pattern of the world. As a reminder from Part I, we are to be IN the world but not OF the world.

Notice the major contrast between being conformed and being transformed. Paul is telling us we cannot be transformed unless we first take ourselves out of conformity. What does this mean?

We are to adhere to two basic levels of nonconformity:

1. Romans 12:2 teaches us NOT to be conformed to this world—to this age.

This nonconformity is the external, big picture of what we are to be OUT OF ALIGNMENT with.

Sometimes our car might pull to the right or left because the wheels are out of alignment. That is the way we should be. We are supposed to be “out of alignment” with the world—we should make the car pull to the right. It doesn’t seem natural, but this verse is saying not to be conformed to this world.

Here is one example of Jesus modeling this action:

John 18:36: Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world <2889>. If my kingdom were of this world, then my servants would be fighting so that I would not be handed over to the Jews; but as it is, my kingdom is not of this realm.

World: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2889 kosmos; orderly arrangement

This scripture references the coming kingdom of God, which will replace this current world order. God will remove the old order; it will no longer exist. It will be replaced with something new. Not conformed, but transformed.

As the Messiah, Jesus was dramatically out of conformity with all that was happening around him. As his footstep followers, we also are to be out of conformity in our time. We are to be radically out of alignment with this world’s precepts and corruptions. Do not be conformed to this world.

The disciples did not understand Jesus' mission. Their expectation was that he would bring down the Roman rule over Israel and establish a Jewish state at that time.

Could there be false expectations today, similar to those of the disciples at Jesus’ first advent?

Yes, like his disciples back then, it is easy to mix our understanding of what Jesus wants from us with our own desires. The purpose of Jesus’ first advent wasn’t to bring about Rome’s downfall. He came to do something much bigger. So there was a disappointment—and a reappointment—of their hopes.

This word for conform is only used one other time in the New Testament.

2. Peter encourages us to be nonconforming in the more personal parts of our lives.

1 Peter 1:13-14: 13 Therefore (because you were called to follow Jesus), prepare your minds for action, keep sober in spirit, fix your hope completely on the grace to be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ. 14 As obedient children, do not be conformed <4964> to the former lusts (longing, desire or craving) which were yours in your ignorance.

In other words, take a stand; walk away from “self.” Don't be conformed to your old ways and worldly mindset.

This is the personal, internal picture of what we are to be OUT OF ALIGNMENT with. We are supposed to be pulling the car to the right, away from alignment with our former self, because we are to be out of alignment with our human nature. We are no longer aligned with what we once knew and followed as acceptable ways of living, thinking and processing our emotions. We now have a higher calling.

The call to Christ involves radical changes. Nonconformity requires a different, higher perspective on what our vocation (what we do for a living) will be. Most people work for a living, but our focus is to be followers of Christ as our primary job.

Let’s look at this new vocation:

Matthew 4:18-20: 18 Now as Jesus was walking by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon who was called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea; for they were fishermen. 19 And he said to them, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men. 20 Immediately they left their nets and followed him.

Their true vocation was to be fishers of men. There is a dramatic difference between our earthly jobs and our true vocations. We are no longer in alignment with our former desires, so our vocation in life should reflect our alignment with the will of God, not our own will. Our own will should be left in the past.

Nonconformity requires a different, higher perspective regarding what our comfort in life looks like:

Matthew 8:18-20: 18 Now when Jesus saw a crowd around him, he gave orders to depart to the other side of the sea. 19 Then a scribe came and said to him, Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go. 20 Jesus said to him, The foxes have holes and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.

Jesus was comfortable with no place to call his own because it was his Father’s will. Let’s remember, the levitical priesthood had no inheritance in the land (Deuteronomy 18:1,2).

Jesus was comfortable not owning anything. However, we are not saying Christians should not own anything. We see that early Christians owned land and had possessions (many used these in service to the brethren—Jesus and the apostles often stayed with their brethren on their journeys). However, their homes, jobs, finances and focus were all dedicated to the will of God through Christ.

That’s nonconformity with our own comfort. We should be uncomfortable if our priority is our own comfort. Our comfort should come from serving God through Christ, rather than from the accomplishments or possessions we have accumulated.

Nonconformity requires a different, higher perspective regarding what our focus in life will be:

Luke 9:23-24: 23 And he was saying to them all, If anyone wishes to come after me, he must deny himself, and take up his cross daily and follow me. 24 For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake, he is the one who will save it.

Our focus in life is to lose ourselves through self-sacrifice, laying down our own interests so that we may become more Christlike. This is what nonconformity, being out of alignment with the world and our own desires, actually means. It is radical, and this is the only way we can get to transformation.

Notice, we haven’t talked about transforming yet, because we cannot get to transforming until we get to NOT conforming. That opens the door.

Nonconformity requires a different, higher conformity to be firmly put in place:

Philippians 4:12-13: (KJV) 12 I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. 13 I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.

You may be thinking, My Christianity doesn't look like this. What should I do? We need to remember that this is not an instantaneous or emotional thing. We have to work at this. We need to intentionally decide to be nonconformists by putting away behaviors, mindsets and even acquaintances that could hinder our growth in Christ.

THE TRANSFORMATIONAL WALK OF TRUE DISCIPLESHIP:

Our transformation begins with the decision to dramatically step out of conformity with the ways and influences of the world, as well as stepping out of conformity with the thoughts, feelings, habits and direction of our individual earthly lives. This nonconformity MUST be INTENTIONAL and not merely consequential!

A good example of this is having a personal trainer. Going to a gym on our own to exercise is different than having a personal trainer. My wife has used a trainer who makes her do exercises she wouldn't normally do and doesn’t want to do. But she does them anyway.

That nonconformity with how we feel opens the door to being able to conform to what we need. We need a clear picture of how all this works, dead-set in our minds, so we understand, If I want to be a true Christian and really follow Christ, these are the things I have to put in place.

This is a big message the Scriptures are presenting loud and clear. True discipleship is not in any way conformed to this world!

Now that we see this powerful message of nonconformity so clearly displayed, how do we translate it into the necessary transformation of discipleship?

It is so important to realize that the genuine transformation of true discipleship cannot begin to firmly take root until we have a working understanding of self-denial and full engagement, along with a grasp of the broad scope of our needed nonconformity. Now we can begin to delve into what the power of transformation in Christ looks like.

Nonconformity is a huge foundation to open the door for transformation.

Here is where nonconformity with the world and our flesh is going to bring us. This is what transformation looks like:

2 Corinthians 5:14-16: 14 For the love of Christ controls us, having concluded this, that one died for all, therefore all died; 15 and he died for all, so that they who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again on their behalf. 16 Therefore from now on we recognize no one according to the flesh; even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him in this way no longer.

The Apostle Paul says that because Christ loved us and all those he died for, his love controls how we should look at others. We no longer recognize people the way they used to be; we look at them with spiritual eyes, seeing them with the same love Christ has for them.

Many people—including Paul himself before his conversion—knew Jesus according to the flesh, meaning they saw him as just a man, a teacher or even a threat. But after encountering the risen Christ, Paul realized Jesus must be understood spiritually—as the glorified son of God.

Therefore, we are no longer conforming to the way we have known one another up until now:

2 Corinthians 5:17: Therefore (because of our nonconformity to our old ways) if anyone is in Christ, he is a new <2537> creature<2937>; the old things passed away; behold, new things have come.

New: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2537 kainos; of uncertain affinity; new (especially in freshness)

Creature/Creation: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2937 ktisis; original formation (properly, the act; by implication, the thing, literally or figuratively)

In other words, you are a fresh, original creation that has never existed before. When God created the heavens and the earth and saw it was very good, that was a finished creation. We are new creations—something that wasn’t created back then. This is something fresh and new. This is why nonconformity to a sinful world and our old lives is incredibly important!

With this glimpse of what a new mind looks like, let’s now further define transformation:

Romans 12:2: And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed <3339> by the renewing of your mind…

Transformed/Transfigured: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3339 metamorphoo; verb to transform (literally or figuratively, "metamorphose")

The King James Version translates this as transfigure 2 times, transform 1 time, change 1 time

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: to change into another form, to transform, to transfigure

This word transformed means to change into another form. It is only used in three New Testament contexts.

The first is in Romans 12:2.

It is also used to describe what happened to Jesus in the vision on the Mount of Transfiguration:

Matthew 17:2: (KJV) And was transfigured <3339> before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light. (Also cited in Mark 9:2)

This was a vision; it didn’t actually happen. In that vision, Jesus went up to the mountain as a man and was changed from an earthly form to a spiritual form. This vision modeled a higher, transformed spiritual way of being.

Paul contrasts the “veiled” approach of Judaism under the Law with liberty in Christ:

2 Corinthians 3:14-18: 14 But their minds were hardened; for until this very day at the reading of the old covenant the same veil remains unlifted, because it is removed in Christ. 15 But to this day whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart; 16 but whenever a person turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. 17 Now the Lord is the spirit, and where the spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. 18 But we all, with unveiled face, beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are being transformed <3339> into the same image from glory to glory, just as from the Lord, the spirit.

The Jews could see the provisions of the Law, but it was as though they were looking through a veil; they couldn’t understand them fully because Christ hadn’t come, and the holy spirit wasn’t yet given to them to help them understand.

This transformation from glory to glory is from human to spirit—a new creation. The human is looked at as “glory” because God created humanity in a glorious fashion to have dominion (to rule responsibly) over the earth. It is a glorious creation. But that glory is transforming into a NEW glory—the new creation.

The Jews of the Old Testament saw God’s plan, but only through a metaphorical “veil” over their hearts. Without the holy spirit working in them, they could not see more. Because of God’s power and influence working in the new creation, faithful followers can see more by His grace, creating a transformation.

Transformation is a gradual process, and even the Apostle Paul had to work on it:

Philippians 3:13-15: 13 Brethren, I do not regard myself as having laid hold of it yet; but one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead, 14 I press on (press also means to flee, pursue or run swiftly) toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus. 15 Let us therefore, as many as are perfect, have this attitude; and if in anything you have a different attitude, God will reveal that also to you.

Leave what was, just like the caterpillar transforms into a butterfly. It's a process of dissolving the old and reforming it into a new being. It’s a complete remaking of what we are. While who we are remains the same, what we are is completely transformed.

Scripturally, the person transforms even to the point of being given a new name:

Revelation 2:17: He who has an ear, let him hear what the spirit says to the churches. To him who overcomes, to him I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, and a new name written on the stone which no one knows but he who receives it.

In the process of our transformation (remember, Revelation is a book of symbols), we are amply fed with the food that brings immortality—that is, hidden manna. The overcomer is identified with a white stone (pure) engraved with a new name.

Being a true follower of Christ takes a lifetime of effort. When we fall, we have to get up and ask for forgiveness and start again, and on and on. It is hard, but SO worth it!

THE TRANSFORMATIONAL WALK OF TRUE DISCIPLESHIP:

Our transformation is a PROCESS that requires our intentional, focused, sacrificial development here and now. While we are not expected to become perfect in this life, we are expected to bend our will, intellect, emotions, words, actions and our character towards Christlikeness, knowing our Father will see our efforts as those of His new creation, not of a fallen human being.

We are thankful that God sees us by looking at the new creature growing within us and not the old creature we are struggling to leave behind. We press toward this incredible transformation of every part of our lives.

This whole concept of being transformed challenges us to see far beyond what is easy and comfortable. We need to stretch!

We are to be nonconformists to the world and our flesh and then transformed by the new mind of Christ. Where does all this lead?

The next piece of this discipleship puzzle that the Apostle Paul is fitting together for us gives us a solid conclusion for our daily Christian lives here and now. As big as the ultimate heavenly results will be later, our focus needs to be on knowing what to do and how to do it today.

Romans 12:2: And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove <1381> what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect.

Prove: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1381 dokimazo; to test (literally or figuratively); by implication, to approve

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to test, examine, prove, scrutinize (to see whether a thing is genuine or not), as metals 2) to recognize as genuine after examination, to approve, deem worthy

Two other examples of this word being used:

1 Thessalonians 5:21: (KJV) Prove <1381> (examine) all things; hold fast that which is good.

1 John 4:1: (KJV) Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try <1381> (scrutinize) the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.

We need to prove, to scrutinize, whether what we are being taught is from God. It is not going to come down in a lightning bolt on our heads so that we always know the correct answer. We have to work at uncovering true understanding through study, prayer and fellowship with our brethren.

Our proving the will of God means we are to LEARN TO KNOW what our right courses of action are.

Romans 12:2: And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good <18> and acceptable and perfect.

Good: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #18 agathos; a primary word; "good" (in any sense, often as noun)

An example of how this word is used:

James 3:17: But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good <18> fruits, unwavering, without hypocrisy.

Our LEARNING TO KNOW the will of God considers only that which is “good” from a godly perspective.

God’s goodness is based on His four main attributes of justice, wisdom, power and love.

Romans 12:2: And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable <2101> and perfect.

Acceptable: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2101 euarestos; fully agreeable

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: well pleasing, acceptable

Examples of how this word is used:

Ephesians 5:10: (KJV) Proving what is acceptable <2101> unto the Lord.

Philippians 4:18: (KJV) But I have all, and abound: I am full, having received of Epaphroditus the things which were sent from you, an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing <2101> to God.

Epaphroditus brought Paul a financial gift from the Philippians to support him while in prison. This was a beautiful and appreciated gift because it was given from pure and godly motives, and it was evidently a sacrifice for the Philippians to send this to help Paul. This made the gift an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice even more acceptable, wellpleasing—not only to Paul—but to God.

We strive to do only those things which are acceptable and wellpleasing to God.

Our LEARNING TO KNOW the will of God follows only that which is acceptable and wellpleasing to God.

Perfect: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5046 teleios; complete

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: brought to its end, finished

Romans 12:2: And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect <5046>.

Examples of how this word is used:

Matthew 5:48: (KJV) Be ye therefore perfect <5046>, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect <5046>.

None of us is perfect; we are to grow toward being complete.

Colossians 4:12: (KJV) Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, saluteth you, always labouring fervently for you in prayers, that ye may stand perfect <5046> and complete <4137> in all the will of God.

We just defined perfect as “complete” or “finished,” but this verse added a different Greek word translated into English as complete.

Complete: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4137 plēroō; to make replete, fill (up)

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to make full, to fill up, i.e. to fill to the full 1a) to cause to abound, to furnish or supply liberally

Think of your spiritual life like a living room undergoing a renovation. First, the construction work is completed: the old walls are removed, new ones are built, the windows are replaced and the flooring is installed. At this stage, the room is structurally sound, stable, and fully developed—nothing is missing in terms of its construction. This is what Paul means by perfect (teleios): mature, well-rounded, brought to full growth.

But even though the room is now beautifully built, it still isn’t ready to be lived in. It needs furniture—a place to sit, a table to gather around, lighting, and the personal touches that make it functional. When all of that is added, the room becomes “complete” (peplērōmenoi; the root word is plēroō)—fully furnished, fully supplied, equipped for its purpose.

In the same way, God not only matures us (building the “room”), but He also equips us with everything necessary for spiritual life and service (furnishing the “room”). The construction makes the room whole; the furnishing makes it usable. He fills our lives with the qualities, experiences and spiritual tools we need to function as mature Christians. The renovation makes us whole, but the furnishing makes us useful.

That’s the difference Paul is highlighting in Colossians 4:12 with the Greek ideas behind perfect and complete.

Our LEARNING TO KNOW the will of God strives towards only that which is complete and wanting nothing in the sight of God.

Now let’s pause a moment and look at what this transformation is NOT. There is another Greek word translated into English as “transformation/transformed.” This, however, is an external change. Though it is sometimes used in a positive sense, it is definitely used as a warning against “outside-in” transformations—transformations that look good from the outside but really aren't.

Transformed: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3345 metaschematizo; to transfigure or disguise; figuratively, to apply (by accommodation)

This transformation can be negative, so we have to be aware of the context and the possible deceitfulness of this transformation.

What is the difference between our transformation and the transformation here?

2 Corinthians 11:13-15: (KJV) 13 For such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves <3345> into the apostles of Christ. 14 And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed <3345> into an angel of light. 15 Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers also

be transformed <3345> as the ministers of righteousness; whose end shall be according to their works.

This transformation is the deceptive kind. Lucifer deceived Eve and made it sound like it was to her advantage to disobey God. Ministers of false Christian ideas can be in this same disguise, knowingly or unknowingly.

We must always test ideas and concepts with the Bible for truth, clarity and harmony with other scriptures, not taken out of context.

Some translations more plainly say, disguising themselves. Satan and his servants do disguise themselves—from the “outside in.” They do NOT become something they’re not; they pretend. They pretend to be angels of light and apostles of Christ.

Why do they do this? TO ATTEMPT TO STOP THE TRUE, “INSIDE OUT” (INTERNAL CHANGE) TRANSFORMATIONAL PROCESS OF THE DEVELOPMENT OF THE TRUE CHURCH!

They want to stop our being NOT conformed to this world and in being transformed into a new creation. We need to be on our guard by continually going to the Bible to determine truth and not just tradition or our own preferences.

Our defense against their disguises is the conviction that a life lived for Christ is a life of ultimate overcoming:

Romans 8:35-37: 35 Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? 36 Just as it is written, FOR YOUR SAKE WE ARE BEING PUT TO DEATH ALL DAY LONG; WE WERE CONSIDERED AS SHEEP TO BE SLAUGHTERED. 37 But in all these things we overwhelmingly conquer through him who loved us.

We conquer not through our own strength, nor even by relying on each other, but through Christ. We need the clarity of this conviction in his ability to conquer all our tribulations, to leave everything else behind and to rely on him to guide us through.

And he will, if we have been given God’s spirit. We cannot be separated from the love of Christ if we choose to remain comitted nonconformists and be transformed into this new creation.

Our defense against Satan’s disguises also comes with the confirmation that NOTHING can separate us from God’s love because we are His!

Romans 8:38-39: 38 For I am convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, 39 nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

I am convinced—the Apostle Paul drew a line in the sand. He decided. He made the choice to be loyal to God, no matter what. Nothing can derail a truly dedicated, sanctified follower of Christ who has God’s power and influence working within him.

Nothing can separate us from the love of God. This is what being a nonconformist to the world, our own feelings and emotions, and our own preferences means. This is what being transformed by the renewing of your mind means.

THE TRANSFORMATIONAL WALK OF TRUE DISCIPLESHIP:

Our transformation is the process of learning to be out of alignment with the world and our desires and instead to be intentionally focused on developing Christlikeness from the inside out. We need to be continually aware of the disguises and deceptions Satan uses while continuously covering ourselves with Christ and light.

Our transformation is continuously fed and encouraged by our heavenly Father and through our Lord Jesus!

How do we know if we are truly following Christ Jesus? This two-part series was designed to analyze just two verses of the Bible. Romans 12:1-2 tell us how to know if we are really following Jesus through God’s grace and mercy.

Get up and walk forward—leave those old inclinations behind. Grab onto godliness instead of humanness and see how you can be blessed!

So, how do I know if I am really following Jesus?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1418-follow-jesus-part-ii/

1. Romans 12:1 Review the foundation by describing the focuses and essential actions found here:

a. Recognition (Romans 11;33)

e. Intentional self-denial (Luke 9:23)

b. Awe (1 Peter 2:10)

f. Adopting a new mindset (1 Corinthians 3:16-17)

c. Gratitude (Ephesians 2:8)

g. Full engagement (Philippians 3:13-14)

d. Humility (1 Corinthians 1:27)

2. Why would dying be considered “gain”? Who is the bride of Christ? For what has she made herself ready? Who “gains” from her death? (Philippians 1:21, Revelation 19:7-8, 21:1-4)

3. Romans 12:2 And do not be conformed to this world…

a. Why is it important we be in nonconformity with the world externally, in the time in which we live? (John 18:36)

b. Why is it important we be in nonconformity with our old selves—the internal part of us that longs for and craves our former lives? (1 Peter 1:13-14)

c. What does nonconformity require of us? (Matthew 4:18-20, 8:18-20, Luke 9:23-24, Philippians 4:12-13)

4. Which “conformities” in your life are hindering your growth in Christ?

5. Romans 12:2 but be transformed by the renewing of your mind…

a. In what way are Christ’s followers “new creatures”? (2 Corinthians 5:17)

b. What practical changes should result as a new creature develops? (Philippians 3:13-15)

6. Romans 12:2 so that you may prove what the will of God is…

a. Why is it important to prove (to try, to scrutinize) whether what we are being taught is truly from God? What does this gain us? (1 Thessalonians 5:21, 1 John 4:1)

b. How do we do this?

7. Romans 12:2 that which is good and acceptable and perfect.

a. What do these things tell us about expectations for our behavior? (James 3:17, Ephesians 5:10,

Philippians 4:18)

b. Are we expected to be perfect in our behavior and mindset as developing new creatures? Explain. (Matthew 5:48, Colossians 4:12) What is the definition of “perfect”?

8. Compare the transformation in 2 Corinthians 11:13-15 with the transformation expected of Jesus’ followers? What are our defenses against these deceptions? (Romans 8:35-39)

9. In what ways do you see transformation happening to you in your walk with Christ? Which activities (like prayer, Bible study, fellowship with other believers) would support and strengthen your transformation?

## Episode 1419 — How Do God’s Promises Change Your Life? (Christian Character Series Part I)
Published: 2026-01-12
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1419-gods-promises/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/09112740/CQ_Rewind_01-12-2026_How_Do_Gods_Promises_Change_Your_Life_Part_I.pdf

How Do God’s Promises Change Your Life? (Christian Character Series Part I)

2 Peter 1:4: For by these He has granted to us His precious and magnificent promises, so that by them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world by lust.

The Apostle Peter began his second letter to all Christians by addressing the very formation of our Christian lives. He proceeded to lay out a deep and profound series of steps for character development to show us how to completely and wholly grow into mature disciples of Christ. To begin this process, his clear message in the first four verses of Chapter 1 verifies that we have been given EVERYTHING we need to be faithful to our call. Peter directly connects God’s promises to our faithfulness. What is it about His promises that has such a powerful influence on the everyday lives of those called according to His purpose? How can we clearly and definitively apply these promises to each and every day of our lives?

1 Peter encouraged Christians suffering from external pressures like persecution

and the challenge of living faithfully in a hostile world. The message was to stand firm, endure and live honorably.

2 Peter addresses internal dangers such as false teachers, moral corruption and

false doctrines. Its tone is more urgent and protective: grow in true knowledge, guard your faith and stay anchored in God’s promises.

Let’s start with a basic answer to our question: How do God’s promises change your life?

They don’t—UNLESS you are in line with His will and are growing into a fully dedicated follower of Jesus.

Now that we have your attention, let’s discover how Peter describes such a follower at the beginning of this letter.

As we read, we will notice MANY important elements of discipleship that have been given to us from God, through Jesus:

2 Peter 1:1–4: 1 Simon Peter, a bond-servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who have received a faith of the same kind as ours, by the righteousness of our God and Savior, Jesus Christ: 2 Grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord; 3 seeing that His divine power has granted to us everything pertaining to life and godliness, through the true knowledge of Him who called us by His own glory and excellence. 4 For by these He has granted to us His precious and magnificent promises, so that by them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world by lust.

Who do these promises apply to?

2 Peter 1:1: …To those who have received a faith of the same kind <2472> as ours...

Of the same kind: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2472 isótimos; of equal value or honor:—like precious

Of the same kind—the Greek adjective here only appears once in the Bible. It’s a powerful word of inclusion, saying, Your faith is of equal worth to that of the apostles. Equally honored, of equal value, of equal privilege. In other words, all believers—Jewish and Gentiles—have the same honored standing before God as the Jewish apostles.

We might be more familiar with the King James Version: to them that have obtained like precious faith.

We have received the same kind of faith as the Apostle Peter! What power!

What does this faith require? A nonconforming, transformed life of discipleship:

Romans 12:1–2: 1 Therefore I urge you, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living and holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service of worship. 2 And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect.

This is written by the Apostle Paul, another individual with that same faith, just like us. In our last two episodes, 1417 and 1418, we went through Romans 12:1,2 in great detail.

This is nonconformity to the external, big picture of what we are to be OUT OF ALIGNMENT with. We are NOT to conform to the world’s ways.

Peter encourages us to be nonconforming on a more personal level in our lives:

1 Peter 1:14: As obedient children, do not be conformed to the former lusts (longing, desire, craving) which were yours in your ignorance.

Peter is telling us that this is the personal, internal picture of what we're supposed to be OUT OF ALIGNMENT with. We are to spiritually live in contradiction to our earthly selves.

We are to be transformed—we are to come from one thing and bcome something else:

2 Corinthians 3:18: But we all, with unveiled face, beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, just as from the Lord, the spirit.

We are transformed from the glory of the human creation to the glory of a new spiritual creation, something that didn’t previously exist in us.

Our faith is the basis for God being able to truly and eternally transform us. This is not a transformation that wears off over time.

We are absolutely being changed from the inside out:

2 Corinthians 5:17: Therefore (because of our nonconformity to our old ways) if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature (a new creation); the old things passed away; behold, new things have come.

To those who have received a faith of the same kind as ours (2 Peter 1:1)—Peter is talking to those who are in the transformation process of being new creatures, those who have God’s spirit working on them from the inside, just like the apostles.

How does this faith come to us? From God ultimately, but through the works of Jesus:

2 Peter 1:1: …by the righteousness of our God and Savior, Jesus Christ: (God here meaning “mighty one,” not Jehovah God)

What was the righteousness… of Jesus? What did he do? He did everything to put us in a position to receive this kind of faith.

God’s justice was perfectly satisfied by the righteous acts of the man Christ Jesus:

Romans 5:18–19: 18 So then as through one transgression (Adam’s) there resulted condemnation to all men, even so through one act of righteousness (Jesus’) there resulted justification of life to all men. 19 For as through the one man's disobedience (Adam) the many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one (Jesus) the many will be made righteous.

2 Peter 1:1 is talking about the righteousness of Jesus Christ, who balanced the “scales” of justice for Adam. This wasn’t easy. It took focused effort, dedication and sacrifice.

This is further verified:

1 Corinthians 15:20–22: 20 But now Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who are asleep. 21 For since by a man came death, by a man also came the resurrection of the dead. 22 For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.

God’s plan and Jesus’ actions make this happen. A faith like the Apostle Peter’s is a faith in the righteous acts of Jesus, who was fulfilling the plan of God.

It is not just running to the promises and holding onto them; we have to learn the plan first! We have to have a faith like the Apostle Peter, based on the righteous acts of Jesus. This is how we begin to move towards claiming those promises of God.

What a strong, fundamental way to open our understanding to appreciate and apply God’s promises in our daily lives!

The Apostle Peter is telling us that faith in the righteousness of Jesus is only a beginning. What does he say follows these things?

Peter’s objective here is for us to have a well-rounded appreciation of the depth of God’s promises. His next words continue to build a basis for being able to accept the true power of not only what God has called us to, but also what He has promised we can rely on.

While he was with Jesus, Peter was known to be impetuous. Here we see him as a mature Christian, showing us something magnificent. Let’s continue with our study in 1 Peter.

2 Peter 1:2: Grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord;

Grace and peace are not just given or added to us; they are multiplied for our benefit. They abound!

Why do they abound? Because we are called by God Himself, and when God is involved in anything, it is not just mere addition; it is multiplication!

2 Thessalonians 2:13–14: 13 But we should always give thanks to God for you, brethren beloved by the Lord, because God has chosen you from the beginning for salvation through sanctification by the spirit and faith in the truth. 14 It was for this He called you through our gospel, that you may gain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Think about this. God has chosen you from the beginning for salvation through sanctification by the spirit and faith in the truth. We are not just “zapped” and changed.

It requires the process of sanctification (setting apart) in which we are made holy by God’s spirit (His power) working within us because we have a faith just like Peter. It is in the truth that Peter, Paul, James and John and all the others preached to us. There is a remarkable power here.

Our lives, therefore, need our daily personal effort and dedication to maintain our focus. This is why it says grace and peace are multiplied to us in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.

Philippians 2:12–13: 12 So then, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your salvation with fear and trembling; 13 for it is God who is at work in you, both to will and to work for His good pleasure.

There’s a direct correlation here between this multiplied grace and peace, with knowledge of God and Jesus. This knowledge is a deep, transformative understanding.

We will talk more about knowledge in this series, but there are those who would love to have these gifts but don’t want to put in the time and effort into study and prayer, or the personal accountability that comes with increased knowledge.

I have a friend who, every time we get together, complains that he doesn’t understand what God is doing in the world and wishes he knew his Bible accounts better. I have asked him, “Well, do you read the book?” His answer was, “Well, no…”

I told him that the Bible is our instruction manual. You have to take time to study. You have to read. You have to fellowship with others who are studying. He just kind of blanks out and says, “Yeah, I don’t understand.” And then he walks away. We have this conversation over and over again. He wants it all without having to do the work.

This is why grace is multiplied in the knowledge of God, because that knowledge of God doesn’t come miraculously for us. It comes through our effort. That’s why Peter calls it a faith of the same kind like ours, because he had to work for it, too.

2 Peter 1:3: seeing that His divine <2304> power has granted to us everything pertaining to life and godliness…

Divine: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2304 theîos; godlike

Not just “a few things,” but we are given everything for the purpose of being faithful. As it says in 2 Thessalonians 2:14—so that we may gain the (same) glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is glory, honor and immortality. It’s interesting that the word divine in the Greek is theîos, meaning godlike. So, divine power is a godlike force.

The faith of the same kind, or like precious faith prepares us for this theme of growth and character that follows in the next verses. Peter is telling us, “You started on the same foundation as we did. You are not behind, you are not less; you have everything you need. Ready, set, grow!”

Peter is talking to us as his brethren—seeing that His divine power has been granted to us—we are in this growth journey together. His divine power gives us everything pertaining to life—our spiritual life. Nothing is left out.

Some would say we aren’t all equal. Some Christians live in more dangerous countries without religious freedom. Some Christians suffer with violence, sickness and bad circumstances. We don’t all have the same degree of difficulties and suffering. Does everybody really get EVERYTHING they need?

YES! Absolutely, unequivocally, beyond the shadow of a doubt! Getting everything we need doesn’t mean our lives are peaceful, wonderful or easy. Those conditions rarely lead to growth. We have to grow in Christ and grow into spiritual maturity. Jesus’ life didn’t end in a very comfortable way, did it? He was tortured and crucified. Experiencing trials is part of what Christlikeness means. With Jesus’ help, during such difficult times we gain spiritual growth.

We may not be able to physically conquer every trial in this life, but using them to increase our faith and draw closer to God will result in eternal favor. We are all equal in this opportunity.

On top of grace and peace being multiplied, we are given every single thing we need to be faithful:

James 1:17–18: 17 Every good thing given and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shifting shadow. 18 In the exercise of His will He brought us forth by the word of truth, so that we would be a kind of first fruits among His creatures.

We grow into being a kind of first fruits among His creatures. This is something entirely new and different, and we are given everything we need to do that growing.

All that we are given puts us in a place of VERY specific privilege:

Ephesians 2:18–22: 18 for through him we both (referring to both Jewish and Gentile Christians) have our access in one spirit to the Father. 19 So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints, and are of God’s household, 20 having been built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the corner stone, 21 in whom the whole building, being fitted together, is growing into a holy temple in the Lord, 22 in whom you also are being built together into a dwelling of God in the spirit.

Take this scripture, read it again, and pause after each phrase. This is talking about us being given everything pertaining to life and to godliness. We have access, we have

citizenship, we have a household, we have a foundation and we’re part of what’s being built. We are completely integrated into God’s plan, given everything we need to spiritually thrive!

Think about Peter and the trials of his life. Think about Paul and the trials of his life. Think about Stephen being stoned to death and how short a time he had. They were all given everything they needed despite their difficult circumstances.

Because of ALL we are given, we are now to apply it through our knowledge of our mighty God:

2 Peter 1:3: …through the true knowledge <1922> of Him who called us by His own glory and excellence.

Knowledge: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1922 epígnōsis; recognition, i.e. (by implication) full discernment, acknowledgement:—(ac-)knowledge(-ing, -ment)

Gnōsis is the normal Greek word for knowledge. Here it adds the preposition epi, which means towards, in the direction of.

Bible Commentary by William Barclay: Epígnōsis then could be interpreted as a knowledge which is always moving further in the direction of that which it seeks to know.

It shows a progression—we are constantly learning this true knowledge.

Our personal responsibility, therefore:

2 Timothy 2:15–16: 15 Be diligent to present yourself approved to God as a workman who does not need to be ashamed, accurately handling the word of truth. 16 But avoid worldly and empty chatter, for it will lead to further ungodliness,

Our true knowledge of God is not natural or easy. Gaining it requires our daily devoted efforts. To emulate a faith like Peter's or Paul's requires working at it. We can see it in their writings and in their experiences. They were constantly challenged and tried, yet they stayed the course and gained the true knowledge of God by living their faith.

Our knowledge of His glory and excellence does not come without severe testing:

1 Peter 5:6–10: 6 Therefore humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that He may exalt you at the proper time, 7 casting all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.

Casting is not a passive or serene act; the word "cast" here implies a forceful physical action, like throwing a football or a fishing line away from yourself so that you no longer possess it. We can do this with confidence because God cares for you, which in the original Greek means He has a profound, deep concern for our well-being.

8 Be of sober spirit, be on the alert. Your adversary, the devil, prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.

Being of sober spirit and on the alert means maintaining a state of mind that is dispassionate, settled and thinking in a mature way.

Peter describes the devil as a roaring lion. Still, it is interesting to note that literal lions roar to intimidate, scare off intruders or warn other lions, rather than when they are actively hunting. Satan uses this "roar" of fear to paralyze us. His goal is to devour our spiritual life, to swallow us up and stop us at all costs.

9 But resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same experiences of suffering are being accomplished by your brethren who are in the world. 10 After you have suffered for a little while, the God of all grace, who called you to His eternal glory in Christ, will Himself perfect, confirm, strengthen and establish you.

Peter offers the perspective that our trials last only for a little while. In the original Greek, this phrase effectively means “puny,” suggesting that even a lifetime of suffering is fleeting compared to the eternal glory that follows.

God carries our anxieties, and He will complete, strengthen and establish us by His own glory and through His own excellence. Peter is building a path towards understanding God’s promises. We haven’t gotten there yet because Peter is giving us all these things to first consider that will make the promises all the more important.

Let’s remember, this is Peter speaking. It’s thought that 2 Peter was written within the last year or two before he was martyred. He’s almost unrecognizable compared to the impulsive fisherman we meet in the gospels, where he was impulsive, overconfident and leading with his emotions. By the time he writes 2 Peter, he has followed Christ for decades and urges us toward patient, disciplined growth in character and true knowledge.

Look at all we are given, and we still have not even begun to describe the role the promises of God will play in our daily lives!

So far, we have been privileged to see how the vast might, providences and grace of God are applied to our lives. What could be better than this?

The incomprehensible magnitude of God will now be further and even more profoundly expressed through the revealment of His promises to us. Peter has masterfully set forth the power of God’s promises by helping us see who it is that makes these promises. What follows now is the absolute assurance of God’s overwhelming power in our lives.

Now we get to the promises!

2 Peter 1:4: For by these (meaning by God’s glory and excellence from verse 3) He has granted to us His precious and magnificent promises...

Of course, a promise is only as reliable as the character of the one who gives it. God’s promises are guaranteed BECAUSE of His glory and excellence!

He is unchangeable, truthful and completely trustworthy. Hebrews 6:18 assures us it’s impossible for God to lie. Because He sees the end from the beginning, we can trust that His long-range plans are as certain as if they’d already happened.

Let’s look at a few scriptures to give us perspective on these precious and magnificent promises:

2 Corinthians 1:20–22: 20 For as many as are the promises of God, in Him they are yes; therefore also through Him is our amen to the glory of God through us. 21 Now He who establishes us with you in Christ and anointed us is God, 22 Who also sealed us and gave us the spirit in our hearts as a pledge.

Being given this spirit as a pledge in this earthly body is a promise of something much more magnificent to come.

What do God’s promises promise? MANY THINGS. The Bible contains hundreds and hundreds of them. We will touch on only a few.

Peace:

Philippians 4:7: And the peace of God, which surpasses all comprehension, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

Notice this doesn’t say the peace of God will guard your body. It guards your hearts and minds, meaning we can go through hard things while still having the peace of God.

Strength and deliverance from trial: Our example will be in 1 Corinthians 10:12-13, but let’s first look at the context. In this chapter, Paul is warning the Corinthians what NOT to do by using Israel’s failures in the wilderness as examples. Earlier in the chapter, he lists how Israel experienced incredible privilege, but many still fell into idolatry, immorality, testing God and grumbling, which led to judgment. His point is that spiritual blessings don’t make anyone immune to temptation or failure.

1 Corinthians 10:12–13: 12 Therefore let him who thinks he stands take heed that he does not fall. 13 No temptation <3986> has overtaken you but such as is common to man; and God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will provide the way of escape <1545> also, so that you will be able to endure it <5297>.

Temptation: Strongs Exhaustive Concordance #3986; peirasmos; a putting to proof

Escape: Strongs Exhaustive Concordance #1545; ekbasis; …an exit (literally or figuratively)

Endure: Strongs Exhaustive Concordance #5297; hupophero; to bear from underneath, i.e. (figuratively) to undergo hardship

Notice that God doesn’t promise there will be no temptations or that each time we are in trouble, we will be miraculously delivered. God never allows a temptation without also providing a real way through it, giving us the strength to endure rather than be overcome.

So, look for the exit strategy! Think of temptation like being in a dark hallway: the moment things feel confusing, God has already lit an exit sign. You may have to slow down and look for it, but the way out is always there. God’s way of escape won’t be a trapdoor that magically (poof!) removes you, but a real, reliable path that lets you move through the situation without being overwhelmed.

This doesn’t mean we won't be tried or have difficulty. It doesn’t mean our way will be easy, or that we will find the exit on the path we are on. We might be going the wrong way! We need to look for His leading. Our way of escape is through His strength, enabling us to endure. The experience may not go away, but we can endure it by holding onto the promise of His strength to lean on.

Instruction and protection:

Psalm 32:8: I will instruct you and teach you in the way which you should go; I will counsel you with My eye upon you.

Think of a well-trained horse. The rider doesn’t have to yank the reins or give loud commands—the horse responds to the smallest shift of posture or the quietest cue because the connection between horse and rider is so close. It moves with confidence, not from force, but from the rider’s steady, attentive watchfulness. That’s the sense of Psalm 32:8: God guides us gently, not by pressure, but by the loving attention of His eye.

We ARE being taught and guided. The question is, are we listening, are we watching for what we are being taught and guided to do? If we are NOT on the right path, we don’t want God’s eyes upon us. We want to hide from God. So this only works if we are doing what we should be doing and are watchful for the slight corrections needed for our missteps.

I will counsel you with My eye upon you—do we want this to happen? We need to want His will to be able to claim His promises.

Deliverance from evil:

Psalm 34:7: The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear Him, and rescues them.

We’re reassured God’s care is both near and ongoing—a protective presence that surrounds His people even when they can’t see it.

This reminds us of Romans 8:31, where Paul writes, If God is for us, who can be against us?

God’s angel encamping around us, rescuing us from evil, provides strong reassurance. We must realize that sometimes our deliverance from evil requires going through it. There are times the results physically might not be happy. We talked about Stephen. Was death his end result? Yes, it was an end result, but not the final result. He was glorified—that was his final result—but it took death to get there. It involved being stoned. It took this horrible experience. His end result, though, was glorious.

Our eternal life is protected—not necessarily this life.

Courage:

2 Corinthians 4:7–10: 7 But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness of the power will be of God and not from ourselves; 8 we are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not despairing; 9 persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed; 10 always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our body.

These verses help us keep the proper perspective when we are going through problems. Courage is not the absence of fear. It is a deliberate process of action, spiritual reliance and psychological reframing. Reframing the experience is really important. It might mean walking towards what we would rather run away from. However, it’s easier to be courageous knowing we are standing behind our older brother, Jesus.

Paul stood courageous because he knew his power was not his own—he saw himself as just a weak jar of clay—an earthen vessel. He was courageous because he saw suffering not as defeat but as participation in Christ’s life and victory. The mission of the gospel was bigger than his fear.

Our faith is modeled after that kind of faith! Courage is not being fearless. Rather, it’s standing firm in the face of fear and uncertainty.

Assurance:

Romans 8:28,35: 28 And we know that God causes all things to work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to His purpose. 35 Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?

None of these can separate us from Christ’s love! Living with this assurance is only tested when our outcomes are not looking at all assured.

We tend to doubt, and that’s okay. When we consider these precious, magnificent and powerful promises from God, our insecurity is answered. We are helped through His power, grace and strength.

Hope and reward:

Romans 8:38–39: 38 For I am convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, 39 nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Nothing can change what He promises us. Our truest Christian hopes are not realized in this life, as our reward is spiritual and eternal.

The Apostle Peter brought us to this place of looking at the promises—but only after he put the work of Jesus in God’s plan and all of God's characteristics in place. There is a reason for this. It helps us see the magnitude of what we are given.

How much more assured than this can we ever imagine ourselves to be? God’s own omnipotent and all-powerful being is the guarantee behind all of His promises!

Now that we have the power of God’s promises laid out right before us, what more can we possibly ask for?

The Apostle Peter doesn’t stop here, nor should we. His next words wrap up the purpose of God’s promises, and then he will again expand our thinking. His next objective will be to set each and every one of us up to thoroughly maximize the power and effects of all he has just written about, by showing us how to grow into these glorious, godly conclusions.

Peter wraps up the power of God’s promises:

2 Peter 1:4: …so that by them (these promises) you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world by lust.

Partakers of the divine nature—to receive an extraordinary opportunity to be transformed from an earthly nature to a divine one—a privilege reserved for the most faithful followers of Jesus. This change in nature is defined by attaining immortality, a state where life is self-sustaining and no longer dependent on an external source. It is gained through a life of self-sacrifice, following Jesus through trials and remaining faithful until death. Its purpose is to serve in heaven alongside Jesus in the work of reconciliation, helping restore resurrected humanity to harmony with God. This is where the promises bring us to— partakers of the divine nature.

The unlikely miracle of this promised divine nature cannot be overlooked:

Ephesians 2:4–8: 4 But God, being rich in mercy, because of His great love with which He loved us, 5 even when we were dead in our transgressions, made us alive together with Christ (by grace you have been saved), 6 and raised us up with Him, and seated us with Him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, 7 so that in the ages to come He might show the surpassing riches of His grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. 8 For by grace you have been saved through faith; and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God.

These verses are telling us we haven’t seen anything yet! That’s how immense the surpassing riches of His grace are. It’s ALL a profound, magnificent and undeserved gift!

That's right, but what does it mean to claim these promises… and what DOESN’T it mean? Aren't they conditional?

When we speak of claiming these promises, it doesn’t mean we get to pick “that” one, or “this” one, or especially “that” one. As followers of Jesus, claiming the promises means we adopt them as God’s promises to us. They become a part of our lives. They are not given to make us feel good; they are given to help us grow towards spiritual maturity.

Yes, they are conditional. Remember, the promises do not affect us unless we are following in Jesus’ footsteps. If we are living a Christlike life, we can then claim the promises as helpful stepping stones along the way so we can grow in Christ. This is how they work.

It is not about how the promises make us feel; it is about what they drive us to do, what they drive us to be, and how they drive our lives.

All of this has been merely an introduction to Peter’s MAIN lesson! Let’s recap our introduction:

2 Peter 1:1-4: (excerpts) 1 To those who have… faith… by the righteousness of our… Savior, Jesus Christ: (We are abundantly given) 2 grace and peace… 3 seeing that God’s divine power has granted to us everything pertaining to life and godliness, through… His own glory and excellence. 4 (Because of this) …He has granted to us His precious and magnificent promises, so… by them you may become partakers of the divine nature…

In God’s lofty character, He presents us with promises that can and will lift us OUT of the corruption of this world stemming from any and all impure human desires. Our being lifted OUT of these insidious traps directly depends on where we decide our ultimate allegiance is focused! Peter’s main lesson here is about where our true allegiance lies. This Christian Character Series will focus on the theme of allegiance—where our allegiance lies as followers of Christ.

Our Ultimate Allegiance: This introduction of 2 Peter 1:1-4 is ALL about where our ultimate day-by-day allegiance is focused. God’s magnificent grace and character are here described as the basis for us being given His promises. BY THESE PROMISES, we are given the opportunity to partake of the divine nature.

The BIG question: What happens as a result of these powerful promises?

To answer this, we will quote Peter’s next words, looking at them in depth throughout this series. They will show us how we can firmly grow in Christ.

2 Peter 1:5–7: 5 Now for this very reason also, applying all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence, and in your moral excellence, knowledge, 6 and in your knowledge, self-control, and in your self-control, perseverance, and in your perseverance, godliness, 7 and in your godliness, brotherly kindness, and in your brotherly kindness, love.

Because of the progression shown here, these are sometimes called a “ladder of virtues,” showing how we mature in Christ, stepping up to the highest rung, which is love.

Each Christian Character trait just mentioned needs to be understood both individually and collectively. They are ALL vital qualities of our ultimate allegiance to God through Christ.

Peter tells us that if we climb this ladder, we can be faithful walking in Jesus’ footsteps. That is what this Christian Character Series will look into—each of these ladder steps and how they relate to one another.

Peter’s conclusion regarding these allegiance qualities is unmistakable:

2 Peter 1:8–11: 8 For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they render you neither useless nor unfruitful in the true knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. 9 For he who lacks these qualities is blind or short-sighted, having forgotten his purification from his former sins. 10 Therefore, brethren, be all the more diligent to make certain about His calling and choosing you; for as long as you practice these things, you will never stumble; 11 for in this way the entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ will be abundantly supplied to you.

For he who lacks these qualities is blind or short-sighted. Peter likens spiritual growth to eyesight. He says that if we increase these “ladder virtues,” we will become fruitful. But if they’re missing, we become nearsighted to the point of spiritual blindness. In other words, without growth, you can only see what’s directly in front of you—your immediate desires, fears, frustrations—while losing sight of the bigger picture of your calling.

Then Peter flips it—as long as you practice these things, you will never stumble. Growing in these qualities doesn’t just make you a better person. It actually stabilizes your entire Christian walk. He says you’ll never stumble, and your entrance into the kingdom will be abundantly supplied—a phrase that pictures a joyful, abundant welcome. You will be full of the fruit of the spirit, and God will say, Well done, good and faithful servant (Matthew 25:21 KJV).

We can liken 2 Peter 1:1-11 to a blueprint—technical drawings used by architects and engineers to construct buildings. Today, the word is used to mean any clear, step-by-step design or strategy. These texts we’ve been reading are a blueprint for spiritual transformation: God supplies the materials, Peter outlines the steps, and the result is a life shaped into Christlikeness with a glorious entrance into the kingdom.

We have a blueprint, a list of qualities, and all these comments at the end that tell us that if we do so, we won’t stumble or fall. We learn how to follow the will of God in our lives.

God’s greatness and His plan, revealed through the righteous acts of Jesus, enable us to be recipients of His powerful, life-supporting and remarkable promises. As amazing as these promises are, we need to recognize that they serve as a foundation for the life-changing work of Christian character building that we, as disciples, MUST engage in. The promises are not the end; they are a tool for our growth. What we have seen thus far is merely the tip of the iceberg!

Do we want to have a faith like the Apostle Peter? If so, we want to engage in the growth process of this Christian character that he is laying out for us.

So, how do God’s promises change your life?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!
