## Episode 1420 — What Steps Help Me Build a Permanent Christlike Character? (Christian Character Series Part II)
Published: 2026-01-19
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1420-diligence-part-ii/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/19215335/CQ_Rewind_01-19-2026_What_Steps_Help_Me_Build_a_Permanent_Christlike_Character_Part_II.pdf

(Christian Character Series Part II) — January 19, 2026

What Steps Help Me Build a Permanent Christlike Character? (Christian Character Series Part II)

2 Peter 1:5: Now for this very reason also, applying all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence, and in your moral excellence, knowledge.

The Apostle Peter began his second letter to all Christians by addressing the very formation of our Christian lives. He proceeded to lay out a deep and profound series of character development steps to show us how to completely and wholly grow into mature disciples of Christ. In Part I of this series, we covered the first four verses of 2 Peter chapter 1. These verses laid a broad foundation for the development of our Christian character, based on who God is, what He promises us and what Jesus has done. The next part of the blueprint for our character development not only shows us the traits needed to be included in our Christlikeness, but also how we are to include them. This episode will reveal how Peter unfolds his spirit-driven, exciting and practical approach to building a true Christlike character.

Let’s briefly recap the Apostle Peter’s foundation with a condensed summation of these texts:

2 Peter 1:1-4: 1 …To those who have… faith… by the righteousness of our… Savior, Jesus Christ: (We are abundantly given) 2 grace and peace… 3 seeing that God’s divine power has granted to us everything pertaining to life and godliness, through… His own glory and excellence. 4 (Because of this) …He has granted to us His precious and magnificent promises, so… by them you may become partakers of the divine nature…

In God’s lofty and unbreakable character, He presents us with promises that can and will lift us out of the corruption of this world stemming from impure human desires. But being lifted out of these insidious traps depends directly upon where we decide our ultimate allegiance is focused!

The Apostle Peter’s main lesson here is about where our true allegiance lies.

When we have true allegiance to something, we are loyal to it. Peter is diving us towards developing, in our Christian character, an abiding loyalty to following God’s will for us.

Our Ultimate Allegiance: This foundation is ALL about where our ultimate day-to- day allegiance will be focused. It is only through God’s magnificent grace and character that we are given His promises. BY THESE PROMISES, we are shown the path we need to take for the opportunity to partake of the divine nature.

What happens as a result of these powerful promises? Let’s look further.

(Christian Character Series Part II) — January 19, 2026

A blueprint describes the appearance and function of something. In 2 Peter 1, Peter describes the ideal appearance and function of our permanent Christian character.

Let’s look at Peter’s “blueprint”:

2 Peter 1:5: Now for this very reason also, applying <3923> all diligence <4710>…

We will pause here to focus on the details to understand the message.

Now for this very reason—what reason? We are told God in His might, power, mercy and grace has given us the power of His providence (oversight) in our lives. This providence comes through the promises which He grants us.

Applying: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3923 pareisphero; to bear in alongside, i.e., introduce simultaneously

Applying here means “bringing something alongside what we have already been given.” Peter is telling us that as we claim the promises of God that we received through the redemptive work of Jesus, we are to simultaneously have diligence.

Diligence: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4710 spoude; "speed," i.e. (by implication) despatch, eagerness, earnestness

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) haste, with haste 2) earnestness

Over the past few years, I have chosen a word to focus on at the beginning of each new year. The word diligence really jumped out at me in this study. Reflecting on its meaning inspired me to make it my New Year's resolution for 2026. I want to be diligent every day in doing God's will and in serving Him and my brethren. This means taking each morning to see how I can do the most important things before my day slips away. This could be preparing for Bible studies, staying close to the Lord in prayer or finding ways to serve my brethren.

One example of this diligence can be found in Hebrews. Paul had been addressing the Jewish Christians, urging them to follow Christ with the same diligence they had previously shown towards the Jewish Law.

Here is how he concludes this thought—showing them they needed to be more diligent in their worship of Christ:

Hebrews 6:10-12: 10 For God is not unjust so as to forget your work and the love which you have shown toward His name, in having ministered and in still ministering to the saints. 11 And we desire that each one of you show the same diligence <4710> so as to realize the full assurance of hope until the end, 12 so that you will not be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.

Sluggish is the exact opposite of diligence, meaning lazy, dull or slothful. We don’t want our days to get swallowed up in sluggishness; rather, we want to be filled with diligently applying godliness.

(Christian Character Series Part II) — January 19, 2026

Our diligence must be focused on inheriting what we have been offered. This is about having unequivocal allegiance to our Father through Jesus. It is about building a permanent, lasting Christian character.

2 Peter 1:5: Now for this very reason also, applying <3923> all diligence <4710>…

Let’s restate this: “Because God in His might, power, mercy and grace has given us the power of His providence in our lives through His promises, we now, while receiving God’s promises, must simultaneously apply diligent earnestness.”

What should we be diligent or earnest about?

2 Peter 1:5: Now for this very reason also, applying all diligence, in your faith <4102> supply moral excellence…

Faith: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4102 pistis; persuasion, credence, moral conviction; reliance (especially upon Christ for salvation), constancy (in such profession)

Apply all diligence to our conviction in Christ, our absolute credence in our Father and in our contancy in the profession of this faith.

Hebrews 11:1: Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction (evidence) of things not seen.

Faith is not a wish; it is based on solid and believable reality.

Applying all diligence (eagerness) in your faith is the beginning.

As we apply God’s promises, the blueprint calls for us to earnestly live our faith—not just feeling it, not just appreciating it, but LIVING it! In Part I, we saw how we have been given a faith just like that of the apostles (2 Peter 1:1). This means our faith needs to be vibrant and alive. It needs to be engaged and strong.

Faith is a gift and is not planted within us as a result of any works of our own:

Ephesians 2:8-10: 8 For by grace you have been saved through faith <4102>; and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God; 9 not as a result of works, so that no one may boast. 10 For we are His workmanship…

We have faith because salvation was freely given by the Father through Jesus. This gift of faith is a real, It is a real gift, not built upon our effort, so that no one may boast.

But this gift must by definition be tested and developed, otherwise it will NOT grow strong:

James 1:2-4: 2 Consider it all joy, my brethren, when you encounter various trials, 3 knowing that the testing of your faith <4102> produces endurance. 4 And let endurance have its perfect result, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.

Can we imagine being joyous in trial? YES! That’s what our permanent Christian character is supposed to look like.

(Christian Character Series Part II) — January 19, 2026

The testing of your faith produces endurance—faith is an attribute of our allegiance to God. We are going to use the phrase “Allegiance Attribute” a lot in this series. These are internal qualities that shape our character.

Faith is an Allegiance Attribute! Applying this gift of our calling requires an allegiance, a loyalty, willing to grind through the many testings of endurance for the sake of being completed in Christ.

This vibrant faith attribute needs to be put into daily use, or it will lose its influence:

James 1:5-8: 5 But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all generously and without reproach, and it will be given to him. 6 But he must ask in faith <4102> without any doubting, for the one who doubts is like the surf of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind. 7 For that man ought not to expect that he will receive anything from the Lord, 8 being a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.

Asking NOT in faith is essentially being double-minded. Asking in faith is being single- minded.

Look at the most successful people in any area of life, and you’ll see they are single- minded or focused on their path. Think of Jesus walking the earth, doing what he did—he single-mindedly followed his Father’s plan and will for our deliverance. The Apostle Peter was very impetuous before Christ died and was raised. But after he received God’s holy spirit, he was single-minded in his mission to spread the gospel. This is where true faith comes into play.

We need that single-mindedness in our faith to build our Christian character.

This vibrant faith must become a foundation for our actions, and therefore our growth:

James 2:18: But someone may well say, You have faith <4102> and I have works; show me your faith <4102> without the works, and I will show you my faith <4102> by my works.

Our faith needs to produce tangible results.

We need to ask ourselves:

- Can the testimony of our faith be seen? - What kind of diligence have we applied to our faith?

When we apply diligence (earnestness)—that focus is obvious to us and to those who see we live a different kind of life than others.

The Allegiance Attribute of Faith: Why is faith so important? Because it forms the foundation upon which other Allegiance Attributes are built. This goes well beyond a New Year’s resolution; this is developing a permanent character of Christlikeness.

(Christian Character Series Part II) — January 19, 2026

In the first few verses of 2 Peter 1, we learned God has granted to us His precious and magnificent promises. We are to take these promises and simultaneously apply diligent earnestness in developing our faith, which will then fully supply our lives for the necessary development of our Christian character.

These verses in 2 Peter provide us with several necessary Allegiance Attributes that are built directly upon this foundation of faith:

2 Peter 1:5: Now for this very reason also, applying all diligence, in your faith supply <2023> moral excellence…

Peter is telling us that as we claim the promises of God (granted us through the redemptive work of Jesus), we are to simultaneously have great eagerness in our vibrant faith to supply something else.

Supply: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2023 epichoregeo; to furnish besides, i.e. fully supply, (figuratively) aid or contribute

King James Version translates this “minister” 2 times, “minister nourishment” once, “add” once, “minister unto” once

Here are two examples of how this word is used:

Paul warns about the temptation of Christians worshipping men in the place of our Lord and head, Jesus:

Colossians 2:19: And not holding fast to the head, from whom the entire body, being supplied <2023> and held together by the joints and ligaments, grows with a growth which is from God.

There is a lot in this one little verse: From whom the entire body, being (fully) supplied through our head, Jesus Christ. His example “fully supplies” us with information, just as our own heads tell our bodies what to do.

We are fully supplied through our head which is Christ Jesus, though we profit from other examples like the Apostle Paul:

1 Corinthians 11:1: Be imitators of me, just as I also am of Christ.

We have our head, Jesus, fully supplying us as the body.

We are also fully supplied by the body of Christ, like the Apostles Peter and Paul and the brethren in our fellowship—the joints and ligaments.

We are required to diligently use our faith to fully supply our Christian character with whatever it needs to grow.

To the best of our ability, this leads us to fully supply others in the body of Christ.

The “fully supplying” here comes from many sources. God fully supplies us as our Father, Jesus fully supplies the body of Christ as our head, and we as members of the body must fully supply to the best of our ability the other body members. Finally, we need to be fully supplying our own character, so we have the capacity to be part of this mutual supplying.

(Christian Character Series Part II) — January 19, 2026

This requires one very specific word—diligence! We also can’t overlook the word applying, which means “alongside of,” and the word supplied, which means “furnished beside.”

Applying + diligence work together, adding depth to our Christlike character.

Now we’re going to jump ahead to the end of this blueprint scenario.

The last verse of this admonition in 2 Peter repeats this word for supplied, but in this case, it is God doing the supplying:

2 Peter 1:11: For in this way the entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ will be abundantly <4146> supplied <2023> to you.

Abundantly: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4146 plousios; copiously

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: abundantly, richly

How can it be abundantly supplied if it’s already “fully” supplied? Remember 2 Peter 1:4: God granted to us His precious and magnificent promises. Whenever we are supplied with anything from God, the supply is not just adequate; it is copiously abundant! This is what abundantly supplied is.

It is overwhelmingly full, and that’s the key to developing a permanent Christian character that will follow Jesus now and for eternity. We need an abundant supply of God’s grace because we are completely overhauling our broken humanity, refashioning it into the likeness of Christ. We are abundantly supplied!

Our mighty God supplies us overwhelmingly—He fully supplies us. We therefore must use our faith, in turn, to fully supply our Christian character, which will bring Him honor and praise eternally! Our Christian walk is all about honoring God for His marvelous promises to us.

(Christian Character Series Part II) — January 19, 2026

In this episode, we have worked on the words that give Peter’s process a way to unfold and move forward:

WHAT are we “fully supplying” to our lives?

- Peter’s blueprint calls for us to use our faith as a basis in applying a diligent earnestness in our personal efforts to develop the character attributes listed in the scriptures that follow.

Fully supplying ourselves is modeled after the Father’s actions of fully supplying us with everything we need. God has unequivocally promised us deliverance from corruption and the gift of divine nature! This deliverance is not a small thing. It required Jesus’ great sacrifice on our behalf. It requires our effort to follow Jesus’ example based on God’s grace, spirit and wisdom.

Alongside our faith we must apply diligence—speedily, eagerly and earnestly!

In our previous episode, we learned about the promises. In this episode, we realized we have to live those promises day by day. Those promises feed our faith. Now, for this very reason also (because God has granted us these promises), applying all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence… (which we will cover in Part III).

Because we are given God’s magnificent promises, we are to simultaneously (and with great eagerness and haste!) engage our faith as a solid foundation that will fully supply the growth of our Christian character. This growth doesn’t happen all at once; instead, it comes in stages, which is why we are reading the Apostle Peter’s blueprint.

So, what steps help me build a permanent Christian character?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

God has granted everything needed for life and godliness through His promises. These promises form the foundation of Christian character. Our response is allegiance—loyal commitment to God’s will.

2 Peter 1:5 is used throughout these questions:

## Episode 1421 — What Does True Christian Moral Excellence Look Like? (Christian Character Part III)
Published: 2026-01-26
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1421_moral_excellence/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/23092616/CQ_Rewind_01-26-2026_What_Does_True_Christian_Moral_Excellence_Look_Like_Part_III.pdf

(Christian Character Series Part III) — January 26, 2026

What Does True Christian Moral Excellence Look Like? (Christian Character Series Part III)

2 Peter 1:5: Now for this very reason also, applying all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence, and in your moral excellence, knowledge.

In 2 Peter 1, the Apostle Peter lays out a phenomenal blueprint for us to follow regarding the how and why of developing a focused and loyal character modeled after Christ. He begins by reminding us of the majesty and power of God, along with the loyalty and sacrifice of Jesus. He tells us that because God is as lofty as He is, we are given incomprehensible promises that can bring us to God’s own divine nature. He then tells us what’s required on our part. Peter explains that because of these promises, we need to apply all diligence, and in our faith we need to supply—we need to develop and live—a character that will nurture and grow specific virtues of Christlikeness.

Here is a portion of the Apostle Peter’s “blueprint” that reveals where our focus should be, so we can understand what our Christian characters are supposed to look like:

2 Peter 1:5: Now for this very reason (because we have God’s promises) also, applying all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence, and in your moral excellence, knowledge.

Let’s restate this, emphasizing the meaning of the key words applying, diligence and supply: While receiving God’s promises, Peter’s blueprint calls for us to simultaneously apply diligent earnestness and haste to our faith as a basis for fully supplying our lives with the fundamental character development needed to truly follow Jesus.

Peter’s teaching now turns away from what God has given us to what we are to give to Him by way of our Christian character. In other words, now that we have God’s promises, what do we need to give back?

Our view of this gift of the promises should be, What am I supposed to do with the privilege of what I have been given? This shows the allegiance of our very being, of who we are, developing step by step into greater Christlikeness. Our faith is where our ability to build a lasting character allegiance to God begins.

We will use the word “allegiance” often in this series. Allegiance in this application means to have total, complete loyalty to God. As we go through these lessons from the Apostle Peter, we’re looking at the different features he’s bringing out. We are calling them Allegiance Attributes, internal qualities that shape our character.

(Christian Character Series Part III) — January 26, 2026

In our previous episode, we talked about the Allegiance Attribute of Faith. This is the allegiance of our direction. Where does our loyalty lie? In what direction is our life going?

Faith is the gift of our calling by God that requires us to fully embrace it. Why? We build all the other Allegiance Attributes upon our earnest development of our faith as the solid base.

Let’s continue following the blueprint!

Now that we have the basis of faith through God’s grace and promises, what do we do?

2 Peter 1:5: Now for this very reason also, applying all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence <703>…

Moral excellence: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #703; arete; properly, manliness (valor), i.e. excellence (intrinsic or attributed)

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) a virtuous course of thought, feeling and action 1a) virtue, moral goodness; 2) any particular moral excellence, as modesty, purity

Allegiance Attribute of Moral Excellence—this is the allegiance of our heart.

We used the metaphor of a ladder, with faith as the first rung. Once we climb to that stable base, it’s time to step higher, right onto the rung of moral excellence.

We’re reading from NASB1995, but other translations say:

goodness virtue moral character noble character worthiness

In Greek, this moral excellence is the word aretē. Peter’s audience, shaped by Greek language and culture, would have understood aretē to mean “excellence,” with the idea of something fully living out its purpose. A knife has aretē if it cuts well. A horse has aretē if it runs fast. Fertile land has aretē.

The Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance definition includes “manliness (valor)” because in early Greek culture, excellence was often measured in heroic action or bravery in battle. A person has aretē if they live courageously and nobly.

So, aretē is something that performs exactly as it was meant to, to its highest purpose.

Peter takes that familiar word and overlays it onto the life of a Christian—once you’ve put your trust in Christ, the next step is to pursue a life that reflects God’s excellence— living in a way that matches the purpose He’s called you to. Living like God’s purpose

(Christian Character Series Part III) — January 26, 2026

actually matters to you. Putting God’s purpose right in front of everything else. It’s about choosing what is noble, courageous and upright in every part of life. It is living up to our highest potential.

We put God first by eagerly and fully supplying moral excellence to the foundation of our faith. This is where we begin to build.

Why is moral excellence the next quality after faith?

Keep this question in mind as we go, because there is a profound connection, and this is the pattern Peter will follow over and over again in these verses as he teaches us how to live.

How do we supply moral excellence? Follow the highest example! Peter explained to us that any true excellence we may develop is fashioned after the excellence of God our Creator.

Let’s go back a few verses:

2 Peter 1:3: seeing that His divine power has granted to us everything pertaining to life and godliness, through the true knowledge of Him who called us by His own glory and excellence <703>.

Peter is shifting his audience from the general excellence of aretē to moral excellence rooted in God’s character. Let’s repeat what we said earlier: it means to pursue a life that reflects God’s excellence—living in a way that matches the purpose He’s called you to. Living like God’s purpose actually matters to you.

We can say aretē is “God-shaped character,” in that God helps to shape it within us through our faith and His promises. It is also “God-shaped” in the sense that it’s modeled after God’s own excellent character—it’s modeled in the shape of God.

It’s exciting! We can’t get a better example. We might think of athletes, physicians, soldiers as heroes at the highest level and highest standard, but God’s character makes all the rest look very puny! We are to be modeled after God’s own excellence.

Next to God’s immutable moral excellence, we have the example of Jesus applying such excellence under great trial and pressure.

While the word for moral excellence is not in this text, the meaning of moral excellence is obvious:

Hebrews 12:1–3: 1 Therefore, since we have so great a cloud of witnesses surrounding us, let us also lay aside every encumbrance and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us, 2 fixing our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. 3 For consider him who has endured such hostility by sinners against himself, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart.

(Christian Character Series Part III) — January 26, 2026

Consider isn’t just a casual thought. It means to meditate on, contemplate or ponder Jesus’ life and experiences. Learn from his strength and character. He absolutely lived in a way that matched God’s purpose for him and reflected God’s own excellence—aretē.

Jesus’ example shows us the definition of “manly valor,” a pattern we want to follow. There is not stronger dedication to godly purpose than what Jesus showed us.

With the two lofty and morally excellent examples of God and Jesus before us, what should OUR moral excellence show?

Our excellence should reflect God’s excellence through Jesus. How do we do that?

1 Peter 2:9,11–12: 9 But you are A CHOSEN RACE, A royal PRIESTHOOD, A HOLY NATION, A PEOPLE FOR God’s OWN POSSESSION, so that you may proclaim the excellencies <703> of Him who has called you out of darkness into His marvelous light;

By the way, aretē is a rare word in the New Testament, used only used five times, so it highlights how intentional Peter and Paul were when they used it.

We need to proclaim God’s excellencies—and then model our lives after them. This is part of learning to step up to this incredible responsibility with incredible privilege.

Because God is SO lofty in His being and plan, and we should keep His example before us as we strive for our own moral excellence. Our own moral excellence needs to be applied around the ungodly; it needs to be applied in action in our everyday lives—a shining example to others.

Let’s continue: 11 Beloved, I urge you as aliens and strangers to abstain from fleshly lusts which wage war against the soul. 12 Keep your behavior excellent <2570> among the Gentiles, so that in the thing in which they slander you as evildoers, they may because of your good deeds, as they observe them, glorify God in the day of visitation.

Excellent: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2570 kalos; properly, beautiful, but chiefly (figuratively) good (literally or morally), i.e. valuable or virtuous (for appearance or use)

Keep your behavior excellent (virtuous)—this is a different Greek word, kalos.

Aretē is fulfilling our intended purpose, our inner character. This is an internal transformation that aligns our life with God’s purpose: you become who God intends you to be.

Kalos is beautiful, honorable, external behavior. Others see God through your actions.

Peter is telling us to keep our conduct so visibly good that even unbelievers can’t ignore it. This is an external witness—goodness that can be seen.

Consider aretē as the root and kalos as the fruit.

(Christian Character Series Part III) — January 26, 2026

Peter told us in 2 Peter 1:5 to supply the root (our faith) with moral excellence—that internal character. Let our faith grow our character so it shows externally. There is a powerful formula Peter is pouring out to us!

By moral excellence (aretē), is my virtuous behavior (kalos) able to be observed and remembered by others?

Does the average person looking at me see something higher, different, something that seems special? Are we showing that by our natural behavior before others?

It’s more than just abstaining from evil; it is living true to our covenant. True excellence of character will mark us as being separate from the world and its spirit. Live the life God designed you for! Show it to others. We can only do that if it really matters to us.

Let’s look at a few examples of what our moral excellence should look like.

James 2:18: But someone may well say, You have faith and I have works; show me your faith without the works, and I will show you my faith by my works.

- James throws down the challenge: Show me your faith.
- Peter just showed us how to do that: aretē is the character that faith grows. Kalos is the conduct that character produces—what others can see.
- James 2:18 is the argument that you can’t separate the two.

Genuine faith inevitably produces inner transformation, which in turn produces outward evidence. It all works together.

We can’t have the external evidence without the internal growth. If someone appears to have external moral excellence without internal growth, they are actors, just like the Pharisees, who appeared righteous but were empty inside (Matthew 23:27).

(Christian Character Series Part III) — January 26, 2026

The Greek word for ‘hypocrite’ is hypokritēs, which originally meant an actor—someone literally wearing a mask on stage. By Jesus’ day it described anyone who performs goodness instead of living it. They’re acting a part rather than cultivating the real excellence Peter calls aretē. Our outside should reflect our inside!

Allegiance Attribute of Moral Excellence provokes us to live what our faith teaches us and to never live below that standard. It’s difficult but worth it. Once put into place, it develops Christlikeness.

Another example of what our moral excellence should look like:

James 1:19–20: 19 This you know, my beloved brethren. But everyone must be quick to hear, slow to speak and slow to anger; 20 for the anger of man does not achieve the righteousness of God.

He’s not talking about righteous anger, like the kind God has or the anger Jesus displayed with the moneychangers. This is our ordinary, reactive, ego-driven anger that rises too quickly and speaks too soon. That’s NOT the kind of anger that grows God’s character in us.

James gives us the conditions allowing our moral excellence to grow:

- We need humility in order to be quick to hear.
- We need self-control in order to be slow to speak.
- We need emotional maturity in order to be slow to anger.

Letting anger lead doesn’t help us develop God’s highest purpose in us—aretē (the inward growth). And it shuts kalos (our outward expression of moral excellence) down—it looks ugly, harsh and reactive. People don’t respond positively to that—they can’t see God with all the “me” blocking the view! The will of God does not follow because we are stuck in anger.

When we live according to our faith, we put aside our human anger, and that is moral excellence. It rises up to live to a standard far higher than anything we have lived to before, and it calls us to do this.

We are not perfect. We fall. But the point is to get up, re-establish that standard and go right back to it.

Allegiance Attribute of Moral Excellence differentiates between our anger and God’s righteousness. Our human anger and God’s righteousness will NEVER agree. His righteousness is always going to be higher.

Another example of what our moral excellence should look like:

Ephesians 4:31–32: 31 Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice. 32 Be kind to one another, tender–hearted, forgiving each other, just as God in Christ also has forgiven you.

(Christian Character Series Part III) — January 26, 2026

This admonition is built upon the same things as the James 1:19-20 texts. We have all these personal things, all parts of our life: bitterness, wrath, and anger, and clamor and slander. We are to put them away, along with all malice. Instead, we are to apply moral excellence, which exhibits kindness, tender-heartedness and forgiveness, just as Christ, in his aretē, his morally excellent character, has forgiven us.

Allegiance Attribute of Moral Excellence recognizes and replaces emotionalism and anger that plague every one of us, with the same grace towards others that God has given us through Christ. That is a powerful principle.

Can I apply the same grace to others that God through Christ has given to me? This is the moral excellence for which we strive.

Galatians 6:9–10: 9 Let us not lose heart in doing good, for in due time we will reap if we do not grow weary. 10 So then, while we have opportunity, let us do good to all people, and especially to those who are of the household of the faith.

God sends rain upon the righteous and the unrighteous… (Matthew 5:45). Let us do good to all people. Let us follow His example.

Because our moral excellence, the allegiance of our heart, is built upon faith, our moral excellence helps us to focus on persevering. It is not easy to not lose heart in doing good. But we know if we continue to do good, in due time we will reap if we do not grow weary. Even when it is difficult we must move forward, keep going, because living up to what God knows we can do, aretē, is what our moral excellence requires of us. We cannot get to that high standard without going on when it gets so tough that it feels like we are done.

Our focus is built around our perseverance, as we KNOW God’s blessing and promises are with us. That is what gives us the strength to keep going.

Our moral excellence is based on our faith and can be further honed through the transformational work of growing the influence of God’s spirit in our lives daily:

1 Thessalonians 5:16–24: 16 Rejoice always; 17 pray without ceasing; 18 in everything give thanks; for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus. 19 Do not quench the spirit; 20 do not despise prophetic utterances. 21 But examine everything carefully; hold fast to that which is good; 22 abstain from every form of evil. 23 Now may the God of peace Himself sanctify you entirely; and may your spirit and soul and body be preserved complete, without blame at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. 24 Faithful is He who calls you, and He also will bring it to pass.

A heart that rejoices, prays, listens and stays grateful is the kind of heart where God can cultivate this excellence. These are daily good habits to build our moral excellence. These were the daily habits of our Lord Jesus. When Jesus was in the same form as we are as a man, he showed us how to reflect the aretē, the moral excellence of

(Christian Character Series Part III) — January 26, 2026

the Father, through the actions of his human life. That gives us the ability to look at his life and realize how these things work. We just have to follow the model. Fixing our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith... (Hebrews 12:2) Follow the model!

Is my moral excellence formed after the image of God—the allegiance of my heart—stronger today than it was yesterday?

Is it building? Am I growing?

Or are we getting a little bit careless, perhaps? A little too comfortable? Then we begin to rationalize. That is not the moral excellence the Apostle Peter means when he says, In your faith, supply moral excellence.

Finally, the Apostle Paul’s teachings dovetail with the Apostle Peter’s, as moral excellence is an integral part of both their “lists” of spirituality.

Let’s look at a list from the Apostle Paul:

Philippians 4:8–9: 8 Finally, brethren, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is right, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is of good repute, if there is any excellence <703> and if anything worthy of praise, dwell on these things. 9 The things you have learned and received and heard and seen in me, practice these things, and the God of peace will be with you.

- Peter told us in 2 Peter 1:5 to add aretē—moral excellence—to our faith.
- Here in Philippians, Paul tells us to think on aretē—moral excellence. Then he says to practice these things. In other words, take the good you’ve seen in my life and make it visible in yours. That’s kalos in action even though the word isn’t used.
- Remember, James said, I will show you my faith by my works. Paul and James both describe the visible outworking of a transformed inner life—kalos.

Let Philippians 4:8 be our mental filter. If we are filling our days with bitterness, fear, comparison, anger, questionable thoughts, worldly activities—it will affect our moral excellence. When our thoughts dwell on what is true, pure and lovely, our life begins to display the goodness our faith claims.

Whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is right, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is of good repute, if there is any (godly) excellence—that is how you qualify what is true, what is really honorable, right and pure. Between Peter and Paul, they have laid out a tremendous guideline that tells us how to build our Christian life.

Let’s revisit our original question. Why is moral excellence the next quality after faith?

(Christian Character Series Part III) — January 26, 2026

Because without a godly standard of moral excellence fashioned in the shape of God’s love for us, everything else we can potentially build upon our faith will crumble. We can’t build moral excellence on top of a cracked, faulty foundation. That’s why we look at the example of God as the Apostle Peter tells us to do.

We are not going to be able to get to that next rung on the ladder if our excellence isn’t “excellent.” We grow into that excellence that reflects God’s character. It is this internal transformation that aligns our lives with God’s purpose for us.

But is the standard too high? This is God’s standard. Is this too much responsibility? Won’t we continually fail?

Yes, we will, but it is NOT too high. How do we know? Why would God give us a standard that ensures we fail? Let’s go back a few verses. Peter assured us that God gives us His exceeding great and precious promises (2 Peter 1:4 KJV). It is because of the work these promises accomplish within us, and because God is with us, that we can eventually attain to the divine nature.

Then Peter says, Add to your faith moral excellence. Yes, it is hard, but we are given every ingredient to make our “plant” of moral excellence grow from root to blossom.

The Allegiance Attribute of Moral Excellence: A mature Christian’s Moral Excellence Allegiance MUST find its fuel through faith in the excellencies of God, our Creator, and Jesus, our Lord. Excellence and virtue can and do abound in many people for many reasons, and we always want to be aware of them and support them. Lots of people who aren’t Christians are moral people! However, we cannot forget the WHY of our seeking such virtue and the loftiness to which we are to strive. Our calling is to godliness, not merely to human moral integrity.

2 Peter 1:5: Now for this very reason also, applying all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence…

Aretē has strongly reminded me that I need to look in the mirror and be the person God intends me to be. I have to live like His purpose actually matters to me. I have to confront the parts of my character that don’t match that purpose— I can’t justify them, make excuses for them, or get lazy. I have to replace them with what God is shaping in me.

This lesson is profound! Inspirational! And we are ONLY on the second rung of the ladder!

Based on our faith, apply this godly moral excellence, this sense of achieving a higher being, so we can truly, every day, work on developing Christlikeness. We say “work on developing it” because we are imperfect and we do fail, and it is okay. We ask for forgiveness—we get up—and God loves us no less as we sincerely try again.

(Christian Character Series Part III) — January 26, 2026

Moral excellence based on God’s example!

So, what does true Christian moral excellence look like?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

## Episode 1422 — How Does Knowledge as a Christian Change My Worldly Life? (Christian Character Series Part IV)
Published: 2026-02-02
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1422-knowledge/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/30160902/CQ_Rewind_02-02-2026_How_Does_Knowledge_as_a_Christian_Change_My_Worldly_Life.pdf

(Christian Character Series Part IV)—February 2, 2026

How Does Knowledge as a Christian Change My Worldly Life? (Christian Character Series Part IV)

2 Peter 1:5: Now for this very reason also, applying all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence, and in your moral excellence, knowledge.

In 2 Peter 1, the Apostle Peter laid out a phenomenal blueprint for us to follow regarding the how and why of developing a focused and loyal character that is modeled after Christ. After reminding us of the incomprehensible promises God brings us through His power and Jesus’ sacrifice, He then focuses us on doing our part. Peter gives us a blueprint for building a virtue “ladder” of Christian character development, with our faith as the first rung. Because we have the firm footing of Christian faith in place, we can then develop “moral excellence,” which in turn gives us the stability to next develop knowledge. As we will continue to see, when followed, the order in which these attributes of our Christian character develop will yield an unbreakable allegiance to daily living God’s will through Christ.

Let’s briefly review the first two rungs of the Apostle Peter’s virtue ladder of Christian character:

The first rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Faith—the allegiance of our life’s direction.

Allegiance means loyalty. If we decide we are living a life of faith, it is necessary that our loyalty is to serve God through that faith.

The second rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Moral Excellence—the allegiance of our heart.

We put God first by eagerly and fully supplying moral excellence to the foundation of our faith. Our heart motivates our direction.

Why is the Allegiance Attribute of moral excellence the next quality after faith? Because without a godly standard of moral excellence fashioned in the shape of God’s love for us, everything else we could potentially build upon our faith would crumble, as it would be built upon a faulty, sinful earthly perspective.

Excellence and virtue can and do abound in many people for many reasons, and we always want to be aware of them and support them. However, we cannot forget the WHY of our seeking such virtue and the loftiness to which we are to strive. Our calling is to godliness, something even higher than human moral integrity.

What’s next after faith and moral excellence?

2 Peter 1:5: …and in your moral excellence, (fully supply) knowledge <1108>.

(Christian Character Series Part IV)—February 2, 2026

Knowledge: Strong’s Exhausti Concordance #1108 gnosis; knowing (the act), i.e. (by implication) knowledge

Moral excellence is the foundation upon which we are instructed to build knowledge. For most of us, knowledge is knowledge—knowing something—so how does moral excellence focus our Christian perspective to change the role of knowledge in our daily lives? What changes with knowledge just because we are a Christian? Why does knowledge need moral excellence to continue in this Christian growth pattern?

The word knowledge generally signifies intelligence and understanding. As far as our Christianity, the deeper we study God’s word with the help of His spirit (His power and influence), the deeper our understanding becomes. It’s important to note that much of the knowledge today is corrupted by worldly perspectives, opinions and social pressures. We need to be discerning about this.

The third rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Knowledge—the allegiance of our intellect.

Why is knowledge the next quality after moral excellence (living up to our highest purpose)?

Let’s begin the answer by looking at a powerful example of knowledge improperly applied without our Christian moral excellence.

1 Corinthians 8:1-2: 1 Now concerning things sacrificed to idols, we know that we all have knowledge <1108>. Knowledge <1108> makes arrogant (inflates), but love edifies (constructs). 2 If anyone supposes that he knows anything, he has not yet known as he ought to know.

Knowledge can inflate someone’s arrogance. In contrast, love edifies or constructs good character. Knowledge in and of itself can be helpful, but if misapplied, it can be detrimental. Misapplied knowledge fuels a hollow character, and a hollow character has no true strength or substance.

When we look at an inflated black balloon from one end, it’s perfectly round, black and shiny. What’s inside that balloon? A lot of air! Let’s tape the balloon to the table and set a black bowling ball next to it. They look similar, but one is full of air and the other is incredibly dense. We want the knowledge we are given through God, His word and His strength to be full of something strong and weighty—not full of hot air! The ball and the balloon look similar but have very different uses.

(Christian Character Series Part IV)—February 2, 2026

In 1 Corinthians, the Apostle Paul is teaching a lesson based on his own failures. Previously known as Saul of Tarsus, he was a prominent Pharisee who used his ego-driven understanding of the Law to make it his personal mission to persecute Christians. His knowledge was misapplied! It lacked the substance needed to make a sound judgment.

From personal experience, he already warned that knowledge can “inflate” or make someone arrogant.

Paul continues his focus on the early church dilemma about eating meat previously offered to idols. Some found it acceptable, while others disagreed:

1 Corinthians 8:7-11: 7 However not all men have this knowledge <1108>; but some, being accustomed to the idol until now, eat food as if it were sacrificed to an idol; and their conscience being weak is defiled. 8 But food will not commend us to God; we are neither the worse if we do not eat, nor the better if we do eat.

Paul is telling us that even though there is nothing wrong with this—because no principles have been violated—we must rise above what we know so that we don’t stumble others.

9 But take care that this liberty of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak. 10 For if someone sees you, who have knowledge <1108>, dining in an idol's temple, will not his conscience, if he is weak, be strengthened to eat things sacrificed to idols? 11 For through your knowledge <1108> he who is weak is ruined, the brother for whose sake Christ died.

This is a powerful statement of responsibility! If we, as mature Christians, similarly influence new or immature Christians into acting in a way that violates their conscience, we may be causing them to sin—he who is weak is ruined. Stumbling another is not acceptable. When someone lacks mature spiritual knowledge, trying to imitate actions that only true understanding can support can cause real harm. Paul cautions us to be mindful of how our behavior might unintentionally mislead or influence others.

Knowledge can easily be misapplied:

1 Corinthians 8:12-13: 12 And so, by sinning against the brethren and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ. 13 Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat again, so that I will not cause my brother to stumble.

This principle emphasizes sacrificing our preferences and being sensitive to the needs of others as we lay down our lives for our brethren.

Our first approach to developing knowledge goes back to a mirror question about moral excellence:

Am I living up to my highest purpose in how I explain myself and what I know? What is the allegiance of my intellect really loyal to? Is it loyal to looking good to others or to being a true and powerful example of appropriately applying and living godly knowledge?

(Christian Character Series Part IV)—February 2, 2026

It is easy to want to look good to others and say, “There’s nothing wrong with me doing this. What’s your problem?” But that’s not the right attitude.

It’s important to recognize that having knowledge doesn't mean we can answer every question or know the depths of every single prophecy, for example. No one has perfect knowledge. Instead, knowledge involves understanding what Christlikeness is and striving to learn and apply it to transform our lives.

Our spiritual knowledge is fed by our faith in the light of God’s glory that shines within us:

2 Corinthians 4:6-7: 6 For God, who said, Light shall shine out of darkness, is the One who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge <1108> of the glory of God in the face of Christ. 7 But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness of the power will be of God and not from ourselves.

This is the key! The light of the knowledge of the glory of God is within us. It doesn’t come from us; it comes from Him, through us. This is the type of knowledge we want. We don’t want this so that we can be boastful about it. These verses say knowledge comes from Him through us, so there is nothing for us to be boastful about.

Because this knowledge, the allegiance of our intellect, comes from God, we need to be humbly subservient to our mighty God through Jesus. This allegiance of our intellect can only thrive when His light fills our emptiness. Don’t be the balloon. Be the bowling ball with substance.

Having our moral excellence firmly beneath us will drive us towards a better understanding of God and His plan.

The godly allegiance of our intellect will recognize that the source of our knowledge ultimately is God:

1 Timothy 2:3-6: 3 This is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior, 4 who desires all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge <1922> of the truth. 5 For there is one God, and one mediator also between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, 6 who gave himself as a ransom for all, the testimony given at the proper time.

Knowledge: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1922 #epignosis; recognition, i.e. (by implication) full discernment, acknowledgement

Thayer’s Greek English-Lexicon: 1) precise and correct knowledge 1a) used in the New Testament of the knowledge of things ethical and divine

The word for knowledge in this text is different. The previous Greek word was gnosis. However, this word is epignosis, meaning “recognition” or “full discernment.” It's a precise and correct knowledge of the truth.

(Christian Character Series Part IV)—February 2, 2026

I have to comment on this verse because it’s one of my favorite scriptures that uses the word "ALL." Paul describes what God's kingdom on earth will be like. It will be a time when every man, woman and child who ever lived will understand the beauty of God's plan and can use their free will to decide whether they want to be part of it.

Come to the knowledge of the truth—a full discernment of truth with nothing hidden; everything will be exposed and explained.

This is a process. We don’t currently know everything, nor are we capable of such. However, we are blessed to know many things through God’s spirit, but not everything.

We journey towards that full knowledge by first recognizing our highest source of authority is the Bible. Here Paul is speaking to Timothy:

2 Timothy 3:15-17: 15 and that from childhood you have known the sacred writings which are able to give you the wisdom that leads to salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus. 16 All Scripture is inspired by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness; 17 so that the man of God may be adequate, equipped for every good work.

Timothy learned about God from his mother and grandmother (2 Timothy 1:5). They passed down great faith and knowledge. Such knowledge can be passed down from generation to generation. Through God’s spirit, this knowledge can be developed in others; it doesn’t have to begin from scratch.

We Christians have a strong foundation from which we can gain knowledge. As people of God, we must fully equip our minds to feed our intellects in a way that honors God at all times. Honoring Him with what we know will drive what we do.

Peter told us in 2 Peter 3:15-16 that our beloved Apostle Paul, according to the wisdom given to him in all his letters, took the Old Testament and explained its connection to Christ. Still, it wasn't easy for the Jewish Christians to understand this connection, but over time, they accepted it. The Old Testament is a vital source for understanding the plan of God.

The New is in the Old concealed, the Old is in the New revealed. — Augustine

We can’t have one without the other. The knowledge of our true Christianity, of our discipleship, is dependent on both the Old and New Testaments. If we don’t read the Old Testament and make the connections with the New, we miss a major contribution to the depth of our becoming Christlike.

Next, we dedicate ourselves to the lifelong journey of comprehending the inspired word. It is one thing to recognize its authority; it’s another to comprehend it:

2 Timothy 2:15-16: 15 Be diligent to present yourself approved to God as a workman who does not need to be ashamed, accurately handling the word of truth. 16 But avoid worldly and empty chatter, for it will lead to further ungodliness.

(Christian Character Series Part IV)—February 2, 2026

When we think about the value of the Old Testament, we think of Jesus. The moment he was baptized, he went into the wilderness to be by himself. But Satan was there to tempt him. Each of the three times Satan tried to tempt him, Jesus quoted Old Testament Scripture. He didn’t want to debate. It was about the Scriptures, the holy word of God. Our knowledge must be founded on God’s word, as Jesus showed us at the very beginning of his ministry.

Our moral excellence fuels the allegiance of our intellect (knowledge) to fiercely and decisively fight off and conquer all that would detour us from the knowledge of God. This is a “present-tense work in progress.”

2 Corinthians 10:3-5: 3 For though we walk in the flesh, we do not war according to the flesh, 4 for the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but divinely powerful for the destruction of fortresses. 5 We are destroying speculations and every lofty thing raised up against the knowledge <1108> of God, and we are taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ.

Paul tells us this is a battle he regularly and constantly fights. There is a problem with taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ—we can work on that today, but tomorrow we will have to work on it again. And the next day, we will have to work on it again because our thoughts are imperfect.

At our home, we have well water from a well that is about 500 feet deep. We get sediment in this well, so we have a water filtration system. I have to change the filter every six months. When we take it out, it has gone from pure white to full of sediment and yucky scum. Unless we continuously filter the water, we will end up with sediment coming through and into the water. This is how we need to treat our mind—it must be constantly filtered so that we’re looking at things appropriately.

We need to not only gain the knowledge of God; we must magnify it mightily in our lives.

Our knowledge of God and His plan are based on His wisdom and knowledge, which helps explain why sin abounds in our world. God’s wisdom reveals why the world is as it is.

Paul talks about why ancient Israel and the entire world is out of favor with God:

Romans 11:32-33,36: 32 For God has shut up (concluded) all in disobedience so that He may show mercy to all.

All are disobedient, yet God will show mercy to all.

33 Oh, the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge <1108> of God! How unsearchable are His judgments and unfathomable His ways! 36 For from Him and through Him and to Him are all things. To Him be the glory forever. Amen.

If we're limiting God's mercy to just Christians, we're missing out—we're taking this incredible knowledge that has been shown to us across all these different scriptures and narrowing it down. Perhaps we need to change the filter so we can filter out the sediment

(Christian Character Series Part IV)—February 2, 2026

of earthly thinking and really see the magnitude of God’s plan for man. If we can do this, we will better understand His heart and His intention for the well-being of mankind.

Does the allegiance of our intellect bring us to this kind of mental space of awe and gratitude? From Him and through Him and to Him are all things. To Him be the glory forever—is this the conclusion of our studies? Do we have the sense of awe that His plan is for everybody?

Finally, this knowledge we are offered is worth leaving all previous accomplishments behind—it’s worth walking away from everything:

Philippians 3:7-11: 7 But whatever things were gain to me, those things I have counted as loss for the sake of Christ. 8 More than that, I count all things to be loss in view of the surpassing value of knowing <1108> Christ Jesus my Lord, for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and count them but rubbish so that I may gain Christ.

When Paul became a follower of Christ, he left behind all his accomplishments and worth he enjoyed when he was known as Saul of Tarsus. He traded it all in to follow Christ. Talk about value!

Paul had a perceived value in his previous life, but really, his life was like that empty black balloon. He traded it in for something of great substance and weight that could change lives! He chose to put everything else he knew aside, because what he was learning while following Christ far surpassed it. We can’t keep both. If we keep what we were, there’s not enough space for us to transform into new creatures (2 Corinthians 5:17).

Knowing the lack of value in what we leave behind, we now look at the value of what is in front of us: 9 and may be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own derived from the Law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which comes from God on the basis of faith, 10 that I may know (<1097> root word for <1108>) him and the power of his resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings, being conformed to his death; 11 in order that I may attain to the resurrection from the dead.

This is the great conclusion of the Apostle Paul’s journey of leaving those things behind. Faith is the basis—through faith in Christ. Although he doesn’t use the words “moral excellence,” it is implied when he says, not having a righteousness of my own derived from the Law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which comes from God on the basis of faith. So, he shows us faith brings us to moral excellence, which gives us the ability to know—the knowledge of what God wants him to be and do.

Peter wrote the blueprint for Paul and the rest of us. Paul is essentially explaining part of that blueprint using his own life experience.

Faith is our basis, and moral excellence is our standard that awakens and drives the allegiance of our intellect—the loyalty of our mind.

Why is knowledge the next quality after moral excellence (living up to our highest purpose)?

(Christian Character Series Part IV)—February 2, 2026

Faith and moral excellence can fully supply our capacity to drink in the knowledge of God over the knowledge of men. It is a different source of knowledge, brought to us in a different way. Without moral excellence built on faith, our knowledge is far too easily subject to the whims, opinions, agendas and imaginations of our sinful world.

Social media is a sad example. There are too many ways to go that aren’t really where we need to be. We want to place ourselves in environments where faith and moral excellence can develop, so that we can learn what we need to know.

The Allegiance Attribute of Knowledge: Based on our pursuit of moral excellence, our efforts should bring us to an ever-growing intellectual appreciation of God’s word, God’s plan, and our putting God first. The stronger our faith and our moral excellence, the stronger our minds will be, and the more substance we can impart to our own hearts and then to others.

Where do we go from here? What's the next rung on the ladder?

The Apostle Peter lays the foundation of faith and says we’ve got to build moral excellence—living up to our highest purpose based on that faith. As we live up to our highest purpose, we are to pour the knowledge of God into us to grow in the right direction.

Peter continues to build the case for becoming Christlike. It isn’t just about believing in and loving Jesus. That is a wonderful place to start, but it’s not where we end. We have to go up this incredible character ladder.

It all comes down to making sure our knowledge is built on the right things: moral excellence based on the faith of those who follow Christ.

So, how does knowledge as a Christian change my worldly life?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!
