## Episode 1423 — What Kind of Self-Control Is Really Required of a Christian? (Christian Character Series Part V)
Published: 2026-02-09
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/self-control/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/09192505/CQ_Rewind_2-9-2026_What_Kind_of_Self_Control_is_Really_Required_Part_V.pdf

(Christian Character Series Part V) — February 9, 2026

What Kind of Self-Control is Really Required of a Christian? (Christian Character Series Part V)

2 Peter 1:6–7: 6 and in your knowledge, self-control, and in your self-control, perseverance, and in your perseverance, godliness, 7 and in your godliness, brotherly kindness, and in your brotherly kindness, love.

The blueprint for Christian character development the Apostle Peter gives us in 2 Peter 1 focuses us on a profound series of steps we need to take in order to be more Christlike. As a basis for this needed growth, we have seen how God’s promises help us to be ready to systematically take the next step up Peter’s ladder of Christian character development. In the previous episodes of this series, we have begun to see how each step up this ladder needs the step before to actually bring us towards true daily discipleship. We now continue this character development process by looking into the fourth step up towards Christlikeness.

2 Peter 1:5: …in your faith supply moral excellence, and in your moral excellence, knowledge.

Our faith is placed in the power and plan of God through the works and example of Jesus. This provides a strong basis for us to practically and prayerfully develop into true disciples of Christ.

Faith is just the beginning. Without a godly standard of moral excellence that is solely driven by that faith, everything else we can potentially build upon our faith will crumble!

Without the moral excellence that is built on faith, our knowledge is far too easily subject to the whims, opinions, agendas and imaginations of our sinful world. Knowing God is true knowledge.

What’s next?

2 Peter 1:6: and in your knowledge, self-control <1466>.

Self-Control: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1466; egkrateia; (noun) from #1468; self-control (especially continence)

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) self-control (the virtue of one who masters his desires and passions, especially his sensual appetites)

(Christian Character Series Part V) — February 9, 2026

Our passions inevitably play a role in any big thing we ever do. We have to learn to control our passions.

This virtue is really the pivot point on Peter’s list. Faith, moral excellence and knowledge are mostly part of our inner transformation. Now, self-control is where we put that transformation to the test “in the real world.”

This Greek word is very specific, meaning inner power, mastery, dominion over oneself. Some translations use temperance. Self-control is the overall ability to govern our desires, impulses, habits, reactions—even our thoughts. If we have self-control, we aren’t dragged around by our impulses. Instead, we guide them to what is good. Think of a rider controlling a strong horse.

In the ancient Greek world, egkrateia meant more than resisting temptation—it was the inner strength to rule yourself. The word comes from kratos, “mastery,” so the idea is having power within, the ability to guide your desires instead of being dragged by them. Philosophers like Plato and Aristotle taught that desires weren’t bad; they simply needed to be ordered, the way a charioteer directs strong horses. A person without this virtue might know the right thing but lack the strength to follow through, which the Greeks saw as a kind of internal slavery. But the person who practiced egkrateia was steady, trustworthy and truly free because their life was governed by what is good rather than by impulse.

Why is self-control the NEXT quality after knowledge?

We ask this question with each of these rungs and will answer as we go. Knowledge is the foundation upon which we are instructed to build self-control. What is there about the self-control a Christian is supposed to have that requires a foundation of Christian knowledge as well as moral excellence?

The beginning of self-control is the mastery of keeping yourself from thinking, saying, doing or dwelling on things that would be harmful or non-productive.

The culmination of self-control is the mastery of thinking, saying, doing or dwelling on things that are spiritual, wholesome and helpful.

We have to pull back from one thing that doesn’t serve us well and push forward with another, more beneficial thing.

(Christian Character Series Part V) — February 9, 2026

Examples might be:

- Someone snaps at you, and your first impulse is to fire back something sarcastic. Instead, you choose a gentle answer (Proverbs 15:1). - You sit down to check one thing on your phone, and suddenly an hour disappears. You didn’t set or stick to a time boundary (Ephesians 5:15-16). - You’re tempted to fire off a comment, a rant, or a sarcastic reply online. Self-control is stopping long enough to ask: Will this reflect Christ or just my frustration? Is this choice feeding my spiritual health, or feeding something that leaves me emptier afterward? (2 Corinthians 5:20)

This reminds us of the mental process we have discussed several times in the past. Life brings us a stimulus, and our reaction rises up almost automatically. But between that stimulus and our action response, there is a small but powerful space before we actually do something. This is where self-control belongs. When we pause in that space, we can choose a response instead of simply feeding the reaction. That’s the heart of what we’re talking about.

Self-control—the allegiance of our passions—begins with focus. We find a small but telling example in Jesus’ life when he had just revealed to the Samaritan woman at the well that he was the Messiah. This was the first time Jesus had said it plainly to someone outside his inner circle.

John 4:30–34: 30 They went out of the city and were coming to him. 31 Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying, Rabbi, eat. 32 But he said to them. I have food to eat that you do not know about. 33 So the disciples were saying to one another, No one brought him anything to eat, did he? 34 Jesus said to them, My food is to do the will of Him who sent me and to accomplish His work.

Their concern was sweet, but they were missing the importance of the moment. Jesus was focused on the next most important thing. He was exhibitimg self-control through his focus on the next most important task he could be doing. He didn’t need to eat right then; he had to stay on target. Jesus is teaching us self-control through his response.

There are many other examples we could have chosen to show how Jesus practiced self- control, such as:

- His silence before Pilate (Matthew 27:12-14, Mark 15:3-5, John 19:9-11). - His refusal to retaliate when insulted or threatened (1 Peter 2:21-23, Luke 23:34,

Isaiah 53:7). - His restraint during the temptations in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1-11,

Hebrews 4:15).

(Christian Character Series Part V) — February 9, 2026

We chose this example after the woman at the well because it occurred early in his ministry. His disciples logically assumed he must be hungry. There is nothing wrong with eating, but Jesus realized the importance and opportunity of sharing his mission with this woman rather than attending to his physical needs.

Jesus took this logical, human thinking and knew there was a higher lesson here. He didn’t need to be focused on food. He needed self-control to only follow his Father’s will.

He set the example early in his ministry, and he continued to exhibit this quality in all subsequent situations.

For God’s spirit to produce self-control within us, we need to apply ourselves to observing and learning what things naturally control our lives, the things that feed our wants and desires. Self-control requires self- examination. Knowledge and moral excellence, based on faith, increase our ability to identify these things!

We believe Peter is putting self-control here in the sequence because with this basis of faith, moral excellence and knowledge, what we should be focusing on becomes much clearer.

We may have idolatrous and selfish thoughts in our imperfect minds. The question is, what do we do with those thoughts? Self-control, the allegiance of our passions, catches those thoughts and denies their passing into the light of day. They are there, but they do not need to be revealed or acted on. We are learning self-control, NOT self-indulgence!

You cannot keep birds from flying over your head, but you can keep them from building a nest in your hair. — Martin Luther

Self-control doesn’t mean we don’t have emotion. Humans are passionate! It is about the mastery of our emotions. Passion doesn’t consume us or control us. That’s the paradox of self-control being freedom, because ironically, the more we yield to our impulses, the less freedom we have. A great example of being enslaved is if we have addictions. Feeding our addictions makes us less and less free.

We often hear, especially on social media, that we should make our own statement, create our own truth. That is not freedom. According to Scripture, that is slavery because inevitably we must put ourselves into the small box of the expectations and impulses of humanity, rather than the goodness of God.

1 Corinthians 6:12: All things are lawful for me, but not all things are profitable. All things are lawful for me, but I will not be mastered by anything.

In other words, just because I can doesn’t mean I should. We have to act by moving forward with what is appropriate. What is appropriate? Faith, moral excellence and

(Christian Character Series Part V) — February 9, 2026

knowledge should be feeding a fruitful tree. Are they? What we are producing reflects what we allow ourselves to be fed. This is where self-control comes in.

Jesus is speaking to the Pharisees who just accused him of casting out demons by Satan’s power. Jesus responds by exposing the absurdity of that claim:

Matthew 12:33–35: 33 Either make the tree good and its fruit good or make the tree bad and its fruit bad; for the tree is known by its fruit.

In Greek, this phrase has the sense of either "acknowledge the tree is good because the fruit is good, or acknowledge the tree is bad because the fruit is bad." In other words, stop pretending you can mix the two.

The fruit reveals the health of the tree, and the Pharisees’ words about Jesus revealed their hearts. What is inside will eventually show on the outside, for good or bad.

Jesus continues: 34 You brood of vipers, how can you, being evil, speak what is good? For the mouth speaks out of that which fills the heart. 35 The good man brings out of his good treasure what is good; and the evil man brings out of his evil treasure what is evil.

The mouth speaks out of that which fills the heart—if our immediate response is revenge, it reveals what is in our heart. If we are professing to be disciples of Christ, we must exhibit self-control. We need to be careful that the fruit of our lives is actually good, godly fruit. This goes beyond human goodness.

The Apostle Paul breaks down the concept of self-control, the Allegiance of our Passions, into pieces:

We must intentionally focus on what is important.

Paul compares our spiritual lives with the focused discipline of an athlete who runs to win a race:

1 Corinthians 9:24: Do you not know that those who run in a race all run, but only one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you may win.

(Christian Character Series Part V) — February 9, 2026

Rick recalls hearing a business leader say, “You have to be specific to be dynamic.” In other words, we have to be specific in what we want to accomplish if we are to be effective.

Run… that you may win. We know the race is for life. We know what kind of pace it requires, and when it’s required. We know where we are going. If we keep that specific destination, that dot on the horizon, in mind, we are running towards something specific. Our focus is clear.

- How clearly do I see the prize for which I say that I am running?
- What greater goal is God inviting me to keep in view right now?
- How would my choices shift if I remember that goal in the moment of

temptation?

We should be mindful of this goal all the time; it should dominate our thoughts and guide our actions.

We must understand the limitations needed to successfully run the race.

To run successfully, there are many limitations to consider:

1 Corinthians 9:25: Everyone who competes in the games exercises self-control <1467> in all things. They then do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable.

Exercises self-control: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1467 egkrateuomai; (verb) to exercise self-restraint (in diet and chastity):—can(-not) contain, be temperate

An athlete doesn’t let lesser desires override the greater goal—that’s how resisting temptation works. When our highest goal stays in front of us, everything else falls into its proper place.

A trained athlete has already made thousands of choices before race day. Similarly, we’re not starting from zero when we face a temptation. We have “muscle memory” of previous, spirit-led good choices. Training is uncomfortable, but it builds strength. Resisting temptation makes us stronger and keeps us from sacrificing the big win for these small wants that come up.

The main thought here is the intentionality of understanding the limitations. We need to be incredibly intentional. For Christians, this requires a deliberate effort every day.

- Have I intentionally limited or eliminated spiritually unproductive thoughts,

words and practices? Have I done that with great intentionality?

- What thoughts do I still need to take captive because they lead me into

unhelpful spirals?

(Christian Character Series Part V) — February 9, 2026

Unhelpful spirals might include catastrophizing, mentally replaying an event over and over, assuming the worst, or letting our thoughts creep into areas we know quickly take us down the wrong path.

When we start spiraling, we get dizzy and then lose control!

We must be “all in” and press on to the finish!

This will require the overwhelming dedication of a superior athlete:

1 Corinthians 9:26–27: 26 Therefore I run in such a way, as not without aim; I box in such a way, as not beating the air; 27 but I discipline my body and make it my slave, so that, after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified.

Athletes still feel cravings, fatigue and thoughts of quitting, but they don’t obey those. Their impulses don’t dictate their actions. Paul refuses to live in an unfocused or impulsive way. He trained his spiritual life the way an athlete trains their body so that nothing would disqualify him from faithfully finishing his race.

Paul was wise. He was in a place of leadership. He was an apostle. He had God’s spirit in great measure. He could perform miracles. He had everything going for him, yet he says, I discipline my body so that I may win this same race.

- Am I running to win, not just to compete? Am I boxing or contending to hit

the target, not just sparring?

- Is my body serving my will in Christ, or is it just serving my will?
- What would it look like to ask God for help before the moment of weakness

and not after?

I’ve had the wonderful privilege of talking with several who are following after Christ who have fought off, and sometimes continue to fight off, addictive behavior. Part of that process is to be determined to put the addictive behavior in the past, and like Paul, say, “I have essentially made my body my slave so that I can be more fully a disciple of Christ.”

Surrendering to God’s will is thoroughly engaging in His work and doing it His way. Jesus showed us:

John 6:38: For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of Him who sent me.

Jesus did not come down to do what HE thought he should do. He came down to do what his Father directed him to do. How clearly are we focused on that same thought process?

(Christian Character Series Part V) — February 9, 2026

Jesus was thoroughly put to the test on this, especially before his crucifixion:

Mark 14:34–37: 34 And he said to them, My soul is deeply grieved to the point of death; remain here and keep watch. 35 And he went a little beyond them, and fell to the ground and began to pray that if it were possible, the hour might pass him by. 36 And he was saying, Abba! Father! All things are possible for You; remove this cup from me; yet not what I will, but what You will. 37 And he came and found them sleeping, and said to Peter, Simon, are you asleep? Could you not keep watch for one hour?

We can hear the incredible self-control Jesus is displaying by essentially saying, “Here is my will, but I give it up to you. I will do Your will instead.”

Peter and the other apostles were not able to stay awake at that time. If we look at what Peter wrote many years later, we can see his incredible growth and maturity. This reminds us we that we need that same clarity of focus to shape our response to a stimulus.

Paul clearly verifies that our self-control is to bring us to God’s will through Christ:

2 Corinthians 5:14–16: 14 For the love of Christ controls us, having concluded this, that one died for all, therefore all died; 15 and he died for all, so that they who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again on their behalf.

Christ's love becomes the controlling force of our lives, not our own passions.

16 Therefore from now on we recognize no one according to the flesh; even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him in this way no longer.

As Saul, the Apostle Paul had been a Pharisee and a son of a Pharisee. As Saul, he persecuted Jesus’ followers. After his conversion, as Paul, he no longer viewed Jesus as merely a human figure but as the risen Lord—completely overturning the hostile, dismissive way he once regarded Jesus and his teachings.

As Christians, we need to be able to see people around us from a higher perspective rather than just through our human eyes, emotions and reactions.

- What does the Allegiance of my Passion, my self-control, reveal about how I

observe and think about others?

- Where do my passions cause me to respond to others with impatience, anger

and judgment; and where do I respond with patience and grace?

Would we verbally express our thoughts if Jesus was standing in front of us? Strive towards this level of self-control.

This is also a necessary characteristic of those who shepherd the flock.

These verses give a description of what pastors and teachers should look like:

(Christian Character Series Part V) — February 9, 2026

Titus 1:7–9: 7 For the overseer must be above reproach as God’s steward, not self-willed, not quick-tempered, not addicted to wine, not pugnacious (ready to pick a fight), not fond of sordid gain, 8 but hospitable, loving what is good, sensible, just, devout, self-controlled <1468>, 9 holding fast the faithful word which is in accordance with the teaching, so that he will be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict.

Self-Controlled: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1468; egkrates; (adjective) strong in a thing (masterful), i.e. (figuratively and reflexively) self-controlled (in appetite, etc.)

Peter is teaching that self-control is a virtue we actively cultivate. In Galatians 5:23, that same word for self-control (#1466) is a fruit of the spirit, where it is a gift of the spirit and a responsibility of the Christian. Self-control is the last item on both lists in Titus and Galatians.

How does the overseer or steward engage with self-control? The steward must be an example of Jesus in all things. But it’s not just about knowing things, it’s about living them in a Christlike fashion.

Those who oversee must have this self-restraint that recognizes what can draw us away from the goal. He puts those aside and replaces them with what brings us forward. There is no better way to teach someone else than to do it ourselves.

Self-control is NOT a stand-alone characteristic; it is a necessary cog in the machinery of spiritual growth. Remember, the fruit of the spirit must work alongside the fruitage of our personal growth. It is critical to being Christlike. We cannot be Christlike without self- control!

Therefore, why is self-control the NEXT quality after knowledge?

Knowledge that is built upon faith teaches us the depths and applications of what true Christian self-control should look like. We cannot build a Christlike character unless we know what one looks like!

We have to have knowledge, Christlike knowledge of God, in order to say, “This is the way my life must be built.”

Knowledge without self-control can become hypocrisy—you know what’s right but choose not to live that way. Self-control without perseverance, which we will talk about in our next eisode, becomes a short-lived effort. So, self-control stabilizes the whole structure.

Do we have to just work on these one at a time? Is this list ONLY sequential and cumulative to be successful?

No, they are not sequential, though they are cumulative. As we walk our Christlike walk, we can be working on any and all of these things at different times. If we are walking through our Christlike life and having trouble with self-control, the Apostle Peter suggests it is because we do not truly know what we are trying to control. And we don’t have the moral integrity to put knowledge in place for that self-control. So if we’re having

(Christian Character Series Part V) — February 9, 2026

a hard time with it, go back to this list. Ultimately, our self-control cannot be at its highest form without knowledge and moral excellence grounded in faith.

2 Peter 1:6–7: 6 and in your knowledge, self-control, and in your self-control, perseverance, and in your perseverance, godliness, 7 and in your godliness, brotherly kindness, and in your brotherly kindness, love.

There are a lot of modern life circumstances the Scriptures don’t directly answer as “yes” or “no.” Peter’s blueprint for Christian character, especially with self-control, helps us determine the boundaries of biblical principles we should stay within.

Self-control is the moment where faith, moral excellence and knowledge start showing up in real-time decisions. My desires don’t get the final say. My habits are being reshaped by Christ.

This is the key to why self-control is right in the middle of this incredible ladder. It is the application of the pieces we have been studying. It sets the tone; it sets the environment for the rest of the pieces to be built upon. The rest cannot be built without the self-control that is driven by God through Christlikeness and following in Jesus’ footsteps. We are to act according to Scripture, not according to what we think, want or feel.

So, what kind self-control is really required of a Christian?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

## Episode 1424 — How Do I Grow in Christian Perseverance? (Christian Character Series Part VI)
Published: 2026-02-16
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1424-perseverance-part-vi/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/13145158/CQ_Rewind_02-16-2026_How_Do_I_Grow_in_Christian_Perseverance_Part_VI.pdf

How Do I Grow in Christian Perseverance?

(Christian Character Series Part VI)

2 Peter 1:6-7: 6 …and in your knowledge, self-control, and in your self-control, perseverance, and in your perseverance, godliness, 7 and in your godliness, brotherly kindness, and in your brotherly kindness, love.

The blueprint for Christian character development the Apostle Peter gives us in 2 Peter 1 focuses us on a profound series of steps we need to take in order to be more Christlike. Based upon God’s power and promises, Peter lays out for us the blueprint for a ladder of Christian character development. Peter has taught us that each rung of this ladder is very important to our success in climbing to the next rung. In the last four parts of this series, we have focused on one rung of this ladder at a time and worked on making the connections between our foundation and how each step makes us more like Jesus. In this episode, we focus on the fifth step.

2 Peter 1:5-6: 5 …in your faith supply moral excellence, and in your moral excellence, knowledge, 6 and in your knowledge, self-control...

Here are the first four rungs of Apostle Peter’s “virtue” ladder of Christian character:

The first two rungs: The Allegiance Attribute of Faith—the allegiance of our life’s direction. The Allegiance Attribute of Moral Excellence—the allegiance of our heart.

Our faith in God’s power and plan is just the beginning. Without a godly standard of moral excellence driven by that faith, everything else we can potentially build upon our faith will crumble!

The third and fourth rungs: The Allegiance Attribute of Knowledge—the allegiance of our intellect. The Allegiance Attribute of Self-Control—the allegiance of our passions.

Moral excellence, built on faith, keeps our knowledge from being subject to the opinions, agendas and imaginations of our world. But faith, moral excellence and knowledge need focus: knowing God is true knowledge. This true knowledge teaches what true Christian self-control should look like so we can build a genuine Christlike character.

What’s next?

2 Peter 1:6: … and in your self-control, perseverance <5281>…

Perseverance: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5281 hupomonē (noun); from #5278; cheerful (or hopeful) endurance, constancy

This noun form is often translated into English as patience.

Perseverance: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5278 hupomeno (verb); to stay under (behind), i.e. remain; figuratively, to undergo, i.e. bear (trials), have fortitude, persevere

The fifth rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Perseverance— the allegiance of our energy.

Why is perseverance the next quality after self-control?

The answer becomes clear as we continue this discussion.

Peter does not list these attributes in random order. Each builds upon the previous.

The Greek word for perseverance means “cheerful endurance” or “constancy.” The verb form means “to stay under,” “bear trials” and “have fortitude.” Sometimes we think of perseverance as drudgery, but it is positive in that there is great strength gained in moving forward, in carrying the load. It does not mean just barely making it.

There is something very inspirational about perseverance.

Peseverance is the act of consciously staying the course and faithfully bearing the weight of a burden. That is the critical element needed to follow our spiritually established self- control.

Perseverance, the allegiance of our energy to the will of God for us, is CRUCIAL in the life of a Christian:

Romans 5:1-5: 1 Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,

Let’s pause and emphasize a simple fact: justification (having been made right with God) brings peace with God.

2 through whom also we have obtained our introduction by faith into this grace in which we stand; and we exult in hope of the glory of God.

Another fact: God’s peace brings His grace. Beyond justification, peace with God allows us to stand in His favor, through His son. These facts now enable our heart to engage.

3 And not only this, but we also exult in our tribulations, knowing that tribulation brings about perseverance <5281>; 4 and perseverance <5281>, proven character; and proven character, hope; 5 and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out within our hearts through the holy spirit which was given to us.

We can see the integrated role that perseverance plays. We receive justification, which brings peace with God; and God’s peace brings His grace. Because of these things, when we have tribulation, we know that God is looking for perseverance, this constancy, going through those trials. They are necessary for our character development. We have hope throughout because His love has been poured out within our hearts through the holy spirit which was given to us.

This is a powerful process. It is not just holding our breath and hanging on. We are supported by our Father’s love in our hearts to persevere, even to carry our burdens with peace and with joy.

Perseverance is only achieved by deciding in our heads and hearts to have it. It has to be a conscious decision. Jesus showed us the template of how to do this:

Hebrews 12:1-3: 1 Therefore, since we have so great a cloud of witnesses surrounding us, let us also lay aside every encumbrance and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let us run with endurance <5281> the race that is set before us, 2 fixing our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured <5278> the cross, despising the shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. 3 For consider him who has endured <5278> such hostility by sinners against himself, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart.

- We need endurance—constancy, perseverance— for the race set before us. How do we do this?
- By fixing our eyes on Jesus… who for the joy set before him endured—he joyfully persevered, not affected by the shame of the cross. He had perseverance, even in the face of the hostility that put him on the cross. We can use his example for inspiration so that we will not grow weary. This is what perseverance looks like!
- Whenever we think we've reached our limit, what should we do? Look at all Jesus endured, which is so much more and beyond what we have gone through. Keep on keeping on!

Perseverance is such an important factor for us to develop in our Christian walk. It is most effective once true knowledge and self-control are put in place. We need to know where we are going and why we are going there. Fixing our eyes on Jesus and having the self- control to stay on target develops and inspires our perseverance.

1. Trials and afflictions: Overcoming requires practical perseverance, the allegiance of our energy.

We focus our energy on overcoming the difficulties before us:

James 1:2-4: 2 Consider it all joy, my brethren, when you encounter various trials, 3 knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance <5281>. 4 And let endurance <5281> have its perfect result, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.

Consider it (our trials) all joy. This is difficult. James says it is the knowing that the testing of our faith produces endurance—perseverance, this constancy, this cheerful endurance— that gives us the strength to persist so that we may be perfect and complete…

This endurance is not automatic. We can’t just flip a switch and get endurance! This is something we have to work on developing. Endurance will keep us going through our trials, difficulties and traumas. It is in these experiences that we must, as Christians, realize—make concrete—the reality of our faith with a long term, endurance-based approach.

Difficult experiences don’t just go away for a Christian. They are needed for our character development; we must learn to work through them. This requires constancy in our faith, perseverance in our pushing towards the goal, and that cheerful endurance that holds on so that we can look up even when it hurts.

Here are the results of those trials and afflictions, as long as we regularly persevere:

James 1:12: Blessed is a man who perseveres under <5278> trial; for once he has been approved, he will receive the crown of life which the Lord has promised to those who love Him.

We are blessed by persevering under trial! God doesn’t just tell us to figure this all out and be happy while weighted down with trials.

Do we carry the weight of our trials until completed, according to God’s standard?

Rick, the other day, you mentioned you saw my wife, Jewel's, recent experience as a practical example of persevering through trials and afflictions. Nine months ago, she severely ruptured a disc in her neck and was in tremendous pain, which affected her ability to sleep. For months she was only able to get two or three hours of sleep each night, which is very debilitating.

The pain made it difficult for her to work on the computer for long periods. This was an issue because she has a weekly role in helping to produce the CQ Rewind Show Notes for each podcast. Despite the difficulties, she has been determined to persevere through the pain and continues her work for the Lord. Thankfully, there are wonderful CQ Rewind partners who work together with her to help carry the load. Jewel is a wonderful example to me of wanting to serve the Lord even through her difficulties.

This certainly hasn’t been easy—it has been extremely painful. She did not have big smiles as she dealt with this, bearing the load of pain. But the joy and the blessing was in working through it and allowing the Lord to touch her and lead her through the experience.

God is not going to make our trials go away, but He will draw us through them, requiring our perseverance. It is also a beautiful example of how those other individuals worked alongside Jewel to help with the extra work. They reached in, said, “We’ve got this!” This is a great practical example of perseverance through a trial.

2. Persecution: To stand under persecution requires principled perseverance, the allegiance of our energy.

John 15:20: Remember the word that I said to you, A slave is not greater than his master. If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they kept my word, they will keep yours also.

As followers of Jesus, we should not expect anything less for ourselves.

Persecution can and often does come from those who are close to us, those whose influence is important in our lives:

Luke 21:16-19: 16 But you will be betrayed even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and they will put some of you to death, 17 and you will be hated by all because of my name. 18 Yet not a hair of your head will perish. 19 By your endurance <5281> you will gain your lives.

We may even face physical death caused by those who hate us, but our eternal life can't be touched as long as we stay faithful. What we are running for is beyond whatever anyone can do to us in this life. We know what they did to Jesus, but he died even FOR those persecuting him.

By your endurance, you will gain your lives—we can see the importance of walking in his footsteps.

When persecuted by those who are close to us, principled perseverance stands firm, as it stands for the name of Jesus! This stand can be VERY challenging.

It's sad, but we can be persecuted even by other Christians who have a disdain for those who don't believe as they do.

Back when Christian Questions was broadcast on local radio stations, people could call in and talk to us live. We also had a listener who would email us regularly. He was not just unhappy with us; he was angry! He was a Christian and he kept calling us a cult and accusing us of misquoting scriptures and so forth. It was difficult because we would have this secondary dialogue going on. For every single email he sent with an accusation, I made it a point to respond with reasoning.

One of his objections was that we were misquoting scripture about Jesus dying for all. He would say, it (Matthew 20:28, Mark 10:45) doesn’t say “all,” it says “many.” He felt that was what a cult does, misquote. I wrote him back with several scriptures and told him to read them (2 Corinthians 5:15 and Hebrews 2:9, for example.) We didn’t misquote them, we actually read them word-for-word.

This was a sad experience because there was no ability to dialogue since he would only contact us by email. We were just covering the one, individual thing he complained about in each email. We could only explain what the Bible says, but had no ability to move forward. That was the sad end result.

We have to stand on the principles not only of what the Bible says, but on how Jesus handled those principles.

Persecution can become a potential breaking point for a Christian who feels alone and even targeted:

2 Corinthians 4:7-10: 7 But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness of the power will be of God and not from ourselves; 8 we are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not despairing; 9 persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed; 10 always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our body.

Paul reminds us that it is God’s power and spirit working in us that gives us the ability to endure—we can’t trust in our own strength. Once again, Paul focuses us on Jesus’ sacrifice, our example of someone persevering through difficulties he did nothing to deserve.

Perseverance, not retaliation, is the personal decision needed to truly fulfill our call to discipleship when faced with persecution. Jesus never retaliated, so we shouldn’t either.

3. The Testing of our Loyalty: Standing in loyalty to God and His purposes requires perseverance, the allegiance of our energy.

We are servants of God with our physical being:

2 Corinthians 6:3-5: 3 Giving no cause for offense in anything, so that the ministry will not be discredited, 4 but in everything commending ourselves as servants of God, in much endurance <5281>, in afflictions, in hardships, in distresses, 5 in beatings, in imprisonments, in tumults, in labors, in sleeplessness, in hunger.

When we read this, we recognize the amount of pressure the Apostle Paul went through. Paraphrasing him, “I need to be careful so that as a representative of the word of God through Christ, I will not be offensive to anybody in any way. I am going to stand above my preferences so that the ministry is not discredited. I can commend myself as God’s servant in all of these things I have gone through: in beatings, in imprisonments, in tumults, in labors, in sleeplessness, in hunger… whatever it is, I will stand above the experience, by the grace of God.” This is what perseverance looks like!

We are thankful we don’t go through all the things the Apostle Paul went through, but his example is so inspiring; it increases our desire to work harder and be stronger.

Loyalty requires deep and passionate perseverance in the hard physical experiences of life! Why? Our objective is for God to be glorified in EVERY experience of our lives! This is a sobering statement, as we have all sometimes failed to glorify our heavenly Father in our experiences.

How do I maintain my goal of glorifying God in every situation?

It begins with prayer and then listening after prayer. It requires meditating and thinking on what Jesus would do to glorify his Father in heaven.

That is such an important principle. Always go to that prayerful attitude during difficult experiences. Sometimes things develop very rapidly, and we start to “go down the rabbit hole” in our heads.

One word that helps us refocus is “or.” I can continue down the awful road, OR I can back up and reset. I can rely on my own strength, OR I can rely on the strength of God through Christ and God’s spirit and do something different.

For Christmas, we gave our 18-year old grandson a calendar with inspirational quotes, and kept a calendar for ourselves. Yesterday’s quote fits this concept so well: “Strength is not measured by muscle, but by the will to keep going.”

Let’s repeat James’ teaching on perseverance through trials and afflictions:

James 1:2-4: 2 Consider it all joy, my brethren, when you encounter various trials, 3 knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance <5281>. 4 And let endurance <5281> have its perfect result, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.

Having joy in trials is a challenge. I can’t help but think of our dear friend, Joanna, who recently passed away from cancer. She was a beautiful example to us of enduring with joy and a smile constantly on her face in all her experiences. I think that smile came from trusting God in everything. She was only in her early 60’s. Her husband had died prematurely from an aggressive form of dementia a few years before that. Here is a Christian woman who had been through many difficult experiences, but we never saw her without a smile on her face because she had the wonderful ability to put things into a godly perspective “from above” instead of “from within.” She was a great example for everybody around her, and we truly love her example.

The testing of our faith produces endurance, and that endurance can make us complete, lacking in nothing.

This perseverance under trials and afflictions is also a testing of our ultimate loyalty:

James 5:7-8, 11: 7 Therefore be patient (forbearing), brethren, until the coming of the Lord. The farmer waits for the precious produce of the soil, being patient about it, until it gets the early and late rains. 8 You too be patient (forbearing); strengthen your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is near. 11 We count those blessed who endured <5278>. You have heard of the endurance <5281> of Job and have seen the outcome of the Lord's dealings, that the Lord is full of compassion and is merciful.

Do I regularly hold back my fleshly desires and persevere through

whatever is set before me?

If we look back on our lives, we will see some examples that are good and some that are not so good.

We’ve talked about this on past episodes. Briefly, our daughter was raped when she had just turned 15-years old. It took several years to put our lives back in order. It was not a happy several years. It was not a clear several years, either. It was very foggy as to what was happening.

There were so many times I didn’t know what was going to happen. I personally had to search for the right thing to do, not what I wanted to do. What was the spiritually sound, Christlike thing to do? This is what kept me going, what kept me able to put my family’s needs in place. It was a great example of learning perseverance. I’m not going to say we mastered perseverance then, because we certainly didn’t, but we learned a whole lot about how to move forward step by small step, by seeking to glorify God.

I can tell you that today our daughter is a very strong, well-adjusted woman who took that horrible experience and has turned it completely around. Now she uses it to help others. It is a beautiful example of perseverance developing strength.

Focusing on Christian Questions every week actually helped with the family’s terrible experience because the required preparation of what was then a two-hour radio program didn’t stop. The deadline didn’t stop.

I had to do the work, and it did help me get out of myself to focus on other things. I also had a job, but it was Christian Questions that helped the most. Matthew 6:33: But seek first His kingdom and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. I quoted this to myself multiple times a day during that experience. Focusing on God helps us get through difficult times.

So, why is perseverance the next quality after self-control?

Self-control is incredibly short-lived without perseverance, as imperfect human thinking and desires can easily derail it. Perseverance, the allegiance of our energy, is the regular restating and reapplying of our discipleship decision. We all fall down, and the point of endurance is to keep getting up.

If perseverance is built on self-control, which is built on knowledge, which is built on moral excellence, which is built on faith, we have a strong reason and capacity to be able to get up and move forward—and keep going in the right direction!

Hebrews 10:35-36: 35 Therefore, do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward. 36 For you have need of endurance <5281>, so that when you have done the will of God, you may receive what was promised.

Don’t let Satan take away your confidence in your Christian walk. Understand that as God’s plan unfolds, Satan has a vested interest in keeping true Christianity from being preached. He will do whatever he can possibly do to attempt to affect our lives. What are we going to do? Never, never, never give up! Put the “first things” first!

The Allegiance Attribute of Perseverance: As we work towards our faith fully supplying us with a morally excellent character, we see that character appropriately absorbing spiritual knowledge, which can direct us towards godly self-control. While self-control is the first step in preventing a thought from becoming an action, perseverance—the allegiance of our energy—is profoundly required to keep ALL of what has already been developed in place and also allow our spirituality to further grow, mature and crystalize.

Perseverance not only is about where we’re going, but it helps us maintain the previous “ladder steps” of character—faith, moral excellence, knowledge and self-control.

Isaiah 40:30-31: 30 Though youths grow weary and tired, and vigorous young men stumble badly, 31 yet those who wait for the LORD will gain new strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles, they will run and not get tired, they will walk and not become weary.

This is the perseverance we are looking for. It comes from above through God’s spirit. It comes because of the sacrifice and example of Jesus. And, it comes to us because we are attempting to walk in Jesus’ footsteps. Make perseverance a part of your life!

So, how do we grow in Christian perseverance?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

### Study Questions

(Christian Character Series – Part VI) https://christianquestions.com/character/1424-perseverance-part-vi/

God has granted everything needed for life and godliness through His promises. These promises form the foundation of Christian character. Our response is allegiance—loyal commitment to God’s will. 2 Peter 1:5-7 is used throughout the questions.

Overarching Question: Why does the Apostle Peter place perseverance after self-control, knowledge, moral excellence and faith in the “ladder” of Christian character development? How does this order impact the way Christians should grow?

1. In what experiences in your life have you experienced perseverance as more than just

“hanging on,” but as a source of strength and inspiration? (Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance for the Greek words hupomonē and hupomeno)

2. When facing tribulation, describe God’s process in our lives outlined in Romans 5:1-5.

What helps us remember God’s love?

3. How do we maintain endurance (constancy, perseverance) even when we feel intense

discouragement? (Hebrews 12:1-3)

4. Why is constancy, this cheerful endurance, needed in a Christian life? What is the result of

perseverance through trial? (James 1:2-4, 12, Hebrews 10:35-36)

5. Can you think of a time when a strong testing of your faith produced endurance? How did

this contribute to your spiritual maturity? What did you learn about yourself and God in the process?

6. How do we stand under persecution from those close to us, those who should understand

us? Why is our reaction so important under this kind of persecution? (John 15:20, Luke 21:16-19, 2 Corinthians 4:7-10, 6:3-5)

can you take to rise about above your personal preferences for His sake? (2 Corinthians 6:3-5, James 1:2-4, 5:7-8, 11)

8. How do you “wait for the Lord” during seasons of weariness or uncertainty? What promises

in Isaiah 40:30-31 encourage you to keep moving forward? How have you experienced God’s renewal?

## Episode 1425 — How Do I Grow in Godliness as a Christian? (Christian Character Series Part VII)
Published: 2026-02-23
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1425-godliness/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/21084730/CQ_Rewind_02-23-2026_How_Do_I_Grow_in_Godliness_as_a_Christian_Part_VII.pdf

How Do I Grow in Godliness as a Christian?

(Christian Character Series Part VII)

2 Peter 1:6–7: 6 and in your knowledge, self-control, and in your self-control, perseverance,

and in your perseverance, godliness, 7 and in your godliness, brotherly kindness,

and in your brotherly kindness, love.

The blueprint for Christian character development given by the Apostle Peter in 2 Peter 1 focuses on a profound series of steps we need to take in order to be more Christlike. With this blueprint, Peter lays out for us a ladder of Christian character development. As we examine it, we find that each rung of this ladder is vital to our success in climbing up onto the next rung. In the last five parts of this series, we focused on one rung of this ladder at a time and worked on making the connections between our foundation and how each step makes us more like Jesus. Now comes the sixth step, and this one really begins to shape what our outward Christian character should look like.

2 Peter 1:5-6: 5 …in your faith supply moral excellence, and in your moral excellence, knowledge, 6 and in your knowledge, self-control, and in your self-control, perseverance, and in your perseverance, godliness.

Here are the first five rungs of Apostle Peter’s “virtue” ladder of Christian character:

The first two rungs: The Allegiance Attribute of Faith—the allegiance of our life’s direction. The Allegiance Attribute of Moral Excellence—the allegiance of our heart.

Our faith in God’s power and plan is our foundation. Without a godly standard of moral excellence driven by that faith, everything else we can potentially build upon our faith will crumble!

The third and fourth rungs: The Allegiance Attribute of Knowledge—the allegiance of our intellect. The Allegiance Attribute of Self-Control—the allegiance of our passions.

Moral excellence, built on faith, keeps our knowledge from being tainted by the agendas and opinions of our world. Knowing God is true knowledge, and this knowledge forms the pivot point of Christian self-control should look like. Here we begin to build a genuine Christlike character.

The fifth rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Perseverance—the allegiance of our energy.

Perseverance is the regular restating and reapplying of our discipleship decisions. It is the act of consciously staying the course and of faithfully bearing the weight of our assigned burdens.

What’s next? 2 Peter 1:6: …and in your perseverance, godliness <2150>,

Godliness: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2150 eusebeia; piety; specially, the gospel scheme

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) reverence, respect 2) piety towards God, godliness

The sixth rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Godliness—the allegiance of our character.

The Strong's Exhaustive Concordance defines godliness as “piety.” Piety makes us think of quiet devotion, personal holiness and a religious feeling, but it’s more active and visible. It's not merely being “good” or being “religious.” It’s a whole life orientation toward God that produces visible fruit.

A practical way to think about piety:

- Reverence for God will reshape how you treat people.
- Devotion to God produces justice, mercy, patience and integrity.
- Worship becomes a lifestyle.

Why is godliness the NEXT quality after perseverance? Keep this question in mind.

We ask this question with each of the rungs and will answer as we go.

When honored and followed, the self-control and perseverance of a true disciple of Christ will combat our imperfect and sinful ways and will inevitably produce godliness if we put all those pieces in order.

Part of being godly is to have an accurate assessment of ourselves (to be humble) as we stand in God’s grace and give Him the true allegiance of our very character. Godliness requires a life of reverence and devotional behavior as we seek God’s will in our lives.

We can view godliness as a result of achieving the previous five attributes.

This is the second mention of godliness by Peter in this teaching.

Peter started this chapter highlighting its importance:

2 Peter 1:3: (KJV) According as His divine power hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness <2150>, through the knowledge of Him that hath called us to glory and virtue <703> (Greek: aretē, moral excellence).

God has given us everything needed for life, and instruction on how we are to live life with godliness. That godliness—reverence or devotional behavior—has to be 24 hours a day.

It is not putting on our “piety suit” to go to church. It is life-changing. It is how we live our lives in reverence to God.

- must be attained as a counterpart to the life opportunity that God gives us through His divine power.
- does not come easily to us—no one is naturally godly; we need to strive for it.
- is an integral part of our character building process.
- is to be prioritized above any earthly ambitions.

How do we develop godliness? By moving away from worldly things:

1 Timothy 4:6–8: 6 In pointing out these things to the brethren, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, constantly nourished on the words of the faith and of the sound doctrine which you have been following. 7 But have nothing to do with worldly fables fit only for old women. On the other hand, discipline yourself for the purpose of godliness <2150>; 8 for bodily discipline is only of little profit, but godliness <2150> is profitable for all things, since it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.

- is seeing things from God's standpoint—through the eyes of eternity and the ultimate well-being of all His creation.

God's word shows us His plan of salvation, that His kingdom will be here on earth as it is in heaven, and He will have all to be saved. This understanding helps shape our godly character.

- is to be constantly nourished on the words of the faith and the words of sound doctrine which you have been following.

The ladder virtues of self-control and perseverance have godliness as their target.

- is the reverential, devotional seeking of God’s will on a daily basis.

Developing and maintaining godliness leads to even deeper growth.

Godliness, true character allegiance to God, can SEEM to be present in some people, but in reality, it is not:

2 Timothy 3:1–5: 1 But realize this, that in the last days difficult times will come. 2 For men will be lovers of self, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, revilers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy, 3 unloving, irreconcilable, malicious gossips, without self-control, brutal, haters of good, 4 treacherous, reckless, conceited, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God,

We’re living in the last days. This is talking about our day here and now. Of course, we recognize these traits are unfortunately all over the world, but we will see who Paul (writing to Timothy) is referring to with this horrific list—the so-called “people of faith,” not humanity in general.

5 holding to a form (appearance) of godliness <2150>, although they have denied its power; avoid such men as these.

In the last days, watch out! There will be much false representation of what true godliness is. Those pretending godliness are putting on a façade, just a show. We have to be careful that the godliness we are seeking after is genuine, scriptural, humble, God-driven, Christlike godliness.

Remember, Satan can appear like an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14). Those with an appearance of godliness are Christians “in name only,” counterfeits of Christ. We want nothing to do with the counterfeit; we want the genuine. These verses warn that godliness will be tested, especially in the last days.

Godliness, true character allegiance to God, is part of the highest standards of true Christianity:

1 Timothy 6:3–4: 3 If anyone advocates a different doctrine and does not agree with sound words, those of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with the doctrine conforming to godliness <2150>, 4 he is conceited and understands nothing;

Godliness has to be built on the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, through doctrines that conform to what is godly, reverential and in accordance with God’s will. How do we do this? By living our lives based only on God’s word. Denominational traditions can be comforting but aren’t necessarily based on God’s word. True godliness comes only from living in God’s word.

However, godliness can be outwardly and partially developed—and thereby misused to pursue earthly gain:

1 Timothy 6:4–5: 4 …but he has a morbid interest in controversial questions and disputes about words, out of which arise envy, strife, abusive language, evil suspicions, 5 and constant friction between men of depraved mind and deprived of the truth, who suppose that godliness <2150> is a means of gain <4200>.

This could apply to Christians accusing other Christians of misrepresenting Christ if they do not share the same beliefs—that action reflects evil intentions, control, power and hatred.

Gain: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4200 porismos; from a derivative of póros (a way, i.e. means); furnishing (procuring), i.e. (by implication) money-getting (acquisition):—gain

Godliness is never a means of material gain! We look to Jesus, who never received money or riches from the gospel message. We look to the apostles and see the same. The mission we follow is higher than earthly standards and earthly objectives.

Such gain might look good, but it is only evil:

Proverbs 25:28: Like a city that is broken into and without walls is a man who has no control over his spirit.

A city without walls is exposed, vulnerable, easily invaded and unable to protect what’s inside. 1 Timothy 6:4-5 is essentially describing what it looks like when the “walls” of a person’s character have collapsed, ruled by impulses instead of God.

It is no accident that the order given to us by Peter is self-control → perseverance → godliness. Godliness is the result of those things that are built on the knowledge of God, which is built on moral excellence, built on true faith. This is why godliness fits in this part of the equation—it is developed by applying all of the previous virtues.

In its appropriate application, our true character allegiance to God does bring great “gain.” Let’s define that great gain:

1 Timothy 6:6–10: 6 But godliness <2150> actually is a means of great gain when accompanied by contentment. 7 For we have brought nothing into the world, so we cannot take anything out of it either. 8 If we have food and covering, with these we shall be content.

The great gain is not acquiring “things”; it is being content. It is in saying, “God is with me in whatever my circumstance; therefore I am content.” This is where godliness can flourish. It’s not about getting; it’s about being godly from the inside out.

9 But those who want to get rich fall into temptation and a snare and many foolish and harmful desires which plunge men into ruin and destruction. 10 For the love of money is a root of all sorts of evil, and some by longing for it have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs.

We can see the dramatic difference between the great gain of godliness… accompanied by contentment versus the temptation and snare of foolish… desires which plunge men into ruin and destruction!

Stepping away from our faith for a time to chase money seems harmless because we can always return later, right? But that's a dangerous lie. Many have followed that voice, wandered from the faith, and ended up with regret.

The problem isn't money itself, but the way the desire for it can lure us away from what truly matters. Very few people can resist that pull, which is why the pursuit of riches becomes such a powerful trap.

This hits home with me. Early in my business career, maybe four or five years after we started Christian Questions on local radio, my senior director asked me to go on a business trip with him.

I was telling him about the exciting things we were doing with Christian Questions, and he said to me, “Look, Rick, you have a lot of talent. If you would be willing to back off from the radio program, just for two years of your time, I can work really hard with you and develop you. You’ll be in such good shape, you’ll be able to do that anywhere you want.”

My answer to him was very clear. “I appreciate the offer, and I’m actually flattered by the fact that you think I have that talent, but you need to understand that those things I’m involved with on Christian Questions are what drive me to do everything else. If I take those things away, I am nothing. So, no, I can’t do that.”

I was a disappointment to him for the rest of the time I worked with him, but I’m not sad about that for a moment! No regrets, whatsoever.

How careful are we to regularly and thoroughly avoid such snares? They can sneak up on us!

Matthew 13:22: And the one on whom seed was sown among the thorns, this is the man who hears the word, and the worry of the world and the deceitfulness of wealth choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful.

As part of the larger Parable of the Sower, Jesus here explains what crowds out our spiritual life—the cares of this world (status, security, identity) and the deceitfulness of riches (the illusion that wealth equals life). This describes someone for whom something other than the word of God has a stronger pull.

We can connect this to Jesus speaking to the rich young ruler in Matthew 19:16-22, who wanted to follow Jesus. He was incredibly wealthy, and Jesus advised him to sell what he had, give it to the poor and follow him. But the young man couldn’t let go of the emotional hold his authority and riches held over him.

We need to be careful about such attachments. There is nothing wrong with dollars and cents. There is nothing wrong with having possessions. But do they hold us, or do we hold them for a specific purpose? How do they fit into our life’s devotion to godliness?

Summing up Paul’s admonition to Timothy to pursue the highest things with our whole being:

1 Timothy 6:11: But flee from these things, (Timothy) you man of God, and pursue righteousness, godliness <2150>, faith, love, perseverance and gentleness.

We added the name Timothy in the verse because Paul was writing to him, which makes it personal. What if we inserted our own name in the verse? For example: But flee from these things, Jonathan, you man of God! This is truly sobering.

To be defined as a man of God—that is godliness! There’s the definition! Can we be defined as men or women of God? Is that what we look like? Is that what comes from inside of us as a witness to those around us?

Timothy was a leader in the early church, and Paul’s admonitions of godliness for him belong to us as well. If we couldn’t honestly be called a man of God or only fit that description part of the time, what do we have to undo? Or redo? What do we have to reapply to get our godliness—our reverence, devotion and continual seeking of God’s will—in order?

Think of how the power of these next texts increases when our perseverance develops godliness:

Ephesians 3:16–19: 16 that He would grant you, according to the riches of His glory, to be strengthened with power through His spirit in the inner man, 17 so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith; and that you, being rooted and grounded in love, 18 may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, 19 and to know the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled up to all the fullness of God.

This is a perfect description of what godliness looks like. This isn’t describing individuals who first learn of Jesus and have only an emotional attachment to claiming him as their Savior. While that's a good place to start, these scriptures describe a more mature Christlike character development rooted in genuine internal godliness.

The growth must come from the inside out, not from an external checklist. Many Christians have been taught to think they are all set if they just do “this, this and this,” almost like checking off the boxes makes you a good Christian. But being Christlike is less about what we are doing and more about who we are and how we are growing. Our actions should reflect our internal growth.

Being only superficially or emotionally attracted to loving God and loving Jesus is like reading a book and getting excited about the description on the book jacket. It’s exciting and we read it over and over, but until we get into the content, we won’t see the depth. We won’t experience the development. The actual content is what will drive us from the inside out. From the Bible we learn reverence, devotion and seeking God’s will in all aspects of our lives—the inside of the book teaches godliness.

If godliness is our true character allegiance to God, then complete transformation is in order:

Romans 12:2–3: 2 And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect. 3 For through the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think

more highly of himself than he ought to think; but to think so as to have sound judgment, as God has allotted to each a measure of faith.

How can we be transformed without being conformed to this world? Does this happen just because we decide it should be done? No. It only happens by the renewing of your mind. How is our mind renewed? We have to reset our focus on our faith in God’s power and plan; we have to keep that moral excellence (our compass), which guides our knowledge (keeping it based on truth); using self-control with perseverance to achieve the objective of godliness.

We have to put ourselves in a position where we are daily living the part, transforming as we go. The transformation doesn’t happen overnight. It has to happen over time and with effort—falling down and getting up, falling down and getting up again and again.

We can’t determine or prove God’s will unless we are in reverent harmony with it. This is “inside out” godliness! This reverence comes from the heart, rather than fulfilling an external responsibility. We don’t just check off the boxes. We need to put our heart into godliness and be genuine.

If we aren’t certain of our authenticity, we need to bring it to the Father in prayer. “Lord, show me if I’m not being genuine. Show me how to be more genuine so that I can serve and honor You.” Faking it doesn’t honor God. We might look good to somebody else, but we are not honoring God. Godliness, by definition, is living in harmony with God’s will and God’s way. That is how we honor Him.

Finally, Peter brings godliness up again as a clear and powerful conclusion to these attributes of loyalty:

2 Peter 3:10–11: 10 But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, in which the heavens will pass away with a roar and the elements will be destroyed with intense heat, and the earth and its works will be burned up.

Let's take a moment to consider what Peter is saying: the current world and its order will eventually be removed. We know the collapse of Satan's present evil world will come to an end, and God’s kingdom of love and peace will ultimately fill the earth.

11 Since all these things are to be destroyed in this way, what sort of people ought you to be in holy conduct and godliness <2150>.

Since these prophecies are going to happen (we can even see them beginning to unfold), Peter asks the question, what sort of people ought you to be in holy conduct? Will you be holy, sanctified, set-apart in conduct and godliness? Will you seek to have reverence, devotion and God’s will in your life so when things start to collapse around you, you can maintain that high level of humility and focus on God?

So, why is godliness the NEXT quality that follows perseverance?

Self-control needs perseverance to be effective. Self-control is great, but without perseverance, it falls flat on its face. Perseverance is MOST effective when there is a CLEARLY-DEFINED OBJECTIVE. Godliness, true character allegiance to God, is that clearly-defined objective. Without a clearly defined objective, our perseverance has no purpose. Godliness follows perseverance as the character attribute that honors God always in all circumstances.

Godliness is not something we only develop on the inside. It has to show. It is a part of who we are, and we can’t be hiding it:

Matthew 5:16: Let your light shine before men in such a way that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

Is this saying that men, seeing our good works, will pat us on the back for such a good job? No, not even remotely close. It’s not about us. This verse is about serving God and having others, seeing us, say, “He/she is a God-honoring individual, and I respect that.” What better compliment could we receive? Of course, it would still be a compliment if they said, “He/she is a God-honoring individual, and I think they are full of baloney!” Both are compliments.

We also want to honor God with our godliness, and our reverent devotion, seeking God’s will in all we think, say and do.

The Allegiance Attribute of Godliness: Godliness is the payoff of perseverance. When we are godly, the fight against our old selves, the world and the devil becomes quickly discernable and quickly remedied, for our very character is now always seeking God. True character allegiance to God is a foundational step in actually living as a true disciple of Jesus.

The whole point of this series is to find out how we can become authentic disciples of Jesus. How do we follow him?

The rungs of the ladder the Apostle Peter gave us lead us to the way to do this:

2 Peter 1:6–7: 6 and in your knowledge, self-control, and in your self-control, perseverance, and in your perseverance, godliness, 7 and in your godliness, brotherly kindness, and in your brotherly kindness, love.

Godliness, that reverent devotion that seeks God’s will every day, is how we develop godliness.

So, how do I grow in godliness as a Christian?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.
