## Episode 1428 — What Does a Fully Supplied Christian Character Look Like? (Christian Character Series Part X)
Published: 2026-03-16
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1428-fully-supplied-christian-character-part-x/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/15110428/CQ_Rewind_03-19-2026_What_Does_a_Fully_Supplied_Christian_Character_Look_Like_Christian_Character_Series_Part_X.pdf

— March 16, 2026

What Does a Fully Supplied Christian Character Look Like? (Christian Character Series Part X)

2 Peter 1:8: For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they render you neither useless nor unfruitful in the true knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.

At the beginning of his second letter, the Apostle Peter reminded us that God, in His power and love, has graciously given us everything we need to be faithful to the calling of discipleship. This walk of sacrifice is supported by the overwhelming gift of God’s precious and magnificent promises. Peter then tells us that because we have such privilege and grace before us, to build on our faith. He tells us that as a result of having this gift of faith, it should help us fully develop moral excellence. That moral excellence should in turn drive us towards spiritual knowledge, which feeds our ability to have self-control. Our outward manifestation of self-control should trigger powerful perseverance, which in turn nourishes a godly and reverent character. This godly character produces an all-encompassing brotherly kindness, which in turn develops the kind of selfless love that our Lord Jesus and our heavenly Father both have.

All of these things were put in place by the Apostle Peter in the first seven verses of this chapter. In this teaching, Peter has revealed an amazing process that, if followed, will literally change our lives. As we have spent several episodes digesting all of this, we now want to focus on how Peter concludes this Christian Character Development Series.

As we will see, his statements in the next several verses solidify the power of the process he has revealed:

2 Peter 1:8-11: 8 For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they render you neither useless nor unfruitful in the true knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. 9 For he who lacks these qualities is blind or short-sighted, having forgotten his purification from his former sins. 10 Therefore, brethren, be all the more diligent to make certain about His calling and choosing you; for as long as you practice these things, you will never stumble; 11 for in this way the entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ will be abundantly supplied to you.

Let’s look closer at verse 8:

2 Peter 1:8: For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they render you neither useless nor unfruitful in the true knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.

What qualities? The attributes identified on the rungs of this ladder.

The first rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Faith—the allegiance of our life’s direction.

The second rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Moral Excellence—this is the allegiance of our heart.

The third rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Knowledge—the allegiance of our intellect.

— March 16, 2026

The fourth rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Self-Control—the allegiance of our passions.

The fifth rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Perseverance—the allegiance of our energy.

The sixth rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Godliness—the allegiance of our character.

The seventh rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Brotherly Kindness—the allegiance of our relationships.

The eighth rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Love—the allegiance of our purpose.

Let’s break down verse 8:

2 Peter 1:8: For if these qualities are yours and are increasing <4121>…

Increasing: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4121 pleonazō; to do, make or be more, i.e. increase (transitively or intransitively); by extension, to superabound: —abound, abundant, make to increase, have over

“Superabound” means to increase—dramatically!

Let’s look at an example:

Philippians 4:17: (KJV) Not because I desire a gift: but I desire fruit that may abound <4121>to your account.

How do we get these qualities to really explode within us into something much more important? Through faith as our foundation. The good news is that we don’t have to have the qualities abundantly at first. All we need is faith and the focus and desire to properly build on that faith.

That’s good news because when I first began studying the Bible, I didn’t have many of these qualities. When someone first finds faith, our emotions are a good thing as we begin to follow Christ. But we need to build our faith beyond our emotions as we mature.

We don’t advance our faith by simply feeling wonderful emotions; it is about character development.

2 Peter 1:8: For if these qualities are yours and are increasing <4121> (IF we are really growing these qualities in our everyday lives, THEN) they render you neither useless <692> nor unfruitful <175> in the true knowledge <1922> of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Useless: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #692 argos; inactive, i.e. unemployed; (by implication) lazy, useless

An example of “useless”:

Matthew 12:36: (KJV) But I say unto you, that every idle <692> word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.

So, being useless or idle is having a lack of purpose for the Lord.

— March 16, 2026

Unfruitful: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #175 akarpos; barren (literally or figuratively)

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: metaphorically without fruit, barren, not yielding what it ought to yield

To be unfruitful means to be barren, not yielding what it ought to yield. Picture a barren tree. It is not doing what it is supposed to do—yield fruit.

What about me? Do I lack fruitfulness?

Be neither useless nor unfruitful—essentially unemployed; not producing, barren.

This is an example of being unfruitful or barren:

Ephesians 5:11: (KJV) And have no fellowship with the unfruitful <175> works of darkness, but rather reprove them.

The works of darkness are not fruitful in the context of spiritual growth. It’s good to come into the faith with emotion, but that needs to be a catalyst to changing, walking away from certain things toward fruitfulness. The Apostle Peter shows us how, because if we are developing the attributes of 2 Peter 1:5-7 we will not be useless nor unfruitful. If we do not have these attributes, we will be useless and unfruitful.

We should be flourishing in the true knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.

True knowledge: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1922 epignosis; recognition, i.e. (by implication) full discernment, acknowledgement

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) precise and correct knowledge 1a) used in the New Testament of the knowledge of things ethical and divine

A great example of true knowledge:

Colossians 1:9-10: (KJV) 9 For this cause we also, since the day we heard it, do not cease to pray for you, and to desire that ye might be filled with the knowledge <1922> of His will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding; 10 that ye might walk worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing, being fruitful in every good work, and increasing in the knowledge <1922> of God.

There is no ambiguity: we need full discernment, a clear understanding. Peter explains that if we are developing these attributes, we won’t be “unemployed” or “inactive” or “barren” in the true knowledge of understanding our Lord Jesus Christ. This maturity allows us to follow Jesus more closely each day.

Developing our Christian character along appropriate lines drives us to a truer and more complete understanding of Jesus. He is our model. Understanding him is understanding what we strive to emulate.

— March 16, 2026

Peter taught us one of the most comprehensive lessons in our Christian lives. He did it succinctly and in a way that can be transformational if we allow it to be.

This is such a high standard that it could sound daunting, which is why not being discouraged with what we don’t have is such an important piece of this. This is all about the encouragement of growth.

Little children see older kids running and want to run too. We are similar. Maybe we are at the crawling stage in our Christian walk, but if we work on these things, we can learn to grow in Christ.

Look at all that we have been given! Our response to these gifts and tools needs to be enthusiasm and determination.

Peter has thus far emphasized the value of having and growing these virtues.

What happens if we don’t work on growing our Christian characters?

The Apostle Peter’s next element of teaching focuses on this very problem, and it is an incredibly important piece of our Christian character puzzle. In any endeavor of life, it is critical to not only know what growth and achievement look like, but also to know what falling short looks like as well. We don’t need to experience it ourselves—we can observe from afar!

This is the disappointing side of the story:

2 Peter 1:9: For he who lacks these qualities is blind or short-sighted <3467>, having forgotten his purification from his former sins.

Short-sighted: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3467 myōpazō; to shut the eyes, i.e. blink (see indistinctly):—cannot see far off

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: to see dimly, see only what is near

— March 16, 2026

If we are called to Christianity and lack these qualities, we either can’t see, or we’re not seeing the bigger picture. Our “vision” is foggy.

Let’s read this again in a different translation:

2 Peter 1:9: (Concordant Version) For he in whom these are not present is blind, closing his eyes, getting oblivious of the cleansing from the penalties of his sins of old.

In other words, we can’t see what is right in front of us!

This reminds us of:

1 Timothy 4:2: (NAS95) by means of the hypocrisy of liars seared in their own conscience as with a branding iron.

To be seared in their own conscience means to be rendered as insensitive. Of course, we don’t want to be blind and insensitive to our own weaknesses. We can choose to remain oblivious, but that won’t help our Christian walk.

Am I blind, short-sighted or even oblivious?

Am I being genuinely transformed and elevated in my response to the call of Christ?

Again, emotions are good but won’t support growth on their own. We must change— transform—from the inside out.

Let’s look at the principle behind a teaching of Jesus that really helps us focus in on this:

Matthew 13:20-23: 20 The one on whom seed was sown on the rocky places, this is the man who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy; 21 yet he has no firm root in himself, but is only temporary, and when affliction or persecution arises because of the word, immediately he falls away. 22 And the one on whom seed was sown among the thorns, this is the man who hears the word, and the worry of the world and the deceitfulness of wealth choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful. 23 And the one on whom seed was sown on the good soil, this is the man who hears the word and understands it; who indeed bears fruit and brings forth, some a hundredfold, some sixty, and some thirty.

Do I have a thorny heart?

Are some of my weaknesses so comfortable that I am I oblivious to what needs to change?

Watch out! It’s easy to become complacent. We must watch out for “thorny hearts” and the short-sightedness that keeps us from being spiritually fruitful.

2 Peter 1:9: For he who lacks these qualities is blind or short-sighted, having forgotten his purification <2512> from his former sins.

Purification: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2512 katharismos; a washing off, i.e. (ceremonially) ablution, (morally) expiation: —cleansing, + purge, purification(-fying)

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: a cleansing, purification, a ritual purgation or washing

This word means the washing, cleansing and ritual purging of our sins. What does having forgotten his purification from his former sins in 2 Peter 1:9 mean?

— March 16, 2026

The next verse helps us understand:

Hebrews 1:3: (KJV) Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he (Jesus) had <2512> by himself purged <2512> our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high.

Peter is saying these people forgot the sacrifice and the merit of what Jesus did to pull us out of death. Discipleship means we have been cleansed from our previous lives to become a new creation! Have we forgotten?

We need to reflect continually on all our Savior did for us. Then we remember where we were when he called us and how he’s helped us up to this point. Self-reflection is so important in not letting former sins creep back into our lives.

It is easy to get comfortable, and the growth process is not necessarily one of great comfort. The comfort during this process comes from honest and reverent service to God, not in resting in our comfort zone. Self-observation is our necessary focus as we move forward.

This cleansing creates a deep personal responsibility to live in accordance with this upward call:

Romans 6:11-13: 11 Even so consider yourselves to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus. 12 Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey its lusts, 13 and do not go on presenting the members of your body to sin as instruments of unrighteousness; but present yourselves to God as those alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness to God.

The principle here is this is where and what you were. Do not go back there! You have been purified. Do not let sin reign in your mortal body. Present yourselves to God through the righteousness of Christ.

Never forget what we have been called to! Peter warns that if we lack these qualities, we are blind, short-sighted and have forgotten this purification Christ has provided for us. Keep this in mind!

Paul’s context in Romans 6:11-13 refers to those who have been in the way for quite a while and relapsed into bad habits. They have forgotten how the blood of Jesus cleansed them and gave them a new start. This describes a lukewarm faith where we relax our vigilance, and then we relapse in our commitment. The apostle warns us not to allow this to happen.

A quick look at the resulting challenges of not working at climbing this virtue ladder. What happens if we stop, get sidetracked or things come up?

1 Corinthians 3:11-15: 11 For no man can lay a foundation other than the one which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.

There is only one foundation here. Again, it’s not about emotion. Emotion alone will not build a strong foundation or sustain our growth. This is about growing our spiritual life based on that one foundation of Jesus Christ.

— March 16, 2026

12 Now if any man builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, 13 each man's work will become evident; for the day will show it because it is to be revealed with fire, and the fire itself will test the quality of each man's work.

This is only talking about those called to follow Christ. Our free will allows us to choose what we will build upon that foundation. Will it be the things the Apostle Peter told us about, or are we starting to mix in other, earthly things? Gold, silver and precious stones (spiritual things) will not burn up when tested with fire, contrasted with building with flammable wood, hay and straw (earthly things).

The fire itself will test the quality of each man’s work—we are on our foundation, but if we are not building with the things from above, our work will be “burned up,” meaning it won’t accomplish what it set out to accomplish.

14 If any man’s work which he has built on it remains, he will receive a reward. 15 If any man’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire.

By God’s grace, this man will still be saved, but through the fire of difficulty.

Will I succeed, or will I fall short?

What “building materials” am I using?

What’s the difference between having high-level and low-level success—between succeeding or falling short—described in these verses?

They are both based on the foundation of Jesus Christ, upon which we are to build a fruitful life of discipleship.

However, what’s missing in those who come up short, those with a lower level of success, is making spiritually-minded choices. These Christians choose to build with earthly and perishable things upon a foundation meant for spiritual and eternal glory. Human comfort, familiarity and desire drive these foolish choices. They might get comfortable, relax and then relapse. They build the wrong kind of structure on this beautiful gift of salvation.

What these Christians have built is easily destroyed in the fire of testing. In spite of this failed structure, these Christians ARE saved from destruction themselves, though this saving is through hard and fiery testing. The realization hits that they have fallen short, and they must get up and get going again.

This is a reality check. It’s such a high standard! Just because we may have been in the way for a long time doesn’t mean we are exempt from this kind of challenge. When we relax, we tend to relapse. We have to rest, instead of relaxing.

Take heart! Even if we find ourselves not doing as well as we should, there is marvelous hope:

Hebrews 4:14-16: 14 Therefore, since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the son of God, let us hold fast our confession. 15 For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who has been tempted in

— March 16, 2026

all things as we are, yet without sin. 16 Therefore let us draw near with confidence to the throne of grace, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.

We’ve got work to do! If we don’t think we need to improve or restart, we’re oblivious to our own situations. This is why the Apostle Peter, in the midst of this beautiful lesson of

2 Peter 1:5-12, includes verse 9 to warn us to be aware, be on guard, as this isn’t automatic. This is something we have to work on.

As we get older, we can’t do all the things we used to do, and we may even have new disabilities. But we cannot use these as an excuse to let weaknesses back in.

At 90 years young, Dorothea is our oldest CQ volunteer.

You can see her hand-drawn images in some of our CQ Kids videos. She says, “I'm just thankful I can still be used in some small way to serve the Lord."

What can I do to focus on the right things?

Focus on:

- We have been purified from our sins. - We have been given God’s spirit. - We have been given this virtue ladder to climb.

Even if we can’t be as active as we maybe once were, that doesn’t mean we can’t be contributing. Even small spiritual contributions are powerful! Remember the example of the widow’s mites? (Mark 12:41-44, Luke 21:1-4) Jesus watched people give offerings at the Temple. Many wealthy people came up and ostentatiously dropped their coins loudly into the metal offering box so that all could hear how much they contributed. But the widow put in two little mites (coins), worth just about nothing.

— March 16, 2026

Luke 21:3,4: (NLT) 3 ...Jesus said, This poor widow has given more than all the rest of them. 4 For they have given a tiny part of their surplus, but she, poor as she is, has given everything she has.

These coins were of great value because she gave all that she had.

Peter’s overall lesson in 2 Peter 1 helps us to understand the difficulties that can challenge us. It is critical we pay attention. Because we live in this sinful and broken world, we always need to be aware of what is around us and what we allow to grow within us.

Seeing the sad potential for getting tripped up can be really discouraging. What is the solution?

Peter, in his deep spiritual wisdom, arranged this teaching to first remind us of God’s GREAT gifts to us. He then showed us what we, as footstep followers of Jesus, are to become as a result. Next, he warned us of the dangers of losing focus. Next, he will reenergize us with the practicality and power of how our call works. If that last segment was kind of discouraging, prepare to be encouraged!

2 Peter 1:10: Therefore, brethren, be all the more diligent <4704> to make certain about His calling and choosing you…

Diligent: VERB Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4704 spoudazō; from 4710; to use speed, i.e. to make effort, be prompt or earnest

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to hasten, make haste

2) to exert one’s self, endeavour, give diligence

Be all the more diligent—strive earnestly; make haste.

Peter is going back to the beginning of his lesson from verse 5.

Now that we have seen the magnitude of God’s gifts and the opportunity we have to respond and to honor Him, let’s remember how to begin:

2 Peter 1:5: Now for this very reason also, applying (meaning, introduce simultaneously) all diligence <4710>.

Diligence: NOUN Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4710 spoudē; "speed," i.e. (by implication) despatch, eagerness, earnestness:—business, (earnest) care(- fulness), diligence, forwardness, haste

This is from the same root word meaning earnestness. Because God in His might, power, mercy and grace has given us the power of His providence in our lives through His promises, we are to apply ALL diligence.

Peter started with diligence in verse 5 and ended with diligence in verse 10. These are wonderful bookends! But if we only do things quickly and forget about earnestness, we lack the sincerity of intentional, God-honoring actions.

— March 16, 2026

Our diligence is supposed to focus us on the fact of God’s care and providence for those who are called:

Romans 8:28-30: 28 And we know that God causes all things to work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to His purpose. 29 For those whom He foreknew, He also predestined to become conformed to the image of His son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brethren; 30 and these whom He predestined, He also called; and these whom He called, He also justified; and these whom He justified, He also glorified.

What a reward we will receive to be the firstborn ones! But it's only if we are faithful and do the work, which is where the diligence comes in. We pour our heart into it. But this doesn’t mean we’re going to do it perfectly. It means if we fall down, we’re going to get up and ask for forgiveness and just keep trying.

Let’s finish the verse:

2 Peter 1:10: Therefore, brethren, be all the more diligent to make certain about His calling and choosing you for as long as you practice these things, you will never stumble <4417>.

Stumble: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4417 ptaiō; to trip, i.e. (figuratively) to err, sin, fail (of salvation):—fall, offend, stumble

We won’t stumble… ever?

James 3:2: For we all stumble <4417> in many ways. If anyone does not stumble <4417> in what he says, he is a perfect man, able to bridle the whole body as well.

Which is it? Do we never stumble or do we all stumble? Is this a contradiction?

No, Peter’s point is that if we truly practice these things, we will be able to continually move forward in spite of our weaknesses. It's not a matter of never having a weakness. It's about having the capacity to get up and keep moving forward as a result.

Romans 2:7: to those who by perseverance in doing good seek for glory and honor and immortality, eternal life.

We aren’t perfect like Jesus. We make mistakes. But when we do, we need to get up, brush ourselves off and grow from the experience.

To keep moving forward we need to practice, be intentionally diligent—in what things? We should be familiar with these by now!

2 Peter 1:5-7: 5 Now for this very reason also, applying all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence, and in your moral excellence, knowledge, 6 and in your knowledge, self- control, and in your self-control, perseverance, and in your perseverance, godliness, 7 and in your godliness, brotherly kindness, and in your brotherly kindness, love.

We keep repeating these qualities because they fit so well together and are in such a profound order that the list of qualities itself can help us whenever we fall. We can analyze ourselves using these character traits to find out where we are deficient. What am I missing?

— March 16, 2026

Maybe we are lacking self-control. Okay, what does my knowledge teach me about self- control? Then get back to it and re-engage perseverance, which brings us to godliness.

Soon we will be back heading in the right direction.

Be diligent in knowing God’s word and will:

2 Timothy 2:15: Be diligent <4704> to present yourself approved to God as a workman who does not need to be ashamed, accurately handling the word of truth.

This is that same earnestness, sincerity. Let God’s word drive us forward, not someone’s opinion or some new thought.

Be diligent to enter into the spiritual rest that discipleship brings:

Hebrews 4:9-11: 9 So there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God. 10 For the one who has entered His rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from His. 11 Therefore let us be diligent <4704> to enter that rest, so that no one will fall, through following the same example of disobedience.

Diligence to enter that rest (King James Version: labor therefore to enter into that rest) sounds like an oxymoron. What does God’s rest look like? It’s knowing God Almighty is handling it, and we’re working our lives within His providence for us. We are following His will through Christ.

Life can be difficult, but that’s exactly where we learn to rest. It’s like this: Jonathan, you need surgery, so you sit down with the surgeon. They walk you through the x-rays, explain what they’re going to do, outline the probabilities of this and that, and by the end of that conversation, you walk away saying, “I can trust this individual. I can rest in their ability to work me through this.” Yes, you’ll need physical therapy afterward, but that’s okay because you trust the surgeon.

In the same way, entering into God’s rest means saying, “I trust my Heavenly Father to oversee and take care of the challenges in my life.” That’s what it looks like to labor to enter His rest.

Be diligent to be mutually engaged in working together as one body with one purpose:

Ephesians 4:1-6: 1 Therefore I, the prisoner of the Lord, implore you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling with which you have been called, 2 with all humility and gentleness, with patience, showing tolerance for one another in love, 3 being diligent <4704> to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace. 4 There is one body and one spirit, just as also you were called in one hope of your calling; 5 one Lord, one faith, one baptism, 6 one God and Father of all who is over all and through all and in all.

The enhancement of our journey works so much better when we decide to work together—to be mutually engaged in working with and handling each other with humility, gentleness and patience, showing that agape kind of love, being diligent to

— March 16, 2026

preserve the unity of the spirit.

Being diligent with God’s word, entering into the spiritual rest of God and working together results in us not being alone. We have the encouragement of working through and growing into all these virtues to become a genuine footstep follower of Jesus.

We keep repeating all these virtues because the Apostle Peter tells us this is a formula we can rely on regularly to keep us on the path to glorifying God.

As hard as this journey is, it is not without anything and everything we might need to continue moving forward in God’s grace!

We have been looking at a remarkable process of Christian character development. If we do these things, what is the end result?

All of what Peter has been teaching us in these several verses leads us to this point. If we do these things—if we take our commitment to be transformed by God’s spirit into true footstep followers of Jesus whose lives are on the path of God-honoring self-sacrifice— what will our lives look like and where will we end up?

That’s the big question, and the Apostle Peter has the big answer!

2 Peter 1:11: for in this way the entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ will be abundantly <4146> supplied <2023> to you.

Abundantly: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4146 plousiōs; copiously Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: abundantly, richly

Supplied: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2023 epichoregeo; to furnish besides, i.e. fully supply, (figuratively) aid or contribute

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to supply, furnish, present

2) to be supplied, ministered to, assisted

— March 16, 2026

This applies to true footstep followers of Christ, not Christians “in name only.” Those who really are walking the walk as best they can, striving upward and looking forward, are abundantly supplied.

Let us pause here to consider this journey and who is involved in it. We will end up entering the kingdom of our Lord Jesus and be with him. However, this entrance into the kingdom is no small thing. This is a dramatic, eternal, life-altering change that can never be undone. That’s how powerful this is. How do we get there? Let’s think about how our Christian lives work for a moment.

First, we are called to follow:

Luke 9:23: And he was saying to them all, If anyone wishes to come after me, he must deny himself, and take up his cross daily and follow me.

This walk is a sacrificial walk, doing God’s will and not our own.

1 Corinthians 1:26: For consider your calling, brethren, that there were not many wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble.

It is an undeserved privilege to be called, but we aren’t special in the world’s eyes. It’s a difficult walk. God doesn’t call the “best of the best”; He calls those who have a heart that can be driven towards God.

The road we are to walk is narrow and difficult:

Matthew 7:13-14: 13 Enter through the narrow gate; for the gate is wide and the way is broad that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter through it. 14 For the gate is small and the way is narrow that leads to life, and there are few who find it.

This is a narrow path. Not many follow through because of its challenges. The difficulty of this road is there to develop our characters into spiritually strong and mature examples of Christlikeness.

Again, this is what Peter’s virtue ladder is all about.

Spiritually, we need to be Christlike:

1 Peter 4:12-13: 12 Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal among you, which comes upon you for your testing, as though some strange thing were happening to you; 13 but to the degree that you share the sufferings of Christ, keep on rejoicing, so that also at the revelation of his glory you may rejoice with exultation.

We know this is going to be hard. Why? The reward is immortality. God is proving heart loyalty that will last an eternity! It is an amazing thought for our little heads to get around. We need to pray in faith, “Lord, whatever Your will is.” We have been given an incredible privilege and want to work towards it every day.

— March 16, 2026

How can we get there? Once again:

2 Peter 1:5-7: 5 …applying all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence, and in your moral excellence, knowledge, 6 and in your knowledge, self-control, and in your self- control, perseverance, and in your perseverance, godliness, 7 and in your godliness, brotherly kindness, and in your brotherly kindness, love.

By doing these things, an abundant entrance into Christ’s kingdom is supplied!

Colossians 3:15-16: 15 Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body; and be thankful. 16 Let the word of Christ richly <4146> dwell within you, with all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with thankfulness in your hearts to God.

This is a “whole person” experience! That is what happens when the word of Christ abundantly dwells within us. That is the kind of entrance that is given us. It’s not some little crawl space we go through.

The abundance of grace and privilege offered as a result of fighting the fight is simply overwhelming. It’s too big to understand. This entrance is going to be supplied, to be furnished—made ready for us.

Colossians 2:19: and not holding fast to the head, from whom the entire body, being supplied <2023> and held together by the joints and ligaments, grows with a growth which is from God.

We are fully supplied through our head which is Christ Jesus! Jesus gives us his example, his being our ransom price for redemption, his paving the road for God’s kingdom to be in heaven and on earth—this is the entrance supplied to us.

While we might fall down, we always get back up. It’s a matter of growing through the challenges of our lives and applying these things so we can be true disciples of Christ.

— March 16, 2026

Here is Peter’s final verse in this context:

2 Peter 1:12: Therefore, I will always be ready to remind you of these things, even though you already know them, and have been established in the truth which is present with you.

This is the conclusion of Peter’s beautiful teaching. Therefore… because we’ve been given every conceivable gift to help draw our thoughts, words and deeds upward; because we are willing to do the consistent work of character transformation; “I, Peter, will regularly remind you of God’s plan and providence for you! You are that important to me.”

This was a personal teaching for Peter. In the next few verses, we see he did not expect to live much longer. It’s as if he is saying, “As long as I breathe, I am going to be with you in these things.” In what things? One more time!

The first rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Faith—the allegiance of our life’s direction.

The second rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Moral Excellence—this is the allegiance of our heart.

The third rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Knowledge—the allegiance of our intellect.

The fourth rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Self-Control—the allegiance of our passions.

The fifth rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Perseverance—the allegiance of our energy.

The sixth rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Godliness—the allegiance of our character.

The seventh rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Brotherly Kindness—the allegiance of our relationships.

The eighth rung: The Allegiance Attribute of Love—the allegiance of our purpose.

The Apostle Peter has given us a template to put every aspect of our lives in order, so that we can fully grab hold of what following Jesus really truly looks like.

Here’s the power of the tools given to us by the Apostle Peter:

Romans 8:35-39: 35 Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? 36 Just as it is written, FOR YOUR SAKE WE ARE BEING PUT TO DEATH ALL DAY LONG; WE WERE CONSIDERED AS SHEEP TO BE SLAUGHTERED. 37 But in all these things we overwhelmingly conquer through him who loved us. 38 For I am convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, 39 nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

— March 16, 2026

Nothing can separate us because we have Jesus as the example. We have God’s spirit working in us, and we know what we need to do. We have this ladder of character virtues to climb each and every day. This is what the Apostle Peter is driving us towards!

So, what does a fully supplied Christian character look like?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

2. How do Matthew 12:36 and Ephesians 5:11 illustrate the seriousness of Peter’s warning against being “useless” or “unfruitful”? Describe what it means to be useless or unfruitful.

3. Why do we need full discernment and a clear understanding? How does growing in the virtues of 2 Peter 1:5-7 lead to “precise and correct knowledge?” (Colossians 1:9-10)

4. How does the description of spiritual blindness in 2 Peter 1:9 expose the danger of losing sight of our calling? Use the Parable of the Sower to illustrate this condition. (2 Peter 1:9, Matthew 13:20-23)

5. In what areas are you spiritually short-sighted? How will remembering Christ’s purification of your sins reshape your perspective? Will you consider setting up a pattern of reflection each day in prayer? (Hebrews 1:3, Romans 6:11-13)

7. How does the repeated call to diligence in 2 Peter 1:5 and 1, frame the entire process of Christian growth?

How do Romans 8:28-30 and 2 Timothy 2:15 reinforce this call to diligence? In what ways do 2 Timothy 2:15, Hebrews 4:9-11 and Ephesians 4:1-6 “enhance” our journey following Jesus’ example?

8. How do we harmonize 2 Peter 1:10 and James 3:2 over “stumbling?” How does practicing the virtues in

2 Peter 1:5-7 enable us to overcome our inevitable stumbling? (Romans 2:7)

9. What are the steps, the “whole person” experience, we go through to attain “an abundantly supplied” entrance into Christ’s kingdom? (2 Peter 1:11, Luke 9:23, Matthew 7:13-14, 1 Peter 4:12-13)

10. How will you let “the peace of Christ rule in your heart… the word of Christ richly dwell within you”? How can you keep “singing with thankfulness in your heart to God?” (Colossians 3:15-16) Then you will never be separated from the love of Christ! (Romans 8:35-39) Think on that!
