### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1430-gods-providence/

1. What is a working definition of “God’s providence”?

2. How does Israel as a nation in the wilderness and Jesus in the Temple at 12 years old help us comprehend

God’s providence? (Deuteronomy 8:2-6, Luke 2:48-51)

3. Compare and contrast Israel in the wilderness for 40 years versus Jesus in the wilderness for 40 days.

(Matthew 4:1-4)

4. When has God provided providential support and then relief during a difficult, challenging, uphill battle

in your life? Have you felt His presence at that time? Looking back, did fighting through the trial like Jesus did give you strength?

5. Why did Jesus have to experience hunger in the wilderness, and what does this teach us about God’s

sustaining power? (Matthew 4:1–4)

6. Answer truthfully to yourself: How do you improve these situations?

a. Do I ever proclaim faith in God’s providence, while standing on the compromised ground of my

own weak decisions?

b. Am I properly asking God to guide my future, but still clinging to habits or choices that keep me

on shaky ground?

c. Do I ask God to bless me with peace, but continue to feed my anxiety with the same unhealthy

patterns that keep me spiritually off-balance?

7. Explain three ways we can identify God’s providence in our lives—where to look, how to apply, and what

we hope to gain. (James 4:13–17; 2 Timothy 3:14–17)

8. How might we misapply Scripture, as Satan did when twisting Psalm 91? How does 2 Timothy 3:14–17 help

us avoid this?

9. What do Jesus’ life objectives teach us about positioning ourselves to receive God’s providence?

(Psalms 40:7-8, John 4:31-34, Matthew 26:36-46, Hebrews 12:4-7, 1 Corinthians 10:12-14)

10. Can you recall a time when God’s providence sustained you through an isolating experience?

11. How can we prepare our hearts to receive God’s providence when He allows hunger, difficulty, solitude,

or the rejection of ease, as Jesus did in the wilderness?

## Episode 1431 — Was ‘Doubting Thomas’ Really a Doubter?
Published: 2026-04-06
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1431-doubting-thomas/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/03092116/CQ_Rewind_04-06-2026_Was_Doubting_Thomas_Really_a_Doubter.pdf

John 20:25: So the other disciples were saying to him, We have seen the Lord! But he said to

them, Unless I see in his hands the imprint of the nails, and put my finger into the place of

the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.

There are many Bible accounts that have gathered a lot of attention over centuries because of their dramatic content. Cain and Abel, Noah and the Ark and David and Goliath are all powerful and dramatic Old Testament accounts filled with action. Two New Testament examples are Jesus in the manger and Jesus on the cross. All of these named stories show us a hero and their experiences. Then we have ‘Doubting Thomas.’ Here was an apostle who did not betray Jesus and who was ultimately faithful to his calling, and yet we know him as ‘the doubter.’ Is this a fair and unbiased way to be remembering one of Jesus’ closest followers? Was Thomas that far off from faithfulness so as to be labeled as a doubter?

Our considerations today will outline five belief lessons that Jesus taught all of us when he addressed Thomas’ inability to comprehend the resurrection.

Let’s first review what we know about Thomas.

You might be surprised that Thomas’ words and actions are recorded only three times in the entire New Testament, all of them in the Gospel of John. The first comes in John 11, when Jesus announces his intention to return to Lazarus in Judea, even though the Jews there had recently tried to stone him.

The apostles were cautioning Jesus against going:

John 11:13–16: 13 Now Jesus had spoken of his [Lazarus’] death, but they thought that he was speaking of literal sleep. 14 So Jesus then said to them plainly, Lazarus is dead, 15 and I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, so that you may believe; but let us go to him. 16 Therefore Thomas, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples, Let us also go, so that we may die with him.

Thomas (Aramaic) and Didymus (Greek) both mean “twin,” so it’s thought he was a twin.

Let us also go, so that we may die with him—this is a statement of courage and connection. If Jesus was walking into danger, Thomas wanted to go with him. He did not want to be separated from Jesus!

Next, we hear from Thomas in the upper room the night before Jesus’ crucifixion:

John 14:3–6: 3 If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and receive you to myself, that where I am, there you may be also. 4 And you know the way where I am going. 5 Thomas said to him, Lord, we do not know where you are going, how do we know the way? 6 Jesus said to him, I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father but through me.

When Jesus is teaching his disciples, it is rare that anybody comes up to him to say, “Wait, wait, we need to fill in that detail…” Thomas jumps in and says, How do we know the way? Jesus doesn’t say, “Shame on you!” He says instead, I am the way, and the truth, and the life. Thomas is reaching out because he didn’t want Jesus to go without him.

This is another statement of courage and connection. Thomas did not want to be separated from Jesus!

These first two examples give us a foundation for understanding who Thomas is.

This brings us to the resurrection appearances of Jesus, and this is where Thomas’ reputation as a doubter is formed. Before we read about this moment, it helps to remember what the disciples had just lived through. They were traumatized, hiding behind locked doors, trying to make sense of the crucifixion. And then, suddenly, Jesus appears to the Ten—alive, standing in front of them, speaking peace over their fear. It is overwhelming, it is unexpected, and it changes everything for them in an instant.

But Thomas wasn’t there, and we’re not told why.

We have the drama of the crucifixion and the bigger drama of the resurrection and appearances, but Thomas wasn’t there. We are going to drop into this account after Jesus appeared to those Ten, where Thomas was not present.

Here is their explanation of what they experienced:

John 20:24–29: 24 But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came. 25 So the other disciples were saying to him, We have seen the Lord! But he said to them, Unless I see in his hands the imprint of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.

We read these words. On the surface, without any other context, these sound like challenging words of great doubt. Unless I see exactly what I say, I won’t believe!

26 After eight days his disciples were again inside, and Thomas with them. Jesus came, the doors having been shut, and stood in their midst and said, Peace be with you. 27 Then he said to Thomas, Reach here with your finger, and see my hands; and reach here your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing. 28 Thomas answered and said to him, My Lord and my God! 29 Jesus said to him, Because you have seen me, have you believed? Blessed are they who did not see, and yet believed.

We see this utterly dramatic turnaround eight days later. We might think Thomas was a terrible doubter but suddenly believed. There is so much more to it than that. Let’s break down these verses and look at this event piece by piece to get an understanding of both where Thomas was in his heart and mind, and what Jesus did about it.

John 20:24: But Thomas, one of the twelve… was not with them when Jesus came.

There may be several perspectives on why Thomas was not there. Because we are not told why he was absent, we can choose to speculate.

The question is, are we speculating from a positive or negative perspective? Was he grieving, or did he have something more important to do? We need to be careful when speculating.

John 20:25: So the other disciples were saying to him, We have seen the Lord!

While the Scriptures do not pinpoint when Thomas came to them, it seems likely that it was later that same day after Jesus had appeared to the Ten. Why do we think this? Because the next verse, John 20:26, says eight days later, which brings us to the following Sunday.

We have seen the Lord! John only records this phrase, but we think it’s reasonable to assume they told Thomas the whole story—the locked door, their fear and Jesus calming them with his words and presence.

Luke fills in a few more details:

Luke 24:38–43: 38 And he said to them, Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? 39 See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself; touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have. 40 And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet. 41 While they still could not believe it because of their joy and amazement (this was the kind of momentary disbelief when something is “too good to be true”), he said to them, Have you anything here to eat? 42 They gave him a piece of a broiled fish; 43 and he took it and ate it before them.

Eating the fish proved to them he wasn’t some vision or hallucination. He was physically resurrected and standing right in front of them! He is present with them! They likely would have told Thomas about Peace be to you, about their commission to be sent out to preach and about Jesus telling them of the comfort of the holy spirit coming to them, and the forgiving of sins. They would have told him everything, so excited and overjoyed to share.

Rather than speculating on the why of Thomas’ doubt, it is far more productive to establish the groundwork of who Thomas was and what he may have needed.

When I see someone who is unsure and in doubt, is it easier for me to speculate, or is it easier for me to pause and consider the whole picture?

Which do we naturally seem to go towards?

What should we spiritually gravitate towards?

The more we are willing to pause and consider the whole story of Thomas, the more we will be able to see the blessings of his learning.

Now we are ready to dive into the plainly stated doubt of Thomas.

What will we find when we get there?

What we will find is a very deep and emotional doubt. As we work at uncovering it, we will need to look under the surface to try and grasp not only why it was there, but what would be needed to handle it. As we go through this exercise, it is imperative that we remind ourselves that Thomas’ doubts were revealed to teach us powerful lessons of faith. Are we paying attention?

We’re not told why Thomas wasn’t with the other Ten, and Scripture never criticizes him for it. Based on what we do know—his courage, his loyalty, his desire never to be separated from Jesus—it’s very likely he was simply crushed by grief and withdrew. Some people run toward community when they’re hurting; others pull away. Whatever the reason, he missed the moment that turned the others from terrified to joyful.

John 20:25: So the other disciples were saying to him, We have seen the Lord! But he said to them, Unless I see in his hands the imprint of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.

And here’s where Thomas earns the nickname that has stuck for 2,000 years! Many Bible commentaries keep reinforcing this myth.

(Source: Eclectic Notes on the Bible) Unless I see… I will not believe Slow of heart to believe, he missed the early taste of the blessing, and abode in the darkness of his own unbelief, whilst the rest were filled with gladness.

“Abode in the darkness of his own unbelief” implies Thomas chose darkness.

(Source: Bible Commentary by J. Vernon McGee) Boy, is he a doubter! He has enough evidence to make him a believer, but he is not. But at least now it appears that he will stay with the other disciples.

“He has enough evidence”—but did he? Thomas only heard traumatized men say something that was unbelievable. We believe commentaries like these are harsh. There has been a long tradition of interpreting Thomas through a lens of failure and not simple humanity.

Two important points:

1. Thomas had just watched the one he loved be brutally killed. People in deep

grief often need more reassurance, not less.

2. The assumption is made that he should have just believed the account of the other apostles who had that personal encounter with Jesus. But those others didn’t believe a personal account either! The women Jesus first appeared to reported the resurrection, but the disciples don’t believe them. Jesus appears, offers the wounds for inspection and even eats fish, and THEN they believe. Thomas wasn’t there, so he’s simply asking for the same experience.

There is certainly more to, Unless I see the wounds and touch them, I won’t believe. Regarding Thomas’ strong reaction, what might be a more positive way for us to look at it?

Maybe he found it difficult to believe the words of anyone who told him that a person whom he had seen dead and laid in a tomb three days before could possibly be alive, especially if that dead man was Jesus, the only human who could raise the dead.

Before Jesus’ crucifixion, he raised Lazarus who had been dead four days. It could be done, but Jesus was the one who did it, and now he’s the one who is dead. How could this possibly change? Perhaps this is what Thomas was thinking, and it was piled on top of his grief and sadness at being left leaderless.

When Thomas says, I will not believe, the Greek phrase is ou mē pisteusō—a conditional expression meaning, “I am not able to believe unless this is shown to me.” So, this isn’t a defiant declaration. It expresses impossibility given the current conditions. It does not mean permanent refusal. It means: “Given what I know right now, belief is impossible for me.” Really what it is saying is, I need help. Show me.

Next, we find that Jesus is ready and able to rise above Thomas’ doubt, grief and frustrated questioning at the appropriate time:

John 20:26: After eight days his disciples were again inside, and Thomas with them.

This is eight days later, again on Sunday. Again the doors were shut and this time the eleven apostles are all there. This means Thomas has had a whole week to replay the crucifixion, question if the others really saw what they said they did, feeling left out of their joy, probably kicking himself for why he didn’t stay with them.

And then Jesus recreates the event. The verse continues with: Jesus came, the doors having been shut, and stood in their midst and said, Peace be with you.

Again, just like the first time, Peace be with you is the introduction. There is nothing better than being given peace by our Lord and Savior, Jesus. This wasn’t something that Jesus just made up in his resurrected appearances. Jesus had spoken about peace in the upper room before his crucifixion.

He planted seeds of peace in their hearts and minds before all the tragedy happened:

John 14:27: (KJV) Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.

Those were the seeds Jesus was going to draw on now after his resurrection, because they had witnessed the horror of the crucifixion. Jesus planted the “peace” seeds beforehand, knowing their belief would soon be profoundly challenged.

In a precise way, Jesus recreated the initial event of eight days earlier, likely for the benefit of Thomas. He had given the others the hope of his resurrection and would do it now for Thomas. This is an incredible lesson of compassion and faith building. Jesus was not there to crush or to correct; he was there to build faith.

John 20:27: (KJV) Then saith he to Thomas, Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.

Here we have the upward steps of faith development: 27 Then saith he to Thomas…

Belief Lesson 1: Jesus first speaks directly to those who have experienced a lack of conviction.

He is talking to Thomas, even though all the rest are in the room. He goes straight to the one with the doubt. This is in direct contrast to his dismissing the fault-finding of the Pharisees. This is encouragement in the face of doubt and compassion in the face of weakness! This is Jesus building and not taking apart.

Jesus treats honest doubt different than hard-hearted resistance. Jesus is trying to steady Thomas’ faith after trauma. But the Pharisees were different. They weren’t struggling to believe—they were refusing to believe. They were trying to trap and undermine Jesus, so he exposed their behavior for what it was and moved on.

Jesus treats Thomas in a compassionate and respectful way. This is a lesson for us: Jesus assures his followers that their personal doubts and confusion are all individually important. Jesus isn’t going to directly speak words to us, but his life example and all the Scriptures “speak” what we need to hear to remove our doubts.

John 20:27: (KJV) …Reach <5342> hither thy finger…

Reach: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5342 pherō; a primary verb; to bear or carry

Belief Lesson 2. Then Jesus invites the doubt to be removed.

The Greek literally means, “Bring your finger here.” It’s not Jesus saying, “Fine, if you insist; go ahead and touch me.” It’s an invitation. Jesus is drawing Thomas close, meeting him in his grief, and giving him exactly what he asked for without even a hint of shaming him. “Bring what you have—your questions, your need, your grief—and come close.”

“Bring your finger here to my hands.” Jesus doesn’t remove the doubt, but he intentionally welcomes Thomas to take the action of reaching out. These gentle instructions demonstrate compassionate accountability.

As Jesus reminds him of his doubts, he simultaneously presents evidence to dissolve them.

John 20:27: (KJV) …Reach hither thy finger, and behold <2396>, (*a form of <1492>) my hands…

Behold here means to grasp, to understand; not just, “I saw something with my eyes.”

Behold: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2396 íde; second person singular imperative active of

#1492; used as an interjection to denote surprise; lo!:—behold, lo, see

#1492 eídō; a primary verb; used only in certain past tenses, the others being borrowed from the equivalent #3700 and #3708 properly, to see (literally or figuratively); by implication, (in the perfect

tense only) to know:—be aware, behold, can (not tell), consider, (have) know(-ledge), look (on),

perceive, see, be sure, tell, understand, wish, wot

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon #1492 1) to see 1a) to perceive with the eyes 1b) to perceive by any of the senses 1c) to perceive, notice, discern, discover

*Different study tools sometimes use different Strong’s Concordance numbers for the word behold or see because the Greek has several verbs that all get translated the same way in English. The tools aren’t disagreeing about the verse—just about which Greek nuance to highlight.

Belief Lesson 3. Jesus then encourages those who doubt to perceive what they are experiencing, so it will stay with them.

It’s not enough to just see it and say, okay, there is a solution. The remedy for doubt is to truly perceive and ingest what we are seeing and experiencing, making it transformational and lasting.

It is one thing to have an experience and another thing for it to take root in you. We think that’s why Jesus waited a full week before addressing Thomas’ doubts. He let Thomas feel the weight of his questions so that when the answer came, it didn’t just pass through him; it transformed him. The delay prepares Thomas to be one of the clearest witnesses to the reality of the resurrection. Thomas isn’t just told the truth—he is standing in the presence of the risen Lord and believes it! He is standing in the presence of the truth, not just hearing it from an intellectual perspective.

This is the same word as eight days earlier when the disciples “saw” Jesus:

John 20:20: The disciples then rejoiced when they saw <1492>* the Lord.

*Some Bible resources show this word as Strong’s 3708 in this and other verses in this chapter.

Greek uses several different verbs for “seeing,” but English flattens them into one word, which makes them look interchangeable. Strong’s 1492 (eidō) comes from an older verb meaning “to see,” but in New Testament Greek it means “to know” or “to perceive mentally.” By contrast, 3708 (horaō) describes truly perceiving or recognizing, and 2334 (theōreō) means to observe attentively. Because Strong’s groups entire word families under one number—and because English translates all of these as “see”—different study tools sometimes assign different Strong’s numbers to the same English word. The Greek verbs themselves aren’t interchangeable; it’s the English that makes them appear that way.

Eight days later means this was a Sunday to a Sunday. Why didn’t this reveal happen on Saturday, the Jewish Law’s Sabbath, the day of rest? We think it’s because this was starting the new age of Christianity, and Sunday was the first day of a new week. This was a new dispensation for the world. It was now the age of the gospel message. This is why Jesus was raised on a Sunday, appeared to the Ten on a Sunday, and then on the next Sunday, appeared to the Eleven. He is teaching them their new life.

So, Jesus is gently saying, “Bring your finger here to me so you can behold my hands, so you can see with your eyes and feel with your own hand the evidence that you felt you so desperately needed.”

When Jesus did appear to Thomas, he offered to have him touch the wounds, though this wasn’t necessary to convince him. He never touched Jesus and immediately recognized him by sight as the Lord. In fact, there is no record that any of the disciples needed to actually touch the wounds.

One of the most beautiful parts of this account is how personally Jesus responds to Thomas, reminding us of:

Belief Lesson 1: Jesus first speaks directly to those who have experienced a lack of conviction.

Instead of feeling left out during those eight days, he is now singled out, but in a personal, compassionate way. Jesus doesn’t give him a lecture, he doesn’t push him away, and he doesn’t shame him for struggling. Jesus acknowledges the doubt is real, brings it into the light and dismantles it step-by-step.

Thomas is singled out so that he can be built up.

For true believers, Jesus will always provide sufficient evidence for us to be able to let go of our doubts.

However, sometimes our hearts are so burdened that we pile doubt upon doubt in our frustration. Thomas seems to have done this eight days previous. The beauty is that this frustration does not lessen Jesus’ ability to solve our dilemmas.

The power of doubt is a formidable foe. It is with a great sigh of relief that we can observe and embrace the compassion and wisdom of Jesus to handle it.

Jesus is now dismantling Thomas' doubt, small step by small step.

How far would he go to rekindle Thomas' faith?

There is a humble and beautiful lesson unfolding here for every true believer who struggles from time to time with doubt. Jesus is plainly showing all of us that he will give us what we need to not only face our doubts, but also to use them in a way that they will press us into a deeper and more active faith. Our job is to pay attention.

Thomas shows us that doubt isn’t the opposite of faith. It can lead to even greater faith. Thomas wasn’t rebellious. He had been shattered by violent trauma; everything he thought he knew turned upside down.

This is the beauty of Thomas’ story: when we bring our questions, our confusion and even our pain to Jesus, he meets us with compassion. For anyone struggling with doubt, we recommend listening to Episodes #1302 and #1303: “How Can I Doubt My Doubts?”

Let’s go back to taking apart verse 27:

John 20:27: (KJV) … behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side…

Belief Lesson 4. Jesus further encourages those who doubt by giving them an even deeper ability to perceive what they are experiencing. Why this step? It shows that the truth and power of Jesus’ life is confirmed by overwhelming evidence!

It’s not just one piece of evidence; it’s many pieces of strong and powerful evidence. Reach hither thy hand—not just a finger. “Bring your hand to this wound so you can be overwhelmed with belief!” What a beautiful, compassionate response focused on Thomas.

Remember, Jesus had given the other apostles this same demonstration of his authenticity:

Luke 24:38–40: (KJV) 38 And he said unto them, Why are ye troubled? and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? 39 Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see… 40 And when he had thus spoken, he shewed them his hands and his feet.

Jesus gave them this opportunity. They were all invited to touch with their own hands so they could perceive and therefore believe. Thomas is given exactly what they were given, the same invitation.

What about us? Do we deeply examine the evidence of Jesus and the gospel being absolutely present in our lives? What are we actually perceiving? Where is Jesus offering evidence in my life that I’m only noticing and not truly perceiving?

There’s a big difference between knowledge that feels good and truth that actually transforms us because it is in our heart.

John 20:27: (KJV) … and be not faithless, but believing.

Belief Lesson 5. The whole reason to allow our doubts is to teach us deeper faith. Jesus continues the lesson by summing up what is now obvious to those who have doubts: God’s will, power and providence are stronger than any human fear or imagination!

Doubt tends to spiral and build more doubt upon doubt, which results in layers of doubt needing to be dismantled.

Thomas, like the other disciples, had fallen into a pattern of doubt. None of them believed the reports of the women about Jesus’ resurrection. Peter didn’t believe even after seeing the empty tomb, though John did. Thomas was simply the last of the eleven to be granted an overwhelming personal demonstration by Jesus that it was really he who was with them again. They needed something personal to guide them. All of Jesus’ appearances after his resurrection did exactly that.

This was not a new way for Jesus to teach his followers.

Throughout his entire ministry, Jesus had given his disciples lessons on developing their faith:

Luke 17:5–6: 5 The apostles said to the Lord, Increase our faith! 6 And the Lord said, If you had faith like a mustard seed, you would say to this mulberry tree, Be uprooted and be planted in the sea; and it would obey you.

Jesus’ analogy: If you have faith like a mustard seed. Notice, it’s not “faith as small as a mustard seed,” as some people assume. It is about faith which, like a seed for a mustard plant, will grow to a good size. This is faith with GREAT growth potential!

Jesus had all along allowed his disciples to have doubts. This wasn’t the first time they had doubts. He allowed those doubts so they could have opportunities to grow their “mustard- seed faith” to a greater magnitude.

We are reminded of Jesus calming the stormy sea, as recorded in Matthew 8:23–27, Mark 4:36–41 and Luke 8:22–25. This was a matter of growing faith. Up to this experience, Jesus had taught and healed as his Father had directed him.

This event, however, would break new ground, as Jesus was about to show them the power of God’s spirit in a whole new way:

Matthew 8:24–26: 24 And behold, there arose a great storm on the sea, so that the boat was being covered with the waves; but Jesus himself was asleep. 25 And they came to him and woke him, saying, Save us, Lord; we are perishing! 26 He said to them, Why are you afraid, you men of little faith <3640>?

Little faith: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3640 oligopistos;

incredulous, i.e. lacking confidence

In the depth of the tumult of the storm, Jesus challenged his disciples regarding their faith. The boat is rocking, the waves are coming over, the wind is howling and Jesus asks, Why are you afraid, you men of little faith?

Why is he challenging their faith at this point? They were frightened for their lives, and the only one who could possibly protect them was asleep! They figured they had to be afraid, because Jesus was asleep and unaware of the danger. But he’s there…!

Little faith sees the magnitude of the experience and knows but does not yet trust in the solution. That is why he said, Why are you afraid, you men of little faith?

Jesus is not ridiculing their doubts; he is using them as a tool to build their faith, and the disciples are following him in this because his guidance is so clear.

Let’s get back to this stormy sea and wrap up this piece of our lesson:

Mark 4:39–41: (KJV) 39 And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. 40 And he said unto them, Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith? 41 And they feared exceedingly, and said one to another, What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

Jesus says, Peace, be still, and all the tumult goes away. Remember when Jesus entered the upper room both times after his resurrection? What did he say? Peace be unto you. There is a theme running throughout that Jesus brings peace, no matter what the circumstance, no matter what the event.

On this occasion, Jesus calms the storm in an instant. His lesson was clear—in his presence there was nothing to fear, even from the arising of a great storm.

- Before he calmed the storm, his message was to rise above fear.
- After calming the storm, his message regarding their lack of faith was a physical verification that they were in the company of God’s chosen one— because nobody else could have done what he did.

This great example of his calming the storm helped prepare them for the tragedies to come later. As we realize the magnitude of any experience, like the disciples, we must learn to also realize the magnitude of the solution, the magnitude of who and what we believe in!

Thomas’ doubt wasn’t rebellion, cynicism or distrust of Jesus. It was a heart trying to reconcile trauma and grief with hope.

Like Thomas, our doubts can feel overwhelming when they are just sitting there before us. Jesus is teaching us to proactively reach out to the evidence of his presence in our lives and the unfolding of God’s plan so those very doubts can be transformed into a growing and healthy faith.

That is what Jesus had taught them all along. The lessons here are nothing short of dramatic. Jesus shows us that our doubts can be opportunities if we reach out in faith!

Jesus had given Thomas everything he needed to extinguish his doubts.

What would Thomas’ reaction be?

The magnitude of this lesson only gets bigger! Thomas had been given dramatic and irrefutable answers to his doubts and now he was ready to respond. As we shall see, his response was overwhelmingly positive and powerful. We need to pay close attention to this so we can use it as a template for our own responses to God through Jesus resolving our own doubts.

Let’s look closer at the verse:

John 20:28: (KJV) And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.

What joy! Thomas’ response, My Lord and my God, is one of the strongest declarations of faith in the entire New Testament. The so-called doubter becomes the apostle who speaks with the greatest clarity.

After all the fear, trauma and confusion of the crucifixion, Thomas finally “sees”—he perceives, he understands—that this is the risen Jesus standing before him, and everything snaps into place. His words are the outpouring of a heart that has been shattered and then rebuilt by overwhelming evidence and overwhelming, individualized grace.

In that moment, Thomas shows us that if we have honest doubt and we bring it to Jesus, it can lead to a deeper and more personal conviction than we ever imagined.

Thomas’ response is proof that his doubt was an honest reaction to grief and frustration and not understanding, versus a doubt that was just skeptical and angry.

For us, the lesson is that our doubts are permitted. Why? To teach us deeper faith.

Jesus begins to wrap up this whole lesson:

John 20:29: (KJV) Jesus saith unto him, Thomas, because thou hast seen <3708> me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen <1492> (or <3708> in some concordances), and yet have believed.

Seen: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3708 horao; properly, to stare at [compare #3700],

i.e. (by implication) to discern clearly (physically or mentally); by extension,

to attend to; by Hebraism, to experience; passively, to appear

Jesus is adding another dimension. You’d think it would be enough to quell the doubts and have everybody say, “We have been so blessed!” But no! Jesus doesn’t stop there; he uses this as a starting point for an even deeper lesson.

The lesson here again is focused on deep and abiding faith that has the potential to grow—mustard-seed faith. Let’s go deeper and see where Jesus is going with this.

Remember, the apostles had up to this point lived at the time of Jewish favor under the Jewish Law. They lived in a time when physical evidences showed God’s favor. This was a time of “seeing is believing.” God’s overruling providence and power were unmistakably with the Jewish people.

Jesus was now showing Thomas and the other apostles that their new experiences would be in the context of “not seeing and yet believing.”

This is a different way of looking at things and applies directly to us in this day, because we are never going to be in that upper room. We will not have the physical experiences the apostles had.

Jesus’ post-resurrection appearances were not only needed to confirm that he had indeed risen—they were also shaping them for the work they would soon do when he would no longer be physically present.

Jesus is clearly using Thomas’ experience to compare these two approaches to faith:

1. Physically seeing something and truly perceiving it, truly grasping what we have seen with our eyes to clearly confirm our faith in what was seen.

John 20:27: (KJV) Then saith he to Thomas, Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.

The nation of Israel had been used to this kind of belief for generations. But Jesus was transitioning the apostles to a different level of faith:

2. Being able to grasp, perceive and truly believe in something with which we have no direct, physical experience. It is this level of belief that we all should strive for, because Jesus calls this level of belief blessed!

This new way to experience faith would now be the responsibility of the apostles to pass along.

The Apostle Paul presses the issue of having faith in that which is not seen. He mentions this several times to the Hebrew Christians.

Let’s just look at a few instances.

Hebrews 3:4–6: 4 For every house is built by someone, but the builder of all things is God.

We know what a house is; we can visualize it, we can mentally walk through the door. Paul next describes a house that is seen.

5 SEEN: Now Moses was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony of those things which were to be spoken later;

Everyone understood that Moses was behind the building of the physical Tabernacle, delivering the Law in stone tablets, the physical aspect of sacrifices—it was all seen; it was in front of them. The Israelites knew what was happening because they could see it.

6 UNSEEN: but Christ was faithful as a son over his house—whose house we are, if we hold fast our confidence and the boast of our hope firm until the end.

Whose house we are—this is something different, something that is not seen, not physical or tangible. Jesus told his disciples in John 14:2, …I go to prepare a place for you. In my Father’s house (you don’t know where it is, or what it looks like) there are many rooms (dwelling places). We are to hold onto the unseen. Thomas is learning that lesson along with the other apostles at this point, because they are recognizing they have to go beyond where they have been; they have to grow.

Jesus said this level of faith in the unseen blessed. Moses’ house was a house of servants. But those of us who follow Christ are referred to as a house of sons. We are considered family!

What evidence has Christ given me that I’ve overlooked, minimized or explained away?

Maybe the evidence is already there:

— in God’s providence we call “coincidence,” — in the strength we didn’t know we had, — in the people placed in our path,

— in the Scriptures that spoke at the perfect moment, — in the emotional healing that happened so slowly we didn’t notice it, such as grief that

softened, fears that don’t have that same hold on us, a sense of peace that didn’t match the circumstances, or — in something that didn’t work out but turned out to be for our protection.

How much doubt has resulted from my not paying attention to the evidence!

One final lesson on having a vital faith in that which you have not physically seen:

Hebrews 12:1–3: 1 Therefore, since we have so great a cloud of witnesses surrounding us,

What witnesses? The previous chapter was all about the faithful individuals of the Old Testament. They are the witnesses. They witness to the faithfulness of God as they worked through very difficult and trying experiences, and we have them to refer to. We can’t see them, but we can read about them and believe even though we do not actually experience their lives alongside them. It is historical evidence.

…let us also lay aside every encumbrance and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us, 2 fixing our eyes on Jesus,

Fixing our eyes on Jesus… can we actually see him? No, but we are fixing our eyes on the vision of who he is, what he stands for, what he did, how he did it, what he taught and how he served his Father with every breath of his life from beginning to end. So, we fix our eyes on that example, not seeing physically, but seeing in a way that we can grasp it with our intellect and hearts.

…the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. 3 For consider him who has endured such hostility by sinners against himself, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart.

And so we will not fall into doubt. Consider him who has endured those difficult things, has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. We don’t even know what that looks like. We can’t even begin to imagine, and yet we believe in this vision even though we cannot actually see it, because we see the evidences of these things. This is the kind of belief Thomas and the other apostles were being told they needed to learn and then teach.

From now on, how about we call him ‘Discerning Thomas’ or ‘Faithful Thomas’!

Faithful Thomas reminds us that Jesus never wastes a doubt. What feels like a setback in our faith can become (if we are humble and reaching) the very place where deeper conviction is born. Thomas walked into that upper room with grief and confusion. He walked out with a faith stronger than ever because he brought those doubts directly to Jesus. His story shows us that honest struggle can press us closer to God, not farther away. If we reach towards the evidence with an honest, humble heart, we will be met with compassion and the personalized strength we individually need to keep believing.

It was an individual lesson taught to Thomas for the benefit of every Christian who has ever lived. Think about the power of that individual lesson and how we can individually apply it.

The lessons we can learn from Faithful Thomas are many.

Let us work at standing firm and hopeful in our personal experiences of faith development, recognizing that we are daily undergoing a process of growing into a faith that can move mountains. Let us more and more see with the eyes of faith, touch with the hands of conviction and act with the zeal of God’s spirit!

This is what Thomas and the other apostles did. They learned that it’s not about physically seeing; it’s about the expansion of faith in the unseen things from above. The resulting growth and development is powerful and life-changing. It is what the gospel message is built upon. It is the good news we are to share with others. So, what are we waiting for!? Let’s remember Faithful Thomas.

So, was ‘Doubting Thomas’ really a doubter?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

## Episode 1432 — After His Resurrection, What Did Jesus Teach Us About Fishing?
Published: 2026-04-13
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/inspiration/1432-why-did-jesus-teach-the-apostles-about-fishing/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/11155251/CQ_Rewind_04-13-2026_After_His_Resurrection_What_Did_Jesus_Teach_Us_About_Fishing.pdf

After His Resurrection, What Did Jesus Teach Us About Fishing?

John 21:6: And he said to them, Cast the net on the right-hand side of the boat and you will find a catch. So they cast, and then they were not able to haul it in

because of the great number of fish.

The crucifixion of Jesus was an event that absolutely overwhelmed his apostles and disciples. Even though Jesus had forewarned them of what was coming, they were still taken by complete surprise. In his great wisdom, Jesus arranged his post resurrection appearances in such a way so as to show them not only who he was, but what was to come. It is fascinating to see how he revealed more and more about their future with each appearance. When we get to his third appearance to a group of his apostles, Jesus came to them as they were fishing. What he did and what he taught related to fishing gave them a pointed and powerful lesson regarding their future.

We are going to look at this appearance of Jesus to a group of his apostles in that 40-day period between his resurrection and his ascension.

Let’s start by reading this account:

John 21:1-3: 1 After these things Jesus manifested himself again to the disciples at the Sea of Tiberias, and he manifested himself in this way. 2 Simon Peter, and Thomas called Didymus, and Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together. 3 Simon Peter said to them, I am going fishing. They said to him, We will also come with you. They went out and got into the boat; and that night they caught nothing.

Let’s start with the first verse and break this down piece by piece:

John 21:1: After these things Jesus manifested himself again to the disciples at the Sea of Tiberias, and he manifested himself in this way.

After these things—what things? This would be Jesus’ third manifestation of his resurrected self to a large group of his disciples, likely three or four weeks after his resurrection.

Jesus first appeared in a group setting to the ten apostles when Thomas was absent (John 20:19-24). A week later, he appeared to the eleven apostles, including Thomas (John 20:26-29). We talked in Episode #1431 about why Thomas should not be labeled “Doubting Thomas,” but rather “Faithful Thomas.” Now, in

John 21:1-14, Jesus appears to seven of his apostles at the Sea of Galilee.

Galilee is a big deal in terms of the gospel. Here are three important details regarding Galilee and the ministry of Jesus:

1. The calling to follow Jesus for several of these disciples began here:

Matthew 4:18-19: 18 Now as Jesus was walking by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon who was called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea; for they were fishermen. 19 And he said to them, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.

At least five of the apostles were explicitly called at or around Galilee (Simon Peter, Andrew, James, John and Philip). Two more (Nathanael and Matthew) were likely called there.

2. The assurance of Jesus being their Messiah was given in relation to the familiarity of their homes:

Mark 14:27-28: 27 And Jesus said to them, You will all fall away, because it is written, I WILL STRIKE DOWN THE SHEPHERD, AND THE SHEEP SHALL BE SCATTERED. 28 But after I have been raised, I will go ahead of you to Galilee.

Jesus tells his disciples what will happen after his crucifixion. They would scatter from panic and confusion. But he would go ahead of them to Galilee after he had been raised. He gave them a comforting reference point to look to for direction after his crucifixion.

3. The reuniting of the apostles with their Lord after his resurrection was to be solidified in this same place. This was the message of the angel to the women at the tomb:

Mark 16:6-7: 6 And he said to them, Do not be amazed; you are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who has been crucified. He has risen; he is not here; behold, here is the place where they laid him. 7 But go, tell his disciples and Peter, He is going ahead of you to Galilee; there you will see him, just as he told you.

Galilee is an important part in the transition from who they had been with Jesus and who they were being shaped to become.

Who was there in Galilee at this time?

John 21:2: Simon Peter, and Thomas called Didymus, and Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.

- Nathanael of Cana is also known by his family name, “Bartholomew,” similar to our present-day last names.
- The sons of Zebedee were James and John, two brothers who were part of Jesus’ inner circle along with Peter.
- The two unnamed disciples are generally thought to be Andrew and Philip. They were both from Bethsaida—a fishing town right on the Sea of Galilee—and they were often found together with Peter, James and John.

Every man in that boat was one of the original apostles. So, this whole fishing scene is a gathering of apostles waiting in Galilee.

Why were these seven in Galilee?

Because Jesus himself told them to meet him there after his resurrection (Mark 14:28,

Matthew 26:32, 28:10). The angel at the tomb repeated this instruction in Mark 16:7.

They clearly informed to wait in Galilee for further instructions.

Here they are, but nothing is happening as day after day goes by:

John 21:3: Simon Peter said to them, I am going fishing. They said to him, We will also come with you. They went out and got into the boat; and that night they caught nothing.

Simon Peter said—this tells us how much leadership was, and is, always needed. We follow a voice that speaks with authority. Some time had gone by without any further direct instructions from Jesus. They needed direction!

Before the crucifixion, Jesus and the apostles were supported by the generosity of believers. But after the scandal of the cross, that support likely dried up to a great extent. With Jesus no longer physically providing direction, and with no clear instructions yet about their future work, the apostles did the practical thing—they went back to what they knew in order to provide for themselves while they waited for Jesus’ next steps.

(Source: Adam Clarke’s Commentary on the Bible) Previously to the crucifixion of our Lord, the temporal necessities of himself and his disciples appear to have been supplied by the charity of individuals: Luke 8:3. As it is probable that the scandal of the cross had now shut up this source of support, the disciples, not fully knowing [how] they were to be employed, purposed to return to their former occupation of fishing, in order to gain a livelihood; and therefore the [seven], mentioned (John 21:2), embarked on the sea of Tiberias, otherwise called the sea of Galilee.

Notice it was Peter who came up with the idea to fish. He was their leader and must have assumed they had to do something productive. But they caught nothing. Catching nothing would have been a clear reminder of just how precarious our human lives can be. They probably hadn’t gone fishing for a long time and would have remembered the unpredictability of this profession.

Following Jesus is no easy task. Jesus knew this and met these seven where they were. From there, he would show them what their new lives would be all about. Jesus was absolutely sensitive to the humanness and habits of his beloved followers and fed them the truth of their mission with their frailty in mind.

We are going to see what we’ve always seen: Jesus will do exactly what is needed at the exact time it’s needed, in the exact way that it will give the biggest, positive lesson—not only for the present, but for the future as well.

Knowing Jesus will again manifest himself to his followers tells us what’s coming: blessings, lessons and clear instructions regarding their future!

Seven men fishing all night without catching anything.

This would normally be considered a failed effort, but was it?

Defining true success and failure in our lives depends on whose perspective we are using. To the human mind, that night of fishing with no catch was a failure, but through the eyes of God and through the presence and efforts of Jesus, that night was a time of successful preparation.

Jesus was waiting for them, and now he would have their attention:

John 21:4: But when the day was now breaking, Jesus stood on the beach; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.

They have been fishing all night, catching nothing. The sun is just cracking through and beginning to shine, and now it’s daybreak. Jesus is standing on the beach, but they don’t yet recognize him. They were just fishing because they were waiting and needed something to do.

This event was similar to when Jesus first drew them to him to become fishers of men three years earlier, as described in the book of Luke. That was at the beginning of the call to follow, on the occasion of Peter’s third drawing to follow Jesus. Peter first met Jesus in John 1 and followed him more closely in Matthew 4.

Now we’re reading from Luke 5 when he was drawn in to completely follow Jesus:

Luke 5:3: And he (Jesus) got into one of the boats, which was Simon’s (Peter’s), and asked him to put out a little way from the land. And he sat down and began teaching the people from the boat.

Jesus is in the boat with Simon Peter, teaching the crowd on the shore.

But after his resurrection, the fishing experience in the book of John was at the beginning of the call to preach and lead.

In this instance, they would recognize him not by his voice or personal appearance but by his miraculous actions:

John 21:5: So Jesus said to them, Children, you do not have any fish, do you? They answered him, No.

These seven apostles are discouraged, have no direction and are unsure of their future. They are even failing at what they know best how to do—fishing.

Jesus calls them children, which functions as a warm familiar address. It’s a term of affection, connection and protection, like saying, “My boys,” or “Dear ones.”

Years later, John uses the word again:

1 John 2:18: Children, it is the last hour; and just as you heard that antichrist is coming, even now many antichrists have appeared; from this we know that it is the last hour.

In the John fishing account after his resurrection, Jesus calls those seven apostles children. John—one of those seven and writing many years later—uses the same term to say, “We’re coming to a transition, children—those I have affection for, who I’m connected to and want to protect—be aware!”

John was preparing his fellow disciples for changes that were coming, just as Jesus had prepared him and his fellow apostles for changes. John remembered how Jesus addressed them.

Jesus begins with this simple, practical question, “Do you have any fish?” It might sound like he’s asking about food or their night’s work, but he’s really drawing their attention to the emptiness of their efforts. It’s his gentle way of asking, “How are your labors going without me?” This sets the stage for the lesson that follows.

Sometimes we go through seasons of spiritual drought, and we don’t feel as close to the Lord as we did. We go back to our normal way of doing things. Maybe we fall back into some old habits, but they don’t feel as fulfilling as they once were. What is our purpose and direction? We shouldn’t be just floating around looking for fish!

John 21:6: And he said to them, Cast the net on the right-hand side of the boat and you will find a catch…

(Source: Bible Commentary from David Guzik) Jesus made a strange suggestion to his disciples. There was no logical reason why fishing in the morning light would be better than fishing at night. There was no reason why fishing on one side of the boat would be better than the other side. It wasn’t even directly a test of trust in Jesus, because they did not know it was him until the fish were caught.

The stranger called from the shore, Cast the net on the right-hand side of the boat and you will find a catch. This was direct guidance that if followed, would produce success and provide the lesson.

Why the right side?

1. It was obviously a completely different and perhaps a less natural approach. (In the

Luke fishing experience, we will soon see they were given the reasonable direction to move out to deep water.) It must have been the side opposite to what they had been doing before—“Cast it on the side you’re not used to.” It was different and caught their attention.

2. Spiritually, the right side was the side of power and authority that Jesus himself

would occupy.

Matthew 26:63-64: 63 …And the high priest said to him, I adjure you by the living God, that you tell us whether you are the Christ, the son of God. 64 Jesus said to him, You have said it yourself; nevertheless I tell you, hereafter you will see THE SON OF MAN SITTING AT THE RIGHT HAND OF POWER…

It seems that in referencing the right, Jesus is showing he is wielding God’s power to draw his followers to the work required ahead.

What did they do?

John 21:6: …so they cast…

It doesn’t say that they deliberated and thought about it. They did it! They listened and immediately obeyed. They didn’t yet know it, but Jesus was showing them a NEW, dramatic and miraculous beginning.

He was using the beginning of the call to follow to teach them about the beginning of the call to preach and lead.

Back to the account of fishing three years earlier when Jesus was in the boat with Simon Peter:

Luke 5:4-5: 4 When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, Put out into the deep water and let down your nets for a catch. 5 Simon answered and said, Master, we worked hard all night and caught nothing, but I will do as you say and let down the nets.

There is a little reluctance, but he did it. Simon was in a position of a humble student here listening to the Master teaching, even though he was the fisherman and knew there weren’t any fish that day! Still, he did what did not seem logical.

What a precursor to what would happen after Jesus’ resurrection!

There are a lot of similarities, but a lot of differences too. Jesus is in the boat in the early account, but not in the latter. They go out to deep sea in the earlier account. In the later account, they are close enough to shore to hear Jesus call instructions to Cast your net.

Putting the two accounts together, we recognize:

The Luke account details the call to follow Jesus. Walk with him and learn from him.

Three years later, in the John account after Jesus’ resurrection, is the call to preach and lead, as Jesus will soon leave them to ascend to the Father.

Jesus used similar fishing experiences for these different objectives.

Learning to truly follow Jesus is accomplished not only by listening, but also by retaining and internalizing what we have heard. Then we need to practically and faithfully apply it all to our lives. These two fishing expeditions were there to teach his disciples how to follow so they could eventually lead!

The similarities and differences between these two experiences should make us pause and consider what Jesus is teaching us, just as he taught his apostles.

This post-resurrection appearance of Jesus seems to have a deep and deliberate

set of lessons for us. Where does it go from here?

The next level of this lesson clearly focused on Peter. Jesus knew that at this very fragile time for his followers, they would need strong leadership, as he would no longer be walking alongside of them as a man. Peter was the beginning of that leadership. He would need to see, comprehend and embrace all that Jesus was showing him, even if it was uncomfortable. He needed to grab hold of these things, and Jesus was there to teach him how.

We are putting the two fishing miracles side by side—one at the beginning of Peter’s journey following Jesus (Luke 5) and one at the end of Jesus’ life, but the beginning of Peter’s ministry (John 21). The back-and-forth will show us how Jesus uses the same kind of moment to shape Peter at two very different stages of his life.

Back to the beginning of the call to follow and the great catch of fish with Jesus in the boat:

Luke 5:6: When they had done this, they enclosed a great quantity of fish, and their nets began to break.

Jesus is in the boat with Peter. Their obedience produced an immense catch. They listened and obeyed with reservations, but the catch was not complete, as the nets broke. The work of being fishers of men would have to continue at a later time.

Traditionally, Christians have thought the breaking of the nets signified the weight of their calling—the work was bigger than they were ready to carry. But remember in both

Matthew 4:19 and Mark 1:17, Jesus said, I will make you fishers of men. So, if the fish represent people, perhaps the nets breaking represents some of the “fish” that got away, namely, the Jewish people who rejected Jesus at that time.

Remember, in the earlier Luke account, Jesus was with them in the boat. Perhaps this represents Jesus’ earthly ministry while he was physically with them. There was great success, even though it ended with his crucifixion and there were “broken nets.” In the later John account, Jesus was on the shore. Perhaps this represents Jesus, now a divine spirit being, guiding them from heaven.

Back to the beginning of the call to preach and lead, and the great catch with Jesus on shore:

John 21:6: …So they cast, and then they were not able to haul it in because of the great number of fish.

What a dramatic reminder this must have been. It would have brought them right back to their beginnings with Jesus! Their obedience gave them such success that the catch was too heavy to hoist on board. They had to drag the nets to the shore through the water.

Even though they hadn’t yet recognized the stranger on shore, they had to realize something unusual was happening as they tried to haul in this great number of fish.

Back to the earlier account:

Luke 5:8-9: 8 But when Simon Peter saw that, he fell down at Jesus' feet, saying, Go away from me Lord, for I am a sinful man! 9 For amazement had seized him and all his companions because of the catch of fish which they had taken.

Peter is awed by the miracle and pulls back, telling Jesus to go away because he feels too sinful. Peter was humbled as he recognized the greatness of the Lord Jesus. He knew his own character. At this point, he could not even see himself following the Lord!

Again, he had great humility but with great energy. This is one of the things that drew Jesus to call him. What a precursor, again, to what was coming! He will go from “following, but not really” to “really following”!

Back to leading:

John 21:7: Therefore that disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, It is the Lord…

At this point, the Apostle John was more tuned into the resurrection and how Jesus was working than the others. They would soon learn!

John really understood. When he and Peter ran to the tomb on the day of Jesus’ resurrection, for instance, the account says John looked in and believed. Here he was the first one to recognize the man on the shore as Jesus. John knew this miracle could not have happened without Jesus. He knew it had to be Jesus on the shore, even though he couldn’t see him clearly.

John 21:7: …So when Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put his outer garment on… and threw himself into the sea.

In the book of Luke, when Jesus called him to follow, Peter responded by saying he was a sinner and unworthy. But here in the book of John, the moment Peter realized it was the Lord, he was completely all in—nothing could hold him back. He threw himself into the water to get to Jesus as fast as he could. He couldn’t wait to be face to face with Jesus again. He needed to see him NOW.

In these two experiences, we can see Peter’s spiritual and intellectual growth.

There was the call to follow while Jesus was walking the earth with them. But now there was the call to preach and lead because Jesus was returning to heaven to be with the Father. He needed Peter to lead, and Peter met that challenge by literally jumping into the water.

We also note the difference between John and Peter. John first recognized the stranger as Jesus. Peter, once told, immediately responds. These two work together to get the job done. John and Peter both contributed in different ways.

This is a tremendous lesson regarding the power of the diversity of the body of Christ:

1 Corinthians 12:14-18: 14 For the body is not one member, but many. 15 If the foot says, Because I am not a hand, I am not a part of the body, it is not for this reason any the less a part of the body. 16 And if the ear says, Because I am not an eye, I am not a part of the body, it is not for this reason any the less a part of the body. 17 If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the sense of smell be? 18 But now God has placed the members, each one of them, in the body, just as He desired.

In the body of Christ, different “parts” serve different functions, yet each are needed as part of the same body, complimenting and supplementing each other. That’s the lesson we are seeing—John said it, Peter did it, and together they got to the Lord with the fish.

Let’s go back three years earlier:

Luke 5:7: So they signaled to their partners in the other boat for them to come and help them. And they came and filled both of the boats, so that they began to sink.

There were so many fish that the boats began to sink! What a magnificent catch! Remember, they caught nothing the night before, but then Peter grudgingly went out and did what Jesus said.

Both boats are filled while still on the restless waters of the sea. Jesus is still with them. Again, perhaps we are seeing a picture of Jesus being present with them in his earthly ministry, surrounded by the “restless waters” of humanity.

Jesus drew crowds wherever he went—while teaching, performing miracles, debating the Pharisees. Their gospel work was just beginning as they together brought their “catch” to shore. Jesus was still with them in that experience. They were being called to follow. Jesus said, “Watch what I do, hear what I say, and understand that it all comes from my Father.” He is modeling for them what they will need to be.

After his resurrection, Jesus is saying, “You’ve seen me work. Now I need you to take my place and be the leaders and teachers who preach the gospel.”

Let’s go back to the after-resurrection fishing experience:

John 21:8: But the other disciples came in the little boat, for they were not far from the land, but about one hundred yards away, dragging the net full of fish.

The nets were heavy, and they were in a small boat with only six workers now. They had to drag the nets behind the boat until they could jump out and hoist them up onto the shore to Jesus who was waiting. They now all knew it was Jesus. We can imagine their excitement!

Perhaps this is a picture of the drawing out of the called-out ones throughout the age of the gospel. They were out in the “restless seas of humanity,” finding those specific called-out ones, bringing them throughout the age to Jesus "on shore,” who was no longer with them. He was waiting on the “solid ground of the heavenly calling” as their Lord! This might represent the true gospel church working together through the last 2,000 years.

The apostles needed to bring the fish to Jesus on stable land, who was waiting for their finished work.

For the apostles, following Jesus began by literally following him around daily. In the long run, this three-year opportunity was there to entrench them into a new way of thinking. With that experience behind them, Jesus would now show them that their following would now come at a distance. Now they would need to take the responsibility of being “fishers of men” upon their own shoulders.

In that second fishing experience, Jesus wasn’t with them; he’s waiting for them. In the first experience, he was with them. Now they are responsible themselves for getting the fish to shore. Jesus is just waiting for the results. It’s the lesson in learning how to lead.

There is a brilliance in Jesus’ teachings and methods that we need to observe with very sober and reverent hearts.

How do these two dramatic fishing accounts end? What were the deepest preaching

and leading lessons that Jesus wanted them to learn?

It’s important that we take a step back to see the big picture here. Jesus was selectively appearing to his followers after his resurrection to prepare them for life without his physical presence. Everything he did in that 40-day period was to spur on that preparation because the changes were monumental. They would become the leaders of the call to follow Christ. They had to step up in a way they never had to step up before.

We can’t overstate how important this was: these followers were becoming the leaders who would establish the entire Christian church after Jesus died. Everything depended on their growth from followers to leaders.

Back to the beginning of the call to follow.

Jesus next reveals the reason for this miracle of these fish to them:

Luke 5:10-11: 10 and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon, Do not fear, from now on you will be catching men. 11 When they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him.

In this second drawing of Peter to Jesus (we read this in the first segment), it said, Follow me and I will make you fishers of men. He had already told them that. Here he tells them the same thing again after this catch of fish. He is reminding Peter of what he has already heard.

Jesus is brilliant at reminding us of the seeds he has already planted. In this experience, he shows them, “Just stay with me. You made it through this incredible experience. I am with you. Follow me. Don’t fear; don’t be afraid. You will be fishers of men.”

They finally DID leave everything. They left their boats and their fishing gear behind and finally, fully and without reservation, followed him.

The call to preach and lead began with these seven apostles. Jesus presents them with a breakfast after fishing and dragging the catch to him on land.

He shows them an end result he had never shown them before:

John 21:9: So when they got out on the land, they saw a charcoal fire already laid and fish placed on it, and bread.

Notice Jesus already had some fish on the fire. Perhaps these fish represent the apostles and disciples who had followed Jesus during his ministry here on earth—the beginnings and leaders of the embryonic church. Jesus is painting a picture of the gospel age work with the fish he acquired during his earthly ministry. These first fish are followed by the massive catch the apostles drag to shore, representing the Christians who follow Christ throughout the age.

Their destination was this solid ground on which Jesus’ power and presence resided. We understand this to show us the heavenly call to the “solid ground” of being with the Lord.

Remember in John 14:3, before the crucifixion, Jesus said, If I go to prepare a place for you, I will come again and receive you to myself. Look what is happening. He is showing them how he’s bringing them to himself along with all these additional fish, these called-out ones.

They are called out of the sea, symbolically a picture of restless humanity. The “fish” are called from all walks of life from our restless human experience to this solid ground of the heavenly call.

Let’s continue in this post-resurrection experience with Jesus on solid ground:

John 21:10: Jesus said to them, Bring some of the fish which you have now caught.

Jesus is now presenting them with the responsibility of being accountable for accurately representing what he had taught them. Jesus showed them the way, and they would follow by preaching and leading others to him throughout the age of the gospel. By doing what Jesus told them to do, they would be accountable to him while they preached without him being present. He puts the responsibility of being accountable for what they say and do on their shoulders.

John 21:11: Simon Peter went up and drew the net to land, full of large fish, a hundred and fifty-three…

Peter led the way, but the pulling in of the fish is teamwork. They are working together. Peter was called on to be accountable first. The beautiful result of Jesus’ preaching would play out in the apostles and disciples bringing all these fish to the Lord. Imagine the weight of the net straining in their hands—heavy, full, almost bursting—yet not a single fish is lost.

Jesus prayed for God’s overruling in their preaching and leading work the night before his crucifixion. It is a touching and moving reference for all of us:

John 17:17-21: 17 Sanctify them in the truth; Your word is truth. 18 As You sent me into the world, I also have sent them into the world. 19 For their sakes I sanctify myself, that they themselves also may be sanctified in truth. 20 I do not ask on behalf of these alone, but for those also who believe in me through their word; 21 that they may all be one; even as You, Father, are in me and I in You, that they also may be in Us, so that the world may believe that You sent me.

Jesus prayed for the work of the gospel to continue after he ascends back to his Father, and in this fishing experience after his resurrection, he is demonstrating this work. He is putting the pieces in place so they can truly understand. It is a beautiful lesson of the importance of the apostles taking the responsibility to stand up for godliness and righteousness in preaching the gospel.

But why specifically 153 fish? Early church writers taught that ancient naturalists believed there were 153 species of fish in the world, so maybe the catch symbolized the gospel reaching and drawing all kinds of people. Through the centuries, people have played with “fish math” to show it is a triangular number, or where it shows up in nature or other places, but we really don’t know what this specific number represents.

Perhaps 153 shows the precision and care with which God’s call will be successful:

Matthew 10:29-31: 29 Are not two sparrows sold for a cent? And yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. 30 But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. 31 So do not fear; you are more valuable than many sparrows.

The message of these simple verses is that the very hairs of our head are numbered if we are one of those called to follow the Lord. Every part of our lives, every part of our experience is overseen by His heavenly providence. So 153 fish may be indicating there is an exact care of those who are drawn.

John 21:11: …and although there were so many, the net was not torn.

All these fish were hauled to the shore to be accountable before Jesus, and yet the net did not break. That’s significant. All the fish were there that were supposed to be there. Not one would be lost. Jesus, as a spirit being, as their Lord, was showing the care and surety with which the call of the true church would be completed by the power of God’s spirit working in them.

Jesus gave the word—cast the net on the right-hand side, on the side of power—and they did. They had the catch, and they recognized the Lord. They brought it to him. They listened to and followed through with all he had said. While the catch was heavy, this time the net wasn’t even torn.

When God calls, nothing can stand in the way of the answer to that call unless we ourselves decide we don’t want to be a part of it. Then we are not one of the fish that is caught in the net. It’s that simple.

Jesus, as a spirit being, as their Lord, was showing the care and surety with which the call of the true church would be completed, by the power of God’s spirit working in them.

John 21:12-13: 12 Jesus said to them, Come and have breakfast. None of the disciples ventured to question him, Who are you? Knowing that it was the Lord. 13 Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and the fish likewise.

He has prepared a meal for them. He welcomes them after their night of fishing with no catch to having this marvelous catch after they follow his instruction. This shows the age of the gospel message going out, with its call to come to Christ. The apostles, first through their ministry in person, then through their writings, brought all those faithful followers, those precious fish, to him, without losing a single one.

Jesus eating with the apostles here reminds us of two other post-resurrection appearances:

- Luke 24:13-35: On the road to Emmaus, Jesus was ready to dine with the two followers but then vanished. -

Luke 24:36-43: When he appeared to the ten apostles to prove who he was, he ate broiled fish and bread with them.

This also reminds us of the message to the Church of Laodicea, the seventh and last stage of the gospel call. In Revelation chapters 1–3, Jesus gives John messages for seven real churches in what is now Turkey. Each message fits the history and struggles of that specific church. But these seven also carry a prophetic meaning, outlining seven successive periods of the Christian church down through the last 2,000 years of the gospel message going out. The story begins at Pentecost with Ephesus and ends with our time, pictured by Laodicea. Each time frame receives a message tailored to the followers living in that moment.

The message to Laodicea:

Revelation 3:20-22: 20 Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and will dine with him, and he with me. 21 He who overcomes, I will grant to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on His throne. 22 He who has an ear, let him hear what the spirit says to the churches.

Those seven churches represent seven stages of the gospel church from the time of the apostles right up to where we are right now. In this last and final stage, Jesus says, Behold, I stand at the door and knock. When somebody is standing at the door and knocking, what does that mean? It means they are there. They have arrived. So, Jesus is calling those to come in and eat with him, to celebrate, to be with him, to fellowship together.

When we look at this experience of this post-resurrection fishing expedition and all the things that happened, we can see the beauty of Jesus showing the apostles, This is what you need in order to lead. This is how you need to preach, so you will gain such results.

“Follow to lead” was the resounding message to Jesus’ followers, not only in this fishing experience after his resurrection, but it was the resounding message in ALL of his appearances after his resurrection. For us, the lesson is simple. Learn to follow Jesus daily, carefully and prayerfully because we also are engaged in the being “fishers of men” now, so that by God’s grace we can be “blessers of men” later!

We need to learn to follow before we can learn to lead. The only way we can learn to lead, and therefore be fishers, is from the example of the apostles and those that followed them in this age of the gospel.

In this episode, we’ve looked at these two events: the earlier experience of Peter fishing in the boat with Jesus, learning to follow him very specifically, and then the fishing experience after Jesus’ resurrection where Jesus turned over the responsibility of preaching and leading in his physical absence.

That was the apostles’ responsibility, and now it is ours.

So, after his resurrection, what did Jesus teach about fishing?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

The two fishing accounts this episode compared:

Luke 5:1-11: 1 Now it happened that while the crowd was pressing around him and listening to the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret; 2 and he saw two boats lying at the edge of the lake; but the fishermen had gotten out of them and were washing their nets. 3 And he got into one of the boats, which was Simon's, and asked him to put out a little way from the land. And he sat down and began teaching the people from the boat. 4 When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, Put out into the deep water and let down your nets for a catch. 5 Simon answered and said, Master, we worked hard all night and caught nothing, but I will do as you say and let down the nets. 6 When they had done this, they enclosed a great quantity of fish, and their nets began to break; 7 so they signaled to their partners in the other boat for them to come and help them. And they came and filled both of the boats, so that they began to sink. 8 But when Simon Peter saw that, he fell down at Jesus' feet, saying, Go away from me Lord, for I am a sinful man! 9 For amazement had seized him and all his companions because of the catch of fish which they had taken; 10 and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon, Do not fear, from now on you will be catching men. 11 When they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him.

John 21:1-13: 1 After these things Jesus manifested himself again to the disciples at the Sea of Tiberias, and he manifested himself in this way. 2 Simon Peter, and Thomas called Didymus,

and Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together. 3 Simon Peter said to them, I am going fishing. They said to him, We will also come with you. They went out and got into the boat; and that night they caught nothing. 4 But when the day was now breaking, Jesus stood on the beach; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus. 5 So Jesus said to them, Children, you do not have any fish, do you? They answered him, No. 6 And he said to them, Cast the net on the right-hand side of the boat and you will find a catch.
