## Episode 1435 — Are Christians Today Really Capable of Healing People and Speaking in Tongues? (Part II)
Published: 2026-05-04
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1435-are-christians-today-really-capable-of-healing-people-and-speaking-in-tongues-part-ii/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/01123916/CQ_Rewind_05-04-2026_Are_Christians_Today_Really_Capable_of_Healing_People_Or_Speaking_in_Tongues_Part_II.pdf

Are Christians Today Really Capable of Healing People

or Speaking in Tongues? (Part II)

1 Corinthians 12:28: And God has appointed in the church, first apostles,

second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healings,

helps, administrations, various kinds of tongues.

Are Christians who claim to heal and who claim to speak in tongues operating within the scriptural guidelines of Christianity today, or have they taken a giant step over the line of appropriate Christian behavior? In our last episode, we observed how the Old Testament established healing as an occasional gift and was not necessarily granted based on faith. We also observed that Jesus healed the masses and generally did not require faith and following to give that gift. We also saw that Old Testament speaking in tongues was absolutely speaking in foreign languages. It was a sign of God’s disapproval when foreign languages were introduced. The Apostle Paul verified that speaking in tongues (in foreign languages) was STILL a sign, but now it was a sign of approval to UNBELIEVERS.

In this episode, we examine healing and speaking in tongues in the New Testament to understand how these gifts functioned in the early church.

FACT #1: FAITH WAS RARELY A REQUIREMENT FOR NEW TESTAMENT HEALING.

Jesus healed out of compassion. Notice there were masses of people healed in these two examples:

Matthew 4:23–24: 23 Jesus was going throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every kind of disease and every kind of sickness among the people. 24 …and they brought to him all who were ill, those suffering with various diseases and pains, demoniacs, epileptics, paralytics; and he healed them.

Matthew 8:16–17: 16 …they brought to him many who were demon-possessed; and he cast out the spirits with a word, and healed all who were ill. 17 This was to fulfill what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet: HE HIMSELF TOOK OUR INFIRMITIES AND CARRIED AWAY OUR DISEASES.

These are just two of the many times Jesus healed numerous people. We have no idea of the actual number healed—hundreds if not thousands! We chose just two incidents in the book of Matthew.

Jesus’ healing work was a sign of fulfilled prophecy. It was a sign that the call to the kingdom was right before all the people who came to Jesus for healing. It was part of the proof that Jesus was the promised Messiah and that his kingdom message was authentic.

What were the Pharisees thinking? They knew the prophecies. These healings were a sign of prophetic fulfillment, and what did they do? They argued with it. They denied it. They didn’t want it to be true. They stuck with their preconceived agenda.

There ARE rare occasions when faith was mentioned as part of healing by Jesus:

Matthew 9:20-22—The woman with the 12-year blood hemorrhage.

Matthew 15:22,28—The Canaanite woman’s faith on behalf of her daughter.

Mark 10:46,52—Bartimaeus pleading for Jesus to heal his blindness.

Luke 17:11,15-19—One of the ten lepers. Nine were healed but only one’s healing was credited to his faith.

Out of the hundreds of people (or more!) Jesus healed, only four were recognized as having faith.

The faith displayed in these examples shows that some would be drawn higher than just receiving a gift of healing. This echoes the gospel call to truly follow Jesus rather than just appreciate him. Lots of people appreciate him. Back then, there were people who followed only for the food and miracles. But Jesus was looking for those who would follow him. There was a difference between the two groups.

Fact #1 Conclusion Jesus primarily healed out of compassion for the sickness and brokenness of the human race as a sign of fulfilled prophecy—nothing more than that.

FACT #2. DURING JESUS’ EARTHLY MINISTRY, THE ONLY GOD-SANCTIONED HEALING RECORDED WAS BY JESUS AND BY THOSE WHOM HE SENT OUT WITH SPECIFIC COMMANDS. THERE ARE ONLY TWO INSTANCES OF JESUS SENDING ANYONE TO HEAL IN THE THREE-AND-A-HALF-YEARS OF HIS MINISTRY.

First, Jesus sent out the 12 Apostles to heal:

Matthew 10:1: Jesus summoned his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every kind of disease and every kind of sickness.

Matthew 10:5–8: 5 These twelve Jesus sent out after instructing them: Do not go in the way of the Gentiles… 6 but rather go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. 7 And as you go, preach, saying, The kingdom of heaven is at hand. 8 Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons. Freely you received, freely give.

Healing was a sign that their Messiah had come! The kingdom is at hand was the very message the apostles were sent to proclaim.

Again, what were the Pharisees thinking? They knew the prophecies. Now they were seeing this healing from others and not just Jesus. They were helpless and hopeless to battle it because they couldn’t change the results and make the people sick again.

Healing was used as the attention-getter for the message: The kingdom of heaven is at hand.

Second, he sent out the 70 disciples to heal:

Luke 10:1: Now after this the Lord appointed seventy others, and sent them in pairs ahead of him to every city and place where he himself was going to come.

Luke 10:8–9: 8 Whatever city you enter and they receive you, eat what is set before you; 9 and heal those in it who are sick, and say to them, The kingdom of God has come near to you.

Healing was a sign that their Messiah was coming.

What were the Pharisees thinking? They knew the prophecies. Now there are 70 out there performing miracles! The 70 disciples came back, amazed that the experience was so remarkable—not just the healing, but the message: The kingdom of God has come near to you.

Fact #2 Conclusion On both occasions, Jesus essentially told them to draw the peoples’ attention by healing, but their mission was to proclaim the fulfillment of prophecy that the kingdom of God has come near to them.

FACT #3. AFTER PENTECOST, THE ONLY RECORDED HEALING EVENTS BY ANYONE OTHER THAN AN APOSTLE WERE DONE BY ONLY TWO INDIVIDUALS, PHILIP AND ANANIAS.

First, Philip witnessed in Samaria.

His healing was done out of compassion in the context of Saul of Tarsus hunting down Christians which caused them to scatter:

Acts 8:6–7: 6 The crowds… were giving attention to what was said by Philip, as they heard and saw the signs which he was performing. 7 For… many who had unclean spirits, they were coming out of them shouting with a loud voice; and many who had been paralyzed and lame were healed.

Philip went to Samara because Saul’s persecution forced him out, not because of a planned mission trip. These healings were not random, were not done in peaceful conditions, or done to impress those who already believed. The miracles validated the message of the kingdom when the church was under attack and were God’s stamp of authenticity of Philip’s preaching.

What was the result?

Acts 8:12: But when they believed Philip preaching the good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were being baptized, men and women alike.

These healings were a sign to the unbelievers, drawing their attention to a message unlike anything they had heard before.

Philip is the only one recorded in the New Testament to perform a public, multi-person healing event, aside from the apostles themselves.

Second, Ananias healed the scales from the eyes of Saul of Tarsus that God

had put there:

Acts 9:17–18: 17 So Ananias… after laying his hands on him said, Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus… has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the holy spirit. 18 And immediately there fell from his eyes something like scales, and he regained his sight, and he got up and was baptized.

In this case, Ananias received a direct command from Jesus in a vision to heal Saul for the purpose of selecting Saul (Paul) as the twelfth apostle to replace Judas.

Fact #3 Conclusion These only-recorded healing events other than by the apostles were very narrow and specific. Of the two, only Philip healed groups of people. While other healing events did occur in the New Testament, we are not given those details. Healing is not highlighted as a strong priority in our Christian walk.

FACT #4. HEALING OTHERS WAS NOT ONE OF THE “GREATER GIFTS” THE EARLY CHURCH WAS GIVEN, AND EVEN AS A LESSER GIFT, IT WOULD END.

1 Corinthians 12:27–28,31: 27 Now you are Christ’s body, and individually members of it. 28 And God has appointed in the church, first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, (now we begin the lesser gifts) then miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, administrations, various kinds of tongues. 31 But earnestly desire the greater gifts. And I show you a still more excellent way.

We will look at what the more excellent way is shortly.

The Apostle Paul gives the structure of the body of Christ—how it is formulated: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles. Following that are gifts of healings, helps, administrations, and various kinds of tongues. After listing all these things, Paul says, And I show you a still more excellent way. He is telling us that we have these opportunities, but there is something much bigger, more important, more life-changing and transformational to come.

Paul explicitly ranks the gifts, placing healing after the foundational teaching roles and after miracles, and then instructs believers to desire the greater gifts—which healing is not part of.

Finally, the following scriptures are often used to say healing commonly took place in the New Testament, but they are NOT about the healing of physical illness:

James 5:13–15: 13 Is anyone among you suffering <2553>? Then he must pray. Is anyone cheerful? He is to sing praises. 14 Is anyone among you sick <770>? Then he must call for the elders of the church and they are to pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; 15 and the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick <2577>, and the Lord will raise him up, and if he has committed sins, they will be forgiven him.

Defining suffering and sick shows that this is not physical illness but spiritual illness.

Is anyone among you suffering?

Suffering: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2553 kakopathéō; to undergo hardship

Is anyone among you sick?

Sick: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #770 asthenéō; to be feeble (in any sense)

The one who is sick:

Sick: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2577 kámnō; properly, to toil, i.e. (by implication) to tire (figuratively, faint, sicken)

When we read those verses, the word for suffering and the two words for sick refer to the hardships of life. They are about being broken and discouraged, not about physical illness. See Bonus Material for more on this point.

Fact #4 Conclusion Healing was not one of the greater gifts. We saw the apostles perform all kinds of healings, but they were the apostles! Outside the apostles, we see only Philip and Ananias. We get the sense that healing was not something to focus on.

The Power, Purpose and Application of Biblical Healing

New Testament healing was a sign that Jesus had come and the call to follow him was open. According to Scripture, healing did not at all dominate the early church’s activities. Once the gospel was established, healing would no longer be a needed sign of discipleship, as the written word of God would continue accomplishing the work.

This makes sense because as footstep followers, we are to walk by faith, not by sight.

Healing was done in the context of an example for unbelievers—it was not what is currently called “faith healing,” which is not scriptural.

Yes, there were a few instances in which faith was a deciding factor in someone being healed, but for the vast majority of those healed, it was a gift from God to preview the kingdom for them.

FACT #1. THE ONE PURPOSE FOR THE GIFT OF TONGUES WAS TO BE A SIGN AND WITNESS OF THE GOSPEL TO FOREIGNERS.

FACT #2. THERE ARE ONLY THREE RECORDED INSTANCES OF SPEAKING IN TONGUES IN THE NEW TESTAMENT.

We will look at these two facts together.

The first instance of speaking in tongues was on the Day of Pentecost. This set the

pattern for its sole purpose—the ability to communicate the good news of the gospel to people of other languages and cultures.

The second instance of speaking in tongues was the conversion of the Gentile

Cornelius to Christianity.

This happened while Peter was preaching about his vision of unclean animals and God’s call being opened to Gentiles:

Acts 10:44–47: 44 While Peter was still speaking these words, the holy spirit fell upon all those who were listening to the message. 45 All the circumcised believers who came with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the holy spirit had been poured out on the Gentiles also. 46 For they were hearing them speaking with tongues and exalting God. Then Peter answered, 47 Surely no one can refuse the water for these to be baptized who have received the holy spirit just as we did, can he?

This was a dramatic miracle! These were the first Gentile converts. This breaks all the pre- set expectations. Once Peter sees this happen, he embraces what he would have rejected earlier. He needed to see this vision of unclean animals in order to shift his perspective.

Observations:

- These Gentiles were likely speaking Hebrew, a language they would have had no use for. Why? Because it says they were exalting God, so those listening would have heard the exaltation of God.
- The description of these events were similar to the Pentecost event. During Pentecost, the hearers heard the disciples speaking in tongues and praising God. In this account, we also have the believers praising God in a foreign language.
- This was positive proof for Peter and the other Jewish Christians who were with him that Gentile and Jewish Christians were equal. This was a paradigm shift for them.
- These followers were now suddenly able to speak the gospel in the languages of the nations around them. It opened a completely new door—reaching people who had never been invited before.

Peter was given the “keys” to unlock the door of the gospel to the Gentiles.

It is a beautiful picture of how the sign of tongues in the Old Testament—which was a sign of God’s disapproval—became, in the New Testament, a sign of God’s approval and the expansion of the gospel. The point of the miracle was to go spread the word!

The third instance of speaking in tongues was when Paul arrived in Ephesus.

He found disciples who were not fully informed and had been baptized with John’s baptism, which was a baptism for the repentance of sins, not a baptism of sacrifice.

Paul witnessed to them about Jesus and baptized them again—this time into Jesus, a baptism of sacrifice:

Acts 19:6–7: 6 And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the holy spirit came on them, and they began speaking with tongues and prophesying. 7 There were in all about twelve men.

(Source: Bible Commentary by J. Vernon McGee) There were many languages spoken there, just as there had been in Jerusalem on the Day of Pentecost. East and West met all along that coast. It was a great city of that day.

Speaking in tongues equipped them to witness.

Modern speaking in tongues is the vocalizing of spontaneous, non-linguistic syllables within gatherings of believers or in private prayer, functioning as a devotional expression rather than the New Testament purpose of communicating the gospel to unbelieving foreigners in their own languages.

Changing the purpose of tongues from a public sign for unbelievers to a private spiritual experience for believers is not scriptural.

So, what do all three of these events (tongues at Pentecost, Cornelius and Ephesus) have in common?

Apostolic preaching Spirit-begotten followers An audience anxious to learn

The one purpose for the gift of tongues was to be a sign and witness of the gospel to foreigners. It was only used a few times.

FACT #3. THIS GIFT OF SPEAKING IN TONGUES WAS SOMETIMES MISUSED, AND IT NEEDED TO BE KEPT IN ITS PROPER SPIRITUAL PERSPECTIVE.

We must apply these precedents to all uses of the gift of tongues.

Paul clearly lays out a scriptural basis to help with our understanding of the appropriate use of this gift:

1 Corinthians 12:28–31: 28 And God has appointed in the church, first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, administrations, various kinds of tongues. 29 All are not apostles, are they? All are not prophets, are they? All are not teachers, are they? All are not workers of miracles, are they? 30 All do not have gifts of healings, do they? All do not speak with tongues, do they? All do not interpret, do they? 31 But earnestly desire the greater gifts. And I show you a still more excellent way.

Paul is laying out the importance of how the church is supposed to work:

1. There is a divide between the “greater” and “lesser” gifts. (For example, in

addition to 1 Corinthians 12:27–28,31 we looked at earlier, 1 Corinthians 14:3-5 highlights prophecy as one of the greater gifts; tongues as one of the lesser.)

2. The path of spiritual gifts is shown to be a lesser path. While they were

miraculous, Paul is laying out the difference and warning the church to keep its priorities straight. A more excellent way exists than these gifts.

3. Paul is teaching by giving his personal experience—I show you a still more

excellent way. In other words, he had experience with this and was sharing it with them.

Paul continues with this more excellent way:

1 Corinthians 13:1–3: 1 If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have love, I have become a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal.

The tongues of men and of angels—what is he talking about? It is likely something

he heard in a vision years before (2 Corinthians 12). He was transported in his

mind to the future and heard and saw things he was not allowed to repeat. So, drawing on this incredible experience, he says, Even if I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, if I am not doing it appropriately, I am just making noise.

2 If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. 3 And if I give all my possessions to feed the poor, and if I surrender my body to be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing.

Love is the more excellent way, specifically agape—that selfless, benevolent, giving love. The miraculous gifts of the spirit were great, but they did not necessarily help one grow spiritually.

Paul goes on to explain the challenges of the misuse of the gift of tongues:

1 Corinthians 14:1–4: 1 Pursue love, yet desire earnestly spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy. 2 For one who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men but to God; for no one understands, but in his spirit he speaks mysteries (it’s valueless—there’s no benefit). 3 But one who prophesies (teaches) speaks to men for edification and exhortation and consolation. 4 One who speaks in a tongue edifies himself; but one who prophesies edifies the church.

We can clearly see the contrast between the greater and lesser gifts. Speaking in tongues is a lesser gift because it does not edify all listeners—only the one who understands that language. Without an interpreter, it is just noise!

1 Corinthians 14:17-19: 17 For you are giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not edified. 18 I thank God, I speak in tongues more than you all; 19 however, in the church I desire to speak five words with my mind so that I may instruct others also, rather than ten thousand words in a tongue.

In other words, be committed to that which is spiritual, not that which might look or feel cool! The apostle was very specific about the appropriate and inappropriate uses of the gifts—and he called out the inappropriate uses.

Fact #4. THIS GIFT HAD A CLEAR PURPOSE. ONCE FULFILLED, THE GIFT WOULD END.

Tongues HAD a place in the early church, but its use ended. How do we know? Because the Apostle Paul told us:

1 Corinthians 13:8–11: 8 Love never fails; but if there are gifts of prophecy, they will be done away; if there are tongues, they will cease; if there is knowledge, it will be done away. 9 For we know in part and we prophesy in part; 10 but when the perfect comes, the partial will be done away. 11 When I was a child, I used to speak like a child, think like a child, reason like a child; when I became a man, I did away with childish things.

Did away with childish things—in other words, grow up! The gifts of the spirit served a purpose, but as a tool to get the gospel message started. When the gifts are abused, they no longer serve a godly purpose.

Paul also warns that these gifts of the spirit are going to cease. Even the gift of knowledge (miraculously receiving knowledge without study) will cease when [that which is] the perfect comes.

Perfect: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5046 téleios; complete

We understand this to refer to God’s Holy Word, from Genesis to Revelation.

Once God’s Word was completed and available, Christians no longer needed

the miraculous gifts. They were supplied to bridge a very small but

timely gap between the very beginnings of the early church and the completion of the writings we now call the Bible. Once that gap was over, the gifts went away, and appropriately so.

The Power, Purpose and Application of Biblical Speaking in Tongues

The New Testament message of the gift of tongues is clear. Speaking in tongues was always the miraculous ability to speak a human language unknown to the speaker. This gift was a sign of God’s approval of the gospel going out through the entire world. It was always to be used only for the furtherance of the gospel. This was a necessary but “lesser gift.”

This gift was important; it played a role. But when the role was over, it went away or ceased, just like the gift of healing. It makes so much sense when we see how these things fit into their scriptural perspective.

Let’s look at the big picture as we wrap this up. Healing and speaking in tongues were both signs of God’s plan unfolding right before the eyes of everyone witnessing them. Jesus showed us a microcosm of a great reality to come in the earthly kingdom. There will be a healing for all.

It’s important to note that those healed by the apostles and disciples became sick again.

The gift of healing gave a glimpse of what prophecy foretold:

Isaiah 35:5–6: (NIV2011) 5 Then will the eyes of the blind be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped. 6 Then will the lame leap like a deer, and the mute tongue shout for joy. Water will gush forth in the wilderness and streams in the desert.

Revelation 21:4: (KJV) And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.

If we take this Old Testament prophecy in Isaiah (we just picked one of many Old Testament prophecies about God’s future kingdom) and this Revelation scripture, we get a hint, a sense, a promise of that which is perfect, of what is to come. We read about this in

1 Corinthians 13:10.

Death… sorrow… crying will all pass away; they will be things of the past. The gift of healing gave the early church a glimpse of what would be permanent in God’s kingdom. This is why Jesus used healing to illustrate the great healing of all in the kingdom.

The gift of tongues gave a glimpse of the pure and complete communication that God had in store for all of humanity:

Habakkuk 2:14: For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea.

Zephaniah 3:9: (KJV) For then will I turn to the people a pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the LORD, to serve him with one consent.

In Part I, we talked about the Tower of Babel, where God confused all the languages to force man to spread out and settle all the earth. But originally, there was only one language. God spoke to Adam, and Adam understood. Habakkuk and Zephaniah above say that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, and that the people will have a pure language. All the miscommunication and frustration of not understanding will be gone.

The ability to speak in tongues was so that the gospel could be understood by all, regardless of where a person came from, the gospel could be understood. Someone who spoke their language was present and explained it to them. In the future kingdom, all humanity will fully comprehend the gospel, as they will all speak one pure language.

Both the gift of healing and the gift of tongues served as signs to those who observed and listened, demonstrating the glory of God's kingdom on earth.

So, are Christians today really capable of healing people or speaking in tongues?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

Additional notes on James 5:13-15.

CONTEXT: James 5 is not about physical sickness; rather, it is a chapter about spiritual endurance:

- endurance under trials - spiritual pressure - weariness of faith - the danger of giving up - the need for mutual support in the church

THE GREEK WORDS: Some Christians use these texts as proof of faith healing, but they are about supporting those who are spiritually weak:

James 5:13–15: 13 Is anyone among you suffering <2553>? Then he must pray. Is anyone cheerful? He is to sing praises. 14 Is anyone among you sick <770>? Then he must call for the elders of the church and they are to pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; 15 and the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick <2577>, and the Lord will raise him up, and if he has committed sins, they will be forgiven him.

These texts prescribe pastoral care for spiritual exhaustion.

Suffering: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2553 kakopathéō; to undergo hardship

Suffering here means to undergo hardship, to experience adversity. It has to do with trials of faith, not physical illness.

For example:

2 Timothy 2:3: Suffer hardship <2553> with me, as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.

2 Timothy 4:5: (KJV) But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions <2553>, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry.

These describe spiritual trials, not physical sickness.

Sick: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #770 asthenéō; to be feeble (in any sense)

While #770 CAN mean either physical sickness or spiritual weariness, it is used far more often to describe spiritual weariness.

For example:

2 Corinthians 12:10: (KJV) Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ’s sake: for when I am weak <770>, then am I strong.

Romans 14:1–3: (NKJV) 1 Receive one who is weak <770> in the faith, but not to disputes over doubtful things. 2 For one believes he may eat all things, but he who is weak <770> eats only vegetables. 3 Let not him who eats despise him who does not eat, and let not him who does not eat judge him who eats; for God has received him.

Sick: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2577 kámnō; properly, to toil,

i.e. (by implication) to tire (figuratively, faint, sicken)

This word is only used two other times and never to describe physical illness:

Hebrews 12:3: (KJV) For consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied <2577> and faint in your minds.

Revelation 2:3: (KJV) And hast borne, and hast patience, and for my name’s sake hast laboured, and hast <2577> not fainted <2577>.

These texts clearly indicate spiritual exhaustion.

ADDITIONAL POINTS:

- The elders are not doctors; they are spiritual shepherds. Their role is prayer, encouragement and guidance.
- James 5:15-16: The result is forgiveness, not physical recovery.
- James 5:17-18: Elijah is given as an example of the power of prayer in times of spiritual pressure. Elijah’s account in 1 Kings 17-19 is about discouragement, fear, exhaustion, feeling alone and wanting to give up. In other words, Elijah experienced exactly the kind of spiritual weariness James is addressing. Elijah is not an example of physical healing.

Are you suffering? Pray.

Are you spiritually weak? Call the elders.

Prayer will restore the weary one.

Confess sins and pray for each other.

Why? Because prayer works—look at Elijah.

THE BOTTOM LINE: When James speaks of calling the elders and anointing with oil, he is NOT describing a faith-healing ritual or an apostolic miracle. Oil was used in the ancient world for physical soothing, but in this context James is addressing believers who are spiritually exhausted, not medically incapacitated. The oil can be understood as a symbolic expression of the holy spirit’s comfort and strengthening influence. When someone is overwhelmed by trials, being surrounded by spiritually mature believers— those who embody and reflect the calming, steadying work of God’s spirit—can help restore their courage and faith. So even if there were accompanying physical maladies involved, James 5 is not a faith-healing ritual. It is describing the pastoral care, prayer and spiritual support that help revive a spiritually weary faith.

--------------------------

Some other instances of Jesus healing the masses in public. He healed out of compassion, not as a result of their individual faith:

Matthew 9:35–38: (KJV) 35 And Jesus went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every sickness and every disease among the people. 36 But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd. 37 Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few; 38 Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.

Mark 3:7–12: 7 Jesus withdrew to the sea with his disciples; and a great multitude from Galilee followed; and also from Judea, 8 and from Jerusalem, and from Idumea, and beyond the Jordan, and the vicinity of Tyre and Sidon, a great number of people heard of all that he was doing and came to him. 9 And he told his disciples that a boat should stand ready for him because of the crowd, so that they would not crowd him; 10 for he had healed many, with the result that all those who had afflictions pressed around him in order to touch him. 11 Whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they would fall down before him and shout, You are the Son of God! 12 And he earnestly warned them not to tell who he was.

Matthew 15:29–31: 29 Departing from there, Jesus went along by the Sea of Galilee, and having gone up on the mountain, he was sitting there. 30 And large crowds came to him, bringing with them those who were lame, crippled, blind, mute, and many others, and they laid them down at his feet; and he healed them. 31 So the crowd marveled as they saw the mute speaking, the crippled restored, and the lame walking, and the blind seeing; and they glorified the God of Israel.

Matthew 19:1–2: 1 When Jesus had finished these words, he departed from Galilee and came into the region of Judea beyond the Jordan; 2 and large crowds followed him, and he healed them there.

## Episode 1436 — How Does Our Free Will Work in God’s Plan? (Part I)
Published: 2026-05-11
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1436-how-does-our-free-will-work-in-gods-plan-part-i/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/11133009/CQ_Rewind_05-11-2026_How_Does_Our_Free_Will_Work_in_Gods_Plan_Part_I.pdf

Joshua 24:15: If it is disagreeable in your sight to serve the LORD, choose for yourselves today whom you will serve: whether the gods which your fathers served which were beyond

the river, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you are living; but as for me and my

house, we will serve the LORD.

The Bible plainly teaches us that God, in His unfathomable wisdom and power, has a clear plan for the destiny of ALL humanity. We also know, according to 1 Peter 1:20, that His plan for the sacrifice of Jesus was clearly in place even before the earth was created. Now, if God’s plan was clear to Him even before humanity existed, how does that fit into our understanding that each and every one of us has free will? Wouldn’t His foreknowledge, by its very existence, make us all puppets in His hands? If He knows how it will all turn out, then aren’t we just playing a predetermined role? Actually, nothing could be further from the truth! As we dig into these questions, we will see that God’s plans and purposes are firmly built around the free will of all of His intelligent creation. Understanding this is life changing!

We face this every day. We pray for guidance but still have to decide. We feel the pull of temptation and the pull of God’s spirit—and our will chooses the direction. And when life goes wrong, we wonder, Was this God’s plan or my mistake? These are real questions, and understanding free will gives us a steadier perspective.

The account of Joshua is so important because his life shows how free will operates within God’s will—through real decisions, real pressures, real consequences. Our theme scripture with its well-known phrase, but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD is Joshua speaking to the Jewish nation. God had chosen him to lead the people after the death of Moses (Numbers 27:18-23), and the people accepted that choice (Joshua 1:16-17).

When Joshua was younger, he and Caleb were the only spies who returned from the land of Canaan with complete faith and confidence in God’s ability to further deliver His people (Numbers 14:6-9). Now, many years later at the end of his life, Joshua calls for the nation to remain faithful. He had done all he could for them by leading, teaching and modeling faithfulness. He had already made his own choice to serve God, but he couldn’t force that choice upon them. The decision was now theirs alone.

Let’s go back to the beginning of Joshua’s leadership, as that beginning teaches us principles of how human free will works within the context of God’s will in this present age of sin and death. We can look at our own ways and compare them to God’s ways to get perspective. The people of Israel had wandered in the wilderness for 40 years and were now ready to receive what God had originally promised them.

God chose His faithful servant, Joshua, to be their new leader:

Joshua 1:1-2: 1 Now it came about after the death of Moses the servant of the LORD, that the LORD spoke to Joshua the son of Nun, Moses' servant, saying, 2 Moses My servant is dead; now therefore arise, cross this Jordan, you and all this people, to the land which I am giving to them, to the sons of Israel.

This was a transition of power. Moses died, and Joshua was being raised up in his place with many responsibilities.

This is an important lesson for us as we begin to understand free will in the context of God’s will.When we make choices to put God first and follow through on them, as Joshua did, God can use our standing before Him as a tool to further accomplish His will.

God’s introduction of Joshua to leadership shows us the principles of godliness at work— and how human free will responds to them.

When God speaks, that is His will. That which He says, He does—period!

God’s will is perfect and His will accomplishes His plan.

When God tells Joshua he would be taking charge but that God would be with him, we know this promise is true.

Human Free Will Principle: We are free to choose a path and to live by our choice.

We can think of free will like holding the steering wheel of a car. God provides the road—His plan—already laid out before us. Joshua stepped onto a road God had prepared long before he was born, and God promised to walk that road with him. Joshua’s free will didn’t create the road, but it determined how faithfully he traveled it.

Rick, I remember when I first came to you with the idea of starting Christian Questions as a weekly radio program. It really came down to two paths: keep looking for a witness opportunity that felt familiar and manageable OR step into a weekly radio program we had no idea how to do. Rick, you dismissed the idea a few times before we finally aired that first episode in June of 1998. And honestly, it was one of the hardest—and scariest—decisions we’ve ever made. We were stepping into something completely unfamiliar, but it became one of the most spiritually rewarding things we’ve ever done. That was a moment where we had to “put our hands on the steering wheel” and choose a path.

It felt like we were driving in completely uncharted territory. What are we doing behind these microphones in this radio studio? It was a very important free will decision. We could have chosen not to do it; I even said, I don’t know, who is going

to do that? We don’t know how to do that—and that was true, but it ended up not stopping us from going in the right direction.

This fits into the Joshua experience. He had not led the people before. He was always behind Moses, doing what Moses told him to do. Now, all of a sudden, Joshua is out in front.

Let’s return to the Joshua account:

Joshua 1:3,5: 3 Every place on which the sole of your foot treads, I have given it to you, just as I spoke to Moses. 5 No man will be able to stand before you all the days of your life. Just as I have been with Moses, I will be with you; I will not fail you or forsake you.

This is the moment when Joshua’s leadership begins. God would be with Joshua just like he had been with Moses. What a powerful message! Joshua could step forward knowing he wasn’t stepping into the unknown alone. God is giving him the assurance of this.

When we have freely chosen to do God’s will, we have chosen to be in His care—just like Joshua. God will oversee all that comes to us.

God’s promise is His will. That which He has promised He will deliver—period!

God’s will is committed and His commitment accomplishes His plan.

When God’s will is committed, it means I will be with you; I will not fail or forsake you. His promise is His will! That is something we can really hold on to.

Human Free Will Principle: Freely doing God’s will opens us up to freely receiving His protection.

But we need to define “protection” because faithful people still suffer. Trials aren’t miraculously removed. Even with these incredible assurances from God, Joshua’s life was anything but easy. By the time we reach our theme text in chapter 24, he has faced battles, setbacks, failures within the camp and the weight of leading a nation that didn’t always want to follow. God’s presence didn’t remove the challenges.

God’s protection acknowledged that leadership would be hard for Joshua. The decisions he would need to make would be difficult. He would fall and have to get back up. God’s protection was that if Joshua would look to Him, God would guide him through all the falling down, trouble and trials.

King David is another good example of this. He found his protection in being able to go back to God no matter what. (Psalms 18:1-3, 32:7, 37:23-24 and many others, for example.) He knew he would be able to stand on his own two feet only as long as he followed God’s will in God’s way. That is where our protection comes in.

Our protection doesn’t keep us from getting hurt. It walks us through our hurt.

Let’s go further in comparing God’s will and the principles of our human free will:

Joshua 1:6-7: 6 Be strong and courageous, for you (Joshua) shall give this people possession of the land which I swore to their fathers to give them. 7 Only be strong and very courageous; be careful to do according to all the Law which Moses My servant commanded you; do not turn from it to the right or to the left, so that you may have success wherever you go.

This was a massive responsibility for one man. Joshua was carrying the weight of an entire nation’s future, and he had to do as well as, or better than, Moses had. Why does God demand courage if He’s in control? Joshua still had to step into the promise with obedience and faith. God’s will requires our active participation. Without it, there would be no character development, no faith and no genuine obedience. We’d be automated.

The Hebrew word for strong here doesn’t just mean “be tough” or “try harder.” It means to grasp firmly—to seize with resolve. Joshua had to take hold of the strength God was providing. The Hebrew word for courageous here carries the sense of standing firm— remaining steady when pressure comes.

So, strong and courageous = active strength + steadfast courage. A simple way to illustrate this is strength is like taking hold with our arms—grasping firmly what God provides. Courage is like standing firm with our legs—remaining steady when obedience is tested.

It is a “whole body” experience! Going back to the early days of Christian Questions, we had to learn to grab hold of the opportunities God provided. Then we had to learn to stand firm. It was not easy, and it took a long time!

When we have freely chosen to do God’s will, by necessity we will need to stand firm with courage. Doing His will is NOT easy in this world! It’s not supposed to be easy.

The key point is that His protection doesn’t necessarily shield us from all of life’s bad experiences. It helps us walk through them and grow through the experience.

Verse 7—do not turn from it to the right or to the left—adds moral courage as another layer. Joshua would face pressures, obstacles and discouragements, and God was preparing him to stand firm in obedience. Strength seizes what God provides; courage holds steady when obedience is tested.

God requires our strength and courage when guiding us in His will, as His

character drives His will.

God’s will is time tested, and that test of time proves His plan.

Sometimes it doesn’t look like His will makes any sense. We can’t see how a circumstance can possibly be God’s will. But just wait. We need time to gain perspective overall and to see the bigger picture. God’s plan is time-tested and always the best way. Why? God knows the big picture.

Human Free Will Principle: A God-driven character is required to appropriately do God’s will.

But is our character “time tested”? How well has Christianity overall done in this test over the course of history? How many times have we seen preachers get involved in money scandals and moral scandals? Why? Maybe they start out with energy and enthusiasm, focused on spirituality, but over time, what happens? That’s the key. Over time, do we stand up with courage, holding on to God’s truth, standing firm, not turning to the right or the left? Or, do we waver back toward other things?

Our human free will principle can choose to do this. We can choose to waver because we’re feeling too comfortable, or we can choose to stand firm in what we know to be the truth according to God’s Word.

Let’s go further:

Joshua 1:8-9: 8 This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it; for then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will have success. 9 Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous! Do not tremble or be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.

More strong and courageous! Joshua was stepping into Moses’ role (big sandals to fill!), and God was commanding him to actively grasp the strength needed for leadership. Joshua could do that because he held God’s Law as that straight-line standard. Anything that didn’t align with God’s Law—and therefore God’s will—was counterfeit. His strength came from anchoring every decision to God’s revealed truth.

We can see that as God prepares Joshua for leadership, He tells him everything he needs to know, everything he needs to rely upon, and everything he needs to watch out for. He gives Joshua the assurance that He will never leave his side; Joshua will not be alone. The LORD your God is with you wherever you go.

Having freely chosen to do God’s will, as Joshua did, obligates us to continually check ourselves against God’s Word, so we can continue to follow His leading at every turn. Our continuous following keeps God’s presence in our lives! We don’t want to end up in a scandal. We want to end up faithful. To do this, we need to keep His presence in our lives.

God’s will is plainly reflected in His Word. His word reflects His plan and His

character.

God’s will is harmonious and the harmony of His Word and actions display the glory of His plan.

Sometimes we can read God’s Word but the actions and experiences in our lives don’t seem to add up. That is when we have to step back and tell ourselves to just wait for it to continue to unfold. The harmony between what God has said and what He does, in its entirety, shows a glorious, magnificent, overwhelmingly powerful, loving and just plan for all humanity.

Human Free Will Principle: Freely doing God’s will requires our intellect to be in harmony with His Word.

Why is intellect so important? Isn’t just the way we feel enough?

No! Simply feeling inspired is great, but is not an adequate basis for doing God’s will. God makes decisions based on justice, wisdom, love and mercy. We have been created in His image and this is how we should be making decisions. Faith built solely on emotion and feeling does not last. What is true, and our understanding of that truth, is what drives godly decisions.

While emotions tied to our faith are essential, we cannot rely solely on emotions to guide our decisions. Do we see the situation intellectually as strongly as we feel emotionally in support of it? If we don’t, then why not? We need to be careful with emotions.

Our Free Will Within the Context of God’s Will:

We truly do have choice, and every choice carries consequences. When our decisions grow out of a godly, well-rounded character and an intellect anchored in God’s Word, we are far better equipped to withstand the challenges that inevitably come. With that strength in place, we can continue to walk in God’s ways.

We have to have it all together. That’s why God was so specific with Joshua about everything he needed to know, understand, look for and do as a result.

Just by looking at one experience with Joshua, we can begin to grasp the great power and responsibility of our free will.

Now that we have a basic understanding of free will in our world,

the next question is, has free will always worked this way?

We can freely choose our path. When we choose God’s way, we open ourselves up to God’s protection. Continuing in His providence requires a godly character and a God-driven intellect. Veering away from any of these things can easily redirect our free will to an alternate path that will draw us away from our God.

Adam and Eve were faced with these very challenges. Remember, this was the first time in human history that free will was being exercised. There was no past failure to learn from, no cautionary tale, no example of what happens when you choose against God.

Now that we’ve learned from Joshua about leadership, let’s go back to the beginning to Adam and Eve. In that context, God would introduce humanity to their responsibility in an environment truly designed for success.

This environment had everything they needed, and it was all presented in a perfect package called the Garden of Eden:

Genesis 2:8-9: 8 The LORD God planted a garden toward the east, in Eden; and there He placed the man whom He had formed. 9 Out of the ground the LORD God caused to grow every tree that is pleasing to the sight and good for food; the tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

The only thing not present in that whole perfect environment was an example of what happens when human free will goes against God. Why? Because it had never happened before! It was the beginning of mankind, so there had never been an opportunity.

Here is part of the wisdom of God that we generally don’t look at: Eden was a perfect package with everything Adam and Eve would need, and it was built around their free will.

God laid out the rules, and the consequences of obedience and disobedience were plainly disclosed:

Genesis 2:15-17: 15 Then the LORD God took the man and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate it and keep it. 16 The LORD God commanded the man, saying, From any tree of the garden you may eat freely; 17 but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat from it you will surely die.

Clear boundaries with clear consequences. Free will was real, but so were the outcomes. Think back to our steering-wheel metaphor. Free will is the steering wheel in our hands. This was the map. In Eden, God placed the map directly in Adam and Eve’s hands—His literal word told them exactly where safety was and where danger lay. Their free will was meant to follow that map with trust.

They were put in a position where they knew and understood everything necessary about their situation. But they were naïve; they lacked direct experience. In their perfection, in being created in God’s image, Adam and Eve were given God’s protection. They were clearly told what not to do.

At this point, their characters and intellect were God-driven because that was how they were created. They did not know anything else BUT to be God-honoring, God-following and God-worshiping. They knew the rules, were clearly given the consequences, but had never experienced them.

We are often asked: How could Adam and Eve have sinned if they were perfect? Please see the Bonus Material. Our website, ChristianQuestions.com, has an entire Q&A section to check out as well.

Another frequently asked question: Since God knows the future, why did God put the forbidden tree in the garden, knowing it would ultimately bring sin, sorrow and death? Please see the Bonus Material.

Human free will would be tested. WHY? Why couldn’t God just give them everything they needed to live happily ever after? Why allow them to choose the ‘not so’ happily ever after? The END RESULT (remember, often when we look at the moment, we don’t see the sense of why something is happening) of God’s plan was, and always will be, to have human free will work within the same parameters as God’s own will, because we were created in HIS image. God was teaching His human creation to learn to always choose correctly, appropriately, justly, lovingly and wisely.

Let’s look at how God’s will worked in all of this:

God’s will is perfect. God’s plan was always for the human will to learn to fully

embrace perfection.

Adam and Eve had perfection, but they had to learn to embrace it through experience.

God’s will is committed. God’s plan was always for the human will to learn

godly commitment.

Adam and Eve understood God’s directions but needed to learn how to commit to Him through all kinds of experiences.

God’s will is time-tested. God’s plan was always for the human will to learn to

be proven (tested, exercised and demonstrated as trustworthy) and faithful not just at the beginning, but consistently over time.

The common denominator is to learn! He wanted them to learn, as He wants us to learn, through experience.

God’s will is harmonious. But His plan did NOT always outwardly reveal this

important trait!

This is why when we look at the experience in the Garden of Eden, we might question WHY God would set it up that way. But the harmony of His plan was not yet to be revealed. It would unfold over time.

The harmony of God’s plans was always there, right from the beginning. Our wise Father who knows all was always there. His plans were in place and human free will needed to be exercised for the learning to begin.

Now the test. Enter Satan, misusing his God-given influence:

Genesis 3:1-3: 1 Now the serpent was more crafty than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said to the woman, Indeed, has God said, You shall not eat from any tree of the garden? 2 The woman said to the serpent, From the fruit of the trees of the garden we may eat; 3 but from the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden, God has said, You shall not eat from it or touch it, or you will die.

Eve repeated God’s command back to him—she knew the rules and the consequence, but her character and intellect were as of yet untested.

Here is one more Bible Q&A: Why didn’t God stop Satan from deceiving Eve? Please see the Bonus Material.

Hint: In God’s plan, free will is everything! God’s free will is expressed in how

He handles situations. His free will is for us to learn and then master our wills

so that we can react as He does.

Satan next introduced a second choice and suggested an alternative ending. This is key in the test and the understanding of free will:

Genesis 3:4-6: 4 The serpent said to the woman, You surely will not die! 5 For God knows that in the day you eat from it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.

The serpent’s lie planted a seed of doubt—a subtle suspicion that God

might be withholding something good. That tiny shift in thinking

opened the door for Eve to step outside of God’s boundaries. But

when Eve listened to another voice, she set the map aside

and steered by her own understanding. Without the

map, even a perfect human can drift off course.

Eve now had “new information.” It contradicted what God told Adam, but this new information was very enticing. This is free will at work—not in a good way—but it is working according to God’s plan.

6 When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was desirable to make one wise…

Her perspective changed. She now evaluated God’s command through self-interest instead of trust. Suspicion brought doubt. Eve ate the fruit and Adam ate with her.

Eve (and now Adam) clearly had a choice and weighed their options as humans. The problem was that they started to put themselves before God. In the deception, Eve had chosen to see God as limiting and not protective, and Adam simply chose to disobey, just as Satan had already done!

We can see how much happened with that one little choice to step away from God’s clearly stated provision for them. They took what was perfect, what was sound and what was given to them by their Creator for their ultimate good and chose to step away from it. Because of “new information,” which was a lie, their whole perspective changed. God knew this was an important test, and that it had to happen for their ultimate learning about how damaging their decision could be.

When our free will is exercised, and we have chosen against ultimate good, the results put us out of harmony with God, and we will rationalize hiding from Him:

Genesis 3:8-11: 8 They heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden. 9 Then the LORD God called to the man, and said to him, Where are you? 10 He said, I heard the sound of You in the garden, and I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself. 11 And He said, Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?

In their sin, their characters and intellects had responded to another voice. Suddenly they felt exposed before God. Of course they hid—they were vulnerable. They were guilty. They were afraid of God who had only ever protected them.

We were created in God’s image. When we follow God’s instructions, we reflect His image in us. His laws are the framework for the best possible life—the life our Designer created us to live. But our fallen nature pushes back. Something in us whispers that God is holding us back from something better. That suspicion is the same seed of deception Eve faced, and it still tempts us today. Complete obedience saves later regret.

Take a moment of emotional reflection: Every time we choose suspicion of God over trust, or self over God, or shortcuts over obedience, we replay a tiny version of that moment in Eden. And yet, God’s response to Adam and Eve—seeking, calling, covering—reminds us that His plan always includes redemption. To get to redemption, though, there had to be a consequence to teach them the way back.

Many of our listeners know that our youngest daughter, Amy, was raped when she was only 15 years old. That created a lot of very hard experiences in our lives. In the process of recovering from all that, she and I had to work together as father and daughter.

There was one period when this really set her off, and she was spiraling downward. She got into a situation where she told me a series of lies to cover for herself so she could do something she was absolutely not supposed to do. As parents, sometimes we find out, and sometimes we don’t, when our kids lie to us. This time we did.

I remember very vividly that I was home, downstairs in our family room. I told Trish to send Amy down when she got home. She came down the stairs, and I looked at her and said, “You lied to me.”

She knew, and she just nodded her head. I said, “You lied to me more than once.” And she nodded her head. And I said, “After all we’ve been through, and what we agreed—that no matter how difficult it is, the truth is going to get us through this—you still lied. That was a betrayal of our agreement.” As her dad, I needed to make a statement.

But I was really upset, so I said, “Okay, I’m done.” I got up, walked up the stairs, out of the house and drove down the road. She was mortified.

I did that for two reasons: One, I needed space because I was really upset—we were too close to losing our daughter.

The second reason I did it was to have her feel the pain of separation. I wanted her to feel what it was like for me to walk out. Now, I was obviously going to come back. And when I did later, it served as a tool to bring us back to working together.

The experience in Eden, like the experience Amy and I had, reminds me of the importance of our free will staying in the context of our Father’s wisdom. It was a great learning experience for both of us and turned out to be one of the turning points that actually saved her life.

It’s important for us to recognize why free will needs to be part of our experience and what the consequences can sometimes be of not following God’s will.

Our Free Will Within the Context of God’s Will:

Adam and Eve had a choice, and they each, in their own way, chose sin. Despite these choices, God’s love provided an eventual way to reclaim them. After all, God’s plan has always been to ultimately develop an unbreakable righteousness within humanity.

We have the picture of our steering wheel as our free will, and our map, of course, is still God’s Word, the Bible. Whose voice are we listening to?

Eve listened to the wrong voice, and so can we. Today, deception is everywhere. So much is fake or engineered to mislead that we can’t always tell what’s real. Our only protection is the same one Adam and Eve and Joshua had—staying close to God’s Word. Anything that doesn’t align with biblical principles is counterfeit—no matter how convincing it looks, or how good it feels.

But that means we must be firm in our biblical principles, or our free will can be steered by the wrong voice.

We have looked at the experiences of Joshua and Adam and Eve, and we’re just getting started! We need to do a second part to get to the core of how to apply all of these learning tools.

God’s will always, eventually, prevails.

When it comes to human free will, we learned from Joshua that the choice to serve God is ours. While serving God with those choices brings us His protection, we also need to develop and apply a godly character and God-driven intellect.

Adam and Eve showed us how easily it is to be distracted from our highest purpose by doubts and suspicions. These alter our perception and lead to compromised choices.

In Part II, we will apply these free will lessons in two ways.

1) To our lives as Christians.

How do we attain and maintain enough godliness to make the right choices?

2) To the lives of the rest of the world in the context of the day of judgment.

Will it be an end for them, or a new beginning?

Human free will is important!

So, how does our free will work in God’s plan?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

BIBLE Q&A If Adam and Eve were perfect, how could they have sinned? Wouldn't a perfect man and woman have acted in a perfect manner?

In Genesis 1:26-27, the Bible says, "Let Us make man in Our image, according to Our likeness... and God created man in His own image..." We know that God is a spirit being with a spirit body, so the statement that man was created in His image does not refer to Adam's body. It therefore must refer to the qualities God gave him in his ability to understand and reason. God possesses these qualities on a much higher level than human beings, but our capacities are similar in type to God's and elevate mankind above the animals. God pronounced His creation "very good" in Genesis 1:31. If in God's eyes it was "very good," it must have been very good indeed! Adam was created sinless and, we believe, with a perfect physical body. If he had continued to obey God and eat the perfect food God provided for him, there would have been no death.

But the similar mental faculties that God gave Adam did not guarantee immunity from temptation. In addition to creating him as a sinless, physically perfect man, God gave him free will. He was not designed as a high-functioning robot. God had made clear the law He expected Adam to follow; the explanation of the law and Adam's understanding of his responsibility to obey it must have been sufficient enough for him to be justly condemned because of disobedience. He was capable of perfect adherence to God's instructions. Otherwise, it would have been unfair of the Father to give Adam the death penalty.

So, why did Adam sin? The Bible doesn't tell us, but there may have been several factors involved. The penalty for disobedience had been described to him, but he did not yet have participatory experience with sin and death and thus may not have been fully able to appreciate the results of his misconduct. He had knowledge of but no familiarity with consequences.

The best clue we have as to why Adam chose to disobey is in 1 Timothy 2:14: For it was not Adam who was deceived, but the woman being quite deceived, fell into transgression. Adam did know that Satan had lied. He did feel guilt after he transgressed or he would not have attempted to hide from God. The best explanation as to why Adam chose to follow Eve in her disobedience may be because he could not bear the thought of life without her. In his perfection, he would have had a great capacity for love and may have willfully chosen to die with her—a form of suicide. At this point there was no mention of a redemption, no hope of resurrection. The prospect of living forever without his beloved companion may have overwhelmed him. This was Adam's first test of character and he failed it. He chose loyalty to Eve over loyalty to God, and thereby condemned the entire human race to death.

Bible Q&A Since God knows the future, why did God put the forbidden tree in the garden, knowing it would ultimately bring sin, sorrow and death?

God placed the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil in the Garden of Eden not as a trap, but as a deliberate teaching tool designed to help Adam and Eve develop moral character, free will and wholehearted devotion to Him. Scripture shows that God desires worship that flows from genuine love and understanding—true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth (John 4:23). For humanity to reach that level of mature, willing obedience, they needed the opportunity to choose righteousness over evil, even when disobedience appeared attractive.

The tree provided that opportunity. It established a clear boundary that would teach obedience, patience and restraint. While the Tree of Life represented the gift of ongoing physical life (Genesis 2:9), the Tree of Knowledge was intended to teach them how to live that life in righteousness. By giving a specific command not to eat from it (Genesis 2:16– 17), God gave His children the chance to choose loyalty to Him over their own impulses.

Without a meaningful alternative, Adam and Eve could not have exercised real moral freedom.

This is why the presence of the tree was essential. God does not create “robots.” To be made in His image, humans had to possess the ability to reason, choose and even disobey. If God had made the understanding of good and evil instinctual, they would have been incapable of choosing otherwise, and moral freedom would have been impossible. Real choice requires at least two options and the possibility of choosing wrongly. Without the forbidden tree, Adam would have had no meaningful way to demonstrate sincere, unforced allegiance to his Creator.

This also created the valuable lesson of the permission of evil. God did not author evil, but He permitted it so humanity could learn—through experience—how terrible sin truly is. Adam and Eve had information about sin, but they did not appreciate its horrors. Now, however, all mankind knows firsthand the suffering, pain and destruction that sin brings. This experiential knowledge is part of God’s long-term plan to produce an eternal appreciation for righteousness. Scripture affirms that God uses even painful experiences to produce lasting discernment (Romans 8:28, Hebrews 5:14).

This educational process continues into the future. During Christ’s 1,000-year reign, when Thy judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world will learn righteousness (Isaiah 26:9), Satan will be bound and humanity will be healed physically, emotionally

and spiritually from the effects of sin (Isaiah 35). At the end of that Millennium, Satan will be released briefly to test the restored human race (Revelation 20:7–9). By that time, mankind will fully understand the difference between good and evil. When confronted with temptation, most will choose obedience, demonstrating the wisdom of God’s permission of evil. Those who stand firm will be proven to love God with mature conviction, having His law written in their hearts and minds (Jeremiah 31:33).

Finally, the tree shows that God’s plan was proactive, not reactive. Because He is omniscient, man's fall did not surprise Him. Jesus is described as the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world (Revelation 13:8), revealing that the remedy for sin was already in place before Adam and Eve were created. In this light, the tree served to initiate the process by which humanity would eventually gain an obedience not based on innocence or ignorance, but on experience, understanding and freely chosen loyalty.

BIBLE Q&A Why didn’t God stop Satan from deceiving Eve? Why did God remove Satan from heaven because of pride but then let him come to earth?

When God sent Lucifer down to earth, Lucifer was not yet sinful. The name “Lucifer” carries the sense of “morning star” or “light bearer.” He became Satan when he lied to Eve. “Satan” means “adversary,” and he became the chief adversary of God.

Ezekiel 28:12-15: (ESV) 12 Son of man, raise a lamentation over the king of Tyre, and say to him, Thus says the Lord GOD: You were the signet of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty. 13 You were in Eden, the garden of God; every precious stone was your covering, sardius, topaz, and diamond, beryl, onyx, and jasper, sapphire, emerald, and carbuncle; and crafted in gold were your settings and your engravings. On the day that you were created they were prepared. 14 You were an anointed guardian cherub. I placed you; you were on the holy mountain of God; in the midst of the stones of fire you walked. 15 You were blameless in your ways from the day you were created, until unrighteousness was found in you.

In these scriptures, the king of Tyre must be symbolic because there was no king of Tyre in the Garden of Eden. These scriptures explain that God placed Lucifer in Eden as an anointed guardian angel. His purpose was to guard and bless Adam and Eve. Instead, Lucifer saw his chance to become a ruler over the human race. That was when unrighteousness was found in him.

Why did God permit Satan to stay as the evil ruler of mankind? Adam and Eve were created perfect (Deuteronomy 32:4) with free will in God’s image. They had the perfect ability to resist the temptation to disobey God. But they did not appreciate the horrible results of sin. They had only experienced the peace and joys of righteousness in Eden. When they sinned, they began to experience the consequences of evil.

Now, all of mankind is learning that disobedience/sin brings pain, suffering, and death. But there is a purpose to God’s permission of evil. In the resurrection, Christ will rule with an iron rod. No sin will be permitted and the willing will learn righteousness.

Jeremiah 31:3: No more shall every man teach his neighbor, and every man his brother, saying, Know the LORD, for they all shall know Me, from the least of them to the greatest of them, says the LORD. For I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin I will remember no more.

Finally, in the little season of Revelation 20:3, Satan will be loosed from the bottomless pit and try to tempt people to sin again. But this time, the results will be different. People will have experienced the consequences of disobedience. The great majority of mankind will choose to love God and righteousness. They will be rewarded with perfect human, everlasting life. (See Revelation 21:4.) Satan will then be destroyed forever.

Isaiah 14:15: (NKJV) Yet you (Satan) shall be brought down to sheol, to the lowest depths of the pit.

example of free will operating within God’s will? (Numbers 27:18-23)

God’s protection actually means for those, like Joshua and like us, who choose to serve the LORD. (Psalms 18:1-3, 37:23-24)

standing firm”? Did you succeed? How could you have improved your reaction?
