## Episode 1437 — How Does Our Free Will Work in God’s Plan? (Part II)
Published: 2026-05-18
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1437-how-does-our-free-will-work-in-gods-plan-part-ii/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/18133757/CQ_Rewind_How_Does_Our_Free_Will_Work_in_Gods-_Plan_Part_II.pdf

Joshua 24:15: If it is disagreeable in your sight to serve the LORD, choose for yourselves today whom you will serve: whether the gods which your fathers served which were beyond

the River, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you are living;

but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

In Part I, we laid out a scriptural foundation for how human free will works by considering two Old Testament accounts. First, we looked at Joshua and how God called him to lead Israel after the death of Moses. His decision to closely follow God’s direction in this task made him a great leader, and it showed us the profound value of always using God’s Word and His will to guide us. Second, we looked at the account of Adam and Eve and their sin. Their poor choices showed us how easy it is for us to apply our free will in self-destructive ways by listening to other voices that oppose godliness. Now we get practical and examine free will in relation to our Christianity, as well as free will in relation to the rest of the world.

The basic principle we have established is that our human free will choices are made based on the input we look for, receive and accept. It’s obvious that this process can be faulty, as we ourselves are faulty. As Christians, we need to be aware of the challenges and traps of our own interpretations and be willing to stand firm in Christ as we seek to correct them and embrace godliness.

As Christians, how do we daily remain aware of our free will, continually turn it back toward God, and make choices based on freedom in Christ?

In Part I, we learned several Human Free Will Principles from Joshua.

Human Free Will Principle: We are free to choose a path and to live by our choice.

We likened our human free will to holding the steering wheel of a car. God provides the road—His plan—already laid out before us.

We decide whether to stay on that road or veer off.

But the Apostle Paul is going to warn us what happens when we stop steering and let the world decide our direction:

Ephesians 4:17–19: 17 So this I say, and affirm together with the Lord, that you walk no longer just as the Gentiles also walk, in the futility of their mind, 18 being darkened in their understanding, excluded from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the hardness of their heart; 19 and they, having become callous, have given themselves over to sensuality for the practice of every kind of impurity with greediness.

Having become callous comes from the Greek word for “hardening,” like a callus on our fingers—a thickening, hard shell that forms over time. Bad choices rarely appear out of nowhere. They are cumulative. This “spiritual scar tissue” forms when we repeatedly ignore God’s leadings.

The natural propensity of our free will is influenced by deceptive, sinful human views of what fulfillment really is. We can pause, consider and reapply ourselves to a higher life, based on freedom in Christ.

God’s will is perfect, and His will accomplishes His plan.

John 8:31: So Jesus was saying to those Jews who had believed him, If you continue in my word, then you are truly disciples of mine.

Yes, we get to choose, but our will should move in the right direction. God gives us the prerequisites to make a godly choice possible. We are called to a higher standard of conscience—but conscience alone is not enough. What guides our conscience? The prerequisite for godly choice is a heart and mind trained by Jesus’ word.

Human Free Will Principle: Freely doing God’s will opens us up to freely receiving His protection.

“Protection” as we talked about in Part I, doesn’t mean we are guaranteed an easy life without challenges and trials. But as Christians, God surrounds our “road” with “guardrails”—His providence. We talked about this in Episode #1430: “How Does God’s Providence Work in Our Lives?” These guardrails don’t force our direction, but they keep us from going over the edge when we drift. Through Scripture, conscience, correction and the influence of His spirit, God lovingly nudges us back toward safety.

This topic about God’s providence as guardrails really hits home for me. A few years ago, we discovered the extent of my sister’s mental illness. She moved in with our elderly parents, claiming to care for them, but the situation became dangerous—she was verbally abusive and neglected their physical needs, which at times risked physical harm. My dad had advanced Alzheimer’s, and my mom pleaded for help. My wife and I recognized we had to intervene and relocate them to our home.

It wasn’t easy. We had to drive several states away, fully aware that my sister would be angry and unpredictable. There were times we felt threatened, but we continued to pray and sensed God urging us, ‘Be strong and courageous—do what’s right, and I’ll be with you.’

When we got to their home, it was tense and painful, but we were able to get my parents out safely with the help of the local police. Looking back, I can see God’s providence all through that experience. He didn’t make it easy, but He protected us through the timing and giving us the strength to keep going. Courage isn’t the absence of fear; it’s choosing obedience in spite of fear. God didn’t force our decision, but I think this is a good example of how our free will and God’s providence work together.

This involved a protective aspect. It was a dramatic step to take into the unknown and something that could have turned out badly. We need to go where God's will is leading us, trusting that He will protect us in His way if we are doing His will.

Paul next takes us into what it means to truly learn Christ:

Ephesians 4:20–21: 20 But you did not learn Christ in this way, 21 if indeed you have heard him and have been taught in him, just as truth is in Jesus.

The point is that we did not learn Christ (learn to follow Christ) through the futility of living the way Paul just described in the previous verses 17-19.

God’s will is committed, and His commitment accomplishes His plan.

John 8:32: and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.

With true freedom comes responsibility. With free will comes both consequences and blessings depending on how we apply that free will. Our free will can be taught to reach for true and eternal freedom from that sad, sinful list of Ephesians 4:17-19.

Human Free Will Principle: A God-driven character is required to appropriately do God’s will.

We have to leave our old ways behind:

Ephesians 4:22: that, in reference to your former manner of life, you lay aside <659> the old self, which is being corrupted in accordance with the lusts of deceit.

Lay aside: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #659 apotithēmi; to put away (literally or

figuratively):—cast off, lay apart (aside, down), put away (off)

Lay aside (put off in the King James Version) describes what you do with clothes. You remove a garment; lay it aside, deliberately put it away. This change is a daily—sometimes hourly—conscious choice. It’s like the spiritual equivalent of, “Take off the old outfit. It doesn’t fit you anymore.” We can now wear the robe of Christ’s righteousness (Isaiah 61:10, Romans 13:14, Galatians 3:27).

The old self which is being corrupted—present tense—it keeps decaying and trying to cling to us. That outfit should feel ugly, itchy and too tight.

And notice it is being corrupted in accordance with the lusts of deceit—these are desires that lie—desires that promise fulfillment but are empty because they are rooted in deception, just as we saw last week when Eve received “new information” from the serpent.

This is why this Human Free Will Principle is so important. Without a God-driven character, any “new information” can look awfully enticing, logical and fulfilling, but it only ends up being awful!

God’s will is time-tested and that test of time proves His plan.

John 17:16–17: (Jesus is talking about his followers the night before his crucifixion.) 16 They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world. 17 Sanctify them in the truth; Your word is truth.

Jesus’ true followers are not about that sad list we read in Ephesians 4:17-19. They are set apart. It might look like they are too small, too fragile. But God’s will is time-tested, and time will prove they can flourish if they remain set apart. The truth will set us free.

As Christians, our free will can be transformed by the holiness of God’s spirit working within us! We need to position ourselves to allow this to happen.

Human Free Will Principle: Freely doing God’s will requires our intellect to be in harmony with His Word.

Ephesians 4:23–24: 23 and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, 24 and put on the new self, which in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of the truth.

Let God reshape the attitude behind our thinking. Paul says to be renewed in the spirit of your mind, which is a full shift in how we process life. Then we put on the new self by choosing thoughts and actions that reflect God’s righteousness.

From a practical standpoint, it’s catching our old reactions—like complaining or reacting harshly—and choosing the Christlike response instead. Renewal is learning to choose the new instinct before the old one takes over. And when our first instinct isn’t great, we don’t give up—we pause, take a breath and move to that second, better thought or word, making immediate corrections.

Take note of the overall pattern of Ephesians 4:

o Put off the old self >> remove old habits o Be renewed in the mind >> rewire your thinking o Put on the new self >> replace your behavior

We repeat this pattern over and over until we are transformed.

To get to the point of being that faithful Christian, we have to work on our intellect, making it in harmony with God’s word. All of these scriptures show us how to find that harmony.

God’s will is completely harmonious.

John 17:18: As You sent me into the world, I also have sent them into the world.

Jesus showed us how to be in harmony. He did not do certain things and have his apostles do something completely different. There is a harmony of self-sacrifice to follow in his footsteps. Our intellect has to understand this in order to grab hold of it.

Do what Jesus did! As Christians, our free will can be energized to carry the gospel and to be its living examples. We are sent by Jesus to carry his message. What an overwhelming privilege to be a part of that work! We are doing what he was doing in a much smaller way. But he gives us the tools.

What is my free will as a Christian focusing on? Is it focusing on these upward things, this godly perspective? Or am I being pulled back into what I once was, like Paul warned us in Ephesians? My choice: Be what I once was or become Christlike.

Paul continues with what our transformed free will produces. This is a process we grow towards.

A TRANSFORMED FREE WILL IS REVEALED IN THE FOLLOWING RESULTS:

Truthful communication:

Ephesians 4:25: Therefore, laying aside falsehood, SPEAK TRUTH EACH ONE of you WITH HIS NEIGHBOR, for we are members of one another.

Our transformed free will gives us that truthful communication—if we follow Scripture.

A spirit of forbearance (hold back what you might be entitled to):

Ephesians 4:26–27: 26 BE ANGRY, AND yet DO NOT SIN; do not let the sun go down on your anger, 27 and do not give the devil an opportunity.

Our Christian free will appropriately holds back even our righteous anger so that we do not sin against another.

Godly morality:

Ephesians 4:28: He who steals must steal no longer; but rather he must labor, performing with his own hands what is good, so that he will have something to share with one who has need.

Don’t steal—not just because stealing is bad, but because we can now honorably help others if we do things honestly. This transformed free will elevates us to a godly morality.

Each of these points is showing us what our transformed Christian free will can produce.

Godly and upbuilding words:

Ephesians 4:29: Let no unwholesome word proceed from your mouth, but only such a word as is good for edification according to the need of the moment, so that it will give grace to those who hear.

Our godly and upbuilding words are valuable to others.

Diligent actions:

Ephesians 4:30: Do not grieve the holy spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.

Give God’s spirit a chance to thrive within us and drive us. A transformed free will is revealed in diligently following after Jesus’ footsteps.

Godly emotions:

Ephesians 4:31: Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice.

This is not saying to remove emotions or become stoic. It says that by removing those destructive emotions, we create an opening in our lives for something else—a loving heart.

A loving heart:

Ephesians 4:32: Be kind to one another, tender-hearted, forgiving each other, just as God in Christ also has forgiven you.

Truthful communication, the spirit of forbearance, godly morality and godly upbuilding words, diligent actions and godly emotions—these all bring us to a loving heart—a transformed free will now working to follow after Christ toward godliness.

Our Free Will Within the Context of God’s Will:

As Christians, we have a profound responsibility to focus our free will solely on accomplishing God’s will in our lives. This can only be accomplished when we offer up the humanness of our will to God and ask that it be replaced with the reverent thoughts and choices of Christlikeness. Such transformation requires clarity, humility, daily diligence and prayer!

Here’s why this matters: God guides our free will because He loves us and knows what leads to our truest joy. We have to look at His boundaries as being protective, not taking us away from something that we think would be better for us. Every nudge of providence and every stir of our conscience is God drawing us back to the life He designed us to thrive in. Our daily choices are where trust grows and where our relationship with Him deepens.

It all comes down to our own free will. We can choose to work on becoming Christlike, or we can choose to serve ourselves.

Which one is going to bring praise and honor to God?

As Christians, our free will can only produce God-honoring results if our freedom is voluntarily made subject to God’s will—period!

If our free will choices need to be overhauled based on godly truth, what about all of the free will choices the rest of the world makes?

This is the really big question!

A skeptic will immediately ask why God lets billions of people make terrible choices with terrible consequences. Some people grow up with loving, moral parents, and others grow up in trauma or spiritual darkness. How can free will be fair when the starting points are so unequal? Bad input produces bad choices.

The short answer is this: God’s will—right from the start—was for humanity to be in line with His plan for their eternal lives. Jesus redeemed Adam from his sin, and thereby redeemed all who were born into Adam’s sin.

So, what do you do with these billions of people?

You raise them from the dead and teach them accountability and righteousness, all to be done within the context of their free will.

And there’s the key: THIS AGE IS NOT THE FINAL JUDGMENT. God allows free will to

operate unevenly now because this is the age of learning through experiencing

consequences. The next age is where God evens the playing field. In our present age, our human free will carries consequences, many of which go unrecognized.

This brings us to the final part of our free will metaphor—the destination. God didn’t give humanity a steering wheel, a road, a map and guardrails just for the journey itself. He’s leading the whole world somewhere.

So, where is He leading them? In our present age, it does seem as though people get away with sinning, but our human free will does carry consequences. There’s more; we need to see the whole picture. The time of resurrection Jesus speaks about opens up those consequences to be dealt with.

First, let’s look at the “how” of the resurrection:

John 5:28–29: 28 Do not marvel at this; for an hour is coming, in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice, 29 and will come forth; those who did the good deeds to a resurrection of life, those who committed the evil deeds to a resurrection of judgment.

Those who seem to get away with something fall under the phrase those who committed the evil deeds to a resurrection of judgment. How does this judgment work?

This judgment was clearly explained by the Apostle Paul when he was in Greece, speaking on Mars Hill to the Gentile thinkers of Athens, including the philosophers of the day.

Paul is directly confronting the idols and false gods surrounding them:

Acts 17:29–31: 29 Being then the children of God, we ought not to think that the Divine Nature is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and thought of man.

Paul reminds them that all humanity is God’s offspring. THE true God can’t be represented by the idols and images their culture has created.

30 Therefore having overlooked the times of ignorance, God is now declaring to men that all people everywhere should repent,

God has not held the world fully accountable in this age. But sin still harms the sinner, and those effects must be addressed.

31 because He has fixed a day in which He will judge the world in righteousness through a man whom He has appointed, having furnished proof to all men by raising him from the dead.

Here is HOW those sins committed in this present age will be given consequences in the future age. Jesus paying the ransom price for Adam gives everybody a resurrection and an opportunity for life. The Day of Judgment (not a literal, 24-hour day, but rather a period of time) will help prepare them for when the world is judged in righteousness at the end of a thousand years. Many Christians look at the Day of Judgment and think it’s a day of horror and misery, but that’s not what the Scriptures say.

Observations:

- It is a fixed “day”—a time period predetermined to happen.
- The judgment of that time will be from Jesus, upon the world and based in

righteousness.

No one “gets away” with anything. Judgment will be focused on what is best for each person.

The resurrection, Judgment Day, the kingdom to come—these are all part of the “destination” God designed for every human being who has ever lived. It’s where His plan has always been heading: mankind restored, instructed in righteousness and brought back into a relationship with Him. It is the destination where every confused human will that has been out of harmony with Him in this life will have the chance to choose God with full understanding.

The purpose of this lifetime is to learn the consequences of our choices and actions, not to receive a final judgment. The resurrection of Jesus by God is God’s guarantee that every person who ever lived will be able to stand before Christ with full clarity and a fair opportunity to choose righteousness with their free will.

This judgment will focus on the free will of every human’s past experience, taking into account all of the circumstances—whether they involve the person’s upbringing, choices or events. (Remember, this segment is about the world in general, not faithful Christians resurrected in heaven.)

Let’s look at the breadth of this judgment:

Matthew 12:36–37: (YLT) 36 And I say to you, that every idle word that men may speak, they shall give for it a reckoning in a day of judgment; 37 for from thy words thou shalt be declared righteous, and from thy words thou shalt be declared unrighteous.

Jesus isn’t saying people will be condemned forever for every careless word. He’s saying every word we speak shapes our character, and character must be addressed in the resurrection. Free will leaves a trail, and every mark it made on our character will need to be faced and worked through.

But God doesn’t condemn people for choices they were never equipped to make. His plan is to restore every confused or wounded will and bring it back to clarity and truth.

Idle words—careless, unproductive words—reveal our habits and unfiltered reactions. Judgment Day is about bringing these instincts into alignment with righteousness.

Nobody “gets away with” anything from this current life. We all want there to be some sort of punishment and justice for the bad deeds of this life, but it will be handled. This means, to the extent that people have made bad choices and hurt others, the resurrection will enable them to correct their faulty human minds and give them clarity. They will be able to look back on their lives and see the damage they did. They will have the capacity and opportunity in God’s kingdom to right their mistakes.

Prophecies point to the people of Israel as the first to be given this opportunity. Let’s look at one of the prophecies where this process is outlined:

Jeremiah 31:27–30: 27 Behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man and with the seed of beast. 28 As I have watched over them to pluck up, to break down, to overthrow, to destroy and to bring disaster, (past actions) so I will watch over them to build and to plant, (future actions) declares the LORD. 29 In those days they will not say again, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge. 30 But everyone will die for his own iniquity; each man who eats the sour grapes, his teeth will be set on edge.

Mankind will no longer be able to blame their bad actions on their past. The proverb about ‘sour grapes’ disappears; no longer will individuals suffer for someone else’s choices. In the kingdom, they can’t blame Adam or genetics or a terrible home life. Each person will face the effects of their own free will decisions, but in a world where clarity, righteousness, and healing finally prevail.

This is a key point. The environment will be positive, upbuilding and godly. Dealing

with all the mess will be possible because the whole of mankind and the

structure they live under will have been lifted up higher.

We went through the Christian focus on free will, starting with the Human Free Will Principles and then comparing them to God’s righteousness. Now we are going to reverse them because now we’re talking about the conditions in God’s future kingdom.

God’s will is perfect and His will accomplishes His plan.

Daniel 2:44: In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which will never be destroyed, and that kingdom will not be left for another people; it will crush and put an end to all these kingdoms, but it will itself endure forever.

Human Free Will Principle: All will be free to choose God’s path and to live by their choice.

The Daniel scripture above says God’s kingdom will replace and put an end to all these [earthly] kingdoms. This means that every human being, resurrected and brought into that world, is given an incredible opportunity to thrive because it is God’s kingdom, and they are living in God’s kingdom—and there is no unrighteousness! There is no sin! But there is clarity and focus. All will be free to choose God’s path. They will remember and be able to use the painful experience of what it was like to live in this present time when they were not “driving”

on God’s path.

God’s will is committed and His commitment accomplishes His plan.

Zechariah 14:9: And the LORD will be king over all the earth; in that day the LORD will be the only one, and His name the only one.

Can you imagine a world without fear? It is a beautiful thing!

Human Free Will Principle: Freely doing God’s will, will give all of humanity His protection.

There will be no fear, but there will be God’s protection because Satan will be bound and eventually completely destroyed. God will be the ultimate source for guidance. He will remove all of the obstacles to godliness. With the experience of sin and death (unlike Adam and Eve had) and the obstacles to righteousness removed, it’s a much clearer path, a clearer decision.

God’s will is time-tested, and that test of time proves His plan.

Psalms 22:27–28: 27 All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the LORD, and all the families of the nations will worship before You. 28 For the kingdom is the LORD’s and He rules over the nations.

Human Free Will Principle: God-driven characters will thrive as God’s will is made plain.

It’s easy to see how this God-driven, human free will principle comes into play when all the families of the nations are worshipping before God. They all have the same objective. There will be NO politics in God’s kingdom. There will not be social clamoring and frustration over things not being our way. ALL the families of the nations will worship before God. His righteous government will rule over everyone.

It will employ the highest principles. God-driven characters will see this, and, based on their experience with free will and all the mess made during their previous lifetimes, they will run to righteousness because they know what the other way looks like. God’s kingdom will seem too good to be true. BUT, it is really too good not to be true!

God’s will is harmonious and the harmony of His word and actions display the glory of His plan.

Isaiah 11:9: They will not hurt or destroy in all My holy mountain, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.

What an interesting choice to compare knowledge with water! You don’t “learn” water— you are surrounded by it. In the kingdom, everyone will be immersed in a righteous environment.

Human Free Will Principle: All human intellect will be in perfect harmony with God’s own word.

We saw the God-driven character through the illustration of families and nations worshipping together. Now we see the intellect; the earth will be full of the knowledge, the understanding, of the Lord as the waters cover the sea. Knowledge and understanding will be plentiful and clear.

All the human free will framework comes into focus and brings us to this beautiful place called the kingdom of God. This is when all the lessons from the mess of today become valuable experiences humanity can look back on and learn from. These lessons will be a great advantage. Adam and Eve had no personal experience or the value of learning from other mistakes.

One of the biggest debates about free will is this: You can say that God is a “benevolent dictator.” His rules, His way. Can you really have free will if the rules are “obey and live; disobey and die”? You have to go along with the program or be extinguished.

God wants humanity to learn from the hard lessons of sin, suffering and death—and to want to choose His will. Not because they’re forced to like robots, but because they finally see that His ways produce the happiest, healthiest, most joyful lives—now and forever. He never takes the steering wheel away. He just removes all the distractions, lies

and emotional blind spots. Everyone will see the road clearly. He really is the best kind of parent!

All of these scriptures give us an understanding that the free will experiences of billions and billions of people who have ever lived, and the mess created on this earth, can actually have a positive, eternal experience.

Back to where we started—Joshua talking to Israel just before he dies. He is telling them they have an important choice to make:

Joshua 24:15: If it is disagreeable in your sight to serve the LORD, choose for yourselves today whom you will serve: whether the gods which your fathers served which were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you are living; but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

Joshua tells them to look back on their past experience. Do they want to serve those gods of the people around them, or do they want to serve the one, living true God?

As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. That is exactly what this kingdom experience, this Day of Judgment, is saying. Look back on your lives and consider the degradation of the things you have seen. Is that what you want? Or, do you want the beauty, righteousness, justice, love, wisdom and power that is right before you? You can choose!

Our Free Will Within the Context of God’s Will:

When the time for the sin and death that originated from Adam’s sin is over, the free will of every human who has ever lived will have been given two things:

First, it has been given the ability to exist. We can look back at our own lives and at the generations that have gone before us and track the mess that has come as a result of the human free will decisions made.

Second, it will be given the ability to be a tool of teaching in God’s hand. Because of Jesus’ sacrifice, every mistake, wrong conclusion and bad decision humanity has ever made can, as each person chooses, drive them towards a newly-educated free will. Then, they can freely and fully choose godliness, and the result will be eternal life!

Choose for yourselves today whom you will serve; but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD. Think about looking at the world around us and the mess it is in. What if God set a plan in place that will enable us to learn from our experiences and live in His kingdom, where all these temptations have been taken away, and all the faultiness of our human imperfection has been taken away?

Imagine where we could go, what we could do and what life would be like. THAT is what is coming. THAT is where free will is going. And THAT is why Jesus said to pray, Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done on earth…

So, how does our free will work in God’s plan?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

Matthew 11:20–24: 20Then he began to denounce the cities in which most of his miracles were done, because they did not repent. 21 Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! Hebrews 4:12–13: (ASV) 12 For the word of God is living, and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, and piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and quick to discern the thoughts and intents of the heart. 13 And there is no creature that is not manifest in His sight: but all things are naked and laid open before the eyes of him with whom we have to do.

will not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set justice in the earth; and the isles shall wait for his law.

## Episode 1438 — Should Women Be Pastors? (Part I)
Published: 2026-05-25
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1438-should-women-be-pastors-part-i/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/22114400/CQ_Rewind_05-25-2026_Should_Women_Be_Pastors_Part_I.pdf

Galatians 3:27-29: 27 For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves

with Christ. 28 There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus. 29 And if you belong to Christ,

then you are Abraham's descendants, heirs according to promise.

The world has changed dramatically over the last 2,000 years. If you are accessing this podcast information, then the world you live in has gone from a very localized environment where the fastest news traveled was by horseback or boat, to a society of instant access to all news and information. Your world has transformed from a patriarchal society where men represented the vast majority of power and influence in life to a society that continues to make all roles equally available for both men and women. So, has Christianity kept up with the times? Have we made all roles, specifically the role of pastor and teacher in the church, equally available to both men and women? If your church has, should it have? If they have not, then why not? There is a clear scriptural answer to this!

There are two major positions in the Christian world, and both sides genuinely believe they are honoring Scripture: egalitarian and complementarian.

Egalitarians say: Men and women are equal in value and equal in calling. God assigns roles based on spiritual gifts—such as teaching, shepherding and leadership—not gender. Women may serve as pastors or elders depending on gifting and calling.

Complementarians say: Men and women complement each other. They are equal in value, but God assigns different roles. A person may be gifted to teach or lead, but gifting does not automatically determine the office. Women should not serve as pastors or elders because those roles are tied to biblical structure, not gifting.

Restating our theme question with more detail:

Should women serve as pastors or elders regarding congregational teaching, and should they have governing authority?

To be transparent up front, our belief is that the Scriptures support the

complementarian view that women should NOT serve in a teaching or

governing role in a church setting.

Let’s begin with a summation of some of the arguments used by those who see men’s and women’s roles in Christianity as interchangeable. We begin with the egalitarian perspective.

Remember, both sides value women. This is about how each side interprets Scripture regarding authority, teaching and church order. The core question: Are these determined by spiritual gifts alone, or by the role structure the Bible gives us?

Egalitarian Point 1: Men and women are equal in value and equal in access to ministry roles.

Galatians 3:27-29: 27 For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ. 28 There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus. 29 And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's descendants, heirs according to promise.

The Apostle Paul does plainly state, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.

The argument is, old roles and distinctions are now gone, and this newness should apply to leadership as well.

Egalitarian Point 2: There were MANY women in leadership roles in both the Old and New Testaments.

- Deborah was an Old Testament judge of the people, and also a prophetess. Judges 4
- Huldah was an Old Testament prophetess. 2 Chronicles 34
- In the New Testament, Priscilla and her husband Aquila taught Apollos and traveled with Paul into great danger. Acts 18, Romans 16:3-4, 1 Corinthians 16:19,

2 Timothy 4:19

- Phoebe was a very faithful and responsible servant of the early church.

Romans 16:1

- Junia was another outstanding example of living a life of Christian sacrifice.

Romans 16:7

These are just a few of the notable women in the bible. So far, there seems to be credibility to the egalitarian perspective.

Egalitarian Point 3: God distributed spiritual gifts without regard to gender, and leadership should follow gifting.

When the spirit came upon the apostles at Pentecost and they began speaking in tongues, Peter quoted Joel’s prophecy to explain what was happening:

Acts 2:16-18: 16 but this is what was spoken of through the prophet Joel: 17 AND IT SHALL BE IN THE LAST DAYS, God says, THAT I WILL POUR FORTH OF MY SPIRIT ON ALL MANKIND; AND YOUR SONS AND YOUR DAUGHTERS SHALL PROPHESY, AND YOUR YOUNG MEN SHALL SEE VISIONS, AND YOUR OLD MEN SHALL DREAM DREAMS; 18 EVEN ON MY BONDSLAVES, BOTH MEN AND WOMEN, I WILL IN THOSE DAYS POUR FORTH OF MY SPIRIT and they shall prophesy.

Sons AND daughters. Both men AND women. This showed that spirit-empowered ministry was not limited by gender. Egalitarians point out that if women could publicly

prophesy, then teaching should be open to them as well. Just for clarification, “prophesy” doesn’t necessarily mean telling the future. The core meaning of prophesy is “to speak on God’s behalf,” meaning to declare His truth, His will or His correction.

Prophecy (noun)—refers to the message itself—a revelation, instruction, warning or encouragement from God.

To prophesy (verb)—refers to the act of speaking that message under the influence of the holy spirit.

This Old Testament prophecy cited in the New Testament puts men and women on an equal footing.

If we look at the broader teaching on gifts, none of these passages restrict gifts to only men:

1 Corinthians 12:7-11: 7 But to each one is given the manifestation of the spirit for the common good. 8 For to one is given the word of wisdom through the spirit, and to another the word of knowledge according to the same spirit; 9 to another faith by the same spirit, and to another gifts of healing by the one spirit, 10 and to another the effecting of miracles, and to another prophecy, and to another the distinguishing of spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, and to another the interpretation of tongues. 11 But one and the same spirit works all these things, distributing to each one individually just as He wills.

1 Corinthians 12:28: And God has appointed in the church, first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, administrations, various kinds of tongues.

Romans 12:6,9: 6 Since we have gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, each of us is to exercise them accordingly… 9 Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor what is evil; cling to what is good.

An egalitarian would say: God Himself arranged the gifts and roles within the church, and He gave these gifts broadly to the whole body without specifying gender.

But from an egalitarian point of view, we see a lot of gender equality so far. It makes sense to take it further.

Notice, we are not yet responding because we want to first clearly represent this perspective.

Egalitarian Point 4: Based on these reasonings, there are other points to consider:

- Christians are redeemed from sin and death; therefore, the New Creation should have a new equality.
- There are several New Testament scriptures we will look at more closely that advise Christian women to learn in silence. The argument is, because this contradicts every aspect of freedom in Christ, they must be referring only to the specific culture in context.
- Why keep any woman from using her teaching gift if it is from God?

Today in many churches, women already lead much of the ministry—children’s work, prayer, counseling, hospitality and missionary work. Many congregations would struggle without their leadership. So some ask, if women already do most of the ministry, why not recognize it formally?

We've stated these four egalitarian points without responding because we want to understand their perspective. We will address each point one at a time and look at it as best as we can through the lens of Scripture.

Establishing the scriptural role of women in the true church:

It is clear that there can be many viewpoints regarding the expansiveness of womens roles in our Christian church communities. As we proceed to clarify these questions, we need to be open to receiving not only what the Scriptures say, but also what they mean across thousands of years of Christian history.

This topic promises to be not only fascinating and emotional, but, at its core, is extremely fundamental and important to our understanding.

It’s time to dig in, so let’s start with our theme text.

Does being “equal in Christ” mean that all roles are open to all Christians?

This is an important and foundational place for us to begin. Paul in Galatians does without a doubt “level the playing field” regarding being in Christ. Now we need to understand what this newly acquired equality actually means so we can rightly apply it to our lives.

Egalitarian Point 1: Men and women are equal in value and equal in access to ministry roles.

Let’s review our theme scripture:

Galatians 3:27-29: 27 For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ. 28 There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus. 29 And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s descendants, heirs according to promise.

Paul is focusing on three important areas. Does this new equality REMOVE what previously existed?

1. There is neither Jew nor Greek—this speaks to heritage:

In other words, our ethnicity does not limit our standing in Christ.

Has our ethnicity been removed?

No. Both Jews and non-Jews are called to the same calling. They will still have the same ethnicity they had before; that is part of who they were, part of what defines them. The ethnicity, the heritage, does not go away.

2. There is neither slave nor free man—this speaks to social status:

In other words, our social status does not limit our standing in Christ.

Has our social status been removed?

No. Both slave and free stand on the same foundation of Christ. There is no distinction.

When Paul speaks of “slaves” and “masters,” he is addressing the everyday working relationships of his time. We aren’t normalizing or excusing slavery. We are looking at the principles that apply to modern employees and employers. There is even a hierarchy among employees in a company.

Jonathan, remember way back in the day when you and I worked at the cabinet shop? I was the general manager and you ran the big, monster electronic saw. I’d come out with the order and say, “Jonathan, here is the cut list.”

Jonathan: And I’d say, “Yes, Sir!”

You never really said that! But the point is there was an order, a hierarchy, and by working together, we got the job done.

With the sense of social status not being removed, how did the Apostle Paul teach?

Ephesians 6:5-6: 5 Slaves, be obedient to those who are your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in the sincerity of your heart, as to Christ; 6 not by way of eyeservice, as men-pleasers, but as slaves of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart.

Knowing Christ doesn’t suddenly free us from our duties; it changes our attitude and perspective, hopefully, making us an even better worker. Paul was saying to those involved in servitude in those days, Do your work well because you now represent Christ.

Now let’s look at how Paul teaches the other side of the social order:

Colossians 4:1: Masters, grant to your slaves justice and fairness, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven.

We can see the equality in these two teachings. Paul is not saying, Do not be the master, or Do not be the worker, the slave. He is not recommending a change of status, only a change of perspective: Do what you are doing to the best of your ability because you represent Christ.

3. There is neither male nor female—this speaks to gender: In other words, our gender does not limit our standing in Christ. But just like you weren’t suddenly no longer Greek, or no longer a servant once you became a Christian, you were still physically either male or female. We are all called to be the bride of Christ under the headship of the bridegroom.

Has gender identification been removed?

No. It is now to be used as a tool of sacrifice and service, just like everything else, like your social position, your heritage.

How does the Apostle Peter teach along these lines?

1 Peter 3:1-2: 1 In the same way, you wives, be submissive to your own husbands so that even if any of them are disobedient to the word, they may be won without a word by the behavior of their wives, 2 as they observe your chaste and respectful behavior.

There are many positive things we could say about the responsibility the wife is given to be an example. It doesn’t take words; it just takes observing who they are to see Christlikeness. That is a high-level application of what we are talking about. It does talk about being submissive, but it also talks about being an incredible example in that context.

The Apostle Paul says this to husbands:

Ephesians 5:25: Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the church and gave himself up for her.

Here we have the other side of the coin. We could say, “Well, all they have to do is love their wives.” But, let’s think about that—just as Christ also loved the church. How does Christ love the church, his faithful followers? He teaches them, guides them, works with them and is an example to them. Above all, he lived and died for them! He never acted against their highest and best benefit. THAT is the standard the Christian husband must meet and uphold. What an an incredible responsibility!

Equality in Christ changes our standing before God, but not the structure of the roles He established.

The equality in Christ expressed in Galatians is not a disregard for heritage, social status or gender. It is an equal invitation for ALL who are called to stand on the one solid foundation of Christ.

This standing doesn’t change our situation in life; rather, it focuses on serving from where we stand. And there is a great freedom in serving from where we stand!

This next scripture makes a big point—equality in Christ does not erase the distinctions God built into the body—it redirects them toward His purpose:

1 Corinthians 12:16-18: 16 And if the ear says, Because I am not an eye, I am not a part of the body, it is not for this reason any the less a part of the body. 17 If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the sense of smell be? 18 But now God has placed the members, each one of them, in the body, just as He desired.

Paul uses an important metaphor. The church is a body, and each faithful Christian is pictured as a different body part with a different function. God Himself places each member where He wants them, with gifts and roles suited to His purpose—as He desired.

Because I am not in that role, and I only play this role, does that mean I am less important? No. It means we are all in this together. Without one, the other cannot function. There is an incredible, intertwined unity. Again, when we look at Galatians 3:27-29, we can see a level playing field in terms of unity, but we can also see what it preserves in terms of diversity within that body.

Establishing the scriptural role of women in the true church:

So far, our foundation is clear. The equality in Christ all Christians have is related to our equal standing upon the merit of Jesus. While this equality does not erase our heritage, social status or gender, it does make those things tools of service as we walk together in Christ.

Our differences are tools of service. When we bring those together, we use those differing tools to work on the same goals in Christ.

Egalitarian Point 2: There were MANY women in leadership roles in both the Old and New Testaments. First, let’s focus on the Old Testament.

Earlier we mentioned Deborah and Huldah.

- Deborah served as both a prophetess and a civil judge in Israel, offering wisdom, settling disputes, and delivering God’s direction during a time of national crisis (Judges 4–5). She courageously supported Barak in battle and played a key role in Israel’s victory over Sisera.
- Huldah was a respected prophetess in the days of King Josiah. When the long-lost Book of the Law was rediscovered, the high priest and royal officials sought her counsel, and she delivered God’s message of both judgment and mercy. (2 Kings 22; 2 Chronicles 34)
- Another example is the wise woman of Abel, who negotiated directly with the captain of David’s army and saved her entire city through courage and wise diplomacy. (2 Samuel 20:14–22)

These women were faithful, courageous and deeply influential, and Scripture honors them for it. Their stories show how powerfully God used women throughout Israel’s history.

At the same time, their remarkable service didn’t include the highest levels of

spiritual authority over Israel. The question here is regarding leadership. None of them—nor any other woman in the Old Testament—were appointed to the leadership roles that represented the nation before God.

This isn’t a dismissal of their value. It simply reflects the consistent structure God established for spiritual authority, even as He used women in significant and meaningful ways.

It is important to recognize how God arranged and placed the roles or offices of His people in a pattern in the Old Testament.

This Old Testament pattern matters because the New Testament consistently builds its teaching about church order on the same creation-based structure, not on cultural norms. It is critical to understand that we have a godly basis that goes back long before culture.

Moses put the Law in place as God told him, and Leviticus records many rules and regulations of the Law. Leviticus 21 thoroughly discusses the limitations that were imposed on those who made up the priesthood. The priesthood is important to consider because it represented the highest spiritual authority in Israel, and its structure reveals God’s intentional design.

If we want to understand the mind of God and the role of humanity, we need to look at how He structured things, especially when it came to directly honoring and worshiping Him, and how He communicated His will to the people.

These verses in Leviticus are obviously for males only. The tribe of Levi consisted of both men and women, but women were NOT part of the priesthood.

Why? This structure was not arbitrary. It reflects the order of creation, the consequences of sin and the roles God established.

It goes back to Genesis, original sin and the consequences both Adam and Eve suffered.

The Apostle Paul speaks of the creation of Adam and Eve:

1 Corinthians 11:7-9: 7… he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of man. 8 For man does not originate from woman, but woman from man; 9 For indeed man was not created for the woman’s sake, but woman for the man’s sake.

As a woman, this passage in 1 Corinthians opened everything up for me. God’s original design for Adam and Eve included headship—(like it or not!) woman was made from man and for man—before sin entered the world. Headship is not about superiority and subservience. It is about a harmonious partnership.

As we will see in Part II, this headship of male and female symbolizes the beautiful picture of the relationship between Christ and his church. He (Adam/man) is the image and glory of God, but the woman (Eve) is the glory of man. We are reading from the New Testament to understand the foundation of both the Old and New Testaments in terms of hierarchy and responsibility. This was a harmonious partnership. It was not a beating down or form of servitude. There was a headship, but the partnership required the unity of two different beings to accomplish what neither could do alone. This was God’s original basis for the relationships between men and women.

But what happened? Eve was deceived by Satan, and Adam sinned willingly.

This resulted in specific consequences for both. Eve’s consequences were pain in childbirth and a new subservient role:

Genesis 3:16: To the woman He said, I will greatly multiply your pain in childbirth, in pain you will bring forth children; yet your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.

- The creation order of God’s design was headship. - The result of sin was subservience.

We can see that one was a glorious partnership of honor, protection and shared purpose, and the other became permission for men to dominate and for women to be diminished. The glory of partnership was replaced by a pattern that could be twisted in countless harmful ways.

God set it up a certain way. As Christians, we respect the word, mind and will of God. We build our understanding and foundation on God’s word, not on man’s interpretation.

Adam’s consequences included pain in providing sustenance and the process of death:

Genesis 3:17-19: 17 Then to Adam He said, Because you have listened to the voice of your wife, and have eaten from the tree about which I commanded you, saying, You shall not eat from it; Cursed is the ground because of you; in toil you will eat of it all the days of your life. 18 Both thorns and thistles it shall grow for you; And you will eat the plants of the field; 19 By the sweat of your face you will eat bread, till you return to the ground, because from it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return.

The fall shows what happens when God's order is ignored. Following the fall, the original beautiful headship was further defined by this decree in Genesis 3:16 (he shall rule over you), which in the fallen state often devolved into the tyranny and conflict observed against women throughout history. God didn’t command men to dominate women;

rather, He predicted that sinful men would do such a thing. Male domination is a result of sin, not God’s original design.

Just as death remains a consequence of sin, the struggle and imbalance between men and women remains as well.

God allowed sin as a learning experience, and made provision so that all will have the opportunity to live in righteousness.

God is as good as His word. We believe Him when he explains how we were created. We believe Him when we tells us about consequences of not following His word. We understand this is all in the ultimate best interest of mankind.

The consequences for sin would remain, even when His chosen people followed Him. Remember, Israel followed Him, but they fell down again and again by idolatry, and they suffered for it. Each time they came crawling back and begged for forgiveness, He would forgive them. But sin is consequential for both men and women.

Establishing the scriptural role of women in the true church:

The Old Testament examples of women who served God in truly remarkable ways teach us that God has, all along the way, used women to directly fulfill His will. These examples reinforce God’s respect for women, as He used them mightily within the context of the original design of creation and the consequences for sin.

We have just touched on the New Testament, but already we have laid a foundation based on some of the viewpoints of the egalitarian perspective, questioning some of their basis. We have looked at the Old Testament and given ourselves a strong foundation for understanding how all this works.

With this Old Testament foundation in place, we can now turn to the New Testament to see how these principles continue and how women served powerfully within that structure. That’s the key. The point of this whole discussion is how are we doing within the structure of what God said and what He wants for us.

In Part II, we will continue our discussion of the differences between these two views on women as pastors. We will begin with New Testament examples of women in influential and leadership roles.

We will discuss the impact of New Testament gifts of the spirit and also weigh in on what it means when Paul says that women should learn in silence.

There is a lot coming up here regarding the true meaning of the relationship between men and women in the true church, who should be pastors and who should not. Much more to come!

So, should women be pastors?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!
