due to feelings of remorse or guilt; twinge of conscience)

The concept of repentance: primary words in the New Testament: #3338 and #3340/3341 (noun/verb)

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon explains the distinction between these two words as emotional vs. actual change:

- 3338 refers to an emotional change; 3340 to a change of choice,
- 3338 has reference to particulars; 3340 to the entire life,
- 3338 nothing but regret even amounting to remorse; 3340 that reversal of moral purpose known as repentance;

#3338 examples:

Matthew 27:3: (KJV) Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself <3338>, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders.

Matthew 21:28-29: (NRSV) 28 What do you think? A man had two sons; he went to the first and said, Son, go and work in the vineyard today. 29 He answered, I will not; but later he changed his mind <3338> and went.

#3340 examples:

Acts 17:30-31: (NRSV) 30 While God has overlooked the times of human ignorance, now He commands all people everywhere to repent <3340>, 31 because he has fixed a day on which He will have the world judged in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed, and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.

Matthew 11:21: (NASB) Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles had occurred in Tyre and Sidon which occurred in you, they would have repented <3340> long ago in sackcloth and ashes.

#3341 example:

Acts 5:31: (KJV) Him hath God exalted with His right hand to be a prince and a saviour, for to give repentance <3341> to Israel, and forgiveness of sins.

David’s Prayer for Forgiveness

Overview, Psalm 51. “To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came unto him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba” (Psalm 51, Title).

David’s prayer for forgiveness after his sin with Bathsheba is rightly considered a model expression of repentance and plea for forgiveness. It is noteworthy that this Psalm is as- signed to the chief musician — as a hymn to be repeatedly sung. There is no attempt to hide or downplay his misdeed, his repentance is both public and, by repetition, enduring.

Nor does he wait for his sin to be discovered, but makes his public confession “when Nathan the prophet came unto him,” upon the first realization of the enormity of his guilt.

“Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy loving- kindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mer- cies blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I acknowl- edge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me.

Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest. Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me. Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom. Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psalms 51:1-7).

SIN AND INIQUITY

In these few verses David uses three different Hebrew words to describe the error of his ways. These are repre- sented by the English words “iniquity,” “sin,” and “trans- gression.” We demonstrate the distinction in these terms in the chart below.

________________________________________________________

Strong English Heb.

No.

Definition

Iniquity Avon 5771 Root: Twist, Distort* Sin Chatah 2403 Root: To miss [the mark] Transgression Pesha 6588 Rebellion

* Definition from Brown, Driver, Riggs Lexicon ________________________________________________________

From the above definitions we can infer that to sin, to miss the mark as an archer with good intent does not always hit a bull’s eye, is to err with no intention of doing wrong; while iniquity, a twisting or distortion of right principles, is more reprehensible.

Verse 5 illustrates a further difference between the words for “sin” and “iniquity.” We are “born in sin,” but “shapened in iniquity.” Behavioral scientists have long recognized that the two vital elements that shape a man’s character are he-

redity and environment. David expresses the same thought.

We are born in sin. Genetically the effects of original sin are passed down from one generation to another. But we are shaped in iniquity. Iniquity is not an inherited trait, it is a result of environmental forces.

TRANSGRESSIONS

The third word the Psalmist uses to describe his wrong- doing is “transgression.” From the table above we see that the Hebrew word used here suggests rebellion. Rebellion is compared to witchcraft in 1 Samuel 15:23, a passage which Adam Clarke translates “As transgression comes from iniq- uity, divination from teraphim, and rebellion from stubborn- ness, so because thou hast rejected the word of the LORD, he hath also rejected thee [Saul] from being king.”

If this is correct, then transgression is an outgrowth of iniquity. Partial willfulness leads to greater willfulness, which in turn leads to stubbornness and its successor, rebellion.

This reasoning suggests that David recognized three gra- dations in sin, pleading guilty to all three — inherited sin (chata, sin), measurable willfulness (avon, iniquity), and stub- born persistence in a wrong course (pasha, rebelliousness).

All three are within the forgiving power of God. “Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children’s children, unto the third and to the fourth genera- tion” (Exodus 34:7).

ANTIDOTES

The verbs the penitent uses in his prayer as he pleads for remedies for his guilt are also instructive. We will examine ten of these antidotes from Psalm 51.

(1) “Blot out my transgressions” (verse 1) (2) “Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity” (verse 2) (3) “Cleanse me from my sin” (verse 2) (4) “Purge me with hyssop and I shall be clean” (verse 7) (5) “Wash me and I shall be whiter than snow” (verse 7) (6) “Hide thy face from my sins” (verse 9) (7) “Blot out my transgression” (verse 9) (8) “Create in me a clean heart” (verse 10) (9) “Renew a right spirit within me” (verse 10) (10) “Deliver me from blood-guiltiness” (verse 14)

(1) “Blot Out My Transgressions” — The allusion is to a charge that is written in a book, as in a court record. He would have these charges removed from the record. This he pleads on the basis of God’s mercy and not on the basis of justice. Isaiah 43:25 states, “I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remem- ber thy sins.” It is a plea to God’s magnanimity (“for mine own sake”) that willfulness can be removed from the annals of the divine court. (2) “Wash Me Thoroughly from My Iniquity” — The Hebrew word for “wash” is kabac (Strong’s 3526) and liter-

ally means “to whiten.” On four occasions it is translated “fuller (dyer).” It would not be inappropriate to render it “bleach.”

The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia has an in- teresting description of the cleansing process used by the fuller. “The Syrian indigo dyer still uses a cleaning process closely allied to that pictured on the Egyptian monuments.

The unbleached cotton is soaked in water and then sprinkled with the powdered ashes of the ishnan, locally called qali, and then beaten in heaps on a flat stone either with another stone or with a large wooden paddle. The cloth is washed free from the alkali by small boys treading on it in a running stream or in many changes of clean water (compare En-rogel, literally, “foot fountain,” but translated also “fuller’s foun- tain” because of the fuller’s method of washing their cloth).”

The earliest soaps were powdered ashes, usually veg- etable but sometimes also from burnt animals. These ashes were called qali, from which we derive our English word alkali, a main ingredient in soap today. Probably from this usage the ashes of the red heifer (Numbers 19:17-19) were used as part of a spiritual cleansing in the Tabernacle.

The word ishnan, used above, is of Indian origin and de- scribes the purification process used by the Sikh community.

The Imperial College Union on London, commenting on this purification ritual, states: “The Sikhs are told to clean the body and mind from vices and sins. The Sikh must wash up the body, clean the mind in nectarine stream and bathe the soul in love of God.”

Thus David is praying for a thorough (Hebrew, repeated) cleansing by the use of symbolic ashes and repeatedly being trod underfoot — a recognition of the need of chastising experiences to correct him from the error of his ways.

(3) “Cleanse Me from My Sin” — One of Professor Strong’s definitions for the word translated cleanse (taher, Strong’s 2891) implies decontamination. Sin is an inherent contaminant. Only the blood of Christ can remove the con- taminant of sin. David desires cleansing from the effects of Adamic sin and the chastisements necessary to remove his willfulness.

(4) “Purge Me with Hyssop” — Though this is possi- bly a reference to the ritual cleansing of ancient Israel through the sprinkling of the ashes of the red heifer mixed with burnt hyssop (Numbers 19:1-14), it more likely refers to the cleansing of the leper where the hyssop was used for sprin- kling blood on the sick man (Leviticus 14:6, 7). Alternatively, it might be a reference to the first Passover in Egypt, when hyssop was used to sprinkle the door-posts and lintels as protection from the death angel of the last plague preceding the Exodus.

The word “purge” is the Hebrew chata, the same word usually translated “sin” or “sin offering.” Adam Clarke trans- lates Psalm 51:7, “Thou shalt make a sin offering for me with hyssop.” It might be worth noting here that the American Standard Version correctly translates Number 19:9, speak- ing of the sacrifice of the red heifer, “it is a sin offering.”1

Leviticus 14:13 similarly relates the offering in the cleans- ing of leper to a sin offering.

The purging which here cleanses evidently refers to the chata of verse 2, alluding to Adamic sin.

(5) “Wash Me and I Shall Be Whiter Than Snow” — As in verse 2, the word “wash” is used to describe the thor- ough washing of the fuller, a whitening or bleaching by the application of an alkaline soap and the trampling under foot to allow the ashes to thoroughly penetrate the pores of the cloth before being rinsed away in cold water. This was not to remove the sin but the concomitant iniquity for which David claimed personal responsibility.

(6) “Hide Thy Face from My Sins” — Only the re- deeming merit of Christ can cover our Adamic weaknesses from the searching eyes of that divine justice which has “purer eyes than to behold evil” (Habakkuk 1:13).

(7) “Blot Out My Transgression” — Recognizing that his own stubborn willfulness had caused him to commit the sin with Bathsheba, he again pleads God’s mercy in erasing that shortcoming on the commitment that David would pledge not to become a repeat offender.

David’s Repentance

(8) “Create In Me a Clean Heart” — Mending the heart was not enough, there was the need for a clean heart to be created. Such a spiritual heart transplant can come only at the cost of the death of the old heart. Paul states the prin- ciple, as applied to another age, thus: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails any thing, nor uncircum- cision, but a new creature” (Galatians 6:15). David knew he could not accomplish this, but that it would need to be created by God alone. (9) “Renew a Right Spirit Within Me” — Here he requests the mending. He once had had a right spirit. He had lost that with his dreadful misdeed. He desired to re- turn to his former spirit and consequent relationship with God. This would require a process in which he would need to cooperate with a determined effort to reform. (10) “Deliver Me from Bloodguiltiness” — Verse 14, in which this expression is found, begins a new section of the Psalm. The writer turns from the sin against Bathsheba to focus on the sin against Uriah, whom David arranged to have killed in battle, hoping to cover up the sin of adultery.

Recognizing his guilt for that blood, he throws himself on God’s mercy and asks deliverance from that burdening emotion.

Guilt has both a proper and improper place in our lives.

This heavy overburdening emotion should, like a weighty load, cause our knees to buckle in prayer. Once it has pro- duced that repentant condition of heart, divine forgiveness must be accepted and the burden laid aside or else we will not be able to rise again. How true it is that “a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again; but the wicked [remaining non-repentant] shall fall into mischief” (Proverbs 24:16).

THE RESULT OF RESTORATION

“Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free spirit. Then will I teach transgressors thy ways; and sinners shall be converted unto thee” (Psalm 51:12, 13). Here is the reason why God permits mistakes in our Christian lives. Lessons learned can become lessons taught.

This is the method by which the Church is trained to be- come teachers with Christ. This is how the Church’s part in the sin offering works.

There is great truth in the tale that is told of the conversa- tion between the disciple and his teacher. Disciple: “Tell me, Master, what is the source of your wisdom.” Master: “Good choices, by son.” Disciple: “And how did you learn to make such good choices.” Master: “By experience.” Disciple: “And how did you receive such experience.” Master: “Bad choices, my son, bad choices.”

Solomon phrased it this way: “And I gave my heart to seek and search out by wisdom concerning all things that are done under heaven: this sore travail hath God given to the sons of man to be exercised therewith” (Ecclesiastes 1:13). To which David agrees, “Before I was afflicted I went astray: but now have I kept thy word. ... It is good for me that I have been afflicted; that I might learn thy statutes” (Psalm 119:67, 71).

ADDITIONAL SCRIPTURAL CONFIRMATION

Three additional scriptures can be cited which imply the same distinction between sin, iniquities, and transgressions.

Isaiah 53:5 — “But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”

It was not Jesus’ death, but his wounding, the daily dealing with man’s condition, which gave him the necessary empa- thy to help us overcome our rebelliousness. “For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succor them that are tempted” (Hebrews 2:18). Likewise, it was his bruising that was especially for our iniquities. The Hebrew daka, here translated “bruised,” literally means to crush under foot. This is the same process that was used in the ancient cloth washing of the fuller, a term we also noted was for iniquities. Jesus suffered at the hands of iniquitous men so as to understand iniquity and help men to overcome it in his kingdom.

Leviticus 16:21 — “And Aaron shall lay both his hands upon the head of the live goat, and confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgres- sions in all their sins, putting them upon the head of the goat, and shall send him away by the hand of a fit man into the wilderness.”

In the offering of the scapegoat on the Day of Atonement, it was not the sins of Israel that were removed. These had been atoned for by the sin offering of a bullock and a goat.

Rather it was the iniquities and the amount of transgression in their sins which were thus taken away. To paraphrase the latter portion of this verse, “confess over him all the partial willful sins and the degree of willfulness in their sinful ways.”

This work is generally, and we believe correctly, applied by Bible Students to the work of the Great Company, as is im- plied in our third text:

Ezekiel 44:10 — “The Levites that are gone away far from me, when Israel went astray, which went astray away from me after their idols; they shall even bear their iniquity.”

This text appears to confirm the identification of the scape- goat with the Great Company, for it is generally agreed that this is the class whom the Levites typify. Here, as with the scapegoat, it is not a sin offering, but to erase iniquity that they are to accomplish. The reason is given as well, “because they went far away from me after their idols” (note also Ezekiel 44:15, 48:11).

How often, in each of our lives, we find ourselves guilty of all three — sin, iniquity, and transgression — Adamic weak- ness, perverse willfulness, and stubborn rebellion. How grateful we are that God has, in Christ, provided a remedy for all three. — Carl Hagensick ___________

(1) Calling the red heifer “a sin offering” should not be confused with the sin offering of Leviticus 16. The Apostle Paul specifies those sin offerings in which “the blood was brought into the sanctuary for sin” (Hebrews 13:11). Israel had many sin offerings, but the one on the Day of Atonement was special and unique.

### Study Questions

1. Why is forgiveness not automatic even for a disciple of Christ? What conditions must be met for

forgiveness and cleansing? (1 John 1:9)

2. How does understanding the Greek word homologeo deepen the meaning of “confession?” How does

“saying the same thing as God” change the way we view our sin? (1 John 1:9)

3. How does King David describe the internal consequences of unconfessed sin? What is the difference if we

confess our sins like David? (Psalms 32:3-5)

4. Why was it necessary for Nathan to confront King David? What was David’s reaction? What does David’s

immediate response teach us about humility and owning consequences? (2 Samuel 12:5-9, Psalm 32:5)

5. What happens to our confessions when we make excuses for our mistakes? How does David’s response

show the difference between excuse-making and true confession? (Psalms 32:1-5, 2 Samuel 12:13-20)

6. If God already knows everything, why does He ask us to confess our sins to Him? What does confession

accomplish in us? (Hebrews 4:12-16, Proverbs 15:3)

7. How does the contrast of light and darkness help us understand why confession is necessary for

fellowship with God? (1 John 1:5-10)

8. What’s the different between confessing our sins to God (Greek: homologeo) and confessing sins to one

another (Greek: exomologeo) What unique benefits come from each? (1 John 1:9, James 5:16)

9. What is the difference between regret and true repentance? Which one describes your usual response to

sin, and how can you move toward genuine repentance? (Matthew 11;21, Luke 22:61-62)

10. How can you be sure that you are truly “saying the same thing” as God about your sin What steps can

help you stop minimizing or justifying it?

## Episode 1442 — How Do I Identify Temptation and Shut It Down?
Published: 2026-06-22
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1442-identify-temptation/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/12165533/CQ_Rewind_06-22-2026_How_Do_I_Identify_Temptation_and_Shut_it_Down.pdf

1 Corinthians 10:13: No temptation has overtaken you but such as is common to man; and God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the

temptation will provide the way of escape also, so that you will be able to endure it.

Temptation is everywhere. In fact, it may be lurking in places that we are not even aware of. Let’s put this in perspective. Who do you claim to be? If you answered that you claim to be a Christian, then the next question is: who do you serve and in whose footsteps are you therefore to walk? Our answer should be that we serve God and walk in the footsteps of Jesus our Lord! Now here’s the test. Let’s think about our associations, our work or school environments, our friends, the shows we watch, the influencers we follow, the music we listen to and the posts we make and read. Where are all these things drawing our minds to? What percentage of all these things are in exact alignment with God our Father and Jesus our Lord? Think! Be honest! You see, temptation IS everywhere!

We’re going to use the metaphor of temptation beginning as a seed—a thought, a desire, a possibility. These “seeds” fall into our lives from three sources:

1. Satan, who plants seeds meant to destroy.

2. God, who sometimes plants seeds of testing or allows them through

circumstances, for the purpose of strengthening and maturing us.

3. Our own imperfect flesh, which produces desires that can grow in either direction.

Here are the fundamental questions that will help us identify temptation so we can shut it down:

- Who do I serve?
- How is what I am thinking, feeling, saying or doing fulfilling my loyalty to God?

Let’s begin by examining the New Testament definition of temptation:

1 Corinthians 10:12–13: 12 Therefore let him who thinks he stands take heed that he does not fall. 13 No temptation <3986> has overtaken you but such as is common to man; and God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted <3985> beyond what you are able, but with the temptation <3986> will provide the way of escape also, so that you will be able to endure it.

Temptation: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3986 peirasmos; NOUN from #3985; a putting to

proof (by experiment [of good], experience [of evil], solicitation, discipline or provocation);

by implication, adversity

Tempter/test: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3985 VERB peirazo; from #3984;

to test (objectively), i.e. endeavor, scrutinize, entice, discipline:—assay,

examine, go about, prove, tempt(-er), try

The Greek word for temptation in its noun and verb forms describes a proving ground— a test that reveals what’s inside and exposes the heart. We often think of temptation only as an invitation to do something wrong, but the New Testament idea is broader—it’s any pressure that uncovers what is already growing in us. That pressure can come from the different sources listed above. That same pressure can either break us or build us, depending on what’s taking root in our hearts.

Now that we have a sense of what temptation is—that it has the capacity to grow, develop and magnify itself—let’s look at the negative and positive uses of this word.

One very negative use that speaks volumes regarding what we must be on the lookout for:

Matthew 4:3: And the tempter <3985> came and said to him, If you are the son of God, command that these stones become bread.

The tempter, with a magnetic drawing power, plants ideas in our hearts and minds that can grow, expand and develop. This is a negative use of the word temptation.

Let’s look at two positive uses that show the value of testing for the sake of strengthening rather than breaking.

God tests to build strength so He can trust our loyalty to Him:

Hebrews 11:17: By faith Abraham, when he was tested <3985>, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the promises was offering up his only begotten son;

The word tested here is the same word translated as tempter in Matthew 4:3. One is to break down and rebuild, the other is to break down and destroy. The same basic word can be used in a positive sense or a negative sense: Satan tempting or God testing.

We can and should put ourselves to the test. We should scrutinize what we think, say and do:

2 Corinthians 13:5: Test <3985> yourselves to see if you are in the faith; examine yourselves! Or do you not recognize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you—unless indeed you fail the test?

Fail the test—this is a good verse to show the expression “once saved, always saved” is not true. We have a relationship that requires ongoing faithfulness and self-examination.

What do we know about temptation so far?

Satan is THE tempter. His objective to undermine God’s will by placing temptations before God’s people is simple and powerful. We must be aware in order to stand and fight against any and all of his temptations!

1 Peter 5:8: Be of sober spirit, be on the alert. Your adversary, the devil, prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.

This situation goes beyond just temptations. This is a spiritual attack of external pressure with the adversary trying to destabilize our confidence, identity or peace. It’s when everything seems to hit us all at once, especially right after making spiritual progress. (Also see Ephesians 6:12.)

Satan is the tempter. His objective is destruction. Temptation is a great way to provoke destruction!

As human beings and disciples of Christ, we are in some ways stuck in between. We have the calling and blessing to follow Jesus, and yet we are still in an imperfect human form. We therefore can be pulled in very opposite directions.

We need to “scrutinize” ourselves and verify our true direction:

Romans 7:21–25: 21 I find then the principle that evil is present in me, the one who wants to do good. 22 For I joyfully concur with the law of God in the inner man, 23 but I see a different law in the members of my body, waging war against the law of my mind and making me a prisoner of the law of sin which is in my members.

Throughout the chapter of Romans 7, Paul shows that even devoted Christians feel a constant pull between the new mind that loves God and the old flesh that resists Him. We are all walking contradictions!

24 Wretched man that I am! Who will set me free from the body of this death? 25 Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, on the one hand I myself with my mind am serving the law of God, but on the other, with my flesh the law of sin.

This law of sin is always present; it pulls in a predictable direction, it resists the new mind, trying to drag us back into old patterns. We have to be aware—it is always there. It never goes away.

God does “test” us for the purpose of teaching and strengthening us. His testing is to be received with gratitude and confidence:

Hebrews 12:6–7: 6 FOR THOSE WHOM THE LORD LOVES HE DISCIPLINES, AND HE SCOURGES EVERY SON WHOM HE RECEIVES (quoting Proverbs 3:11-12 from the Greek Septuagint). 7 It is for discipline that you endure; God deals with you as with sons; for what son is there whom his father does not discipline?

When God allows testing, we can receive it with gratitude because He uses it for our growth. It is in His hands, from His perspective; therefore, we can trust in this testing.

We need to understand the difference between temptation, spiritual attack and testing.

- Temptation pulls us away from God through desire (James 1:14–15). Temptation weakens us.
- Spiritual attack comes from the adversary and aims to destabilize our identity and confidence, especially when we’re tired or discouraged, likened to the roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8). Spiritual attack rattles us.
- Testing pulls us toward God through discipline and growth (Hebrews 12:6–7). Testing strengthens us.

Knowing the difference helps us respond wisely:

- Temptation requires escape. - Spiritual attack requires resistance. - Testing requires endurance.

So far, the equation is simple; no matter which way we turn, there will be tests or temptations. Let’s work at making them work for us.

Now that we know the sources of our many testings, how do we determine

what to do to diligently identify and handle them?

Lucifer’s pre-satanic fall was a growing, festering and deadly desire that was fed by his own intellect.

The context of these next verses is the prophet Isaiah using Lucifer’s rebellion as a comparison to the king of Babylon.

Isaiah looks back at Lucifer’s pride and self-exaltation to show what happens when any being tries to rise above the place God has given them:

Isaiah 14:12–15: 12 How you have fallen from heaven, O star of the morning, son of the dawn! You have been cut down to the earth, you who have weakened the nations! 13 But you said in your heart...

The deadly spread of sinful desires that give birth to thoughts and plans:

- You said in your heart—it always begins in the heart when we entertain dark desires.

...I will ascend to heaven; I will raise my throne above the stars of God, and I will sit on the mount of assembly in the recesses of the north. 14 I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High.

Notice how many “I’s” are used:

- I will ascend to heaven—he was already privileged to be God’s earthly representative. - I will raise my throne above the stars of God—he was already one of the high and lofty “stars” of God, but it wasn’t enough! - I will sit on the mount of assembly in the recesses of the north—where God abides. - I will ascend above the heights of the clouds—above the influence of God’s presence with man. - I will make myself like the Most High—not replacing, but rivaling the Most High.

15 Nevertheless you will be thrust down to sheol, to the recesses of the pit.

The inevitable end result of these dark desires is destruction. Destruction will always follow unbridled temptation and action!

So, Lucifer was looking for dominion, power and authority and to usurp the rights of his Creator, who he had been honored to represent and work for.

Identifying human temptation begins with identifying where our desires are leading us. Lucifer’s fall from glory as a bright star of the morning began with his own prideful desires that started in his heart. Leaving those desires unchecked led to prideful actions.

John gives us clear warnings of this:

1 John 2:15–17: 15 Do not love the world nor the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. 16 For all that is in the world, the lust <1939> of the flesh and the lust <1939> of the eyes and the boastful pride of life, is not from the Father but is from the world. 17 The world is passing away, and also its lusts; but the one who does the will of God lives forever.

Lust: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1939 epithumia; NOUN from #1937;

a longing (especially for what is forbidden)

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) desire, craving, longing, desire for what is forbidden, lust

Lust: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1937 epithumeo; VERB from #1909 and #2372;

to set the heart upon, i.e. long for (rightfully or otherwise)

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to turn upon a thing 2) to have a desire for, long for, to desire

3a) of those who seek things forbidden

Temptation is based on desire. The Greek sense of the word adds the idea of a desire that swells and grows when fed.

The Greek picture is richer, describing a desire that swells, expands and grows when fed. Classical writers like Plato and Philo used this word to describe passions that intensify when indulged, showing that this word carries the idea of an appetite that enlarges itself when given attention.

Scripture shows how external temptation and internal desire interact, for example,

James 1:14-15: 14 But each one is tempted when he is carried away and enticed by his own lust. 15 Then when lust has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and when sin is accomplished, it brings forth death.

Lust “conceives” and “gives birth” to sin—a picture of something that grows when nurtured.

1. Temptation can come from outside us, but it only becomes powerful when it

connects with a desire inside us.

2. Desire doesn’t instantly become sin. This is good news because we can uproot it at

any stage.

The key is that sin always starts with desire; the lust (desire) of the eyes, the lust of the flesh, the boastful pride of life… It starts with that longing. This is where temptation can find its roots and grow if we allow it.

All sin is based on desire and has similar ingredients. Satan was even subject to these elements:

Isaiah 14:13–14: 13 But you said in your heart, I will ascend to heaven; (lust of the eye—he had his sights set on something higher) I will raise my throne above the stars of God, (lust of his being—he wanted to elevate himself) and I will sit on the mount of assembly in the recesses of the north. 14 I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High (the boastful pride of life—look at me!)

This is what happened to Satan, the tempter, which is a huge warning sign. If Satan was overcome by temptation, it could certainly happen to us. We must remain aware. Any one of these three elements can be a temptation if “desire” is behind it.

Humanity fell right into the trap of desire, as Satan deceived and tempted:

Genesis 3:4–6: 4 The serpent said to the woman, You surely will not die! 5 For God knows that in the day you eat from it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil. 6 When the woman saw that the tree was good for food (lust of the flesh), and that it was a delight to the eyes, (lust of the eyes) and that the tree was desirable to make one wise, (the boastful pride of life) she took from its fruit and ate; and she gave also to her husband with her, and he ate.

Satan opened Eve’s mind up to an alternate perspective of life (not the godly perspective), one that was not based on truth. Once she considered this alternative approach, her desires were awakened, and she was tempted.

The lust of the flesh—the tree was good for food.

The lust of the eyes—it was a beautiful piece of

fruit.

The boastful pride of life—it would make her wise.

The problem with temptation is that it is all lies we tell ourselves to justify our actions.

We have seen where temptation comes from and are beginning to understand how to recognize it. What are we going to be able to do about all this?

Understanding how temptation is driven by desire is an important step toward putting things in order so we can deal with whatever comes our way.

This is, at the very least, disturbing. Any and all of our human desires can, in the wrong environment or circumstances, lead us to fall.

So, my own personal desires are at the root of my own personal temptations.

Now that I know this, how do I handle them?

Here is where the real work begins. This work cannot be successful without a willingness to be thoroughly open before God in laying out our weaknesses. As a matter of fact, our degree of openness before God is directly related to how readily we will be able to grab hold of our temptations and shut them down!

Each of the following steps is about dealing with temptation at the seed stage—before it grows into something that chokes our spiritual life.

Shut it down!

Make a clear decision.

Don’t try to examine it or rationalize with it!

The principles for shutting down our temptations are clearly laid out by the Apostle Peter:

2 Peter 1:5–7: 5 Now for this very reason also, applying all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence, and in your moral excellence, knowledge, 6 and in your knowledge, self-control, and in your self-control, perseverance, and in your perseverance, godliness, 7 and in your godliness, brotherly kindness, and in your brotherly kindness, love.

What does this have to do with temptation? This is a formula for character development. We went through these verses in our Christian Character Series, beginning with Episode #1419.

We have faith, and that groundwork of faith establishes moral excellence. Moral excellence is a great way to avoid temptation, but it doesn’t stop there. We need knowledge on top of that. Then, with knowledge based on moral excellence and faith, comes self-control. How do we deal with temptation? We need self-control, but it doesn’t stop there!

We also need perseverance to plow through the daily temptations. But that perseverance has to be based on the faith, moral excellence, knowledge and self-control we’ve been working on. Now that leads to godliness, and then we can develop from there. These verses give us a clear focus on what we need to do to work through these temptations.

Let’s get into the actual temptations and what we need to do about them. These next scriptures give us the steps to take to shut down our temptations:

James 4:7–10: 7 Submit therefore to God. Resist the devil and he will flee from you. 8 Draw near to God and He will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners; and purify your hearts, you double-minded. 9 Be miserable and mourn and weep; let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy to gloom. 10 Humble yourselves in the presence of the Lord, and He will exalt you.

There is a lot of direction here. Notice all the action words, like submit, draw near, cleanse, purify and more. Let’s take apart these verses and see the progression in how to understand, face, deal with and dismiss temptations.

Shut it down! Stop thinking; start doing. Stop wondering. Do it.

SHUT IT DOWN! How? Remember, all temptation begins in our hearts with desire:

James 4:7: Submit therefore to God…

We won’t recognize temptation clearly unless our default direction is walking in God’s ways. Submit therefore to God. That’s a good way to start recognizing temptation.

At a time when we are NOT in a temptation battle, have a personal honesty session. Bluntly determine what kind of desires are tempting for YOU.

If we are serious about avoiding temptation, we want to prevent the possibility of the seeds even getting into the ground.

Psalms 1:1–3: 1 How blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand in the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers!

This man is blessed because he has resisted the temptation, but someone else might walk in the counsel of the wicked—they’re talking to somebody as they’re walking along with them.

Nor stand in the path of sinners—the wicked person’s conversation is so interesting that the person stops to continue the conversation.

Or sit in the seat of scoffers! Now this person is sitting down, off-guard, not going anywhere. They have been sucked in.

Walk—stand—sit. Potential temptation can progress when we slow down from walking in God’s direction to entertain something else. How should we have reacted?

2 But his delight is in the law of the LORD, and in His Law he meditates day and night. 3 He will be like a tree firmly planted <8362> by streams of water, which yields its fruit in its season and its leaf does not wither; and in whatever he does, he prospers.

Planted: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #8362 šāṯal; to transplant:—plant

This isn’t a wild tree; the Hebrew word for planted here means “transplanted, intentionally placed, carefully set.” God, as our Master Gardener, sets us by His nourishing water, so we fight temptation by guarding the soil and staying near His water of truth.

This is a tree deliberately moved by a gardener. Those streams of water in Hebrew (Strong’s #6388) are divided channels for irrigation, man-made waterways. So, the water supply is intentional. The righteous person is like a tree that God Himself planted by nourishing water. We fight temptation by guarding the soil, staying near water of truth and letting God shape our growth.

There is a tremendous difference between walking, standing and sitting with the scoffers versus being a tree that’s specifically transplanted to grow and prosper. Godly focus and attention can fill us and leave no extra room for temptation if we allow it to. When our mind is filled with God’s truth, there is simply less room for temptation to settle in. We crowd it out by filling the space with something better. It is imperative to not allow temptation to open a door to fill a void. Recognize it so we can shut it down.

That’s pretty simple—REMOVE OURSELVES. But that is sometimes easier said than done.

SHUT IT DOWN! How? Make the choice to take intentional corrective action when the tempting desire awakens:

James 4:7: …Resist the devil and he will flee from you.

Intentional, corrective action!

Change your posture, your environment, your company or your input. Be specific!

Disrupt the process. Don’t go peeking under that crime scene tape. It’s not for you. This is one of the strongest findings in modern psychology, and it’s amazing how closely this aligns with Scripture. Studies show people resist temptation far more effectively by changing their environment than by relying on willpower.

(Source: Psychology Today, Willpower: It’s in Your Environment, Susan Weinschenk, Ph.D., August 2012)

Resisting and removing ourselves from the temptation opens the door to preemptive strikes against it. When we take that preemptive strike, we solve the problem BEFORE it blows up!

Before it overwhelms us, we have taken it out:

Colossians 3:2–5: 2 Set your mind on the things above, not on the things that are on earth. 3 For you have died and your life is hidden with Christ in God. 4 When Christ, who is our life, is revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory. 5 Therefore consider the members of your earthly body as dead to immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed, which amounts to idolatry.

Set your mind on the things above, not on the things that are on the earth. We are supposed to be beyond such things. Once we act on our temptations, the tidal wave of consequences and grief will inevitably follow. We all know this. Only resistance based on submission to a higher cause can avert this storm—and that storm will come unless we take that intentional action in terms of removing ourselves!

Sometimes temptation sneaks up so fast that we have to say, “What just happened? How did I let that door open?”

So last Friday morning, right before the three of us got together to discuss this topic, I dropped my wife Jewel off at the airport. She’s going to be away for a few days. And as I’m driving away, this little thought pops into my head: “I’m on my own! I can eat whatever I want today!”

Okay, so you had a shift in circumstance, and suddenly, the world opened up with all kinds of opportunities! We all know that eating anything we want is not the best thing. But we take this little piece and see it as a principle for how temptation works in a much bigger way. In our lives, the way it works is that suddenly the world opens up with all kinds of opportunities because we perceive that something is giving us permission to go in a direction we ought not to go.

Then the GPS takes me on some bizarre back road. I’m 15 minutes out of my way, frustrated, annoyed, not in my normal state of mind. And that’s when it hit me: my mindset had already shifted. I wasn’t thinking spiritually—I was thinking emotionally. I was irritated, tired and off-balance. I was miserable.

That’s exactly how it works. Vulnerability grows when those things happen. Frustration, fatigue and irritation create openings.

So, I’m driving along this weird route, and suddenly I pass a bakery. And instantly my brain goes: “Cinnamon rolls! Cherry pie! I deserve this!”

Now normally, that wouldn’t even tempt me—Jewel and I are trying to eat healthier. But because she wasn’t home…and because I was so frustrated… that cherry pie suddenly looked like the answer to all my problems.

And that’s the point. “Cherry pie” becomes a euphemism for all kinds of things we normally wouldn’t consider but suddenly feel justified to experience because our circumstances changed, especially when we add in a bunch of strong emotions.

But I caught myself. I literally said out loud, “Nope. I’m going home and eating my yogurt.” And I kept driving.

Was it cherry yogurt?

No, it was plain yogurt!

But that’s the victory! You recognized the shift, reassessed your emotions and shut it down before it grew. Such a little experience, but such a BIG LESSON!

This lesson has another layer—it shows how critical your wife’s input is when the two of you are making mutual decisions. Mutual accountability gives us the support we need to deal with and resist temptations.

SHUT IT DOWN! How? “Nope, I’m going home to eat my yogurt!”

We need to honestly reassess our emotions and thought processes regarding a temptation.

Prayerfully and honestly examine how the door to temptation was opened. Then, decide to shut it down!

James 4:8: Draw near to God and He will draw near to you…

Face the reality of how temptation came to life. Phone?

Website? Memories? Social Media? Friends? Old habits?

Addictive behaviors? A change in circumstance that brought new opportunity?

Expose the process so we can build walls—or spiritual crime tape—around it!

Psychologists note that we are most vulnerable to temptation when we’re tired, stressed, or emotionally off-balance—which is exactly when the adversary tries to rattle us.

(Source: Psychology Today, HALT: Hungry, Angry, Lonely, Tired, Beverly D. Flaxington, 2019)

Sometimes temptation feels comforting, familiar and even like something we should be entitled to, just like “everybody else.” That’s why shutting temptation down requires honesty.

We might stop and pray, “Lord, this desire feels good to me right now, but I know it won’t lead me to You.” We have to drag the temptation into the light and honestly examine it.

Where do I live? Is it in the treacherous lair of my own desires or is it in God’s protective shadow? What is my address?

Psalms 91:1–4: 1 He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty. 2 I will say to the LORD, My refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust! 3 For it is He who delivers you from the snare of the trapper and from the deadly pestilence. 4 He

will cover you with His pinions, and under His wings you may seek refuge; His faithfulness is a shield and bulwark.

Where we dwell is where we live; therefore, abide in the shadow of the Almighty. If we honestly reassess our emotions and thought processes regarding our temptations, we should want to go back home. We should want to return to that spiritually-based place where we can thrive.

Giving in to temptation only produces lies, deceit and misery. On the contrary, seeking God’s sacred presence here and now produces a fortress of protection and righteousness that was described in Psalm 91 above.

Temptation pushes momentum the other way. Reassess and then take action!

So, the bottom line here is, it’s a process; it’s always a process! Let’s face it: to walk in God’s grace with purity is absolutely worth whatever it takes!

We’ve learned to recognize our temptations, remove ourselves from them and then

reassess our emotions. What’s next?

The next several steps are in place to take what we’ve discovered and shape that discovery into a new practical and practicable pattern of response and behavior. All of this sure seems like a lot of work. Newsflash—it is! The key here is how the sincere and godly effort we put into abandoning our temptations brings us into reverent harmony with God through Christ.

In gardening, this is the moment we amend or enrich the soil—add what’s missing so the right plants can grow. Reshape the handling of our emotions and thought processes.

SHUT IT DOWN!

How? Surrender to God’s will, God’s way, God’s strength and God’s providence!

James 4:8: …Cleanse your hands, you sinners…

Intentionally adopt a new approach to the challenge. Write it down, seek accountability, seek support or get needed guidance. Don’t get stuck in reacting; respond instead!

Don’t get stuck with the reaction. That is where temptations really come in. We have something happen—the stimulus—then we have an immediate gut reaction inside ourselves. We cannot control the gut reaction, but we can ‘pause and consider.’ “How do I choose to respond instead of just reacting?” Don’t get stuck reacting. Take a breath… and then respond.

Our friend Cher-El gave a great real-life example while helping a 12-year-old prepare for Bible camp. She used a simple scenario: you’re doing great with healthy eating… and suddenly someone brings out your favorite ice cream. That’s the temptation. How do you fight it? The same way Jesus did — with Scripture you’ve already planted in your heart. Verses about self-control, wisdom and faithfulness come to mind, and suddenly you’re responding with truth and not reacting to the ice cream. The temptation loses its power because God’s Word was already in place before the moment arrived.

If we are in a testing time or experience with harsh consequences, we need to turn the reins over to our Father, lest we bury ourselves in ever deeper sin! It’s a choice:

James 1:2–4: 2 Consider it all joy, my brethren, when you encounter various trials <3986>, 3 knowing that the testing (a testing, by implication trustworthiness) of your faith produces endurance <5281>. 4 And let endurance have its perfect result, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.

Endurance: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5281 hupomonē; NOUN cheerful (or hopeful)

endurance, constancy:—enduring, patience, patient continuance (waiting)

The word for endurance here describes strength that stays under pressure without breaking. It’s the spiritual steadiness that keeps the seed of desire from sprouting.

Take the necessary actions. Don’t just think about it and feel bad. Don’t just hope it will be different the next time. If we are God’s through Christ, we CAN change our state of mind. God promised us HIS care, and we are to apply ourselves to standing in the power of His promises. Don’t get stuck reacting—RESPOND!

Whom do I serve?

How is what I am thinking, feeling, saying or doing fulfilling my loyalty to God?

What are the consequences if I continue on this path?

SHUT IT DOWN! How?

Open our eyes to the long-term habits and brokenness that come from giving into our temptations.

James 4:8: …purify your hearts, you double-minded.

James is describing someone trying to serve God and self at the same time, someone pulling in two directions internally. This inner conflict makes them spiritually inconsistent.

“Roll the tape forward.” Deliberately let yourself feel the potential negative consequences of our actions if you were to give in to your temptation. Dwell on the darkness and loneliness of that potential reality. Feel its pain, and then run from it!

The necessary long-term purification of our minds can only come to us through humility:

1 Peter 5:6–8: 6 Therefore humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that He may exalt you at the proper time, 7 casting all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you. 8 Be of sober spirit, be on the alert. Your adversary the devil, prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.

We return to these texts because we need to refocus our minds on the big picture and forcefully take the step of casting our issues into the hands of our benevolent heavenly Father.

What will my life look like if I move forward with this behavior?

Research shows that long-term thinking reduces impulsive behavior. Psychologists call

this Delay Discounting—the normal tendency to choose immediate gratification over

long-term good. We devalue or discount the long-term reward because the short-

term one is right in front of us.

(Source: Psychology Today, Why We Give In to Temptation, Shahram Heshmat, Ph.D. July 2017)

Psychology shows us if we take the time and intentionally do the things we need to do, like reminding ourselves of the long-term consequences, it can be a strong deterrent for something that might be disastrous.

Retraining ourselves comes after we remind ourselves of the consequences, after we roll the tape forward and visualize what will happen if we continue on this path. We find the motivation to say, “I don’t want to be in this place anymore. This is too hurtful. It never works out well. I want to be retrained.”

SHUT IT DOWN! How?

Embrace the pain AND forgiveness of our failure just as David and Paul did. They both committed ugly, mortifying sins, and instead of letting them ruin their relationship with God, they repented and used them to push forward towards holiness.

James 4:9: Be miserable and mourn and weep; let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy to gloom.

Feel the pain and focus on new habits that are spiritually driven. Journal, use Post-It notes, institute pre-determined changes in thoughts and actions. Be accountable!

Thousands of years ago, James had the answer, but today this is called Future Self Continuity. Psychologists note that when we picture our “future self,” we make wiser choices and resist short-term impulses. Long-term thinking increases self-control. Connecting with your future self reduces impulsive choices. This is the antidote to Delay Discounting.

(Source: Psychology Today, Your Future Self Is Watching You, Hal Hershfield, Ph.D., 2018)

When we retrain ourselves towards spiritually sound long-term results, we are building our ability to resist. We have reshaped our handling of emotions. We’re reminding ourselves of potential consequences, and now we are actually building something.

This is painful, especially if we have addictions or similar struggles in our past. If we have lived a broken life and are now truly fighting it by following these steps and scriptures, then we need to understand that our life isn’t broken; it just hurts. There’s a difference. Let the hurt motivate growth. We are not broken if we are fighting. Keep moving forward!

Changing any habit of reaction requires new habits and responses:

2 Peter 1:5–7: 5 …applying all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence, and in your moral excellence, knowledge, 6 and in your knowledge, self-control, and in your self-control, perseverance, and in your perseverance, godliness, 7 and in your godliness, brotherly kindness, and in your brotherly kindness, love.

We come back to these verses because they show us how to retrain ourselves. Build upon your faith moral excellence, and then knowledge, and then self-control, etc.

James 1:12: Blessed is a man who perseveres under trial; for once he has been approved, he will receive the crown of life which the Lord has promised to those who love Him.

The results of systematically fighting temptation are dramatically glorious! There is incredible wholesomeness, victory, calm, happiness, peace and godliness from retraining ourselves.

SHUT IT DOWN! How? Heavily rely on the redeeming price that Jesus paid for us and follow him:

James 4:10: Humble yourselves in the presence of the Lord, and He will exalt you.

There’s the recommitment! Be humble so God can lift us up. We can’t lift ourselves up.

Wake up each morning to a newly created, godly routine. Maybe we wake up and say, “This is what I’m NOT going to do today.” Build other new routines that crowd out the dark desires that fuel temptation. Know your weaknesses—because Satan surely does.

Research shows that accountability and value-based identity significantly increase self-control. People make better choices when they remember who they want to be, connect their actions to their values, and have supportive relationships.

(Source: Psychology Today, The Power of Accountability, Steven Stosny, Ph.D., 2014)

Create new routines. Start with one and build with others. Here’s a way to put the commitment in place:

Galatians 2:20: I have been crucified with Christ; and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me; and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.

I have been crucified with Christ, and that is the life that I am pursuing. God’s power can and will overwhelm temptation at any stage only if we let it. We simply need humility, focus and passion for God’s ways. We need to follow these steps and execute them in order. He will overrule our experiences, and we need to follow His leadings. While not easy, it is attainable.

We ARE blessed! When we have to deal with the temptations of our lives, we must recognize we are not alone because we have God through Christ. If we choose to, we can rely on other like-minded Christians around us. We can have accountability and share friendship and encouragement. Maybe we need some professional help. Whatever it is, we do not have to be alone. The Scriptures give us a step-by-step process in which we can identify, deal with, focus on and overcome these temptations and live a life that brings glory to God. Isn’t that the most important thing?

So, how do I identify temptation and shut it down?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.
