Now a masterful example of overcoming temptation:

Luke 4:1–13: (ASV) 1 And Jesus, full of the holy spirit, returned from the Jordan, and was led in the spirit in the wilderness 2 during forty days, being tempted of the devil. And he did eat nothing in those days: and when they were completed, he hungered. 3 And the devil said unto him, If thou art the son of God, command this stone that it become bread. (lust of the flesh) 4 And Jesus answered unto him, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone. 5 And he led him up, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time. (lust of the eyes) 6 And the devil said unto him, To thee will I give all this authority, and the glory of them: for it hath been delivered unto me; and to whomsoever I will I give it. 7 If thou therefore wilt worship before me, it shall all be thine. 8 And Jesus answered and said unto him, It is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and Him only shalt thou serve. 9 And he led him to Jerusalem, and set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said unto him, If thou art the son of God, cast thyself down from hence: (pride of life) 10 for it is written, He shall give His angels charge concerning thee, to guard thee: 11 and, On their hands they shall bear thee up, Lest haply thou dash thy foot against a stone. 12 And Jesus answering said unto him, It is said, Thou shalt not make trial of the Lord thy God. 13 And when the devil had completed every temptation, he departed from him for a season.

How did Jesus overcome?

1. He answered based on Scripture—that is, his reasons were based on an authority

higher than himself—the authority of the word of God.

2. Jesus didn’t engage in debate, rationalization and conversation. He answered and

then closed the door.

Jeremiah 6:16: (NRSV) Thus says the LORD: Stand at the crossroads, and look, and ask for the ancient paths, where the good way lies; and walk in it, and find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk in it.

3. Jesus had ALREADY DECIDED who his God was. He knew who Satan was.

There was no reason for any other consideration.

Even though the tempter tried, Jesus proved faithful throughout his entire life:

Hebrews 4:15–16: 15 For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who has been tempted <3985> in all things as we are, yet without sin. 16 Therefore let us draw near with confidence to the throne of grace, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.

Now let’s look at our Christian testings and temptations:

James 1:12–15: 12 Blessed is a man who perseveres under trial <3986>; for once he has been approved, he will receive the crown of life which the Lord has promised to those who love Him. 13 Let no one say when he is tempted <3985>, I am being tempted <3985> by God; for God cannot be tempted by evil, and He Himself does not tempt <3985> anyone. 14 But each one is tempted <3985> when he is carried away and enticed by his own lust. 15 Then when lust has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and when sin is accomplished, it brings forth death.

The reason for our testing and temptation is our own imperfect selves. Why? So we can learn how to truly be overcoming disciples of Jesus!

### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/character/1442-identify-temptation/

1. How does just reading 1 Corinthians 10:13 shape your understanding of temptation, particularly regarding

God’s faithfulness and the “way of escape”?

2. How does the Greek word for temptation/testing expand our understanding beyond simply doing wrong?

(1 Corinthians 10:12-13, Hebrews 11:17)

3. What are the three sources of temptation or testing, and how does each source differ in its purpose or

intent?

a. Matthew 4:3

b. Hebrews 11:17

c. 2 Corinthians 13:5

4. Describe the differences between temptation, testing and spiritual attack. What response does each

require of us? (James 1:14-15, 1 Peter 5:8, Hebrews 12:6-7)

5. How does Romans 7:21-25 describe the internal struggle between the flesh and the spiritual mind of the

new creature? What does this say about persistence on the part of the struggle and on our part?

6. Where does temptation begin, and how does desire progress toward sin if it is allowed to grow?

(James 1:14-15, 1 John 2:15-17)

7. What can we learn from examining Lucifer’s fall? How did he display “the lust of the eye,” “the lust of the

flesh” and “the boastful pride of life”? How did he later use these same elements to tempt Eve? (James 1:14-15, Isaiah 14:12-15, Genesis 3:4-6)

8. Based on James 4:7-10, list seven steps to shut down temptation. Then add how to shut it down with the

appropriate scripture for each and the practical point given to help us do this.

9. How does 2 Peter 1:5-7 help us to shut down temptation? Why does this process, practiced over a long

period of time, help us resist negative temptation?

10. What practical changes (environment, habits, accountability or mindset) can you implement this week to

“set your mind on things above,” to prevent temptation from taking root? (Colossians 3:2-5)

## Episode 1443 — What Is the ‘Fear of the Lord’?
Published: 2026-06-29
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1443-fear-of-the-lord/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/22152833/CQ_Rewind_06-29-2026_What_Is_the_Fear_of_the_Lord.pdf

2 Corinthians 7:1: Therefore, having these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from

all defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.

If we are not careful, it can be easy to misrepresent God. So often we hear people proclaim that God is a God of anger and wrath, a God who demands that we fear Him. While God does absolutely and ultimately demand that all will eventually honor and reverence Him, we need to grasp what He requires of humanity now. The Bible, if carefully understood, supplies these answers. By examining what ‘fear of the Lord’ looks like first in the Old Testament and then in the New, we can receive a clear picture of what He demands. What does this picture show us? It reveals His power, His authority and His overwhelming benevolence.

In many ways, the phrase ‘fear of the Lord’ in the Old Testament defines itself. Outside the prophetic meanings of some scriptures, this phrase was defined for His people, Israel, through the context of their receiving physical fulfillments of His promises.

While these physical blessings applied only to Israel, the underlying principle still carries forward to us as Christians in that we receive spiritual blessings.

The physicality of Israel’s experience and the spirituality of our calling need to be kept distinct yet viewed together, so we can see the fuller picture of what ‘fear of the Lord’ truly means.

Let’s begin with the different forms of the word “fear.” Collectively, they mean fearing; morally, reverent.

The Hebrew Lexicon adds:

- In the negative sense, fear is a terrifying thing. - In the positive sense, reverence shows respect and to stand in awe of.

Fear: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3374 yir’ah; NOUN feminine of 3373;

fear (also used as infinitive); morally, reverence

Brown-Driver-Briggs Hebrew Lexicon: 1) fear, terror… 1b) awesome or terrifying thing

(object causing fear) 1c) fear (of God), respect, reverence, piety

Fear: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3373 yare’; ADJECTIVE from 3372;

fearing; morally, reverent

Fear: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3372 yare’; VERB a primitive root; to fear;

morally, to revere; cause to frighten

Brown-Driver-Briggs Hebrew Lexicon: 1) to fear, revere, be afraid 1a2) to stand in awe of,

be awed 1a3) to fear, reverence, honour, respect

Could the frightening fear be our conscience telling us that God is not pleased with us when we are doing wrong?

We might have that negative sense of fear, but we’re going to find out that it’s the positive sense we need to focus on.

For example, King David had a great fear. When Nathan pronounced, Thou art the man, he had fear over what he had done, rightfully so (2 Samuel 12:1-7). Yet that fear brought him to a reverence and a respect, which we will unfold as we go.

‘Fear of the Lord’ was the very foundation for applying the Law given to Israel:

Deuteronomy 6:1-2: 1 Now this is the commandment, the statutes and the judgments which the LORD your God has commanded me to teach you, that you might do them in the land where you are going over to possess it, 2 so that you and your son and your grandson might fear <3372> (reverence) the LORD your God, to keep all His statutes and His commandments which I command you, all the days of your life, and that your days may be prolonged.

Reverence for God is meant to keep our focus steady to help us live and act in a godly way. Think of the peace that such reverence brings! It is an important foundation on which to begin; it is the very foundation upon which the Law was given. Reverence for God is high, lofty and wonderful, guiding our hearts into that kind of peace.

‘Fear of the Lord’ brings His truth, His lovingkindness and His deliverance:

Psalms 86:11-13: 11 Teach me Your way, O LORD; I will walk in Your truth; unite my heart to fear <3372> (reverence) Your name. 12 I will give thanks to You, O Lord my God, with all my heart, and will glorify Your name forever. 13 For Your lovingkindness toward me is great, and You have delivered my soul from the depths of sheol.

Reverence brings total reliance on God. That reverence opens us up to His truth, His loving-kindness and His deliverance. David is poetically showing us a place of deep reverence. This isn’t about being afraid and shaking before Him.

‘Fear of the Lord’ brings confidence and abundant life:

Proverbs 14:26-27: 26 In the fear <3374> (reverence) of the LORD there is strong confidence, and his children will have refuge. 27 The fear <3374> of the LORD is a fountain of life, that one may avoid the snares of death.

So, the fear (meaning reverence) of the Lord shows trust.

We initially asked: What is the ‘fear of the Lord’?

The answer, unequivocally and repeatedly throughout this episode, is simple:

It is honoring and worshipping Him with reverence, not something over which we shake in fright. It instills confidence and strength because we see how small we are and how big God is. Proverbs says it brings us confidence and an abundant life. It is a positive sense in our lives. If you've been afraid of God before this,

take a breath, let the Scriptures sink in. They will help you to see more clearly and change how you feel about God.

‘Fear of the Lord’ brings instruction, prosperity, generational inheritance and God’s promised protection:

Psalms 25:12-15: 12 Who is the man who fears <3373> the LORD? He will instruct him in the way he should choose. 13 His soul will abide in prosperity, and his descendants will inherit the land. 14 The secret of the LORD is for those who fear <3373> Him, and He will make them know His covenant. 15 My eyes are continually toward the LORD, for He will pluck my feet out of the net.

When we are afraid, our eyes aren’t fixed on what scares us. Our instinct is to try and get away from it. Our backs are turned to it as we run away.

Here in Psalms, our reverence draws us toward Him because of His instruction and goodness. For Israel, that reverence brought physical inheritance, promises and protection. For us, it becomes the pathway to living in the transforming ‘fear of the Lord.’

‘Fear of the Lord’ fits precisely into the context of all other directions that Israel received from God:

Psalms 19:7-10: 7 The law of the LORD (the law of love) is perfect, restoring the soul; the testimony of the LORD (His instruction) is sure, making wise the simple. 8 The precepts of the LORD (His appointed plans) are right, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of the LORD (His teaching) is pure, enlightening the eyes. 9 The fear <3374> of the LORD is clean, enduring forever; the judgments of the LORD are true; they are righteous altogether. 10 They are more desirable than gold, yes, than much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and the drippings of the honeycomb.

Here we see aspects of God's overruling providence for Israel, and, essentially, for us Christians as well. The law of love, the instructions and the teachings are all beautiful.

The fear of the LORD is clean—what a great description. There is cleanliness and purity in having this reverence. It is enduring because His judgments are true and righteous, and more desirable than gold.

So, we are not afraid of Him. We want to honor, worship and serve Him.

‘Fear of the Lord’ can bring us a fearless approach to our challenges:

Psalms 27:1-3: 1 The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear <3372>? The LORD is the defense of my life; whom shall I dread? 2 When evildoers came upon me to devour my flesh, my adversaries and my enemies, they stumbled and fell. 3 Though a host encamp against me, my heart will not fear <3372>; though war arise against me, in spite of this I shall be confident.

Think about how powerful and freeing it is for those who follow God's directions!

Sometimes when we have deep, hard challenges in life, being reverent just doesn’t cross our minds because we’re so emotionally overwhelmed and distraught.

When our youngest daughter was assaulted at 15 years old, it blew our lives to pieces. And I remember very vividly not knowing what to do. I was shaking on the inside with the trauma of what had happened. But for me, what helped was prayerful consideration before taking the next step, based on scriptural principles, and just having faith.

When I read these scriptures about this giving us a fearless approach to our challenges, it brings me back to that time. Afterward, people would ask how I knew what to do. My answer was, “I didn’t!” But I prayed, looked at the Scriptures and took that step in faith. It was the reverence for God—just knowing He’s there—that drove us to rely on Him, pulling us through that horribly difficult time in life. This is very personal and special for me to reflect on reverencing the Lord in relation to challenges.

‘Fear of the Lord’ will, in God’s due time, be spread throughout all nations to their benefit:

Psalms 67:3-7: 3 Let the peoples praise You, O God; let all the peoples praise You. 4 Let the nations be glad and sing for joy; for You will judge the peoples with uprightness and guide the nations on the earth. Selah. 5 Let the peoples praise You, O God; let all the peoples praise You. 6 The earth has yielded its produce; God, our God, blesses us. 7 God blesses us, that all the ends of the earth may fear <3372> Him.

This prophetic view is a perfect conclusion to what God will ultimately bring about in His kingdom on earth with the nations under the New Covenant. The people will reverence Him from their hearts.

This ‘fear of the Lord’ is positive. It brings people up. He blesses them. They praise Him with reverence—they’re not shaking—they praise Him with awe for all of their blessings. What a great example!

The fear of the Lord opens the door to that sigh of relief that says, Our God is over all, with us and guiding us. What a message from the Old Testament! People say God is a God of anger and wrath, yet all these scriptures show that, behind all the justice that had to happen in the Old Testament, this is the true God!

As we move into the New Testament, consider these two important details:

1. The theme of fearing the Lord is the same.

2. Fearing the Lord is a less common teaching.

Fear: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5401 phobos; NOUN from a primary phebomai

(to be put in fear); alarm or fright

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) fear, dread, terror 1a) that which strikes terror

2) reverence respect (including reverence toward one’s husband)

Fear: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5399 phobeo; VERB to frighten,

i.e. (passively) to be alarmed; by analogy, to be in awe of, i.e. revere

The Greek verb phobeō is related to the English word “phobia,” which comes from the same Greek root. It can describe being alarmed or frightened, but it can also mean to stand in awe of or to revere, depending on the context. Again this word can be both negative and positive.

When we hear the word phobia, we naturally think of something entirely negative. But the Greek root behind that word has a wider range of meaning.

In previous episodes, we’ve looked at an Old Testament text and then examined how that same passage is quoted or used in the New Testament. Those “transition scriptures” help us see how Jesus and the first-century Jewish believers understood the original meaning— and in the case of ‘fear of the Lord,’ they consistently understood it in the positive sense of reverence, not terror.

When Scripture talks about the ‘fear of the Lord,’ it’s important to recognize that the Hebrew and Greek words for “fear” can carry either a negative or a positive meaning. The same root can describe terror, dread or danger—but it can also describe reverence, awe and deep moral respect. The key is always the context. Whenever the Bible uses the phrase, the surrounding language consistently points to the positive sense. In Proverbs, for example, this “fear” is paired with wisdom, knowledge, confidence and life—not panic or avoidance. In the Psalms, those who ‘fear the Lord’ are described as blessed, protected and secure. Even in the New Testament, when the Greek phobeō is used in this phrase, it is always positive, linked with obedience, devotion and spiritual maturity. So while the word itself can go either direction, the biblical authors never use ‘fear of the Lord’ to mean terror of God’s punishment. Instead, it describes the posture of a heart that recognizes God’s greatness, trusts His character and responds with humble loyalty. This distinction matters, because it shows that the “fear” God desires is not the fear that makes us run away from Him, but the reverence that draws us closer.

Let’s look at a few examples of this reverent “fear” in the New Testament:

1. The transition from Old Testament thinking:

Acts 13:15-16: 15 After the reading of the Law and the Prophets the synagogue officials sent to them, saying, Brethren, if you have any word of exhortation for the people, say it. 16 Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said, Men of Israel, and you who fear <5399> God, listen.

This is a great transitional scripture. Paul is in the synagogue speaking to Jews (men of Israel) and God-fearing Gentiles (you who fear God) who attended synagogue but had not fully converted to Judaism. So when Paul uses phobeo here, he is using it in the positive sense, describing those who revere, respect and worship the true God.

It shows that in the New Testament, the phrase who fear God carries the same positive meaning as the Old Testament phrase ‘fear of the Lord.’

2. The Apostle Paul had just written to the Corinthians to not be “unequally yoked” (overly involved) with unbelievers:

2 Corinthians 7:1: Therefore, having these promises, beloved (the promises of being God’s sons and daughters), let us cleanse ourselves from all defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear <5401> of God.

Having the promises of being God’s sons and daughters is a positive experience. It doesn’t make us shake with terror. It makes us want to to run toward our Father. We’ve been given these promises; let’s clean ourselves up and become more worthy of receiving God in reverence. We want to approach Him and serve Him because we love Him. That is what the fear of God means in this scripture.

3. Peter shows us this reverent awe is to be an integral part of our Christian character:

1 Peter 2:16-17: 16 Act as free men, and do not use your freedom as a covering for evil, but use it as bondslaves of God. 17 Honor all people, love the brotherhood, fear <5399> God, honor the king.

What does honor all people and honor the king mean? Honor here means “to prize or value.” So, if we prize and value all people and those in authority as we reverence God, this should bring peace in our lives. Reverence Him, but also prize and value those around you.

Understanding this New Testament fear as reverence and awe instead of terror is not only appropriate for Christians; it is a necessary state of heart and mind.

Positive “fears” we should have:

- Reverence—dealing with godly things reverently, not casually - Awe - Wonderment - Acknowledging God’s sovereignty with reverence

Because we have this reverence for God through Christ, there are other kinds of fear we should NOT have. Let’s look at two negative examples.

1. The kind of fear we don’t have to have:

2 Timothy 1:7-8: 7 For God has not given us a spirit of timidity <1167, but of power and love and discipline. 8 Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord or of me his prisoner, but join with me in suffering for the gospel according to the power of God.

What is this spirit of timidity? (King James Version: spirit of fear.)

The word Paul uses for timidity here is a noun that appears only once in the New Testament. It is not the same word as phobos or phobeo. This is a different kind of fear— the negative kind.

Fear/timidity: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1167 deilia NOUN

from 1169 (meaning cowardly); timidity:—fear

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) timidity, fearfulness, cowardice

Fear/timidity: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1169 deilos; from deos (dread); timid, i.e. (by implication) faithless:— fearful

When Paul says God has not given us a spirit of cowardice, he is describing those moments when we feel like cowering or hiding. This is not what God gives us. Faith in Him should result in reverence, not cowardice. Because of that, we are called to rise above our fear.

I was thinking about being at Bible camp years ago, and Rick, your children were playing by a little stream. All of a sudden, these hornets came out of the ground and started stinging your children. Trish, your wife, had no cowardice—she ran right in, grabbed them up and took them away from danger.

I saw the bees and was cowardly. I ran! I didn’t even think. I reacted cowardly, and I feel ashamed to this day for doing that. But I need to be vulnerable and confess my mistakes, Brother.

That was a really dramatic experience, because all of a sudden there was this swarm! Trish darted right in and got the kids out; there was chaos! She got stung about 40 times. We ended up going to the hospital just in case. She was able to do this without cowardice because she is a mother and had to take care of her children. She saw what happened, swallowed her fear and instantly responded, taking care of things.

I forgot all about that—what a dramatic memory!

2. The apostles were fearful when they were in the boat with Jesus during a storm:

Mark 4:39-41: (KJV) 39 And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. 40 And he said unto them, Why are ye so fearful <1169>? How is it that ye have no faith? 41 And they feared <5399> exceedingly, and said one to another, What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

In this account, we see both kinds of fear in the same passage.

Fear/timidity: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1169 deilos; from deos (dread); timid, i.e. (by implication) faithless:— fearful

Fear: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5399 phobeo; VERB to frighten,

i.e. (passively) to be alarmed; by analogy, to be in awe of, i.e. revere

First, Jesus asks, Why are ye so fearful, using the word deilos for dread or acting cowardly. Then, after he calms the storm with Peace, be still, the apostles feared exceedingly, and this time the word is phobeo, meaning reverence or awe. Once the wind ceased and a great calm settled over the sea, they were overwhelmed with awe and asked one another, What manner of man is this? They were astonished that, through the power of God, Jesus could command even the wind and the waves. This second fear was the right kind—their initial terror was transformed into deep reverence.

This cowardly type of fear is seldom used in the New Testament.

- It is cowering away when our response should be to stand firm. - It is giving in to emotions instead of seeking clarity to face outward circumstances.

All the scriptures we’ve discussed give us the confidence to stand in the Lord to fight and be strong and stable, because we reverence Him and won’t let cowardice stop us.

Unfortunately, the false doctrine of hellfire instills the wrong kind of fear. God is love; He is not a monster. The doctrine doesn’t belong to God and completely destroys the scriptural description of His character. It’s simply not taught in Scripture, and the concept doesn't fit the description of the heavenly Father, Jehovah God, in all His mighty wisdom and power.

If we are following Christ, we are MOST privileged, and therefore should have the deepest of reverence and awe for our God:

1 Peter 1:17-19: 17 If you address as Father the One who impartially judges according to each one's work, conduct yourselves in fear <5401> … 18 knowing that you were not redeemed with perishable things like silver or gold from your futile way of life inherited from your forefathers, 19 but with precious blood, as of a lamb unblemished and spotless, the blood of Christ.

If (we) address as Father the One who judges everything, we should conduct (ourselves) with reverence, because this is OUR Father.

Our Father provided for all of us to be redeemed through the sacrifice of His son, Jesus— not through a simple transaction of buying back Adam’s sin, but with the blood of his sacrifice. That brings us to absolute reverence. The ‘fear of the Lord’ is a wonderful reverence!

Let us work hard to fulfill the gracious will and desire of God our Father on our behalf:

Philippians 2:12-13: 12 So then, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your salvation with fear <5401> and trembling; 13 for it is God who is at work in you, both to will and to work for His good pleasure.

Fear and trembling, or “reverence” and trembling. Trembling is the anxiety one feels when they don’t trust their own ability, yet still do everything they can to carry out their duty. In other words, the anxiety we feel when we just don’t feel like we can.

I always had a reverence for God from childhood, but that changed when high school began. Trying to find myself, trying to fit in and be accepted by my peers, I went down a selfish and destructive road until I hit bottom without God. Then I refocused. I only had one way to look—and that was up! I remember my past with fear and trembling, but now I want to live with reverence for God as I originally thought in my youth. My prayer was, “God, give me direction,” and He certainly did!

That gives us the ability to step up and live reverentially. That is what ‘fear of the Lord’ is!

What is the ‘fear of the Lord’? We can put all these pieces together to get a proper understanding. God, the Creator of all things, deserves our reverence, respect, wonder, awe and recognition of His sovereignty.

As Christians, we should live with this running through our veins. In every experience, we need to live in fear and reverence of the Lord and stand in the confidence that reverence gives us.

So, what is the ‘fear of the Lord’?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

Many of our topics are compiled with a Word Study using several concordances and other Bible helps. We see how a particular word is used in both the Old and New Testaments. Understanding how the words are used not only tells us what they mean, but it gives us the nuances of the original Hebrew or Greek when comparing how the writers of the Bible use them in different contexts. We can also learn more by seeing the origins of a particular word, providing a depth of understanding that just reading scriptures in English cannot provide.

1 Peter 2:18: Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear <5401>; not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward.

1 Peter 3:2: While they behold your chaste conversation coupled with fear <5401>.

1 Peter 3:14-15: 14 But and if ye suffer for righteousness’ sake, happy are ye: and be not afraid of their terror <5401>, neither be troubled. 15 But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear <5401>.

1 John 4:18: There is no fear <5401> in love; but perfect love casteth out fear <5401>: because fear <5401> hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love.

Jude 1:23: And others save with fear <5401>, pulling them out of the fire; hating even the garment spotted by the flesh.

Revelation 11:11: And after three days and an half the spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet; and great fear <5401> fell upon them which saw them.

Revelation 18:10: Standing afar off for the fear <5401> of her torment, saying, Alas, alas, that great city Babylon, that mighty city! For in one hour is thy judgment come.

Revelation 18:15: The merchants of these things, which were made rich by her, shall stand afar off for the fear <5401> of her torment, weeping and wailing.

### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1443-fear-of-the-lord

1. What does the ‘fear of the Lord’ (reverence) provide in each of these examples?

a. Deuteronomy 6:1-2: What foundational purpose did reverence serve for Israel?

b. Psalms 86:11-13: How does reverence open the heart to God’s truth, lovingkindness and

deliverance?

c. Proverbs 14:26-27: How does reverence produce confidence and become a “fountain of life”?

d. Psalms 25:12-15: What instruction, prosperity and protection come from reverencing God?

2. Psalms 19:7-10 lists several aspects of God’s guidance—His law, testimony, precepts, commandment,

reverence and judgments. What does each of these provide, and how do they together reveal God’s overruling providence for Israel and for Christians today?

3. Why do you think the fear of the Lord is “clean” and “enduring”? How does reverencing God bring purity,

stability and peace in your own life? (Psalms 19:7-10)

4. In Psalms 27:1-3, how does reverence remove dread and produce confidence? How will reverence

transform the world under the future New Covenant? (Psalms 67:3-7)

5. Explain how these New Testament uses of the Greek phobeo and phobos show either positive or negative

connotations: Acts 13:15-16, 2 Corinthians 7:1, 1 Peter 2:16-17

6. What kind of fear ought we NOT to have? Use 2 Timothy 1:7-8 and Mark 4:39-41 to show how both

appear in the same narrative.

7. If we are following Christ, how should the fear of the Lord inform our decisions, our sense of

responsibility and our awareness of God working in us? (1 Peter 1:17-19, Philippians 2:12-13)

8. Where in your life do you struggle with the negative kind of fear (cowardice, dread, avoidance)? How can

confidence in God’s greatness and goodness reshape your response?

9. Philippians 2:12-13 tells us to “work out your salvation with fear and trembling.” What current

responsibility or spiritual challenge causes you to “not trust your own ability”? How can you lean more fully into allowing God to work with you over this?

## Episode 1444 — Do the Ten Commandments Apply to Christians Today?
Published: 2026-07-06
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1444-first-commandment-christians-today/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/27125549/CQ_Rewind_07-06-2026_Do_the_Ten_Commandments_Apply_to_Christians_Today.pdf

(The Ten Commandments Series Part I)

Exodus 20:1–3: 1 Then God spoke all these words, saying, 2 I am the LORD your God,

who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.

3 You shall have no other gods before Me.

The giving of the Ten Commandments to the people of Israel after their miraculous deliverance from slavery in Egypt was part of one of the most memorable series of events in the entire Old Testament. Here were millions of people who were now free from bondage but as yet with no home and no way to take care of themselves other than trusting in Moses, who was following God’s instructions. The giving of these ten foundational laws would set them up to understand who God was and what He would expect of them regarding how they honored Him and respected one another. These Ten Commandments were God’s directive to His people after He delivered them. They would stand the test of time.

Are the Commandments optional or even outdated? Why does this topic matter for our discipleship today? Are we bound by these laws for our own deliverance from sin and death?

We’re going to see that the answer is a resounding yes! We’re not under the Law of Moses, but the Ten Commandments reveal God’s character, and Jesus built his teachings on those same principles.

This episode explores how God delivered the Ten Commandments to Israel and why that foundation is still essential for Christians. We then take a deeper look at the First Commandment as the opening part of our 10-part series on each of the Commandments.

Let’s grasp the relevance of these Commandments to us by grasping how they were presented to Israel. Seeing Israel’s responsibility and purpose will help us see our own.

To illustrate this connection, we will view the context of Moses giving the Law to the people from God as a representation of Jesus sending out the call to discipleship, as directed by his Father.

Exodus 19:1–2: (ASV) 1 In the third month after the children of Israel were gone forth out of the land of Egypt, the same day came they into the wilderness of Sinai. 2 …they encamped in the wilderness; and there Israel encamped before the mount.

In the two months leading up to the Sinai experience, God had walked Israel through seven powerful experiences to prepare them for a covenant relationship with Him.

1. He delivered them through the Red Sea (Exodus 14:13-31).

2. He sweetened the bitter waters of Marah (Exodus 15:23-25).

3. He refreshed them at Elim (Exodus 15:27).

4. He fed them with manna (Exodus 16:4-18).

5. He brought water from the rock at Horeb (Exodus 17:1-7).

6. He gave them victory over Amalek (Exodus 17:8-13).

7. He established wise leadership through the appointment of judges (Exodus 18:13-

26).

Through these seven lessons, God showed that He delivers, provides, refreshes, teaches, protects, empowers and organizes His people. In the two months between their deliverance and their reaching the Sinai, they had already seen His character in action and were ready to hear His covenant.

These events provided evidence of God's powerful presence among them. They were not alone.

Let's begin to unfold how God will present the Ten Commandments:

Exodus 19:3–6: (ASV) 3 And Moses went up unto God, and Jehovah called unto him out of the mountain, saying, Thus shalt thou say to the house of Jacob, and tell the children of Israel: 4 Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I bare you on eagles’ wings, and brought you unto Myself.

God is emphatically reminding them: You've seen what I did to get you to where you are. You need to recognize the context in which you are living and the fact that you are free.

5 Now therefore, if ye will obey My voice indeed, and keep My covenant, then ye shall be Mine own possession from among all peoples: for all the earth is mine: 6 and ye shall be unto Me a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation. These are the words which thou shalt speak unto the children of Israel.

As Jesus' disciples, we are called to be different and to be witnesses, just as Israel was set up to be separate from the world. When Israel later rejected Jesus, they were themselves cast off for a time. This opened the door for Jesus’ call to discipleship to go to the Gentiles, who would be described in much the same way.

Compare how Israel was described with the chosen ones who were to follow Jesus:

1 Peter 2:9–10: 9 But you are A CHOSEN RACE (King James Version says, a chosen generation), A royal PRIESTHOOD, A HOLY NATION, A PEOPLE FOR God’s OWN POSSESSION, so that you may proclaim the excellencies of Him who has called you out of darkness into His marvelous light; 10 for you once were NOT A PEOPLE, but now you are THE PEOPLE OF GOD; you had NOT RECEIVED MERCY, but now you have RECEIVED MERCY.

Peter uses the same covenant language originally spoken to Israel and applies it to Christian disciples, showing that the church now fulfills the spiritual purpose pictured in Israel’s national calling.

What Israel was called to be nationally, the church is called to be spiritually. This is a huge connection!

Israel enthusiastically responded to this invitation to serve Jehovah as their one and only God.

Next, they were to be sanctified so they could receive the holy Law of God:

Exodus 19:14: (ASV) And Moses went down from the mount unto the people, and sanctified the people; and they washed their garments.

Their washing showed that meeting with Jehovah required both inward and outward preparation. They had to physically be clean.

Christians are also to be cleansed in order to be sanctified and receive God’s holy law.

However, our cleansing is given as a result of Jesus’ ransom and in the form of God’s spirit and truth:

John 15:3–4: 3 You are already clean because of the word which I have spoken to you. 4 Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it abides in the vine, so neither can you unless you abide in me.

Abiding in Jesus is the cleansing action of sanctification.

It goes further that same evening when Jesus talks to his apostles before his crucifixion. He prays for his followers:

John 17:16–19: 16 They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world (just like Israel was not of the world). 17 Sanctify (cleanse) them in the truth; Your word is truth. 18 As You sent me into the world, I also have sent them into the world. 19 For their sakes I sanctify myself, that they themselves also may be sanctified in truth.

The parallel is dramatic: being physically clean for Israel before God and being spiritually clean by washing our robes through Christ’s precious blood.

Sanctify them in the truth; Your word is truth—the giving of the Law is “truth” for us. We are set apart because Jesus made that sacrifice. It gives us a powerful connection between what happened to physical Israel before they received the Law and our calling to discipleship in Christ.

Let's continue with the Christian perspective on this. While we are under grace and not the Law, we find that the Ten Commandments are all principles of godly righteousness and do not involve any of the Law’s rituals.

By “under grace,” we mean that Christians are no longer bound to the Law Covenant given at Sinai, but live under God’s favor through Christ. Yet, Jesus built the gospel’s teachings on these same moral principles. The Law Covenant itself was far more than the Ten Commandments. It included hundreds of instructions—civil, ceremonial and moral— designed to teach Israel how to live in a covenant relationship with God. The Ten Commandments were given first, before the rest of the Law.

The Ten Commandments are the foundation.

Moses is speaking at the end of his life:

Deuteronomy 18:15: The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your countrymen, you shall listen to him.

For the New Testament connection, the Apostle Peter identified Jesus as the fulfillment of this Deuteronomy prophecy in Acts 3:22. Also, Stephen, in his defense before the

Sanhedrin in Acts 7:37, quoted this text and applied it to Jesus.

There is an undeniable connection between Moses as a mediator and Jesus as a mediator.

The beginning of the Law was the Ten Commandments, and they applied to Israel. Our Christian lives begin with the principles of the Ten Commandments on a spiritual level to follow in Christ's footsteps.

We need to unequivocally align with these principles and be ready to listen, absorb and act.

There is a sober reverence in how God instructed Moses to prepare the people to receive these Commandments. We need to pay attention!

Paying close attention to God delivering the Ten Commandments

is obviously important. What can we learn?

Let's take God delivering the Ten Commandments through Moses to Israel personally. We see God proclaiming ten powerful principles for our Christian lives through Jesus. Each and every principle will add to our foundation and further enable us to walk more fully in Jesus' footsteps.

We are explaining why this is an important foundation for Christians. Often, we look at the Ten Commandments and think, That's old stuff. No, it’s Christian stuff. It is the Christian foundation.

We are going to look closely at how God gave these Commandments, beginning in Exodus 20. Take note of the first thing God tells the people. This proclamation would be the foundation for all of the Commandments to Israel, as well as the foundation for all of the teachings of the gospel.

This is a critical verse. The Commandments are introduced with this proclamation from God:

Exodus 20:2: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.

This powerful and miraculous deliverance was a historical marker that clearly established God’s sovereignty for all to see. It is one of the most often quoted events in the Old Testament and among the strongest pieces of evidence of God’s sovereignty.

By reminding Israel of this deliverance before giving the Law, God grounded His Commandments in relationship—He had already proven His love, protection and covenant commitment.

Let’s fast forward to Christianity. We have also been brought out of the darkness of slavery to sin by answering the call to follow Jesus:

1 Peter 2:9: But you are A CHOSEN RACE, A royal PRIESTHOOD, A HOLY NATION, A PEOPLE FOR God’s OWN POSSESSION, so that you may proclaim the excellencies of Him who has called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.

We have been called out using the same descriptions. Why were we called out? To proclaim the excellencies of Him who called us out of darkness into His light—from where we were into a place where we can stand and be protected, loved and directed by God Himself.

The words of Jesus to Saul of Tarsus at the time of his conversion:

Acts 26:17–18: 17 rescuing you from the Jewish people and from the Gentiles, to whom I am sending you, 18 to open their eyes so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the dominion of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those who have been sanctified by faith in me.

Natural Israel was brought out of Egypt and slavery.

We are brought out of the darkness of the world and the slavery of sin. Cleansed,

washed by faith in Jesus, we owe our loyalty to God Almighty. What a gift!

From the darkness to the light, from the dominion of Satan, just like slavery in Egypt, to this new living way. This is another powerful connection.

When God says, I'm the One who brought you out of the land of Egypt, we, as Christians, need to see that God is speaking to us. He brought us out of sin and death—from slavery to Satan—to something new and beautiful in the light.

The First Commandment:

Exodus 20:1-3: 1 Then God spoke all these words, saying, 2 I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. 3 You shall have no other gods before Me.

At this point in history, every surrounding nation was polytheistic. Egypt, Canaan and Mesopotamia all worshiped large pantheons of gods tied to nature, fertility, war, storms and even specific regions. Their deities were territorial—the gods of Egypt, gods of Canaan, gods of Babylon—each was believed to have power only within their own land.

Jehovah, by contrast, was not a local deity but the sovereign God over all creation. This was radically unique and set Israel apart from the entire ancient world. So, the First Commandment was a declaration that Israel’s God was utterly unlike the gods of the nations.

No other gods before Me—meaning, I am first in your mind, your instinctive go-to source of strength, courage, calm, wisdom, insight and direction. I alone am the worthy recipient of your praise and thanksgiving, and I alone am worthy of all of these things.

How do we know Have no other gods before Me means no other gods at all, rather than “no gods higher than Me, but lesser gods are okay?” Check out the detailed Q&A in the Bonus Material.

As Christians, this commandment means we are drawn away from our previous associations to now be under God's law through Christ.

1 Corinthians 9:21: to those who are without law, as without law (the Gentiles), though not being without the law of God but under the law of Christ, so that I might win those who are without law (the Gentiles).

Paul is explaining how he adapts to different audiences without ever compromising God’s moral standards. When he is with the Jews, he adapts to their customs, but he’s not under the Mosaic Law. When he is with the Gentiles, he adapts to their customs, but he’s not lawless. In every situation, he is under the Law of Christ—the expression of God’s righteousness now revealed through Jesus. Paul adapted to their customs but not to their gods.

The theme of God being above all for all time is entirely consistent between Judaism, Israel and Christianity:

Mark 12:28–31: 28 One of the scribes came and heard them arguing, and recognizing that he had answered them well, asked him, What commandment is the foremost of all? 29 Jesus answered, The foremost is, HEAR, O ISRAEL! THE LORD OUR GOD IS ONE LORD; 30 AND YOU SHALL LOVE THE LORD YOUR GOD WITH ALL YOUR HEART, AND WITH ALL YOUR SOUL, AND WITH ALL YOUR MIND, AND WITH ALL YOUR STRENGTH (quoting from Deuteronomy 6:4-5). 31 The second is this, YOU SHALL LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF. There is no other commandment greater than these (quoting from Leviticus 19:18).

Love the Lord your God; love your neighbor. The First Commandment demands exclusive loyalty to God: You shall have no other gods before Me.

Jesus expresses that same truth from a positive standpoint, showing what exclusive

loyalty looks like: wholehearted love, total devotion and “God first” in every part of life. Instead of merely forbidding other gods, Jesus reveals the heart behind the command: Love God with everything you are. And if God is truly first, His character naturally shapes how we treat others.

The First Commandment establishes who God is, His rightful place and His exclusive authority. Jesus affirms that everything else in the Law hangs on this foundation.

The simple, systematic structure of the Ten Commandments:

- The First and Tenth Commandments are “internal instructions,” fulfilled within our heart and mind.
- Commandments Two through Nine are “external action instructions.” Their fulfillment can be outwardly seen.
- Commandments One through Four guide our relationship with the one Almighty God.
- Commandments Six through Ten guide our relationship with our human family.

So, we begin and end with an “internal instruction,” and everything in between is what we do. We have a sandwich effect. Surrounding all of our outward actions are the internal desires of our hearts and minds.

Jesus didn't say to Christians, “You need to live according to the Ten Commandments.” The Apostle Paul didn't say this either, but both of them showed us how to do so. They both showed us what the most important thing is. That's what we need to take away from this and work with as we look at this now.

We have barely scratched the surface and there is already much to learn. Time to dig into the details!

As we now begin to focus on having no other gods besides God,

what are the main points we need to look for?

First and foremost, we need to be as clear as possible as to what having NO other gods before God means for Israel and for us. The concept is simple. God always comes first. Period. How can we possibly mess that up? Actually, it’s easy. Once this is established, we need to truly grasp the magnitude of this Commandment being an “internal instruction.”

Because this First Commandment begins on the inside, it helps to picture the kind of structure God builds within us. Just as our bodies rely on bones for strength and movement, our spiritual lives depend on God’s moral framework for our freedom. The Ten Commandments aren’t restrictive—they’re the structure that lets us live and move with purpose. Without that framework, life collapses into chaos. God’s laws are the dependable skeleton of righteousness, helping us stand upright and walk in His ways. With that inner structure in mind, we’re ready to see how God spoke this command directly to Israel’s hearts.

Exodus 20:3: You shall have no other gods before Me.

These words were spoken directly to the people of Israel. They heard them in a dramatic manner:

Deuteronomy 5:2–5: 2 The LORD our God made a covenant with us at Horeb. 3 The LORD did not make this covenant with our fathers, but with us, with all those of us alive here today. 4 The LORD spoke to you face to face at the mountain from the midst of the fire, 5 while I was standing between the LORD and you at that time, to declare to you the word of the LORD; for you were afraid because of the fire and did not go up the mountain…

Moses reminds Israel that the covenant at Sinai wasn’t a distant or inherited agreement— it was God Himself addressing the very people standing before Him that day. They personally heard God’s words directly.

When someone in authority speaks directly to you, it carries a different weight. That’s what God did here. When God speaks directly, it becomes personal. It demands attention, reflection and ultimately, a response from the one who heard it.

When you were a kid in grade school, did you ever get called to the principal's office?

That happened to me. The principal is talking, and I’m nervous, because the authority is powerful.

Imagine the authority of God giving these commands to them.

It's powerful!

What is meant by other gods? The elevation of anyone or anything in our lives that would challenge God’s sacred and rightful ascendancy. These people or things can rival His power, justice, wisdom and love in our mind.

No other gods before God means we worship only Him in His overwhelming sovereign power.

What about Jesus? If we are to worship only God, what about Jesus?

Yes, there are scriptures that tell us to worship Jesus. Is this a contradiction? No.

Philippians 2:8-9, for example, describes Jesus by being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even a death on a cross. We see his incredible humility in always doing the will of God. For this reason, God highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name which is above every name.

Here comes the worship part:

Philippians 2:10,11: 10 so that at the name of Jesus every knee will bow, of those who are in heaven and on earth and under the earth, 11 and that every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord…

If we stop reading, it sounds like we are worshiping Jesus, but let’s continue.

…to the glory of God the Father. We are actually worshiping God through our reverence for the actions, life, death, faithfulness and loyalty of Jesus. It is entirely appropriate to worship Jesus in that context, because he is the one who always stands for God Almighty!

Worshiping Jesus is, in effect, worshiping the Father, as Jesus is the conduit through which we approach God.

Let’s pick back up where we left off:

No other gods before God means we worship only Him in His overwhelming sovereign power. Why?

God is stronger than the rest. He is the one who chooses, gathers, protects, strengthens and upholds:

Isaiah 41:8–10: 8 But you, Israel, My servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, descendant of Abraham My friend, 9 you whom I have taken from the ends of the earth, and called from its remotest parts and said to you, you are My servant, I have chosen you and not rejected you. 10 Do not fear, for I am with you; do not anxiously look about you, for I am your God. I will strengthen you, surely I will help you, surely I will uphold you with My righteous right hand.

This is written to Israel in the Old Testament, but Christians can spiritualize this passage because the New Testament explicitly applies Israel’s covenant language to the church. As we read, Peter used the very same titles God gave to Israel—chosen, holy, His possession— and applied them directly to Christians in 1 Peter 2:9–10. This means the spiritual purpose behind God’s promises to Israel now extends to the followers of Christ—not as a replacement but as an addition.

The power of this promise is simple. Is there any other “mighty one” at any time or under any circumstance, who could do the things in this verse? Absolutely not. This passage describes God's unequivocal power and strength in terms of the protection and overruling that He provides for His people.

No other gods before God means we worship only Him in His overwhelming sovereign power. Why?

God is wiser than the rest. There is no other mighty one who knows the beginning from the end:

Isaiah 55:8–11: 8 For My thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways My ways, declares the LORD. 9 For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are My ways higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts. 10 For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven, and do not return there without watering the earth and making it bear and sprout, and furnishing seed to the sower and bread to the eater; 11 so will My word be which goes forth from My mouth; it will not return to Me empty, without accomplishing what I desire, and without succeeding in the matter for which I sent it.

When God says something that hasn't yet happened, it's a guarantee it will in the future. Who else can do that? No one! Is there any other mighty one whose word is driven by such eternal power? No. Only our Jehovah God.

This is God's wisdom; His ability to know, comprehend, to plan and acts on those plans; to overrule, protect, guide and give all that is needed. This can only come from God, who has a plan. That's the wisdom of our Almighty God. This is why we worship Him.

No other gods before God means we worship only Him in His overwhelming sovereign power. Why?

God is more compassionate than the rest. Only God has a plan for ALL of humanity:

Paul here is acknowledging that Israel rejected Jesus as their Messiah, which opened the way for the Gentiles, but the Jewish rejection wouldn't be permanent. In fact, nothing could alter the fact that they were and are God's chosen people and have a place in His plan.

Romans 11:32–36: 32 For God has shut up all in disobedience so that He may show mercy to all. 33 Oh, the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments and unfathomable His ways! 34 For WHO HAS KNOWN THE MIND OF THE LORD, OR WHO BECAME HIS COUNSELOR? 35 Or WHO HAS FIRST GIVEN TO HIM THAT IT MIGHT BE PAID BACK TO HIM AGAIN? 36 For from Him and through Him and to Him are all things. To Him be the glory forever. Amen.

In the end, Paul shows that God has arranged it so that ALL—Jew and Gentile— experience disobedience, making His mercy the only basis of salvation for everyone.

This mercy and compassion are the expression of God's justice and love. If we add those to His power and wisdom, there is no other God worthy of our heart loyalty. He does everything for His people's eternal well-being.

Is there any other mighty one whose word is so sound and who can display foresight that will bring all of humanity to an opportunity for eternal life?

No, there isn't! You shall have no other gods before me.

This is where God’s internal instruction becomes real, in how He steadies and redirects us in everyday life. Rick, you said earlier that “having no other gods before Him means God becomes our instinctive go-to for strength, courage, calm and direction.” That struck me, because I lived through a time when fear tried to take that place.

Years ago, I went through a legal situation that became very personal and very stressful. I found myself accused of something I hadn’t caused, and the whole process felt overwhelming. There were endless details to navigate and a constant

uncertainty about what would happen next. Fear—and sometimes panic—began consuming my time and emotions.

I had a lot at stake financially, and it could affect my professional reputation. I started to realize that fear was becoming the first voice I listened to, the thing I obeyed. False gods try to get you to listen to them first.

Through the experience, God didn’t remove the stress, but I learned to trust Him no matter the outcome. That is the heart of the First Commandment: choosing God first when something else is fighting for that place.

The situation was eventually resolved, and the real lesson was how God sustained me: I prayed to be a good example even when things felt bitter, staying grounded in Bible study because I needed something steady, and simply doing the next right thing instead of letting fear—or even the pull toward revenge—rule me. Ironically—providentially—this was also around the time when I first started volunteering for Christian Questions. That work kept my mind anchored in God’s lessons at a time when fear was trying to dominate my thinking. That was God’s internal instruction acting as a guardrail, keeping my loyalty where it belonged and lifting my perspective higher.

That's a powerful story. Julie, I don't know if you remember, but the very first part of your contribution to Christian Questions was for an episode about wisdom. It fits well with your experience. I remember that vividly because we had just started working together on creating the CQ Rewind Show Notes. That was the first one. Your story shows the sovereignty of God in the life of someone who was struggling, yet held on and found a way.

Do the next right thing. Take the next step. Keep looking up. The First Commandment is simple, but it demands everything. It begins in the heart. It begins from the inside out.

The heights, depths, power and wisdom of God should be clearly before our eyes and hearts. Let’s appreciate what we have!

Having no other gods before God is pretty clear. How do we take this clarity and

transform it into an “internal instruction”?

The difference between knowing the sovereignty of God and actually living according to His sovereignty is the difference between being one who knows and one who does. As Jesus’ disciples, we are required to both know who God is and do His will, just as Israel was required to know and to do His will.

It’s one thing to acknowledge God—even to recognize Him as the Creator of everything— but it’s something entirely different to submit to His authority. Accepting God as “God” means accepting His right to define how life works, what is right, and what leads to blessings. His rules, His way.

Let’s begin this “internal instruction” exploration with an example of the “knowing” part.

Our example will be King Nebuchadnezzar with his response to Daniel. Early in the book of Daniel, the king has a dream and then forgets it. He calls his wise men, but no one can recount the dream or interpret it. Daniel, by God's grace, is able to both describe the dream and interpret the meaning of its mighty image. Humble Daniel gave God all the credit, saying in Daniel 2:28, there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries.

King Nebuchadnezzar’s response after Daniel interpreted the dream of the image:

Daniel 2:46–48: 46 Then King Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face and did homage to Daniel, and gave orders to present to him an offering and fragrant incense. 47 The king answered Daniel and said, Surely your God is a God of gods and a Lord of kings and a revealer of mysteries, since you have been able to reveal this mystery. 48 Then the king promoted Daniel and gave him many great gifts, and he made him ruler over the whole province of Babylon and chief prefect over all the wise men of Babylon.

Daniel was rewarded as King Nebuchadnezzar recognized and appreciated that the God of Daniel is the God of all gods. Unfortunately, Nebuchadnezzar would later forget this appreciation and end up being punished for it.

Knowing and appreciating who God is is good, but it is not complete. In comparison, Daniel himself lived his entire life with a heartfelt communion with God. He was always in tune with God’s will, not the will of the king or anyone else.

The First Commandment is an internal instruction. Internal instructions are driving forces in our lives, not merely thoughts or feelings.

Having no other gods before Me means we need to define how our worship works and what drives it.

Three basic questions:

What is the object of our worship? How do we know?

What are the reasons for our worship? Are they clear, honorable and uplifting?

What are the methods of our worship? What do these methods reveal about us?

1. What is the object of our worship?

What we worship is whatever we trust—what we protect, fear losing, sacrifice for and quietly obey. Whatever gets our first loyalty, our first emotional reaction or our instinctive trust—that is our god.

Obvious objects of worship include money, success, celebrities, influencers, political figures, our possessions or our addictions.

But remember, this is about other voices competing for our attention. The more subtle objects of worship might also include fear, control, comfort, approval from others, or self-reliance—using God as a backup plan instead of the first place we turn.

These subtle gods show up in the motives behind our worship.

Do I seek God only for what He gives me? Do I turn to Him only when my life is falling apart? Do I worship to avoid guilt or to maintain an image? Do I study Scripture to hear Him, or just to confirm what I already think I know?

2. What are the reasons for our worship? Are they clear, honorable, uplifting and godly?

❑ Do I seek God because of what He can give me, or do I seek Him because He alone

is worthy? ❑ Am I hoping for prosperity just because I go to church or give donations? ❑ Do I believe that being obedient means life will always be easy? ❑ Do I treat God as a way to fix my problems?

This exposes the false gods of comfort, prosperity or control.

❑ Am I using God as my safety net, turning to Him only when life falls apart? ❑ Do I treat prayer like a spiritual vending machine to get what I want?

This exposes the false god of self-reliance.

❑ Do I worship to avoid guilt rather than to pursue a real relationship with God? ❑ Am I checking the boxes to feel “safe”? ❑ Do I worship out of fear of punishment now or in the afterlife?

This exposes the false god of fear.

❑ Do I want others to see me as a “good Christian”?

This exposes the false god of self-image.

Consider the reasons for your worship. Why am I drawn to following after (in effect bowing down to) who or what I worship? Bravely asking ourselves these types of questions can be the beginning of understanding and corrective action.

3. What are the methods of our worship? What do these methods reveal about us? How I worship shows whether I’m fitting my life into God—or trying to fit God into my life! Worship is proven in the small, consistent choices I make.

❑ Do I worship on Sunday but live independently the rest of the week? ❑ Do I act first and then pray, perhaps, for forgiveness later? ❑ Do I give God my best—or my leftovers? The leftovers usually show up after we’ve

spent half the evening scrolling, binge-watching or “just checking one more thing” on our phone.

Whenever comfort, control, approval or self-reliance shape our actions more than God does, we quietly violate the First Commandment. This can be subtle, as it always happens as an internal instruction!

Violation of this First Commandment is the beginning of the downfall of any individual or civilization. History has proven it and will continue to prove it until God's kingdom.

Lucifer (Satan) before he became sinful, is an example:

Isaiah 14:13–14: 13 But you said in your heart, I will ascend to heaven; I will raise my throne above the stars of God, and I will sit on the mount of assembly in the recesses of the north. 14 I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High.

Satan’s internal instruction (his instruction to himself) was to rival the Almighty. You can’t worship what you want for yourself because, intrinsically, that is self-worship and therefore violates the First Commandment. That was Satan’s downfall.

Now we can explore what internal instructions look like when the “knowing” and the “living” aspects are both fully in order.

Recognize not only who God is, absorb what He does and how He does it:

Psalms 121:1–8: 1 I will lift up my eyes to the mountains; from where shall my help come? 2 My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth. 3 He will not allow your foot to slip; He who keeps you will not slumber. 4 Behold, He who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep. 5 The LORD is your keeper; the LORD is your shade on your right hand. 6 The sun will not smite you by day, nor the moon by night. 7 The LORD will protect you from all evil; He will keep your soul. 8 The LORD will guard your going out and your coming in from this time forth and forever.

When we read these verses, we see how the Lord is always with us. He will protect, He won't allow, He will do, He will be, He is always there. We begin to understand who He is and take in what He does and how He does it.

Teach others. There's no better way to create a stronger internal instruction than to teach others what you have learned.

The following verses are part of Moses’ farewell advice to Israel, reminding them of the covenant and calling them to wholehearted obedience. He’s 120 years old and knows he’s not going to enter the Promised Land with the people. Joshua has already been appointed as the new leader.

Deuteronomy 6:1–2: 1 Now this is the commandment, the statutes and the judgments which the LORD your God has commanded me to teach you, that you might do them in the land where you are going over to possess it, 2 so that you and your son and your grandson might fear the LORD your God, to keep all His statutes and His commandments which I command you, all the days of your life, and that your days may be prolonged.

You can know. Your son can know. Your grandson can know. Pass on the greatness of the sovereign Jehovah God who is before us, who is from everlasting to everlasting, who put this whole plan in place. Teach it to others. There's no better way to have it really sink in than when you passionately teach something to someone else.

Seek God’s strength and help as we enthusiastically protect ourselves with His providence:

Ephesians 6:10–13: 10 Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of His might. 11 Put on the full armor of God, so that you will be able to stand firm against the schemes of the devil. 12 For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the powers, against the world forces of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. 13 Therefore, take up the full armor of God, so that you will be able to resist in the evil day, and having done everything, to stand firm.

Do we stand firm because we are so strong? No. Is it because we are so determined? No. It is because God Almighty protects us.

Be strong in the Lord and the strength of His might. Put on His armor to be protected from anything and everything He permits to come your way. Seek His strength. Seek His help.

Constantly apply the power of God’s presence as we walk through ALL of life’s experiences:

Earlier in the podcast when Julie related her experience with fear and anxiety, she described how these emotions were mitigated by constantly applying the power of God's presence instead of being overwhelming.

Colossians 1:10–14: 10 so that you will walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, to please Him in all respects, bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God; 11 strengthened with all power, according to His glorious might, for the attaining of all steadfastness and patience; joyously 12 giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified us to share in the inheritance of the saints in light. 13 For He rescued us from the domain of darkness, and transferred us to the kingdom of His beloved son, 14 in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.

Essentially, we're ending right where we began. Remember, Israel was delivered from the darkness of slavery in Egypt. We are delivered from the darkness of the slavery of sin and death.

He rescued us from the domain of darkness and gave us the gift of light through the sacrifice of His son. Constantly apply the power of God's presence as we walk through each and every experience. That's putting Him first. You shall have no other gods before Me.

We often talk about following Jesus, but it is really all about God our Father. This is true because no other gods come before him. Jesus' entire existence was to serve God. We should do exactly the same with every ounce of energy we have.

Have no other gods before Me.

So, do the Ten Commandments apply to Christians today?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

CQ Q&A: Does the First Commandment mean "Have no other Gods at all" or just "Have no other God's that are higher than Me, but lesser gods are fine"?

Understanding the First Commandment begins with understanding what God actually said. When God declared, You shall have no other gods before Me, the key phrase before Me (Strong's Exhaustive Concordance #5921 plus 6440) comes from the Hebrew expression that literally means “in front of Me,” “in My presence” or “in My sight.” Because God is omnipresent, everything is in His presence. This means the command is not about ranking God above other deities; it is a command to have no other gods at all. The wording itself rules out the idea of “lesser gods” being acceptable.

The grammar reinforces this. The Hebrew phrase for “other gods” refers to any gods besides Jehovah, without qualification or hierarchy. It means "no gods besides Me in any category." If God had meant “no gods higher than Me,” Hebrew has clear ways to express that idea, but none of those forms appear here. Instead, the construction is absolute: no other gods in any category, in any capacity, under any circumstances.

The context of the passage also makes the meaning unmistakable. Immediately after the First Commandment in verse 3, God forbids making images, bowing down to anything or serving anything besides Him. These commands only make sense if God is prohibiting all forms of worship directed toward anything else. If “lesser gods” were allowed, the next verses would contradict the very system God was establishing.

This is a blanket prohibition, not a ranking system. The flow of the text shows a complete rejection of the polytheistic worldview Israel had just left behind.

This matters because the ancient world was filled with ranked pantheons. Egypt, Canaan and Mesopotamia all believed in hierarchies of gods. Some were more powerful than others, some less, each tied to specific regions or specialty functions. Israel’s God was radically different. He was not a local deity or a member of a divine council. He was the Creator, the Sovereign, the One who brought them out of Egypt by His own power. The First Commandment was a declaration of His uniqueness and exclusivity, not His position within a larger spiritual ecosystem. It is "I am the only God," not "I am the highest God."

The rest of Scripture consistently interprets the First Commandment this way:

Deuteronomy 6:4: The LORD is one.

Isaiah 455-6: Isaiah repeatedly declares, There is no God besides Me.

Hosea 13:4: You shall know no God but Me.

1 Corinthians 8:4: Paul writes, There is no God but one.

Nowhere does the Bible treat the First Commandment as a ranking system. It always presents it as a call to exclusive allegiance.

Jesus reinforces this understanding. When asked about the greatest commandment (see

Mark 12:28-30, Matthew 22:36-38 and Luke 10:27), he quotes Deuteronomy 6:4-5 and says we must love God with all our heart, soul, mind and strength. That is not a command to love God most; it is a command to love God entirely. Jesus does not leave room for divided loyalty or secondary deities. He reveals the heart behind the First Commandment: wholehearted devotion to the one true God. Love God with everything.

Finally, the First Commandment is an internal instruction. It begins in the heart, where loyalty is formed long before actions are visible. Internal loyalty cannot be shared or ranked. If God is first in the heart, nothing else can occupy that place. The command is about giving God the exclusive devotion He alone deserves.

Taken together, (Hebrew grammar, ancient context, scripture interpreting scripture, and Jesus’ own teaching) the meaning is clear. The First Commandment does not allow for multiple gods with God at the top. It calls for one God, one loyalty and one devotion.
