## Episode 1445 — How Do I Keep Idols Out of My Life?
Published: 2026-07-13
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1445-second-commandment-no-idols/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/05160412/CQ_Rewind_07-13-2026_How_Do_I_Keep_Idols_Out_of_My_Life.pdf

(The Ten Commandments Series Part II)

Exodus 20:4: You shall not make for yourself an idol, or any likeness of what is in heaven

above or on the earth beneath or in the water under the earth.

In our last episode, we unfolded the revealing of the Ten Commandments to the nation of Israel after they were miraculously freed from Egyptian slavery. We observed how God powerfully reminded them that their deliverance came from Him, and how their loyalty to Him was to be reflected by the First Commandment’s instruction to have no other gods before Him. As Christians, we were also rescued from the “slavery” of sin and death by God through the sacrifice of Jesus. We are therefore required to follow this Commandment and have our loyalty solely focused on God through Christ. The Second Commandment instructs us to have NO idols in our lives and builds squarely upon the First. Practically speaking, what does being idol-free look like? What are the dangers of not living up to this standard?

The Ten Commandments’ structure first honors God and then focuses on respecting our human family.

This is an "internal instruction." It is fulfilled within our hearts and minds. This establishes the necessity of having our loyalty and worship clearly fixed on God through Jesus.

Because this is an internal instruction, people do not necessarily see us fulfilling it. It is an internal formulation of loyalty. To keep this Commandment, we need to know who God is and immerse ourselves in living according to that knowledge.

Violation of this First Commandment is the beginning of the downfall of any

individual or civilization.

As we examine the Second Commandment, let’s do so with both the nation of Israel who received these commandments, AND Christianity in mind:

For I Jehovah thy God am a jealous God—this means protective, covenant loyalty, like a husband guarding a marriage; not the emotional insecurity of jealousy.

There is something unique about this commandment. It comes with the longest explanation of any of the Ten Commandments. God pauses to spell out the why, the danger and the generational impact. Idolatry is what we might call a “root” sin. It misdirects the heart before any other sin even begins. We’re already turned in the wrong direction, heading toward the wrong address. If you’ve ever wondered why certain sins keep repeating in your life, this might be the reason. The heart’s direction was off from the beginning, and then it spread. Idolatry establishes patterns and loyalties that can affect children, grandchildren and way beyond.

The First Commandment, Have no other gods before Me, was an internal instruction. The Second Commandment not to make idols is an “external action instruction.” This action can be outwardly observed.

To “make” an idol is to create a physically or emotionally tangible object of worship, to physically or emotionally bow down <7812> and serve <5647>, as used in Exodus 20:5 quoted earlier.

Bow down: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #7812 shachah; a primitive root;

to depress, i.e. prostrate (especially reflexive, in homage to royalty or God)

Serve: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5647 abad; a primitive root; to work (in any sense);

by implication, to serve, till, (causatively) enslave, etc.

To bow down is more than just bending your knees. It means lowering yourself, yielding or placing yourself under the authority of whatever you bow to. It is the posture of giving something your awe, your trust and your loyalty.

To serve means devoting yourself, working for, or even becoming bound to whatever you serve. It is the language of commitment and even slavery.

So, God is commanding: Do not lower yourself before anything created, and do not bind your life to anything that will rule you.

Let’s consider the essence of this commandment. The idea of serving is to take care of, to have responsibility towards.

One specific example:

Genesis 3:23: (KJV) Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till <5647> the ground from whence he was taken.

Adam was bound to the ground. To have the ground support him, he had to pour his energy into it. This is a positive use of the Hebrew word abad.

Bowing down and serving an idol means that a person is pouring their energy into something. This is the word used in a negative sense.

The expansiveness of idolatry is more fully explained in Deuteronomy. Moses is re- explaining this to Israel much later in his life:

Deuteronomy 4:15–20: 15 So watch yourselves carefully, since you did not see any form on the day the LORD spoke to you at Horeb from the midst of the fire,

They heard God on Horeb but did not see Him. Moses is saying, You don’t even

know what God looks like! You didn’t see Him. You were just instructed by Him.

16 so that you do not act corruptly (meaning “decay or ruin”) and make a graven image for yourselves in the form of any figure, the likeness of male or female,

Making idols would corrupt, decay and ruin Israel. Moses’ point was that they

couldn’t see God, so how could they possibly think about making an image of Him?

17 the likeness of any animal that is on the earth, the likeness of any winged bird that flies in the sky, 18 the likeness of anything that creeps on the ground, the likeness of any fish that is in the water below the earth.

God went through the details to make sure idols were not fashioned after

anything. There is a lot in creation that could be made into an image, but God did not want them to make representations of living things that could be worshipped.

19 And beware not to lift up your eyes to heaven and see the sun and the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, and be drawn away and worship them and serve them…

Don’t worship the stars, sun or moon either! Our loyalty is to God and Him alone.

20 But the LORD has taken you and brought you out of the iron furnace, from Egypt, to be a people for His own possession…

God described their slavery in Egypt as an iron furnace because He was using that

intense experience to shape Israel into a people who would bear His name and reflect His character. Since humanity is already made in God’s image, they didn’t need to create an image of Him. They were meant to be His living representation. That’s what makes the Second Commandment so serious: idolatry replaces the true image of God with something we create, and it corrupts the very purpose for which Israel was rescued from Egypt and we have been rescued from the slavery of sin.

Idolatry is not just about statues or symbols; it is anything we construct—physically or emotionally—that competes with God for our loyalty. Idols are an insult to our Creator!

Our “external action instruction” from Jehovah God tells us that NOTHING should be construed or constructed that would interfere with or ruin our singular loyalty to Him. This is what this Second Commandment is all about.

The first physical idol we know the exact shape of is the golden calf (Exodus 32:1-6). It is a clear example of idolatry used as a shortcut. Moses was taking too long, so the people demanded something they could see immediately. The tragedy of the golden calf is that they traded the glory of God who rescued them for a man-made object that reflected their impatience and fear. Idolatry still works this way today—it offers quick reassurance, while God calls us to the slower, deeper work of real transformation which takes time.

Our idols are a lot more sophisticated today. They're bigger, yet far more subtle—and we can take them with us wherever we go. Some potential “other” gods include ego, people, success, comfort, wealth, power, social media and social position. We can idolize those things.

Other possible idols include possessions, objects, pictures or symbols. These can all enhance ego. Such idols can unduly elevate people and depict success, comfort, wealth, power or social position.

Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) can become an idol—not because the technology is

inherently evil, but because it offers what idols have always offered: a shortcut. Idols let us bypass the slow, personal work of trusting God. Instead of waiting, listening or growing, idols give us something quick and reassuring—something that feels immediate and under our control.

Are we turning to AI first for direction or reassurance? AI lets us shortcut work, learning and even spiritual life—giving instant answers without the deeper discipline of prayer and meditation.

AI is powerful, but it can’t sanctify us. It can’t shape our character. It can’t replace the long labor of learning obedience by walking with God. When we let a shortcut stand where only God belongs, we’ve stepped right back into the ancient pattern of idolatry in a modern form.

AI is a tool—but this modern idol is much more devious than building a simple physical idol. We must exercise caution in not building ourselves up by taking credit for work that AI actually did.

People might say, “Look how eloquently they expressed themselves!” We must be careful, especially in the context of our spirituality, not to let AI be what speaks for us. We need to speak from our hearts, driven by God’s spirit.

Rick, you’re a great writer. Have you ever been tempted to type your subject title into AI? There are pastors who have AI create their sermons for them. Have you ever been tempted to do that?

No, never. As a matter of fact, it scares me to death, and I am very emphatic because, in my own experience, my study, my writing, I truly believe, are coming from understanding and studying the Scriptures with God’s spirit working within me.

Why would I take something that artificially gathers pieces of knowledge together when I can have the genuineness of God’s word and the beauty of His spirit that provokes me to dig deep into His word to express something?

It may not come out as eloquently or as impressively, but it’s genuinely working to honor God. So, no. Never have I ever been tempted that way. It scares me; I’m afraid of it. I’ll use it to help me understand a word here or there, and that’s about as far as I can go.

There is a simple and devious pattern that runs through every example of our attraction to idolatry:

- Observation: Seeing someone or something attractive that begs for admiration - Feeling and Thinking: Purposefully holding in awe the image of that which is attractive. - Rationalizing: Convincing ourselves that we owe attention and loyalty to that which is attractive. - Action: Transforming wrongly placed emotional worship into an outward sin of active worship.

The end result? We become idolatrous.

The Second Commandment was clearly stated throughout the Old Testament. It is referred to with the same intensity in the New Testament. The Apostle Paul in Athens not only states this but also shows us how to approach it. Let’s apply his teaching on idolatry to those around us and to ourselves.

Acts 17:16–17: 16 Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was being provoked within him as he was observing the city full of idols. 17 So he was reasoning in the synagogue with the Jews and the God-fearing Gentiles, and in the market place every day…

City full of idols—the Greek idea behind the word idol is an appearance or likeness that looks like something real but isn’t the real thing. It’s like a shadow that resembles reality but with no substance.

Paul looked around Athens and saw all the idols. He knew this was not good and knew he needed to do something. So, he started conversations.

We also need to intentionally seek to be aware of the depth of idolatry that may surround us. Take a look around your own life for a moment. What are the “idols in the marketplace” for you? What fills your environment, your schedule, your mental space?

Modern humans may not carve statues, but our hearts haven’t changed—we still crave something tangible to trust. Instead of wood and stone, we turn to screens, brands, entertainment, habits, identities and comforts. These things give us the same sense of immediacy and reassurance that physical idols once did for ancient humans.

That’s why modern idolatry is often more subtle and more dangerous. We don’t bow to statues; we bow to whatever captures our time, attention, loyalty and emotional energy. The temptation is the same as it was in Exodus: to let something created take the place of the Creator. NO!

Back in Athens…

Through his conversations, Paul’s intensity against idolatry was recognized. He was then invited to speak publicly about this. He had the opportunity because he recognized it. He acted quietly by starting conversations with those around him. In Paul’s approach to the Athenians, he respectfully addressed those who may have been open to listening.

Dealing with others who may have an issue with idolatry: Respectfully address those around us who may be open to listening. When we are in an environment where there is an overt amount of idolatry around us, we might try the same approach as Paul.

How do we take this lesson of looking at it on the outside and applying it to the inside?

For us personally, internally: We need to recognize what potential idolatry might be developing in our hearts. We need to look in the mirror. Example: Maybe I own a phone—or does my phone own me?

My friend Harrison calls our phones the “pocket god.” I've left the house without my phone. And I have felt very uncomfortable to the point of being anxious. And I was with other people who had phones, so it wasn't like I was afraid of being in an emergency with no call for help. I've had to really take a look in the mirror and see how dependent am I am on this little pocket god.

Let’s see what Paul did:

Acts 17:22–23a: 22 So Paul stood in the midst of the Areopagus and said, Men of Athens, I observe that you are very religious in all respects. 23 For while I was passing through and examining the objects of your worship, I also found an altar with this inscription, TO AN UNKNOWN GOD.…

Notice Paul is not calling these “idols,” a false, empty image, even though he knows they are and must have been horrified by what he saw. He’s calling them objects of your worship, or in Greek, the “things you revere.” Paul clearly saw the idolatry but spoke to the people gently. This is a model for us. We can recognize false worship for what it is without demeaning those who are caught up in it. This is meeting people where they are. That's exactly what Paul did. He used the Athenians’ own thinking and habits to stimulate them to listen, so he could draw them up higher and away from their deeply idolatrous ways. This is a great example of what we can do with others.

Here’s one that affects many of us. Doesn’t it feel good to be validated and have someone say, “You’re right!” There’s a danger when you’re looked upon as the “expert” in the room—at work, in church, in our relationships, in the advice we give to others. And sometimes it’s not even about being right; it’s about having the last word, making sure we really get our point across, or that our perspective is the one that stands. That pressure to be right—and to stay right—can quietly become an idol.

In some of my counseling experiences, we talk about personal validation. We rehearse where our validation should come from. It should come from God above. What other people say and think should not be what drives us. It should be about honoring Him. Let Him bless us in His way. That is not as tangible a validation, but it is a powerful validation and a great example.

Let’s look at idolatry and its power in the New Testament in relation to us:

1 Corinthians 6:9–10: 9 …Do not be deceived; neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, (and a long list follows…) 10 …will inherit the kingdom of God.

So idolaters are on the list of those who will not inherit the kingdom. If we are a Christian, we must take that to heart. We need to be aware of the potential for idolatry in our own hearts.

Dealing with others who may have an issue with idolatry: Tactfully inform those who listen of God’s sovereignty by telling them who God is, small step by small step.

What about when we're dealing with the idolatry on the inside? How do we take Paul's lesson and apply it to ourselves?

For us personally, internally: Isolate it and treat. Hold our own idolatrous actions up to the light of God’s sovereignty.

How Paul explained who the UNKNOWN GOD was:

Acts 17:23–26: 23 …Therefore what you worship in ignorance, this I proclaim to you. 24 The God who made the world and all things in it, since He is Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made with hands; 25 nor is He served by human hands, as though He needed anything, since He Himself gives to all people life and breath and all things; 26 and He made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth…

Paul gave this beautiful, gentle introduction. He explains that they are actually looking for Jehovah in this idol to the UNKNOWN GOD.

God, who is the ultimate Creator of all, does not dwell in temples made with hands... That is a very kind way of saying all the things they were building did not represent God. He is above all. Further, God created one man, and all were born through that man, so we ALL therefore owe our loyalty to that one unknown God. Paul met them where they were. What a beautiful way to introduce truth to the Athenians and open up the opportunity to follow Jesus. It was like a giant arrow pointing, “This way!” We can take that same approach.

Here’s another “bad” list:

Galatians 5:19–20: 19 Now the deeds of the flesh are evident, which are: immorality, impurity, sensuality, 20 idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, disputes…

We don’t want anything to do with what is on this list! Idolatry shows up again. It is always on the bad lists, in the middle of things. If we give allegiance to something that conflicts with our ultimate loyalty to God, we build a bridge to our own destruction. This is what our idols really are.

Dealing with others who may have an issue with idolatry: Invite those who listen to genuinely seek after this one, loving, powerful and accessible God. Paul continues to teach them, showing them that this is the One God, the Creator of all men, who doesn’t dwell in the temples they built. He is far beyond and above such things.

Meet those who will listen where they are and find a way to give them logic and clarity.

For us personally, internally: Repent. Unequivocally change direction and resume walking in the light.

In Episode 1441: “Is It Necessary to Confess My Sins?” we saw how important confession is to help see ourselves the way God sees us, leading to repentance, leading back to a relationship with God. Walking in the light keeps us spiritually awake and accountable.

Paul invites them to genuinely seek God:

Acts 17:27–28: 27 that they would seek God, if perhaps they might grope for Him and find Him, though He is not far from each one of us; 28 for in Him we live and move and exist, as even some of your own poets have said, For we also are His children.

Paul quotes their own poets—again meeting them where they are. He tells them they might have to grope for Him because this was unfamiliar to them, but He is accessible. He can be found because He is real. Paul gave the Athenians an invitation to develop a relationship with God.

To understand why this mattered so much, we need to step into their world for a moment. In the ancient world, idols were believed to become living containers of a god’s presence. Through well-documented rituals like the “opening of the mouth” ceremony, priests would symbolically open the idol’s eyes, ears and mouth so the deity could enter it. Once “activated,” the idol was treated as a living divine presence, being washed, fed, clothed and consulted. This is the world that surrounded Israel, and the Second

Commandment was a radical rejection of the idea that God could be summoned, contained in an object, or that the worshiper could control access to the divine.

If we find ourselves struggling with idolatry today, we might be wanting a god we can control—something visible or emotionally immediate—rather than trusting the God who cannot be contained or manipulated. Modern idols work just like the ancient ones: they promise comfort, control or reassurance, but they end up shaping us in their image rather than allowing God to shape us in His.

The context is of not being unequally yoked with unbelievers; not becoming immersed in the world around us because of the idolatry:

2 Corinthians 6:16: Or what agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God…

Idols HAVE temples, but we ARE the temple. God dwells in us, not in objects.

Dealing with others who may have an issue with idolatry: Conclude with gently stating the irrefutable evidence against idolatry and reaffirming God’s love.

For us personally, internally: Restart. Embrace the purity of no other gods before God! Figure out what those other gods are for you.

Paul finishes with the following:

Acts 17:29–31: 29 Being then the children of God, we ought not to think that the Divine Nature is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and thought of man. 30 Therefore having overlooked the times of ignorance, God is now declaring to men that all people everywhere should repent, 31 because He has fixed a day in which He will judge the world in righteousness through a man whom He has appointed, having furnished proof to all men by raising him from the dead.

Paul talks about idolatry, saying the divine nature is not formed by the art and thought of man. He introduces Jesus and the miracle of him being raised from the dead. Of course, some wanted to hear more, but others wanted nothing to do with it, and that was okay.

Paul concluded by giving the Athenians irrefutable evidence of Jesus’ resurrection. He informed them of a new and higher way to live. He showed them the way to follow God’s “external action instruction” of not worshiping idols.

We are not to make or participate in anything that gets in the way of our relationship with God.

Not all idols are “anti-God.” In Greek, “anti” means “in place of.” Today’s idols might not look like they’re against God at all—so we have to look for what’s competing with Him. Something might not even be obviously sinful. There is a danger of even good things—like family, work, comfort, being the smartest one in the room—becoming idols when they become the ultimate things. That’s why the foundation of the First Commandment is so important—to have no other gods before Him.

Ephesians 5:5: For this you know with certainty, that no immoral or impure person or covetous man, who is an idolater, has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.

When we are idolatrous, we are inevitably coveting something, be it comfort, direction, recognition or whatever it is. We need to stay away from those and look to our heavenly Father through Jesus for our blessing.

The bottom line is simple. The First Commandment is, Have no other gods before Me. The Second Commandment is to make no images or idols of anything that would put any other god before THE God, the Creator of all things.

Why would we want to worship an idol? Because we are sinful, broken and insecure. Idolatry grows out of insecurity. True godliness grows out of the security and faith in our heavenly Father through Jesus.

So, how do I keep idols out of my life?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1445-second-commandment-no-idols/

1. What is the Second Commandment, and why does God give it the longest explanation of all ten?

Explain how is this commandment functions as an “external action instruction” and why idolatry is described as a root sin with generational impact.

2. According to Exodus 20:4-6 and Genesis 3:23, what does it mean to “make” an idol? Describe how bowing

down and serving an idol involves lowering yourself and binding your energy to something created.

3. Using Deuteronomy 4:15-20, restate the Second Commandment in your own words for modern

Christians. How does idolatry corrupt the purpose for which God rescued Israel—and for which Christ rescued us?

4. How does the golden calf reveal why idolatry is so appealing? Explain how idolatry acts as a shortcut,

offering quick reassurance instead of the slower, deeper work of transformation.

5. Describe the four-step pattern of idolatry as described in the Rewind. How does this pattern show the

subtle way idolatry forms in our lives? (Exodus 32:1-6)

6. Describe Paul’s awareness of the idolatry he saw around him in Athens. How did he address the

Athenians respectfully, meeting them where they were? Can you think of a situation where you could use Paul’s approach with others? (Acts 17:16-28)

7. How can we recognize our own idolatry developing in our hearts? How should we respond when we

identify idolatry within ourselves? (Acts 17:27-28, Galatians 5:19-20)

8. Where have you allowed a desire for control, reassurance or immediate answers to replace trust in God?

9. What modern ‘idols’ (objects, habits, comfort, validation, technology, identity) might be shaping your

choices? What steps can you take to shut them down completely rather than leaving a small pathway open? controlling you?

## Episode 1446 — Do I Ever Take God’s Name in Vain?
Published: 2026-07-20
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1446-taking-gods-name-in-vain/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/04210304/CQ_Rewind_07-20-2026_Do_I_Ever_Take_Gods_Name_In_Vain.pdf

(The Ten Commandments Series Part III)

Exodus 20:7: (ASV) Thou shalt not take the name of Jehovah thy God in vain;

for Jehovah will not hold him guiltless that taketh His name in vain.

As we continue our Ten Commandments Series, we are focusing on how each and every Commandment given by God to Israel after they were freed from slavery has direct and profound meaning for us as Christians. While we live in a very different world, the principles of each of those commandments are powerfully important for us to follow in our walk as disciples of Jesus. The Third Commandment tells us not to take God’s name in vain. For the most part, we might think, I don’t use God’s name in any inappropriate way, so I’m fine! Well, the reality is, taking God’s name in vain is far deeper, far more subtle and far more destructive than the words we use. We need to pay close attention!

The First Commandment is an “internal instruction” and is fulfilled within our hearts and minds. It establishes the necessity of having our hearts and minds clearly fixed on God through Jesus as our only object of loyalty and praise.

The Second Commandment is an “external action instruction.” Its fulfillment can be outwardly observed. To “make” an idol is to create a physically or emotionally tangible object of worship, to physically or emotionally “bow down to” or “serve.”

God is commanding: Do not lower yourself before anything created, and do not bind your life to anything that will rule you.

Connecting the first two commandments: God must always be first in our hearts and minds. Idolatry is an outward manifestation of an inward lack of fidelity to the one God. It sets us on a path that will further degrade and disregard the sacred loyalty any human can ever be privileged with.

The Third Commandment is also an external instruction. We are to thoroughly live what we proclaim to be. Don’t just say it, do it.

We may have thought this means we shouldn’t say, “OMG” or carelessly use the name “God” or “Jesus” in our conversation. We shouldn’t, but this goes much deeper. Let’s look at the Hebrew words used for take and vain.

Take: Brown-Driver-Briggs Hebrew Lexicon #5375 nasa'; 1) to lift, bear up, carry, take 1a1) to lift,

lift up 1a2) to bear, carry, support, sustain, endure 1a3) to take, take away, carry off, forgive

Take in this verse means “to lift up, to carry, to bear.” It is used throughout the Old Testament to describe carrying physical loads, bearing guilt or carrying another person’s burden.

For example:

Genesis 4:13: (KJV) And Cain said unto the LORD, My punishment is greater than I can bear <5375>.

That’s the same word. The Third Commandment is not primarily about speech. It’s about carrying God’s name—representing Him—in a way that is not empty, false or worthless. Don’t live in a way that misrepresents the God whose name you bear. This is hypocrisy!

As Christians, when we “take” the Lord’s name, it becomes a symbol of our identity. It could be considered as a form of our signature.

If I am signing my name, I am Rick, the disciple of Christ; that's my signature. Is that signature real? Is that signature genuine? Am I holding that representation in its highest form?

Vain: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #7723 shav’; from the same as #7722 in the sense of

desolating; evil (as destructive), literally (ruin) or morally (especially guile); figuratively idolatry (as false, subjective), uselessness (as deceptive, objective;

also adverbially, in vain):—false(-ly), lie, lying, vain, vanity

Brown-Driver-Briggs Hebrew Lexicon: emptiness, vanity, falsehood, worthlessness (of conduct)

This is a sad word and means empty, false or deceptive; something hollow, without substance. It is used in the Old Testament to describe false oaths, empty promises and worthless action. The thing described does not fulfill its purpose.

The commandment becomes much deeper than “don’t swear using God’s name.” It means do not carry God’s name in a way that is empty, false or misleading. Do not misrepresent Him.

So, the idea behind vain is that of a falsehood or an exaggerated and fantasy view of what is real.

Do I, Rick, the disciple of Christ, ever have that false representation? Does it always mean “Rick, the disciple of Christ,” or is it simply a label I can hide behind when other things are happening?

Israel had been given these commandments after being freed from Egyptian slavery. It is a brand new beginning, and they say, “Yes, we're in! We're going to follow it.” Yet how often did Israel as a nation promise fidelity to God and then turn to idolatry? Again and again! No wonder their consequences were always severe!

As Christians, we need to make sure that we're focused clearly on these first three Commandments.

Let’s look at another example. God’s prophet Jonah fell prey to his own empty idolatry. As a designated representative of God, he declined to do God’s will. He ran in the other direction.

Here is a portion of his repentant prayer to God after he ran away and was swallowed by the fish:

Jonah 2:1–2, 7–9: 1 Then Jonah prayed to the LORD his God from the stomach of the fish,

The LORD his God signaled that Jonah had finally turned back to Jehovah. He was no longer running from Him.

2 and he said, I called out of my distress to the LORD, and He answered me. I cried for help from the depth of sheol; You heard my voice. 7 While I was fainting away, I remembered the LORD, and my prayer came to You, into Your holy temple. 8 Those who regard vain <7723> idols <1892> forsake their faithfulness, 9 but I will sacrifice to You with the voice of thanksgiving. That which I have vowed I will pay…

Idols: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1892 hebel; from #1891; emptiness or vanity; figuratively,

something transitory and unsatisfactory; often used as an adverb

Here the word for idols (hebel) means emptiness or vanity, something transitory and unsatisfying—a false substitute. What vain idol caused Jonah to run?

He was describing himself. In effect he said, “I'm in distress, I'm crying, and the Lord is answering me. Those who follow the useless vanity of their own desires forsake their faithfulness.”

By not preaching to Nineveh, the “vain idol” he is referring to is his own will! Not only did he not do what God told him, but he went in the opposite direction!

He was stuck in his own head, and he knew it. He recognized it and showed faithfulness by acknowledging he followed the emptiness of his own vanity. What a powerful admission!

Idolatry brings emptiness. It involves taking God's name without meaning what we say; not protecting it, and instead using it frivolously. Jonah was a prophet of God yet did not hold that responsibility as sacred. He was in that fish because he ran from the mercy God wanted to show the Ninevites and Jonah himself. Idols both mislead us and rob us because we walk away from the mercy God gives us.

Why would we do such a thing? Because we get stuck and focused on how good the idol looks, and we end up not living in accordance with what we say we stand for.

Let's look more deeply at taking God's name in vain. It continues to be a destructive, commandment-breaking process that ends in broken loyalty:

- Doubting God within your heart and mind. The First Commandment is being violated.
- Looking for other more tangible objects of worship and security. The Second Commandment is being violated.
- Continuing to outwardly carry the name of God while finding security and fulfillment in earthly things. This is hypocrisy! The Third Commandment has been violated.

These are purposely interconnected. God put them in this sequence to show the process that leads us to become a false representative of Him.

How do we get from being in this difficult place to where we need to go? Is there a reset? The first step is to figure out how we got here. How can this happen to a disciple of Christ?

o Through my own desires o Through worldly influences o Through the leadings of others that slowly, quietly wear us down

What will be my true signature for each of these influences?

o My own desires

Philippians 3:4–6: (This is the Apostle Paul describing himself when he was known as Saul.) 4 although I myself might have confidence even in the flesh. If anyone else has a mind to put confidence in the flesh, I far more: 5 circumcised the eighth day, of the nation of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the Law, a Pharisee; 6 as to zeal, a persecutor of the church; as to the righteousness which is in the Law, found blameless.

Imagine someone today with the perfect résumé—top education, top performance, widely respected, disciplined and admired. The kind of person who always succeeds and always gets recognized. That was Paul; that was Saul! If anyone could have relied on their achievements for spiritual security, it was Paul. But all of that was a forgery of godliness. His signature looked impressive, but it wasn’t the signature of a representative of God.

It wasn't even the signature of a Jewish individual rightfully handling the Law. He took the Law into his own hands, persecuting Christians. He broke the very Law he was powerfully defending, and did so with pride. It was an absolute forgery.

What do we do if our own desires lead us to that forgery scenario?

The antidote for our personal desires is to focus on God. Simply back up and return to the First Commandment—have no other gods before Him.

Philippians 3:7–8: 7 But whatever things were gain to me, those things I have counted as loss for the sake of Christ. 8 More than that, I count all things to be loss in view of the surpassing value of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord, for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and count them but rubbish so that I may gain Christ.

Paul says in these verses that all his credentials and accomplishments and every bit of status are nothing compared to knowing Christ. He realized that even the best version of himself could not save him. His success wasn't bringing him closer to God; in fact, it was the opposite. His success had become an idol, and he had to let it go.

His signature as a servant of God was a forgery. Then, when he came to Christ

and began truly serving God, what happened to him? He was persecuted,

beaten, imprisoned and shipwrecked. He said all of that before was nothing— I count them but rubbish—because his new signature is Paul, the servant of God through Jesus, and it’s genuine. He took care of his own desires, put them behind him and was able to move forward.

Consciously consider the eternal weight of what we have gained—to be able to honor God through Christ—compared to the passing successes of our personal earthly ambitions. Our signature must be genuine.

Our own desires come from within. Worldly influences come from the outside.

o Worldly influences:

Ephesians 4:17–19: 17 So this I say, and affirm together with the Lord, that you walk no longer just as the Gentiles also walk, in the futility of their mind, (in other words, don’t go back to the way you used to live) 18 being darkened in their understanding, excluded from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the hardness of their heart; 19 and they, having become callous, have given themselves over to sensuality for the practice of every kind of impurity with greediness.

Paul isn’t describing unbelievers “out there.” He’s warning Christians not to return to the emptiness from which they were rescued. Paul’s message: You belong to Christ now. That’s your new signature. The old way has to go. Don’t drag God’s name through the mud. Don't live in the emptiness that you were saved from. Don’t attach God’s name to a life that contradicts Him.

Let’s read these same verses from the New Living Translation: 17 With the Lord’s authority I say this: Live no longer as the Gentiles do, for they are hopelessly confused. 18 Their minds are full of darkness; they wander far from the life God gives because they have closed their minds and hardened their hearts against Him. 19 They have no sense of shame. They live for lustful pleasure and eagerly practice every kind of impurity.

Worldly influences are everywhere. They're all around us, and we can't get away from them, no matter what we do. We need to be able to look at them and ask:

The antidote to the worldly influences is to have no idols—no graven images.

Understand what is important:

Hebrews 12:2: fixing our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, despising the shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.

Fix your eyes. When worldly influence is strong, fix your eyes on your target: it's Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith. He endured everything for our sake and now is at the right hand of the throne of God.

Jesus draws us to God. Fixing our eyes on Jesus brings us to the heavenly Father. The son brings us to the Father every time. Focus through the noise and stimulation of our present, overstimulating world and realize the empty promises they make. Focus through the confusion to see Jesus as our only way to satisfy ourselves so that we can stand before our Father and hold His name with integrity, love, compassion and praise.

Deal with the worldly influences by enforcing the Second Commandment. Have no idols!

o The leading of others:

The influence of others can draw us away from godliness and tempt us to use God’s name in vain, turning our signature into a forgery.

The Apostle Paul is giving his farewell warning to the elders of the church of Ephesus that dangerous leaders would arise from within the church:

Acts 20:29–30: 29 I know that after my departure savage wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock; 30 and from among your own selves men will arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them.

We see this same pattern in our own time. When leaders in modern churches misuse their position—whether through moral failure, financial abuse or manipulating people in God’s name—they are carrying God’s name in a way that empties it of truth. This is exactly what the Third Commandment warns against.

And again, there's forgery when they twist Scripture for their own benefit. It's bad enough to say something for our own benefit, but it is far worse to take God's Holy Word and knowingly misrepresent it “in the name of Christ.” We have to be careful.

This was already happening in Paul’s time when he was putting the ministry in place. Already some of the leaders were not genuine followers.

The antidote to letting others influence us is the Third Commandment—do not take God's name in vain. Be a genuine representation of Him and stand for what we profess.

Colossians 1:9–10: 9 …we have not ceased to pray for you and to ask that you may be filled with the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding, 10 so that you will walk in a manner worthy <516> of the Lord, to please Him in all respects, bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God.

We must strive to be genuine Christians. These texts are loaded with ways to put that into practical use, so that you may be filled with the knowledge of His will—understanding His will. We have to study God’s word to understand His will, and then we let that knowledge transform into godly wisdom.

Worthy: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #516 axiōs adverb from G514;

appropriately:—as becometh, after a godly sort, worthily(-thy)

Walk in the manner worthy of the Lord—the Greek word axiōs means “worthy, fitting, consistent with.” Therefore, live in a way that matches the values of the One you represent. This is the positive version of the Third Commandment and the direct opposite of the wolves in Acts 20:29 who misrepresent Christ.

Bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God—there is godly fruitage when we carry God's name with integrity, spirituality and genuineness. That is a genuine signature and not a forgery.

These texts in Colossians are basically telling us to diligently seek God's word as our sole guide. Jesus told us we would be sanctified by the truth of God's word. (John 17:17: KJV Sanctify them through Thy truth; Thy word is truth.) We need to shun the teachings of those who would make the word of God a tool of personal benefit. Walk away. Those teachings have no redeeming power. They are a false representation; a false signature claiming you represent something you really don't.

In every case, the sacredness of God’s name has the power to completely reset our thinking. Let it do its work:

Matthew 6:7–9: (Jesus teaches us to pray) 7 And when you are praying, do not use meaningless repetition as the Gentiles do, for they suppose that they will be heard for their many words. 8 So do not be like them; for your Father knows what you need before you ask Him. 9 Pray, then, in this way: Our Father who is in heaven, hallowed <37> be Your name.

Hallowed: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #37 hagiazo; from #40; to make holy,

i.e. (ceremonially) purify or consecrate; (mentally) to venerate

Hallowed, also translated as sanctify, means to make holy, to treat as holy, to set

apart as sacred. Jesus begins the Lord’s Prayer with another positive version of the

Third Commandment, essentially saying: “Father, may Your name be treated as holy, not dragged around in the mud,” the opposite of that sad Hebrew word shav, or emptiness. This is God’s reputation, and we are to carry the name with reverence and honor.

Hallowed be Your name is the positive representation of the Third Commandment. The first two Commandments have a positive representation as well.

It begins with the simple words, Our Father (have no other gods before Him).

Our Father shows that closeness we should feel to Him as our life-giver. Therefore, He deserves our eternal dedication and loyalty.

Our Father, who art in heaven (do not make, bow down to or serve idols).

Deuteronomy 4:15-16 makes clear that it is impossible to make an idol of God because we do not know what He looks like. We do not need idols because God’s presence in our lives is enough.

Then comes the Third Commandment—hallowed be Thy name. It’s right here at

the beginning of the Lord's Prayer. That’s powerful!

It is no accident that the veneration of God’s name should be the opening of our prayers!

Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be Thy name. Let these words inspire us to think more deeply about the veneration we owe to our Father, and let these thoughts plant the seeds of integrity, spirituality, humility and reverence.

The name we carry—our true signature—must always reflect that which we most highly honor:

1 Peter 3:15–16: 15 but sanctify <37> Christ as Lord in your hearts, always being ready to make a defense to everyone who asks you to give an account for the hope that is in you, yet with gentleness and reverence; 16 and keep a good conscience so that in the thing in which you are slandered, those who revile your good behavior in Christ will be put to shame.

Sanctify (set apart) Christ as Lord in your hearts. Who is Jesus? He is the son of the living God. Where is Jesus? At the right hand of the power of the living God. Remember this so we can be clear, powerful, unequivocal representatives, and not forge our name.

I don’t want to sign my name, Rick, the disciple of Christ, and then have it be found out that I looked like a disciple of Christ, but the works of my life and results of the imaginations of my heart did not match my signature. This is far too sacred to take lightly!

If we truly say we are disciples of Christ, we are saying that I, as a Christian, have no other gods before God. I will not build idols in any way, and I will carry the name of God with respect, honor, dignity, integrity, faith and humility so that His name can be seen through me. This is what it means to not take God's name in vain.

So, do I ever take God’s name in vain?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

### Study Questions

(Ten Commandments Part III)

https://christianquestions.com/character/1446-taking-gods-name-in-vain/

1. How does redefining “take” as “carry” deepen our understanding of what it means to bear God’s name?

(Exodus 20:7, Genesis 4:13)

2. In what way can our outward religious identity become “empty” or “false?” (using the definition of “vain”)

3. How does Jonah’s confession in Jonah 2:7-9, reveal an internal idolatry? What is the lesson for us?

4. Describe the decline into hypocrisy caused by chasing our own “vain idols.” How does this happen to a

disciple of Christ? (Philippians 3:4-6, Ephesians 4:17-19, Acts 20:29-30)

5. What are the antidotes to the reasons for this decline into hypocrisy?

a. Personal desires: Philippians 3:4-8

How can personal success become an idol that corrupts our “signature” as Christ’s disciples? Where in my life am I carrying God’s name outwardly, while inwardly allowing personal desires, comfort or pride shape my true signature?

b. Worldly influences: Ephesians 4:17-19, Hebrews 12:2

How can worldly influences reshape our “signature”? Where do they belong in our life? What protects us and preserves the integrity of the name we carry?

What worldly influences have moved into the center of my life, affecting my choices, priorities or loyalties?

c. Leading of others: Acts 20:29-30, Colossians 1:9-10

How can spiritual leadership become a place where God’s name is most easily forged? What does it mean for our Christian life to be consistent with the value of who we represent?

6. Why is the veneration of God’s name placed at the beginning of Jesus’ teaching us the Lord’s prayer?

How is this the positive fulfillment of the Third Commandment? (Matthew 6:7-9, Deuteronomy 4:15-16) In what specific ways can I more intentionally “hallow” God’s name in my daily conduct, relationships and decisions?

7. Who is it that our true signature must reflect? How can you do more of this in your daily life?

(1 Peter 3:15-16)

## Episode 1447 — Does Honoring the Sabbath Apply to Christians Today?
Published: 2026-07-27
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1447-sabbath-rest/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/16153028/CQ_Rewind_07-27-2026_Does_Honoring_the_Sabbath_Apply_to_Christians_Today.pdf

(The Ten Commandments Series Part IV)

Exodus 20:8: (ASV) Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.

Although the Ten Commandments are well known, the sad reality is they certainly are not well practiced. In our current Ten Commandment series, we are examining each one and how it relates to our Christian lives here and now. So far, we’ve covered the first three and found them to be deeply connected and incredibly relevant to our everyday lives. We now look at the Fourth, the command to remember the Sabbath day and to keep it holy. As Christians, the issue here should be obvious. The Jewish Sabbath is Saturday, and we have our day of worship and rest on Sunday. Are we wrong in this approach, or is our remembering the Sabbath supposed to be expressed in entirely different terms?

Let’s begin by tying the lessons of the first three commandments together:

Having no other gods before God is an “internal instruction” and is fulfilled by having our hearts and minds clearly fixed on God, through Jesus, as our only object of loyalty and praise. This Commandment is the basis for ALL of the rest.

Having no idols is an “external action instruction” and can be outwardly observed. To “make” an idol is to create a physically or emotionally tangible object of worship. It is an outward manifestation of an inward lack of fidelity to the one God.

Not carrying, or bearing, God’s name in an insincere way is an “external action instruction” to thoroughly and genuinely live what we proclaim to be.

The Christian bottom line on this Commandment:

This is the first “do” Commandment after a string of three “don’t” Commandments. The first three demonstrated an alarming and degrading human pathway away from God.

Violating the First Commandment, having other gods in our lives, opened the door to violate the Second Commandment, which was establishing those other gods as idols. These decisions set up the utterly hypocritical environment for us to violate the Third Commandment and become a walking contradiction of proclaiming faithfulness but not living it.

Remembering the Sabbath is a critical element in identifying that destructive pattern that brings us to such hypocrisy. The Sabbath allows us to reevaluate and break the pattern.

Back in the Old Testament, remembering the Sabbath Day gave Israel a chance to stop, look to God and take a break from daily work. It was also a time to ask, “Am I putting something before God and becoming idolatrous? Am I honoring His name?” By interrupting constant busyness, the Sabbath helped them refocus on God.

Stopping the mundane daily activities helped them refocus and do nothing else but reflect and correct what might have been going wrong. It’s brilliant! Let’s look at how it was structured. God explained in detail what this Sabbath Day was to look like for the Jewish nation.

We will first look at the Jewish perspective before we move on to the Christian Sabbath:

Exodus 20:8-10: (ASV) 8 Remember the Sabbath <7676> Day, to keep it holy. 9 Six days shalt thou labor, and do all thy work; 10 but the seventh day is a sabbath <7676> unto Jehovah thy God: [in it] thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy man-servant, nor thy maid-servant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates.

Sabbath: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #7676 šabāṯ; intensive from Old Testament #7673;

intermission, i.e (specifically) the Sabbath

Sabbath means to take an intermission; rest and pause. Even the animals stopped working on this day.

Stop ALL physical labor for a day! Why was this so specific? God continued:

Exodus 20:11: (ASV) For in six days Jehovah made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: wherefore Jehovah blessed the sabbath <7676> day, and hallowed it.

Even God Himself rested after the creative days. He blessed the sabbath day (the intermission), and hallowed it. Why did God rest on the seventh day? Was he tired? Did He need a breather?

God introduces the concept of “rest” after the creative process, long before it is given in the Commandments:

Genesis 2:2-3: 2 By the seventh day God completed His work which He had done, and He rested <7673> on the seventh day from all His work which He had done. 3 Then God blessed the seventh day and sanctified <6942> it, because in it He rested from all His work which God had created and made.

Rested: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #7673 shabath; a primitive root; to repose, i.e. desist from exertion; used in many implied relations (causative, figurative or specific)

Sanctified: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #6942 qadash; a primitive root;

to be (causatively make, pronounce or observe as) clean

He sanctified—made clean—the seventh day and rested from all His work. This defines exactly what He rested from: the earthly, physical, creative process (from all His work which God had created and made). Israel also was supposed to rest from their physical, creative processes. There is a similarity.

God rested, not because He needed rest, but because He would now put His creative work into the hands of the created, allowing them to make their choices. After putting everything in place, He would step back to see how His creation would respond. This seventh-day rest would shape eternity!

God sanctified the seventh day as a day that would reflect the eternal unfolding of His will. God rested from His physical creation of the earth but still worked on the accomplishment of His plan.

God said that everything He made was clean and in order. It was declared to be good, and in the case of mankind, very good. When He completed His work, He looked at it with pleasure.

For those who know me, I'm kind of a clean freak. I ran a specialty cleaning service for many years, so everything needs to be neat and orderly.

(Rick) Let me just define Jonathan’s “neat and orderly,” okay? We used to work together long ago, and at times I’d go to visit him and not a thing was even remotely out of place on his desk. I would walk in, and just when Jonathan would turn away, I’d move a pencil just a little bit, maybe quarter of an inch, just so it was not quite in line. Sure enough, he’d notice it just like that. He would put it back and I’d smile, then when he wasn’t looking again, I’d try to turn something else.

Yeah, you tried to drive me crazy! Back to my story, when I’m done with a project of any kind, I like to look at my finished work. Then I ask my wife to come see what I’ve done. I sometimes wonder if she’s thinking, That's all you did? But seriously, she is very supportive and appreciative of what I attempt to do.

Looking at your work and reflecting on it is a small example of what God did. He purposely looked upon His work.

Within Israel’s ceremonial Law, the Sabbath was the primary observance. Their religious life included many appointed rituals, but the Sabbath was the central piece—the weekly pause that framed all other ceremonies. This fact is crucial to our understanding of how it does—and does not—apply to our Christian lives.

This passage illustrates just one of the many Sabbath observances found in the Jewish Law:

Leviticus 23:23-25: 23 Again the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, 24 Speak to the sons of Israel, saying, In the seventh month on the first of the month you shall have a rest <7677>, a reminder by blowing of trumpets, a holy convocation. 25 You shall not do any laborious work, but you shall present an offering by fire to the LORD.

Rest: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #7677 šabāṯôn from Old Testament #7676; a sabbatism or special holiday

The Law included many such Sabbath times, all tied to its ceremonial structure: weekly Sabbath Days, the Feast of Pentecost, Sabbath years every seventh year, and the Jubilee in the 50th year. Each represented a divinely appointed period of rest—sometimes for the people, sometimes for the land, and often for both.

With so many Sabbath observances built into the Law, it’s helpful to notice how different groups within Israel experienced them. Since the Aaronic priesthood had no inheritance in the land, they were exempt from the literal Sabbath because they served God on the Sabbath and labored for God. The Aaronic priesthood did NOT have the Sabbath off.

Their responsibilities had nothing to do with the land (unlike the other Israelites who were working the land and needed the rest for themselves and for the land) because the priesthood did not own land. Their work was all about spiritual responsibilities.

Is there a connection to Christianity in this thought? Yes. The Apostle Peter describes true Christians in 1 Peter 2:9 as a chosen race, a royal priesthood. We are put in the same category as the Aaronic priests; not being bound by the physical responsibilities towards the things of the land. Our responsibilities are to higher spiritual principles.

Christian Sabbath Principles: God rested and yet continued working. How? He rested from the physical creation but continually worked on the accomplishment of His plan.

In the “cleanness” of that seventh day, He showed us His plan in a new, higher way.

A great example of our rest in Christ can be found in doing good works:

Ephesians 2:10 (ASV): For we are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God afore prepared that we should walk in them.

What kind of works did God prepare for us? Not works in the physical world, although they may include doing good for others; rather, works of spiritual importance.

Jesus worked on the Sabbath and told us God was still working as well:

John 5:15-17: 15 The man went away, and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well. 16 For this reason the Jews were persecuting Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath.

Jesus heals a man, so why is he being persecuted for doing something good? The Law had been interpreted over time to say that the Jews could not lift a finger for any reason or else it would be considered “working” on the Sabbath. But that was not what the Sabbath was for!

The Law allowed necessary acts of mercy on the Sabbath. Caring for animals, rescuing them from danger and helping someone in need were never forbidden. Jesus reminded the Pharisees it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath (Matthew 12:11-12). Jesus showed them that the higher spiritual works are entirely acceptable. The scribes and Pharisees wrongfully persecuted Jesus for these Sabbath Day acts of mercy because he was making them look bad. Jesus showed us his responsibilities on the Sabbath, which, in turn, are our responsibilities.

Jesus replied: 17 But he answered them, My Father is working until now, and I myself am working.

Jesus’ answer shows that God is still working. He rested from the physical creation of the world, but He has continued working ever since—carrying out the spiritual side of His plan through and with Jesus.

God’s work after creation was to prepare the coming of Messiah and then to work through Messiah. Jesus was foreshadowed throughout the Old Testament—seen in Isaac as the promised seed of Abraham, reflected in the Tabernacle sacrifices, and pictured in many literal events that pointed forward to him.

So the work God invested in His people on a spiritual level was all part of preparing Israel—and ultimately the world—for Messiah. He was laying the groundwork for the age to come. This was profound and purposeful work, but it was not the physical work of creation. He rested from that physical work.

A Christian’s Sabbath rest is defined and applied very differently than the Jewish Sabbath. How do WE enter into God’s rest? Only through Jesus and being part of his continuing the work of God. It is through him and his work that we enter into God’s rest.

When God works in us, we find rest:

Philippians 1:6: (ASV) being confident of this very thing, that He who began a good work in you will perfect it until the day of Jesus Christ.

In other words, our spiritual life is defined by God’s ongoing work within us. It sounds like everything is about work, doesn’t it? And it is—spiritual work. We don’t stop living faithfully or stop growing. But our rest comes within that work, not apart from it. How is that possible?

Jesus gives us the answer:

Matthew 11:28-30: 28 Come to me, all who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you rest <373>. 29 Take my yoke upon you and learn from me...

Rest: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #373 anapauo VERB; (reflexively)

to repose (literally or figuratively (be exempt), remain); by implication, to refresh:—take ease, refresh, (give, take) rest

At first this seems contradictory. Jesus promises rest, yet immediately tells us to take up his yoke, an image of labor. It feels like he’s saying, “I’ll give you rest… now get to work!”

But it actually makes perfect sense. The rest Jesus gives is relief from everything that burdens us—fear, guilt, anxiety, striving and the weight of our own failures. The yoke he gives is the life of discipleship, walking in his footsteps and doing the work God sets before us.

So, we rest from the things that drain us, and we work in the strength he provides.

...for I am gentle and humble in heart, and YOU WILL FIND REST <372> FOR YOUR SOULS. 30 For my yoke is easy and my burden is light.

Rest: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #372 anapausis; NOUN

intermission; by implication, recreation

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: intermission, cessation of any motion, business or labor

You will find rest for your souls—a rest from worldly cares, ambitions and the worldly things that need to be done, because our focus now is on something different.

Remember when Jesus was with the apostles and they urged him to eat? He responded in

John 4:32,34: 32 …I have food to eat that you do not know about. 34 My food is to do the will of Him who sent me and to accomplish His work.

Jesus was refreshed and rested because he didn’t need to worry about earthly things when he was engaged in the work of his Father. That is our calling as well. His yoke—his work, pictured by the harness used to plow a field—is easy, and his burden is light.

We find rest and refreshment when we set aside earthly cares and take up that work. That is Christian rest.

The book of Hebrews compares Old and New Testament Sabbath resting:

Hebrews 4:3: For we who have believed enter that rest, just as He has said, AS I SWORE IN MY WRATH, THEY SHALL NOT ENTER MY REST <2663> (quoting from Psalm 95:11), although His works were finished from the foundation of the world.

Rest: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2663 the noun form of 2664: katapauo; from 2596 and

3973; to settle down, i.e. (literally) to colonize, or (figuratively) to (cause to) desist

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon for Strong’s #2664: 1) to make quiet, to cause to be at rest, to grant

rest 1a) to lead to a quiet abode… 2) to rest, take rest

The Apostle tells the Hebrew Christians that we enter that rest through belief in Jesus. Israel did not enter His rest because they failed to live in harmony with God’s commandments.

Hebrews reminds us that His works were finished from the foundation of the world. God’s physical works were done, and His rest from that physical creation is on-going. Even though He rested from creating the world, He has continued working on spiritual things ever since.

Though God’s physical works were “finished,” His full plan had not yet been revealed. The Old Testament slowly revealed what would come through Messiah, and we are part of His works still being revealed.

There’s a subtle yet important difference between the word for rest Jesus gives in

Matthew 11:29 and the rest in Hebrews 4:3. They shall not enter My rest uses a word closely related to the Sabbath rest—a cessation, a putting down of things, a time to stop and reflect. The rest Jesus offers in Matthew, rest for your souls, is a slightly different word with a more uplifting, restorative sense. Looking at these two words side by side shows an important connection:

The two Greek verbs—anapauo and katapauo—both share the root pauo, meaning “to cease” or “to stop,” but their prefixes give them different shades of meaning.

Anapauo emphasizes restoration and refreshment—an uplifting pause. This is the kind of rest Jesus offers. Even when we are working, it is restful because we are working with him. We follow him, he leads us, and he is our Lord.

Katapauo emphasizes cessation or stopping. It can be positive, as in God’s rest, but it carries the thought of not doing something. This is the idea behind the Sabbath rest—a deliberate putting down of activity.

So Sabbath rest is about ceasing. The rest Jesus gives involves setting aside earthly things, but then taking up his work—something higher, different and spiritually refreshing.

Jesus gives us a positive, uplifting pause because becoming his disciples elevates us to a higher life. Living a life of sacrifice and following Jesus now let’s us participate in the work of restoring God’s favor to humanity.

Does resting in God’s work mean we don’t have to do anything to sustain ourselves and our family on a daily basis? NO. The New Testament is clear: if anyone does not provide for his own… he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever (1 Timothy 5:8). We have to work to take care of our own needs and the needs of those dependent on us. But that is not our sole objective in life. It is not what drives us. We rest in God because our lives are about being a new creature.

2 Corinthians 5:17: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature; the old things have passed away; behold, new things have come.

We don’t have to worry. We still live in the world, but that’s not where our worry belongs. That’s not where we toil. We do the work that needs to be done, but our real labor—our real effort—is in Christ, empowered by God and His spirit. That is what it’s about.

In Philippians 4:8, the Apostle Paul told us to think on those things that are true, honorable, right, pure, etc.

Here is the next verse:

Philippians 4:9: (ASV) The things which ye both learned and received and heard and saw in me, these things do: and the God of peace shall be with you.

These things DO—we never stop “working” at doing the will of God. We never take a day off. But we do need to put our earthly labors in their appropriate context.

Our Sabbath rest is more about reprioritizing the normal activities of living so we can refocus on the higher gifts and blessings from God through Jesus. We should do this every day.

This is a real true struggle of mine. There are a lot of things on my plate. I run a business and have many responsibilities. I’m not complaining, but sometimes I get overwhelmed. And when I get overwhelmed and the pile starts to get too big, I

start to rush. And when I start to rush, I get careless. When I get careless, I make mistakes and don’t take care of things the way I should.

Interestingly, in the last several weeks, I’ve observed my rushing and seeing how I’m starting to get careless. I actually say out loud, “SLOW DOWN!” It’s a reset that helps me to put aside my earthly thinking.

The pile doesn’t get smaller. It’s still just as big and intense, but slowing down gives me the ability to think clearly. This is a spiritual thing. This is resting in the Lord by putting away the earthly demands and my reactions to them.

In the last several weeks some amazing, beautiful things have happened by slowing down. It didn’t make the pile go down or go away, but it enabled me to deal with my responsibilities, by putting “Rick” away and relying on the peace of Jesus.

Hebrews continues by revealing the transition of rest in God from Israel to Christianity:

Hebrews 4:4,6-7: 4 For He has said somewhere concerning the seventh day: AND GOD RESTED <2664> ON THE SEVENTH DAY FROM ALL HIS WORKS. 6 Therefore, since it remains for some to enter it, and those who formerly had good news preached to them failed to enter because of disobedience, 7 He again fixes a certain day, Today, saying through David after so long a time just as has been said before, TODAY IF YOU HEAR HIS VOICE, DO NOT HARDEN YOUR HEARTS.

He is talking about Israel’s seventh-day rest and the fact that they were given the opportunity to enter God’s rest but did not take it. Because of their disobedience, they failed to enter. Paul then quotes David, who says prophetically in effect, “Today is another opportunity. Do not harden your hearts when God offers you His rest.”

We rest in the strength of Jesus:

Philippians 4:13: (ASV) I can do all things in him that strengtheneth me.

This isn’t about stopping; it’s about doing. We take care of our earthly cares by the grace of God through His spirit, putting our energy into the new mindset of that holy nation and royal priesthood. Our rest comes from relying on His strength as we carry out the work He gives us.

Back to Israel, Joshua did bring the people into the Promised Land, but they never maintained full “rest” in God:

Hebrews 4:8-9: 8 For if Joshua had given them rest <2664>, He (God speaking through David in the previous verse) would not have spoken of another day after that. 9 So there remains a Sabbath rest <4520> for the people of God.

Joshua’s rest refers to Israel entering the Promised Land—a physical cessation from wandering and war. God’s rest, however, is deeper. Even after Joshua led them into Canaan, God still spoke of another day of rest that was spiritual and ongoing. This “other day” connects directly to the katapauo rest—the divine cessation from self-driven works and striving, entering into harmony with God’s completed word.

Christians ARE the people of God to whom this rest now applies—through Jesus, God had His Sabbath rest: resting from His earthly creation while continuing His work on the new creation. We have our Sabbath rest by resting from our earthly creation—our old life— and living with a new focus. We still take care of our responsibilities, but our work is now driven by being “in Christ.” That is the difference.

Rest: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4520 sabbatismos; from a derivative of 4521;

a "sabbatism," i.e. (figuratively) the repose of Christianity (as a type of heaven)

Hebrews 4:10-11: 10 For the one who has entered His rest<2663> (we have entered His Sabbath kind of rest) has himself also rested from his works, as God did from His.

We put aside our earthly cares because our minds are focused on something higher where our hearts are. This doesn’t mean we don’t take care of responsibilities. It means we do them in a godly fashion. That was how Jesus took care of everything in his earthly care, with that godliness.

11 Therefore let us be diligent to enter that rest <2663>, so that no one will fall, through following the same example of disobedience.

We are invited into God’s rest but are then required to actively step into it. That means deliverately laying down self-driven striving and choosing to rely on Christ’s strength instead of our own, so that we don’t repeat Israel’s pattern of disobedience.

For me, it’s verbally saying, “SLOW DOWN!” I take “me” out to allow the principles and the heart of Jesus to rule inside me in order to deal with exactly what I have to deal with in a completely different way. It is transformational.

It all comes down to Jesus. God’s work is through him, and our work and growth are through him. That’s the lesson God has been teaching throughout this entire age after He finished His creative work. He has shown us Messiah’s coming, Messiah’s presence, Messiah’s sacrifice and Messiah now in heaven. At present, Jesus is drawing those who follow him to be part of the work of the next age.

This reminds us of the following verses:

Revelation 14:12-13: (ASV) 12 Here is the patience of the saints, they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus. 13 And I heard a voice from heaven saying, Write, Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from henceforth: yea, saith the spirit, that they may rest from their labors; for their works follow with them.

We never rest in our spiritual labors. Our rest is in doing spiritual work every day of our lives. That is where our focus, our energy, and our peace come together—resting from the old life while faithfully working in the new one.

This doesn’t mean we don’t ever take time out to pause and consider, worship and pray. We know the early church did that. The early church chose Sunday, the first day of the week, as a day to gather, study, reflect, pray and praise because it was the day Jesus was resurrected. Spiritual work on Resurrection Day!

Resurrection Day unfolded the work of God’s previously unknown plan:

Acts 20:7: On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul began talking to them, intending to leave the next day, and he prolonged his message until midnight.

He spoke until midnight! This shows Paul was speaking and “working” on the Christian Sabbath. We observe our Sabbath on that day because that was the day the world was changed. Jesus died and the moment he was raised, the world was forever changed.

1 Corinthians 16:2: On the first day of every week each one of you is to put aside and save, as he may prosper, so that no collections be made when I come.

Paul tells the Corinthians that when they gather on the first day of the week, they should set aside contributions for the poor and for Jerusalem so that everything would be ready when he arrived. He wasn’t telling them to stop doing anything; he was telling them to do work of spiritual value. He was directing them towards activity that served God’s people.

Christian rest isn’t inactivity. It’s a state of peace and purpose found in spiritual labor. We devote ourselves to God’s work by building character, serving others, spreading truth—we participate in God’s ongoing creative work. We rest by working in harmony with Him. Our rest is found in doing God’s spiritual work so the kingdom can be ushered in, not in ceasing all motion like the literal Sabbath of old. That’s the beauty of the Christian Sabbath.

How many days a week are we supposed to do that?

Every day. We are to rest every day. On Sundays, there is generally a special time where we have praise and prayer, but that doesn’t mean we can’t have rest every day.

Every day of our lives we are serving God. We can never take time off from that, even during our own leisure time. But we rest in God’s presence in our lives, in His spirit working in us, in His word showing us how, and in putting aside our own earthly ways and ambitions.

We need to take care of our earthly business, but we take care of it in the context like

Jesus said in John 4:32,34: 32 …I have food to eat that you do not know about. 34 …my food is to do the will of Him who sent me and to accomplish His work.

How am I living my Christian life every day? Is every day a day of resting in the Lord? Am I getting frustrated and anxious about all the pieces of life? If so, maybe we aren’t resting in the Lord as we should.

Instead, let’s attempt to approach those frustrations, difficulties and challenges with the rest of God through Christ. Let’s see how that transforms us from being frustrated to a footstep follower of Jesus.

So, does honoring the Sabbath apply to Christians today?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!
