### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1447-sabbath-rest/

1. What similarities exist between God ceasing His creation on the seventh creative day and Israel being

commanded to observe a sabbath in Exodus 20:8-11? (Genesis 2:2-3)

2. What is the deeper meaning of God’s rest? Why did God sanctify the seventh day? (Genesis 2:2-3,

Exodus 20:11)

3. How could the Sabbath serve as a safeguard against violating the first three commandments?

(Exodus 20:3-8)

4. There were many Sabbath observances in Israel’s Law. Some were for the people, some for the animals,

and some for the land itself. Why was the Aaronic priesthood unique in all of Israel in regard to the Sabbath? (Leviticus 23:23-25, 1 Peter 2:9)

5. Contrast the nature of Christian work with the ceasing of physical labor on the Sabbath that Israel

practiced. What is the relationship between spiritual work and Sabbath rest? (Ephesians 2:10, John 5:15-17,

Matthew 12:11-12)

6. Why are Jesus’ rest and the taking up his yoke not a contradiction, but rather essential parts of each

other? (Matthew 11:28-30)

7. What practical changes can I make this week to “rest in the Lord”? (Hebrews 4:10-11, John 4:32,34)

8. Compare the two forms of “rest” in Matthew 11:29 and Hebrews 4:3. How does entering into God’s rest

different from the rest Jesus gives us when we become his followers? (Philippians 4:13, Hebrews 4:8-9)

9. What does it mean to “rest now while we do God’s work”? Why do Christians observe our Sabbath day on

Sunday rather than Saturday? (chart at end, Acts 20:7, 1 Corinthians 16:2)

10. How can I more intentionally enter into the rest Jesus describes in Matthew 11:28-30 when life becomes

busy, stressful or overwhelming?

## Episode 1448 — What Does Honoring Our Parents Really Mean?
Published: 2026-08-03
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1448-honoring-parents/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/24134001/CQ_Rewind_08-03-2026_What_Does_Honoring_Our_Parents_Really_Mean.pdf

(The Ten Commandments Series Part V)

Exodus 20:12: (ASV) Honor thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long in the

land which Jehovah thy God giveth thee.

The Fifth Commandment God gave to Israel after He freed them from slavery was a simple statement of respect. God instructed each and every individual to honor their parents. To really understand the import of this Command from God to His people of Israel—and to us—it is important to do two things. First, recognize that appropriate “honor” for one’s parents really has its foundation in the previous four Commandments. Second, we need to be aware that while honoring our parents is based on honoring God, we must recognize that any and all honor we give them reflects how and why we honor God. So, how and why do we as Christians honor our parents?

Exodus 20:3: (ASV) Thou shalt have no other gods before Me.

God is sovereign. This “internal instruction” is the basis for ALL of God’s other Commandments.

Exodus 20:4: (ASV) Thou shalt not make unto thee a graven image…

God’s sovereignty is never to be shared or diminished. This “external action instruction” (what we do) is outwardly observed when we refrain from creating a physically or emotionally tangible object of worship.

Exodus 20:7: (ASV) Thou shalt not take the name of Jehovah thy God in vain…

This external action instruction focuses us on NEVER representing the holiness of God’s name carelessly, foolishly or with any hint of irreverence.

Exodus 20:8: (ASV) Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.

This is also an external action instruction.

God rested after His creative work of the earth and human life, though He continued to prepare and provide for the Messiah. We also are to rest, to not be driven by the toil of our physical lives, but “rest” in the redemption and calling that Jesus has provided. We rest in the blessed work and sacrifice of taking his yoke upon us.

The first four commandments focus on who God is and give us instruction in how to thrive spiritually. They are our foundation and encompass the sanctity that His sovereignty holds in our lives. They teach us to always reverence Him with our

everyday thoughts, words and actions.

Now comes the Fifth Commandment. It is also an external action instruction and is the first step in establishing how to physically thrive as a people in relation to one another. All of the six final Commandments will show us what governs successful interpersonal relationships.

Exodus 20:12: (ASV) Honor <3513> thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long in the land which Jehovah thy God giveth thee.

What does it mean to honor your father and mother? This word honor can be positive or negative.

Honor: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3513 kabad or kabed; a primitive root; to be heavy, i.e. in a bad sense (burdensome, severe, dull) or in a good sense (numerous, rich, honorable);

causatively, to make weighty (in the same two senses)

Brown-Driver-Briggs Hebrew and English Lexicon: to be heavy, be weighty, be grievous,

be hard, be rich, be honourable, be glorious, be burdensome, be honoured

Honor in a bad sense:

Exodus 8:32: (KJV) And Pharaoh hardened <3513> his heart at this time also, neither would he let the people go.

Here the Hebrew word is used in a negative, even dangerous, sense.

Honor in a good sense:

Proverbs 3:9: (KJV) Honour <3513> the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase.

This word for honor means to give weighty, meaningful reverence to God with our substance, our very being, and with the firstfruits of whatever we produce. Put Him high above everything, at all times.

This is a powerful word, however it is used.

Just as the principle of reverencing God is the spiritual foundation for society, so the honoring of parents is the physical foundation for human societal interaction. Both are needed.

If we are truly to understand “honoring our parents,” we need context. This next set of scriptures puts it all together in a beautiful way.

These scriptures are also part of the Jewish Law:

Leviticus 19:1–4: 1 Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying: 2 Speak to all the congregation of the sons of Israel and say to them, You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy (set apart. In other words, you shall be set apart, just like God is set apart. As a people, you're different from everyone else.) 3 Every one of you shall reverence his mother and his father, and you shall keep My sabbaths; I am the LORD your God. 4 Do not turn to idols or make for yourselves molten gods; I am the LORD your God.

All of the first five commandments are reflected in this summation.

In ancient Israel, the honor due to parents was a pivotal part of establishing and maintaining a God-revering society. It could even have been looked at as a matter of national security! They had to honor their parents to keep their nation intact, because the nation was built on honoring God, the ultimate Father.

(Source: jewishstudiesforchristians.com) In the Hebrew, honoring our parents carries the

profound idea of “weight” or “heaviness.” First and foremost in the mind and heart, to

ascribe weight, substance and supreme importance to one’s parents. It involves refusing

to view them as fleeting shadows; but rather, as vital anchors in our lives, deserving our deepest respect and devotion.

This gives the sense that our parents are our strong anchors. An anchor holds us in place. From the standpoint of Israel and Jewish Law, that is the concept.

Now let’s focus on our Christian responsibility to honor our father and our mother.

New Testament honor:

Honor: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5091 timao; to prize,

i.e. fix a valuation upon; by implication, to revere

Matthew 15:4: For God said, HONOR <5091> YOUR FATHER AND MOTHER, and, HE WHO SPEAKS EVIL OF FATHER OR MOTHER IS TO BE PUT TO DEATH.

Well, that’s harsh! But what if someone's parents are awful parents? We will address this important question after setting some groundwork.

Matthew 15:4 quotes the Fifth Commandment, and the Greek word for honor means “to prize” or “to revere.” As Christians, we should view this commandment in the context of this definition.

This shows how this word can be applied in its highest sense:

John 5:23: so that all will honor <5091> the son even as they honor <5091> the Father. He who does not honor <5091> the son does not honor <5091> the Father who sent him.

This is a strong statement by Jesus, essentially saying he is connected to the Father. Therefore, if we truly revere the Father, we honor Jesus because the Father sent him.

Having respect for our parents opens positive doors for all involved:

Proverbs 23:22–23: 22 Listen to your father who begot you, and do not despise your mother when she is old. 23 Buy truth, and do not sell it, get wisdom and instruction and understanding.

This gives us a sense of “Pay attention!” Notice those who are naturally there for us. Such a level of honoring begins in a sincere heart and is expressed as an external action. Honoring our parents is not only inward; it is shown by how we live and how we express ourselves.

(Source: jewishstudiesforchristians.com) Parents are the first divine representatives we encounter—the ones who give us life, exercise authority over us, provide care and hold out the promise of a bright future. They act on behalf of God for a significant portion of our lives. This reality establishes the family as the primary training ground for moral character, where a child learns how to relate to others in appropriate ways.

That’s a beautiful way to put it. Parents were the first ones in line. As Christians, just like the Jews who were given that commandment back in the Old Testament, we should have this sense of reverence in relation to our parents. How do we put this into practice in our everyday lives?

We brought my parents to live with us because they needed care. My dad had Alzheimer’s for seven years but was always gentle. After eight months with us, he passed away peacefully at home, all with the help of wonderful caregivers and God's guidance. My mom stayed with us for three years. She loved having Bible studies at our house, waving to people from the porch and being pampered. We did our best, but caring for her was sometimes hard because she needed a lot of attention. It took patience from all of us, especially my wife.

I remember once when Jewel was working in another room, and Mom was in the living room watching TV. She called out for Jewel and asked specifically for three Raisinets (chocolate-covered candy) in a dish. Of course, Jewel didn’t count them out. By the way, Mom was capable of walking. We all called her Queen, and she loved that. Looking back, we have no regrets. God gave us the strength to honor both my parents. It wasn’t always easy—and sometimes it was exhausting—but the point is, it was the right thing to do.

Let’s go back to Jesus as an example. At age 12, he had been left behind in Jerusalem, and his parents were very worried.

His response to their worry and then his life after:

Luke 2:49–52: 49 And he said to them, Why is it that you were looking for me? Did you not know that I had to be in my Father’s house?

Jesus was saying, “Where else would I be? I'm not interested in anything other than being close to my heavenly Father.”

50 But they did not understand the statement which he had made to them. 51 And he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and he continued in subjection to them; and his mother treasured all these things in her heart. 52 And Jesus kept increasing in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men.

Jesus was perfect, but he didn’t know everything. By the age of 12, he likely had an intellectual capacity beyond most human beings. The beauty of this scripture is that they didn't understand what he said, but he continued in subjection to them until his time came. He looked to his parents as his earthly examples. They taught him what he needed to know about human life. Jesus kept increasing in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men, which is a testimony to his parents’ input and his receiving it with that honor. It is a beautiful example. He was an example of a calm, quiet young man, open to learning.

That was the first instance we have of Jesus interacting with his parents. Now let's fast forward. The last time Jesus interacts with his mother is when he's on the cross.

At the very end of his life, he continued to be the example of what honoring our parents should look like:

John 19:25–27: 25 …But standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. 26 When Jesus then saw his mother, and the disciple whom he loved (the Apostle John) standing nearby, he said to his mother, Woman, behold, your son! 27 Then he said to the disciple, Behold, your mother! From that hour the disciple took her into his own household.

A child dying before the parent is unnatural. Jesus, even while in the midst of agony and pain, was concerned for his mother's well-being. He turned over the responsibility for caring for his mother to the Apostle John, whom he trusted with her life. John was the only apostle at the cross. John lived longer than any other apostle, giving him the time to care for Mary, Jesus’ faithful mother.

He did not act on the spur of the moment; there was thought and care behind his words. It shows the honor and respect Jesus had for his mother, up to almost his dying breath.

Our respect for our parents must filter through our recognition of their best yet imperfect efforts.

This scripture is talking about being disciplined:

Hebrews 12:9–11: 9 Furthermore, we had earthly fathers to discipline us, and we respected them; shall we not much rather be subject to the Father of spirits, and live? 10 For they disciplined us for a short time as seemed best to them (in other words, they did the best they could), but He disciplines us for our good, so that we may share His holiness. 11 All discipline for the moment seems not to be joyful, but sorrowful; yet to those who have been trained by it, afterwards it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness.

The comparison is that our earthly parents disciplined us for a short time as seemed best to them. These verses allow for imperfection. It assumes our parents were doing the best they could when they disciplined us, and we needed to learn from it. All discipline for the moment seems not to be joyful, but sorrowful—we may not have always agreed with their parenting decisions, but we should honor our parents’ best intentions. If we want to be judged in our own lives based on that standard, we need to apply it to others, especially our parents.

Though wisdom is never complete in any of us, it generally dwells in those with greater experience:

1 Timothy 5:1–2: 1 Do not sharply rebuke an older man, but rather appeal to him as a father, to the younger men as brothers, 2 the older women as mothers, and the younger women as sisters, in all purity.

When we need to correct an older person, it has to be done respectfully, and with honor and wisdom.

It is appropriate to respect our elders. My mother-in-law was a devoted Christian. We had the privilege of having her live with us for 13 years after my father-in-law passed away. She faced many physical challenges and needed our help. I always enjoyed discussing the Scriptures with her. She had much wisdom to share.

I knew your mother-in-law well. Over those many years, I was able to see the great mutual respect everyone had. You and Jewel lifted her up to a position of great honor. Your example stays with me to this day.

These 1 Timothy texts talked about having to direct somebody who's older. Let me give you just an example from my own life experiences with my mom. Jonathan, you know my mom very well. She is the most generous, hospitable person you’ll ever meet anywhere. If you look up “hospitality” in the dictionary, there is her picture! But as people get older, their reflexes start to slow down. They don’t necessarily realize it.

A few years ago, when she was older than 70-years old but less than 90 (I’m not revealing her age!), it became obvious that driving was probably no longer a good idea.

I had a conversation with her one day about the concept of slowing down reflexes and the potential to hurt someone without meaning to. I said, "Mom, I want you to think about this, because I want it to be your decision." I thought it was really important to be her choice. A few days later, we were sitting and talking—I go visit her every morning. She said, “Oh, you know what? I thought about what we talked about and here’s what happened. I was driving with Joy (her daughter, my sister). Joy was driving, and somebody just cut out in front of us. Joy had to stop suddenly. I realized I would never have been able to stop in time.”

So, she made the decision. I could have approached her and demanded she give me her license, but that would not have been the respectful thing to do. That incident really stuck with me in terms of how to deal with things from a perspective of honor.

Jonathan: I love your mom. She is always encouraging when she sees me.

How do we know? Let’s go back to the Scriptures:

Ephesians 6:1–4: 1 Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. 2 HONOR YOUR FATHER AND MOTHER (which is the First Commandment with a promise), 3 SO THAT IT MAY BE WELL WITH YOU, AND THAT YOU MAY LIVE LONG ON THE EARTH. 4 Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.

Obey your parents in the Lord for this is right—then the Apostle Paul quotes the Fifth Commandment. After that, he warns, Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.

When a parent is destructive, abusive and not abiding by righteous principles (and it breaks our hearts to even talk about this), we have to be able to step back and not blindly follow. Any destructive parenting issue can be a real challenge.

As Christians, we should always look to those who would give godly instruction for help when faced with such a prospect:

Galatians 6:2: Bear one another’s burdens, and thereby fulfill the law of Christ.

(Source: jewishstudiesforchristians.com) Honor can mean being sad about the loss of the ideal parent or respecting your own God-given worth by setting limits. To break the cycle of abuse is a very honorable thing to do. It indicates that you care about the relationship and want to make things better in the future. The process of healing becomes a sacred task as it brings the damaged relationship before God... When we listen with intention, forgive with generosity, set healthy boundaries where needed, and remain faithfully present.

There is no greater honor than helping someone up and putting them on the right path. If it is our parents, let’s do it with love and respect, taking a stand on the foundation of godly righteousness, rather than on what we think, feel or resent.

So, honoring our parents cannot be done without godliness.

Now on to our second caution. We must make clear that these two cautions are very different. They need to be kept separate at all times.

Sometimes we can have a resentment that overwhelms us, but is not based in godliness. Maybe our parents were doing the best they could toward righteousness, but we rejected their approach. Now we have built up a resentment. We have to be careful. This is not an excuse to cast our parents aside.

Jesus addresses this in talking to the Pharisees:

Mark 7:9–13: 9 He was also saying to them, You are experts at setting aside the commandment of God in order to keep your tradition. 10 For Moses said, HONOR YOUR FATHER AND YOUR MOTHER; and, HE WHO SPEAKS EVIL OF FATHER OR MOTHER, IS TO BE PUT TO DEATH; 11 but you say, If a man says to his father or his mother, whatever I have that would help you is Corban (that is to say, given to God), 12 you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or his mother; 13 thus invalidating the word of God by your tradition which you have handed down; and you do many things such as that.

The Pharisees taught the people to contribute to the temple treasury to further God’s work, even if it was at the expense of helping parents. The Pharisees said their parents could be told it was Corban—that is, “I’m giving the money I would have used for you to the temple to honor God.” Jesus saw through this. That is NOT what the Commandment was about. The Pharisees had created a giant loophole to get around the responsibilities the Law, which demanded the care of parents. “Give the money to us, not to your parents.”

Source: Eclectic Notes: Corban The Law did not give offerings the precedence over moral duties. For it had the Decalogue at its heart. But the inventions of the scribes had so perverted the moral intelligence that it had come to be a recognized thing that to declare any possession Corban left one free to refuse to use if for the help even of father or mother.

It is easy to fall into our resentment if we are frustrated and remembering difficult experiences. Sometimes we were rebellious as kids, right? We didn’t follow along, and then resented the correction. This is not a valid excuse. Perhaps our parents were trying hard to keep us on the righteous path.

Wisdom is clearly required to choose the right path when faced with highly emotional issues:

Galatians 6:7–8: 7 Do not be deceived, God is not mocked; for whatever a man sows, this he will also reap. 8 For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the spirit will from the spirit reap eternal life.

God is not mocked. What we sow, we reap. What we put out, we get back. God knows whether we are acting out of resentment, frustration or spite.

Christians are to honor their parents from the heart. We need to recognize whether our heart is tainted in any way. If it is, we have to work on correcting it so we can be honorable, as the Scriptures teach us.

Child-to-parent honor and parent-to-child respect that is pleasing to the Lord is our clear, focused and primary objective:

Colossians 3:20–21: 20 Children, be obedient to your parents in all things, for this is well- pleasing to the Lord. 21 Fathers, do not exasperate your children, so that they will not lose heart.

This is similar to Ephesians 6:4 we read earlier about fathers not provoking children to anger. This is obviously important, as Paul was inspired to share this twice.

Paul is talking to Gentile Christians who do not have any sense of the Jewish heritage of honoring their parents. He is laying out all the groundwork of what a true Christian life looks like from all perspectives. This helps us to also see the most important things.

All we do must be done with the full intention of pleasing God, including honoring our parents from our hearts:

Colossians 3:23–25: 23 Whatever you do, do your work heartily, as for the Lord rather than for men, 24 knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance. It is the Lord Christ whom you serve. 25 For he who does wrong will receive the consequences of the wrong which he has done, and that without partiality.

(Source: jewishstudiesforchristians.com) For when families reflect the weight of genuine honor, they become places of healing, hope and light—illuminating the way toward deeper harmony with God and one another. Let us carry this commandment forward with joy, knowing that in honoring our parents, we honor the God of Israel who first gave us life.

This is a choice we can make in applying this particular Commandment of honoring our father and mother in our own lives, no matter our age. This is what Jesus taught us to do.

Honoring our parents comes because we honor God. We do not have idols; we do not take His name in vain by misrepresenting Him because we rest in Jesus. Honoring our parents is built on these Christian principles.

Honoring our parents is a joy, a treasure, a brilliant opportunity and a responsibility.

So, what does honoring our parents really mean?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1448-honoring-parents/

1. How do the first four commandments (honoring God through reverence, worshiping Him exclusively,

respect for His name and Sabbath rest), prepare us for the Fifth Commandment, to honor our parents correctly? Why might God place reverence for parents within this context? (Exodus 20:3-8, 12, Leviticus 19:1-4)

2. How does the concept of “weight” or “heaviness” explain both positive and negative uses of the Hebrew

word, kabad? How do we give our parents “weight” in our lives? (Exodus 20:12, 8:32, Proverbs 3:9)

3. How does the New Testament concept of honor (timao – “to prize or revere”) deepen our understanding

of the Fifth Commandment? (Matthew 15:4, John 5:23)

4. What are some practical behaviors found in Proverbs 23:22-23 we can use to honor our parents?

5. How did Jesus honor his earthly parents in his youth and in the final moments of his life? (Luke 2:49-52,

John 19:25-27)

6. How can we more closely follow Jesus’ example of respectful, thoughtful and loving honor? How can you

make sure you aren’t primarily motivated by duty, family expectation, and instead by a desire to honor God? (John 19:25-27, Colossians 3:23-25)

7. Hebrews 12:9-11 says earthly fathers discipline “as seemed best to them.” How should this perspective

influence our judgments of our parents?

8. What guidance does 1 Timothy 5:1-2 provide for interacting with older family members? How can we

retain a respectful attitude even when difficult conversations are necessary?

9. What are the biblical limits of obedience, especially to abusive parents? How can honoring parents

coexist with setting healthy, godly boundaries? (Ephesians 6:1-4, Galatians 6:2)

10. How can we distinguish between honoring parents in difficult circumstances and falling into ungodly

resentment or avoidance?

11. Are there any unresolved resentments toward my parents that may hinder my ability to honor them from

the heart? What godly steps can I take toward healing, forgiveness and/or establishing appropriate boundaries? (Galatians 6:2, 7-8)

12. What was Jesus’ warning concerning excuses for neglecting parents? How can resentment, self-interest,

or even religious rationalization lead us to avoid our responsibilities toward parents today? (Mark 7:9-13)

13. How does honoring parents ultimately reflect our honor for God?

## Episode 1449 — What Makes Christians Guilty of Murder?
Published: 2026-08-10
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1449-christians-guilty-of-murder/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/03162352/CQ_Rewind_08-10-2026_What_Makes_a_Christian_Guilty_of_Murder.pdf

(The Ten Commandments Series Part VI)

Exodus 20:13: You shall not murder.

In this Ten Commandments series, we are looking at each commandment individually to see how they all apply to our present-day personal Christian lives. In our systematic examination of each of the first five commandments, we have seen a powerful interconnectedness that deepens their meaning for us. The first three focus us on God as our sole object of ultimate worship and loyalty. The Fourth Commandment to remember the Sabbath teaches us, as Christians, to rest in God through Jesus, ensuring our motivations in life remain spiritually focused. The Fifth Commandment to honor our father and mother was the first to fully focus on our interpersonal human relationships. This respect and honor towards parents is the clear foundation for the rest of the commandments, which set rigid guidelines for the mutual respect we should have for all humanity.

The Sixth Commandment is straightforward:

Exodus 20:13: You shall not murder <7523>.

Murder: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #7523 ratsach; a primitive root;

properly, to dash in pieces, i.e. kill (a human being), especially to murder

The King James Version translates this as put to death, kill, (man-) slay (-er), murder (-er)

“To dash in pieces”—this root word literally means to shatter a life. It has the sense of violently crushing or breaking a life, not merely killing.

This “external instruction” (action) is a direct command to honor the sanctity of human life and is given in the powerful context of honoring the sovereignty of God.

There are many words for kill or slay in the Old Testament, but God used ratsach for this Commandment.

Ratsach describes a person who takes the life of another outside the limitations of the Law and implies passion and rage behind the deed.

You shall not murder is the only Commandment repeated in some form in all five books of the Torah, the first five books of the Bible.

Starting in Genesis, after Noah and his family come off the Ark, this is one of God’s commands:

Genesis 9:6: Whoever sheds <8210> man’s blood, by man his blood shall be shed <8210>, for in the image of God He made man.

Shed: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #8210 šāp̄aḵ; a primitive root; to spill forth (blood,

a libation, liquid metal; or even a solid, i.e. to mound up); also (figuratively) to expend

(life, soul, complaint, money, etc.); intensively, to sprawl out:—cast (up),

gush out, pour (out), shed (-der, out), slip

From this we learn human life is sacred because we bear God’s image. Anything that destroys human life, dignity or crushes the vulnerable violates the image of God.

The prohibition against murder is again found in Exodus 20:13, Leviticus 24:17,

Numbers 35:30 and Deuteronomy 5:17.

How can the God who forbids killing also order it? He commanded Israel to kill surrounding pagan nations, asked Abraham to sacrifice Isaac, and allowed Jesus to be killed on a cross as part of the bigger plan. Is God contradicting Himself?

There’s a difference between human violence and divine judgment. God knows all, is above all, and is wise, loving, compassionate, merciful and just. His judgments have much deeper reasons behind them than our imperfect reactions.

Killing in war, for judicial justice or by accident among humans is never labeled in the Bible by this word ratsach for murder or murderer.

It is important to recognize that God’s understanding is far superior to ours. This category of “murder” applies only in specific circumstances, specifically to the unlawful destruction of human life driven by anger, rage or personal retribution.

This is an example of looking at God’s justice:

Psalms 94:1-2: (NLT) 1 O LORD, the God of vengeance, O God of vengeance, let your glorious justice shine forth! 2 Arise, O judge of the earth. Give the proud what they deserve.

We might feel, as David did here, that the proud and evil should get what we think they deserve. But God’s justice isn’t like that; His justice is eternal. His plan is for the salvation of every man, woman and child who ever lived.

If God says this or that nation had to suffer because of their wrongdoings in this life, it was with His plan and His full knowledge that those people will be raised later and go through a future reconciliation. God’s judgments have the eternal picture in mind. Only God can see what is needed in this life to secure their salvation in the future. When we react, we only see the immediate picture without this future understanding.

The Sixth Commandment is testifying to the sacredness of human life as a direct creation of God. It warns against acting on one’s own passion, rage and sense of personal retribution.

This Old Testament standard regarding murder in the Sixth Commandment is a definitive line in the sand. It is a line that has been drawn clearly—something we simply cannot do.

When someone was appropriately judged to be guilty of murder, the Law called for the death of that person. That was how serious it was!

For example:

Numbers 35:30: If anyone kills <5221> a person, the murderer <7523> shall be put to death at the evidence of witnesses, but no person shall be put to death on the testimony of one witness.

Takes/kill: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5221 nakah; a primitive root;

to strike (lightly or severely, literally or figuratively)

Brown-Driver-Briggs Hebrew and English Lexicon: to strike, smite, hit, beat, slay, kill

In other words, if someone strikes/kills (nakah) another person in a way that causes death, if it is determined to be an unlawful killing, that person is a murderer.

Numbers chapter 35 draws a clear legal line between accidental killing and murder. Jesus takes that line and moves it inward—into the heart.

Jesus’ teachings for his followers move that line in the sand to a higher, more challenging position. As we continue, we will see just how challenging it is!

Let’s go to the New Testament. In the Beatitudes, in his Sermon on the Mount, Jesus taught his followers how different our calling is.

We would become the light that shows the way back to God for Israel and for the whole world:

Matthew 5:14,16: 14 You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden; 16 let your light shine before men in such a way that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

We are to be light-bearers!

We are to let our light shine before men. As we go through how Jesus teaches us—You shall not murder—keep in mind that we are to be light-bearers. That light should be something others see, which illuminates our good works to glorify God, not ourselves.

Jesus next gave a series of practical examples of what standards of godliness would look like for his disciples. Matthew 5:21-22, 27-28, 38-39, 43-44 (and others) all have a similar theme, building upon, correcting and lifting the requirements of the Old Testament Law to a new and higher Christian standard.

He taught this with a very simple phrase, for I say to you (or, but I say unto you— depending on the translation). When we see that phrase, stop and think; be ready to be taught.

Matthew 5:20: (YLT) For I say to you, that if your righteousness may not abound above that of the scribes and Pharisees, ye may not enter to the reign of the heavens (King James Version: kingdom of heaven).

Jesus tells them that unless their righteousness surpasses that of the scribes and Pharisees, they would not enter the kingdom.

This would have been a shocking statement for Jesus’ listeners. They had been taught their whole lives that these elevated religious people were the most righteous in Israel. But in reality, they often twisted God’s Law with loopholes and man-made traditions that distorted its purpose and meaning.

Christians are called to a level of spirituality higher than any other standard, then and now:

Matthew 5:21: (YLT) Ye heard that it was said to the ancients: (Jesus quotes the Commandment:) Thou shalt not kill <5407> (murder; not just any kind of killing) and whoever may kill shall be in danger of the judgment.

Kill: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5407 phoneuo; from 5406; to be a murderer (of)

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to kill, slay, murder 2) to commit murder

The judgment—the lowest, local court that handled ordinary civil and criminal cases in several cities in the area. Made up of seven judges, they had limited authority.

Matthew 5:22: (YLT) …but I--I say to you, that every one who is angry <3710> at his brother without cause, shall be in danger of the judgment (the court mentioned above).

Angry: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3710 orgizo; from 3709;

to provoke or enrage, i.e. (passively) become exasperated

Jesus connects anger without cause to this first level of judgment in the local court. The Law said You shall not murder. But I say to you… Jesus brings it to a higher level. Everyone angry, provoked, enraged or exasperated with his brother without cause is in danger of being liable of judgment from the local court.

Let’s look at how that teaching of Jesus is repeated:

Ephesians 4:26-27: 26 BE ANGRY <3710>, AND yet DO NOT SIN (Paul is quoting from

Psalm 4:4 in the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint); do not let the sun go down on your anger (rage, indignation), 27 and do not give the devil an opportunity.

Jesus raised the standard. The Apostle Paul here repeats the raised standard. He wants us to recognize that this is really important. Don’t be angry or exasperated with your brother without cause, and do not let the sun go down on your anger—in other words, though we all have feelings of exasperation and frustration, don't let the sun go down before we resolve these feelings.

Christian Responsibility to the Sanctity of Life: If our anger or exasperation with our brother is not appropriately checked, it can bring us to the same moral category as murder!

Think about driving. Driving these days has become like a blood sport! Someone cuts you off. Before you even have time to think, out comes something like, “What a jerk!” or “What a moron!” Then you start driving aggressively, taking it out on other drivers. That moment shows how fast anger can turn into contempt, and how easily contempt can turn into dangerous behavior. Road rage has led to literal murder, but even when it doesn’t, that instinctive anger without real cause is exactly what Jesus warns us about.

In principle, we need to be careful about how we react because our reactions may easily invite a response based on them. It comes down to recognizing, as Jesus says, that if we are exasperated or angry, we are on the same level as murder.

We need to stop and think … Okay, I’m overreacting. Maybe I need to back up a little, especially when driving. Take a breath. I wonder what kind of day that person’s having. What’s on their mind? Maybe they are having a really bad day, or maybe they are just angry; whatever it is, I don’t want to enter into that!

Unchecked anger can lead to contempt, which can lead to dehumanization. This happens when we reduce people to stereotypes or label them as “those people.” In our polarizing politics, it’s easy to look at someone who sees things differently and think, How can they be so blind? Why don’t they get it? Don’t they see what I see?

Jesus doesn’t stop there. When we said he was going to raise the level, he raises the level!

Matthew 5:22: (YLT) …and whoever may say to his brother, Empty fellow! shall be in danger of the Sanhedrin…

Young’s Literal Translation uses the phrase empty fellow here, but the underlying Aramaic word Jesus spoke was raca—a common insult meaning “empty headed” or “worthless.” This captures the everyday contempt people show toward one another. It would be like us saying under our breath, “What an idiot!” This was a real-world, personal insult.

The Sanhedrin was the highest Jewish court, handling major religious and national cases. It was located in Jerusalem. It would be like us going before the Supreme Court in the United States.

Jesus was talking to the Jewish society of his day, using systems they understood to make his point. He quantified the seriousness of anger and rage against our brothers in terms of their legal system to get their clear, focused, undivided attention.

It’s a metaphor. Anger is like being liable to the local court, but now contempt for your brother is like being liable to the Sanhedrin. Human laws could only address the outward act of taking a life, but Jesus taught that God’s standard goes much deeper. God judges the inner attitudes and the beginnings of anger that lead to murder long before any blood is shed.

Let’s see what James says:

James 1:26: If anyone thinks himself to be religious, and yet does not bridle his tongue but deceives his own heart, this man's religion is worthless.

We see that what Jesus taught, his truest followers (like the Apostle Paul and James) took to heart. Then they spent a lot of time re-teaching and reminding us. James tells us if we do not bridle our tongue, we are not living up to our religion—it’s worthless. It’s like taking God’s name in vain, the Third Commandment.

Christian Responsibility to the Sanctity of Life: If our insulting and degrading speech against our brother is not appropriately checked, it can bring us to the same moral category as murder!

Eventually, contempt comes out in our words. Sometimes the people we hurt most are the ones closest to us. With family or church family, we drop the verbal filters we’d use with strangers. We get too casual, too sarcastic, too quick with a quip or an insult. Familiarity makes us careless, and careless words can cut deeply and hurt. Jesus’ warning about contempt isn’t just for strangers—it’s especially for how we treat those we live and worship with.

This is a big thing for me. I’ve had many wonderful privileges working with the brotherhood on all kinds of issues. A lot of times it is something like this: In a marriage, where filters get dropped, habit sets in, and the partners are just shooting poison arrows at one another. Breaking down those habits, rebuilding healthier patterns, and working on the language used is very difficult.

That is why I am very careful when responding to things, because I have seen it too often. I’ve watched the pain and suffering, and sometimes irreparable damage. So, in written correspondence with my church family, I always sign my name as “Brother Rick” to signal our Christian relationship. If it is something more casual, it’s “Rick.” If I write "Brother Rick," it’s because I want to make sure that if we are having challenges, we just need to settle down and take a breath. So, this is really important to me.

We “murder” with words when we tear down someone’s identity—telling them they’re worthless, mocking their abilities or using sarcasm that wounds. Online, the damage multiplies through cyberbullying, shaming or comments meant to humiliate. Scripture says reckless words are like sword thrusts (Proverbs 12:18). Even without physical violence, words can break a person down. Words cut, hurt and scar.

Sometimes these words come from our own hurt. When we react, we need to pause before responding. Reaction. Pause. Respond. We all react, sometimes, without thinking. We can’t take that back, but we can pause and not follow through. If we do follow through, we show disdain for our brother or sister. This is not spiritually healthy.

Let’s see what John says about this idea of potential murder of our Christian brother or sister:

1 John 3:15-16: 15 Everyone who hates <3404> his brother is a murderer <443>; and you know that no murderer <443> has eternal life abiding in him.

Hates: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3404 miseo; from a primary misos (hatred);

to detest (especially to persecute); by extension, to love less

Murderer: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #443 anthropoktonos;

from 444 and kteine (to kill); a manslayer

This Greek word for hate can sometimes mean “detest” or “love less,” but the context of 1

John 3:15 makes it clear that John is talking about active hostility—the kind of heart-level rejection Jesus identified as the root of murder.

16 We know love by this, that he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.

Jesus laid down his life for us. Instead of getting lost in hate, frustration and contempt, we ought to think about laying down our lives for the brethren by putting them first and being humble. Consider that Jesus and his disciples writing the New Testament are teaching us a lesson about personal humility.

Jesus continues raising the standard:

Matthew 5:22: (YLT) …And whoever may say, Rebel! (King James Version: Thou fool) shall be in danger of the gehenna (utter destruction) of the fire.

Here, if someone calls another Fool, they shall be in danger of gehenna, or utter destruction, of losing everything as a result of God’s judgment against them!

We started with the lower court, next the high court of the Sanhedrin, and now to the danger of losing everything. We see how Jesus is elevating the Law.

Talking about somebody as being a fool means we have lost respect for them. If they are our brother, who do we think we are? What right do we have to lose respect for others? We do not have that right. God is the judge, not us.

Let’s look at what James says about this very thing:

James 3:8-10: 8 But no one can tame the tongue; it is a restless evil and full of deadly poison. 9 With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in the likeness of God;

As we discussed earlier in Genesis 9:6, God forbids murder because human life bears His image, and only He—not human rage—has the authority over life and death.

10 from the same mouth come both blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not to be this way.

There is a fundamental contradiction when the same mouth brings blessing and cursing. If we are engaging in rage and in diminishing others, in contempt and divisiveness, it renders our profession of religion worthless.

Jesus started this discussion in this way:

Matthew 5:14,16: 14 You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden; 16 let your light shine before men in such a way that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

Because we are called to be light-bearers, Jesus shows us how You shall not kill reaches deeper than the outward behavior of actually killing someone. Cursing those who have been made in the likeness of God does not bring honor and glory to God.

And isn’t that the whole point? Such behaviors are contrary to our purpose of bringing glory to God by being the light of the world.

Christian Responsibility to the Sanctity of Life: If our contempt and disdain for anyone is not appropriately checked, it can bring us to the same moral category as murder!

Jesus wasn’t just tweaking the Law or saying Christians had to be more careful. He was revolutionizing it for his followers. The standard is raised so much higher, as reinforced throughout the New Testament.

Modern life makes this commandment even more challenging. Have you thought of what it means to murder someone’s hope and potential? It happens when we tell someone they’ll never change, crush their confidence with constant criticism (like parents to children or among spouses), or when our digital world overwhelms teens with impossible beauty standards and fake comparisons. AI now accelerates these harms by spreading damaging content and misinformation faster than the truth can catch up.

In 2024, YouTube had 2.5 billion active users, meaning even a small amount of harmful content—self-harm videos, bullying, despair-reinforcing messages—can reach millions of vulnerable people. (Source: DataReportal, 2024 global YouTube usage metrics.)

When we strip away someone’s belief in their own worth or future, we commit a quiet kind of “murder”—the killing of potential. When our words diminish someone’s worth, Scripture calls it slander, and slander is a form of spiritual harm.

In calling them a fool, we diminish them before themselves. When we plant a seed of doubt in someone’s heart and mind, we have no idea how deeply that can damage and destroy.

James 4:11: (NIV2011) Brothers and sisters, do not slander one another. Anyone who speaks against a brother or sister or judges them speaks against the law and judges it….

There we have it—a simple statement. Do not slander one another. All of these things we have discussed fall into the category of slander, belittling our brethren before God.

For Jesus’ disciples, belittling, contempt and slander towards our brother or sister can be a recipe for attempting spiritual murder.

Jesus finishes this teaching with a solution—humility:

Matthew 5:23-24: (YLT) 23 If, therefore, thou mayest bring thy gift to the altar, and there mayest remember that thy brother hath anything against thee, 24 leave there thy gift before the altar, and go—first be reconciled to thy brother, and then having come bring thy gift.

A Rick Interpretation: “Therefore, do NOT be content with outwardly serving God while you are not in harmony with your brother or sister. Instead, approach him, work to make things right and you will be living your dedication to God instead of just making a presentation to God that outwardly looks good.”

The Third Commandment, Thou shalt not take the Lord’s name in vain is appropriate here. We can’t carry the name of Christian unless we are actually acting as a Christian should. Humility is required.

Let’s go to Peter for his concept of a Christian murderer:

1 Peter 4:15-16: 15 Make sure that none of you suffers as a murderer <5406>, or thief, or evildoer, or a troublesome meddler; 16 but if anyone suffers as a Christian, he is not to be ashamed, but is to glorify God in this name.

Murderer: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5406 phoneus; from 5408; a murderer (always of criminal [or at least intentional] homicide; which 443 does not necessarily

imply; while 4607 is a special term for a public bandit)

Murder begins with attitudes that diminish life. As disciples called to be the light of the world, our words, thoughts and actions must protect the worth of every person made in God’s image. This is a high standard!

- Work to lift others up. - Give people the benefit of the doubt. - Look at our own self to see what is causing us to have such negative reactions.

Let’s be careful to honor—not harm or diminish—the lives and dignity of others.

So, what makes a Christian guilty of murder?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1449-christians-guilty-of-murder/

1. How does the Hebrew word ratsach distinguish murder from other forms of killing in Scripture?

(Exodus 20:13, Numbers 35:30)

2. What is the significance of human beings being made in God’s image in the command against murder?

What broader implications does this fact have in the way we treat the dignity, vulnerability and worth of others? (Genesis 9:6, Exodus 20:13)

3. Does God contradict Himself in forbidding murder while commanding killing in certain cases? What is

the difference between the violence as a result of human anger and God’s justice, which operates with the eternal picture rather than the immediate one? (Psalms 94:1-2, Genesis 9:6)

4. How does Jesus take the Old Testament “line in the sand” regarding murder and move it inward into the

disciple’s heart, using escalating legal imagery to show the increasing seriousness of anger, contempt and disrespect? Explain each example below: (Numbers 35:30)

a. Needing to be more righteous than their spiritual leaders: Matthew 5:20

b. Anger against a brother or sister: Matthew 5:22, Ephesians 4:26-27

c. Calling someone an “empty fellow,” or raca: Matthew 5:22, James 1:26

d. Hating our brother—using words as “sword thrusts”: 1 John 3:15,16, Proverbs 12:18

e. Calling someone, “Thou fool” or “Rebel”: Matthew 5:22, James 3:8-10

5. How does speech (destructive words, sarcasm, insult, slander) function as a form of murder according to

the principles Jesus sets down? (Proverbs 12:18, James 1:26, 4:11)

6. What is Jesus’ solution at the end of his teaching on murder? What is required of us if we wish to carry

the name of “Christian” and truly be “light-bearers”? (Matthew 5:23-24, 1 Peter 4:15-16)

7. How have I allowed my anger, frustration or exasperation toward another remain unresolved? What can I

do to address this appropriately before the “sun goes down”? (Matthew 5:22, Ephesians 4:26-27)

8. Do my words build others up and honor their God-given worth, or have I used sarcasm, criticism,

contempt or slander to tear them down? What changes can I make so my words are God-honoring? (James 1:26, 3:8-10, 4:11)

9. Is there anyone with whom I need to pursue reconciliation so that my service to God reflects genuine

humility and Christian love—rather than just an outward devotion—and so my light can shine clearly before others? What next steps need to be taken? (Matthew 5:23-24, 1 John 3:16)

## Episode 1450 — Is Adultery More Subtle than We Think?
Published: 2026-08-17
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1450-bible-says-about-adultery/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/07110002/CQ_Rewind_08-17-2026_Is_Adultery_More_Subtle_than_We_Think.pdf

(The Ten Commandments Series Part VII)

Exodus 20:14: You shall not commit adultery.

As we continue our Ten Commandments series, we are now at the point of deeply examining the Commandments that directly govern our interpersonal human relationships. This began with honoring our father and mother, as a basic tenet for living respectful lives. Next was the clear command not to murder. We found that Jesus, in his Sermon on the Mount, seriously elevated the responsibilities of that command—to not even be angry with, insult or degrade our brothers or sisters. Now, we examine the Seventh Commandment, You shall not commit adultery. As emotional as it was to discuss how Jesus raised the bar for his followers regarding treatment of the brotherhood, this subject breaks entirely new ground for what is required of faithful Christians to live clean and faithful lives.

If you think the Seventh Commandment is only for married people, you’re about to be surprised!

The Seventh Commandment is another “external instruction” because it addresses what we do or don’t engage in. This Commandment is the foundation of the human family relationship, as it is based on the sacred marriage covenant between husband and wife.

Adultery: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5003 na’aph; a primitive root; to commit adultery;

figuratively, to apostatize:—adulterer(-ess), commit(-ing) adultery,

woman that breaketh wedlock

Apostatize: (verb) means to abandon or renounce one’s religious faith, beliefs or loyalty; to defect from a previously held commitment.

Adultery means a married person having sexual relations outside their marriage. The Hebrew word goes further. It also means betraying God by turning away from Him. It is the spiritual equivalent of adultery: giving our devotion, trust or worship to someone or something other than God. This is why every Christian needs to pay attention to the Seventh Commandment, not just those who are married. We are talking about covenant faithfulness to God, not just misdirected human desire.

This is a big addition to what many of us think of when we hear this Commandment.

In the Law, adultery was clearly defined as a sin both men and women could commit. As such, the penalty was also the same:

Leviticus 20:10: If there is a man who commits adultery <5003> with another man's wife, one who commits adultery <5003> with his friend's wife, the adulterer <5003> and the adulteress <5003> shall surely be put to death.

This is the same penalty we talked about on our last episode for committing murder. So, adultery was just as heinous. God had very high standards for His chosen people for specific reasons. These standards maintained the integrity of their social environment, which is why the penalties were so serious.

This societal command has its basis in the marriage covenant expressed at humanity’s beginning:

Genesis 2:23-24: (KJV) 23 And Adam said, This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called woman, because she was taken out of man. 24 Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave <1692> (to cling or adhere) unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.

Cleave: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1692 dāḇaq; a primitive root; properly, to impinge, i.e. cling or adhere; figuratively, to catch by pursuit:—abide fast, cleave (fast together), follow close (hard after), be joined (together), keep (fast), overtake,

pursue hard, stick, take

Adultery can break us to our very core! Even if someone is never caught, they still suffer consequences:

Proverbs 6:32-33: 32 The one who commits adultery with a woman is lacking sense <3820>; He who would destroy himself does it. 33 Wounds and disgrace he will find, and his reproach will not be blotted out.

Sense: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3820 leb; a form of #3824; the heart; also used

(figuratively) very widely for the feelings, the will and even the intellect;

likewise for the center of anything

On a different Old Testament level, adultery was also considered apostasy, meaning to abandon your faith, beliefs or loyalty. It was apostasy when the Jewish nation strayed from adherence to God’s Law and betrayed their covenant relationship with God.

That was called adultery because Israel was described as God’s wife. When the nation worshiped idols, the prophets called it adultery because it broke the covenant—the sacred relationship God formed with Israel—just like marital unfaithfulness. God describes both Israel and Judah as unfaithful wives.

See Jeremiah 3:6-8, for example.

There is this spiritual kind of adultery that is just as difficult, just as dramatic—just as wrong—because it is violating a relationship with God Himself.

The dramatic conclusion is that when Old Testament adultery is committed, be it on a physical level or a spiritual level, its results were ALWAYS disgraceful and severe consequences would surely follow.

We now move to the Sermon on the Mount in the New Testament where Jesus will teach us the Christian meaning of adultery. Jesus is addressing what the standards of godliness would look like for his disciples. He quotes portions of the Law and then raises the meaning for his followers with the words—but I say to you.

So, whenever we read, especially in Matthew 5, Jesus saying, You have heard such and such said, but I say to you...he’s telling us to listen carefully because this is what it means to be a disciple of Jesus.

Jesus transforms the “external instruction” of the Seventh Commandment into an “internal instruction” as well:

Matthew 5:27-28: (YLT) 27 Ye heard that it was said to the ancients: Thou shalt not commit adultery; 28 but I--I say to you (this “stutter” is in the Young’s Literal Translation), that every one who is looking on a woman to desire <1937> her, did already commit adultery with her in his heart.

Desire: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1937 epithumeo; VERB from #1909 and #2372; to set the

heart upon, i.e. long for (rightfully or otherwise): —covet, desire, would fain, lust (after)

King James Version translates this as “desire” 8 times, “covet” 3 times, “lust” 3 times,

“lust after” 1 time, “fain” 1 time

Thayer’s Greek English Lexicon: 1) to turn upon a thing… 3) to lust after, covet

3a) of those who seek things forbidden

To paraphrase: But I say to you, I, Jesus, am telling you, my disciples, that YOU REPRESENT ME. Here is MY teaching regarding what you have always known as “adultery,” which looks at this commandment from a higher level. Even if you think about desiring someone and do not act on it, you are violating your marriage covenant in a very disturbing way.

This Greek word for desire is also translated lust. It means “to set the heart upon, to long for.” It can be used in a positive sense, as in 1 Timothy 3:1 about a man desiring to be in service as a servant in the church.

1 Timothy 3:1: (NASB) It is a trustworthy statement: if any man aspires to the office of overseer, it is a fine work he desires <1937> to do.

In a negative sense, it happens when we allow desire for someone outside our marriage covenant, feeding an emotional or sexual attachment we aren’t entitled to. As with murder, adultery begins in the mind, long before the act itself. This is an intentional, well- fed desire.

We heard a sobering thought: “Lust trains the heart to want what God forbids.” This isn’t just a passing or involuntary thought, or something briefly catching our eye. This is a cultivated, intentional desire.

Desire can be good, but it can also bring us to a place we do not belong.

Social media algorithms make this dangerously easy. They notice what we pause on and keep sending more of it. Curiosity can soon be cultivated into desire. And the whole digital world works the same way—websites, ads and apps all track our habits and keep offering us more of whatever we seem interested in. It’s a system designed to insidiously feed desire.

When I prepare for these various podcast episodes, I think twice as I type in what I am looking for when we are studying subjects like demonism or adultery. I might be looking up information on the effects of pornography, and all of a sudden I am bombarded with site after site on the subject and more. These algorithms set a person who shows interest up for failure.

Back to Jesus’ words in Matthew 5:28 (YLT), every one who is looking on a woman to desire her did already commit adultery with her in his heart—Jesus is saying this is an internal attraction—there has not yet been an action taken. The foundation of adultery is an internal attraction we have been drawn to and are giving attention to.

Jesus is speaking plainly. For his disciples, looking upon another person with inappropriate desire is to commit a sin of the heart. Remember that phrase: a sin of the heart.

→ Are you guilty of actually committing adultery? No. → Are you guilty of compromising the principles of discipleship? Yes, absolutely! → Are you guilty of severely compromising the principles of the marriage covenant?

Yes!

How can we say this if no act was actually committed?

Jesus speaking to the Pharisees about marriage:

Matthew 19:5-6: 5 And said, FOR THIS REASON A MAN SHALL LEAVE HIS FATHER AND MOTHER AND BE JOINED <2853> TO HIS WIFE, AND THE TWO SHALL BECOME ONE FLESH? 6 So they are no longer two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let no man separate.

Jesus quotes the “leave and cleave” passage of Genesis 2:24. In Hebrew, cleave was “to cling or adhere.” Here in the New Testament Greek, be joined means “to glue to; figuratively to adhere.”

Whenever I hear these verses, I think of my past as a fine furniture maker. I went to school for this and learned how to do things by hand, with accuracy and artistry.

When we were taught to glue a cabinet or case together, one of the rules was to build the case in such a way that the case, drawers, everything included, holds itself together without glue. When we put the glue on, it made the item firm and immovable. So, when I see this concept of “being joined,” or “glued” to your spouse, I think of the firmness of the lives you have already interlocked.

Your lives are interlocked, and now it's firm, it’s solid, and it can't be moved. The glue joint is not stressed because there is an interlocking of the wood—so the glue joints don’t ever wear out.

When you build it this way and then glue it together, it is the final step that makes it something unbreakable. To me, it’s a beautiful thought.

This photo is a picture of a jewelry case Rick made for Trish around 1978. Notice how the joinery holds the case together, and the glue makes it all “one.”

So, adultery violates a union that is meant to be “glued together” at the deepest level, whether physical adultery or spiritual adultery. It’s attaching yourself where you do not belong.

How should we reply to someone who says, “Well, I’ve already committed adultery in my heart, so I might as well do it for real!

A sin is a sin.”

Even if someone has committed adultery in their heart, it doesn’t mean the door is automatically open to go further.

There is a difference between thinking about a sin and actually acting on it—external versus internal. If we give in to this satanic thinking, we are stuck in the sin. If we instead stop and turn toward repentance, we can back up and work our way back to God. It's like saying, I've reached the cliff and fallen down the first part. I might as well jump off the cliff. No, that doesn't make any sense.

Adultery in the heart is not the same as physical adultery.

Reparation for adultery in the heart is an easier process

than the reparation for physical adultery.

James focuses us on what Jesus said about internal and external adultery in a broader application. Again, adultery happens first on the inside. Stop it there before it happens on the outside, where it's even more difficult.

James 1:14-15: 14 But each one is tempted when he is carried away and enticed by his own lust <1939> (noun form of <1937>). 15 Then when lust <1939> has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and when sin is accomplished, it brings forth death.

Lust—sin—death…What a progression! James is describing the moment desire stops being a thought and becomes a “plan.” That’s the conception. Lust moves from temptation to a decision to act on it. We need to stop the thought when it is in the percolation process. James warns us that when desire has conceived, then it gives birth to sin. But it has to be conceived first, which means you have to have entertained it. You have to have fed it. This is a dangerous process that we ALL are subject to.

Our desires can conceive what leads to bad actions, which, if continued, lead to spiritual death and destruction.

Jesus’ next statement emphatically teaches us what to do about this dilemma:

Matthew 5:29: (YLT) But, if thy right eye doth cause thee to stumble, pluck it out and cast from thee, for it is good to thee that one of thy members may perish, and not thy whole body be cast to Gehenna (meaning, utter destruction).

Jesus isn’t saying to literally poke out your eye. This is metaphorical. In the ancient world, the right side represented power, honor and priority. Your right eye was considered your best eye.

This first instruction is an “internal” instruction: Stop looking, if what you see draws you to sinful desire! Your spiritual life depends on it. Stop the inputs that can lead us further. “Pluck out” the eye! Watch your inputs.

Maybe it’s time to disable or delete your social media accounts.

Maybe it’s time to delete certain apps because they keep putting temptation

in front of you.

Humanity is curious, and we tend to wonder about things, especially those that are forbidden. Wondering draws these temptations towards us, algorithms keep them right in front of us, and, “I wonder” can become “I wander.”

If we feed wondering, we end up wandering. Wandering is never good based on this kind of wondering. Imagination is strong. Stop looking!

Matthew 5:30: (YLT) And, if thy right hand doth cause thee to stumble, cut it off, and cast from thee, for it is good to thee that one of thy members may perish, and not thy whole body be cast to Gehenna.

Again, this is a metaphor, not actual mutilation. Remember it is the right hand, generally the dominant hand. We are not just putting it behind our backs or covering it with a big mitten; we are cutting off its ability to cause us a problem. Remember how lust conceives an action when we let a desire grow. Don’t feed it. Don’t revisit it. Don’t consider it. Don’t imagine it. Don’t give it any space to develop; it just snowballs down that hill too fast.

Jesus breaks it down metaphorically with dramatic language—gouging out eyes, cutting off hands.

The first instruction is internal—stop looking.

The second instruction is external—stop doing what is unrighteous, and cut off the ability to continue doing it.

Your spiritual life depends on it!

Maybe it’s time for your spouse to set up parental controls on your TV,

phone and computer.

Maybe it’s time to install accountability software that sends your browsing

history to someone you trust.

Maybe it’s time to block certain sites entirely, even if you think you can

handle them.

Rick, in your role as a minister, you counsel many people who are often in an emotional or vulnerable situation. Attraction can surprise even the most faithful person. How do you protect your heart and your ministry from that danger?

I have found that I have to be painstaking about every tiny detail. These are the rules I put in place:

- Transparency with Trish, my wife. Trish knows everybody I am talking to. Those I am talking to also know she knows. She doesn’t know all the details; those remain private, but she knows of the conversations.
- Maintaining “Brother Rick” formality—not just “Rick” like in a more casual setting. This is a formal undertaking to examine a challenge spiritually.
- There are never inappropriate comments, innuendos or jokes that could be misinterpreted.

This is a scary thing. Trish and I are very open with one another. Right after I finish a conversation, I usually tell Trish the gist of what I was talking to so-and-so about. We share everything.

I noticed before we go on air, you take your phone and hand it to Trish.

Maybe it’s time each spouse has passwords to each other’s phones and

computers for more transparency and accountability.

Trish has my phone and email passwords. There is nothing to hide because “the two have been joined.” We have been glued together, and the two are one. That makes life free— there is no second-guessing.

https://scienceinsights.org/the-real-psychology-behind-cheating-in-relationships/ Research on social media and relationships has found that many people now believe evidence of infidelity can be found on a partner’s phone, which creates a cycle: ambiguous online behavior triggers suspicion, which leads to surveillance (reading texts, checking DMs), which partners then justify as “a right to the truth.” This dynamic can erode trust even when no actual cheating has occurred. The core psychological issue is that couples often haven’t explicitly agreed on what counts as crossing a line in digital spaces, leaving both partners operating under different assumptions about what’s acceptable.

James helps us remember that spiritual adultery is also a significant challenge for believers:

James 4:4: You adulteresses, do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility <2189> toward God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.

Hostility: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2189 echthra; hostility; by implication,

a reason for opposition:—enmity, hatred

This Greek word for hostility here is a deep, active opposition. Aligning ourselves with the world’s values puts us in an adversarial position against God. That is how serious spiritual adultery is.

Satan is our adversary (1 Peter 5:8), and he is called that because he is in an adversarial condition with God. Friendship with the world means essentially joining Satan.

Seeking to fulfill sinful desires while being God’s child violates our covenant with God!

Any adultery committed by a Christian—be it spiritual, physical or mental—reveals our choice to open our hearts and minds to sin, giving the sin an open invitation to flourish.

We want to touch on four basic points to help us understand when we might fail: Three of the points are internal, and the last one is external because Jesus made the application of this Commandment both internal and external.

Internal Point We may love righteousness, but we don’t truly hate iniquity:

Psalm 45:7: You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of joy above your fellows.

Because we love righteousness AND hate iniquity, we are raised to a higher level. If we are in this liminal state of being able to go one way or another, we have not hated iniquity nearly enough. We have to HATE it. That’s an internal thing. Nobody else sees this; it happens inside our heart.

Internal Point We may hear and appreciate the word, but we are not fully committed to living it:

James 1:22: But prove yourselves doers of the word, and not merely hearers who delude themselves.

We must be doers of what we hear. It is not enough to go to church and nod and smile and feel good. We have to LIVE it. Decide that we will fully commit to what we learn from the word of God.

Internal Point We may love God, but we haven’t permitted our devotion to undo our earthly desires:

1 John 2:15-16: 15 Do not love the world nor the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. 16 For all that is in the world, the lust <1939> of the flesh and the lust <1939> of the eyes and the boastful pride of life, is not from the Father, but is from the world.

- How do you maintain a secret relationship while still genuinely loving your spouse?
- How can you be a Christian who deeply loves God and yet still participates in contradictory thoughts and actions that He hates?

In modern psychology, this is called compartmentalization, putting conflicting parts of your life into separate “mental boxes” so they never touch. It’s a way to avoid feeling the conflict altogether. This is a scary place to be as a Christian!

We have to permit our devotion to God to undo and dismantle our ungodly, earthly desires. By examining these points, we can see where we can potentially go wrong on the inside, so we stop ourselves from going wrong with our external actions.

External Point We may know what’s right, but we haven’t permitted our knowledge to transform us:

Colossians 3:5: (WEY) Therefore put to death your earthward inclinations—fornication, impurity, sensual passion, unholy desire, and all greed, for that is a form of idolatry.

Paul ends this list by calling these desires idolatry, because they replace God with something else. Adultery and idolatry share the same root problem: misdirected loyalty. We see the same pattern in human relationships. It is surprising how often these two words are found intertwined in Scripture.

Idolatry and adultery, in all cases, end up with misery and difficulty. We may know what is right, but not follow it. Our knowledge of God should transform us into something better.

https://scienceinsights.org/the-real-psychology-behind-cheating-in-relationships/ Technology has introduced a gray area that previous generations didn’t have to navigate. The concept of “micro-cheating,” liking an ex’s photos, maintaining flirtatious text conversations, or keeping active dating profiles, reflects how digital interactions have made the boundaries of fidelity harder to define.

The Apostle Paul taught about the sin of physical adultery in the context of our spirituality:

1 Corinthians 6:15-16: 15 Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take away the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? May it never be! 16 Or do you not know that the one who joins <2853> (to glue) himself to a prostitute is one body with her? For he says, THE TWO SHALL BECOME ONE FLESH.

Joins: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2853 kollao; from kolla ("glue");

to glue, i.e. (passively or reflexively) to stick (figuratively)

The King James Version translates this as “join (one’s) self” 4 times, “cleave” 3 times, “be joined”

2 times, “keep company” 1 time, “reach” 1 time

Thayer’s Greek English Lexicon: 1) to glue, to glue together, cement, fasten together

2) to join or fasten firmly together 3) to join one’s self to, cleave to

This gives us the sense of corrupting the body of Christ, much like the potential of corrupting our marriage relationship. When someone joins (glues) himself to a prostitute, they have unglued themselves from their original covenant!

As a cabinet maker, if the construction is done well, to unglue the joint is to destroy it. There is no way to pull the pieces apart. The joint has to be broken. Then this brokenness is glued to something else…? What a horrific ending place for us to be.

This powerful reminder of the original model of marriage fidelity is being written to those whose backgrounds were deeply pagan. Many of these Gentile Christians had no sense of the Jewish Law, so they had to be brought up to speed. Paul gives them blunt, straightforward admonitions. They needed to see the clear line of fidelity God had drawn both on the physical and spiritual levels.

In the next verses, Paul is following Jesus’ example, as he raises the standard even higher:

1 Corinthians 6:17-18: 17 But the one who joins <2853> (glues himself spiritually) himself to the Lord is one spirit with Him. 18 Flee immorality...

RUN AWAY from anything immoral.

Sensuality-based thinking needs this blunt and unmistakable reminder regarding what is and is not acceptable Christian behavior. My body is the dwelling place of God’s spirit—it is sacred!

Whether it is literal adultery or spiritual adultery...

Maybe it’s time to bring someone into your struggle so that you’re not

fighting alone.

That someone needs to be an individual who has their feet solidly on spiritual ground, scriptural ground, who is not afraid to help you walk away from such things.

Maybe it’s time we put things in order and decide that no matter what

happens, no matter what comes our way, we are walking behind Jesus.

If we walk behind him, we see only him and will be protected!

So, is adultery more subtle than we think?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

Many of our topics are compiled with a Word Study using several concordances and other Bible helps. We see how a particular word is used in both the Old and New Testaments. Understanding how the words are used not only tells us what they mean, but it gives us the nuances of the original Hebrew or Greek when comparing how the writers of the Bible use them in different contexts. We can also learn more by seeing the origins of a particular word, providing a depth of understanding that just reading scriptures in English cannot provide.
