1. How does the Hebrew word for adultery (Strong’s #5003), broaden the meaning of the Seventh

Commandment beyond marital unfaithfulness? (Exodus 20:14, Jeremiah 3:6-8)

2. What does the public penalty for adultery under the Law reveal about God’s view of the marriage

covenant? Why was the stability of marriage so important in society and before God? (Leviticus 20:10,

Genesis 2:23-24)

3. What are the personal consequences for adultery in Proverbs 6:32-33, and why do they occur even if the

persons involved keep the adultery hidden from others?

4. In what way did Jesus elevate the 7th Commandment from an external act to an internal responsibility?

Explain. (Matthew 5;27-28)

5. What distinguishes righteous desire from sinful desire, and how does intentional cultivation turn desire

into lust? (Strong’s #1937, Matthew 5:28, 1 Timothy 3:1)

6. How does the illustration of interlocking wood and glue in cabinetry deepen our understanding of Jesus’

words on the permanence and sanctity of marriage (two becoming “one flesh” and “joined together”) in

Matthew 19:5-6?

7. What practical lessons can we draw from James 1:14-15? Describe the progression of temptation.

8. How do Jesus’ warnings in Matthew 5:29-30 teach us the best way to deal with temptation? In what ways

do these metaphors emphasize both internal and external action against sin?

9. Identify the specific dangers described for us in each of these areas, and explain how each can lead to

subtle forms of adultery: Psalm 45:7, James 1:22, 1 John 2:15-16, Colossians 3:5.

10. How does James 4:4 define spiritual adultery, and why does friendship with the world place us in an

adversarial position toward God?

11. How does “compartmentalization” allow contradictory desires to coexist, and why is this spiritually

dangerous for Christians? (1 John 2:15-16)

12. What practical steps can I take to “pluck out the eye” or “cut off the hand” in my own life by removing

sources of temptation before they become sinful actions? (Matthew 5:29-30)

13. In what areas of my life am I merely hearing God’s word rather than allowing it to transform my

thoughts, desires and behavior? (James 1:22, Colossians 3:5)

## Episode 1451 — Do We Ever Steal Without Realizing It?
Published: 2026-08-24
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/program/1451-do-not-steal/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/14120409/CQ_Rewind_08-24-2026_Do_We_Ever_Steal_Without_Realizing_It.pdf

(The Ten Commandments Series Part VIII)

Exodus 20:15: You shall not steal.

We are now ready to consider the Eighth Commandment in our Ten Commandments Series. Through the first seven, we have seen that honoring God from our hearts and with our actions is our foundation. The Sabbath was created to remind us of this sacred responsibility. We are then taught to honor our parents as the basis for all our human interactions. Next came the clear commands not to murder and not to commit adultery, and we found that Jesus, in his Sermon on the Mount, seriously elevated the responsibilities of these specific commands. As we examine the next Commandment, “You shall not steal,” it will quickly become evident that these four words are not simple general guidance. On the contrary, they teach us the fundamentals of civility and respect. As usual, Jesus will take this lesson and elevate it even further for his followers.

The Eighth Commandment is a foundational “external—what we do—instruction” designed to clearly establish and recognize the personal rights of those in our community:

Exodus 20:15: You shall not steal <1589>.

Steal: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1589 ganab; a primitive root; to thieve

(literally or figuratively); by implication, to deceive

This word for steal has a VERY broad meaning and is explained in several other scriptures. As we go through some in the Old Testament that refer to the concept of “stealing,” notice the differences in circumstances and consequences.

“You shall not steal” applies to the lives of our fellow man. Each has a right to live according to the Law:

Exodus 21:16: He who kidnaps <1589> a man … shall surely be put to death.

The word for kidnap is the same as steal. There is no greater “stealing” than the taking of another human. It is punishable by death.

“You shall not steal” applies to how we treat others within the context of the general business of life. Simple honesty and respect should prevail:

Leviticus 19:11, 13: 11 You shall not steal <1589>, nor deal falsely, nor lie to one another. 13 You shall not oppress (defraud, violate) <6231> your neighbor, nor rob <1497> him. The wages of a hired man are not to remain with you all night until morning.

Oppress: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #6231 ashag; to press upon, i.e. oppress, defraud,

violate, overflow:--deceive

Rob: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1497 gazal; a primitive root; to pluck off; flay, strip or rob

It comes down to respect for those in our lives. There is no defrauding. We can’t

just pluck things off someone—almost like a pickpocket! On whatever level, we just don’t take advantage of someone in any way. The next sentence is about the wages of a hired man—we need to pay them the day they do the work. We do not take advantage.

“You shall not steal” applies to the specifics of buying, selling and trading. Be precise; have integrity:

Leviticus 19:35–36: 35 You shall do no wrong in judgment, in measurement of weight, or capacity. 36 …I am the LORD your God, who brought you out from the land of Egypt.

This tests our standard of righteousness. If we use a measurement of weight or capacity while trading or selling, we must be precise. Do not shade things toward our own benefit; that is out-and-out stealing!

I am the LORD your God, who brought you out from the land of Egypt—the message is: Do NOT even bend the Law or the rules a little, because I, the Lord your God, gave you freedom, and you owe Me your allegiance. You must live up to the power and strength of My Law. Do not cheat one another in any way, shape or form.

“You shall not steal” applies to many general experiences of taking what is not yours:

Leviticus 6:1–3,5: 1 Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, 2 When a person sins and acts unfaithfully against the LORD, and deceives his companion in regard to a deposit or a security entrusted to him, or through robbery <1498> (plunder), or if he has extorted <6231> from his companion, 3 or has found what was lost and lied about it and sworn falsely, so that he sins… (he must return what he stole), and 5 …he shall make restitution for it in full and add to it one-fifth more. He shall give it to the one to whom it belongs…

What causes this behavior? Selfish motives that lead to dishonesty. These verses describe different circumstances so things are not left to the imagination. They do not allow anything contrived to go against the standards of the LORD God who brought you out from the land of Egypt. This you shall not steal commandment has many facets and applies to every aspect of life.

Restoration of what was stolen plus 20 percent was required, but that’s not all. You now must make it right before God:

Leviticus 6:6–7: 6 Then he shall bring to the priest his guilt offering to the LORD, a ram without defect from the flock… for a guilt offering, 7 and the priest shall make atonement for him…

Not only was this a sin against a person, but it was also a sin against God. The person had to bring a guilt offering to say, “I am guilty of violating Your command.”

The one guilty of stealing had to fully replace what was taken and more. He was to give the best of his own flock—a ram without defect—to God as a sacrifice to show repentance. It had to cost him something. He had to feel the pain of the transgression.

“You shall not steal.” To steal from a family’s livelihood and profit from it brought a much higher penalty than anything but kidnapping.

God’s Law was built to protect families and communities:

Exodus 22:1,4: 1 If a man steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters it or sells it, he shall pay five oxen for the ox and four sheep for the sheep. 4 If what he stole is actually found alive in his possession, whether an ox or a donkey or a sheep, he shall pay double.

This reminds us of when the prophet Nathan was sent to King David in 2 Samuel 12:1-6. Nathan told him a story about a rich man who stole the only ewe lamb from a poor man.

2 Samuel 12:1-4:

David reacts to Nathan’s story with righteous indignation and goes along, exactly quoting the Law. He was so upset at what the rich man did to the poor man's family and said, Surely the man who has done this deserves to die. And he must make restitution for the lamb fourfold. Then, Nathan said these cutting words: David, YOU are the man, and you’ve done much worse! He said this because David had stolen Uriah's wife, Bathsheba, and had him killed in battle.

This shows us the depth of taking from another’s ability to support themselves. We simply should not do that! You shall not steal is not about just little things; it’s about all different areas of life.

“You shall not steal.” Negligence that results in another’s losses is stealing. Integrity must prevail:

Exodus 22:5: If a man lets a field or vineyard be grazed bare and lets his animal loose so that it grazes in another man's field, he shall make restitution from the best of his own field and the best of his own vineyard.

If we’re lazy and do not keep up our fields and our animals eat all that is in our pasture, and then we let them graze in another’s pasture—there is a Law against that. We are being negligent and need to give the best of what we have to God to make up for it.

The concept of you shall not steal in the Old Testament covers a wide variety of situations in our lives, from little things to very big things. All of it is in the context of I AM the Lord your God who delivered you out of the land of Egypt, so you owe Me your loyalty to hold My Law to its sacred standard.

You shall not steal gives us an overview of the Old Testament. Now we want to take a look at the New Testament.

To grasp what Jesus taught about stealing, we need to look at:

his broader perspective regarding our human interactions

his approach to this Eighth Commandment

First, the broader perspective. After explaining a parable about what defiles a man, Jesus said:

Matthew 15:19–20: 19 For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, slanders. 20 These are the things which defile the man; but to eat with unwashed hands does not defile the man.

Jesus’ broad perspective for the Christian who is following in his footsteps is that all these wrong actions begin in our hearts. He illustrates this concept by his teachings and his actions.

It’s not a matter of do and don’t—it’s a matter of what is stirring in our hearts and what seed has been planted within us, and whether that seed will produce fruitage that is unprofitable or even wretchedly wrong.

It’s no surprise that Jesus turns You shall not steal into an “internal instruction” as well as an “external instruction” for his followers.

Now let’s look at how he sums up the entire Law:

Matthew 22:35–40: 35 One of them, a lawyer, asked him a question, testing him, 36 Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law? 37 And he said to him, YOU SHALL LOVE THE LORD YOUR GOD WITH ALL YOUR HEART, AND WITH ALL YOUR SOUL, AND WITH ALL YOUR MIND. 38 This is the great and foremost commandment. 39 The second is like it, YOU SHALL LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF. 40 On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets.

One of the lawyers of the Jewish Law thought he could trap Jesus by asking: which is the great commandment in the Law? Jesus sums up the whole Law with these two commandments: How do you love God, and how do you love your neighbor? He says their thinking is inside out! They need to BE the fulfillment of the Law, not DO the fulfillment of the Law. That’s the importance of following in his footsteps now.

Because Jesus came to fulfill the Law, his teaching here is vital. He explains that the primary purpose of the Law AS A WHOLE is:

1. To honor God and

2. To thoroughly respect those around us.

These two halves cannot be separated without degrading the meaning of the whole. Each is important—we cannot have the whole if we degrade the meaning of either half.

Why does stealing happen in the first place? Stealing happens because of what we want, what we perceive we need, or what we actually need. Sometimes there is a need and a temptation because of that need. This is an understandable circumstance.

Let’s look at a dramatic example of stealing to satisfy a desire:

The following scriptures were written by the Apostle Paul to the Corinthian

church. They had come from a very pagan background and had to be taught many things to achieve a Christlike character. Before their conversion, they had grown accustomed to taking what was not theirs.

We are dropping into the middle of a lesson here:

1 Corinthians 6:10–11: 10 nor thieves <2812>, nor the covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers <727>, will inherit the kingdom of God. 11 Such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the spirit of our God.

Thieves: Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) an embezzler, pilferer 1a) the name is transferred to false teachers, who do not care to instruct men,

but abuse their confidence for their own gain

Swindlers: Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: an extortioner, a robber

This word gives the sense of embezzling and also of a swindler, which is really extortion. Paul is saying none of these levels are acceptable. If we are following Jesus, we have to be on a higher level than we previously were.

When we come to Christ, we lay all our past before God, and we leave it there. We then walk in accordance with the footsteps of Jesus. He showed us how to live.

INTEGRITY LESSON: Heaven is closed to thieves. It is one thing to have been a thief, and it is an entirely different thing to continue being one after knowing Christ.

We must change our ways in order to be acceptable before God. Just as the Jewish Law elevated the people to that physical standard, we who attempt to follow Jesus are elevated to a spiritual standard.

Let’s look at a few modern examples:

- This is a huge new issue! Some shoppers are now committing “friendly fraud” by buying items and then disputing the charge instead of returning them. This practice lets people keep merchandise for free while credit card companies unknowingly enable the theft. Businesses are hit hard, losing the product, the payment and paying penalty fees on top of it.

We can’t even fathom what is in the minds of these people! They must somehow justify this behavior to themselves, but it is certainly not proper. They are not just stealing from that merchant or that credit card company; they are stealing from God, our Father!

- Another big one is self-checkout: Not scanning items, scanning cheaper items instead or “accidentally” misweighing products. This is becoming such an issue that some stores are reverting to cashiers and closing self-checkouts.

The self-checkout method is efficient but assumes a simple principle of personal human integrity.

- Digital theft: sharing paid streaming logins, downloading movies or music illegally, or using software without a license.

If I can get away with it, why not? Because it is wrong—it is really that simple! If we follow in Jesus’ footsteps, we don’t walk in that direction.

For those who take because they see themselves as privileged or spiritually superior:

Matthew 21:12–13: 12 And Jesus entered the temple and drove out all those who were buying and selling in the temple, and overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those who were selling doves.

This is a case where the merchant was cheating the consumer. Two things were going on here:

1. The merchants were price gouging because the pilgrims had no other place to buy

their animals for sacrifices.

2. The money changers were using false weights to extort the people.

13 And he said to them, It is written, MY HOUSE SHALL BE CALLED A HOUSE OF PRAYER; but you are making it a ROBBERS’ DEN.

In verse 13, Jesus quotes two verses.

1. Isaiah 56:7—MY HOUSE WILL BE CALLED A HOUSE OF PRAYER—God is telling

Isaiah that even those who were not natural Jews but sincerely practiced the faith would be deeply blessed in God’s sacred house of prayer. Whatever their background, if they were sincere in following the Jewish faith, they would be welcome and blessed. But they had polluted God’s house with their practices. Jesus is calling them out on this.

INTEGRITY LESSON: ALL are welcome to this sacred place!

2. Jeremiah 7:11—God is telling Judah to stand for His righteousness, and not their

own deceptive words and pagan practices and then hypocritically come to God’s house. They could not live in an ungodly way, then come in and worship God— Jesus would not accept that desecration of his Father’s house by turning it into A ROBBERS’ DEN.

Jesus is taking two significant Old Testament events and saying, You're doing both of these things. Think about the importance of such a lesson.

INTEGRITY LESSON: You (the religious leaders of Jesus’ day) are robbing the people by way of false pretenses. Robbing the people this way is stealing from God as well. If we steal, even in a small way, we are stealing from our heavenly Father. And we are stealing from Jesus because we are taking our commitment to be Christlike and are polluting it. That is stealing his reputation.

Pay close attention to those who exploit followers of Christ. They steal from others and from God!

Titus 1:10–11: 10 For there are many rebellious men, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision, 11 who must be silenced because they are upsetting whole families, teaching things they should not teach for the sake of sordid gain.

This brings to mind churches pressuring families to tithe beyond their means. Tithing is not a New Testament requirement; it was a Jewish requirement to support those serving in the Tabernacle who did not receive an inheritance in the land. By the way, it was never money that was given to support the priesthood.

The damage caused by this pressure is incalculable. I remember a sister in Christ who has since passed away. She was meeting with us, but had been in a church before where they demanded 10 percent tithes. She was a woman with almost nothing, and she went hungry because she gave that 10 percent. Once she understood the truth of the matter, she was very happy with the simplicity of true giving.

There is a difference between hearing a biblical word, using it, and truly following biblical truth. Those who do things for gain might have some biblical reasons, but they are not following true biblical teaching.

INTEGRITY LESSON: When biblical truth is neglected, the temptation may arise to take what is not ours. Let us deeply consider our “why” before we allow ourselves to engage in a sinful “what.”

Time for some more modern examples:

- My wife was recently at the grocery store to pick up a few things. She put one item in the cart and the other items in the top section by the handle. After paying and heading to the car, she noticed the one item at the bottom was never taken out of the cart. She went back to customer service to explain and pay for it. She thought it was odd they didn’t thank her for coming back to make it right.
- Back when I was around 12 years old, we used to drive to church and would stop at the store on the way because my grandfather liked to read the New York Daily News. I would run in, get the newspaper and run back to the car. Then we would finish the drive to church. One Sunday, I ran in, grabbed the paper and paid the 25 cents. I ran back out, got in the car, and we continued on to church. Then I noticed I had grabbed two papers instead of one. I asked my dad, What do I do?

He said not to worry; next week I should just give the clerk two payments. The next week, I’m feeling embarrassed because I shouldn’t have grabbed two papers, but I remember walking into the store, picking up one newspaper, and giving the guy 50 cents instead of 25. I explained I had made a mistake and taken two papers the week before. I remembered my dad telling me not to worry, which gave me the courage to actually do it. Walking out, I felt good about actually following through and standing up for my mistake.

It’s time to take a stand, even regarding the little things that don’t seem that bad! We need to apply discipline:

Ephesians 4:27–28: 27 and do not give the devil an opportunity. 28 He who steals must steal no longer; but rather he must labor, performing with his own hands what is good, so that he will have something to share with one who has need.

Instead of being a stealer of others, be a steward for others. Don’t take from others—take care of them.

INTEGRITY LESSON: How persistently do we go to any length to legitimately take care of ourselves? Even if I am in a tough spot now, is my objective to work through it and to help others as I go?

He who steals must steal no longer, but go to work so he can take care of himself and have something to give to others in need. Turn the tables on your life—come as you are, but do not stay in the same sinful circumstance; become Christlike. Focus on giving, not taking.

We need a sense of selflessness, being a steward for others, and stand up for the standards given to us.

We need to make a paradigm shift from selfishness to personal responsibility, which leads to selflessness.

This brings to mind the story of the widow’s mite in Luke 21:1-4. The widow had almost nothing, but she gave the little she had. Jesus’ response was that she was focused on truly supporting godliness, and she would be blessed. This is a small but powerful example of the way our hearts and minds should be working.

One last modern example:

- Time theft at work: Taking long breaks, doing personal things on company time, or the latest thing called “quiet quitting” while still collecting full pay.

That’s when employees do only the bare minimum needed to keep their job, never going “above and beyond.”

As Christians, it’s our responsibility to do all things as unto the Lord (Colossians 3:23). “Quiet quitting” is not for Christians. We need to stand up and put in our effort, even if we are not happy with the job, employer or whatever it is, because we do those things as unto Christ. That is the important thing. For us, it would be stealing to do the bare minimum when we can do so much more.

If anyone feels shame or guilt after realizing past mistakes, learn from them! None of us are perfect along these lines. We need to remember how wrong stealing is so we can overcome in the little things of life. We really need to focus on the little things to make sure we’re not bending the rules: Can I do this better? Can I do this in a more Christlike way as if Jesus were sitting next to me looking over my shoulder?

How strongly can we rise to a level of Christian character that does not seem to be constantly trying to make up for its lack, but instead simply loves our brethren—and all people?

Romans 13:8–9: 8 Owe nothing to anyone except to love one another; for he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. 9 For this, YOU SHALL NOT COMMIT ADULTERY, YOU SHALL NOT MURDER, YOU SHALL NOT STEAL, YOU SHALL NOT COVET, and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying, YOU SHALL LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF.

This is how the whole Law is summed up—Love your neighbor as yourself.

INTEGRITY LESSON: Loving our brother means helping them in their needs in appropriate ways. Loving them also means receiving their help in our needs. It’s a two-way street. We all should be stewards one to another.

This is so important. The main issue is You shall not steal—but it is not that simple. We shall live in a way of standing for a high level of giving, integrity and spirituality and work on developing a sacred character that reflects God through Christ.

We look at the previous commandments, and we see:

Loving God comes first.

The Sabbath gives us rest and reflection.

Loving and respecting our parents helps us with our human family relationships.

Do not commit adultery.

Do not steal.

These must be put into the perspective of putting God, through Christ, first in every aspect of our lives.

Every day we have a choice. We must live in a Christlike way. Let us not steal.

So, do we ever steal without realizing it?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

## Episode 1452 — What Does It Really Mean to Bear False Witness?
Published: 2026-08-31
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1452-bear-false-witness/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/24150243/CQ_Rewind_08-31-2026_What_Does_It_Really_Mean_to_Bear_False_Witness.pdf

(The Ten Commandments Series Part IX)

Exodus 20:16: You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.

Our Ten Commandments series has now brought us to the Ninth Commandment, regarding not bearing false witness against our neighbor. To properly dig into the meaning of this command, we need to remember its context. After the first several commandments taught us about our spiritual connection with God, the next several focused on our human connections with one another. While this Ninth Commandment may not seem as dramatic as do not murder, do not commit adultery and do not steal, it raises our thinking and instruction to a new level. This level is not only about our thoughts and actions toward one another; it also applies to behavior in a clear legal sense. So, what did this mean for Israel and, more importantly, what does it mean for us as disciples of Christ?

We have to appreciate the Ten Commandments because they cover every aspect of life. If we have a question about life, we can turn to the commandments to learn how to act, how to be, and what to seek.

Now we consider this Ninth Commandment, another “external action command” that focuses on how to contribute to and maintain a just and respectful society:

Exodus 20:16: You shall not bear <6030> false <8267> witness <5707> against your neighbor.

Bear: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #6030 anah; a primitive root; properly, to eye or (generally)

to heed, i.e. pay attention; by implication, to respond; by extens. to begin to speak;

specifically to sing, shout, testify, announce

False: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #8267 sheqer; an untruth; by implication,

a sham (often adverbial)

Witness: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5707 ed; concretely, a witness; abstractly, testimony;

specifically, a recorder, i.e. prince, witness

It’s saying don’t testify to an untruth or sham if you are a witness in a dispute. We are not to be part of a sham (a deliberate fraud) to cover something else up during a testimony.

This commandment has a clear focus on legal settings. Do not testify to any form of untruth if you face a situation where you are called on to testify against your neighbor because of some wrongdoing.

This obvious “external action” is a premeditated evil.

What could motivate someone to do this? Envy, jealousy, hatred or testifying falsely for profit.

The point is that it is a premeditated evil. The Law was specific about forbidding this behavior.

Our first example seems to begin in a social setting where mob mentality can easily develop. This mentality can then be displayed in a legal setting:

Exodus 23:1-3: 1You shall not bear a false <7723> report …

False: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #7723 shav’; in the sense of desolating; evil (as destructive),

literally (ruin) or morally (especially guile); figuratively idolatry (as false, subjective), uselessness

(as deceptive, objective; also adverbially, in vain):—false(-ly), lie, lying, vain, vanity

The word for false is the same as in “do not take the LORD’s name in vain.” “Vain” is a falsehood or an exaggerated fantasy view of what is real.

… do not join your hand with a wicked man to be a malicious (violent, unjust) witness <5707>. 2 You shall not follow the masses in doing evil, nor shall you testify (answer) in a dispute so as to turn aside after a multitude in order to pervert justice; 3 nor shall you be partial to a poor man in his dispute.

This is saying: Get it right and don't let evil or mob mentality influence you. The last point says that just because someone is poor doesn't mean we should bend toward them or be partial in our testimony. Having pity on someone is one thing, but the truth is another.

We have to resist either side. If we are pushed by mob mentality to testify to the mob viewpoint, or pressured by feeling sorry for someone who is down on their luck, we must still remember that TRUTH IS TRUTH. God makes this point through all His commandments!

Now take all of the input and influence from the emotionally driven—and stand only for the truth:

Exodus 23:6–9: 6 You shall not pervert the justice (a verdict pronounced judicially) due to your needy brother in his dispute. 7 Keep far from a false <8267> charge, and do not kill the innocent or the righteous, for I will not acquit the guilty. 8 You shall not take a bribe, for a bribe blinds the clear-sighted and subverts the cause of the just. 9 You shall not oppress a stranger, since you yourselves know the feelings of a stranger, for you also were strangers in the land of Egypt.

In Exodus 23, Israel was told NOT to pervert justice. They were to keep far from a false charge. God tells them clearly He will not acquit the guilty because they do this on purpose. They must face consequences if they transgress this edict. Do not kill the innocent or oppress a stranger. Be 100 percent truthful. The reason? For you were also strangers in Egypt. God reminds Israel of the loyalty owed to Him, as in Exodus 20:2: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.

It is tragic how full of global injustices our world is today, particularly when false accusations are used to advance selfish agendas. We are so used to this that we don’t give it a second thought, and that is where the great danger lies. Things fall apart when we don’t abide by the truth.

The Law also focused on the need to stand justly in individual matters:

Deuteronomy 19:15–17: 15 A single witness shall not rise up against a man on account of any iniquity or any sin which he has committed; on the evidence of two or three witnesses a matter shall be confirmed. 16 If a malicious <2555> (violent, cruel, unjust) witness <5707> rises up against a man to accuse him of wrongdoing, 17 then both the men who have the dispute shall stand before the LORD, before the priests and the judges who will be in office in those days.

According to Jewish Law, if there is a dispute between two people, the responsibility of those in authority is to scrutinize both parties with the same level of integrity. Both sides must be weighed very carefully.

Justice would be served in handling an individual dispute by seriously questioning both sides:

Deuteronomy 19:18–21: 18 The judges shall investigate thoroughly, and if the witness <5707> is a false <8267> witness <5707> and he has accused his brother falsely <8267>, 19 then you shall do to him just as he had intended to do to his brother. Thus you shall purge the evil from among you. 20 The rest will hear and be afraid, and will never again do such an evil thing among you. 21 Thus you shall not show pity: life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot.

Israel’s Law was based on a stringent code of justice. The Law said that if someone brought a false charge against another that was so egregious as to cause that person to lose his home, the accuser should then also lose his home.

The Law is specific and designed to make all in Israel think hard about telling the truth. Jewish Law was based on clear-cut integrity and truth.

The preparation for this episode once again reminded me of my daughter’s story, which we have talked about many times on Christian Questions. Our daughter, Amy, was raped at age 15. This was one of the hardest experiences of our lives. The recovery went on for years.

I remember right after finding out, Amy was home, and the family was sitting around the table, and we did not have any idea what to do. My son was sitting next to me, and he got a phone call. I could hear what was being said. A deep voice on the other end said, “I understand you have a problem.” I knew exactly what was happening: someone wanted to help by illegally hurting the offender. Part of me wanted to ignore what I heard because I wanted the young man to be hurt. He hurt my daughter, and I wanted him to feel the same.

Even though there was no bearing of witness at this point, in my heart I had a choice. I could be quiet, pretend I didn’t hear, and essentially advocate violence because the young man “deserved it.” I felt like he did. But by God’s grace, I recognized my feelings were wrong. So I told my son, “No, call off the dogs. This is not happening on our watch. We’re doing this the right way.”

But I was fighting against letting that mob mentality we were just talking about expand and do damage. It felt like it would have made me feel good for a moment, but I would have regretted it the rest of my life.

Now as we move to the New Testament and the teachings of Jesus, the first thing we will notice is that Jesus did not directly expand on this commandment. Why? There was no direct teaching needed. The summation of his other teachings powerfully prepared his true disciples to follow this commandment without even having to think.

A text from our last episode illustrates this:

Matthew 15:19–20: 19 For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness <5577>, slanders. 20 These are the things which defile the man…

False witness: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5577 pseudomarturia; from #5575; untrue

testimony

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) false witness, false testimony

As we said earlier, Jesus didn't elaborate on this commandment of being a false witness, but he did remind us of how it defiles those who engage in it.

I can speak to my own experience in the experience I shared. I wanted that young man to be hurt, physically. I knew that was wrong, and only by God’s grace was I able to push those feelings aside. It was a battle, though, and the battle continued.

Now let’s look at “how” Jesus summed up the entire Law when answering a question about its importance:

Matthew 22:37–40: 37 And he said to him, YOU SHALL LOVE THE LORD YOUR GOD WITH ALL YOUR HEART, AND WITH ALL YOUR SOUL, AND WITH ALL YOUR MIND. 38 This is the great and foremost commandment. 39 The second is like it, YOU SHALL LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF. 40 On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets.

We can bear false witness against ourselves by dwelling on our failures and

putting ourselves down after we have already repented and asked forgiveness. This is an interesting way to look at this. The original intent of Jewish Law did

not address this aspect, but it is an important part of what Jesus taught us.

Applying this principle to ourselves means if we are forgiven, then we are forgiven. It is a legal experience. When Jesus took sin away from us, he took it away. We no longer have a right to that sin, or to dwell on it. This is a powerful and personal way to see how both parts of the commandments—loving God and loving our neighbor as ourselves—work together.

Jesus taught that the primary purpose of the Law as a whole is:

1. To honor God.

2. To respect those around us.

We can’t have one without the other. Jesus is adamant that we cannot love God without loving our neighbor. We cannot truly love our neighbor unless we first love God. The two cannot be separated.

The night before his crucifixion, Jesus gently reminded his disciples of what was most important:

John 14:5–6: 5 Thomas said to him, Lord, we do not know where you are going, how do we know the way? 6 Jesus said to him, I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father but through me.

Jesus is simply saying, Look at what I say, look at what I do and where I go, and look at how I act. This is the way.

That is why Jesus didn’t have to explain every detail. He gave us the living human example, the path we need to follow. He paved this incredible path and told us to walk in his footsteps, and we would be fine.

With Jesus as the way, it’s obvious how his teachings lock us into striving for a purity of heart and mind that is rarely seen. He lived all of the commandments.

What about those who opposed him?

Those who opposed Jesus will be judged with righteousness in the kingdom of God. In addition, they will have the ability to repent and live that repentance.

Going back to Amy’s story: We realized we needed to report this to the police, and it was difficult to make Amy go through it all again.

I took her downstairs to the family room, just the two of us, and had her tell me everything she could remember so I could write it down. Having my daughter tell me about being violated is one of the hardest things I’ve ever done.

I had to sit there and couldn’t even look at her. I just looked down and wrote what she said. The temptation was to finish her sentences because she didn’t remember much due to the trauma. Even though I thought I knew what had happened, I did not do this, knowing it would mean making assumptions.

Writing this statement, this experience she and I went through, painful step by painful step, was handed over to the police department as a written testimony of the truth so it could not be embellished by a single word.

Again, that was hard because she didn’t remember everything. When we talk about not letting our emotions take over, I can identify with how that happens. I’d lived it, and it was uncomfortable.

Keeping in mind how hard it was to keep to just the truth with no embellishment, let’s go back to the religious leaders of Jesus’ time.

The only way the religious leaders of Jesus’ day could be rid of him was for them to energetically pursue the breaking of this very commandment:

Matthew 26:59–63: 59 Now the chief priests and the whole Council kept trying to obtain false testimony <5577> against Jesus, so that they might put him to death. 60 They did not find any, even though many false witnesses (#5575 in KJV, #5577 in NASB) came forward. But later on two came forward, 61 and said, This man stated, I am able to destroy the temple of God and to rebuild it in three days. 62 The high priest stood up and said to him, Do you not answer? What is it that these men are testifying against you? 63 But Jesus kept silent.

They were the religious leaders of the Jewish nation, and said truth didn't matter because the greater good was the extermination of Jesus. They looked for lies and promoted them, but producing false witnesses did not work.

Their pursuit of slander and lies could not stand legally, so the high priest was forced to go in a different direction:

Matthew 26:63–66: … And the high priest said to him, I adjure you by the living God, that you tell us whether you are the Christ, the son of God. 64 Jesus said to him, You have said it yourself; nevertheless I tell you, hereafter you will see THE SON OF MAN SITTING AT THE RIGHT HAND OF POWER, and COMING ON THE CLOUDS OF HEAVEN.

He said it because it had to be said. The religious leaders could not find anything to convict him of that was worthy of death. Jesus knew from the prophecies that his time was up according to God's will and plan. This shows that Jesus gave a 100 percent willing sacrifice. The priests didn’t corner him or surprise him; he voluntarily gave himself over to their maliciousness, their darkness, evil and pride, so that God’s will would be done.

How could that be God’s will? Because the lamb had to be sacrificed so all of this sinful world could eventually be made right.

65 Then the high priest tore his robes and said, He has blasphemed! What further need do we have of witnesses? Behold, you have now heard the blasphemy; 66 what do you think? They answered, He deserves death!

How dramatic. What a show. This display ignited a mob mentality. Remember in Matthew 23 when Jesus pronounced all the woes against the religious leaders? He ended it with this statement: For I say to you, from now on you will not see me until you say, BLESSED IS HE WHO COMES IN THE NAME OF THE LORD! Even his murderers will be given an opportunity to turn their lives around in God's kingdom.

That is why Jesus willingly gave his life and why he is the example and no one else. Jesus gave the high priest something to build a corrupt and vile case upon, because the religious leaders had no evidence and their hearts and minds were firmly set on unjustly getting rid of him.

The Law said, You shall not bear false witness. And yet, it didn't matter because the religious leaders had a bigger agenda.

This shows Jesus’ surrender in doing God's will to pay the ransom price for Adam and the entire race. What a savior! He knew the consequences of telling the truth and was willing to bear them. He knew his time had come and gave his enemies the desire of their hearts.

We have to wonder here how many commandments they broke in their pursuit of Jesus’ life.

This comes back to Amy again. We did what we needed to do. We submitted the police report. The guy was arrested, but he ended up leaving the country. There was no justice served.

I could look at this and think, he got away with it. Maybe I should have made the story bigger because he deserved punishment. Maybe I should have embellished. Maybe I shouldn’t have stopped my son from listening to the guy on the phone. I had all these second thoughts. But the bottom line is it would have been wrong. It would not have been following a standard that has been laid out for us very clearly. And just like the religious leaders, that young man will have to face what he did to Amy on the day of judgment, in the day of reconciliation. And by God's grace, he will hopefully be able to be reconciled. But for us, we need to have that forgiving attitude because we leave it in God's hands.

Now, onto the disciple Stephen. The only way the Jewish religious leaders could quiet him down was to pointedly pursue the breaking of this very commandment—bearing false witness. In so doing, they revealed the process by which we rationalize bearing false witness and recruit others to do so as well.

HOW DOES THIS RATIONALIZATION PROCESS WORK?

1. We have a passionately held position we believe is unshakable:

Acts 6:8–9: 8 And Stephen, full of grace and power, was performing great wonders and signs among the people. 9 But some men from what was called the Synagogue of the Freedmen… rose up and argued with Stephen.

The men from the synagogue saw the great wonders and signs, and yet they argued. It is okay to argue if you have a different perspective. Express it, but do so with integrity.

2. When met with overwhelming logic, we stoop down to defend rather than stand up to discuss. Watch what happens now:

Acts 6:10–11: 10 But they were unable to cope with the wisdom and the spirit with which he was speaking. 11 Then they secretly induced men to say (Wait a second! They did what?), We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and against God.

They secretly induced men to lie! This would make the whole thing a legal matter so they could say, We have heard him speak blasphemous words.

It's bad enough to be a false witness, but to talk others into it is on a whole other level. They joined the Pharisees in that, didn’t they?

3. We take the exaggerated and false statements we have encouraged and fuel the fire of our threatened position to create a frenzy of massive emotion:

Acts 6:12–14: 12 And they stirred up the people, the elders and the scribes, and they came up to him and dragged him away and brought him before the Council. 13 They put forward false <5571> witnesses who said, This man incessantly speaks against this holy place and the Law; 14 for we have heard him say that this Nazarene, Jesus, will destroy this place and alter the customs which Moses handed down to us.

False: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5571 pseudés; untrue,

i.e. erroneous, deceitful, wicked:--false, liar

They put forward more false witnesses again with new lies!

The Law was clear and they did not give it a thought! They just didn’t abide by it. To them, their interpretation of the truth and their agenda was more important. Real truth, real integrity didn’t matter whatsoever.

4. The result of this unrighteous exercise is a complete abandonment of integrity for the purpose of extinguishing a legitimate question or perspective. They killed him.

The evidence they came up with wasn't worthy of a death sentence. And this was done in the name of godliness? We have seen this behavior from church systems, especially during the Dark Ages. It was built on idolatry and taking the Lord's name in vain by torturing and murdering Christian martyrs for power and control.

What we see in Scripture has been repeated time and again through history. This should be a warning sign for all of us. We need to hold onto what the Scriptures teach us.

Let’s end on a positive note:

Ephesians 4:29–30: 29 Let no unwholesome word proceed from your mouth, but only such a word as is good for edification according to the need of the moment, so that it will give grace to those who hear. 30 Do not grieve the holy spirit of God, by which you were sealed for the day of redemption.

Our responsibility is to let no unwholesome word proceed from our mouth. Remember, words are provoked by emotion and thought. That is what Jesus taught us. Cleanse our hearts and stand for a higher standard so we honor God rather than destroy Him in what we say and do.

That is the message from this concept of the Law: the Ninth Commandment says, You shall not bear false witness. The positive way of saying this is that we shall always speak truth with integrity, no matter the end result for ourselves.

That’s what we need to do because that is what Jesus did.

So, what does it really mean to bear false witness?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1452-bear-false-witness/

1. Explain the Ninth Commandment. In what way does it have a legal focus? (Exodus 20:16)

2. What factors can pervert justice? What did the instructions in Exodus 23:1-9 warn Israel (and all

believers) against when testifying against a neighbor? Why was this important?

3. How did the principles in Deuteronomy 19:15-21 regarding witnesses and disputes safeguard justice?

What would the effect be of the harsh penalties on a society?

4. In what way can we bear false witness against ourselves?

5. What does Matthew 15:19-20 teach about the relationship between inner motives and outward acts of

dishonesty?

6. How does Jesus’ summary of the Law in Matthew 22:37-40 deepen our understanding of the Ninth

Commandment?

7. What significance does Jesus’ statement, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” have in our lives?

(John 14:5-6)

8. How did the religious leaders violate the Ninth Commandment in their efforts to condemn Jesus?

What can we learn from Jesus’ responses during his trial? (Matthew 26:59-66)
