## Episode 1453 — What’s Wrong With Wanting What Others Have?
Published: 2026-09-07
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1453-covet/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/04123846/CQ_Rewind_09-07-2026_Whats_Wrong_With_Wanting_What_Others_Have.pdf

(The Ten Commandments Series Part X)

Exodus 20:17: You shall not covet your neighbor’s house; you shall not covet your

neighbor's wife or his male servant or his female servant or his ox or his donkey

or anything that belongs to your neighbor.

We are now ready to address the last of the Ten Commandments that God presented to Israel after miraculously delivering them from the slavery of their Egyptian captors. We have seen many important and guiding connections between these Commandments, each building on the previous ones. These connections were profoundly important to the nation of Israel, as they created a foundation for their civil laws. As Christians, we appreciate how Jesus elevated these Commandments as the basis for our spiritual lives. Now, as we consider the final Commandment, “You shall not covet,” we will observe how it ties everything together for both Israel and the disciples of Christ.

The Tenth Commandment is similar to the Second Commandment (“Do not make any idols”) and the Fourth Commandment (“Remember the Sabbath”) because it does more than simply give a command. It also expands on the meaning of the command.

Covet: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2530 chamad; a primitive root; to delight in

This word for covet is not negative by definition; it’s not a bad thing. However, when this emotion is applied inappropriately, it brings only trouble and never ends well.

God built perfect humanity to desire—to covet—the beauty and goodness of His creation:

Genesis 2:9: Out of the ground the LORD God caused to grow every tree that is pleasing <2530> to the sight and good for food; the tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

God built the desire into human nature to be drawn to beauty, to want it. This is a good desire God placed in the hearts of humanity.

But Satan twisted that delight towards perceptions and applications that were NOT God-sanctioned:

Genesis 3:6: When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight (delight here is a different Hebrew word) to the eyes, and that the tree was desirable <2530> to make one wise (coveting wasn't there until Satan gave the evil suggestion), she took from its fruit and ate; and she gave also to her husband with her, and he ate.

The desire to see the beauty of the tree positively in Genesis 2, then to desire it negatively in Genesis 3, creates a powerful contrast. The coveting of the wisdom the tree could give her—beyond what God had already given her at the time—wasn’t hers to be had, and may even have been beyond her ability to use. Satan took a good desire and twisted it into something bad that served him.

The next use of the word covet in the Old Testament is in the Tenth Commandment. Here, inappropriate desire appears again in the Law as a major commandment.

Inappropriate coveting is an internal sin of the heart, just as breaking the First Commandment—having no other gods but God—is a sin of the heart. The Tenth Commandment is an “internal instruction” with many applications.

Exodus 20:17: You shall not covet <2530> your neighbor's house…

First of all, who is our “neighbor”?

Jesus taught the Parable of the Good Samaritan in response to a lawyer who challenged him on the Law’s greatest Commandment. In the parable, a man is robbed and beaten on the road. A priest and a Levite pass by and ignore him. A Samaritan cleans his wounds and brings him to a place of rest and care.

Then Jesus asked the lawyer:

Luke 10:36-37: 36 Which of these three do you think proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell into the robbers' hands? 37 And he said, The one who showed mercy toward him. Then Jesus said to him, Go and do the same.

Jesus is setting a broad standard of mutual care, and such a standard has no room for coveting! Our neighbors, then, are those around us whether we like them or not.

To covet your neighbor’s house is to deeply desire their life for your own. It means wanting to be who they are and to experience what you perceive they experience. You have everything. If only I could be you or have your (money/house/car/job/spouse/…).

Satan was the original coveter. Despite what he had been given, he wanted the power, authority and majesty of his Creator. These weren’t his to have:

Isaiah 14:13-14: 13 But you said in your heart, I will ascend to heaven; I will raise my throne above the stars of God, and I will sit on the mount of assembly in the recesses of the north. 14 I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High.

Right then, we see coveting gone awry. If we get into that frame of mind, we are thinking in a satanic way. I’ll make myself be that person. I want what that person has.

Satan wanted to be in God's place by usurping His authority. How selfish and arrogant to step over God despite all He did for him. Talk about a superiority complex!

When we covet maybe just a little and feel discontent, we might think, Well, what’s wrong with this? We need to remind ourselves that coveting is based on a satanic principle.

Let’s get practical. We talked about coveting our neighbor’s house—in effect, desiring their life for our own. The world we live in is not equal. Christianity is made up of individuals from all walks of life, from those with authority and earthly influence to those who must submit to authority and simply work hard.

The Scriptures address this from a New Testament perspective:

Ephesians 6:5-8: 5 Slaves (meaning indentured servants), be obedient to those who are your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in the sincerity of your heart, as to Christ; 6 not by way of eyeservice, as men-pleasers, but as slaves of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart. 7 With good will render service, as to the Lord, and not to men, 8 knowing that whatever good thing each one does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether slave or free.

Paul is essentially telling the working class to serve as unto the Lord and do their best in whatever work they are given. So, what might some of the worst-case scenarios look like when someone allows coveting to take over in the workplace?

There might be dissatisfaction with how the business is run. “I can goof off if I like. It’s not my business—in fact, I should be running it! I don’t need to contribute; it’s a mess anyway.” There may also be a sense of entitlement or sabotage of the business or others’ work due to coveting.

In these cases, we need to question our motivation. What good is this attitude? How is this Christlike? Or… how is this Satan-like?

“Am I not happy with my life? Do I think if I had someone else’s life, I could live it better than they are living it?” We can’t go down that road. If we have that basic discontent with our own lives, we need to address it in a more positive way.

It hurts to think about that. But we easily fall into this kind of thinking: “If I had that opportunity, you should see what I could do!” This is talking like Satan in Isaiah 14:13-14.

“I” will sit on the mount of assembly in the recesses of the north. “I” will ascend above the heights… If we think like this, we think like Satan. That is why this is the last Commandment. It really gets our attention.

If we answer these mirror questions in the affirmative, we may have pride and arrogance like Satan, which is the opposite of humility.

1 Peter 5:6: …Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God that he may exalt you at the proper time.

God exalts us; we don’t exalt ourselves. It is up to Him. Let God be the designer of our life experiences.

Even if it is below what we might desire, if God puts us there, we should embrace what He has given us so we can grow into whatever He has set up for us, rather than desiring what would be contrary to His will.

Coveting the lives and experiences of the rich and famous, especially in our world today, is not only frequent but also a taught behavior.

The first detail of not coveting has been stated in the broad terms of our neighbor’s

house. Now the Commandment will go deeper. What comes next?

Remember that even though the thought of desiring is not inherently bad, this Commandment only deals with specific danger zones of coveting. This message should be loud and clear in the ears of every disciple of Jesus: Do NOT go down these roads of desire, or delight in things that violate the integrity of our faith and our calling! Coveting inappropriately in not harmonious with our calling as Christians.

Exodus 20:17: …you shall not covet <2530> your neighbor's wife…

To covet your neighbor’s spouse is to, in effect, desire their strongest earthly attachment for yourself, which was sealed by “a covenant of God.”

This reminds us of the words of Jesus in relation to the Seventh Commandment:

Matthew 5:28: But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lust <1937> for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

Lust: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1937 epithumeo; to set the heart upon,

i.e. long for (rightfully or otherwise)

We discussed this scripture in great detail on the podcast about the Seventh Commandment, but the word for lust (also translated desire) here is like the word for covet in the Old Testament. It is not automatically a negative word. Rightly applied, it is an appropriate and helpful human emotion.

Let’s look at one example:

1 Timothy 3:1: It is a trustworthy statement: if any man aspires to the office of overseer, it is a fine work he desires <1937> to do.

Desiring the office of a shepherd or pastor isn’t wrong. It’s a good thing to set our heart upon. This is an office of service and responsibility, but it’s not an office of elevation above others. It is a responsibility requiring someone to help, build up, guide and direct. It takes a lot to desire, to be able to want to give and sacrifice in that way. This is a good desire.

Again, the word itself is not bad. It is how it is applied that makes it either a danger zone of coveting or something that should be worked towards.

To desire what is not and cannot be ours because of a solemn promise (like the covenant of marriage) before God is a deeply sinful place to go.

This desire is much more than just sexuality. What about personality, social skills, wit or their ability to prepare food? What about their career success? Do I desire their ability to engage in activities, or do I desire them for their athletic ability? Or, do I desire their ability to be supportive, or to lead, or their example? These are all things that can be part of this inappropriate coveting. We need to inspect our hearts to make sure we do not miss these subtle things we don’t normally think about.

We might start with: If only my spouse were… Then perhaps we look around and start comparing them with other spouses. This might lead to desiring the other person for those skills, which might not seem harmful. But we are engaging in a desire outside of a covenant, and it doesn’t serve anyone well at any time.

Instead of this, we need to put our own spouses in a position of being lifted up in our hearts and minds—exactly the opposite of coveting.

James helps us see what this commandment is driving us to comprehend—that coveting opens the doors to sin:

James 1:14-15: 14 But each one is tempted when he is carried away and enticed by his own lust <1939> (noun form of <1937>). 15 Then when lust <1939> has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and when sin is accomplished, it brings forth death.

This is the pattern of inappropriate desire:

- enticed by his own lust
- desire begins to grow
- it gives birth to sin
- sin is acted upon
- it brings forth death

Shouldn’t this be our attitude? Instead of coveting what belongs to our neighbor, we should focus on improving our own situation and being thankful for what we have rather than comparing ourselves to others. Find the positive in your spouse instead of looking elsewhere!

Sometimes we get into very negative patterns. This is where inappropriate coveting can come into play. When was the last time you spoke to your spouse and directly told them about the good things you appreciate, how they help you, how important they are to you? When someone expresses this to us, we feel appreciated. When we feel appreciated, we tend to contribute more. It’s a building-up process.

We can either be inappropriately coveting and tearing down, or we can be going in the other direction by building up. When we give true compliments, our spouses give us more respect because we have identified and see the value they bring to the marriage. It elevates the whole marriage. This should be a constant way of life.

Exodus 20:17: You shall not covet <2530>… his male servant or his female servant...

To covet your neighbor’s servants in today’s world is a desire for the status others possess. In ancient times, having servants showed family stability and success. Today, we see this as a desire for our neighbor's or spiritual brother's status.

As Christians, we need to be aware and respectful of what we are, what we are not and the contributory role we all can play:

1 Corinthians 12:14-16: 14 For the body is not one member, but many. 15 If the foot says, Because I am not a hand, I am not a part of the body, it is not for this reason any the less a part of the body. 16 And if the ear says, Because I am not an eye, I am not a part of the body, it is not for this reason any the less a part of the body.

There are benefits to being different. We should complement each other, not covet; be harmonious, not harmful.

Rick and Jonathan are so different, but they share the same objective in producing the Christian Questions podcast. Each brings what they can to the table, and together they can build what is God-honoring. Rick is Rick, Jonathan is Jonathan, and together they build up as different parts of the body.

To desire a “higher” position within the body is to ask for greater responsibility. The question is, should we really be asking for greater responsibility? Are we meant for that higher position? Am I wanting this to increase my status, or does the heavenly Father want this for me? He is the One whose opinion matters.

It is one thing to want to learn how to be like someone else. It is another to want their position. When we start to do that, we are stepping outside of Apostle Paul’s explanation of how the body of Christ operates. If I am a “foot,” I can’t be a “hand.” Even if the foot is always stuck in the sandal and in the dirt, I can’t be a hand! I need to accept it and get my work done.

We have to be careful with our thoughts. We don’t want to think like Satan who wanted God's opportunity to rule the world.

Paul simplifies all of this with two basic admonitions:

Have a clear life perspective:

1 Timothy 6:7-8: (This refers to what we have) 7 For we have brought nothing into the world, so we cannot take anything out of it either. 8 If we have food and covering, with these we shall be content.

This says we were all essentially born the same way. We need to be content with the gifts, blessings and providences God places before us.

As our friend Mark says: “Have you ever seen a hearse pulling a U-Haul? You can’t take it with you!”

Have a clear objective regarding our everyday thoughts:

2 Corinthians 10:5: We are destroying speculations and every lofty thing raised up against the knowledge of God, and we are taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ.

God’s Word is our manual for how we think and live. That’s why, at Christian Questions, we study subjects topically from a biblical perspective, seeking to let the harmony of God’s Word shape our understanding.

We must let the harmony of God’s Word—not our opinions, desires or insecurities— shape what we desire and how we act in relation to those desires. It is not about someone else’s status, but about our own status before God Almighty and how we use His spirit in our lives.

A desire to serve the Lord more is good. Pray on it and watch for God’s providential direction as He opens doors in response to your sincerity. He did it for us with Christian Questions. We didn’t know what we were doing, and we had to learn as we went along, letting His guidance open the doors.

The bluntly stated bottom line here is that if we covet another's relationships and status, we are essentially telling God He didn’t treat us fairly and we should get what we want. Ouch!

We’ve reviewed wanting another’s life, their spouse and their status.

If we can’t covet those things, can we covet their success?

The beauty of this Tenth Commandment is that it breaks down our human desires toward what others may have into several distinct categories of attraction. The lesson should be obvious, as God is showing us His knowledge of humanity's imperfections and how to be on guard against them. How well are we paying attention to what we are being taught?

Let’s look at our next lesson:

Exodus 20:17: You shall not covet <2530>… his ox or his donkey.

It's like saying, “It's not fair. I want that ox and that donkey. If I had them, I would be even more successful than him. I deserve them!”

To covet your neighbor’s ox or donkey in our world today is to essentially desire the success in business that our neighbor maintains. It is looking at their success and thinking they are successful because of what they have been given. “If I ran that business instead of them, look what I could do!” It is switching our perspective of our neighbor’s success from godliness to selfishness.

For most people, “getting rich” in business requires serious focus and dedication. Focus and determination are good, but what do they draw us toward?

1 Timothy 6:9-10: 9 But those who want to get rich fall into temptation and a snare and many foolish and harmful desires which plunge men into ruin and destruction. 10 For the love of money is a root of all sorts of evil, and some by longing for it have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs.

Wanting to get rich can be a snare, a temptation that can derail our Christian walk. We want to be clear: there is nothing wrong with working hard and finding success. But it comes down to our real motivation. There is nothing wrong if we have been blessed with wealth, but what are we doing with what we’re blessed with? How do we use it for the benefit of God’s work? Are we putting ourselves in a position where we can be a benefit to others?

Do you look at yourself and think, I’m in a dead-end job. Do you have opportunities? Can you apply yourself to something differently? What are your options without getting into a situation of inappropriate desire? We have to parse through this and think about it in an appropriate way.

Do I want another’s earthly or spiritual opportunity? If I want what you’re doing because I think I can do it better than you, I’ve already lost the battle.

Jealousy is a big part of coveting.

The answer as to our desire to be “rich” was in the previous verses:

1 Timothy 6:6-8: 6 But godliness actually is a means of great gain when accompanied by contentment. 7 For we have brought nothing into the world, so we cannot take anything out of it either. 8 If we have food and covering, with these we shall be content.

That inordinate desire for something somebody else has cannot overcome us if we are truly content. When we look at the business success of our brother or neighbor, we need to be content with what God has given us to thrive. This doesn’t mean we have to stay where we are. It doesn’t mean we cannot change and do better. But let’s do it for the right and appropriate desires, not the inappropriate jealousies of wanting what someone else has.

I used to be a cabinet and countertop maker, but I changed careers many years ago. I got into a service business because I saw an opportunity to control my time so I could do things for the Lord. I had no idea what, but I knew if I could have more control of my time, I would have more opportunities.

At the shop, I worked on salary, and that meant I never saw a 40-hour week in my life, even when it was only a four-day week! It was always 50, 55 hours. So I looked for something else and made a change because I truly wanted to serve God.

It didn't work out great at the beginning (don’t ask my wife!). It took several years, but after we got used to it, it actually worked out. A lot of people ask me, how are you able to work on Christian Questions while working full-time? One of the answers is that I run my own business by God’s grace and therefore control my own time, so I can carve out time to do the work. But it took years to get there. So, we do not have to stay put, but we have to be aware of what is driving our hearts, how we desire and what we are desiring to achieve.

Exodus 20:17: You shall not covet <2530>… anything that belongs to your neighbor.

To covet anything of your neighbor’s is to dwell on a basic dissatisfaction with your own life and focus your attention on what someone else has. Coveting at any level reveals a lack of contentment.

Again, an appropriate desire to change can be good if our situation is difficult and we can’t find contentment in the environment. But an inappropriate desire to take what someone else has so that we can have it is not! We have to separate the two very clearly.

In our Christian fellowship, many of our issues with one another can be connected to coveting:

James 4:1-3: 1 What is the source of quarrels and conflicts among you? Is not the source your pleasures <2237> that wage war in your members? 2 You lust <1937> and do not have; so you commit murder. You are envious <2206> and cannot obtain; so you fight and quarrel. You do not have because you do not ask. 3 You ask and do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives, so that you may spend it on your pleasures <2237>.

Pleasures: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2237 hedone; from handano (to please);

sensual delight; by implication, desire

King James Version translates this as lust, pleasure

Envious: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2206 zeloo;

to have warmth of feeling for or against

Jesus says in Matthew 7:7: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find. James tells us we are not receiving because we are asking with the wrong motives. He says there is inappropriate coveting that doesn’t belong among the brotherhood. It is creating friction, problems, disunity and a godless environment!

If we are envious of our neighbor’s success at something, instead of being jealous, we can approach the brother or sister and ask if they can help us learn to do what they do so well. Turn that inordinate desire into a shared learning experience. It’s a huge change.

Am I a troublemaker within the body of Christ because I think things should be the way I think they should be? We cannot covet positions and authority that don’t belong to us!

Continuing:

1 Timothy 6:11-12: 11 But flee from these things, you man of God, and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance and gentleness. 12 Fight the good fight of faith; take hold of the eternal life to which you were called, and you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.

Passion is appropriate as long as it’s directed towards pursuing godliness and the hope set before us. Absolutely have passion, but let it be in the desire to do the will of God at the expense of your own will. That is how we turn the tables on this.

Stephen showed remarkable passion as he witnessed the beautiful truths at the Temple, but his message was not well received (Acts 7:51-54). The Apostle Paul also had passion, as did the Apostle Peter. It cost Stephen his life. We might think he was foolish to push his beliefs so hard that he became a martyr, but look at the glory he was given. It’s incomprehensible. It is not about the here and now, today. It’s about God’s plan and eternity. That is where our true desire should be.

Finally, let us do what Jesus did and bend all our personal desire toward fellowship, godliness and self-sacrifice, using desire in an appropriate way:

Luke 22:14-15: (NKJV) 14 When the hour had come, he sat down, and the twelve apostles with him. 15 Then he said to them, With fervent desire <1937> I have desired <1937> to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.

This is a good desire. Jesus desired to be with his apostles before his greatest trial—the one that would take his life. That is the kind of desire we want for ourselves. That is what we want to focus on as we walk in Jesus’ own footsteps.

To conquer coveting is no small task. It requires not only perseverance, but a fundamental honesty and humility to set our sights and move in the right direction.

We have examined and discussed each of the Ten Commandments and applied

them to Israel and ourselves. How do we put this all together?

Let’s begin with a simple pattern. Breaking the First Commandment, having no other gods before God, happens within us and cannot be seen by others until our actions change. We call it an “internal instruction.”

The next eight Commandments are all “external action instructions” as they are readily visible by those around us.

The Tenth Commandment is like the First Commandment, as it is an “internal instruction.”

The first and last Commandments create a kind of “sandwich effect”—the desire to serve God on one side and the desire not to serve ourselves on the other.

You shall have no other gods before me. For the Jews, this is an “internal instruction,” fulfilled within the heart and mind.

That same principle carries directly into the Christian life. It establishes the necessity of having our hearts and minds firmly fixed on God through Jesus as our only object of loyalty and praise.

Violation of this First Commandment is the beginning of the downfall of any individual or any civilization.

You shall not make unto thee a graven image (KJV). For Israel, this is an “external action instruction.” To “make” an idol is to create a physically or emotionally tangible object of worship, to physically or emotionally “bow down to” and “serve.”

For Christians, this also becomes an “internal instruction” to firmly and consistently seek out and destroy any forms of idolatry lurking in the corners of our hearts, minds or desires. We must uproot them from the inside out.

Thou shalt not take the name of Jehovah thy God in vain (KJV). For Israel, this is an “external action instruction” to thoroughly live what they proclaim to be.

The name carried must always reflect that which we most highly honor. For Christians, this becomes an “internal instruction” to carry the name of God essentially as the signature of our life and NOT have it be a forgery (not saying we are something we really are not), a false or frivolous representation of being a disciple of Christ. Do not take God’s name in vain. Be genuine in how we walk in His son Jesus’ footsteps.

Connecting the first three Commandments: These first three demonstrated an alarming and degrading human pathway away from God.

Jesus connected them clearly in the Lord’s prayer:

Matthew 6:9: Pray, then, in this way: Our Father who is in heaven, Hallowed be Your name.

1. “Our Father” — First Commandment

“You shall have no other gods before Me.” → Have no other gods before God.

2. “Who is in heaven” — Second Commandment

“You shall not make for yourself an idol…” → Make no idol or image of He who is in heaven.

3. “Hallowed be Your name” — Third Commandment

“You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain.” → Reverence and honor His sacred name.

These three commandments are the basis for our entire life.

Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. For the Jews this “external action instruction” is the first “Do” commandment after a string of three “Don’t” commandments. For Israel, it was a solemn reminder to pause, consider and fully keep the first three Commandments. The Sabbath was critical to them.

For Christians this becomes an “internal instruction” as well, because we rest now while doing God’s work. We rest because we have nothing to fear and because we know we must “do with our might what our hands find to do” (Ecclesiastes 9:10) while leaving all else in God’s hands. There is a great rest in this.

The first four commandments are all about how to thrive in relation to spirituality and to who God is.

Honor thy father and thy mother (KJV). For Israel this is an “external action instruction” and is the foundation in establishing how to thrive as a physical people in relation to one another.

All of the final six Commandments will show us what governs successful interpersonal relationships. (Remember, the first four were about spiritual relationships with God.)

As Christians, respect for our parents must filter through our recognition of their best, yet imperfect, efforts. While honoring a destructive parent is NOT a biblical principle, we must NOT confuse this challenge with our own potential resentment or frustration against them. The honor that we give to our parents must come from our hearts.

You shall not murder. For Israel, this is an “external action instruction” to thoroughly honor the sanctity of human life. The penalty for breaking this Commandment was severe!

Jesus raised the bar by making this an “internal instruction” and teaching his disciples that anger and slander were akin to murder for them.

For Christians, if our contempt and disdain for anyone is not appropriately checked, it can bring us to the same moral category as murder! Unchecked disrespect for our brother or sister can bring disastrous results, as we may end up “murdering” their reputation and all aspects of their worth before others. You shall not murder in this way!

You shall not commit adultery. For the Jew, it is another “external action instruction,” as it addresses what we do or don’t engage in. This Commandment is the foundation of the human family relationship, as it is based on the sacred marriage covenant between husband and wife.

Jesus transformed this into an “internal instruction” as well. For his disciples, even looking at another person who is married (or if WE are married) with inappropriate desire is adulterous and can lead to spiritual death and destruction. Even more important is the higher necessity regarding our internal and external fidelity to God. We should not adulterate our relationship with God either.

You shall not steal is an “external action instruction” for the Jews that establishes the personal rights of our community. It applies to the general business of life, the specifics of buying and selling, to stealing from a family’s livelihood and to negligence that results in another’s losses.

Jesus transformed this Commandment into an “internal instruction” as well. Let us be clear: heaven is closed to thieves. The question, then, is not merely, “What am I doing?” but “WHY am I doing it?” Before a sinful “what” ever becomes an action, it often begins with a subtle thought, need or desire taking root in the heart. The lesson begins with becoming aware of our motives before they lead us into sinful action.

You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor is another “external action instruction” for Israel. This legal focus is on the sin of publicly and legally accusing your brother on the basis of preplanned falsehoods, for the purpose of publicly and legally damaging or destroying him.

Jesus again made this an “internal instruction.” No matter how driven we are about our positions regarding serious disagreements with others, speaking falsehoods is NEVER appropriate. Even exaggeration is speaking a falsehood. Elevating things to a formal level with ANY HINT of malice or contempt is diametrically opposed to our discipleship!

You shall not covet is an “internal instruction,” like the First Commandment. For the Israelites to desire something is not inherently bad, but coveting anything that is your neighbor’s—his house, his wife, his servants or his cattle—amounts to dishonoring your neighbor and God.

Jesus’ standards are those of mutual care, and such standards have no room for coveting or inappropriate desire! Again, to stand for Christ is to stand in support of and love for the brotherhood. If our focus is always on standing for Christ, we will not have either the time or inclination to allow coveting even to begin to take root.

As we have looked at these Ten Commandments over the last ten episodes, we see a dramatic story unfold of how God, in His incredible wisdom, laid out these civil laws for the Jewish nation and spiritual laws for us as well.

Let’s go back to what Jesus said about these Commandments:

Matthew 22:37-40: 37 And he said to him, YOU SHALL LOVE THE LORD YOUR GOD WITH ALL YOUR HEART, AND WITH ALL YOUR SOUL, AND WITH ALL YOUR MIND. 38 This is the great and foremost commandment. 39 The second is like it, YOU SHALL LOVE YOUR

NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF. 40 On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets.

Jesus takes all Ten Commandments and puts them into these two simple statements:

1. YOU SHALL LOVE THE LORD YOUR GOD WITH ALL YOUR HEART, AND WITH

ALL YOUR SOUL, AND WITH ALL YOUR MIND.

2. YOU SHALL LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF.

Then he states that on these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets. When we look at the Ten Commandments, let’s not think of them as something old- fashioned and no longer relevant. As Christians, we should take them seriously and approach them with reverence as we seek to follow God through Christ.

So, what’s wrong with wanting what others have?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/character/1453-covet/

1. How do Genesis 2:9 and Genesis 3:6 contrast godly desire with sinful coveting?

2. In what way is the Tenth Commandment similar to the First Commandment? (Exodus 20:3,17)

3. Who is our “neighbor”? Explain how Jesus’ words leave no room for coveting. (Luke 10:36-37)

4. What warnings can we draw from Satan’s ambition? Why does this reveal the essence of coveting?

How can we fall into satanic thinking? How can we avoid it? (Isaiah 14:13-14, 1 Peter 5:6)

5. Give some practical examples of coveting that can arise in the workplace. What should our attitude be

when we are working? (Ephesians 6:5-8)

6. How does Jesus expand the command against coveting a neighbor’s spouse beyond physical attraction to

include desires related to personality, abilities and other qualities? How can we combat this in our own marriages and relationships? (Matthew 5:28, James 1:14-15)

7. How does Paul’s illustration of the body of Christ help believers avoid coveting another person’s status,

role or opportunities within the church? (1 Corinthians 12;14-16)

8. What is the connection between contentment and freedom from coveting? If we fall into coveting

someone else’s success, what does this say to God? (1 Timothy 6:6-10, 2 Corinthians 10:5)

9. What leads to issues and conflict in our Christian fellowship? What might the deeper heart issue be

behind quarrels and division? (James 4:1-3, Matthew 7:7)

10. When I admire a quality, position or accomplishment in another person, do I respond with gratitude and

a desire to learn from them; or with jealousy and a desire to possess what is theirs? (1 Corinthians 12;14-16,

James 4:1-3) How can I change this attitude?

11. How can we ensure our strongest desires are directed toward serving God and His people as Jesus did,

instead of toward advancing our own will and ambitions? (Luke 22:14-15, 1 Timothy 6:11-12)

## Episode 1454 — Can Death and Hope Actually Work Together?
Published: 2026-09-14
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1454-death-and-hope/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/05195203/CQ_Rewind_09-14-2026_Can_Death_and_Hope_Actually_Work_Together.pdf

John 12:24: Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies,

it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.

When we look at the world around us and the powerful influences of darkness and evil that dominate it, we can easily get discouraged. Why would God allow so much to be so wrong for so long? Thinking about faith is helpful, but it doesn’t alleviate the nagging questions about how darkness and sin seem always to be winning.

So, what if… ?

o What if we apply our faith to a broader perspective and look at the world’s history

as the beginnings of an eternal plan for all of humanity? o What if we mark specific cycles of this history as steps that God is having His

human family take? o What if each step in God’s plan after Adam and Eve were created is marked by

death, and that death would bring the seeds of renewal and hope for the next step? o What if this process shows us the mind, power, love and mercy of God?

What is the basis for looking at our dreadful world in this way? God’s own words that describe His character and His foresight!

He knows the end from the beginning, AND He has a purpose!

Isaiah 46:9–10: 9 …For I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is no one like Me, 10 declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times things which have not been done, saying, My purpose will be established, and I will accomplish all My good pleasure.

So God's got this, and His good pleasure will happen!

He is above us, and His words are guarantees of what will come to pass:

Isaiah 55:9–11: 9 For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are My ways higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts. 10 For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven, and do not return there without watering the earth and making it bear and sprout, and furnishing seed to the sower and bread to the eater; 11 so will My word be which goes forth from My mouth; it will not return to Me empty, without accomplishing what I desire, and without succeeding in the matter for which I sent it.

These two passages in Isaiah show that God knows the end from the beginning. He has a purpose—His words and ways guarantee that His plan will be accomplished.

In the second citation, God describes His words as the rain and the snow come down from heaven, and do not return there without watering the earth. God’s word has a purpose—to water the earth so it can bear and sprout. He essentially said that the cycles of nature are His signature, reminding us that He has a plan.

Let’s lay out the process that needs to take place.

“What if” we start at the beginning? Before there was death, there was life— perfect, harmonious human life:

Genesis 2:8–9: 8 The LORD God planted a garden toward the east, in Eden; and there He placed the man whom He had formed. 9 Out of the ground the LORD God caused to grow every tree that is pleasing to the sight and good for food; the tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

God sets it up; all is good, perfect and harmonious. God’s intention is very beautiful. Everything is supplied. He creates this beautiful place for man, but things don't go as intended.

Let’s go now to the point where man becomes part of God’s intentionality:

Genesis 2:16–17: 16 The LORD God commanded the man, saying, From any tree of the garden you may eat freely; 17 but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat from it you will surely die (King James Version: Dying thou shalt die).

What happened? Adam and Eve sinned and were sentenced to a life that would ultimately end in death. So, the sentence was a life that would degrade itself until death took them.

God’s perfect intention and preparation existed from the beginning. But then sin entered. Did that mess up God’s entire plan? What now?

Don’t worry! Remember the “what if… ?” God has the ability of foresight!

With this sentence of death (they were not yet dead; they were dying) came an actual death—the sacrifice of an animal to cover the recognition of their own sins:

Genesis 3:21: The LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and clothed them.

The death of an animal was the first recorded death in the Bible. It was sacrificed to provide a covering for sin. Because Adam had named all the animals in the garden and cared deeply for them, witnessing death for the first time must have been traumatic.

It would have been a real wake-up call! This was completely contrary to the environment of the Garden of Eden. Sin had created an entirely new condition.

When we consider God and His wisdom, as described in the previous Isaiah scriptures, we have to wonder, how would He make this right?

The answer is that He knew the nature of free will in advance and already had a plan in place. The death of the sacrificed animal symbolized the beginning of life under a sinful condition.

Adam and Eve’s environment would change, and they needed to be covered:

Genesis 3:22–23: 22 Then the LORD God said, Behold, the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil; and now, he might stretch out his hand, and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever— 23 therefore the LORD God sent him out from the garden of Eden, to cultivate the ground from which he was taken.

God didn’t abandon him. Instead, God took Adam from the perfect garden, where everything was supplied, into a new environment where Adam would need to take responsibility for his own preparation and survival.

Adam and Eve went from that perfect, beautiful paradise into a world in shambles. Things had fallen apart. God had this all under control, but it certainly didn’t look that way at that moment.

As time progressed, this downward trend would unfold.

Even spirit beings would follow Satan’s lead and become involved in that same cycle of putting self before God:

Genesis 6:1–3: 1 Now it came about, when men began to multiply on the face of the land, and daughters were born to them, 2 that the sons of God (referring to fallen spirit beings) saw that the daughters of men were beautiful; and they took wives for themselves, whomever they chose. 3 Then the LORD said, My spirit shall not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; nevertheless his days shall be one hundred and twenty years.

God allowed the fallen spirit beings to interfere with humanity—but only for a limited time. This intentional turning toward sin and darkness initiated by those spirit beings who followed Satan would not continue indefinitely. God said it would stop! He had a plan to deal with disobedience. But this hybrid race—half fallen angel and half human—went beyond the realm of what creation was designed to be. The world was heading into a deep, dark situation.

All of this corrupted spiritual activity added to dramatically corrupting the people:

Genesis 6:11–12: 11 Now the earth was corrupt in the sight of God, and the earth was filled with violence. 12 God looked on the earth, and behold, it was corrupt; for all flesh had corrupted their way upon the earth.

God stopped this corruption by allowing the Flood and the death it brought. Remember, our theme is the concept of death and renewal.

This would be the end of an age—a massive period of time—ending in death.

However, in the midst of all the death and destruction, there was hope:

2 Peter 2:4–5: (WEY) 4 For God did not spare angels when they had sinned, but hurling them down to Tartarus consigned them to caves of darkness, keeping them in readiness for judgement. 5 And He did not spare the ancient world, although He preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when He brought a deluge on the world of the ungodly.

The Flood brought massive death and destruction to man and beast. This marked the end of an era and brought about a profound change.

But all was not lost! Throughout this very dark and depressing time, there remained a thread of hope, pictured in Noah—the one individual who would carry forward the line of righteousness.

Let’s pause and sum things up at this point. We have this age of time stretching from Adam all the way to Noah, and we see many events taking place during this period.

The genealogies in Genesis clearly establish that the timeline from Adam’s creation to the Flood was a total of 1,656 years. See Bonus Material for more.

Think about the long period of time that had begun with a beautiful, perfect life. Then sin entered and corruption began. That corruption grew deeper and deeper until God brought it to an end through the dramatic, large-scale Flood. Yet, in the midst of all that darkness, there was this tiny thread of hope—and his name was Noah. He and his family—the other seven—were spared so that all was not lost. There was still an opportunity for renewal to come later.

This can be a hard concept to follow, as we need to keep God’s perspective of time and eternity clear in our minds—when we want immediate results!

So, the death at the end of that first age with the Flood was dramatic!

Can we expect the renewal of the next age to be just as dramatic?

While having dramatic renewal would be glorious for our human minds, we need to recognize that God’s plans always work through small beginnings. We need to look for what God will do with the renewal and who will carry its message. Remember, whenever there is any major shift in how God’s plan is being fulfilled that is marked with death, it always precedes a renewal that brings hope, and His plan one step closer to His eternal objective.

We are looking at a process that repeats itself—the details might look different but have the same elements. Each time this happens, the process brings us to where God has known He would bring us all along!

Back to the death that ended the previous age. The great deluge wiped out the wickedness and evil that had been perpetrated by fallen spirits who had gained control over the people. God put a stop to it and limited their abilities going forward. He held these spirits in darkness (Jude 1:6), stopping them from creating any hybrid race. We’re watching what God did in this step-by-small-step process. The heavenly Father, who sees the end from the beginning, is unfolding His plan.

The systems and corruption of that age were removed. Their death was necessary

to provide a new beginning where God’s plan could flourish without the

influence of these fallen spirits. Noah would carry renewed hope. Remember,

when there is death, there is always someone to carry the torch of renewal!

The renewal of this new age began with Noah and his family as life-givers:

Genesis 8:15–17: 15 Then God spoke to Noah, saying, 16 Go out of the ark, you and your wife and your sons and your sons’ wives with you. 17 Bring out with you every living thing of all flesh that is with you, birds and animals and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth, that they may breed abundantly on the earth, and be fruitful and multiply on the earth.

Genesis 9:1: And God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth.

This is exactly what God told Adam and Eve: Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth. We can see God renewing the opportunity He originally put in place. Though the scenario is different, He is renewing it. We must follow the way God sees, thinks and directs it.

The responsibility of renewing the earth was given to Noah and his family. As a result, life would continue.

Noah is incredibly grateful, so he builds an altar and offers a sacrifice of praise to God. God’s renewal came with a promise:

Genesis 9:8–11: 8 Then God spoke to Noah and to his sons with him, saying, 9 Now behold, I Myself do establish My covenant with you, and with your descendants after you; 10 and with every living creature that is with you, … of all that comes out of the ark, even every beast of the earth. 11 I establish My covenant with you; and all flesh shall never again be cut off by the water of the flood, neither shall there again be a flood to destroy the earth.

This refers to the rainbow of promise. It was a symbol God put in place to help people understand and remember the lessons of the Flood. It was also meant to provide the security of knowing that God would never again destroy the world in this way. Throughout history, God has put certain things in place to reassure mankind. This rainbow promise was the first one.

This promise was a step toward the life God planned for His creation. God’s renewal process develops one step at a time—so, no, the fulfilment of His plans will not be accomplished tomorrow.

“What if” God had this all planned out—the pattern of death followed by renewal? Could there be something more to this? Now that we have begun, let’s trace the next steps and see how one builds upon what was previously there, and how the brightness of the renewal grows each time.

We just discussed the first major time division or “epoch” of God’s plan. 2 Peter 3:6 (KJV) refers to this pre-Flood epoch as the world that then was—(we will refer to this as the “the world that was,”) from Adam to the Flood.

The second epoch is referred to by Galatians 1:4 (KJV) as this present evil world.

At the beginning of this new epoch, God clearly dealt with and worked through faithful individuals, such as Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph. They are often referred to as the patriarchs, so we will call this the Patriarchal Age.

Let’s trace the pathway of God’s renewal and hope through Abraham. This torch of renewal gets passed on:

Genesis 12:1–3: 1 Now the LORD said to Abram, Go forth from your country, and from your relatives and from your father’s house, to the land which I will show you; 2 and I will make you a great nation, and I will bless you, and make your name great; and so you shall be a blessing; 3 and I will bless those who bless you, and the one who curses you I will curse. And in you all the families of the earth will be blessed.

This is so much bigger than when God said be fruitful and multiply. Now, All the families of the earth will be blessed! It is not just the people who have lived, but all the people who would live in the future.

God’s plan of renewal and hope was becoming more focused. It moved from the promise to never again destroy the earth to the promise to Abraham that he would be blessed and, in that blessing, become the conduit for blessing ALL the families of the earth!

All of them! What a marvelous hope!

When God says something, it’s simply history that hasn’t been recorded yet because His word doesn’t return to Him unfulfilled.

God restated this promise of blessing to Isaac, Abraham’s son, and to Isaac’s son, Jacob, whose name was changed to Israel. When Jacob died, we see a marked change in how God’s plan would unfold.

Instead of blessing one faithful person at a time, God, through Jacob (Israel), blessed all 12 of his sons:

Genesis 49:1–2: 1 Then Jacob summoned his sons and said, Assemble yourselves that I may tell you what will befall you in the days to come. 2 Gather together and hear, O sons of Jacob; and listen to Israel your father.

This is significant! Jacob calls himself Israel. With his death, something bigger is established—the opportunity for renewal on a different level.

Israel (Jacob) then speaks prophetically to each of his sons. When he finishes, he prepares to die:

Genesis 49:28–29: 28 All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father said to them when he blessed them. He blessed them, every one with the blessing appropriate to him. 29 Then he charged them and said to them, I am about to be gathered to my people; bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite.

These were essentially Jacob’s last words.

Israel’s death signified the ending of the Patriarchal Age. God’s dealings with individuals would now be expanded to dealing with an entire nation. The death of Israel, the man, would now translate into God dealing with Israel, the nation.

Once again in God’s plan, a death marks a transition. The death of Jacob wasn’t dramatic like the Flood; it was subtle. But the change it brings is dramatic. God is altering the way He will deal with humanity. Instead of working primarily through individuals, He will now work through a large group of people who will become a nation. Renewal no longer rests with individuals.

The connections between death, renewal and hope must be observed and appreciated if we are to truly see God’s wisdom at work.

At the end of the first age, we saw Noah carry the torch of renewal to the next age.

Who would carry that torch to the following age?

The torch would be carried by Joseph. Remember, he was the son of Israel who was sold into slavery by his jealous older brothers before his father died. His life of faithfulness, despite all the challenges laid before him, put him in a position of influence and power in Egypt. He would go on to save the world, including his family, from seven years of famine.

Back to the death that ended the previous age.

Joseph had risen to power in Egypt and brought his family there to care for them during the drought. Soon afterward, his father, Israel, died:

Genesis 50:1–2: 1 Then Joseph fell on his father’s face, and wept over him and kissed him. 2 Joseph commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father. So the physicians embalmed Israel.

It is interesting how one of Jacob’s sons became the torchbearer of renewal. Joseph saved the world because God worked through him. It was remarkable what Joseph did with the opportunity he was given. So, the renewal for this next age began with Joseph, who had been spared by God and put in place as a savior of his family. (Who does that remind us of? Jesus!)

Joseph eventually died. At that time, the people of Israel were thriving in the land of Goshen in Egypt where Joseph had arranged for them to settle.

Before Joseph died, he renewed God’s promise to his brothers:

Genesis 50:24: Joseph said to his brothers, I am about to die, but God will surely take care of you and bring you up from this land to the land which He promised on oath to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob.

Hope is coming through his great-grandfather, his grandfather and his father. Now it belonged to those sons as the beginning of the nation, carrying the torch of renewal, carrying hope. Joseph’s death was obviously a very somber occasion, and it opened the door for some difficult things to happen.

After Joseph’s death, Israel would eventually become enslaved by the Egyptians. Just when they had hope—it seemed to be dashed! Many years later, Moses would deliver them. Joseph had carried the torch of renewal, providing Israel with a place where they could flourish. Later, Moses would carry that same torch of renewal, leading them out of slavery and firmly establishing them as a nation.

The transition from God dealing with individuals to dealing with millions of people is huge. Think about the hope Israel must have felt when God delivered them from more than a hundred years of slavery.

After leading them out of Egypt, Moses delivered God’s Law to the people of Israel, His chosen nation—they are now His people:

Exodus 19:3–6: 3 …Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob and tell the sons of Israel: 4 You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles’ wings, and brought you to Myself. 5 Now then, if you will indeed obey My voice and keep My covenant, then you shall be My own possession among all the peoples, for all the earth is Mine; 6 and you shall be to Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. These are the words that you shall speak to the sons of Israel.

Moses was the great torchbearer for Israel, carrying forward that renewal. He carried it in the form of God’s Law, elevating Israel above the other nations and giving them a civil consciousness of how to conduct themselves and handle life. The Ten Commandments were given, deliverance after deliverance came, and yet, all too often, the people responded with disobedience. That is human nature in a sinful state.

Sadly, even Moses was disobedient to God and was not allowed to enter the Promised Land. So God passed the torch of renewal to Joshua, who would lead the nation into the Promised Land and toward greater heights.

The renewal is never lost. Sometimes it has to be transitioned and passed on. Despite sin and difficulty, there is this torch of renewal that brings hope. God points us toward something beyond.

God led Israel as a nation, and we refer to this the “Jewish Age.”

The nation of Israel eventually demanded a king like the surrounding nations had, and this was followed by periods of faithfulness and unfaithfulness. God sent prophets to Israel; sometimes Israel listened to them and sometimes they didn’t.

The prophet Amos reminds us of God’s patience and faithfulness to the nation:

Amos 3:1–2: 1 Hear this word which the LORD has spoken against you, sons of Israel, against the entire family which He brought up from the land of Egypt: 2 You only have I chosen among all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.

Israel was given both opportunity and responsibility. That is the pattern we have seen throughout this unfolding of God’s plan.

- Adam—opportunity and responsibility.
- Noah—opportunity and responsibility.
- Abraham—opportunity and responsibility.
- Joseph—opportunity and responsibility.
- Israel, as a nation—opportunity and responsibility.

There is an opportunity for renewal that brings hope, but that opportunity also carries a responsibility to respond—to move forward in harmony with God’s purpose.

We’re rapidly covering Israel’s long history of obedience and disobedience in the Old Testament.

Fast forward to the beginning of the New Testament. John the Baptist would carry the torch of renewal even further, as Israel’s greatest opportunity yet was about to appear on the scene—Jesus, their Messiah.

The Gospel Age begins!

Jesus IS the torch of renewal:

Mark 1:1–3: 1 The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the son of God. 2 As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: BEHOLD, I SEND MY MESSENGER (John the Baptist) AHEAD OF YOU, WHO WILL PREPARE YOUR WAY; 3 THE VOICE OF ONE CRYING IN THE WILDERNESS, MAKE READY THE WAY OF THE LORD, MAKE HIS PATHS STRAIGHT.

This is quoted from the book of Malachi, the last book in the Old Testament, written 400 years before. This last Old Testament prophecy is about John the Baptist coming to introduce the Messiah. The first public event in the New Testament is the exact same thing the Old Testament ended on!

The Old Testament speaks and says, Watch out, Behold, I send my messenger—then there is silence for 400 years. The next public event is John the Baptist fulfilling that prophecy. Talk about a torch of renewal and hope!

God brings the hope of renewal again at the appropriate time. BUT, Israel rejected their Messiah. Really!? This is how it works in a world of sin. God knows this, and His foresight is so magnificent that He will continue to build hope despite people’s difficulties!

Jesus knew this rejection was coming, and he willingly gave his life as a ransom for them as well as for every other human being ever born in Adam.

Remember, back at the beginning, we talked about how God sacrificed an animal to provide a covering for Adam and Eve’s sin. This reminds us of the death of the Passover lamb, which was sacrificed before Israel could be delivered from slavery in Egypt. And now we have come to the time when the Lamb of God, Jesus, offered himself as the great ransom sacrifice before the next renewal could begin.

Jesus comes to earth—and then He dies. That is a hint. Here is the torchbearer who is going to die—and He IS the torch! His death tells us that we are coming to the end of

another age and the beginning of a new period of time.

Here is the death that would bring renewal and hope. Jesus describes his own death in a very significant way:

John 12:23–25: 23 And Jesus answered them, saying, The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. 24 Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. 25 He who loves his life loses it, and he who hates his life in this world will keep it to life eternal.

Jesus had to die before life could flourish. He is telling them exactly that. He is talking about the pattern God has laid out: Noah picked up that little thread of hope. Just a tiny thread of hope. Then, when Jacob dies, the favor is passed to his sons, who become the nation of Israel. Now the nation has come to the point where they have rejected their great hope—their Messiah. When we look at that rejection, we must think everything is dashed.

Yet this thread of hope is even stronger because Jesus presents a humble, willing and complete laying down of his perfect life.

And it was the life of the ONLY man who had ever fully kept the Law of Moses:

John 12:27–28: 27 Now my soul has become troubled; and what shall I say, Father, save me from this hour? But for this purpose I came to this hour. 28 Father, glorify Your name…

We read here of a beautiful acquiescence to the will of God. This torch of hope and renewal is essentially saying, “I can be put out.” Apparently, this was true for a time, because that was the necessary price that needed to be paid.

Why? To glorify God’s name.

Why? Because what if, from the very beginning, God had this all planned and had put the pieces in place? And now the Savior of Israel, the One who was rejected, dies—and it looks hopeless.

But “what if” it’s not only NOT hopeless, but also a magnificent NEW BEGINNING?

The drama of Israel’s deliverance from slavery compared to their rejection of their Messiah is dramatic. And, no, God is not finished blessing them yet!

How is this all working? It sure seems like every time there is death and renewal,

there is also a turning away from that renewal! Where’s the hope?

Every time God puts renewal and hope in place, man seems to find a way to disrupt them! Yes, that’s true. But that, too, is part of the scope of God’s plan.

The key point here is that God’s plan has been unfolding in stages. Adam sinned,

and that sin led to a degraded world, with spirit beings later interfering with the evil that already existed. God stopped that and proceeded to deal with individuals according to His promises to them. When Jacob (later named Israel) died, God now had a family that would become a nation. From that nation, despite their stubbornness, God would bring forth the Messiah. Jesus came, remained faithful, and died as the necessary price for Adam’s sin.

God’s plan continues to progress through each transition. Death, depression and sadness accompany those endings, but with those comes something else: renewal. And with renewal comes hope.

God's plan is becoming bigger and clearer as we go. Back to the death that ended the previous age:

1 Timothy 2:3–6: (KJV) 3 For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour; 4 who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth. 5 For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; 6 who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time.

We can see the harmony between the promise made to Abraham and Paul’s writings: In thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed. That seed—that grain of wheat— bears much fruit.

As we go through this, we know what is going to happen because we have the notes! So, when we come to the sadness surrounding the death of Jesus—the depression and anxiety that would follow—we can say, “Just wait! The next chapter is going to build to something that has never been seen before!” And then that, in turn, is going to build to something else that has never been seen before. That is the way all of this is working.

This is the message of renewal: ALL are redeemed from death through Jesus. Now God’s step-by-step plan can begin to be seen more clearly, more understandably, and more fully. It can begin to make sense when we follow the pieces of Scripture—not tradition, but the scriptural pieces.

The renewal of the next age, following the age of Jewish favor, began with the results of Jesus’ sacrifice. Who would carry the torch?

The torch of renewal would now be carried by those who were called to walk in the sacrificial footsteps of Jesus, beginning with his apostles. This all began at Pentecost, when God’s spirit was given to the apostles.

This is where Christianity was born, and torchbearers were called into service:

Ephesians 1:18: I pray that the eyes of your heart may be enlightened, so that you will know what is the hope of His calling, what are the riches of the glory of His inheritance in the saints,

Paul is writing, I pray you can see what this incredible opportunity is, not only for you, but for all. You can see what you are a part of, what this torch of renewal actually looks like, what it brings.

This calling must be understood as a calling to the sacrifice of earthly lives and ambitions in exchange for doing God’s will, no matter what the cost:

Romans 12:1–2: 1 Therefore I urge you, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living and holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service of worship. 2 And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect.

This beauty, this renewal, this hope comes through following in the footsteps of Jesus, whose path led to a difficult end and to complete self-sacrifice.

To what end do these torchbearers carry this torch of renewal? To the end of establishing hope. But there is a pattern here: hope would always require death first. Death had to come before renewal could have free rein.

There are two kinds of death here that are important:

First, the death of those who follow Jesus, so they can be raised to their

heavenly reward. They have to cease to exist as humans and be raised by the

heavenly Father through Christ.

Romans 8:35–36: 35 Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? 36 Just as it is written, FOR YOUR SAKE WE ARE BEING PUT TO DEATH ALL DAY LONG; WE WERE CONSIDERED AS SHEEP TO BE SLAUGHTERED.

Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world—John 1:29. Jesus was that sacrifice as the Lamb of God. We also are as sheep. We have to be willing to follow in his sacrifice. This is part of the death, the cost of getting to the next level of renewal.

But we know Jesus promised, If I go, I go to prepare a place for you in heaven—John 14:3. So, this difficulty brings something much more glorious!

Second, the death and destruction of the spiritual and earthly kingdoms

of this earth. They are not able to develop the kingdom of God that Jesus told

us to pray for.

Daniel 2:44: In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which will never be destroyed, and that kingdom will not be left for another people; it will crush and put an end to all these kingdoms, but it will itself endure forever.

This is similar to the death at that first age, the “world that was,” where all those kingdoms in existence before the Flood were destroyed. But then God’s kingdom will take their place and endure forever! What a powerful promise. It sounds scary to think of all the social structures being destroyed, but what follows it is not scary.

What follows this death? Renewal and great hope. It cannot even begin to be described, but we’re going to try!

The following scripture is a Messianic prophecy of the next age.

This describes the transition from the collapse of Satan’s present evil world to the establishment of God’s kingdom on earth.

Isaiah 35:8–10: 8 A highway will be there, a roadway, and it will be called the Highway of Holiness. The unclean will not travel on it, but it will be for him who walks that way, and fools will not wander on it. 9 No lion will be there, nor will any vicious beast go up on it; these will not be found there. But the redeemed will walk there, 10 and the ransomed of the LORD will return and

come with joyful shouting to Zion, with everlasting joy upon their heads. They will find gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing will flee away.

This is an overwhelming renewal for humanity. No lion means no Satan to interfere. No vicious beast means no false religions to confuse the people. No fear; just joy and gladness with eternity before them.

Because Jesus paid the price, he brought mankind to that opportunity. That is really what the Day of Judgment is about—it will be a time of reconciliation and renewal. It is not judgment in the sense of, You’re bad; you’re going to die! Rather, it is an assessment and judgment of what each person has done and an opportunity to work through the problems that have resulted from sin, ultimately reaching a beautiful renewal and hope.

This final scripture gives us a very different symbolic perspective of this:

Revelation 21:1–4: 1 Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth (“new” means made fresh, renewed; not brand new); for the first heaven and the first earth passed away, and there is no longer any sea (symbolic of restless humanity).

Simply stated, Satan's evil world died, came to an end and God's kingdom on earth replaced it. All freshened up.

2 And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, made ready as a bride adorned for her husband. 3 And I heard a loud voice from the throne, saying, Behold, the tabernacle of God is among men, and He will dwell among them, and they shall be His people, and God Himself will be among them,

Remember, God was walking in the garden with Adam. Talk about renewed hope!

4 and He will wipe away every tear from their eyes; and there will no longer be any death; there will no longer be any mourning, or crying, or pain; the first things have passed away.

An important thing to remember is that mankind will have to learn to be reconciled to God. They will have to become responsible for their past baggage and learn to live according to God’s will. Just as Israel had the opportunity to follow God’s Law after He redeemed them from slavery, the world of mankind, God’s people, will need to conform to the New Law Covenant from their hearts.

They will have the opportunity for life and the responsibility to learn godliness. God is among men, and He will dwell with them, and they shall be His people. This renewal reaches its grand completion in restoring what God began with Adam in the Garden of Eden.

So, we see the pathway of sin and death was not the end! It was the pathway through which mankind would learn lessons that would last for eternity.

We can play a part in this. Adam had opportunity and responsibility, and he sinned.

The “world that was” ended with massive death and destruction, but there was still a thread of hope, with Noah carrying forward that righteousness.

Then came the Patriarchal Age, with the fathers of faith—Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and others. They carried the promise forward. Jacob’s death began the transition into the Jewish Age, a time of God’s favor toward the nation of Israel.

That age came to an end with the rejection of Jesus. He willingly gave himself as the ransom in the Gospel Age. Then this torch of renewal burst into a massive flame of hope! Now those who are begotten by God’s spirit carry the message of God’s kingdom, pointing forward to that next Messianic Age.

It is a dramatic story of how God takes something small, something sad and depressing— and says, “Let me work with it. Let me show you how I can take this hardship and turn it into something positive, something hopeful.”

The resurrection is for all mankind because Jesus died for every human being who ever lived. All those who have sinned and made mistakes have that opportunity.

That’s renewal. That’s hope. That’s what God intended all along. Just read it in His Word, because the story is already written—it is history that has not yet been fulfilled!

So, can death and hope actually work together?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.
