## Episode 1455 — What Big Lessons Can We Learn from the Little Book of 3 John?
Published: 2026-09-21
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1455-book-of-3-john/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/11112701/CQ_Rewind_09-21-2026_What_Big_Lesons_Can_We_Learn_From_the_Little_Book_of_3-John.pdf

What Big Lessons Can We Learn From

the Little Book of 3 John?

3 John 1:4: I have no greater joy than this, to hear of my children walking in the truth.

Some of the most significant lessons can come from the smallest things. The Bible is a big book made up of 66 books. The shortest of these is the book of 3 John. This letter, consisting of less than 300 words, was written to a Christian named Gaius. John describes him as a disciple whose life and example are truly Christlike. John then sharply contrasts him with another Christian leader whose example is exactly the opposite, as he seemingly dominated those around him. As John concludes this letter, he introduces the example of a third Christian as a contrast for Gaius to observe. These three examples show us the depths of Christian character, the power of biblical truth, the danger of mixing pride and power with discipleship and the impact of leading by example.

The Apostle John wrote the Gospel of John, 1 John, 2 John, 3 John and Revelation. He was older when he wrote 3 John and was thought to be the last surviving apostle at that time. He had watched generations of Christians grow up in the faith. We can think of him at this point like a father or even a grandfather, nurturing and guiding the followers of Christ.

This short letter of John is divided into three parts:

1. John’s wonderful description of Gaius.

2. John warns about a brother named Diotrephes who is NOT standing for the truth

of the Gospel and who is damaging the church in the process.

3. John speaks of Demetrius, another example of true Christianity in action.

3 John 1:1-4: 1 The elder to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth. 2 Beloved I pray that in all respects you may prosper and be in good health, just as your soul prospers. 3 For I was very glad when brethren came and testified to your truth, that is, how you are walking in truth. 4 I have no greater joy than this, to hear of my children walking in the truth.

The first verse of this little book speaks volumes:

3 John 1:1: The elder <4245> to the beloved <27> Gaius...

Elder: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4245: presbuteros comparative of présbys (elderly); older;

as noun, a senior; specially, an Israelite Sanhedrist (also figuratively, member of the celestial

council) or Christian “presbyter”:—elder(-est), old

Beloved: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #27: agapetos; from #25; beloved: the adjective of agape

Agape is the root word. Agapētos is the person who receives that love—the one who is loved with agape. (Same root; different parts of speech.)

John refers to himself as the elder. He could have used “John the Apostle” or “John the last surviving eyewitness of Christ,” but he never used titles to elevate himself. The elder is a title of relationship: I am the elder brother among you, someone who cares for you, someone who loves you, not someone above you.

Another observation is that when he wrote 1, 2 and 3 John, he never used his name. Even in his Gospel, he never identifies himself by name; instead, he describes himself as the disciple whom Jesus loved. What humility there was in his character.

Beloved in Greek is the adjective of the root word agape, the highest form of benevolent love. We talk about agape a lot. John calls Gaius beloved four times! In other words, You are the one who is deeply loved with the love of God.

John the Apostle is probably in his 80s at this point. He has been a Christian for 55 to 60 years. He has all this experience, and he personally walked with Jesus.

In the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, this word for beloved explicitly or implicitly is used only to describe Jesus as God’s beloved son. We'll see Jesus' teachings reflected through John as he writes this incredible letter to Gaius.

3 John 1:1: The elder to the beloved Gaius, whom I love <25> in truth <225>.

Truth: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #225 aletheia; from #227; truth

In other words, love is based not on emotion, but on the common bond of God’s truth. This word for truth appears in the New Testament a little over 100 times. In this tiny, 300- word letter of 3 John, it appears six times. In 1 and 2 John, it appears 14 more times. That means 20 of the 100 or so instances where the word truth appears are found in John’s three letters.

Let’s look at why John was fixated on passing on godly truth:

John 8:32: and you will know the truth <225>, and the truth <225> will make you free.

John 14:6: Jesus said to him, I am the way, and the truth <225>, and the life; no one comes to the Father but through me.

John’s opening theme in his letter is to show Gaius that John loves him with the fatherly love God has for Jesus, and that this love is based on the unequivocal truth of God as shown to us through Jesus.

3 John 1:2: Beloved <27>, I pray that in all respects you may prosper and be in good health, just as your soul prospers.

John calls Gaius beloved a second time. John’s profound love for Gaius is multifaceted.

→ First, he desires that Gaius be supplied in ways that would help him

continue to be an example. Let’s go back to the words of his mentor, Jesus:

Matthew 6:31–32: 31 Do not worry then, saying, What will we eat? or What will we drink? or What will we wear for clothing? 32 For the Gentiles eagerly seek all these things; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things.

John prays, knowing God will supply all that Gaius needs and that Gaius will be able to receive and accept whatever the Father’s will supplies for him.

→ Second, John observes that Gaius’ life is modeled appropriately, and that

model is noticeable:

3 John 1:3: For I was very glad when brethren came and testified to your truth <225>, that is, how you are walking in truth <225>.

So, this was obvious to the brotherhood. He upheld a high standard in Christ and had leadership qualities.

Walking in truth is a conviction that guides every decision of life.

John is fixated on truth. He is fixated on God's love for Jesus and how Jesus lived that love and passed it on to John himself.

When we have that truth, nothing else really matters:

Matthew 6:33: But seek first His kingdom and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.

Perhaps John is thinking about this concluding thought from Jesus as he writes to Gaius. Seek first His kingdom and His righteousness. Don’t worry about anything else.

This scripture has played an enormous role in my daily life, especially through the Christian Questions endeavor over the last 28 years. It has always been in the back of my mind. I have it on a plaque right behind me.

Throughout this episode, we're going to ask ourselves some self-examination questions to help us stay focused on John’s message in 3 John.

How aware am I of the lives and examples of my family in Christ? How often do I encourage them?

I was thinking about this question this week and wondered: when was the last time I thanked the person who comes in early to church on Sunday to set up what we need? Or the one sister who quietly stays late to clean up after everyone has left?

We want to look for Christ in others. Notice the good in others. Affirm their faithfulness. Speak well of their character and service. Encourage them by acknowledging how God is visibly working in and through them.

The Apostle John observed how Gaius was walking in the truth.

Our theme text:

3 John 1:4: I have no greater joy than this, to hear of my children walking in the truth <225>.

Did you catch all of this?

Verse 1: … whom I love in truth Verse 3: … brethren… testified to your truth, that is, how you are walking in truth Verse 4: … no greater joy… to hear of my children walking in the truth

Truth, truth, truth—this is John’s heartbeat. For the beloved Gaius, the truth was intertwined in his life in such a way that it couldn’t be separated.

When we look at what John wrote and how he wrote it, we see patterns of deep concern for the highest levels of fidelity to the cause of Christ. His constant example and writings provided continuous reminders. Walking in truth is EVERYTHING! This is what was important to the Apostle John in the later years of his life as he saw Christianity develop and face challenges.

Let’s go to an example of this great joy when walking in truth:

1 John 2:15–17: 15 Do not love the world nor the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. 16 For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes and the boastful pride of life, is not from the Father, but is from the world. 17 The world is passing away, and also its lusts; but the one who does the will of God lives forever.

There is a dramatic contrast in John’s first epistle between what has been—where they have all come from—and where they are now. Stay away from worldly thoughts, worldly desires and worldly pulls; stay focused on the truth from above. Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world.

Does my daily walk through life clearly define the truth that I profess to stand for? Can others see it? Is my light shining?

Think about the everyday moments that test us:

Driving in bad traffic.

Being on hold with the phone company.

Having to stand in a long line.

How we react when our printer keeps jamming or wi-fi keeps dropping. Lashing out when we’re tired or hungry.

Do we reflect Christ, or do we reflect our own impatience?

Let’s read the next four verses and then look more closely at each:

3 John 1:5-8: 5 Beloved, you are acting faithfully in whatever you accomplish for the brethren, and especially when they are strangers; 6 and they have testified to your love before the church. You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God. 7 For they went

out for the sake of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. 8 Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers with the truth.

3 John 1:5: Beloved <27>, you are acting faithfully in whatever you accomplish for the brethren, and especially when they are strangers.

During John’s time, traveling brethren depended entirely on the kindness of fellow Christians for lodging, meals, safety and support.

When they are strangers—the brotherhood is the brotherhood, whether we personally know someone or not.

John’s focus on how Gaius served those in need shows us how important it is to LIVE the gospel. He lived the gospel in all aspects of his life, and this letter of 3 John focuses specifically on the hospitality he gave others.

This is part of a bigger picture:

Ephesians 2:12: remember that you were at that time separate from Christ, excluded from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world.

The Apostle Paul is talking to those Christians who came from other countries and out of paganism. He tells them that they were strangers who were without God in the world.

Paul then describes how the blood of Christ brought strangers into unity with one another:

Ephesians 2:18–20: 18 for through him we both have our access in one spirit to the Father. 19 So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints, and are of God’s household, 20 having been built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the corner stone.

The Apostle Paul states that we both (you Gentiles who were strangers and those of us who were Jews) have access in one spirit to the Father. We ALL are of God’s household having been built on the same foundation. An incredible unity and coexistence is unmistakable. This is an important principle to note as John develops his discussion with Gaius.

Am I an outward example of welcoming all who truly profess Christ regardless of their background?

Rick, your parents were a personal example of this to me. They invited me to live with them when I was a young man who had just come from a sordid past. They were willing to look beyond my past and see me for who I could become. I am forever grateful!

It was no surprise to me. You were a good friend of mine. When we talked to them about your past and our friendship, they were, of course, welcoming because that was the driving force in their lives.

We have someone in my congregation who is in a wheelchair, so many physical forms of service aren’t available to him. But every Sunday, he arrives early and positions himself at the front door so he can personally greet everyone who walks in with an encouraging, comforting word. It is a beautiful way to start my Sunday worship! Hospitality is about how we choose to bless others.

3 John 1:6: and they have testified <3140> to your love <26> before the church (meaning, those in the church have witnessed to Gaius’ agape love for them). You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God.

Testify: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3140 martureō; to be a witness, i.e. testify (literally or figuratively):—charge, give (evidence), bear record, have (obtain, of) good (honest) report, be well

reported of, testify, give (have) testimony, (be, bear, give, obtain) witness

Martyria: the root idea is someone who gives a witness. Early Christians who bore witness to Christ under persecution were called martys. Over time, because so many early Christians gave their testimony even to the point of death, the word martys (witness) came to mean someone who dies for their testimony. That’s how the English word “martyr” developed.

Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3140 martureō (verb) — to testify (the act of testifying) Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3141 martyria (noun) — a testimony (the testimony itself) Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3144 martys (noun) — a witness (the person who testifies) (English) martyr— one who dies for their witness

Gaius’ hospitality made such an impact that people talked about it when they got home. They were credible witnesses to the love they experienced from his care. His love was so tangible it could be seen, confirmed and witnessed by others. Gaius made that kind of lasting impression on those he served.

Paul also encouraged such an example:

Galatians 6:8–10: 8 For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the spirit will from the spirit reap eternal life. 9 Let us not lose heart in doing good, for in due time we will reap if we do not grow weary. 10 So then, while we have opportunity, let us do good to all people, and especially to those who are of the household of the faith.

Do good to all, and especially to those who are of the household of faith—whatever the need, whatever the case, whatever the circumstance—Paul is calling us to stand up and be counted, caring for those around us.

Do my actions of support and care for the brotherhood stimulate a memorable and lasting impression?

I can answer this for both of you. I would say, absolutely yes! I know that both of you open your homes for meals or overnight stays whenever someone needs it. I’ve been in both of your homes when, literally, there were no more chairs that could fit into the room because you had everyone over for Bible study or fellowship. It takes a lot of effort to make things appear effortless, and I know how much work it is for both of you and your wives!

John helps us see that Gaius reflects all these things we are talking about. This is why he is beloved of John like Jesus was beloved to God. It is the same kind of connection.

3 John 1:7–8: 7 For they went out for the sake of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. 8 Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers <4904> with the truth <225>.

The Greek word for fellow workers is sunergos, a co-laborer—one who works alongside another. Our English word “synergy” comes from this same root idea: people working together in such a way that their combined effort produces more than any of them could accomplish alone.

Fellow Workers: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4904 sunergos; a co-laborer, i.e. coadjutor

John speaks of Jesus as the Name. This only appears once in Scripture. Why? Perhaps John was drawing on his own experiences WITH Jesus and then his experiences FOR Jesus.

First, before the crucifixion—an experience WITH Jesus:

John 15:21: (This is Jesus speaking.) But all these things they will do to you for my name's sake, because they do not know the One who sent me.

For my name’s sake—we wonder if John remembered these words and thought about working for Jesus’ name. Jesus was crucified the next day.

The next experience—after Pentecost, FOR Jesus:

The apostles, including John, had been imprisoned for preaching, but an angel set them free and they went right back to preaching the next day. When they were brought before the Sanhedrin and threatened with further punishment, the council listened to the counsel of Gamaliel, a respected Pharisee and teacher of the Law. He warned them not to overreact—if this new Christian movement was merely human, it would fade away; but if it was from God, they would be fighting against God Himself. The council accepted his advice, so the apostles were flogged and then released rather than executed.

We pick up with that experience:

Acts 5:40–41: 40 They took his advice; and after calling the apostles in, they flogged them and ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and then released them. 41 So they went on their way from the presence of the Council, rejoicing that they had been considered worthy to suffer shame for his name.

Perhaps John is drawing on this experience as well, when they were told not to speak in the name of Jesus, but they walked away rejoicing that they had been considered worthy to suffer shame for his name.

It might be that John’s letter to Gaius was a personal testimony, that Gaius is living in the same way as John and the other apostles.

John’s encouragement to Gaius was to support those who were engaged in parts of the work that others may not have the privilege of sharing in. This is the power of true brotherhood—and this is what John saw in Gaius.

How clearly am I focused on truly contributing what I can, where I can and when I can for the sake of the Gospel, for the name of Jesus? Am I contributing to the synergy of the brotherhood?

Two of our CQ volunteers are busy ministers in our congregation. Most people have no idea how many late-night hours they spend working on our various websites and apps for public witness work. It’s tedious and often thankless, but it’s a behind the scenes service that is essential. This is synergy! This is contributing where you can, when you can, for the sake of the Gospel.

These pilgrims in Gaius’ time weren’t traveling for money or to build a personal following. This is why Gaius’ work was so important: he was supporting men who carried the authority, name and message of Christ.

Not everyone preaches, but everyone can support the work. Supporting the work makes you PART of the work. Let the brotherhood know that their contributions matter.

John’s example of showing Gaius his value is striking and inspiring. He is really showing us how to help others strive more strongly toward faithfulness.

So far, all that we have read from 3 John is not only positive, but very encouraging!

How will John follow that theme?

John, as the wise elder, has laid the groundwork for Gaius to see and understand a very difficult challenge. This wisdom needs to be observed and copied, for John has effectively told Gaius that he is capable and strong in Christ and can therefore be equipped to understand and prepare for problems. This specific problem was named Diotrephes.

John will now unveil the challenge true Christians face when confronted with prideful, controlling leadership:

3 John 1:9-11: 9 I wrote something to the church; but Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, does not accept what we say. 10 For this reason, if I come, I will call attention to his deeds which he does, unjustly accusing us with wicked words; and not satisfied with this, he himself does not receive the brethren, either, and he forbids those who desire to do so and puts them out of the church. 11 Beloved, do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. The one who does good is of God; the one who does evil has not seen God.

3 John 1:9: I wrote something to the church; but Diotrephes, who loves to be first <5383> among them, does not accept what we say.

Who loves to be first: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5383 philoproteuo; from a compound of

#5384 and #4413; to be fond of being first, i.e. ambitious of distinction

This is the only place in the Bible this word is used. Greek readers would have understood it instantly; he fused two root words together: (It’s as if you hadn’t heard the word “self-promoter” or “first-place-lover,” in English, you would still know what was meant.)

philos — “loving, fond of” #5384 prōtos — “first, chief, preeminent” #4413

Put together, it describes someone who loves being first, someone who craves the top position, someone who pushes themselves into prominence.

Beyond pride, Diotrephes had ambition that pushed others down. This is the opposite of the humility shown by Gaius and even John himself, who simply refers to himself as the elder. It is a stark contrast. John wastes no time in saying here is the problem: Diotrephes loves to be first and does not accept what we say.

John begins his description of Diotrephes with a pointed warning that references both Jesus’ own words (which John personally heard) and the downfall of Satan:

Matthew 23:10–12: 10 Do not be called leaders; for one is your leader, that is, Christ. 11 But the greatest among you shall be your servant. 12 Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled; and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted.

John’s example shows how he took what he learned from Jesus and carried that standard forward. This was a crucial responsibility.

The warning is clear: Be aware of anyone who craves position, power and prominence! How contrary this is to the way the apostles themselves worked.

The Apostle Paul:

1 Corinthians 15:9: For I am the least of the apostles, and not fit to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.

Yet he went from country to country, demonstrating and preaching the gospel. It wasn’t about him—it was about the gospel.

The Apostle Peter:

1 Peter 5:1: Therefore, I exhort the elders among you, as your fellow elder and witness of the sufferings of Christ, and a partaker also of the glory that is to be revealed.

Did Peter say, “I exhort you because I am the Apostle Peter, the rock...?” No! He says, as your fellow elder.

We have letters from three apostles in the New Testament—Paul, Peter and John. All three present themselves with humility and with the thought of serving the body. Three apostles; one consistent message.

Considering John was most likely the last surviving apostle to have literally walked in Jesus’ footsteps, for Diotrephes to refuse to accept John’s instruction is shocking and a clear sign of deep discord developing in the early church.

Yet this gives us an important insight into how the early church was to function. The apostles did not rule by force. There was no hierarchy in which one man was elevated above the others. They understood themselves as servants of the body—not rulers over it.

Do I ever entertain thoughts or desires for position, power or prominence within the brotherhood? Am I truly aware of how contrary this is to the template for the church that the apostles set up?

Maybe we are disappointed when our ideas aren’t chosen or when our efforts go unnoticed. We all need encouragement to feel valued and to have self-worth, but when does it cross the line into resentment or pride? Perhaps the question to ask is, “Would I still do this joyfully if no one but the Lord noticed?” Greatness in Christ is about being faithful, not about recognition.

It is important to understand what should drive our faithfulness. We already see, in this first description of Diotrephes, the dramatic contrast between him and Gaius.

Now the Apostle John goes further in his description of Diotrephes:

3 John 1:10: For this reason, if I come, I will call attention to his deeds which he does, unjustly accusing us with wicked words; and not satisfied with this, he himself does not receive the brethren, either, and he forbids those who desire to do so and puts them out of the church.

John lays out three treacherous results of Diotrephes’ desire for position, power and prominence:

First Treacherous Result: … unjustly accusing <5396> us with wicked words…

The New International Version translates this as spreading malicious nonsense.

Unjustly Accusing: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5396 phluareo; to be a babbler or trifler,

i.e. (by implication) to berate idly or mischievously

(Source: Albert Barnes' Notes on the Whole Bible: Unjustly accusing) This occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, this means to "overflow with talk," to talk much without weight, or to little purpose; to be loquacious; to trifle; or, to use an expression common among us, and which accords well with the Greek, to run on in talk, without connection or sense. The word does not properly imply that there was malignity or ill-feeling in what was said, but that the talk was of an idle, foolish, and unprofitable character. As John here, however, specifies that there was a bad spirit in the manner in which Diotrephes expressed himself, the real thing which is implied in the use of the word here is, that there were much talk of that kind; that he was addicted to this habit of "running on" against the apostle; and that he was thus constantly undermining his influence, and injuring his character.

This nonsense wasn’t a one-time thing; this was his habit. Imagine if he had social media! He was an “influencer” in his time, and his influence wasn’t good! It wasn’t godly, and it wasn’t in line with what they were supposed to be doing according to the Scriptures they already had.

James 4:11–12: 11 Do not speak against one another, brethren. He who speaks against a brother or judges his brother, speaks against the law and judges the law… 12 There is only one Lawgiver and Judge, the One who is able to save and to destroy; but who are you who judge your neighbor?

We have to be respectful, even when criticism may be needed. Our mission is to build up, not to tear down. It is important to recognize the mission. Diotrephes showed us what the mission is NOT. Sometimes seeing the contrast between the two helps us focus more clearly.

Second Treacherous Result: Not satisfied with this, he himself does not receive the

brethren.

Diotrephes refused to show this expected hospitality to his fellow Christians. Perhaps he resented the travelers. Maybe he feared people might admire them more or that their influence could challenge his control. He didn’t even want an apostle to have authority over “his” church. Remember, this was someone who loved to be first!

This sounds like the Pharisees. They loved to be first and did not want anybody else to have the influence they had:

Matthew 23:13: But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut off the kingdom of heaven from people; for you do not enter in yourselves, nor do you allow those who are entering to go in.

Those who had the desire to go into the kingdom of heaven were shut off by the Pharisees. Diotrephes had the same attitude: “If you don’t do it my way, under my words, and my direction and guidance, you don’t do it at all!” This is as un-Christian as it gets!

Be receptive and welcoming, as we are all in Christ and therefore interactive parts of the body. Diotrephes decided to make up his own rules. This is unacceptable.

Third Treacherous Result: He forbids those who desire to do so and puts them

out of the church.

He is not only putting up a wall; he is saying, “You are out! You cannot even be here.”

Let’s go back to Jesus’ words in Matthew:

Matthew 7:15–18: 15 Beware of the false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves. 16 You will know them by their fruits. Grapes are not gathered from thorn bushes nor figs from thistles, are they? 17 So every good tree bears good fruit, but the bad tree bears bad fruit. 18 A good tree cannot produce bad fruit, nor can a bad tree produce good fruit.

John really brings out the comparison between Gaius and Diotrephes. It is a dramatic difference—not even close. It is not, there is some good here and a little good there. It is black and white—you do this and don’t do that.

John’s message is: Be rewarding, not rejecting, when we see others serving in ways we are not serving. Diotrephes was shutting down other servants of God in arrogance.

John finishes this portion of the letter with a strong admonition towards godly righteousness:

3 John 1:11: Beloved <27>, do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. The one who does good is of God; the one who does evil has not seen God.

These encouragements are so wonderful for Gaius.

John never makes things about John. It’s always about truth, the Name, and how to keep walking correctly.

Every time John starts a sentence with Beloved, we can now picture in our mind the love John had for Jesus. John was a walking epistle. He walked with our Lord and took all those experiences to heart. Now, all these years later, with maturity, he pours those experiences out to his beloved spiritual grandson, Gaius.

John is urging a complete shutting down of any and all destructive thoughts and behavior:

1 Peter 3:8–9: 8 To sum up, all of you be harmonious, sympathetic, brotherly, kindhearted, and humble in spirit; 9 not returning evil for evil or insult for insult, but giving a blessing instead; for you were called for the very purpose that you might inherit a blessing.

It sounds like Peter picks up exactly where John left off in his commentary, with his own experience with Jesus—not returning evil for evil or insult for insult, but giving a blessing instead.

John is sending us a message that there can be clear and present danger when we are involved with those whose lives do NOT reflect Christ. We need to pay attention!

The contrast between Gaius and Diotrephes is dramatic.

How will John conclude this lesson and draw positive conclusions?

There is no doubt that the church John was speaking about was facing very difficult challenges, with seemingly few options for repair. John will now bring up another brother in his letter. While we cannot be sure, it does seem like the apostle is suggesting that the church should rely on this individual as a way to face and overcome their problems.

3 John 1:12-14: 12 Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself; and we add our testimony, and you know that our testimony is true. 13 I had many things to write to you, but I am not willing to write them to you with pen and ink; 14 but I hope to see you shortly, and we will speak face to face.

Let’s look closer:

3 John 1:12: Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth <225> itself; and we add our testimony, and you know that our testimony is true.

John never says outright, “Replace Diotrephes with Demetrius,” but it is implied. After exposing Diotrephes’ harmful behavior, John immediately presents Demetrius as a man with a strong testimony from everyone, the kind of brother the church could trust.

Again, this gives us insight into how the early church operated—the apostles didn’t impose leadership by force. John suggests the brethren look at those whose character matches the truth, and then act accordingly when choosing their leaders. He is leaving it to them. There is liberty and wisdom in this arrangement.

Although we don’t know anything more about Demetrius, what we are told here is a powerful testimony to his character.

Just as John had mentioned three areas of challenge that Diotrephes had, he also mentions three clear commendations for the character of Demetrius:

First Commendation: Demetrius has received a good testimony <3140> from

everyone…

In other words, he had a godly reputation.

Just as Gaius received a positive witness from others in the brotherhood, Demetrius received the same. This good testimony from everyone is an expression from the heart of what is visible and a truth people are willing to stand for.

John is pointing to embracing and using the perspectives of those involved as a guide for finding solutions. Go to those who can be helpful.

This idea of having a “good report” is important. Remember when the apostles asked the congregation to select deacons to serve:

Acts 6:2–3: 2 So the twelve summoned the congregation of the disciples and said, It is not desirable for us to neglect the word of God in order to serve tables. 3 Therefore, brethren, select from among you seven men of good reputation <3140>, full of the spirit and of wisdom, whom we may put in charge of this task.

When choosing deacons, the congregation was to choose seven men of good reputation or good report; the same Greek word as the good testimony Demetrious received. This is a high-level recommendation.

John is encouraging the brethren to look around them and chose those who are godly.

How well does my character speak for my Christlikeness? Can others see Christ in me, and more importantly, can they rely on Christ in me? If someone trusts us with something confidential, do we keep it that way?

The relationship between John and Gaius reminds us of the trust Paul had in Timothy— like a fatherly love for a son.

When we promise to help but it’s inconvenient, do we follow through without secretly complaining?

Sometimes Christlikeness shows not only in how we help others, but in how we allow others to help us. When we’re struggling, do we reach out for prayer or support, or do we try to handle it alone? It takes humility to ask for help and great wisdom to keep things quiet when they need to be.

There is such a power in all of this. John, in his incredible wisdom, is pointing out those individuals who have these kinds of characteristics.

Second Commendation: … and from the truth <225> itself…

John adds the “testimony” is from the truth itself! How does “the truth” testify in someone?

John is saying that Demetrius’ character, conduct and teaching were so consistent with the truth of Christ that anyone who knew the truth could see it reflected in him. His character and actions matched the message.

We saw that in Jesus—his character and actions matched every word he said. These are examples of Christlikeness. Likewise, the truth testifies for us.

The truth “testifies” by our knowledge of it:

2 Timothy 2:15: Be diligent to present yourself approved to God as a workman who does not need to be ashamed, accurately handling the word of truth.

We are told to accurately handle the word of truth, not accurately handle traditions or opinions, or things we would like, but accurately handling the word of truth, the word of God. Jesus is the truth (John 14:6). This was shown in both Gaius and Demetrius.

Is my knowledge of the truth growing in such a way that I can see it clearly leading me? Or am I choosing pieces of the truth so I can make my choices?

John says Demetrius has a good testimony from the truth itself, it means he was daily living what the Scriptures taught him.

The truth “testifies” by our diligent application of it as we walk the path of discipleship:

2 Peter 1:5–8: 5 Now for this very reason also, applying all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence, and in your moral excellence, knowledge, 6 and in your knowledge, self-control, and in your self-control, perseverance, and in your perseverance, godliness, 7 and in your godliness, brotherly kindness, and in your brotherly kindness, love. 8 For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they render you neither useless nor unfruitful in the true knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.

We recently aired our Christian Character Series, starting with Episode #1419, breaking down all of these characteristics. What a great lesson that was! We saw that knowledge only becomes Christlike when it’s built on faith and moral excellence.

Truth is the template, and we need to be the exact copy of that template that came from Jesus. A template is the model of what the final project will be. We make that model come alive day by day, experience by experience. John is showing Gaius that Demetrius is just like him in these ways.

Does my life not only reflect the humility and sacrifice of Jesus, but also the depth of dedication that he had to doing only God’s will? His life was truth! How about mine?

When others look at my daily life, do they see something that reflects God’s truth in every aspect of my life, integrity in my dealings, in my language, actions, thoughts and direction? Or do they see me as someone who is conflicted?

Third Commendation: … and we add our testimony, and you know that our

testimony is true.

John himself testified to the spiritual maturity of Demetrius and therefore to his availability to help. His qualifications were impeccable. What better human testimony could there have been at that time than that of one of the Twelve Apostles!

This was an apostolic stamp of approval from one who had been an apostle for around 60 years and who had personally walked with Jesus. John is essentially saying that Gaius is beloved in the truth, and Demetrius is someone who is an accurate representation of that truth.

Can I be relied upon by those who stand for the highest spiritual standards? When faced with difficult situations, do my Christian brothers and sisters feel comfortable asking me for prayer or guidance? Do they feel confident that I won’t overreact, gossip or give unscriptural advice?

This is a big responsibility for Jonathan and me as ministers in our congregations. One of the things that has been helpful to me is assuring people that there’s no judgment here. When someone comes to me and I sense there is something very challenging in their situation, I assure them, “There’s no judgment here. Let’s just talk about what’s happening. Let me hear what is going on.” Then I listen. And by God’s grace, we are able to put guidance in place. It takes a lot to live up to this kind of standard.

Let’s finish up the letter of 3 John:

3 John 1:13–14: 13 I had many things to write to you, but I am not willing to write them to you with pen and ink; 14 but I hope to see you shortly, and we will speak face to face.

We don’t know if John ever did get to see Gaius face to face. And we could find no historical record of what happened to Diotrephes.

John gives us three examples in this little short letter that is almost a postcard:

Do we identify with one more than the other? John called on us to imitate what is good, reject what's evil and strengthen the body of Christ through truth, love and service. How are we doing? Do we have some of Diotrephes in us? What are we doing to put it aside?

Do I stand up and respond to the challenges that come to my brethren in the same way that John is instructing Gaius?

So, what big lessons can we learn from the little book of 3 John?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

## Episode 1456 — Can Christians Lose Their Salvation? (Part I)
Published: 2026-09-28
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1457-can-christians-lose-their-salvation-part-i/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/18143115/CQ_Rewind_09-28-2026_Can_Christians_Lose_Their_Salvation_Part_I.pdf

Hebrews 10:26: For if we go on sinning willfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth,

there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.

Every professed Christian acknowledges that they have been saved as a result of Jesus’ sacrifice. The big questions come after that acknowledgment. How is someone saved, is there a cost for this salvation, or is it a free gift? What are we saved from? Is there a way to lose this salvation or is it an unbreakable and permanent protection no matter what we do? If we go to various denominations with these questions, we will receive a wide variety of answers. The challenge is, all these answers do have some basis in scripture. What do we do now? We look at scripture as a whole and find the recurring themes that explain how all of these moving parts come together.

Salvation is one of the most important subjects in all of Christianity—and one of the most misunderstood. Scripture gives us strong assurances, strong warnings and sometimes seemingly contradictory statements. Here in Part I, we will establish the “what, how and who” of salvation: what salvation is, how it works and who benefits from it. This foundation will set up Part II’s “why” and “how” of maintaining or losing salvation.

We believe Christians can lose their salvation. We will establish the scriptural basis for this understanding over the next two episodes.

What is this salvation from? We need salvation from eternal death:

1 Corinthians 15:22: For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.

It’s important to recognize two points right away:

1. ALL is a huge word. ALL die in Adam and ALL are made alive in Christ—

every single human being.

2. This text contrasts death and life, not eternal hellfire with life.

Adam’s sin brought death to all, and Jesus’ sacrifice guarantees life to all. This is the foundation for understanding how salvation works in Scripture.

What are we ALL—both Christians and everybody else—saved from? Death. Salvation in Scripture always means deliverance—deliverance from sin, deliverance from Satan’s influence, and ultimately deliverance from death itself. The Greek words used for save and salvation literally mean “rescue” or “deliverance,” which fits perfectly with the idea of being rescued from the death we all inherited from Adam.

This message of salvation was made plain by an angel right at Jesus’ birth:

Luke 2:10-11: 10 But the angel said to them, Do not be afraid; for behold, I bring you good news of great joy which will be for all the people; 11 for today in the city of David there has been born for you a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.

Again, Jesus died for ALL the people, every single human being, not just Christians.

Is there a cost to being saved, or is it a free gift? Yes to both!

How is someone saved? Many people look at the following verses separately and assume each one fully explains salvation:

All we need to do is to accept salvation as a free gift of God:

Romans 6:23: For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

All we need is the redemption of Jesus’ blood:

Romans 3:23-24: 23 For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, 24 being justified as a gift by His grace through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus.

All we need do is call upon the name of Jesus:

Romans 10:12-13: 12 For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, abounding in riches for all who call on him; 13 for WHOEVER

WILL CALL ON THE NAME OF THE LORD WILL BE SAVED.

All we need to do is confess Jesus and believe in our hearts:

Romans 10:9: That if you confess with your mouth Jesus as Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.

And these are just the ones in Romans! The Bible gives many more statements that sound effortless, or effort-ful, conditional or universal.

When we attempt to over-simplify salvation, we can run into the challenge of conflicting messages like in the four verses above. To sell Christianity to the masses, it needs to be made easy to swallow. But Christianity was never meant to be sold to the masses!

How can all these various single-instruction statements be true and in the same letter Paul wrote to the Romans?

Throughout Romans, Paul restates to his readers the building blocks of what the gospel is and how it works.

After 11 chapters, he draws ALL of these statements together in chapter 12:

Romans 12:1: Therefore (whenever we see this word, we need to ask, “What is it there for?”) I urge you, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living and holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.

Paul’s therefore in this verse is the conclusion of what he had written in the previous eleven chapters.

Let’s sum up those eleven chapters briefly:

- Because the world is in the darkness of sin and Israel is under the shackles of the Law...
- Because God is merciful and impartial and true justification comes by faith...
- Because we are called to live in Christ and to be united with him…
- Because we must fight our old nature to seek for daily victory in Christ…
- Because, in spite of the tragedy of Israel’s rejection of Jesus, they are promised redemption…

Because of all these things… we come to Romans 12:1.

Romans 12:1: Therefore I urge you, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living and holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual <3050> service of worship <2999>.

Spiritual: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3050 logikos; rational ("logical")

The King James Version translates this as “reasonable” 1 time and “of the word” 1 time

Service of worship: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2999 latreia;

ministration of God, i.e. worship

The King James Version translates this as “service” 4 times and “divine service” 1 time

Thayer’s Greek English Lexicon: 1) service rendered for hire

1a) any service or ministration: the service of God

The King James Version calls this your reasonable service. Salvation is a gift, but based on what we’ve learned so far, we have responsibilities with this gift. No matter which translation we look at, there is a continuous theme of service. When we perform a service for someone, it is an obligation we fulfill. Present your bodies a living and holy sacrifice— this goes beyond just showing up for church or reading our Bibles.

Jesus tells us what this spiritual service of worship looks like:

Luke 9:23-24: 23 And he was saying to them all, If anyone wishes to come after me, he must deny himself, and take up his cross daily and follow me. 24 For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake, he is the one who will save it.

Paul: Be a living sacrifice.

Jesus: Deny yourself, take up your cross and follow me every day.

Jesus took up his cross and walked knowingly and willingly towards torture and death. Following him is not easy—it means the sacrificing of our lives to do the will of God.

Paul is basically repeating what Jesus said. There was no clearer picture of a living sacrifice in those days than someone carrying his cross toward his own crucifixion!

Salvation is more than just accepting a gift. It requires a lifetime of commitment and transformation.

Before we go any further, we need to define who we’re talking about when we ask, “Can a Christian lose their salvation?”

Who is a Christian? Is it everyone who goes to a church? Everyone who grew up with Christian parents?

A true Christian is someone who has been called by God, who has presented themselves as a living sacrifice to do God’s will, not their own. That is what the sacrifice is about. If God accepts them, He gives them His holy spirit. That’s when they become a new creature or new creation (depending on the translation) according to

2 Corinthians 5:17. They have new desires, new priorities and a new direction, trusting in Jesus as their Savior and walking in his footsteps.

THE NEW CREATION: Those who hold the “once saved, always saved” view take this a step further. They reason that if a Christian is a new creation, then losing salvation would require destroying that new creation. Is God going back on what He gave?

The words of both Jesus and Paul require us doing our part—to take up our cross daily and to present our bodies as a living (continual) sacrifice. This requires action. It is not that God takes something away; it would be us not doing our part.

Becoming a new creature is a beautiful transformation, but it doesn’t remove our free will. God doesn’t destroy the new creation, but He also doesn’t force us to keep it. The new life He begins in us can be abandoned if we choose to walk away from it.

REDEMPTION: Another point from the “once saved, always saved” viewpoint has to do with redemption. They reason that if Jesus purchased us with his own blood, how could God revoke that purchase? The blood has already been spilled.

That’s a great point: God won’t revoke that purchase. However, we have to understand that the ransom of Jesus is freely given and must be freely received. However, if we don’t follow through with the responsibilities that accompany that gift, God will not override our own free will and force us to accept it.

Jesus’ sacrifice purchased the entire human race. But this redemption is applied differently at different times. Those that choose to follow Christ at this time receive the benefits now, in this lifetime; while the rest of the world receives redemption after they have been resurrected in God’s future kingdom.

God never revokes the redemption. But God does not forcibly hold someone who chooses to walk away. He does not “take salvation back,” but an individual CAN reject the relationship that redemption opened, whether it be now for those following Christ, or in the future for the world of mankind in general.

Let’s return to what our spiritual service of worship looks like in daily life.

The Apostles Peter and Paul tell us what this looks like:

1 Peter 2:11-12: 11 Beloved, I urge you as aliens and strangers to abstain from fleshly lusts which wage war against the soul.

Peter urges his readers to stay away from those things that are at war with the Christians’ new way of life. In other words, do not be tempted. Do not put yourself in situations where you might be tempted to turn left when you should turn right. Personal responsibility is required.

Now from Paul:

Philippians 1:21: For to me, to live is Christ and to die is gain.

To live is Christ, and to die is gain—do we assume personal responsibility to follow Paul as he followed Christ? Whether living or dying, it doesn’t matter as long as we are following in the footsteps of Jesus.

Again, this is about personal responsibility—the daily discipline of Christlikeness. Are we being Christlike in everything we think, say and do?

Romans 8:35-36: 35 Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? 36 Just as it is written, FOR YOUR SAKE WE ARE BEING PUT TO DEATH ALL DAY LONG; WE WERE CONSIDERED AS SHEEP TO BE SLAUGHTERED.

SEPARATION: These texts are often cited by those who say Christians CAN’T lose their salvation. Obviously, the Apostle Paul here is asking rhetorical questions, saying that NOTHING can separate a true Christian from God; therefore, wouldn’t his or her salvation be secure?

Correct—nothing EXTERNAL can separate us. No enemy, no circumstance, no persecution. But notice what Paul is actually saying: nothing outside of us can tear us away from Christ. But remember, God does NOT override our free will. God will not permit others to separate us from His favor, but He does allow us to walk away if we choose. This distinction becomes essential as we move forward.

As an example, we see Lucifer, who had a glorious heavenly position as a morning star (Isaiah 14:12). Yet, he chose to follow his own will instead of God’s will, and as Satan, he will eventually be destroyed. God allowed him to make the choice to rebel. God allowed both the choice and its consequences.

As another example, God allowed Adam to make the wrong choice and to suffer the consequences.

So, yes, none of what is listed in Romans 8:35-36 can separate us from God, unless we make the choice to walk away.

JUSTIFICATION: Closely related to redemption is the question of justification. Justification simply means being declared righteous in God’s sight—having a clean standing before Him because of Christ. The “once saved, always saved” view reasons that if God has declared someone righteous, He would never reverse His own verdict.

And He won’t reverse His verdict! If we have been declared righteous, we are righteous. Justification is absolutely a gift of grace (the scriptures tell us this plainly in Romans 5), but it is only applied to those who have been called and have given their lives in sacrifice—take up your cross daily and follow me. Once that commitment has been accepted, we have to get to work.

Justification is not yet applied to the world. We are going to get into the scriptures that show that justification can be forfeited if someone knowingly abandons the righteousness they once embraced. God doesn’t arbitrarily “un-declare” righteousness, but He does accept the resignation of someone who chooses to reject the standing He graciously provided.

The message thus far is not about gain, but about receiving a gift that opens a door to eternity through self sacrifice.

If salvation costs so much for Christians now, what happens to everyone else?

Is humanity just doomed if they don’t answer this call?

One of the enormous advantages of studying the Bible as a whole, instead of just picking scriptures to read and follow, is that combining all of Scripture will give us whole answers. As we further develop the concept of salvation, we need to pay particular attention to the breadth and depth of God’s wisdom and love. He created humanity for a very good reason and His objective will come to fruition.

Let’s first ask, what does the call of those who are following in Jesus’ footsteps look like?

Our mission is to follow the path on which Scripture, not church traditions, leads us:

2 Timothy 2:15: Be diligent to present yourself approved to God as a workman who does not need to be ashamed, accurately handling the word of truth.

The King James Version expresses this as rightly dividing the word of truth. So, we need to divide the many salvation-related scriptures between the true followers of Christ and non- believers.

God’s proclamation to Satan after the original sin of Adam and Eve was the first spoken hint of how His plan would unfold:

Genesis 3:15: And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed; he shall bruise you on the head, and you shall bruise him on the heel.

This is a battle between the serpent (Satan) and the seed of the woman (through her lineage, Jesus). There is active hostility between the two (evil versus righteousness), and there is injury, too. Jesus, the seed of the woman, is bruised on his heel. It is a wound, but not a mortal one. The serpent’s head is bruised (crushed in several other translations), a death blow. This is a battle of light versus darkness. God has allowed this battle to be fought.

God allows even spirit beings to have free moral choice. Let’s walk through history and see how Scriptures verify this truth.

Generations after Adam and Eve, God clarified the Genesis 3:15 proclamation with His promise to Abraham. God is speaking to Abraham through an angel:

Genesis 22:17-18: 17 Indeed I will greatly bless you, and I will greatly multiply your seed as the stars of the heavens and as the sand which is on the seashore; and your seed shall possess the gate of their enemies. 18 In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you have obeyed My voice.

The Bible is written as a continuous message from beginning to end. To understand the full message of salvation, it is essential to go back to Genesis and creation, and to the promise God gives to Abraham about his son Isaac and succeeding generations. There is a theme from the beginning when God promised Eve her seed, Jesus, would eventually crush the serpent’s head. Abraham’s son Isaac carried the promise in his generation, representing Jesus.

Generations after Abraham and Isaac, the prophets wrote about this plan as well. Here is one example:

Isaiah 42:1,4: 1 Behold, My servant, whom I uphold; My chosen one in whom My soul delights. I have put My spirit upon him; He will bring forth justice to the nations. 4 He will not be disheartened or crushed until he has established justice in the earth; And the coastlands will wait expectantly for his law.

My servant, whom I uphold—Jesus will bring justice to the nations and establishes justice in the earth, revealing the future phase of God’s plan when all humanity receives the opportunity for life under Christ’s righteous rule. Salvation is not only personal; it will be global. It will be universal, already anticipated in the Old Testament.

Generations after the prophets, Jesus fulfilled this plan talked about in the Old Testament:

Romans 5:18-19: 18 So then as through one transgression there resulted condemnation to all men, even so through one act of righteousness there resulted justification of life to all men. 19 For as through the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one the many will be made righteous.

Adam’s free choice brought death to all humanity, and Jesus’ free choice brings life to all humanity. Salvation exists because of these two pivotal decisions.

We’ve traced this thread from Genesis through Abraham and into the prophets, all pointing to the same plan. Jesus sacrificed his life, and the Apostle Paul draws the conclusion: all die in Adam, and all are given life in Christ. This is the consistent, unfolding story of God’s salvation for the entire human family.

The many were made sinners—Paul uses the many as a way of saying “the whole group considered as a unit.” Through Adam, all became sinners—there’s no one outside that category. So when Paul says the many will be made righteous, he’s referring to the same group. Everyone who was condemned in Adam is included in the righteousness offered through Christ. It’s the same “many,” and it means everybody.

Paul is writing to the Roman Christians at that time. He did not say, the many are being made righteous. He said the many will be made righteous. The Greek makes this point unmistakable. When Paul says the many were made sinners, he uses a past tense—a completed fact for all humanity. But when he says the many will be made righteous, he switches to a future tense. He’s pointing to something still ahead: the full, universal application of Christ’s righteousness in God’s future kingdom.

1 Peter 3:18: For Christ also died for sins once for all, the just for the unjust, so that he might bring us to God, having been put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit.

The just for the unjust—this is a very sweeping statement. Who kept God’s Law in the history of humanity? Nobody except Jesus, the just. Who has fallen in sin and shapen in iniquity throughout all the generations (as the King James expresses it in Psalm 51:5)? Everybody.

How does this salvation work? In two stages:

1. Salvation by invitation—this kind of salvation applies now to only a few.

2. Salvation by just and merciful inclusion—this kind of salvation applies in the

future to the rest of mankind.

Salvation by invitation is only for a few:

John 6:44: No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him; and I will raise him up on the last day.

Does this mean not everyone is invited? Yes! No one comes to Jesus unless the Father… draws him. This is by invitation only.

Salvation by invitation shows us that most are NOT drawn—and that is the clear intention of God in His plan.

Scripture shows two distinct salvations—one for the church now, by invitation, and one for the world later, by inclusion. Mixing these two leads to confusion about who can—and cannot—lose salvation.

Can a non-Christian lose salvation in this life?

No, because they haven’t yet been given salvation. They’re not on trial for eternal life. They remain under the condemnation of Adam until their resurrection. You can’t lose what you’ve never received.

Present salvation is a privilege only for those whom God is calling now. Now is the time when God is calling out the true church—this is the church’s judgment day—not the world’s. Only spirit begotten Christians are on trial now.

We have made some strong statements about how the plan of God works.

Now let’s prove them with Scripture:

John 12:36-40: 36 While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may become sons of light. These things Jesus spoke, and he went away and hid himself from them. 37 But though he had performed so many signs before them, yet they were not believing in him. 38 This was to fulfill the word of Isaiah the prophet which he spoke: LORD, WHO HAS BELIEVED OUR REPORT? AND TO WHOM HAS THE ARM OF THE LORD BEEN REVEALED? (quoting from

Isaiah 53:1) 39 For this reason they could not believe, for Isaiah said again, 40 HE HAS BLINDED THEIR EYES AND HE HARDENED THEIR HEART, SO THAT THEY WOULD NOT SEE WITH THEIR EYES AND PERCEIVE WITH THEIR HEART, AND BE CONVERTED AND I HEAL THEM (quoting from Isaiah 6:9-10).

Jesus is talking to his disciples at the beginning of the quote when he refers to the sons of light. But then he talks about those who didn’t believe in him despite the miracles he performed for them. This is partially because God covered their eyes and didn’t allow them to see or understand. But is that fair?

Yes, as God’s plan always unfolds in stages. We are in the stage where He is choosing only a few by invitation.

Salvation by invitation shows us that the drawing is purposefully very selective:

Matthew 11:25-26: 25 At that time Jesus said, I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that You have hidden these things from the wise and intelligent and have revealed them to infants. 26 Yes, Father, for this way was well-pleasing in Your sight.

Why would God hide these things? Because His plan is bigger than we can imagine. We need to give it time to unfold and see the reasons why the call is happening now, and how that call will later affect those people ignorant of it now.

If non-Christians aren’t saved now, what happens to them?

Their salvation comes later, in God’s kingdom on earth. Jesus’ ransom guarantees that every human being will be awakened from the grave. But that awakening

doesn’t guarantee eternal life. It’s the beginning of their first real opportunity for salvation, when they receive accurate knowledge of the truth and are judged under the New Covenant. This new law will be written upon their hearts.

Let’s put scriptures to our statements about God’s plan for the rest of His human creation.

Salvation by just and merciful inclusion shows us the vast plan of God for all of His human creation:

1 Timothy 2:3-6: (KJV) 3 For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour; 4 Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge <1922> of the truth. 5 For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; 6 Who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time.

Knowledge: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1922 epignōsis; recognition, i.e. (by implication) full discernment, acknowledgement:—(ac-)knowledge(-ing, - ment)

We have seen scriptural evidence that God hides the call to be a follower of Jesus (Matthew 11:25-26), but we are promised He will have ALL men to be saved and come to a knowledge of the truth.

The Greek word for knowledge here means “full discernment,” which indicates a deep, accurate understanding and not merely awareness.

There is no special calling for this future salvation as there is for the followers of Jesus now. Notice the order: non-Christians are saved (redeemed) first, then taught later. For the Christian now, it is believe (knowledge) first and then be saved. The order is different for these two different phases of salvation.

The trial for eternal life for non-Christians happens in the future, after they are raised from the dead, not now. The world’s future judgment is fair because when they are raised, Satan will be bound (Revelation 20:1-3), and they will finally come to full, accurate knowledge of the truth. They are raised from the dead under uncontaminated conditions, then fully taught righteousness before they are judged worthy for eternal life. This is very different from the experience of those who follow Christ now in a sin-sick world.

Salvation by just and merciful inclusion shows us that those invited now are uniquely privileged:

1 Timothy 4:10: For it is for this we labor and strive, because we have fixed our hope on the living God, who is the Savior of all men, especially of believers.

This text is so clear—all men, especially of believers—two distinct groups. Believers receive salvation now, and the rest of humanity receives salvation later. Present salvation comes through God’s calling and the work He begins in a Christian’s life. Future salvation comes through resurrection and the restorative work of the future kingdom.

The awakening of the non-Christian world is salvation from the grave, but it is not the final salvation of eternal life. It begins their opportunity to walk the metaphorical Highway of Holiness (Isaiah 35:8) and choose life under Christ’s righteous rule.

The further we open the Scriptures, the more we see that being called to follow Christ is a massive opportunity that needs to be handled with focus and reverence!

What is this higher and privileged way? Are there dangers along this path that can

result in the loss of our capacity to stand before God through Jesus?

As we have thus far seen, the call to Christian discipleship is, in Jesus’ own words, a limited call to a comparatively small number of people throughout the entire world. As we shall now see, Jesus also clearly revealed both the rewards and the challenges to those who would follow this path.

Remember, during this Gospel Age, only the called-out, spirit-begotten Christians are being judged for eternal life. The rest of the world’s judgment comes later in the kingdom.

- Non-Christians cannot lose salvation now because they do not possess it. Their salvation is in the future kingdom, after they are resurrected.
- This may sound surprising, but only spirit-begotten Christians can lose salvation now, because only they are on trial for eternal life.

(Also see 1 Peter 4:17 that states judgment must begin at the house of God [the church, the true followers of Jesus], but it doesn’t end there, as the world’s judgment comes later.)

If salvation is such a profound privilege for the called-out ones, what dangers exist that could cause a true Christian to lose it?

First, a glimpse of the challenges:

Matthew 7:13-14: 13 Enter through the narrow gate; for the gate is wide and the way is broad that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter through it. 14 For the gate is small and the way is narrow that leads to life, and there are few who find it.

Many people read this verse and conclude that the broad way represents the masses who are headed for destruction, and in a general sense that’s true. But Jesus’ words here are not describing the final destiny of all humanity. Instead, he is talking about the experience of an individual who is called to follow him. The narrow gate represents the difficult, disciplined path of discipleship. It isn’t easy, and it isn’t meant to be. It is a challenging way of life that requires sacrifice and commitment—yet it is also deeply blessed for those who walk it.

Jesus explains:

Matthew 10:37-39: 37 He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and he who loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. 38 And he who does not take his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me. 39 He who has found his life will lose it, and he who has lost his life for my sake will find it.

This is a matter of our loyalty, our willingness, to put Christ above everything else. This is the kind of loyalty required. This is part of what it means to be a living sacrifice, taking up our cross daily.

A glimpse of the rewards:

John 15:7-9: 7 If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. 8 My Father is glorified by this, that you bear much fruit, and so prove to be my disciples. 9 Just as the Father has loved me, I have also loved you; abide in my love.

If we abide in Jesus and in his words, we will be blessed beyond our comprehension. But what did Jesus’ words bring him to? Sacrifice and death. While our path of sacrifice follows the same pattern, we will be incredibly blessed and have much help along the way if we abide in his love.

This fruitage comes from God’s spirit working in the called-out ones, whom God begets with His spirit:

2 Corinthians 5:17-19: 17 Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature; the old things passed away; behold, new things have come. 18 Now all these things are from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation, 19 namely,

that God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and He has committed to us the word of reconciliation.

These verses show what the new creature, or new creation, really is. When God gives us His spirit, He begins a new life within us. It’s a transformation that comes with responsibility. God reconciles us to Himself through Christ, and then He gives us the ministry of reconciliation—the work of helping the world of mankind find their way back to Him in the kingdom.

For now, we live out the character of Christ as a witness to that coming work. This is why the Christian walk is so serious. It’s a life that must be protected and lived with intention.

There are several scriptures that show us the work of today is for the purpose of the reconciliation of tomorrow. We need to understand how this fits together. That is why God’s spirit works within us and will guide us—as long as we allow it to. We can’t get in its way! That would be like having a GPS and then turning right when it tells us to go left. We have to follow what we are given.

These are the beautiful rewards. Having God’s spirit in our lives is completely life-altering because it raises us up and helps us see things from a different perspective.

Jesus showed us what the eternal future would hold for the faithful, which is a different reward from the rest of the world:

John 14:1-3: 1 Do not let your heart be troubled; believe in God, believe also in me. 2 In my Father's house are many dwelling places; if it were not so, I would have told you; for I go to prepare a place for you. 3 If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and receive you to myself, that where I am, there you may be also.

Heaven is hard to comprehend, but think about this part; I will come again and receive you to myself, that where I am, there you may be also. We get to be with Jesus in this reward! How unbelieveably awesome and beyond our comprehension! What a great reward for a life of sacrifice.

So, if this calling is so filled with blessing and support, what can happen to make someone lose it? Jesus shows us the hope set before the faithful, but he also shows us the seriousness of the path that leads there.

First of all, no enemy can ever take this gift from us:

Romans 8:38-39: 38 For I am convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, 39 nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

These are definitive statements: nothing can separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus, our Lord. The only thing not on this list is our own personal choice.

We can give our “birthright” away like Esau. The story of Esau giving away his birthright is found in Genesis 25:29–34, with the consequences shown in Genesis 27, and the spiritual lesson explained in Hebrews 12:16–17.

Esau and Jacob were brothers. Esau was older, and the inheritence normally went to the oldest. But Jacob was prophesied to inherit it. Esau gave his birthright away, the greatest blessing in his life, because he was hungry. It was his free will choice.

This shows us the concept of losing something of incredible value, a free gift, because our choice brings us in the wrong direction. Our choices are critical.

In Part I, we have focused on trying to define what salvation is.

Part II will dive into the depths of how and why our salvation can be lost, even though it is a free gift. We will look at the strongest arguments from those who say a Christian can’t lose their salvation. We’ll put those arguments side-by-side with the passages that warn about losing it and let Scripture show us how all of it fits together.

Actually, we should be putting everything we do against Scripture, asking what the word of God says versus what we would like it to say, or what we are used to thinking it says. Let’s let the word of God do the speaking. In relation to salvation, one thing is true: Jesus Christ died for the sins of Adam and that covers every man, woman and child who ever lived because they are all victims of Adam’s sin. Jesus provides that release to ALL at the appropriate time.

So, can Christians lose their salvation?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.
