------------ The actual New Testament words for save and salvation are very general.

Save: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4982 sozo; from a primary sos (contraction for obsolete

saoz, "safe"); to save, i.e. deliver or protect (literally or figuratively)

The King James Version translates this as “save” 93 times, “make whole” 9 times,

“heal” 3 times, “be whole” 2 times, and “misc” 3 times

King James Version:

Matthew 1:21: And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save <4982> his people from their sins.

Matthew 8:25: And his disciples came to him, and awoke him, saying, Lord, save <4982> us: we perish.

Matthew 9:21: For she said within herself, If I may but touch his garment, I shall be whole <4982>.

Salvation: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4991 soteria; feminine of a derivative of #4990

as (properly, abstract) noun; rescue or safety (physically or morally)

The King James Version translates this “salvation” 40 times, “the (one) be saved” 1 time,

“deliver” 1 time, “health” 1 time, “saving” 1 time, “that (one) be saved” 1 time

Acts 27:34: Wherefore I pray you to take some meat: for this is for your health <4991>: for there shall not an hair fall from the head of any of you.

Romans 1:16: For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation <4991> to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.

Saved from what? From a death that has no resurrection:

1 Corinthians 15:21-22: 21 For since by a man came death, by a man also came the resurrection of the dead. 22 For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.

2 Corinthians 2:15-16: 15 For we are a fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved <4982> and among those who are perishing; 16 to the one an aroma from death to death, to the other an aroma from life to life. And who is adequate for these things?

Saved from the broken systems and thinking of a sinful world:

1 Corinthians 1:18-19: 18 For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved <4982> it is the power of God. 19 For it is written, I WILL DESTROY THE WISDOM OF THE WISE, AND THE CLEVERNESS OF THE CLEVER I WILL SET ASIDE.

### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1456-can-christians-lose-their-salvation/

1. What is “salvation,” and from what does humanity need to be saved? Why is there an emphasis on “ALL?”

(1 Corinthians 15:21-22)

2. How does Romans 12:1 bring together what seem like separate statements in Romans 3:23-24, 6:23 and

10:9-13? What does Romans 12:1 tell those who are called to Christ what is expected of them? (also use 1

Peter 2:11-12, Philippians 1:21) Is this salvation a free gift?

3. What distinguishes a true Christian from someone who simply identifies with Christianity? How is our

“new creature” different from our old selves according to 2 Corinthians 5:17?

4. Compare Jesus’ words in Luke 9:23-24 with Paul’s words in Romans 12:1. How are these instructions

different from simply accepting the gift of salvation? (1 Peter 2:11-12, Philippians 1:21)

5. What is the only way a true Christian can lose salvation? How does the example of Esau illustrate this?

What are we protected from? What cannot take away our redemption or our salvation? Does God ever revoke the efficacy of the ransom (redemption) or our ultimate salvation? (Romans 8:35,38-39)

6. Discuss how Genesis 3:15, 22:17-18, Isaiah 42:1,4, Romans 5:18-19 and 1 Peter 3:18 can be connected to show

God’s plan of salvation from Genesis through Christ.

7. Compare the present “salvation by invitation” with the future “salvation by just and merciful inclusion.”

Why is most of humanity NOT invited at this time? (John 6:44, 12:36-40, Matthew 11:25-26, 1 Timothy 2:3- 6, and 4:10)

8. What are the privileges, responsibilities, dangers and rewards of those called to follow Christ now?

Include Matthew 7:13-14, 10:37-38, John 14:1-3, 15:7-9, 2 Corinthians 5:17-19 in your discussion.

9. In light of Romans 12:1 and Luke 9:23-24, what in your life reflects these ideals? What areas could use

improvement? Consider your thoughts, priorities, relationships, decisions, habits or use of time. What is one specific change you can make to more intentionally “take up your cross” this week?

10. Which choices or attitudes in your life could potentially pull you away from faithfully following Christ?

(Romans 8:35, 38-39) What practical steps can you take to remain attentive to God’s direction, allowing His spirit to guide your daily decisions?

## Episode 1457 — Can Christians Lose Their Salvation? (Part II)
Published: 2026-10-05
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1457-can-christians-lose-their-salvation-part-ii/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/25082938/CQ_Rewind_10-05-2026_Can_Christians_Lose_Their_Salvation_Part_II.pdf

Hebrews 10:26: For if we go on sinning willfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.

Salvation is a foundational belief every Christian stands upon. We all claim renewal as a result of Jesus dying for our sins. Sounds simple and straightforward—until we begin to ask the hard questions about how salvation actually works. In Part I of this two-part series, we took a hard scriptural look at the mechanics of salvation. We’ll begin Part II by briefly summarizing our Part I conversation regarding what we believe the whole Bible from Genesis to Revelation teaches us about salvation. Next, we will dive deeply into the very controversial question about a Christian’s ability or inability to ever lose that salvation. Answering this question needs clear and plainly stated biblical support. Let’s find it!

Christians can lose their salvation.

What is this salvation from? We need salvation from eternal death:

1 Corinthians 15:22: For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.

All die/all will be made alive. This applies to ALL; every man, woman and child who ever lived. Also notice this text contrasts death and life, not eternal hellfire with life.

How is someone “saved”? Is there a cost or is it a free gift?

It is a free gift:

Romans 6:23: For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

And there is a cost:

Romans 12:1: Therefore I urge you, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living and holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.

So, yes it’s given freely, but that doesn’t mean there isn’t work required on our part.

How does this salvation work? In two stages:

1. Salvation by invitation—this kind of salvation applies now to only a few.

2. Salvation by just and merciful inclusion—this kind of salvation applies in the

future to the rest of mankind.

1. Salvation by invitation is only for a few:

John 6:44: No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him; and I will raise him up on the last day.

As we have accepted this free gift, our mission is to follow the path that biblical scriptures lead us on. There is work to be done:

Luke 9:23: And he was saying to them all, If anyone wishes to come after me, he must deny himself, and take up his cross daily and follow me.

Jesus took up his cross and walked knowingly and willingly towards torture and death. Following him is not easy—it means the sacrificing of our lives to do the will of God.

Revelation 2:10: Do not fear what you are about to suffer… be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life.

2. Salvation by just and merciful inclusion shows us the vast plan of God for ALL His human creation:

1 Timothy 2:3-6: (KJV) 3 For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour; 4 Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge <1922> of the truth. 5 For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; 6 Who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time.

Knowledge: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1922 epignōsis; recognition, i.e. (by implication) full discernment, acknowledgement:—(ac-)knowledge(-ing, - ment)

The Greek word for knowledge here means “full discernment,” which indicates a deep, accurate understanding and not merely awareness. Notice the order: non-Christians are first saved, then taught after. For the Christian now, the order is believe (knowledge) first and then be saved. These two different phases of salvation are the end result of Jesus paying the ransom for ALL.

1 Timothy 4:10: For it is for this we labor and strive, because we have fixed our hope on the living God, who is the Savior of all men, especially of believers.

All men, especially of believers—here are the two distinct groups. Believers receive salvation now; and the rest of humanity, all men, receives salvation later.

How does this two-stage salvation work together? Those who respond now to the call of salvation by invitation to be disciples of Jesus are called for the purpose of becoming faithful ahead of time and will play a powerful role assisting in the salvation by just and merciful inclusion for the world, the “everybody else,” later.

Here’s how the two are connected:

2 Corinthians 5:17-19: 17 Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature; the old things passed away; behold, new things have come. 18 Now all these things are from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation, 19 namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and He has committed to us the word of reconciliation.

When God gives us His spirit, He begins a new life within us. We become a new creature. It’s a transformation that comes with responsibility. God reconciles us to Himself through Christ, and then we are given the ministry of reconciliation—the work of helping the world of mankind find their way back to Him in the kingdom.

We’re invited; they’re included!

The invitation of the few now is to teach the rest of mankind as students, like Jesus did with his disciples. These students learn, prove themselves faithful, and then become teachers of the next group of students—the rest of the world of mankind. This is how the Bible describes salvation, in two pieces.

Romans 5:19: For as through the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one the many will be made righteous.

Adam’s free choice brought death to all humanity, and Jesus’ free choice brings life to all humanity. The same many who became sinners in Adam are the many made righteous in Christ—meaning everyone.

We ended Part I with this next text. These next verses give a beautiful picture of love and protection. If this calling is so filled with blessing and support, what can happen to make someone lose it?

First, let’s establish that no enemy can ever take this gift from us:

Romans 8:38-39: 38 For I am convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, 39 nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

The Apostle Paul is listing external forces—things outside of us—that can’t sever the relationship God has established. HOWEVER, as we started to talk about last week, God does NOT override our free will. We saw that principle exemplified in Lucifer, Adam and Esau.

Once we get on track following after our Lord, we are impervious to outside attacks separating us from God. But we are not impervious to what comes from within ourselves!

We see that first wave of salvation prepares for the second, much greater wave of salvation, putting the teachers in place for the future.

With this scriptural basis set, we need to make sure that our personal beliefs are firmly rooted in what the Bible teaches.

So far, we have seen that power, privilege and personal accountability are all results of our salvation here and now. Does this mean we can lose that salvation?

We need to answer this question very carefully. We cannot lose our salvation arbitrarily, by accident. However, we can give it away. The Scriptures show us that we can consciously reject this powerful and freeing gift given from God through Jesus. Christians can only lose their salvation by their own choices and free will.

We alone have the power to reject the gift after we once received it, as seen by the various scriptures we are about to review.

Let’s set the groundwork for understanding how one would choose to put this gift aside if they are among the few who are called by invitation now to be the future teachers.

Remember, this ONLY applies to those who have God’s spirit here and now in this life:

Hebrews 10:23-25: 23 Let us hold fast (don’t let go!) the confession of our hope without wavering, for He who promised is faithful; 24 and let us consider how to stimulate one another to love and good deeds, 25 not forsaking our own assembling together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another; and all the more as you see the day drawing near.

The entire chapter of Hebrews 10 is addressed to Christians who have already been enlightened, sanctified and brought into a covenant relationship with Christ. A command to hold fast only makes sense if we could let go! We are urged to stay connected because wavering is a real spiritual danger.

These verses tell us to not forsake gathering together with other Christians. There is much more strength when we surround each other with hope, love and encouragement.

It’s important to note the context of Hebrews 10. It very clearly addresses those in Christ.

The position of many who claim “once saved, always saved” is that a TRUE Christian cannot willfully sin. If they do, it is reasoned, then they were never truly spirit-begotten to begin with and therefore couldn’t lose the salvation they never had.

But Hebrews 10 is clearly speaking to those who have already been sanctified and enlightened, and the Apostle Paul is warning them about the danger of willful sin. You don’t warn people about something that can’t happen.

The next verse pushes this concept even deeper:

Hebrews 10:26: For if we go on sinning willfully after receiving the knowledge <1922> of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins,

The Greek word here for knowledge, meaning full discernment, is the same one we read earlier in 1 Timothy 2:4 (who have all been saved and come into the knowledge—full discernment—of the truth). So, the warning here in Hebrews is directed at those who are still sinning willfully after having being enlightened.

There no longer remains a sacrifice for sins—there isn’t another Jesus who will die for you! Jesus died once for all (Hebrews 7:27). Hebrews 10:23-25 is a warning about taking our salvation, given once through Christ, and essentially throwing it away.

Does this mean knowingly committing a sin automatically negates our salvation?

No. It is important to recognize if we commit a willful sin, we can repent from that willful sin. We will be forgiven and can stand up again. The key is to avoid a life of willful sinning with no repentance. That is the warning.

Let’s look at the scriptures those who believe “once-saved, always-saved” might bring up to prove their viewpoint:

Romans 8:29-30: 29 For those whom He foreknew, He also predestined to become conformed to the image of His son, so that he would be the firstborn among many brethren; 30 and these whom He predestined, He also called; and these whom He called, He also justified; and these whom He justified, He also glorified.

Here’s the argument: Those God predestined He also called, justified and glorified. This is a guarantee that those who are justified are glorified. It’s a completed chain. No one drops out. If you can lose your salvation, then this text is wrong.

If we just read through this quickly, we can see how someone could come to that conclusion. However, we need to take the scripture in its appropriate context, because that is not what it is saying. This view is a misapplication of these verses.

These verses are addressing the body of Christ as a completed whole. They are not focused on individuals; they are describing the body of Christ as a complete unit. This “predestination” began in the mind of God ages before it came to pass. God engineered, or predestined, the plan ahead of time, and the Apostle Paul is explaining the big picture. He is talking about all of the called-out ones together. This group, the firstborn, was predestined to be called out of the world and to go through the stages of justification and glorification. Paul is showing the overall picture.

We as individuals are not glorified now. The whole group as the body of Christ is predestined to be glorified after resurrection.

Glorified in Romans 8:30 is past tense because God’s plan is complete in His foreknowledge, not because each Christian is already glorified or is guaranteed to be.

The Apostle John subtly explains what individual glorification looks like and when it happens:

John 12:16: These things his disciples did not understand at the first; but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things were written of him, and that they had done these things to him.

When Jesus was glorified, then they remembered… Jesus was not glorified before he died; he was glorified after he was raised from the dead. Jesus’ walk, being the first of the faithful ones, shows us the pathway of offering, sacrifice and then being raised and glorified.

Paul was not yet glorified:

Philippians 3:12: Not that I have already obtained it or have already become perfect, but I press on so that I may lay hold of that for which also I was laid hold of by Christ Jesus.

Glorification is conditional:

Romans 8:17: and if children, heirs also, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him.

Paul is describing the church as a completed body in God’s plan, not the guaranteed outcome of each individual. The group is predestined, but individuals must remain faithful.

What the world considers acceptable is not what we as Christians are to consider acceptable. The following temptations are danger zones!

1 Corinthians 6:9-11: (WEY) 9 Do you not know that unrighteous men will not inherit God's kingdom? Cherish no delusion here. (Other translations use, Do not be deceived, or Do not be led astray.) Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor any who are guilty of unnatural crime, 10 nor thieves, nor avaricious people, nor any who are addicted to hard

drinking, to abusive language or to greed of gain, will inherit God's kingdom. 11 And all this describes what some of you were. But now you have had every stain washed off: now you have been set apart as holy: now you have been pronounced free from guilt; in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and through the spirit of our God.

Cherish no delusion—do not go back to what you were. You have been cleaned, so stay cleansed! Paul wouldn’t be encouraging or admonishing someone to stay cleansed if it was impossible for them to go back to their old ways.

The admonishment is not to let any of those past doings come into our hearts or minds. even one iota. The potential to fall is there.

Paul is saying, “Don’t go back to what you were,” not, “You could never go back even if you tried.” He’s not claiming that a spirit-begotten Christian is incapable of willful sin. Free will is still in play.

Paul is powerfully announcing that unrighteousness does not inherit God’s kingdom. He tells the brotherhood to cherish no delusion, meaning they should never even entertain these sins a little bit. Why say this? Because it could happen! We could lose our salvation by going down these roads again, even though we had already been cleansed from them.

Another text used by those who say we cannot lose our salvation:

Philippians 1:6: For I am confident of this very thing, that He who began a good work in you will perfect it until the day of Christ Jesus.

Here’s the argument: God finishes what He starts. If He began the good work, He guarantees the end.

But notice, Paul is expressing confidence in God’s faithfulness—not saying the outcome is automatically guaranteed. God finishes His work in those who continue to cooperate with Him. Because God is faithful, YOU must be faithful, too!

God has promised that He will not give up on us. We should hold that close because it helps keep us headed in the right direction.

In the very next chapter, Paul continues encouraging the brotherhood to rise above challenges, meaning these challenges could make them fall:

Philippians 2:12-13: 12 So then, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out <2716> your salvation with fear <5401> and <2532> trembling <5156>; 13 for it is God who is at work in you, both to will and to work for His good pleasure.

Work out: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2116 katergazomai; to work fully, i.e. accomplish; by implication, to finish, fashion:—cause, to (deed), perform, work (out)

If the outcome is already guaranteed, why would we have to work out our salvation with fear and trembling?

The counterargument: “Work out” means “work outward,” in other words, display the salvation you already possess. It does not mean to maintain or guard it, or take it seriously because danger exists.

Yes, but if Paul meant “work outward,” he would have said “live out” or “show” your salvation. But he used a verb that means to finish; to carry something through to its intended end.

A second counterargument: “Fear and trembling” means having reverent awe and deep respect, not actual fear of falling away. Because God is doing the work, salvation can’t be lost.

Fear: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5401 phobos; from a primary phébomai (to be put in fear); alarm or fright:—be afraid; and as a result of an idiom peculiar to the Hebrew: exceedingly, fear, terror

And: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2532 kai; apparently, a primary particle, having a copulative and sometimes also a cumulative force; and, also, even, so then, too, etc.; often used in connection (or composition) with other particles or small words:—and, also, both, but, even, for, if, or, so, that, then, therefore, when, yet

Trembling: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5156 tromos; a "trembling", i.e. quaking with fear:— and as a result of an idiom peculiar to the Hebrew: tremble(-ing)

But the Greek really does mean fear and trembling.

Paul uses the phrase three other times (2 Corinthians 2:3; 7:15 and Ephesians 6:5), and it always means “with seriousness and caution,” never “reverent awe.”

This shows how important it is to listen to what the Scriptures are teaching. We have to look up the words, understand what they mean and accept them. If our perspective does not line up with what we read, we need to carefully examine it to see if it needs changing.

Look back at creation. God said at the end of the sixth day that His work was very good. Now, when God says something is very good, we can be sure it is completely awesome! Yet, He allowed sin to enter. Why would He do that if His work was very good? Because part of His plan is the allowance of free will. This is why we see Adam sin, Lucifer (Satan) fall from grace and all the rest of sin’s degradations happen.

Those who have been called by God also have free will.

God is absolutely capable of seeing His plan for you through to the end. Paul is encouraging the brotherhood as a whole, not removing personal responsibility. The same Paul immediately says, Work out your salvation with fear and trembling. God works in us, but He does not override our choices.

That is part of the amazing greatness and wisdom of God. It’s such a big picture with eternity in mind. Our free will should make positive choices towards that goal.

We can’t get stuck in how we would prefer to think or what we would prefer to have. It is NOT about us; it is about walking in the footsteps of Jesus.

These scriptures show us the depth of sober thoughtfulness required to follow Jesus. This is not to be taken lightly!

How serious are these warning signs? What conditions of a true Christian’s heart and mind would have to be in place to cause concern?

The first thing to note here, is that the depth of concern for this potential loss of salvation is only reserved for those who have truly been called by God, who have answered that call in this gospel age since Jesus’ death, and have actually been begotten by God’s spirit. Every other human being will have their time of testing on the Day of Judgment after their resurrection. Right now, we are just talking about those who have been called by God in this life.

Let’s look at another text used by those who believe “once-saved, always-saved”:

Ephesians 1:13: In him (Jesus), you also, after listening to the message of truth, the gospel of your salvation—having also believed, you were sealed in him with the holy spirit of promise.

The argument: Having a seal means permanence. If God seals you, you cannot be unsealed. It’s finished, locked, irreversible. Therefore, salvation cannot be lost.

But the next verse explains what the seal actually is: 14 Who is given as a pledge <728> of our inheritance, with a view to the redemption of God's own possession, to the praise of His glory.

Pledge: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #6162 arrabōn; of Hebrew origin; a pledge, i.e. part of the purchase-money or property given in advance as security for the rest:—earnest

Arrabōn always means a pledge, a down payment, a first installment. In Greek business and marriage contracts, an arrabōn was binding and serious but not the final covenant.

This is something that guarantees God’s intention, but it is NOT the completed inheritance.

Some translations use the word guarantee instead of pledge:

- New International Version: …a deposit guaranteeing our inheritance until the redemption… - English Standard Version: …the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it… - New American Standard Bible: …a first installment of our inheritance… - Christian Standard Bible: …the down payment of our inheritance…

However, even translations that say guarantee are describing the function of a pledge, not changing the meaning of the Greek word. A guarantee of something is not the thing itself. The spirit is the guarantee that God will do His part, but Scripture repeatedly shows that humans can reject the pledge before the inheritance is given.

The spirit is a pledge—an engagement promise, not the completed marriage. Nothing external can remove the seal, but we can choose to let go of what we were given. The seal guarantees God’s faithfulness, but doesn’t override our free will.

The spirit is like a down payment, as explained by Ephesians 1:14. The spirit is given as a pledge of our inheritance, with a view to (until) the redemption (deliverance) of God’s own possession (mankind)… with a view to what’s coming in the future. It’s not solid, sealed and delivered completely now. The spirit is given in view of what is coming in the future.

The “rest of the payment” of our inheritance comes after we have proven faithful. If we don’t prove ourselves faithful, then we don’t inherit!

The Apostle Paul says we are sealed but then explains the seal is a pledge, not the actual inheritance. God guarantees His part, but He never overrides our free will. Receiving God’s spirit is the down payment, but faithfulness is required in order to get the full inheritance.

Let’s further focus on the biblically stated conditions that exist when this tragic loss takes place:

Hebrews 6:4-6: 4 For in the case of those who have once been enlightened and have tasted of the heavenly gift and have been made partakers of the holy spirit, 5 and have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, 6 and then have fallen away, it is impossible to renew them again to repentance, since they again crucify to themselves the son of God and put him to open shame.

Let’s first notice how many times and is used in these verses. If someone has ALL these advantages, and then falls away…

So it is not one or the other; it is all of them.

Let’s examine this verse piece by piece:

…those who have once been enlightened

Meaning, those whose eyes and minds were not blinded to truth:

2 Corinthians 4:3-4: 3 And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing, 4 in whose case the god of this world (Satan) has blinded the minds of the unbelieving so that they might not see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.

Jesus made a clear distinction of those whom the Father calls (John 6:44, 6:45). Everybody else can’t see or understand spiritual things because their minds have been blinded by Satan. Those who have… been enlightened are privileged to understand spiritual things.

But, what about this other once-saved, always-saved argument?

John 10:27-29: 27 My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; 28 and I give eternal life to them, and they will never perish; and no one will snatch them out of my hand. 29 My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all; and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand.

The argument: Because Jesus gives eternal life, it must not be able to be lost.

But eternal life describes the kind of life God offers, not an automatic guarantee that a believer cannot walk away from it. Our reward can be lost:

Revelation 3:11-12: 11 I am coming quickly; hold fast what you have, so that no one will take your crown. 12 He who overcomes, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he will not go out from it anymore; and I will write on him the name of my God…

Hold fast. Don’t let go. Keep hold of it with all our strength. Why? Because there are repercussions if we let go. Our crown, that glory, can be lost. Both these John and Revelation scriptures are the words of Jesus, who does not contradict himself. The glorified Jesus warns us to hold fast—hang on tightly—so as not to lose our crown.

Having a crown means you were called and accepted as a Christian, so there is a crown reserved for you; it has been pledged to you. However, you can forfeit your reserved crown, and it will go to someone else.

…and have tasted of the heavenly gift

Those who have had God’s blessings and favor made manifest to them as they sought to do God’s will in His way from their hearts:

Romans 5:1-2: 1 Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, 2 through whom also we have obtained our introduction by faith into this grace in which we stand; and we exult in hope of the glory of God.

How we look forward to seeing the glory of God in the future! These verses show us being made right before God—we are justified by faith. Having been made right in God’s eyes means He no longer sees us as sinners. He sees us as followers of Christ, as that new creation.

…and have been made partakers of the holy spirit

Having been redeemed by Jesus, these are now seen in the light of Jesus’ righteousness and have God’s spirit working within them as their guide:

1 Thessalonians 5:19-22: 19 Do not quench <5670> the spirit; 20 do not despise prophetic utterances. 21 But examine everything carefully; hold fast to that which is good; 22 abstain from every form of evil.

Quench: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4570 sbennumi; a prolonged form of an apparently primary verb; to extinguish (literally or figuratively): quench, go out

Do not quench the spirit, meaning, do not extinguish it. Paul is talking to Christians who already have God’s spirit.

Paul follows this warning with two commands: hold fast to that which is good and abstain from every form of evil. These are responsibilities. Nothing external can take the spirit away, but we can let go of it by neglect, by compromise, or by walking away from the narrow path of sacrifice. We can essentially put out the “flame” God ignited within us. Our free will has a voice.

It is our responsibility to direct our free will to respond to Thus sayeth the Lord. What did Jesus do when Satan tempted him in the wilderness? He always went back to Scripture. He always went back to, “But the Lord says,” or “God’s word says…”

If we are warned not to quench the spirit, then it CAN be extinguished.

Another “once saved, always saved” point around a very specific circumstance:

1 John 2:19: They went out from us, but they were not really of us; for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us; but they went out, so that it would be shown that they all are not of us.

We have been saying that Christians can lose their salvation because they have free will. They can habitually willfully sin, and they can even change their minds and outright deny the faith.

The argument: A true, spirit-begotten Christian will NOT live in continual, unrepentant sin (1 John 3:6). And anyone who departs the faith proves they were never truly saved.

1 John 2:19 says, They went out from us, but they were not really of us. If they had been true Christians, they would have remained. Therefore, those who fall away were never saved in the first place.

Let’s go to the context. John isn’t talking about ordinary Christians who stumble and sin. He is talking about outsiders who actively oppose Christ and deliberately deceive the church. These are wolves in sheep’s clothing (Matthew 7:15).

The previous verse shows who is being spoken of:

1 John 2:18: Children, it is the last hour; and just as you heard that antichrist is coming, even now many antichrists have appeared; from this we know that it is the last hour.

The Greek prefix "anti" primarily means “opposite” or “instead of.” In the context of antichristos, John is describing those who stand in opposition to the true Christ— individuals whose teachings or claims place them instead of Christ and therefore against him. In John’s day, there were already many who positioned themselves as “opposites” to the true Christian message, which is why he said that many antichrists had arisen.

These aren’t Christians who are weak or confused. These are people who are hostile opponents of Christ. John explains they left because they weren’t ever, not at all, a part of the true brotherhood.

If we are going to build an argument by quoting a scripture, it needs to be quoted in context. This context is clearly focusing on those who are outsiders coming into the church to take advantage of it.

John is describing a specific circumstance of deceivers and enemies of Christ—not spirit-begotten Christians who tragically fall away. This passage has nothing to do with our question of whether a true, spirit-begotten Christian can abandon their calling.

…and have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come

And… and… and… all of these incredible blessings, opportunities and privileges are piled one on top of another, showing a great progression in the way of Christ. Who has tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come? Those who have experienced forgiveness of sins and the profound blessings of being restored to God’s favor as sons. Sonship with God was lost to the world of mankind when Adam sinned. But Jesus tells us we can call God “Father.”

We are restored to a level of sonship that is above and beyond anything humanity had ever seen until Jesus:

1 Peter 2:3-5: 3 If you have tasted the kindness of the Lord. 4 And coming to him as to a living stone which has been rejected by men, but is choice and precious in the sight of God, 5 you also, as living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house for a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

You… are being built up as a spiritual house… to offer up spiritual sacrifices— we saw what that means back in Romans 12:1, where we are to present your bodies a living sacrifice, which is your spiritual service of worship.

We sacrifice ourselves, our own will, to walk in the footsteps of Jesus.

…and then have fallen away

But if, after all of these blessings, leadings and experiences combined:

Hebrews 6:6: And then have fallen away, it is impossible to renew them again to repentance, since they again crucify to themselves the son of God and put him to open shame.

So if someone has received all of these things, but then they have fallen away, it is impossible to renew them again to repentance.

This is a very sad end result of having been given and accepted all the wonderful gifts and opportunities of sonship and then walking away and giving it all back.

We feel the depths of sadness caused by the free will choices of one who abandons Christ:

Hebrews 10:29-30: 29 How much severer punishment do you think he will deserve who has trampled under foot the son of God, and has regarded as unclean the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has insulted the spirit of grace? 30 For we know Him who said, VENGEANCE IS MINE, I WILL REPAY. And again, THE LORD WILL JUDGE HIS PEOPLE.

This is elsewhere described as the sin leading to death:

1 John 5:16-17: 16 If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask and God will for him give life to those who commit sin not leading to death. There is a sin leading to death; I do not say that he should make request for this. 17 All unrighteousness is sin, and there is a sin not leading to death.

We get a lot of listeners who write in, upset that they have commited some sort of sin. They are so distraught because they are afraid they have commited a sin leading to death, from which there is no return. We tell them, if you are upset about this, you haven’t committed that sin unto death because you are still in the game! They are repentant, picking themselves up and trying to do better.

That is not the person talked about in these verses. This is someone who has outright rejected (trampled on) the blood of Christ shed for him or her.

What exactly happens to the former Christian who, after having accepted the call, decides to “trample the blood of Christ”?

For someone who has had all these gifts, one piled on top of the other, but then walks away, it says it is impossible to renew them again to repentance. Jesus died for them. His sacrifice was given to them and they were seen in God’s eyes as a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17), rescued from death caused by Adam’s sin.

Once we chose to forfeit the application of Jesus’ sacrifice, there is no more sacrifice left. Jesus isn’t going to die for you again.

Their end result is, unfortunately, second death.

Revelation 2:11: He who has an ear, let him hear what the spirit says to the churches. He who overcomes will not be hurt by the second death.

Revelation 20:6: Blessed and holy is the one who has a part in the first resurrection; over these the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ and will reign with him for a thousand years.

We know from 1 Corinthians 15:22, as in Adam all die, even so in Christ all will be made alive. We were raised from death and the sin of Adam by accepting the call to follow Jesus. But then, if we choose to not be obedient and we turn our back on that first redemption, we die a second time. Our life is extinguished. It’s done. It’s over. We go out of existence (Acts 3:23).

We continue to repent and fight against sin. We must get up when we fall, ask for forgiveness and WALK AWAY from that sin.

Let’s address another common argument raised by those who believe “once saved, always saved.”

Jesus spoke to Nicodemus about being born again… or did he?

John 3:3: Jesus answered and said to him, Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born <1080> again he cannot see the kingdom of God.

(Read John 3:1-7 for the context.)

Born: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1080 gennaō; to procreate (properly, of the father, but by extension of the mother); figuratively, to regenerate

The argument: Nicodemus immediately takes Jesus literally and says a person cannot be physically born a second time. A birth is final and irreversible. You cannot be “unborn.” Therefore, once someone is born again, salvation cannot be lost.

Jesus does say we must be “born again,” but the Greek word He uses is gennaō, which means to beget or to conceive in this context, not “to give birth.” Nicodemus’ confusion shows Jesus is talking about a spiritual conception, not a completed birth. A conceived life is real and precious—but it can tragically die before birth. Spirit-begettal happens now, when God’s spirit begins its work in us; spirit-birth happens at the resurrection, when we are fully transformed into spirit beings.

Gennaō is a verb that can mean “to beget,” “to give birth,” or “to be born,” depending on context. In this passage, Jesus is using the male sense of the word—begetting—to describe the beginning of spiritual life. Just as human life begins with begetting before birth, spiritual life begins when God begets us by His spirit. This is why Nicodemus’ confusion about literal birth shows Jesus is speaking of a spiritual begetting now, with the full “birth” into spirit life occurring at the resurrection.

The phrase born again in John 3:3 would be better translated “begotten from above,” which matches both the Greek and the context. Jesus is describing the beginning of spiritual life, not its completion.

The argument “you can’t be unborn” doesn’t apply, because we are not spirit-born yet. We are spirit-begotten—in the developmental stage—and Scripture warns that this developing life must be nurtured, protected and held fast.

This is what we were talking about earlier with the “down payment.” The begettal is the down payment; the birth is the glorification.

We are “begotten” now, not “born” now. The “you can’t be unborn” argument collapses because it is based on a mistranslation of the Greek word and context.

We’ve talked about a lot of things that feel rather depressing. How do we even stand a chance? We stand a chance because we are in Christ, we are begotten by the spirit and we have been given blessings and forgiveness. But we need to work together!

No wonder the scriptures implore us to be engaged with one another to support and build each other up in the body of Christ:

Galatians 6:1-5: 1 Brethren, even if anyone is caught in any trespass, you who are spiritual, restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; each one looking to yourself, so that you too will not be tempted. 2 Bear one another's burdens, and thereby fulfill the law of Christ. 3 For if anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. 4 But each one must examine his own work, and then he will have reason for boasting in regard to himself alone, and not in regard to another. 5 For each one will bear his own load.

We are imperfect, we will fall, we will make mistakes, we will sin—and it is imperative that we work through those things as best we can. Think about how much stronger our work can be when somebody reaches their hand out and says, Here, let me give you a hand, and then pulls you up and helps you to walk.

We have tried to find every scripture that could be used to support the viewpoint that once we have been saved, we cannot lose our salvation.

We present one more:

Jude 1:24: Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling, and to make you stand in the presence of His glory blameless with great joy.

The argument: Jude says God is able to keep Christians from stumbling and to present them blameless. If God is able to keep us from falling, then salvation cannot be lost. God’s power guarantees our perseverance.

When we take a phrase and build a doctrine out of a phrase, we are not following God’s word, His will and His way.

Let’s look at the verses immediately preceding this powerful proclamation:

Jude 1:21-24: 21 Keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting anxiously for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to eternal life. 22 And have mercy on some, who are doubting; 23 save others, snatching them out of the fire (meaning, pulling them away from the influence and snares of the adversary. Yes, we are our brother’s keeper!); and on some have mercy with fear, hating even the garment polluted by the flesh. 24 Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling, and to make you stand in the presence of His glory blameless with great joy.

Look at the activity we are to be doing in this verse—this is an active process of growing. We are not given God’s spirit because we are fully grown. We are given it because we are babies and need to learn how to “grow up” in Christ, and to become mature men and women in Christ. All of us can contribute to becoming the body of Christ because we follow our head, Jesus.

Yes, God is fully able to keep us from stumbling, as we keep ourselves in His love. But again, He does not use His power to override our choices.

We need to be fully engaged! Our full engagement provokes us to let go of all that we used to be, to do, to hope for—and to press forward:

Philippians 3:13-14: 13 Brethren, I do not regard myself as having laid hold of it yet; but one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead, 14 I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.

The Apostle Paul had been preaching Christ at this point for about 25 to 30 years or so.

I do not regard myself as having laid hold of it yet—I haven’t finished the work of growing that I need to do.

Therefore, I forget what lies behind (I move on from my mistakes) and reach forward to what lies ahead… I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.

That is what our lives are called to be. That is why, yes, we can lose our salvation, BUT there is so much in place to protect and guide us, and give us strength and encouragement that we are able to succeed. We are able to succeed through prayer and through working with our fellow soldiers in Christ, relying on each other for help and comfort.

It comes down to making sure we are not about ourselves, but are instead about the whole body of Christ:

Romans 12:2: And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect.

Our salvation is a free gift. It is given to us. Through God’s spirit—His power and influence—we are given the ability to grow and become strong in Christ. We help others grow along with us. This gift cannot be taken from us.

However, we CAN lose this gift if we reject it and give it away. Stand strong in Christ!

So, can Christians lose their salvation?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

God’s spirit is the power and influence of God. We saw its power in creation as the spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters… God’s power and influence always work in conjunction with His character, which is based upon His justice, His wisdom, His power and His love.

While these characteristics are all powerful, we see that God does NOT use His power and influence to crush the ability of His created beings to make choices. Instead, He systematically and over history teaches each and every being endowed with freedom of choice that their choices do have consequences. In His benevolence, He also shows them what the consequences are and how they can make righteous choices, and therefore choose to live eternally. ------- The sin unto death:

1 John 5:16-17: 16 If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask and God will for him give life to those who commit sin not leading to death. There is a sin leading to death; I do not say that he should make request for this. 17 All unrighteousness is sin, and there is a sin not leading to death.

There are various types of relationships people can have with God. This is similar in some ways to our own relationships. We can have distant acquaintances, friends and close family.

In order to be considered sons of God (i.e. close family members) an individual must have devoted his or her life to Him. This is described in Romans 12:1 as “presenting our bodies as a living sacrifice to God.” Once this is done, that person is generally baptized as a symbol of their devotion. If God accepts this decision, then the individual is “justified” by Christ’s blood.

This is described in Romans 5:9: Being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from the wrath of God through him. This justification means the individual is considered righteous in God’s eyes and a personal relationship is established.

After justification, the individual then receives a measure of the holy spirit—God’s power and influence—and is considered a “son of God.” At this time, the “sin unto death” referenced in several scriptures is only applicable to those who have followed these important steps and are now under the blood.

If they should completely turn their backs on what they professed, go into unbelief and “trample the blood of Christ,” there is no longer any blood available to justify them. However, most are not even aware of the process and have not dedicated their lives to God and been justified, so we understand this to apply to very few in this age.

## Episode 1458 — What Does It Mean to Be Baptized Into Christ’s Death?
Published: 2026-10-12
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1458-baptized-into-christs-death/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/04233220/CQ_Rewind_10-12-2026_What_Does_it_Mean_to-be_Baptized_Into_Christs_Death.pdf

Romans 6:3: Or do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus

have been baptized into his death?

Baptism plays a vital and sacred role in the lives of Christians. John the Baptist introduced baptism into the New Testament as a symbol of repentance, in preparation for Jesus coming on the scene. Jesus then took that symbol and amplified it to include the sacrificial aspects of following him as a disciple. Throughout the New Testament, the concept of baptism is described in several ways. So, what does it all mean? What should we as Christians understand about the broad meaning of baptism? How should we go about daily living what it tells us to stand for? How do I, as an individual Christian, embrace being baptized into Christ’s death?

John identified himself as the forerunner of the Messiah. His work was to prepare Israel:

Mark 1:4–5: 4 John the Baptist appeared in the wilderness preaching a baptism of repentance <3341> for the forgiveness <859> of sins. 5 And all the country of Judea was going out to him, and all the people of Jerusalem; and they were being baptized by him in the Jordan River, confessing their sins.

There was a massive call to repentance! John prepared the people to recognize their need for repentance, so that they could receive forgiveness through Jesus’ sacrifice. It was the set-up to get them ready for Jesus’ message.

Repentance: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3341 metanoia; from #3340; (subjectively) compunction (for guilt, including reformation); by implication reversal (of [another's] decision)

Let’s look at an example of repentance:

Hebrews 6:1: (KJV) Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance <3341> from dead works, and of faith toward God.

A person doesn’t spiritually progress without repentance as a foundation.

Repentance makes us ready to receive forgiveness because it means we’ve recognized our sin, admitted our need and turned our hearts toward God. John’s baptism laid that foundation of honest repentance so the people would then be ready to receive forgiveness of sins.

Forgiveness/Remission: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #859 aphesis; from #863;

freedom; (figuratively) pardon

Forgiveness means freedom from our sins. It is a pardon from sin; those sins are behind us, gone and no longer attached to us.

Jesus’ words spoken near the beginning of his public ministry help us see this:

Luke 4:18: (KJV) The spirit of the Lord is upon me, because He hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; He hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance <859> to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty <859> them that are bruised.

The words deliverance and liberty also convey the thought of forgiveness. This pardon was directed toward the brokenhearted, the captives and those who were hurting, with the purpose of offering freedom in Christ.

John couldn’t do that. He could help them open their hearts and minds through repentance, but Jesus was the one who would deliver that freedom. In Luke 4, Jesus is describing part of his ministry. He is quoting an Old Testament prophecy about himself from Isaiah 61:1-2.

Jesus’ words, spoken shortly before his ascension, take this further:

Luke 24:47: (KJV) And that repentance <3341> and remission <859> of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem.

Jesus spoke these words after he had been resurrected from the dead and was about to be raised up to heaven. He was giving the disciples their mission: to preach repentance and the remission of sins through Jesus Christ.

John’s baptism was only about repentance. It would be replaced by Jesus’ baptism—a baptism of repentance, forgiveness and a life of self-sacrifice.

As a reminder, we understand that John the Baptist was one of the last prophets of the Old Testament. God’s holy spirit worked with him like the Old Testament prophets. With Jesus, it was entirely different.

John is introducing Jesus to the nation of Israel. He is handing off his part in God’s plan to Jesus, who would take it further and begin the next phase of the plan.

How did Jesus personally apply and describe baptism?

Jesus was baptized to mark the beginning of his ministry:

Matthew 3:13–15: 13 Then Jesus arrived from Galilee at the Jordan coming to John, to be baptized by him. 14 But John tried to prevent him, saying, I have need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me? 15 But Jesus answering said to him, Permit it at this time; for in this way it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness. Then he permitted him.

We can understand John’s concern. Jesus was perfect and not tainted by Adamic stock, and he never sinned, so he had nothing to repent for. John was a little confused here!

Jesus says, I have need to be baptized by you. John is confused because Jesus did not need to repent—he had never done anything that required repentance!

That is why Jesus had to say, Permit it at this time, because it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness. He didn’t need to repent because he hadn’t sinned, but John trusted in Jesus’ judgment.

Jesus’ baptism was an act of obedience, not repentance. It symbolized the complete surrender of his human will in order to do the Father’s will perfectly, even unto death. It also served as God’s public endorsement of Jesus.

So, Jesus’ baptism was to mark the beginning of his ministry. After his baptism, the spirit of God descended like a dove and landed on him. God’s voice said, This is my Son in whom I am well pleased.

This is the beginning. This is the symbol.

Jesus spoke of another baptism, the baptism of suffering.

James and John were prompted by their mother to ask Jesus for positions at his right and left hand in God’s future kingdom.

Here was Jesus’ reply:

Mark 10:38–40: 38 But Jesus said to them, You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized? 39 They said to him, We are able. And Jesus said to them, The cup that I drink you shall drink; and you shall be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized. 40 But to sit on my right or on my left, this is not mine to give; but it is for those for whom it has been prepared.

The cup and baptism are not literal here. Jesus is talking about life experience. He is showing them that the “cup” and the “baptism” mean much more than a physical cup and the physical experience of being immersed in water.

They are symbolic of a voluntary acceptance of this cup as our designated path of discipleship. Being baptized is symbolic of accepting and enduring possibly harsh trials that may cost us our very life.

Jesus tells James and John they do not know what they are asking for, as they will be tested in these ways. The baptism Jesus was baptized with was a challenging way of life.

Here Jesus does not mention baptism, but he does dwell on the cost of following him:

Luke 14:27–30: 27 Whoever does not carry his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple. 28 For which one of you, when he wants to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the cost to see if he has enough to complete it? 29 Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who observe it begin to ridicule him, 30 saying, This man began to build and was not able to finish.

In other words, be careful; think this through, as this is a major decision. Why? Because a cross pictures suffering and death. Once you accept God’s invitation and calling to walk in Jesus’ footsteps, there’s no turning back.

Jesus is making a very clear point here. He is not inviting everyone to come and follow him. There is no hype, no excitement—just a deliberate and calculated statement of what this life will mean.

It is important that we understand what the symbol of baptism really means. Jesus’ description of carrying a cross represents the suffering of the baptism Jesus spoke about in Mark 10.

His warning is clear: do not commit to this “narrow way” before clearly counting the cost!

Matthew 7:14: 14 For the gate is small and the way is narrow that leads to life, and there are few who find it.

The symbol of baptism—being immersed in water— through all the experiences of life, shows us the life Jesus led and the life we are to lead as well.

Is our baptism into Christ a one-time event, or is it a process that unfolds throughout our lifetime?

There is a lot of confusion surrounding this debate. One practice we need to consider is infant baptism. This one can be emotional, but for those who understand baptism to be a one-time event, infant baptism is a common example.

With infant baptism, there is no counting the cost, nor is there an acceptance of the call through the symbol. This doesn’t fit into the context of the Scriptures.

There may be a few passages of Scripture that could be construed to include infants, but the context shows otherwise. There is NO scriptural example or requirement of infant baptism.

We return to Mark 10:39: The cup that I drink you shall drink; and you shall be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized.

God does not interfere with human free will. Those who are called to Christ need to count the cost of following Jesus’ walk—they are not coerced into it. They indicate their willingness to accept this call through the symbol of baptism.

Baptism is a serious decision that is indicative of something much bigger.

After the initial symbol of water immersion—not just a sprinkling, but a complete submersion—baptism describes a continuously unfolding life experience for us, as its reality is expressed over and over again in our lives. We live the baptism shown to us by the symbol, just like Jesus did.

Before we move forward, we need to state a hard truth: There should never be a baptism into any church, organization or group—only into Christ. We will see this clearly as we go through the Scriptures.

Let’s start with a foundational principle of Christianity: actual baptism into Christ. Before his ascension, Jesus gave these instructions:

Matthew 28:18–20: 18 And Jesus came up and spoke to them, saying, All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. 19 Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and the son and the holy spirit, 20 teaching them to observe all that I commanded you; and lo, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.

Based on everything Jesus has said so far, before we dedicate our life to Christ in the symbol of baptism, consider asking ourselves three questions:

1. Do I realize I am a sinner born in Adam?

2. Do I accept Jesus as my personal Savior?

3. Am I making a lifelong commitment to do God’s will by laying down my life and

following in Jesus’ footsteps?

These three questions show us the thought and prayerful consideration that go into making such a decision. It is not a casual life choice, nor a choice made in order to be a member of a church or organization. It is much bigger than that.

Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and the son and the holy spirit.

1. This does NOT say to baptize them into the name of a church group or denomination. It means baptizing them into God’s authority.

2. There are many New Testament scriptures that say that they were baptized into Christ. See the Bonus Material. Does this contradict Jesus’ instruction to baptize in the name of the Father and the son and the holy spirit?

No, these Scriptures do not contradict Jesus’ instruction. Baptizing them in the name of the Father and the son and the holy spirit describes the authority under which baptism happens. Baptized into Christ describes the relationship and identity with Christ the Christian enters through baptism.

Jesus shows us the magnitude of what baptism into Christ is: a declaration that we belong to the Father, are redeemed by the son and guided by the spirit. We are baptized under this authority, and through that baptism the Christian becomes united with Christ.

Let’s look at other aspects of our baptism experience mentioned by John and Jesus.

John the Baptist spoke of a baptism of the holy spirit:

Matthew 3:11: As for me, I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, and I am not fit to remove his sandals; he will baptize you with the holy spirit and fire.

The baptism of the holy spirit for disciples was unquestionably performed on the day of Pentecost. It established Christianity, and its effects would continue all through this age of the gospel.

Many Christians speak of the “baptism of fire” as the power of the holy spirit. However, we need to pay attention to the context. John is relating this baptism of fire to his audience— the nation of Israel. When they rejected Jesus, Israel suffered national destruction, and the people were dispersed throughout the nations of the world.

John predicts this prophetically in the next verse:

Matthew 3:11: His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly clear his threshing floor; and he will gather his wheat into the barn, but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.

Unquenchable fire pictures the rejection of Israel, the nation that stood in opposition to Jesus, their Messiah. Gather his wheat pictures the ongoing effort to find new wheat, since Israel as a nation chose to reject the call to become “wheat.” The call would eventually have to go outside of Israel, and Gentiles would be included to make up the remainder of Christ’s church.

Always check the context!

This baptism of the holy spirit comes upon the true church. They are begotten by the spirit and have it dwelling within them.

The baptism of fire was destructive—a removal of things that were in the way so that the plan of God could continue. This does not mean that Israel was cast off forever. At that time, with their rejection of their Messiah sent by God, there was a destruction of their national polity. But at the end of their time of punishment, they will once again be restored to a relationship with God.

The result of an appropriate Christian baptism is the establishment of a new creation’s beginning:

2 Corinthians 5:17–19: 17 Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature; the old things passed away; behold, new things have come. 18 Now all these things are from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation, 19 namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and He has committed to us the word of reconciliation.

These verses show us the two aspects of salvation: those who are saved first will become the teachers and guides for those who are saved later.

Baptism is the foundation of the new creation—the spirit-begotten ones who are now learning in the school of Christ. In the kingdom of God, they will pass on to mankind the teaching of how to come back into harmony with Him. That is why they are given a ministry of reconciliation. We learn this ministry by living a life of sacrifice, by living what baptism into Christ’s death means every day.

Baptism clothes us with the merit of Jesus’ perfect sacrifice as our protection and justification—it clothes, protects and covers us:

Galatians 3:27–29: 27 For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ. 28 There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus. 29 And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s descendants, heirs according to promise.

Being “clothed” in Christ pictures Christ’s imputed robe of righteousness, which covers our sinful flesh. Christ’s merit gives us a standing with God. The symbol of baptism is an outward display of the baptism of the heart.

By Christ’s “merit,” we mean the worth or value he earned by living a perfect, sinless life and offering that life in sacrifice. Humanity doesn’t have this kind of spiritual credit on its own, so Christ’s merit is what gives Christians acceptance before God. “Imputed” simply means that God credits Christ’s perfection to us—like placing his righteousness into our account even though we didn’t earn it. This is why the Bible uses the picture of a robe: Just as a clean white garment covers up stained or worn clothing, Christ’s imputed righteousness acts like a robe covering our human flaws, giving us a right standing with God.

Baptism is a symbol of our life that unfolds every day. It is not once and done. It is a symbol of having Christ clothe us and of being acceptable before God because of Jesus’ merit in our lives.

Romans 5:1: Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,

When we are clothed in Christ’s righteousness, we have recognition before God. The blood of Jesus justifies us before God, and if we are justified, we can have peace with God. What a beautiful, grand picture of what baptism means. We are now living on a different level, living a different life.

I have told my story about the past, how I lost my way. This went on for years until I hit bottom. I begged the Lord for help and direction and He came through. It took some time to learn what being a follower of Christ looked like, but I realized God was calling me. So I decided to give my life to Him and be baptized.

I told my parents, and they wanted to support me. They did not understand the depth of the commitment, but they were happy I turned my life to God.

This was an important experience because so many of us go through that same kind of thing. Jonathan’s parents saw the baptism of John in his repentance, but they did not see the depth of commitment—the baptism into Christ’s death. They grew to see what the actual baptism meant as he grew up in Christ before them: justified, made right with God, and being clothed with the righteousness of Jesus. This is what true baptism into Christ’s death means.

Our baptism is a commitment to be dead with Jesus to our earthly lives and alive in a new way:

Romans 6:3–4: 3 Or do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death? 4 Therefore we have been buried with him through baptism into death (meaning our humanity is over and done—why?), so that as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.

We see the decision-making process here. Referring back to infant baptism, it does not fit into the equation of consciously choosing to be buried with him through baptism into the death of our humanity, so we too might walk in newness of life.

We are to be “dead” to our old earthly self so the new life we lead can be a vital, shining example:

Romans 6:5–6: 5 For if we have become united with him in the likeness of his death, certainly we shall also be in the likeness of his resurrection, 6 knowing this, that our old self was crucified with him, in order that our body of sin might be done away with, so that we would

no longer be slaves to sin.

THIS IS A CONSCIOUS DECISION. Our baptism into Christ has to be

lived every day. We are not baptized and now we are saved. We are baptized as a symbol of our decision to walk with Christ—what we have now, and what we will become by God’s grace!

Our baptism means we are now prospective members of the body of Christ—this is an unbelievable reward:

Colossians 2:10, 12: 10 and in him you have been made complete, and he is the head over all rule and authority… 12 having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised up with him through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.

Jesus is the head, and we are part of the body of Christ. Paul talks about this in

1 Corinthians 12:12. In addition, he says in verse 13: For by one spirit are we all baptized into one body.

We were one thing, and now we are something else—and we are part of the body of Christ. This is another reason we can’t be baptized into a church or organization, because we are part of a single entity—the one body of Christ. It has to fit the way Jesus described it to us.

Our baptism opens up the restoration of our lives to favor with God and the renovation of our minds, enabling us to receive the guiding and protective power and influence of God’s spirit.

Titus 3:4–6: (YLT) 4 and when the kindness and the love to men of God our Saviour did appear 5 …He did save us, through a bathing of regeneration, and a renewing of the holy spirit, 6 which He poured upon us richly, through Jesus Christ our saviour.

Through a bathing of regeneration—that really describes baptism beautifully. Regeneration means the restoring of our lives to something higher, better and stronger. And a renewing of the holy spirit—that word renewing appears only twice in the New Testament: here in Titus 3:5 and in Romans 12:2.

Romans 12:2: 2 And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing (the renovation) of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect.

Be transformed by the renovation of your mind—baptism is a symbol of that transformation. We go down underneath the water, symbolizing death. Then we come up out of the water, symbolizing life in Christ.

When we look at the whole concept of baptism, we need to recognize that it includes repentance and the forgiveness of sins. But, in accordance with what Jesus taught us, it is also about following in his footsteps—a life of sacrifice, a life that takes away what used to be and puts on what is new, the new creation. It means putting our lives in the hands of God through Christ.

The begettal of God’s spirit is at the center of all of this. It is the middle part of the process, the power that shapes and guides our everyday lives. Baptism means giving our lives fully into God’s hands through Christ, and allowing His spirit to work within us. This

is what baptism into Christ’s death means—and this is what our everyday lives need to reflect if we have truly made the decision to be baptized into Christ’s death!

So, what does it mean to be baptized into Christ’s death?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

What exactly does baptism symbolize?

Romans 12:1–2: 1 Therefore I urge you, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living and holy sacrifice ...

We present ourselves into the hands of our baptizer—trusting them with our very life: ... acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.

We are only acceptable through Christ and his ransom price paying for our sins, shown as we lay down our lives in the immersion process: 2 And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind,

Not conformed but transformed, like a caterpillar to a butterfly.

Our minds are renovated by the begettal of the holy spirit, shown by being pulled up out of the water, cleansed: ... so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect.

Now we can live differently than before!

2 Timothy 2:11–12: 11 It is a trustworthy statement: For if we died with him, we will also live with him; 12 If we endure, we will also reign with him; If we deny him, he also will deny us.

Whose name are we to be baptized in? The Father, son and holy spirit or just the name of Jesus?

When given instructions about “how to baptize,” some say Jesus gave instructions the apostles did not follow. This would seem odd. Why wouldn’t they follow what the risen Lord had said? Was it not important? Did they forget?

Jesus’ specific instructions given at his ascension:

Matthew 28:19: Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and the son and the holy spirit.

Never in the New Testament are those words (baptizing them in the name of the Father and the son and the holy spirit) actually recorded. Here is what those with the question cite:

Peter at Pentecost:

Acts 2:38: Repent, and each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.

Peter with Cornelius:

Acts 10:48: And he ordered them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.

Paul at Ephesus:

Acts 19:5: When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.

Paul to the Romans:

Romans 6:3: …all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus.

Peter and John visiting Samaria:

Acts 8:16: (ASV) only they had been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.

Important observation: The Bible focuses us on the most important details of important lessons. Let’s start here:

Paul to the Romans:

Romans 6:3: Or do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death?

Because this text does not recount any specific baptism event, it shows us the principle of being baptized INTO Christ. We see this as a clarifier that works alongside of and in the names of the Father, son and holy spirit.

Peter at Pentecost:

Acts 2:38: Peter said to them, Repent, and each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins; and you will receive the gift of the holy spirit.

Why leave the others out? The KEY point for those at Pentecost was raising them up from the Law and into Christ. They all knew John’s baptism. This was new, higher and thoroughly Christ-centered.

Peter with Cornelius:

Acts 10:47–48: 47 Surely no one can refuse the water for these to be baptized who have received the holy spirit just as we did, can he? 48 And he ordered them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ…

The same point is the focus here—Cornelius was adhering to Judaism from a distance and Peter now showed him that Jesus and not the Law had become his center.

Paul at Ephesus:

Acts 19:4–5: 4 Paul said, John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in him who was coming after him, that is, in Jesus. 5 When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.

Simply referring once again to the MOST IMPORTANT difference between the Law and Jesus.

Peter and John visiting Samaria:

Acts 8:14–16: (ASV) 14 Now when the apostles that were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent unto them Peter and John: 15 who, when they were come down, prayed for them, that they might receive the holy spirit: 16 for as yet it was fallen upon none of them: only they had been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.

The point is, the Samaritans were “nominally Jews” and were unequivocally pointed to Christ, not the Law.

- No actual act of baptism is revealed in any of these accounts. We believe the words of Jesus were cited.
- There should never be any baptism into any church or group—only into Christ! - We believe the following words should be used in our day to fulfill scriptural baptism: “In the name of the Father, the son and the holy spirit, by this authority I baptize you in symbol into Christ.”

Baptism Conclusion: Jesus is the centerpiece. Our baptism brings us into Christ (not any church or organization) and that is done in the name of the Father, the son and the holy spirit.
