1. What are the similarities and the differences between John the Baptist’s kind of baptism and the baptism

Jesus introduced? What was the purpose of John’s mission? Use Mark 1:4-5, Hebrews 6:1, Luke 4:18, 24:47, and Romans 6:3 to support your answers.

2. Why did Jesus insist he be baptized even though he had never sinned? (Matthew 3:13-14)

3. Describe all that is included in being “baptized into Christ Jesus, …being baptized with the baptism” he

experienced. Use Romans 6:3, Mark 10:38-40, Luke 14:27-30, and Matthew 7:14 in your answer.

4. How does infant baptism differ from the conscious, voluntary baptism Jesus speaks of? What should we

think about before we consider baptism? What questions should we ask ourselves? (Mark 10:39, Romans 6:3-6, Luke 14:27-30)

5. Many churches require baptism to join their church. What should we be baptized into? Explain Matthew

28:19’s injunction to the apostles, compared to Acts 10:48 and other scriptures that talk about being baptized into Jesus. Are these different baptisms?

6. How does baptism symbolize death and then “newness of life”? What does it mean to be “baptized into

his (Christ’s) death”? (Romans 6:3-6, 12:1-2, Colossians 2:10,12, 2 Timothy 2:11-12, Galatians 3:27-29)

7. What does it mean that we, “who were baptized into Christ have clothed” ourselves, “with Christ”?

(Galatians 3:27-29)

8. Discuss Titus 3:4-6 and Romans 12:2. How does a “bathing of regeneration” and “the renewing of our

minds” affect our everyday lives?

If you are a sincere Christian who has been baptized, or is contemplating baptism:

9. What areas of your old life still need to be surrendered to God? What would it look like to more fully

place one specific area of your life in God’s hands through Christ, to allow His holy spirit to transform it?

10. Are you living out the commitment represented by your baptism daily, or have you allowed baptism to

become something that is a past event? What can you do to better fulfill this?

## Episode 1459 — Are Both Unity and Diversity Possible in Today’s Christianity?
Published: 2026-10-19
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1459-christian-unity-and-diversity/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/12220428/CQ_Rewind_10-19-2026_Are_Both_Unity_and_Diversity_Possible_in_Todays_Christianity.pdf

Ephesians 4:4-6: 4 There is one body and one spirit, just as also you were called in one hope

of your calling; 5 one Lord, one faith, one baptism, 6 one God and Father of all

who is over all and through all and in all.

John 3:16 tells us, For God so loved the world, that He gave His only begotten son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish, but have eternal life. You would think that having such a loving God and such a selfless and loving Redeemer as Jesus, we as Christians would all be unified and be working together to spread the good news and build one another up in faith. Yet, here we stand in countless camps of denominationally divided believers. Why? The answer comes down to the fundamental question of how we decide what is and is not required of us as Christians. A simple observation: we believe that Christianity, Christian unity and diversity must be labeled by Scripture and Scripture only. If we put aside traditions and denominations, what will we find to guide us in building biblical unity and diversity in Christ?

To begin addressing this, we will walk through a good portion of Colossians 3.

As we go, we will frequently pause and ask these questions:

1.

What has the Apostle Paul just defined Christianity as including or excluding?

Inclusive statements: What Paul tells us to put on, pursue, accept or embrace.

Exclusionary statements: What Paul tells us to put off, reject, avoid or leave behind.

2. Based on these biblical descriptions, what does Christian unity accept or oppose?

3. Based on these biblical descriptions, what does Christian diversity accept or

oppose?

We’re going to take Colossians apart piece by piece, read a few verses, and then pause to ask what Paul just said. From there, we’ll bring in additional supporting scriptures and ask how it all applies to Christian unity and diversity.

Let’s begin:

Colossians 3:2-4: 2 Set your mind on the things above, not on the things that are on earth. 3 For you have died and your life is hidden with Christ in God. 4 When Christ, who is our life, is revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory.

1. What has the Apostle Paul just defined Christianity as including or excluding?

What is Paul telling us should be part of our Christian lives, and what should not? We can see that verses 2 and 3 are mainly INCLUSIVE statements—set your mind on the things above, not on the things that are on earth, and Christ…is our life. These are simple, fundamental Christian truths.

(Source: Bible Commentary by William Barclay) From now on the Christian will view everything against the background of eternity and no longer live as if this world was all that mattered. … Sometimes we say of a man, “Music is his life—sport is his life—he lives for his work.” Such a man finds life and all that it means in music, in sport, in work, as the case may be. For the Christian, Christ is his life.

A Christian’s life MUST be about serving God through Jesus and nothing less:

Romans 12:1-2: 1 Therefore I urge you, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living and holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service of worship. 2 And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect.

Colossians 3:2-4 says, Set your mind on the things above, not on the things that are on earth. Romans 12:1-2 says, present your bodies a living and holy sacrifice and do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed. Both are straightforward statements from the Apostle Paul: set our minds on things above and make sure Christ is our life.

Colossians 3:5-6: 5 Therefore consider the members of your earthly body as dead to immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed, which amounts to idolatry. 6 For it is because of these things that the wrath of God will come upon the sons of disobedience.

1. What has the Apostle Paul just defined Christianity as including or excluding?

This is an exclusionary statement. We certainly do not want these things to be a part of our lives!

People might think, Well, my specific sin isn’t listed here, so maybe I’m off the hook. But the Greek words Paul uses are broad categories that cover almost everything. As an example, immorality is translated from the Greek word porneia, from which we get the English word “pornography.” This word is broad, covering all sexual activity outside of

God’s design for marriage, which began with Adam and Eve. There are no loopholes here to find.

As we go through these verses, we will see that things are either inclusive or exclusionary—there are no statements in-between. We need to understand what the foundation is: what is being included and what is being excluded.

A Christian MUST, with great intention and discipline, walk away from their former self:

Galatians 5:19-21: 19 Now the deeds of the flesh are evident, which are: immorality, impurity, sensuality, 20 idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, disputes, dissensions, factions, 21 envying, drunkenness, carousing, and things like these, of which I forewarn you, just as I have forewarned you, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

This is where Christian unity often gets misunderstood. In today’s world, “unity” is sometimes taken to mean accepting everyone exactly as they are with no expectations, no boundaries and no call to change. But Christian unity doesn’t mean embracing behaviors that Scripture identifies as sinful.

We have often said on this podcast that Christianity is “come as you are,” but it’s NOT “stay as you are.” Unity isn’t overlooking or condoning sin. It’s not lowering the standard to include everyone; it’s helping them rise up to the standard in Christ. We don’t have a right to redefine the line that Scripture draws.

What is a practical example of what we need to leave behind from our former way of life as we come to Christ?

One common practice in society today is living together outside of marriage. Christian principles and the biblical foundation are specific: this practice has no place in Christianity. Galatians 5 (above) also makes clear that enmity, strife, anger, etc., are not part of Christian behavior. The same is true for drunkenness and carousing. These behaviors are not Christlike.

Paul goes even further:

Colossians 3:7-9: 7 ...and in them you also once walked, when you were living in them. 8 But now you also, put them all aside: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and abusive speech from your mouth. 9 Do not lie to one another, since you laid aside the old self with its evil practices.

1. What has the Apostle Paul just defined Christianity as including or excluding?

These are obviously exclusionary statements. We should be excluding all these things because we’ve laid aside our old self with its evil practices.

We aren’t adding or deleting from the Apostle Paul’s own words, as they are inspired by God as part of God’s holy word!

This is all about personal transformation, and specifically what destructive behaviors we have to remove in order to bring about that personal transformation. And they must be removed—not just reduced or kept hidden on Sunday and practiced Monday through Saturday. We can’t have just “a little bit” of these behaviors.

Now, none of us is perfect. Maybe we will never completely overcome our weaknesses.

But we, as Christians, MUST continually work at releasing destructive emotions, actions and intentions:

2 Timothy 3:1-4: 1 But realize this, that in the last days difficult times will come. 2 For men will be lovers of self, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, revilers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy, 3 unloving, irreconcilable, malicious gossips, without self-control, brutal, haters of good, 4 treacherous, reckless, conceited, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God…

Why is the Apostle Paul saying this to Christians? Wouldn’t they look at this list and think these things were obvious? Well, obviously not! Have we allowed any of these things to settle in with us? Paul knows that in the last days difficult times will come. We certainly see these around us now. Paul is building on what he said earlier in Colossians 3:2-9.

→ Based on these biblical descriptions, what does Christian unity accept or oppose?

Christian unity opposes dissensions brought on by unscriptural, self-driven or power-driven teachings. Unity won’t happen if we are driven by self-interest:

Romans 16:17-18: 17 Now I urge you, brethren, keep your eye on those who cause dissensions and hindrances contrary to the teaching which you learned, and turn away from them. 18 For such men are slaves, not of our Lord Christ but of their own appetites; and by their smooth and flattering speech they deceive the hearts of the unsuspecting.

Unity requires us to guard the body by recognizing what doesn’t align with sound teaching and turning away from it.

→ Based on these biblical descriptions, what does Christian diversity accept or

oppose?

Christian diversity opposes ungodly morality that draws us away from reverent obedience to Christ:

Ephesians 5:3-5: 3 But immorality or any impurity or greed must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints; 4 and there must be no filthiness and silly talk, or coarse jesting, which are not fitting, but rather giving of thanks. 5 For this you know with certainty, that no immoral or impure person or covetous man, who is an idolater, has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.

Take note of the power of these Colossians 3 texts and their supporting scriptures. They remind us again and again that there are things that do not belong in a Christian’s life. We can’t try to find a way to let them squeak in just a little bit. It’s either yes or no.

Remember after listing immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire and greed, Paul said in

Colossians 3:7, and in them you also once walked, when you were living in them. Jonathan has been open with our audience about how he lived this. His story shows exactly what this looks like in real life.

Yes, this part of the conversation is personal for me. I grew up in a Christian home, but as a young man, I fell hard. I made many bad lifestyle choices—I was a mess. I was broken. I hit bottom. Then God directed me to a Bible study group that opened my eyes to a proper way of living.

If the people there had looked at me and said, “Your kind isn’t wanted,” I don’t know where I’d be today. But they didn’t. They welcomed me. They taught me. They showed me what living for Christ actually looked like. At one point, because I was relocating to a new area for a new job, I was invited to live with Rick’s parents for a while. They accepted me for who I was.

I was given room to learn, grow and transform. I changed my life completely.

So, when we talk about unity, this is what we mean: not accepting sin, but accepting broken people—people just like I was—who are trying to find Christ.

The beauty of that story is that you were not a finished product. First of all, you’re not a finished product yet. Neither am I. Neither is Julie. You were a diamond in the rough, though. Those around you saw the potential in you and showed you how to trim away the unwanted habits and then live in the way you should. It is not about beating someone down with what the Bible says; it is about showing them by example. I watched this happen with you—the beauty of living out the example of what Christlikeness really is.

I’ve also experienced the opposite of Jonathan’s story. There was a person who came to the congregation I belong to as a “former” witch. She seemed sincere and was searching, and many people—including you, Rick, spent much time and effort with her. But in the end, she could not accept that following Christ meant she had to completely leave the principles of witchcraft behind. Eventually, we had to ask her not to attend our services.

Unity cannot embrace behaviors that openly oppose Christ. Jonathan chose the path of transformation. This other person refused it. Both illustrate the sides of what Paul means when he says, “You once walked in these things, but now put them aside.”

We often want to bring some of our old habits along on our Christian transformation. Instead, we must leave those things behind and press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God … Philippians 3:14.

These first few verses in Colossians 3 have shown us a lot of things that simply do not belong in the life of a Christian.

We can’t build unity on top of a pile of unremoved sin and destructive habits. This is why the Apostle Paul starts by clearing the area, making room for a solid foundation on which unity can be built. Then he shows us what true Christian unity and diversity look like.

The details of what we are to avoid are dramatic. These graphic descriptions are there to get our attention and set us on the right path.

The Apostle Paul is getting our attention so we can truly absorb big lessons. Now that we know what to avoid, what are we to follow after and embrace?

By emphatically beginning with identifying the things that need to be put out of our lives, Paul is encouraging us to remove them and make room in our hearts and minds for genuine Christlikeness. All calls to diversity and unity must begin with this approach.

We simply cannot be unified in Christ unless we are actually in Christ first.

Colossians 3:10-11: 10 …and have put on the new self who is being renewed to a true knowledge according to the image of the One who created him— 11 a renewal in which there is no distinction between Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave and freeman, but Christ is all, and in all.

1. What has the Apostle Paul just defined Christianity as including or excluding?

We will break this into two sections.

Paul is showing that Christianity includes a life being renewed—a new self that God is remaking from the inside out.

It is not simply about doing what needs to be done; it is about becoming the person we need to be so that we CAN do what needs to be done.

A Christian’s life MUST continually submit to being continually renewed in Christ. And make no mistake; it is a battle!

2 Corinthians 4:16-18: 16 Therefore we do not lose heart, but though our outer man is decaying, yet our inner man is being renewed day by day. 17 For momentary, light affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory far beyond all comparison, 18 while we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen; for the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.

This is practical advice. Paul says our inner man is being renewed day by day—meaning real, lasting change takes time. We can’t expect it to happen just because we are a Christian. We learn to shift our focus from the temporary to the eternal. That shift shows up in the choices we make, how we respond to pressure and discouragement, and what things we allow to capture our attention. We have a new perspective!

Fighting this battle requires a “true knowledge” of how and why to fight:

2 Timothy 2:15-16: 15 Be diligent to present yourself approved to God as a workman who does not need to be ashamed, accurately handling the word of truth. 16 But avoid worldly and empty chatter, for it will lead to further ungodliness.

Be diligent to present yourself approved to God as a workman—we have to DO the work. We are not handed the work already done. This is what the renewal of our lives is about— doing the work.

Let’s look at the next inclusive part of Colossians 3:10-11.

(Paraphrasing Barclay commentary): Paul lists the major divisions of the ancient world— ethnic, religious, cultural and social. The ancient world was full of barriers. Greeks looked down on anyone who didn’t speak Greek—they called them “barbarians.” Jews saw themselves as God’s chosen people. Scythians were considered the worst of the barbarians, the most savage and uncivilized people imaginable. Slaves weren’t even viewed as human beings in ancient law. They were just living tools with no rights of their own.

Paul’s point is clear: Christ breaks down every barrier, even the ones we think are impossible—like the Scythians!

A Christian’s life MUST be lived by recognizing that each of us is but one ingredient in the body:

1 Corinthians 12:12-14: 12 For even as the body is one and yet has many members, and all the members of the body, though they are many, are one body, so also is Christ. 13 For by one spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free, and we were all made to drink of one spirit. 14 For the body is not one member, but many.

What encouraging texts! When we come into Christ and see others who are much further along than we are, we can become discouraged, thinking we could never be like that. But we CAN be the person God has called us to be, one small step at a time, developing from the inside out as we leave those ungodly things in our lives behind us.

It is a beautiful example of being part of something bigger than ourselves, driven by Christlikeness.

→ Based on these biblical descriptions, what does Christian unity accept or oppose?

Christian unity embraces the varied contributions needed for our Christian mission to be fulfilled:

Ephesians 4:11-13: 11 And He gave some as apostles, and some as prophets, and some as evangelists, and some as pastors and teachers, 12 for the equipping of the saints for the work of service, to the building up of the body of Christ; 13 until we all attain to the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the son of God, to a mature man, to the measure of the stature which belongs to the fullness of Christ.

Until we all attain to the unity of the faith—no one is left out; no one is “less unified” than another. It is one body of Christ together. To become mature Christians, we are working together and drawing each other up. This is the unity the Apostle Paul is describing.

→ Based on these biblical descriptions, what does Christian diversity accept or

oppose?

Christian diversity strongly embraces the call of Christ going out to every culture and level of society:

Galatians 3:27-29: 27 For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ. 28 There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus. 29 And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's descendants, heirs according to promise.

It doesn’t matter what our heritage, lineage or social status is if we belong to Christ. We are all heirs according to the promise. Everyone is there together because they are in Christ—not because of their own worldly thinking.

Paraphrasing William Barclay commentary: As a former Pharisee, Paul would have grown up saying a certain morning prayer (Tosefta Berakhot 6:18 and Babylonian Talmud, Menachot 43b) where a man thanked God he was not a Gentile, not a slave, and not a woman. Paul takes these categories and removes their power to mark someone’s identity. In Christ, these kinds of distinctions no longer determine value, identity or a standing before God. Social boundaries don’t define you anymore. As we read before, Christ is our life.

And so, the “mature in Christ” Apostle Paul is talking to himself as he talks to us, reminding us of what he used to be and what he has grown into. What an encouragement for us! He had a long way to go, and so do we.

There are a lot of things to be put aside, as we listed in the first segment. Once we have taken those things out of the way, we can stop focusing on them and begin focusing on our growth. That is how we begin to grow.

When we compare what we have given up with all that we are receiving in Christ, this really becomes an easy decision to make.

We have accepted the comparison between life in the world and life in Christ.

So, what do we grow into next?

For us to find and actually rejoice in the unity and diversity that life in Christ provides, we need to next focus on making this renewal a way of life for ourselves as well as for those we walk alongside.

Now comes the deep dive into the character development that provokes true Christian unity and embraces true Christian diversity:

Colossians 3:12-13: 12 So, as those who have been chosen of God, holy and beloved, put on a heart of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience; 13 bearing <430> with one another, and forgiving each other, whoever has a complaint against anyone; just as the Lord forgave you, so also should you.

Bearing: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #430 anéchomai; to hold oneself up against,

i.e. (figuratively) put up with:—bear with, endure, forbear, suffer

Paul says to “put on” these Christlike qualities. It’s like putting on new clothes. Changing our character doesn’t happen automatically—we have to make a conscious choice to put on these qualities and live them out in our personal relationships. This is what it means to be made alive in Christ—a new wardrobe of the heart.

1. What has the Apostle Paul just defined Christianity as including or excluding?

A Christian’s life MUST be grounded in compassionate communication based in scriptural principles:

Ephesians 4:25-27: 25 Therefore, laying aside falsehood, SPEAK TRUTH EACH ONE of you WITH HIS NEIGHBOR, for we are members of one another. 26 BE ANGRY, AND yet DO NOT SIN; do not let the sun go down on your anger, 27 and do not give the devil an opportunity.

Lay aside falsehood, speak truth because we belong to each other. We are connected. We do get angry at times, but don’t sin. Put things in order so we can leave the past behind and move forward. This is what putting on a heart of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience looks like.

Paul continues with another inclusionary statement:

Bearing with one another basically means putting up with each other—enduring with patience. Paul uses a Greek form of the word that implies continual action. If we can do this for each other, it gives us room to grow while we are being transformed.

And notice Paul is not so subtle about why we are to forgive others—because we ourselves were forgiven. We must, in turn, be forgiving.

A Christian’s life MUST be able to work past its own friction-causing emotions and support others:

1 Corinthians 3:3-7: 3 For you are still fleshly. For since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not fleshly, and are you not walking like mere men? 4 For when one says, I am of Paul, and another, I am of Apollos, are you not mere men? 5 What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? Servants through whom you believed, even as the Lord gave opportunity to each one. 6 I planted, Apollos watered, but God was causing the growth. 7 So then neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who causes the growth.

Paul gives an example of that fleshly attitude: dividing themselves over leaders, saying I am of Paul, or I am of Apollos. But Paul and Apollos are just servants. One planted, one watered, but only God makes anything grow.

This is friction caused by emotions: I like the way Paul does it better, Apollos is better, I’m with Christ! Stop! We have to swallow our pride and look to the scriptural principle—God causes the growth. It doesn’t come from us. It comes through us by His grace.

→ Based on these biblical descriptions, what does Christian unity accept or oppose?

Christian unity embraces the “new creation” in our brotherhood even when we may not like them:

Ephesians 4:31-32: 31 Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice. 32 Be kind to one another, tender-hearted, forgiving each other, just as God in Christ also has forgiven you.

We embrace those with different personalities. It’s a GOOD thing that everyone isn’t like us! This is diversity.

We can’t be unified if we’re full of bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander.

→ Based on these biblical descriptions, what does Christian diversity accept or

oppose?

Christian diversity thoroughly embraces the uniqueness and variety in the lives of our brotherhood and how their different approaches are also focused on sacrificially serving God through Christ:

Romans 14:4,8: 4 Who are you to judge the servant of another? To his own master he stands or falls; and he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand 8 for if we live, we live for the Lord, or if we die, we die for the Lord; therefore whether we live or die, we are the Lord's.

Paul explains that Christians may differ in how they handle certain practices—and that’s okay! What matters is that our choices are made for the Lord, with a sincere desire to honor Jesus and a clear conscience before God.

We don’t have to deal with our fellow Christians eating meat offered to idols like Paul did, but today, maybe some choose to fast and some don’t. Some abstain from alcohol entirely, while others feel that some wine with dinner is just fine. We have different clothing preferences, make different medical decisions, we decide how to spend our free time and our money, and even the style of our worship music, just to name a few. Christians differ in choices involving matters of conscience, and we aren’t supposed to judge one another for those differences.

We come from such different backgrounds, and that is one of the reasons our congregation has a devotional meeting every three months or so. That Sunday gathering is focused entirely on devotion. The assignment is for anyone who would like to bring a song, poem or something else that is inspiring to them. The rule for all of us is to accept the style, whatever it is. We listen to it, and the individual explains what it means to them. And we get a wide variety. We have older brethren and younger brethren from different cultures. We’ve had rap, classical, country and gospel music. Sometimes it’s just a straightforward hymn. But it is a beautiful combination because everyone is contributing and listening to what others have brought. We find appreciation in each contribution because it came from someone’s heart. That is part of the diversity we are truly looking to develop.

Unity grows when we treat each other with compassion and forgiveness. Diversity works when we give people space to serve God in ways that fit their own conscience. Notice how all of this is based on Christlike principles—what we leave behind and what we build our foundation upon.

There is a lot to be said for growing into genuine Christlikeness. Without it, the ideas of unity and diversity simply remain ideas.

Without developing a true Christian character, we cannot expect to experience true

Christian unity and diversity. What comes next?

This is such an important point. So much of the “unity” and “diversity” we now see in many Christian circles is based on meeting people where they are and not lifting them out of their fleshly lives.

Returning to Colossians, we see this lifting can only take place when selfless love is at work in a Christlike character:

Colossians 3:14-15: 14 Beyond all these things put on love, which is the perfect bond of unity. 15 Let <1018> the peace of Christ rule <1018> in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body; and be thankful.

1. What has the Apostle Paul just defined Christianity as including or excluding?

Paul has been building layer after layer—putting off the old self, putting on the new self, learning compassion, patience, forgiveness—and now he ties it all together with love. Here’s where the unity comes in.

This tells us a Christian’s life MUST grow to be driven by selfless love. There is no other way:

Ephesians 4:15-16: 15 But speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in all aspects into him who is the head, even Christ, 16 from whom the whole body, being fitted and held together by what every joint supplies, according to the proper working of each individual part, causes the growth of the body for the building up of itself in love.

We are to grow up. This means leaving behind everything in the negative list in the beginning of Colossians 3.

Literally the Greek means, “Let the peace of Christ be the umpire in your heart.” Sporting events were a big part of Greek society in Paul’s day.

Let rule: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1018 brabeúō; to arbitrate, i.e. (genitive case) to govern (figuratively, prevail):—rule

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1. to be an umpire; 2. to decide, determine;

3. to direct, control, rule

(Source: Commentary by William Barclay) He uses a verb from the athletic arena; it is the word that is used of the umpire who settled things in any matter of dispute. If the peace of Jesus Christ is the umpire in any man’s heart, then, when feelings clash and we are pulled in two directions at the same time, the decision of Christ will keep us in the way of love and the church will remain the one body it is meant to be. The way to right action is to appoint Jesus Christ as the arbiter between the conflicting emotions in our hearts; and if we accept his decisions, we cannot go wrong.

A Christian’s life must surrender to the peace of Christ reigning over us and guiding our efforts toward unity. Unity doesn’t happen simply because we’re in the same room. It happens because, despite being naturally different, we choose to work at it.

We need to have the peace of Christ as the basis for our working together toward this unity:

Ephesians 2:14-16: 14 For he himself is our peace, who made both groups into one and broke down the barrier of the dividing wall, 15 by abolishing in his flesh the enmity... so that in himself he might make the two into one new man, thus establishing peace, 16 and might reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, by it having put to death the enmity.

Make the two into one man—what a strong, united effect! Christ himself is our peace. We are called to one body, and we must act like what we were called to be. That requires us to follow the instruction and direction of the Scriptures, putting aside traditions and

denominationalism. We follow the Scriptures so we can walk toward the true Christian unity we are called to develop.

Colossians 3:16-17: 16 Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you, with all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with thankfulness in your hearts to God. 17 Whatever you do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks through him to God the Father.

1. What has the Apostle Paul just defined Christianity as including or excluding?

Paul is saying that Christianity includes letting the word of Christ take up full residence in us—not just visiting on Sundays, but actually living in us in a way that shapes our thinking, our priorities and how we react. When something “richly dwells within us,” it means it has decorated the inside of our hearts and minds. It influences who we are and what we become.

A Christian’s life MUST be driven by seeking opportunities to serve and sacrifice for our brotherhood. Let’s look at how Jesus supports this thought:

John 13:14-16: 14 If I then, the Lord and the teacher, washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet. 15 For I gave you an example that you also should do as I did to you. 16 Truly, truly, I say to you, a slave is not greater than his master, nor is one who is sent greater than the One who sent him.

There is an emotional release in singing with thankfulness in our hearts to God. We

can build each other up this way—with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs. We are thankful for God’s grace, strength, guidance, providence and spirit.

A Christian’s life MUST learn to be inspired by God’s word and to share that inspiration with others:

2 Peter 1:2-4: 2 Grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord; 3 seeing that His divine power has granted to us everything pertaining to life and godliness, through the true knowledge of Him who called us by His own glory and excellence. 4 For by these He has granted to us His precious and magnificent promises, so that by them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world by lust.

If we look at His precious and magnificent promises for those who follow in Jesus’ footsteps, they provide guidance, strength, encouragement and inspiration through every part of our lives and every trial we face. God does not promise to take away our trials, but He does provide the ways and means to get through them by His grace. We need to be inspired by these promises and allow them to strengthen us.

Don’t just say it—be an example of what it looks like in action.

A few years ago, I went to see a client who is a Christian. When I was ready to go, he asked if he could pray for me before I left. I said sure, and he started praying. But he prayed the kind of prayer sometimes called a “decree and declare” prayer, where he declared that the traffic would be cleared, that my way would be safe, and so on.

He finished, I thanked him, and walked out to my car. Once I got there, I bowed my head and asked the Lord to forgive that prayer. We have no right to decree and declare anything from God other than, “Let Your will be done.”

A Christian’s life MUST learn to stand strong in God’s grace with humble acceptance of one another. This is the context for our theme scripture:

Ephesians 4:1-6: 1 Therefore I, the prisoner of the Lord, implore you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling with which you have been called, 2 with all humility and gentleness, with patience, showing tolerance for one another in love, 3 being diligent to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace. 4 There is one body and one spirit, just as also you were called in one hope of your calling; 5 one Lord, one faith, one baptism, 6 one God and Father of all who is over all and through all and in all.

This gives us a sense of the humble acceptance we need to have for one another to find true Christian unity in the midst of our diversity.

→ Based on these biblical descriptions, what does Christian unity accept or oppose?

Christian unity embraces the contributions of the brotherhood that are unique to each of them:

1 Corinthians 12:21-23: 21 And the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you; or again the head to the feet, I have no need of you. 22 On the contrary, it is much truer that the members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary; 23 and those members of the body which we deem less honorable, on these we bestow more abundant honor, and our less presentable members become much more presentable.

How good are we at looking at those who may seem to have less to offer or who are not as eloquent? Maybe they don’t have the education or the means to do this or that. Should we look at them on the same level as those who are more talented? No. We should put them on an even higher level because they may be working so much harder!

That is true unity. Stop being full of ourselves and start being full of the fellowship we share in the body of Christ.

→ Based on these biblical descriptions, what does Christian diversity accept or

oppose?

Christian diversity thoroughly embraces the challenge of inclusion even when we stand apart, see things differently or have struggles with one another:

1 Corinthians 1:10-13: 10 Now I exhort you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all agree and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be made complete in the same mind and in the same judgment. 11 For I have been informed concerning you, my brethren… that there are quarrels among you. 12 …That each one of you is saying, I am of Paul, and I of Apollos, and I of Cephas, and I of Christ. 13 Has Christ been divided? Paul was not crucified for you, was he? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?

Let’s put the pettiness aside. The strength of the brotherhood is built on Christlikeness and scriptural principles. We must work together based on those scriptural principles and build true unity by treasuring our true diversity, each bringing our unique talents to the body.

Before we end, what is the answer to our theme question? Are both unity and diversity possible in today’s Christianity—are we supposed to work hard to bring all denominations and sects together as one?

Our focus is to find the foundation of true Christianity in Scripture, to stand firmly and only on that foundation, and to draw together those who likewise stand for these things.

Frankly and bluntly, there are many denominations that look at diversity as "Come as you are, and basically stay as you are; and it's okay, we're all in this together." It has to be that we come together, we come as we are, but we don't stay that way. We have to grow in Christ.

We have quoted many scriptures to show how the Bible describes this life.

What do the Scriptures teach us about Christian unity and Christian diversity?

How well am I walking along those lines, essentially ignoring and putting everything else behind me?

The Bible defines every part of our lives in a scriptural fashion so we can build unity and accept diversity within the context of being a true disciple of Christ.

That is our mission. That is what our lives are about. That is what we are called to: Be not conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your minds…

Thereby, find unity and find diversity in Christ!

So, are both unity and diversity possible in today’s Christianity?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.
