## Episode 1460 — What is the Balance Between Pride and Humility?
Published: 2026-10-26
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1460-pride-and-humility/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/16161104/CQ_Rewind_10-26-2026_What_is_the_Balance_Between_Pride_and_Humility.pdf

Matthew 23:11–12: 11 But the greatest among you shall be your servant. 12 Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled; and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted.

Jesus emphatically taught us that personal humility is a primary ingredient in the life of anyone professing to be his disciple. His own humble example was an unmistakable illustration of what our lives are supposed to look like. When it came to pride and self-exaltation, he was just as emphatic. As we strive to understand how to apply humility and avoid pride, several questions come to the surface. First, what does true humility mean? Is it a self-deprecating behavior that renounces our ability to do or accomplish anything good? And what about pride? Are we never to be “proud” of anyone or of any accomplishment in our lives? As usual, when we examine the Scriptures, the answers to these questions about humility and pride will all present themselves with great clarity!

As we consider humility, we need to begin with the strongest source—Jesus’ own example and words:

John 13:12–17: 12 So when he had washed their feet, and taken his garments and reclined at the table again, he said to them, Do you know what I have done to you? 13 You call me Teacher and Lord; and you are right, for so I am. 14 If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. 15 For I gave you an example that you also should do as I did to you. 16 Truly, truly, I say to you, a slave is not greater than his master, nor is one who is sent greater than the one who sent him. 17 If you know these things, you are blessed if you do them.

If you know these things—great! But you are blessed if you do them.

According to Jesus’ actions, what does humility look like?

It’s impressive that the son of God humbled himself to teach sinful humanity how to serve one another. Jesus, God's co-Creator, was willing to lower himself to this level. It is mind- boggling! God's beloved son, washing feet like a servant. What a beautiful demonstration of humility and love.

He put himself in the lowest position. The others who had their feet washed were vying for position and status, but Jesus lowered himself beneath everyone. He then showed them how to serve one another and said, If I then… washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.

A few weeks prior to the washing of the feet example, Jesus was speaking to his disciples and the people, in the company of the scribes and Pharisees.

His words delivered a pointed lesson in humility aimed towards the scribes and Pharisees:

Matthew 23:8–12: 8 But do not be called Rabbi; for one is your Teacher, and you are all brothers. 9 Do not call anyone on earth your father; for One is your Father, He who is in

heaven. 10 Do not be called leaders; for one is your Leader, that is, Christ. 11 But the greatest among you shall be your servant. 12 Whoever exalts <5312> himself shall be humbled <5013>; and whoever humbles <5013> himself shall be exalted <5312>.

One is your Teacher—Jesus. One is your Father—God. One is your Leader—Christ. The scribes and Pharisees had taken these titles for themselves among the Israelites. But who was the ultimate Teacher, Father, and Leader of the nation of Israel? It was God.

Jesus addressed the arrogance of the scribes and Pharisees as they sought to exalt their positions and in effect take God’s place here on earth. Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled… They knew he was talking about them!

Let’s briefly introduce the meaning of exalt, which we will examine more deeply later.

Exalt: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5312 hupsoo; to elevate (literally or figuratively)

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) to lift up on high, to exalt 2a) to raise to the very summit of opulence

and prosperity 2b) to exalt, to raise to dignity, honour and happiness

To exalt means to elevate. If someone exalts himself, he lifts himself to a higher place, to the summit of prosperity, raised to a place of dignity and honor. But Jesus was saying that if we exalt ourselves, we will be humbled, or brought low.

What about humility?

Humbles: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5013 tapeinoo; to depress;

figuratively, to humiliate (in condition or heart)

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) to make low, bring low… 1b1) to assign a lower rank or place to 1b2) to abase 1b3) to be ranked below others who are honoured or rewarded… 1c2) to have a modest

opinion of one’s self 1c3) to behave in an unassuming manner 1c4) devoid of all haughtiness

It means to make low, bring low, to have a modest opinion of oneself, or to behave in an unassuming manner. We can see the contrast between exaltation, self-exaltation and humility.

There is no dishonesty or exaggeration when defining humility. Humility is about learning

to honestly assess, in a godly manner, who we are and what we are capable of. It’s not exaggerating by saying, “I’m useless.” It is understanding what we can become and then moving forward toward that realization with God’s guidance.

Humility doesn’t mean we have no value; it simply means we maintain an honest assessment of our value. If our heavenly Father has called us to be disciples of Jesus, we have potential.

Here is Jesus’ own humility explained:

Philippians 2:5–8: 5 Have this attitude in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, 6 who, although he existed in the form of God, did not regard equality with God a thing to be grasped, 7 but emptied himself, taking the form of a bond-servant, and being made in the likeness of

men. 8 Being found in appearance as a man, he humbled <5013> himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.

This shows Jesus’ pre-human status and then explains what he did with it. He did not seek equality with God; he was a spiritual being working alongside God.

Yet he voluntarily took that position and laid it aside to take on the humanity he was given. Then he even laid that aside in death. He humbled himself completely. This describes the humility of Jesus.

There is great humility in his greatness, and that is what makes his greatness so great.

We’ve looked at Jesus’ words describing humility, examples of how he challenged those who weren’t being humble, and a description of his own humility.

Now let’s look at how Jesus explains his own humility:

Matthew 11:27–30: 27 All things have been handed over to me by my Father; and no one knows the son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father except the son, and anyone to whom the son wills to reveal Him.

Does the fact that Jesus explained it take anything away from his humility? Is he bragging here?

No! In saying, all things have been handed over to me by my Father; and no one knows the son except the Father; nor… the Father except the son… he gave an accurate assessment of himself and the role he was privileged to have been given.

28 Come to me, all who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you rest. 29 Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble <5011> in heart, and YOU WILL FIND REST FOR YOUR SOULS. 30 For my yoke is easy and my burden is light.

Humble: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5011 tapeinos; depressed,

i.e. (figuratively) humiliated (in circumstances or disposition)

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) not rising far from the ground 2) metaph. 2a) as a condition, lowly, of low degree … 2c) lowly in spirit, humble 2d) in a bad sense, deporting one’s self abjectly,

deferring servilely to others

We saw in Philippians 2:5-8 that he brought himself to a lower position—the form of a bond-servant. So when he says, Come to me, all who are weary and heavy-laden… for I am gentle and humble in heart, he is saying, “Come to me because I know who I am, what I’ve been given, and my responsibility of what I am to give to you.”

This makes him incredibly approachable. This truly humble man could describe the power and authority he was given without any arrogance or self-interest. We can feel embraced in his presence.

In this first segment, we’ve looked at Jesus’ humility—what he said, what he did and how the Scriptures describe him. This provides a strong foundation for understanding what true humility encompasses.

Jesus emptied himself, going from a mighty spirit being to a human being. And we, too, have to empty ourselves of our own will and ego so we can be used by God. This is a lifelong process.

That is why we are trying to understand pride and humility—how the two work together or fail to work together. When we start with Jesus, we get the clearest picture of humility in action on every level.

Jesus always shows us the way. Our job is to pay attention as we learn to embrace what he said and how he lived as a pattern for our own lives!

Jesus’ example is absolutely inspiring!

How do we make that example real and practical in our own lives?

The best way to follow the example of our perfect Lord Jesus is to follow the examples of those who were our original Christian teachers. They, like us, were imperfect and subject to the failures that we are subject to. Paying close attention to their experiences and their wise words will guide us as we seek to progress step by step along our path of discipleship.

Following Jesus’ perfect example of humility can be discouraging because it is perfect! Let’s look at those who weren’t perfect so we can relate to their struggles.

◼ Be drawn to those who are good examples of living a humble life.

Romans 12:14–16: 14 Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse. 15 Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep. 16 Be of the same mind toward one another;

do not be haughty in mind, but associate with the lowly <5011> (humble). Do not be wise in your own estimation.

Associate—be drawn to those who can show us what humility looks like and how they live it. As we spend time with them, their example of Christianity will help us improve our own behavior. That’s a good place to start when choosing our associations.

◼ By truly and sincerely humbling ourselves after the example of Jesus, we are drawn into God’s favor.

Here’s what happens when we put ourselves in that position:

James 4:6–7: 6 But He gives a greater grace. Therefore it says, GOD IS OPPOSED TO THE PROUD <5244>, BUT GIVES GRACE TO THE HUMBLE <5011>. 7 Submit therefore to God.

Resist the devil and he will flee from you.

Proud: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5244 huperephanos; appearing above others

(conspicuous), i.e. (figuratively) haughty

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) showing one’s self above others, overtopping, conspicuous

above others, pre-eminent

The devil, Satan, is identified in the Bible as the first being to possess pride. We need to flee from his influence. God is opposed to the proud. The word proud means “appearing above others.” God is opposed to those who conspicuously display their haughtiness. Haughty means “self-important.” Yet God gives grace to the humble. This lesson draws us toward God’s favor by encouraging us to work on our humility.

Now some steps to bring us to a more humble life:

James 4:8–9: 8 Draw near to God and He will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners; and purify your hearts, you double-minded. 9 Be miserable and mourn and weep; let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy to gloom.

This is the process of changing from self to selflessness. This almost sounds depressing: Be miserable and mourn and weep; let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy to gloom. Is this really the way we are supposed to live?

The point here is to be serious, be humble and not be double-minded. Be reverent as we assess who we are, what we’re doing, how we’re acting and how we’re coming across to others. We need to come across as Jesus did and follow the example of other faithful Christians in the Scriptures.

Don’t get overexcited by accolades or by people thinking we are awesome Christians. This is not what we seek. God draws us to Him by giving grace to those who are humble.

◼ A promised result of living a humble life as a true disciple of Jesus is God lifting us up!

We don’t elevate ourselves. Only God will lift us up.

James 4:10: Humble <5013> yourselves in the presence of the Lord, and He will exalt <5312> you.

God lifts us up. Humility doesn’t mean we should never receive recognition. On the contrary, recognition may come—but it should NOT come from us about ourselves. It might come through whatever position God puts us in where others can see something different about us.

I work in a service business with a lot of other people. Several years ago, a very quiet individual worked with us. He would just watch. One day, he walked up to me and asked, “Rick, where do you go to church?” I said, “A non-denominational church that studies the Scriptures, but why do you ask?” He said, “Because I want to go to church where you go so I can be like you are.”

I wasn’t walking around preaching at work, saying, “Let me show you Jesus!” It was a matter of living righteously—with integrity, kindness and clarity—and trying to be as wise as I could. He saw those characteristics without a single religious word being spoken and wanted that for himself.

It startled me. It wasn’t about trying to impress everyone with my religiousness. It was about letting my life say, Let me be like Jesus. God is the one who does the lifting!

◼ Always relate to one another from the basis of equality and the attitude of service.

1 Peter 5:1–5: 1 Therefore, I exhort the elders among you, as your fellow elder and witness of the sufferings of Christ, and a partaker also of the glory that is to be revealed, 2 shepherd the flock of God among you, exercising oversight not under compulsion, but voluntarily, according to the will of God; and not for sordid gain, but with eagerness; 3 nor yet as lording it over those allotted to your charge, but proving to be examples to the flock. 4 And when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory. 5 You younger men, likewise, be subject to your elders; and all of you, clothe yourselves with humility <5012> (modesty) toward one another, for GOD IS OPPOSED TO THE PROUD <5244>, BUT GIVES GRACE TO THE HUMBLE <5011>.

Humility: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5012 tapeinophrosune; from a compound of #5011 and

the base of #5424; humiliation of mind, i.e. modesty

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) the having a humble opinion of one’s self

2) a deep sense of one’s (moral) littleness

Clothe yourselves with humility is a beautiful phrase. Our humility should be something others can see; something that you're “wearing” they notice and can relate to.

Peter begins, I exhort the elders—those who have responsibility for guiding, directing, teaching and leading others in the flock. He speaks to them as a fellow elder, not from a position of superiority as “the Apostle Peter.” It’s as if he’s saying, “Here is what we need to do. Here is our example.” He exhorts them to be examples to the flock, not to create distance between those who lead and those who are members. The elders should be among them.

Clothing ourselves with humility is exactly the point. Be like the positive scriptural examples we have been given. Show Christlikeness by simply being a part of things. It is a beautiful thought. And again, God gives grace to the humble. This “humiliation of mind” (as defined in Thayer’s) means seeing ourselves as no higher in status than others. This is so important.

Again, we see the same equation appearing—humbling ourselves brings exaltation from God:

1 Peter 5:6–7: 6 Therefore humble yourselves <5013> under the mighty hand of God, that He may exalt <5312> you at the proper time, 7 casting all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.

Humble yourselves, and don’t worry about the exalting part. It’s not our concern if we are casting all our anxiety on Him, because He cares for us. Do we need to be exalted if we know God is caring for us? His care is all the exaltation we need.

◼ Recognize that our humility is one of many factors in our being called and chosen by God to follow in Jesus’ footsteps.

Colossians 3:12–14: 12 So, as those who have been chosen of God, holy and beloved, put on (or “clothe yourselves with”) a heart of compassion, kindness, humility <5012>, gentleness and patience; 13 bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, whoever has a complaint against anyone; just as the Lord forgave you, so also should you. 14 Beyond all these things put on love, which is the perfect bond of unity.

We have heard from Peter, James and Paul, all telling us the same things. Be a humble person. Put on humility and make it part of who we are, just like Jesus did. Remember how he lowered himself to become a man to save mankind?

We need to have that same humble attitude.

Humility is right in the middle of the list above, and each of the qualities listed works better in combination with humility. If we are arrogant, having a heart of compassion, kindness, gentleness and patience will not develop as it should. But with humility, these qualities flourish.

◼ See our fellow disciples through the lens of them “having higher value” than we do. Why? We can’t read anyone’s heart or intentions, so we need to give them the benefit of the doubt.

Philippians 2:2–3: 2 make my joy complete by being of the same mind, maintaining the same love, united in spirit, intent on one purpose. 3 Do nothing from selfishness or empty conceit, but with humility of mind <5012> regard one another as more important than yourselves;

The followers of Jesus are precious to our heavenly Father. They should be precious to us as well. If they belong to Him, they belong to us. When we have the utter privilege of working, living or contributing alongside those who belong to God, think of how we can honor and praise Him through the way we honor, teach and care for them. It comes down to being thankful for the opportunity to interact with others of God’s children.

These are the lessons from those who have gone before us, who walked in Jesus’ footsteps, and by their example, showed us how to do it.

We can’t look at others with the thought, They don’t know what I know. Instead, view them as God’s children, doing what they are capable of doing when they are capable of doing it.

Humility requires a lot from us. We need to learn to embrace these requirements as coming from God through Jesus and envision ourselves living this way.

We have seen many aspects unfold as to what our humility is to look like. What about pride? Is there any kind of pride that is acceptable for a Christian?

The gut reaction to this is no! There is no place for pride in the life of a Christian. However, we need to carefully unpack exactly what pride means and what it doesn’t mean. Once again, the Scriptures give us very specific and strong guidance regarding how we as

Christians should respond to any goodness, blessing and accomplishments that come our way.

As we get into the topic of pride, we need to understand it and recognize that some forms of it may be valuable, while others are not. Again we turn to Jesus’ words.

In this short parable, Jesus illustrates the fundamental value of humility, as well as the value of appropriate exaltation:

Luke 18:9–14: 9 And he also told this parable to some people who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and viewed others with contempt: 10 Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. 11 The Pharisee stood and was praying this to himself:

➢ God, I thank You that I am not like other people: swindlers,

unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. ➢ 12 I fast twice a week; ➢ I pay tithes of all that I get.

13 But the tax collector, standing some distance away, was even unwilling to lift up his eyes to heaven, but was beating his breast, saying, God, be merciful to me, the sinner! 14 I tell you, this man went to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts <5312> himself will be humbled <5013>, but he who humbles <5013> himself will be exalted <5312>.

Jesus unfolds this simple little story by contrasting the words and actions of one who saw himself as above the other with those of one who saw himself as unworthy. Jesus shows us that when we pat ourselves on the back we are exalting ourselves, and we’ve lost sight of humility. On the contrary, when we are just trying to climb into God’s favor because we are so needy that we cannot even look up as we pray, we are made right.

Again, Jesus says here, he who exalts himself will be humbled. And he who humbles himself will be exalted. The exaltation comes from above, from God, not from ourselves.

The Pharisees put themselves in the seat of Moses (Matthew 23:2-3; meaning a position of authority in teaching and interpreting the Law of Moses), but they forgot that Moses was one of the meekest men on earth when God called him to lead.

When God called Moses, he essentially said, “God, you’ve got the wrong guy. I’m not your man. I can’t do that.” But God asked him, What is that in your hand? Moses answered, A staff. God showed Moses that He could use that staff—and Moses himself—to accomplish His purpose. God had to help Moses see what he was capable of with His guidance. (Exodus 4:1-4)

The Pharisees put themselves in the seat of Moses, but with the opposite attitude—one of arrogance and entitlement. If we approach responsibility with humility and a willingness to seek God’s direction, we can serve in a position of responsibility with reverence.

Let’s begin with some of the more dramatic kinds of pride mentioned in Scripture:

1 John 2:15–17: 15 Do not love the world nor the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. 16 For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes and the boastful pride <212>, is not from the Father, but is from the world. 17 The world is passing away, and also its lusts; but the one who does the will of God lives forever.

Boastful pride: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #212 alazoneia; from #213; braggadocio,

i.e. (by implication) self-confidence

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) empty, braggart talk… 3) an impious and empty presumption which

trusts in the stability of earthy things

The words boastful pride come from the Greek word alazoneia, meaning self-confidence and empty, braggart talk. Someone who has braggadocio has an overabundance of self- confidence. It just pours out of them. This is what John calls the boastful pride of life. He is warning us to stay away from this kind of attitude.

Paul is writing about some who have rejected God and godliness:

Romans 1:29–31: 29 being filled with all unrighteousness, wickedness, greed, evil; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malice; they are gossips, 30 slanderers, haters of God, insolent, arrogant <5244>, boastful <213>, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, 31 without understanding, untrustworthy, unloving, unmerciful.

Boastful: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #213 alazon; from ale (vagrancy); braggart

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) an empty pretender, a boaster

Remember, the word for arrogant means “appearing above others” or “self-important.” Boastful means someone who brags. “Look what I can do. Look what I’ve done. Look how good I am. Did you notice? It’s all about me!”

When we take God out of the center of our lives, the propensity to become prideful grows. Is this kind of pride acceptable within Christianity? No, not in the slightest! We can't go there. But if we do, we should immediately go to the throne of grace and ask for forgiveness.

It is important to know that we can fall. Our world today teaches us arrogance. It teaches us to be comfortable in our arrogance—in “my truth,” my way, and the idea that I am the center of my world. It is easy to get caught up in arrogance when it feels comfortable and good.

How about this kind of pride:

Conceit: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5187 tuphoo; from a derivative of #5188;

to envelop with smoke, i.e. (figuratively) to inflate with self-conceit

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: to be puffed up with haughtiness or pride

The idea of “enveloping with smoke” is like creating an illusion. What we have going on is not what it’s supposed to be. We can’t see it for what it really is.

Paul describes to Timothy the qualifications for elders in the true church:

1 Timothy 3:4, 6: 4 He must be one who manages his own household well, keeping his children under control with all dignity 6 and not a new convert, so that he will not become conceited <5187> and fall into the condemnation incurred by the devil.

He will not become conceited refers to this kind of pride that becomes inflated with self- conceit. In other words, showing something that isn’t really there.

This person wants to believe he has qualities he either does not possess or does not possess to the degree he believes he does. He has allowed himself to become entranced by an exaggerated view of his own accomplishments.

We need to be careful about whom we place in positions of responsibility within the body of Christ. Maturity needs to come before responsibility in Christ!

Paul describes those who do not stand for the original doctrines of Christ:

1 Timothy 6:3–5: 3 If anyone advocates a different doctrine and does not agree with sound words, those of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with the doctrine conforming to godliness, 4 he is conceited <5187> (pretending to be something he’s not) and understands nothing; but he has a morbid interest in controversial questions and disputes about words, out of which arise envy, strife, abusive language, evil suspicions, 5 and constant friction between men of depraved mind and deprived of the truth, who suppose that godliness is a means of gain.

Paul goes all out when he describes this conceited approach!

Is this kind of pride acceptable within Christianity? No. None of these traits are godly or Christlike. Paul is describing wolves who devour the flock.

What about this kind of pride:

Self-exaltation: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5229 huperairomai; middle voice; to raise

oneself over, i.e. (figuratively) to become haughty

2 Corinthians 12:7–9: 7 Because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, for this reason, to keep me from exalting myself <5229>, there was given me a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to torment me—to keep me from exalting myself <5229>! 8 Concerning this I implored the Lord three times that it might leave me. 9 And he has said to me, My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness. Most gladly, therefore, I will rather boast about my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.

What a journey Paul took, from Saul of Tarsus, persecutor of the early church, to the Apostle Paul, one of Christianity’s greatest missionaries and leaders! He was transformed by Christ and learned to rely on Christ, not himself.

So, when he talks about being given a thorn in the flesh… to keep me from exalting myself— from raising himself above others and becoming self-important, the message is profoundly clear. He was given this weakness that made his life harder to help keep him focused on and relying on things that were above, rather than on his own talents, which might have led him to become something he should not have been.

Is this kind of pride acceptable within Christianity? Absolutely not! No one is better than anyone else in Christ, regardless of the amount of talent or ability someone has. We are all equally sinners. Without Jesus, we are all sentenced to death in Adam.

God uses the talents He gives us in His service. This is where reverence, not pride, needs to develop.

Paul said, to keep me from exalting myself. He recognized that he needed outside help with this and thanked God for the trial that helped keep him humble.

Proverbs 16:18 tells us pride goes before destruction. This is a powerful message for any and every Christian walking in Jesus’ footsteps!

These examples of the dangers of pride are really eye-opening! Is there any kind of

pride at all that is considered acceptable within true Christianity?

We want to be careful as we answer this. Paul does give examples of satisfaction with accomplishments that are acceptable. The key here is to understand what these examples show us, and what they mean regarding how we look at ourselves and others.

Now we are going to take a different look at pride because there are some forms of pride that ARE acceptable. We are going to focus closely on Paul’s meaning and application in his teachings.

These next verses are an example of leadership, not arrogance. Notice the guidance and encouragement that accompanies the strong direction:

Philippians 4:9–14: 9 The things you have learned and received and heard and seen in me, practice these things, and the God of peace will be with you. 10 But I rejoiced in the Lord greatly, that now at last you have revived your concern for me; indeed, you were concerned

before, but you lacked opportunity. 11 Not that I speak from want, for I have learned to be content in whatever circumstances I am. 12 I know how to get along with humble means, and I also know how to live in prosperity; in any and every circumstance I have learned the secret of being filled and going hungry, both of having abundance and suffering need. 13 I can do all things through him who strengthens me. 14 Nevertheless, you have done well to share with me in my affliction.

The things you have learned and received and heard and seen in me, practice these things— in other words, this is what you need to do. That sounds pretty arrogant, but it’s not! He is showing us through his example. He explains that he knows what it’s like to have nothing, to be starving and imprisoned. He also knows what it’s like to have things go well. The bottom line is to follow in Jesus’ footsteps, regardless of external circumstances.

I can do all things through him (Christ) who strengthens me. Paul is showing us leadership, not arrogance. He encourages the Philippians, and us, not to follow him, Paul, but to follow him only as he follows Christ.

Paul tells us when “boasting” is appropriate. Watch this concept unfold:

1 Corinthians 1:26–31: 26 For consider your calling, brethren, that there were not many wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble; 27 but God has chosen the foolish things of the world to shame the wise, and God has chosen the weak things of the world to shame the things which are strong, 28 and the base things of the world and the despised God has chosen, the things that are not, so that He may nullify the things that are, (Why did God call the weak? Here’s the answer:) 29 so that no man may boast <2744> before God. 30 But by His doing you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification, and redemption, 31 so that, just as it is written, LET HIM WHO BOASTS <2744>, BOAST <2744> IN THE LORD.

Boast: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2744 kauchaomai; to vaunt (in a good or a bad sense)

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) to glory (whether with reason or without)

2) to glory on account of a thing 3) to glory in a thing

There IS appropriate boasting! To paraphrase Paul, “Let’s face the facts. Most of you are not the cream of the crop of the world. Why? Because God is not looking for those who will boast in themselves. He is looking for those who will give glory to God.” Those who, though weak, lean on God’s strength and shame the things which are strong.

The word for boast here means to glory on account of something. Paul is saying we should not look at ourselves and say how awesome we are. Instead, we should look at God’s glory, providence, direction, wisdom and spirit as to what is awesome.

Paul is quoting from Jeremiah about how and when to “boast.” Let’s read the original source:

Jeremiah 9:23–24: 23 Thus says the LORD, Let not a wise man boast <1984> of his wisdom, and let not the mighty man boast <1984> of his might, let not a rich man boast <1984> of his riches; 24 but let him who boasts <1984> boast <1984> of this, that he understands and knows

Me, that I am the LORD who exercises lovingkindness, justice and righteousness on earth; for I delight in these things, declares the LORD.

Boast: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1984 halal; a primitive root; to be clear (orig. of sound,

but usually of color); to shine; hence, to make a show, to boast; and thus to be (clamorously)

foolish; to rave; causatively, to celebrate; also to stultify

Boasting in God and in Jesus is appropriate because of all they have done for us.

The word boast here means shining, celebrating or exulting. It should ALWAYS be based on glorifying God! If it expresses appreciation for and recognition of God’s goodness, then it is appropriate—not only to recognize God’s goodness, but also to draw attention to it because it is from Him.

We are going to go through several more scriptures where the Apostle Paul talks about boasting. In studying for this episode, we were surprised how often he talks about boasting. He is teaching us how to do this in a reverential, humble manner.

How did the Apostle Paul personally apply this? We are to exult in God’s hope and in our trials:

Romans 5:1–5: 1 Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, 2 through whom also we have obtained our introduction by faith into this grace in which we stand; and we exult <2744> in hope of the glory of God. 3 And not only this, but we also exult <2744> in our tribulations, knowing that tribulation brings about perseverance; 4 and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope; 5 and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out within our hearts through the holy spirit which was given to us.

Exalt: to raise someone or something in rank, power, status or to praise and glorify them with high honor.

Exult: to feel, show, or express lively, triumphant joy, elation, or great happiness, especially as a result of a success, victory, or someone else's failure.

Merriam-Webster.com

Exult (not “exalt,” this is a different word) here is the same Greek word as boast. Exult means “to rejoice greatly.” We are to exult in the hope of the glory of God… but we also exult in our tribulations.

The reason we rejoice is because God is present in our broken experiences. He is with us, and sometimes that is when we most clearly see and feel His presence. People often can’t understand how we can be content in our difficult experiences. They do not understand that we have God’s guidance to walk us through them. God doesn’t promise to take away the difficulty; He promises to walk with us and strengthen us.

With humility, we can exult, knowing that tribulation brings about perseverance… proven character… hope, because we are following Him and the love of God has been poured out within our hearts.

This is an appropriate boast; an appropriate exulting or rejoicing.

How do we understand Paul’s “boasting/exulting” in these next verses?

2 Corinthians 10:8, 12–13: 8 For even if I boast <2744> somewhat further about our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you,… 12 For we are not bold to class or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves;… 13 But we will <2744> not boast <2744> beyond our measure, but within the measure of the sphere which God apportioned to us as a measure, to reach even as far as you.

The Corinthians were having trouble staying with the truth. External influences were guiding them inappropriately, and Paul was attempting to get them back on the right path. He was warning them of his authority, which might sound like boasting. But actually, he was saying he was only using the authority the Lord gave him to bring them to Christ. Because he was their teacher, he felt the responsibility to keep them on track. He wouldn’t boast about accomplishments or recognition like others do. He only boasts about the work God had sent him to do to bring them to Christlikeness.

In his “boasting,” Paul is fulfilling his responsibilities of leadership. He is urging the Corinthians to follow only what has come from God through Christ. He is asking them to remember how they all worked together with him to get their church in Corinth started. He wants them to come back to their roots.

2 Corinthians 10:15–18: 15 not boasting <2744> beyond our measure, that is, in other men's labors, but with the hope that as your faith grows, we will be, within our sphere, enlarged even more by you, 16 so as to preach the gospel even to the regions beyond you, and not to boast <2744> in what has been accomplished in the sphere of another. 17 But HE WHO BOASTS <2744> IS TO BOAST <2744> IN THE LORD. 18 For it is not he who commends himself that is approved, but he whom the Lord commends.

Notice how many times he says the word boast. Paul is pleading for them to come back and work together with him again. He wants them to return to the fundamentals of their Christianity and work with him to preach the gospel even to the regions beyond Corinth. He warns against the others who are influencing them. It is not he who commends himself that is approved, but he whom the Lord commends. God had sent Paul to them to teach and nurture.

Paul AGAIN quotes Jeremiah 9 here—but let him who boasts boast of this, that he understands and knows Me, that I am the LORD. This shows us the clear grounding of how to properly exult or rejoice.

Appreciating God's blessings in our lives is a good thing, and we should use the talents we've been given. One of the talents God helped me develop is being a harmony man. Musically, I learned how to enhance a lead vocalist with subtle harmonies that bring out the best in them. My goal was to encourage and motivate them to be even better than they could be on their own, helping them shine even brighter. Over time, God showed me how to apply that same ability to encourage and support my Christian brethren in their service to Him.

This is important because not everybody can be the one who is out in front. Those who are out in front need others behind them to support and enhance their efforts, expanding what they are capable of accomplishing. That is why Jesus sent the apostles and disciples out two by two. They could supplement, balance and complement each other’s abilities. They could recognize and analyze situations together, and the two would be greater than simply one plus one. It is a powerful lesson.

(Now we are back to the words exaltation and exalted.)

The greatest example of appropriate exaltation in all of history is focused on Jesus. He humbled himself more than ANY other being in God’s entire creation for the sake of fulfilling God’s will. In return, he was rewarded with the greatest exaltation that God’s entire creation would ever witness!

From the greatest humility to the greatest exaltation:

Philippians 2:8–11: 8 Being found in appearance as a man, he humbled <5013> himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. 9 For this reason also, God highly exalted <5251> him, and bestowed on him the name which is above every name, 10 so that at the name of Jesus EVERY KNEE WILL BOW, of those who are in heaven and on earth and under the earth, 11 and that every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

This is the only place in the New Testament where the words highly exalted are used!

Exalted: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5251 huperupsoo; from #5228 and #5312;

to elevate above others, i.e. raise to the highest position

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) metaphorically to exalt to the highest rank and power,

raise to supreme majesty 2) to extol most highly

Jesus did not do this for himself! He simply did the will of his Father, no matter the cost, the circumstances or the level of humility required. The exaltation came from God. That is THE lesson for us about pride versus humility. Jesus is the greatest example of humility and the greatest exaltation of a being that God’s creation has ever seen.

The key is to apply ourselves all to the glory of God. If we can apply ourselves, with a humble assessment of our responsibilities and talents, to be all that we can be to the glory of God, we will be in a position to exult in God’s providence in our lives. To do this, we have to understand who we are and what we’ve been given, reverentially recognizing and using it.

Let’s exult in that and nothing else!

So, what is the balance between pride and humility?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.
