### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/character/1460-pride-and-humility/

1. What was the purpose of Jesus washing his disciples’ feet? How did his actions contrast with the disciples’

actions and the Pharisees’ actions? (John 13:12-17, Matthew 23:11-12)

2. Jesus was humble, yet he was fully aware of his mission, authority and relationship with his Father. What

does Jesus' example teach us about the difference between humility and having a low opinion of ourselves?

3. Why is self-exaltation spiritually dangerous? (Matthew 23:8-12)

4. Using Philippians 2:5-8, explain how Jesus’ willingness to “empty himself” models honest self-assessment.

Why does Jesus’ humility make him approachable to weary believers? (Matthew 11:27-30)

5. Give the practical steps toward humility outlined in James 4:6-10 and Romans 12:16. If we follow these

steps, what are we promised?

6. Explain the metaphor “to clothe yourselves with humility” in 1 Peter 5:5. What does it imply about the

visibility of humility in a Christian’s daily conduct? How does this apply to church leadership and those they serve?

7. How does humility affect our relationships with fellow Christians? Why is it essential to have

compassion, kindness, patience and unity? (Colossians 3:12-14, Philippians 2:2-3)

8. In the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector, what attitudes distinguished the two men?

Why was the tax collector justified rather than the Pharisee? (Luke 18:9-14)

9. Describe these unacceptable forms of pride. Give the characteristics of each, and why they are

incompatible with a Christlike walk:

a. Boastful pride: 1 John 2:15-17, Romans 1:29-31

b. Conceit: 1 Timothy 3:4,6; 6:3-5

c. Self-exaltation: 2 Corinthians 12:7-9, Proverbs 16:18

10. What is an appropriate kind of boasting? How did Paul model proper rejoicing, confidence and

leadership while maintaining humility? (1 Corinthians:26-31, Jeremiah 9:23-24, Romans 5:1-5,

Philippians 4:9-13, 2 Corinthians 10:8,12-18)

11. Do I honestly assess my strengths, responsibilities and opportunities as gifts from God, or do I sometimes

take personal credit for them? What would it look like to “boast in the Lord” instead?

12. How can I better “clothe myself with humility” in my relationships with others this week?

## Episode 1461 — Do I Ever Mix My Christianity with Paganism?
Published: 2026-11-02
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1461-christianity-and-paganism/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/25213139/CQ_Rewind_11-02-2026_Do_I_Ever_Mix_My_Christianity_With_Paganism.pdf

Isaiah 52:11: Depart, depart, go out from there, touch nothing unclean; Go out of the midst

of her, purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the LORD.

One of the foundations of true Christian discipleship is the obvious focus on following in Jesus’ footsteps. Jesus himself taught us about leaving the world behind and being willing to live a life of dedication and sacrifice as he did. One important but sometimes overlooked challenge to this is the practicality of what it means to leave the world behind. This is where an understanding of paganism needs to come into play. It's important to realize that paganism is not a single, unified religion; rather, it is a broad umbrella encompassing many different spiritual beliefs and practices, often connected by a reverence for nature and the natural world.

So, what are the differences and what are the similarities between paganism and Christianity?

Let’s begin by generally defining the very broad topic of paganism.

(Source: www.paganclub.com, excerpts from “Paganism Overview: Exploring Earth-Centred Spirituality”) Paganism, derived from the Latin word paganus, meaning “country dweller” or “rustic,” was a term in use by early Christians to describe the polytheistic and animistic religions of Europe, the Middle East and Northern Africa.

These traditions were seen as the beliefs of rural or backward peoples as Christianity spread across the Roman Empire and beyond. In reality, however, pagan traditions were the dominant spiritual systems in many societies long before the rise of monotheistic religions like Christianity, Judaism and Islam.

One of the hallmarks of ancient paganism is its polytheistic nature. In other words, the belief in and worship of multiple gods and goddesses. Ancient pagans would look up to deities, of course. This is because they often linked them to natural elements like the sun, moon, wind and earth.

This is a broad overview of the earth-based foundation of paganism. We will get into more details as we go along.

Let’s now look at the context of our theme scripture.

The release of Israel from the 70-year captivity in Babylon was prophesied in Isaiah. Isaiah describes the responsibilities of this newly-given freedom:

Isaiah 52:11-12: 11 Depart, depart, go out from there, touch nothing unclean; Go out of the midst of her, purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the LORD. 12 But you will not go out in haste, nor will you go as fugitives; For the LORD will go before you, and the God of Israel will be your rear guard.

Isaiah is saying, Go back to your land, renewing your service to and faith in God! When Israel left Babylon to return to their land, they were to touch nothing unclean. They were to purify themselves, separate themselves from the pagan influences of Babylon, and follow only the Lord who would go before them. This was a dramatic change—not just relocating, but reallocating their hearts and minds toward God.

The generation of Israelites taken captive had been idolatrous. Their idolatry was one of the primary reasons God sent them into captivity. The generation that would be freed 70 years later had essentially grown up surrounded by idolatry.

(Source: Biblical Commentary by Albert Barnes) Though the captivity was at first attended with every circumstance suited to give pain, and though they were subjected to many privations and sorrows in Babylon (see Psalm 137), yet… many of them became strongly attached to a residence there, and were strongly indisposed to return. They were there seventy years. Most of those who were made captive would have died before the close of the exile. Their children, who constituted the generation to whom the command to return would be addressed, would have known the land of their fathers only by report. It was a distant land… They had been born in Babylon. It was their home… many, it is probable, had lands, and friends and property in Babylon.

They weren’t only leaving behind a place, they were leaving behind a way of thinking that had become normal to them. It’s what they knew. Seventy years is a long time. They had become accustomed to a way of life, but now God reminded them how they were His chosen people. What they had grown comfortable with must be left behind.

In 2 Corinthians, the Apostle Paul takes this ancient event from Isaiah 52:11-12 and brings its lessons and principles into play in our current everyday Christian lives. Before reading his message, we again need background. Why would he quote Isaiah? To understand 2 Corinthians, we have to go back to 1 Corinthians.

1 Corinthians was written to a church whose priorities were very confused. They closed their eyes to dark moral sin while engaging in a sectarian brand of Christianity that was not disciplined. They were stuck in spiritual pride, misuse of the gifts and neglect of the most important things. The Apostle Paul wrote to them firmly to straighten them out.

Corinth was a major Greek city in the Roman Empire. The Christians there were living in a culture saturated with pagan religion. They were accustomed to it. It was “normal,” much as it was for the Israelites during their captivity in Babylon in the Old Testament. They were familiar with their surroundings, having grown up in that environment. We can see why the Apostle Paul draws on this well-known period in the Old Testament to make his point.

2 Corinthians was later written to them after they had heeded Paul’s warnings and were beginning to grow in Christ. Paul loved them unconditionally and encouraged them to continue putting away their humanness. He gave general admonitions that would clearly apply to the context of their lives and their deeply pagan background.

1 Corinthians was written to help them understand the big picture, while 2 Corinthians was more like saying, “Good, good! Keep going, keep going. Keep walking away, keep walking away.”

We’re going to look at several verses in 2 Corinthians and take them apart piece by piece:

2 Corinthians 6:14: Do not be bound together <2086> with unbelievers <571>…

Bound together: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2086 eterozugew heterozugeo; from a compound of 2087 and 2218; to yoke up differently, i.e. (figuratively) to associate discordantly

The Greek words for bound together refer to being yoked together, like animals joined in the same harness. Paul is warning against being connected to someone who is moving in a different spiritual direction. Animals were yoked in this way to do a specific job. If they are tied together but going in different directions, the job will not get done.

The King James Version says, Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers. The root words in the New Testament are always tied to a committed relationship, either in a positive or a negative sense.

Positive example:

Matthew 11:29-30: 29 Take my yoke <2086> upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and YOU WILL FIND REST FOR YOUR SOULS. 30 For my yoke <2086> is easy and my burden is light.

We are to be yoked to Christ in a position of submission and discipleship. We work with him and follow in his footsteps so the work of the gospel is accomplished.

Negative example:

Acts 15:10-11: (Here the Apostle Peter describes the Jewish Law as a yoke): 10 Now therefore why do you put God to the test by placing upon the neck of the disciples a yoke <2086> which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? 11 But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, in the same way as they also are.

The Law was a yoke, meaning a burden that sinful people were unable to bear because they could not keep it perfectly. Peter was addressing the efforts of Jewish and Gentile Christians to work out their understanding of the gospel. He warned the Jewish Christians not to place this yoke—the Jewish Law—upon the Gentiles. Jesus emphasized the spirit of the Law, and his followers were to walk in his footsteps. Rather than placing the burden of the Law upon one another, they needed to be yoked together in following Jesus.

Unbelievers: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #571 apistos; from 1 (as a negative particle) and

4103; (actively) disbelieving, i.e. without Christian faith (specially, a heathen);

(passively) untrustworthy (person), or incredible (thing)

Do not be bound together with unbelievers—When Paul says unbelievers, he uses a word meaning those who do not share faith in Christ. He is warning against binding ourselves into partnerships where our deepest spiritual commitments are fundamentally different.

In other words, do not be tied together with those who do not share the same belief system. This does not mean we stay out of the world or refuse to go to work tomorrow based on this text. Rather, it means we do not want to make spiritual choices that join us to the wrong thinking and the wrong belief systems that conflict with our Christian beliefs.

How do the Scriptures describe “unbelievers”? Here are just two examples:

Matthew 17:17: And Jesus answered and said, You unbelieving <571> and perverted generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I put up with you? Bring him here to me.

Jesus is referring to the Jewish people who did not believe he was the Messiah in spite of obvious evidence.

1 Corinthians 6:5-6: 5 I say this to your shame. Is it so, that there is not among you one wise man who will be able to decide between his brethren, 6 but brother goes to law with brother, and that before unbelievers <571>?

Before unbelievers—before Gentiles.

In the first example, Jesus is referring to unbelieving Jewish individuals.

In the second, Paul is speaking about unbelieving Gentiles.

The admonition is to ensure our focus is to be tied together with the appropriate people. Both those who were Jews in name only and those who are simply outside of the Christian faith are considered unbelievers.

Are we to look at unbelievers and consider them to be “bad” people? No! They are simply unbelievers. God has salvation planned for them in a different way and at a different time.

So to sum up, paganism in both ancient Israel and the early Christian church was something people lived alongside every day. It was easy to get used to and easy to stop noticing how it could negatively influence their thinking, and ultimately their relationship with God. We certainly experience this in our day.

And that's the key we're looking for: What is my individual fidelity to my faith?

To grow in Christ requires a solid foundation to build upon. Defining what we walk toward and what we walk away from gives us something firm to stand upon.

As we begin to compare the fundamentals of paganism and Christianity,

what impact do the belief origins have?

The impact is enormous, as the origins of a belief establish the foundation for that belief. As we now begin to dig a bit more deeply into the “how” and “why,” we will begin to understand why the Apostle Paul made such a clear statement about not being bound together with unbelievers.

Let’s expand our understanding of paganism by continuing with this article, written from the perspective of those who hold these beliefs.

(Source: www.paganclub.com, “Paganism Overview: Exploring Earth-Centred Spirituality”) …At the core of many ancient pagan traditions was animism—the belief that all elements of the natural world—rivers, trees, mountains, animals—possess a spiritual essence or consciousness. This reverence for nature manifested in countless ways, from the worship of the Egyptian sun god Ra to the sacred oak trees of the Druids…

…The 20th century saw a renewed interest in ancient pagan traditions, often called the “pagan revival” or “neo-paganism.” This revival emerged out of a longing to reconnect with nature, reject the dogma of organized religion, and explore alternative forms of spirituality. Neo- paganism is diverse, encompassing a variety of movements, each drawing from different ancient traditions…

“Neo” just means “new,” so this is referring to the modern adaptation of paganism.

Paganism has been around for a very long time. Neo-paganism is a revival of these older traditions, with some adaptations to fit into modern day.

One particularly interesting belief is that elements of nature—such as rivers, trees, mountains and animals—possess a spiritual essence or consciousness. Keep that idea in mind as we examine these scriptures and consider them from a biblical perspective.

2 Corinthians 6:14: … for what partnership have righteousness and lawlessness…

What partnership have righteousness (a spiritual state of being made right with God) and lawlessness (literally, illegality; in a spiritual sense, meaning a state of disfavor with God)?

This is a contrast between spiritual righteousness and spiritual lawlessness in relation to godliness. This does not imply that those who are not believers are bad people—they are simply outside of favor with God. From a Christian perspective, this is a bad condition to be in. Christians seek a relationship with God by pursuing godliness. Unbelievers, however, do not share this belief in God and therefore do not pursue that same relationship.

As Christians, it is important that we treat pagans with respect. Many are good people. However, we are not to become involved in pagan beliefs or practices.

What partnership have righteousness and lawlessness? Paul is asking the Corinthians—and us—to think about what we once were and compare it with what we are becoming.

We have covered some of the origins of paganism, including beliefs associated with the natural world and the newer adaptations of those traditions.

Now, let’s turn to the origin of Christianity. From the beginning, there was intentional action by the one God. This is a very different approach from that which is found in historical pagan traditions.

The Bible’s creation account in Genesis:

Genesis 1:1-3: 1 In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. 2 The earth was formless and void, and darkness was over the surface of the deep, and the spirit of God was moving over the surface of the waters. 3 Then God said, Let there be light; and there was light.

The first four words of the Bible help us understand the basis of Christianity: In the beginning, God. We put Him at the center as the Creator, the Designer and the Executor who brought all things into existence. Let there be light. God did this. This was intentional action that created the vast ecosystem of our planet.

Let’s look at why He created the vast ecosystem of our planet:

Genesis 1:11-12: 11 Then God said, Let the earth sprout vegetation, plants yielding seed, and fruit trees on the earth bearing fruit after their kind with seed in them; and it was so. 12 The earth brought forth vegetation, plants yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit with seed in them, after their kind; and God saw that it was good.

God put the elements in place and built in the perpetuation of life through the seed system. As a result, we have beautiful, intentional vegetation growing into place by the design of the Creator.

The comparison shows a stark contrast. If all the elements of the natural world—rivers, vegetation, mountains and animals—possess a spiritual essence or consciousness, the implication is that these elements developed independently of one another but somehow work together.

Rather, it makes sense that if all things were created by one Creator, they would be part of a balanced system, designed specifically to work together.

Why? Biblical creation continues with the direct creation of humanity:

Genesis 1:26-28: 26 Then God said, Let Us make man in Our image, according to Our likeness; and let them rule over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the sky and over the cattle and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth. 27 God created man in His own image, in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them. 28 God blessed them; and God said to them, Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth, and subdue it…

There is a difference with the creation of humanity. While all of creation was intentional, the creation of mankind was unique. Humans were given dominion over the earthly creation so that this system would sustain and nurture them. This was not an invitation to abuse nature, but rather a responsibility to work together with it—a God-driven, intentional ecosystem with mankind at the center of it all.

Pagan beliefs differ considerably, but many forms of paganism explain the origin and sustaining of life in terms of various gods, goddesses, spirits or supernatural powers, depending on the specific tradition.

The Bible tells us that God created the earth and its abundance as a support system for His directly-created human family. That support system itself (sky, sun, moon, vegetation, animals, etc.) can hardly be “the gods”—that puts things in a backwards perspective. When we read the Bible’s account of creation about how God brought things into existence, it is easy for us to choose what to believe in.

We don’t often see an average Christian going out and worshiping a tree, so how does this affect me?

We don’t want to have the tendency to, even casually, attribute guidance or destiny to cosmic powers, saying things like:

"The universe is trying to tell me something."

“I want to put good energy out into the universe.” "My computer isn’t working. Mercury must be in retrograde.”

Christians might credit "Mother Nature" without even thinking about it.

Let’s understand the foundation of what we believe and always return to the Founder, God Almighty, the Father of Jesus Christ. Let us give Him the praise and honor, and let the awe inspired by everything else in creation draw us upward to Him.

2 Corinthians 6:14: …or what fellowship has light with darkness?

Fellowship: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2842 koinōnía; from 2844; partnership, i.e. (literally) participation, or (social) intercourse, or (pecuniary) (financial) benefaction

What partnership can light have with darkness? None! Darkness cannot abide in the presence of light. From a spiritual perspective, light overcomes darkness. This is a picture of two very strong opposites.

Spiritually, what constitutes light and darkness?

Ephesians 5:6-9: 6 Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. 7 Therefore do not be partakers with them; 8 for you were formerly darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light 9 (for the fruit of the light consists in all goodness and righteousness and truth).

This is not necessarily referring to the physical world, but rather contrasting the spiritual darkness that covers the world with the light of God’s plan of salvation for all through Jesus.

They are clear opposites. Darkness is described as the absence of the light of God. The light of God is inherently good, righteous and truthful. Keep in mind that we are drawing a spiritual picture here. People of all faiths, as well as those who do not believe, can have a good conscience and do what is right. That is praiseworthy. We are talking, however, about reaching for a higher level of motivation. This is where the light of God helps us.

Another scripture that helps define this difference between light and darkness:

Isaiah 60:1-3: 1 Arise, shine; for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD has risen upon you.

The light is God’s light—this is a spiritual picture.

2 For behold, darkness will cover the earth and deep darkness the peoples; But the LORD will rise upon you and His glory will appear upon you.

This glory is God’s glory. Darkness will cover the earth... and the peoples. This is not

talking about a literal eclipse of the sun. Rather, it speaks of the goodness of God

and His plan, which remain unseen by the world. Yet, we have God’s glory upon us!

3 Nations will come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.

What a beautiful prophecy of what is to come! This is a prophecy of the coming

kingdom of God through Christ. Nations will come to your light—the spiritual light of God through Jesus. This light does not—and cannot—mingle with darkness!

These are questions we need to consider and ask ourselves so we can be sure our Christianity does not have little pieces of paganism creeping in.

The Bible clearly states our God-driven, God-created system is the absolute basis for all we hold sacred. Let’s stand on that obvious foundation.

So far, we’ve established a foundation of beliefs relating to our origins and the

fundamental differences between Christian and pagan beliefs. What are the

differences regarding our individual Christian or pagan approach to life?

Here is where we need to pay very close attention to what many may consider to be subtleties. Our technologically advanced world has brought the ability to choose ways of thinking before us that have never been so easy to access. As Christians, caution should guide our thinking!

(Source: www.paganclub.com, “Paganism Overview: Exploring Earth-Centred Spirituality”) While ancient paganism became community-focused, modern paganism tends to be more individualistic. This means practitioners craft their own rituals and belief systems. However, many key elements remain consistent across various pagan traditions.

These key elements include: Reverence for Nature: Whether through seasonal celebrations like the equinoxes and solstices, or daily rituals that honour the earth, modern pagans maintain a deep connection to nature. This often extends into environmental activism, with many pagans committed to ecological causes.

It is not a surprise that modern paganism tends toward being more individualistic. The range of beliefs is broad, allowing individuals to choose what appeals to them. They can take a piece of it and create their own gods, rituals or belief system.

As Christians, we need to be very cautious about this individualistic approach. We can’t simply create our own rituals and belief systems. We have been given guidelines in the Scriptures we need to cling to and embrace.

Our clear focus as Christians is to respect nature as it was created by God for humanity’s good:

Romans 1:18-21: 18 For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men who suppress the truth in unrighteousness, 19 because that which is known about God is evident within them; for God made it evident to them. 20 For since the creation of the world His invisible attributes, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood through what has been made, so that they are without excuse. 21 For even though they knew God, they did not honor Him as God or give thanks, but they became futile in their speculations, and their foolish heart was darkened.

Paul is essentially saying that we have ample evidence of the power of our one God as demonstrated through His creation. When we look at nature, especially in the 21st century, we can see that this ecological system—despite the destruction caused by mankind—is still self-perpetuating. It can’t be by chance that the system repairs itself when given time. It has to be because the design is God’s. In the Romans scriptures above, it says the Designer can be understood through what has been made. It warns about walking away from God and as a result, becoming futile in their speculations.

In paganism, practitioners craft their own rituals and belief systems based on what they feel is right.

Christians should be grateful for creation and care for it responsibly, but we worship the Creator, not the creation. There is nothing wrong with enjoying hiking or gardening or bird watching. But we don’t want to start thinking there is inherent spiritual energy in a crystal, a tree, a mountain or a body of water. The issue is not in appreciating creation, but whether creation begins to receive the honor that belongs to God alone.

We should have an awestruck respect for nature, but always in the context of godliness. Observing and appreciating nature should be used as a means to bring us closer to God.

Continuing with the rest of the key elements from the article:

(Source: www.paganclub.com) Magic and Spellwork: Magic—often spelled ‘magick’ within pagan communities to distinguish it from stage magic—is viewed as a natural extension of one’s will, intent and energy. Spellwork can involve various tools like candles, herbs, crystals and incantations. The focus is generally on personal growth, healing and harmony rather than controlling others.

Divination: Many pagans practice forms of divination, such as tarot, rune casting or scrying, to gain insight into the future or their own subconscious.

Ethics and the Rule of Three: While ethical systems vary across pagan traditions, Wicca (“white” witchcraft) is known for the “Rule of Three.” This states that whatever energy a person puts into the world—positive or negative—will return to them threefold. Other pagans follow similar principles, emphasizing personal responsibility and harm reduction.

Many aspects of paganism involve personal will, taking control of our lives, and even rising above our human station. We can understand why people might be attracted to these ideas. They often emphasize personal power, individual action and the ability to control circumstances or even one’s own destiny. And, of course, we would all love to know the future.

Let’s now examine a few of the practices that were forbidden by God’s specific instructions. Remember, forbidden means prohibited, not permitted or allowed; we can’t have it.

These prohibitions are found in the Old Testament and are reaffirmed in the New Testament:

Deuteronomy 18:10: There shall not be found among you anyone who makes his son or his daughter pass through the fire, one who uses <7080> divination <7081>, one who practices witchcraft <6049>, or one who interprets omens, or a sorcerer.

Uses: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #7080 qacam; a primitive root; properly, to distribute,

i.e. determine by lot or magical scroll; by implication, to divine

Divination: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #7081 qecem; from Old Testament #7080;

a lot: also divination (including its fee), oracle

Witchcraft: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #6049 `anan; a primitive root; to cover; |

used only as a denominative from Old Testament #6051, to cloud over; figuratively,

to act covertly, i.e. practice magic

The prophet Jeremiah later warned God's people not to listen to enchanters, diviners or sorcerers in Jeremiah 27:9 and Jeremiah 29:8.

Jeremiah 27:9: (KJV) Therefore hearken not ye to your prophets, nor to your diviners, nor to your dreamers, nor to your enchanters <6049>, nor to your sorcerers, which speak unto you, saying, Ye shall not serve the king of Babylon.

Jeremiah 29:8: (KJV) For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Let not your prophets and your diviners <7080>, that be in the midst of you, deceive you, neither hearken to your dreams which ye cause to be dreamed.

Jeremiah also condemned false prophets who relied upon false vision and divination rather than God's revelation in Jeremiah 14:14.

Jeremiah 14:14: (KJV) Then the LORD said unto me, The prophets prophesy lies in my name: I sent them not, neither have I commanded them, neither spake unto them: they prophesy unto you a false vision and divination <7081>, and a thing of nought, and the deceit of their heart.

Divination is the practice of obtaining supernatural knowledge apart from God.

The New Testament continues to reject occult practices. Here are a few examples:

- Acts 13:6-12: Paul condemns Elymas the sorcerer. -

Acts 16:16-18: Paul casts out a spirit of divination from a slave girl. -

Acts 19:19: New believers publicly burn their books of magic. They renounced these practices rather than incorporating them into Christianity. -

Galatians 5:19-21: Sorcery is listed among the works of the flesh. -

Revelation 21:8; 22:15: Sorcerers are condemned.

We looked at just a few Old and New Testament scriptures that clearly state these practices are forbidden. They are contrary to the teachings of Judaism in the Old Testament and to Christianity in the New Testament.

2 Corinthians 6:15: Or what harmony <4857> has Christ with Belial or what has a believer in common <3310> with an unbeliever?

Harmony: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4857 sumphonesis;

from 4856; accordance:— concord

In common: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3310 mer-ece’; a portion

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) a part as distinct from the whole

2) an assigned part, a portion, share

Harmony is an interesting word.

Who is Belial?

(Source: Matthew Poole’s English Annotations on the Bible) Belial: The term is used only in this place in the New Testament, but very often in the Old Testament, to express men notoriously wicked and scandalous, Deuteronomy 13:13, Judges 19:22, 1 Samuel 1:16, 2:12, 25:17, 2 Samuel 16:7, 2 Chronicles 13:7.

There is no subtlety here. The Apostle Paul is telling us that this is not something we need to parse through to understand. The point is dramatically clear! What harmony can there be between those who are under Christ and a world under Satan’s rule?

Ours is a “spiritual symphony.” If we add instruments that do not belong and create discord, we disrupt the harmony and ruin the message of that symphony.

The appeal of horoscopes, so-called “angel numbers” (where you see the same number over and over again and think it has special meaning), crystals, energy healing and manifesting often lies in the promise of answers or a sense of control over situations we cannot control. Manifesting is increasingly popular, promoting the idea that visualizing what we want can make it come true. It can replace prayerful submission to God’s will with confidence in our own ability to shape reality.

See Bonus Material for a link to an excellent article at ChristianQuestions.com about manifestation.

We should also ask whether we are drawn to these things because they seem mysterious, ancient, forbidden or sexy. For some, the idea of possessing secret knowledge is hard to resist.

Are these practices truly harmless, or do they reveal a desire to look beyond God’s providence for answers or control?

Rather than being satisfied and allowing God’s will to unfold, are we taking matters into our own hands, attempting to use some kind of energy or power to make things happen? This is a very pagan approach, in contrast to the Christian approach of submitting to the will of God.

As Christians, we seek spiritual harmony in accordance with God’s word and will— this is what should drive us:

1 Peter 1:13-16: 13 Therefore, prepare your minds for action, keep sober in spirit, fix your hope completely on the grace to be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ. 14 As obedient children, do not be conformed to the former lusts which were yours in your ignorance,

We once lived according to our former lusts because we didn’t know any better. But now, because we are in Christ, we know better.

15 but like the Holy One who called you, be holy yourselves also in all your behavior; 16 because it is written, YOU SHALL BE HOLY, FOR I AM HOLY.

Remember our discussion about Israel’s captivity in Babylon? They had to walk away from their former way of life and establish new habits. We might also have had to walk away from a former way of life. We had to establish new habits.

When we walk away from something, by definition, we leave it behind. The place we walk toward is holy—it is sanctified; set apart for the purposes of God—to work actively in our lives.

We can see how the differences between paganism and Christianity are growing more and more dramatic. We really do need to pay attention!

After reviewing many aspects of paganism through a lens of biblical perspective,

what is the bottom line?

First of all, it bears repeating that we should always respect our fellow human beings as they seek to follow what they believe to be good and righteous.

Everything we have seen regarding pagan beliefs can be summed up in one clear biblical teaching: Flee from idolatry! This is based in the Old Testament and repeated in the New Testament.

Let’s go to the Old Testament origin from the Ten Commandments:

Exodus 20:4: (ASV) Thou shalt not make unto thee a graven image, nor any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth.

Remember how the second generation of Israelites who left Babylon were warned to leave behind the pagan practices they grew up with? Similarly, Moses restated the Second Commandment as a warning to the second generation of Israelites who grew up in the wilderness, just before entering the Promised Land. He went into more detail in

Deuteronomy 4:15-20. They were not to make images of God or be drawn into worshipping the sun, moon, stars, animals or other parts of God’s creation. God’s invisible nature (we have no idea what He looks like!) distinguished Him from the many pagan religions that represented their gods through idols and images. We don’t need to make an image of God.

The Scriptures are clear on the importance of avoiding idolatry, but idolatry can involve more than physical idols. Other potential “gods” in our lives could include ego, people, success, comfort, wealth, power, social media or social position. These can become “gods” or “idols” when we prioritize them over our relationship with our heavenly Father.

In my opinion, paganism seems to especially appeal to the ego. It offers a sense of power and strength, along with the ability to divine or direct outcomes. Other forms of idolatry can also feed the ego by placing undue importance on people, success, comfort, wealth, power and social position.

All of these can fall under the heading of idolatry. If we are serving the one God through Jesus, we must recognize these influences and turn away from anything that draws us away from Him.

2 Corinthians 6:16: Or what agreement <4783> has the temple of God with idols?...

Agreement: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4783 soong-kat-ath’-es-is; from 4784; a deposition

(of sentiment) in company with, i.e. (figuratively) accord with

How do these two things work together? They don’t!

A temple is where religion is kept. For religious people, including pagans, a temple signifies a place of sacred meaning and worship. Where is the temple of God that the apostle references in this verse? Paul’s answer is in the next phrase of this verse:

2 Corinthians 6:16-17: 16 …For we are the temple of the living God; just as God said, (quoting from Isaiah 52:11-12 that we already read) I WILL DWELL IN THEM AND WALK AMONG THEM; AND I WILL BE THEIR GOD, AND THEY SHALL BE MY PEOPLE. 17 Therefore, COME OUT FROM THEIR MIDST AND BE SEPARATE, says the Lord. AND DO NOT TOUCH WHAT IS UNCLEAN; and I will welcome you.

The Apostle Paul is essentially applying Isaiah's command to Christians. Just as Israel was called to leave Babylon behind, we are called to leave behind any worldview that competes with wholehearted devotion to God.

I am not my own. Therefore, I must be and do only what is in accord with sanctification— with being set apart for a holy purpose. I am called to be a temple, and I am obligated to live accordingly. This is the reason I was called, and I MUST therefore sanctify myself, setting myself apart for that holy purpose, because that is what I promised to do. I promised to walk in Jesus’ footsteps, and that is exactly what he did.

What agreement has the temple of God (us) with idols? None whatsoever!

As Christians, our lives are SO much bigger than the spiritual searching associated with paganism. We have the spiritual clarity that comes from true Christianity:

1 Peter 2:4-5, 9, 11-12: 4 And coming to him as to a living stone which has been rejected by men, but is choice and precious in the sight of God, 5 you also, as living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house for a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

We are being built up as a spiritual house—a temple. For what reason? For a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus. We have a higher way of life.

9 But you are A CHOSEN RACE, A royal PRIESTHOOD, A HOLY NATION, A PEOPLE FOR God's OWN POSSESSION, so that you may proclaim the excellencies of Him who has called you out of darkness into His marvelous light…

We are called out of the darkness into this spiritual life. Those who faithfully follow Jesus are called a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, a chosen race. We have become something different! We cannot mix what we have left behind in our lives—or whatever else is out there—with what we have been given.

11 Beloved, I urge you as aliens and strangers...

In other words, we are now foreign to the world in which we were once comfortable. Paul urges us to live as aliens and strangers in this world. Our purpose is different from that of the world around us.

What is that purpose?

...to abstain from fleshly lusts which wage war against the soul. 12 Keep your behavior excellent among the Gentiles, so that in the thing in which they slander you as evildoers, they may because of your good deeds, as they observe them, glorify God in the day of visitation.

This is a great responsibility. It will be costly and difficult to maintain such a high standard while living in the midst of darkness. Yet, at the same time, we are set free in Christ.

There is a cost—the world slanders those who keep their behavior excellent. But because of who we are as followers of our Lord, because of what we stand for and what we do in his service, we can serve as an example to them.

In the day of visitation (the day of judgment in the future), they will remember our behavior now and how we were aliens and strangers in this world, setting an example of godliness. That is the point. We must stay away from the pull of the world and run toward Christ—there is no middle ground.

What is the result of all of this setting apart of our lives?

2 Corinthians 6:18: And I will be a Father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to Me, says the Lord Almighty.

It is truly unbelievable—it is hard to get our heads around the depth, clarity, focus, sincerity, promise and magnitude of being able to call the Creator of all things, “Father.”

Earlier we quoted Genesis 1:1: In the beginning, God created… Now, we are being told that if we walk away from these fleshly lusts, which wage war against the soul, we can be His children. That means we are His family. And it all came about because of Jesus.

It’s clear that we live in a world with all kinds of belief systems with their promise of power, influence and belonging. And then you have true Christianity, which says to follow something higher so that in the future, we can bless the whole of mankind.

Flee idolatry, flee pagan beliefs and trust in God through Christ.

So, do I ever mix my Christianity with paganism?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1461-christianity-and-paganism/

1. Why was the Israelites’ departure from Babylon and return to the Promised Land more than simply a

physical relocation? How had 70 years influenced them? What did they need to change? (Isaiah 52:11-12)

2. Are there any ideas, expressions, habits or practices I have accepted because they are popular, familiar,

entertaining or culturally normal, without carefully examining whether they align with my Christian faith?

3. Relate how the concepts of 2 Corinthians 6:14 and Matthew 11:29-30 support each other. How can

Christians maintain respectful relationships with others while remaining faithful to Christ?

4. How does the biblical account of creation establish God as the Creator and Designer of the earth and its

living systems? How does this differ from pagan beliefs? What responsibilities does the God-given dominion over the earthly creation demand of man? (Genesis 1:1-3, 11-12, 26-28)

5. What does it mean to “walk as children of light”? What is the fruit of this walk? Explain the spiritual

contrast between light and darkness. Why should a Christian’s motivation be at a higher level than even a good and moral person? (2 Corinthians 6:14, Ephesians 5:6-9, Isaiah 60:1-3)

6. How can Christians appreciate the beauty and wonder of nature while ensuring their gratitude and

worship remain directed toward the Creator? (Romans 1:18-21)

7. Which kinds of pagan practices are forbidden in the Old and New Testament? (Deuteronomy 18:10,

Jeremiah 14:14, 27:9, 29:8; Acts 13:6-12, 16:16-18, 19:19, Galatians 5:19-21, Revelation 21:8, 22:15)

8. In what way can things in our lives become idols? Can this happen with things not inherently wrong?

(2 Corinthians 6:16-18, 1 Peter 2:4-5, 9, 11-12)

9. Why would anyone choose to become a Christian with all the restrictions they must submit to? What is

promised to those who choose to live a life set apart for God? (1 Peter 1:13-16, 2 Corinthians 6:16-18)

10. What specific steps can I take to separate myself from influences which compete with God for my deepest

loyalty, so that I can walk more faithfully in Jesus’ footsteps and truly be a “temple of God”?

## Episode 1462 — Are Gossip and Slander Part of My Social Connections?
Published: 2026-11-09
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1462-gossip-and-slander/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/01133335/CQ_Rewind_11-09-2026_Are_Gossip_and_Slander_Part_of_My_Social_Connections.pdf

Ephesians 4:31: Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander

be put away from you, along with all malice.

There are many thoughts and actions in this life that can short circuit our Christian lives. We can have weak priorities, we can mismanage our time, we can put forth effort into spiritually unprofitable things, we can improperly use our resources, we can give in to laziness and lethargy. All of these things can reduce our daily strength and focus and have a direct influence on us while also negatively impacting others. There is another thought and action combination that can prove to not only hurt us but also hurt those around us in a deep and long-lasting way. This thought and action combination is common, easy to engage in, and can feel fun and inclusive, while insidiously destroying others AND OURSELVES. We are talking about gossip and slander.

There are many ways the Bible describes gossip and slander. The definitions range from careless whispering to harmful talk behind someone’s back to deliberate character assassination. The least abrasive definition of gossip is hushed, idle and careless talk. It’s the creating or repeating of things that should not be said because they are not true, not the whole story or because they are no one else’s business. Gossip happens easily and is sometimes unintentional.

When you think about “gossip,” you might picture two people whispering in a hallway, but of course, gossip isn’t limited to private conversations. It can take place through text messages, email chains, social media posts, comment sections, private groups and online forums. Technology has changed the tools, but not the heart behind the behavior.

Slander goes a step further by attacking another person's reputation through falsehood, distortion or malicious accusation. It is much harder (though not impossible) to slander someone unintentionally.

In the digital age, slander can spread much farther than a spoken rumor. A misleading post, an unfounded accusation, an edited clip taken out of context or spreading unverified claims can affect thousands of people in a matter of minutes.

Recognize that in the 21st century, we engage in gossip and slander by talking, writing and posting!

We can easily justify things that, according to Scripture, are not appropriate for Christians!

James 3:1–18 reveals the darkness of gossip and slander, how they work and how to stop them.

First, an introduction by James and some general observations regarding negative words:

James 3:1–2: 1 Let not many of you become teachers, my brethren, knowing that as such we will incur a stricter judgment.

This is talking about those who have been given the privilege and responsibility of leadership, of shepherding. James is warning that not many should be willing to accept this duty because there is a stricter judgment for those who are teachers. It is a powerful responsibility.

2 For we all stumble in many ways. If anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect <5046> man, able to bridle the whole body as well.

Perfect: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5046: téleios, complete (in various applications of

labor, growth, mental and moral character, etc.); completeness:—of full age, man, perfect

The word translated as perfect (teleios) is used in the sense of a mature, complete, fully developed person. It doesn’t mean sinlessly perfect. James isn’t sarcastically saying, “Oh sure, if anyone can control his tongue, he’d be perfect!” He’s suggesting our speech accurately indicates our spiritual condition. Does the way we speak to and about others reveal our spiritual maturity (or lack thereof?)

Gossip and slander can be defense mechanisms: Perhaps I feel inferior to someone, and as comparisons arise I let a little unverified story slip out about them to give others reason for doubt.

It’s nothing too significant, but, you know, they did fail quite often before this…

Maybe someone in our church is receiving appreciation for their service. Feeling overlooked, I casually mention one of their past mistakes to tamp down the praise they're receiving. After all, the past mistakes were pretty big, but we don’t want to say too much…

Leadership in the body of Christ can be a dangerous and heady thing. But it should be a humble thing! Paul knew this because this “headiness” was in his background:

1 Timothy 1:13: even though I was formerly a blasphemer <989> and a persecutor and a violent aggressor. Yet I was shown mercy because I acted ignorantly in unbelief;

Blasphemous: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #989 blasphemos; scurrilous, i.e. calumnious

(against men), or (specially) impious (against God)

Thayer’s Greek Lexicon: 1) speaking evil, slanderous, reproachful, railing, abusive

The Greek word translated blasphemer describes abusive and defamatory speech directed against God or people. We might think scripturally of blasphemy as only directed against God, and while that’s often true, the word is broad and can include abuse towards other people. This gives us a deeper responsibility to watch what we say and how we say it. The Apostle Paul tells us here that he used to be that way. He is a great example of humility.

While gossip, slander and blasphemy are not identical, they all share a common thread: the misuse of speech to tear down rather than build up.

James 3:3–5: 3 Now if we put the bits into the horses’ mouths so that they will obey us, we direct their entire body as well. 4 Look at the ships also, though they are so great and are driven by strong winds, are still directed by a very small rudder wherever the inclination of the pilot desires. 5 So also the tongue is a small part of the body, and yet it boasts of great things. See how great a forest is set aflame by such a small fire!

The principle James taught about controlling the tongue is just as relevant when our communication happens through keyboards and screens. We have to control our typing fingers!

Gossip and slander can feed one’s ego: We have a perceived need to establish our own importance, so we do so—not by focusing on our own contributory value—but by diverting attention to another’s perceived or made up, or improperly reported faults or shortcomings.

Information can be a form of social currency. If people are coming to me for information, that makes me feel important, valued, part of a group. Am I talking about others because I like that feeling of being “in the know”?

The warning here in James began with those who have the most responsibility. With great responsibility comes great temptation.

Just look at the Pharisees when they sought to stone Stephen:

Acts 6:10–11: 10 But they were unable to cope with the wisdom and the spirit with which he was speaking. 11 Then they secretly induced men to say, We have heard him speak blasphemous <989> words against Moses and against God.

The Pharisees persuaded people to tell lies about Stephen. These were trumped up charges. Ironically, those claiming to defend God's honor were bearing false witness against God's servant. They had to slander God’s servants so they could make their point that they were the righteous ones!

Does my ego ever minimize someone else so I can shine? When we look in the mirror, nobody else should be in the reflection but ourselves.

Ego might be disguised as concern or a desire to “keep others informed” when I really just want the recognition or influence or superiority. How often when I am trying to “keep others informed” am I telling a story that is not mine to tell?

James 3:6: And the tongue is a fire, the very world <2889> of iniquity <93> (moral wrongfulness); the tongue is set among our members as that which defiles <4695> (stain or soil) the entire body, and sets on fire the course of our life, and is set on fire by Gehenna.

James is becoming very descriptive here with the tongue setting on fire a world of moral wrongfulness, soiling our entire person because it is a derogatory experience that helps no one and hurts everyone, especially the one speaking it.

Gossip and slander can be passive-aggressive weapons: Maybe we’re engaged in disagreement, and we’re trying to solidify our perspective as being the correct one. We share a little gossip or slander with others, as an emotional barb against those we disagree with.

They don’t generally follow through, but that’s not what matters.

I wouldn't want to judge them (but I will), but I've heard they're not very trustworthy.

We use that little passive-aggressive thing to justify our slander as not being so bad. Did Jesus ever say, “Don’t say anything that is ‘not so bad’?” Or, did he tell us to speak righteously?

If we plant a seed, it has the opportunity to grow. Our words can sow a seed of discord to discredit someone. Now we are responsible for that seed being there.

Our words, be they spoken or written, are the most volatile and contagious factors in our lives!

They can become a “soiling stain” (defiles <4695>) upon us. They can begin a course that leads directly to our spiritual destruction!

Jesus is chastising the Pharisees:

Matthew 15:11: It is not what enters into the mouth that defiles the man, but what proceeds out of the mouth, this defiles the man.

Homeland Security is the part of the United States government responsible for protecting the country from threats, securing its borders, responding to disasters and helping keep people safe.

Several years ago, we received a visit from a Homeland Security agent. We had a brief association with someone from another country, and our home address was involved in that association. Someone that person knew in their home country was handing out counterfeit money. Homeland Security followed the trail and came to ask us questions.

After we dealt with that and did everything we needed to do to make sure things were understood, I had a responsibility to talk to one of the other brothers in Christ who was deeply involved in missionary work throughout the world.

I was very cautious when I approached this individual. I gave him a little bit of information and asked if he needed more details. He said, “Yes, but only tell me what I need to know.” So, very cautiously and carefully we discussed the matter. He understood and knew what to do from there.

It was a great example of the appropriate way to handle negative information about someone else. I was afraid to just blab things, but his questions and comments were well thought out, and he only wanted to know what he needed to know to do whatever was necessary to protect others involved.

This was an unusual experience, and the only experience I’ve ever had with Homeland Security!

This person responded in a sensitive and godly way asking for only necessary information. Gossip needs both a speaker and a receiver.

Proverbs 18:8: (also nearly identical in Proverbs 26:22) The words of a whisperer are like dainty morsels, and they go down into the innermost parts of the body.

Gossip was “juicy” even in ancient times. It’s tasty to consume, but the problem is, once heard, gossip can be hard to forget, even if it turns out to be false.

Proverbs 17:4: An evildoer listens to wicked lips; a liar pays attention to a destructive tongue.

Do I passively encourage gossip by listening to it, enjoying it, or asking for more details instead of redirecting the conversation? We often focus on the person speaking, but gossip survives because it has an audience. Spiritual maturity isn’t only about being the source of gossip. What about our willingness to consume it?

James 3:8–10: 8 But no one can tame the tongue; it is a restless evil and full of deadly poison. 9 With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in the likeness of God; 10 from the same mouth come both blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not to be this way.

Deadly poison illustrates how damaging words can be. But men, who have been made in the likeness of God explains why we should care in the first place. This should affect how we speak to one another. When we carelessly tear down others, we are speaking against those whom God created in His image. This was the same reason murder is forbidden according to Genesis 9:6. How we treat people matters because of whose image they bear.

Gossip and slander can be deflectors of attention: When we are not comfortable being the focus of attention, revealing dramatic sounding “information” about someone else can ease that discomfort. Calling gossip “information” makes it sound legitimate, but it’s still gossip.

Maybe a discussion reveals an area where I am falling short spiritually. Rather than examining myself, I bring up another person's inconsistency or mistake. It's easier to talk about their shortcomings than confront my own.

Understand how insidious this is. Gossip and slander easily slip right into the conversation.

James 3:8-10 calls our words a restless evil, an unstable and destructive force dripping with poison. Poison kills! We use our words to bless God and then to curse His human creation. This is hypocrisy! We can’t call ourselves Christians and behave this way.

Let’s look at another example:

2 Corinthians 12:20: For I am afraid that perhaps when I come I may find you to be not what I wish and may be found by you to be not what you wish; that perhaps there will be strife, jealousy, angry tempers, disputes, slanders <2636> (defamation), gossip <5587> (whispering), arrogance, disturbances.

The Apostle Paul is talking about visiting the Corinthian church. He warns that perhaps he will not find they are doing what they should be (unrepentant sinning), and they will not like his strong rebuke. (1 Corinthians 4:21: What do you desire? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?) He is trying to rein in the emotions so they can start focusing on the higher things and not the strife.

Words invite actions! Words of gossip, if unchecked, will bring us to actions of unrighteousness, which will bring us to a state of rationalizing and acceptance towards godless behavior. The recipe for godlessness can easily start with gossip and slander, and then we become godless individuals.

Do I ever put somebody in the crosshairs because I don’t like them, and they don’t deserve this or that?

Proverbs 11:9: With his mouth the godless man destroys his neighbor…

It's easy to think of examples of people using words as weapons—think about national politics.

I'd rather think about someone who used words as tools for peace. I think of our friend Joanna. She spent years volunteering for Christian Questions responding to difficult and sometimes hostile comments online. Yet her words were never weapons. She always responded with patience and kindness. She could disagree without being disagreeable. Even when others seemed determined to argue, Joanna left them with something scriptural to consider and an example of genuine Christian character. Whenever I respond to anyone online, I always ask myself, “Would Joanna say it this way? Is this the way she would write it?”

She reminds us of someone who had a velvet hammer. Even though she was giving some hard truth, it felt good; it was so nice. This is an important way to respond when we are in those difficult situations that become so negative.

James now begins to develop the solution for the rabid results of words spoken and written without godliness:

James 3:11–13: 11 Does a fountain send out from the same opening both fresh and bitter water? 12 Can a fig tree, my brethren, produce olives, or a vine produce figs? Nor can salt water produce fresh. 13 Who among you is wise and understanding? Let him show by his good behavior his deeds in the gentleness of wisdom.

James has just laid out the horrors of the power of the tongue and then talks about being wise and understanding… showing by his good behavior his deeds in the gentleness of wisdom. What a powerful theme to think about!

Gossip and slander can be the result of spiritual indifference: We can easily “go along for the ride” in our Christianity. Maybe the work is too hard or monotonous, so we begin to gravitate towards stories or hearsay that are appealing, and now we have something else to focus on and share. We get to be a part of something which makes us feel included. Gossip can be the result of spiritual indifference when our attention goes elsewhere.

I didn’t spend any time preparing for the Bible study. To prevent others from noticing, I deflect the conversation to gossiping about someone else.

Gossip can derail us from the work God has given us to do. If we’re constantly monitoring what others are doing, we can lose focus on what WE should be doing. Watching the work is not the same as doing the work.

Are they a reflection of the deep principles of Christ’s teachings?

1 Timothy 6:3–4: 3 If anyone advocates a different doctrine and does not agree with sound words, those of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with the doctrine conforming to godliness, 4 he is conceited and understands nothing; but he has a morbid interest in controversial questions and disputes about words, out of which arise envy, strife, abusive language <988> (blasphemy), evil suspicions.

If we don’t agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus, and we don’t conform to godliness as he modeled for us, then we are in this place of destructiveness. A big part of that destructiveness is abusive language. We can be abusive to others. We need to look hard at our words.

Are they reflective of the gentleness of wisdom?

1 Peter 3:16–17: 16 and keep a good conscience so that in the thing in which you are slandered <2635> (slander), those who revile your good behavior in Christ will be put to shame. 17 For it is better, if God should will it so, that you suffer for doing what is right rather than for doing what is wrong.

We can’t control others talking about us, but we can control our responses to what others are saying. We could easily get into the same boat they are in with an angry response. Or we can choose to stay above and beyond it with godly actions.

Do I sometimes speak before I think?

This is an example of what I am calling “accidental gossip.” Recently, someone asked me a doctrinal question and briefly mentioned that some of our congregations had split over the issue; they stopped meeting together because the topic was so contentious.

I knew we were going to talk about this topic soon, so, not wanting to get involved in gossip, I didn't ask for details and paid little attention to that part of the conversation. Later, I told you, Rick, how encouraged I was by the person's sincere spiritual questions, and I casually repeated the comment about the congregations. Naturally, you asked, "Which ones?" Concerned there might be a current problem, I mentioned a name and then realized I was mixing details from completely unrelated conversations. You immediately corrected me before I accidentally turned a vague comment into a specific rumor. As it turns out, the incident had happened more than 50 years ago!

That was a great lesson for me. Gossip doesn't always begin with bad motives. Sometimes it begins when we repeat information we don't know well enough to repeat. I need to keep my mouth shut!

It’s easy to take a thought that seems in harmony with our point and just bring it into the conversation without thinking. We need to examine all of our words and actions.

James 3:14-16: 14 But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your heart, do not be arrogant and so lie against the truth. 15 This wisdom is not that which comes down from above, but is earthly, natural, demonic. 16 For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there is disorder and every evil thing.

Gossip and slander can be expressions of jealousy: “We’ve had enough of that person. You know the one I’m talking about, right?” The one who seems to outshine us and seems to get what we want or think we deserve. We “expose” them with a story or two that is a little exaggerated, incomplete or just plain none of anyone’s business.

One of the biggest problems with gossip and slander is that we talk or write about what should be none of our concern.

What fills your heart? Can we honestly and humbly see what is there?

1 Peter 2:12: Keep your behavior excellent among the Gentiles, so that in the thing in which they slander <2635> you as evildoers, they may because of your good deeds, as they observe them, glorify God in the day of visitation (the day of judgment).

Slander: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #2635 katalaleo;

from #2637; to be a traducer, i.e. to slander

Even in the circumstances when we are falsely judged, hurt or slandered, our heart should be able to rise above those accusations as a witness because that is what Jesus did. It really is that simple. If we are walking in his footsteps, we need to do what he did when he was spoken about so poorly.

Label it clearly so there is no mistaking what the source is, as each of our hearts are driven either by the “wisdom” of Satan or the wisdom of God:

James 4:11: Do not speak against <2635> one another, brethren. He who speaks against <2635> a brother or judges his brother, speaks against <2635> the law and judges the law…

Gossip is speaking against someone. We MUST NOT DO THIS! We need to be clear and label this behavior as speaking against our brother, or judging our brother. That is NOT our job. Label it what it is.

Interestingly, the Greek word often translated Devil is diabolos, which means “slanderer” or “false accuser.” (See Matthew 4:1, Ephesians 6:11, James 4:7 and 1 Peter 5:8.) This word is applied to humans in 1 Timothy 3:11, 2 Timothy 3:3 and Titus 2:3. We certainly don’t want the Devil’s title applied to us!

Do we want to follow the Devil’s “wisdom” or God’s wisdom?

Do I ever selfishly reduce someone else’s value so I can feel a little bit better? Gossip and slander do that.

James 3:17–18: 17 But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, unwavering, without hypocrisy. 18 And the seed whose fruit is righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

We talked about planting seeds before. This is the spiritually-founded seed.

Gossip and slander can be the result of carelessness and opportunity: It is carelessness by overhearing one end of a conversation and jumping to conclusions. It is opportunity because there’s something in our experiences that cause doubt and this carelessly adopted story can easily mask that self-doubt.

We need to make sure we are accurately representing what has happened to us.

I’m a supervisor in the business I work in and my associate, I’ll call him Bob, had a legitimate problem with the home office that messed something up. He was angry and absolutely had a right to be. He explained to me what he was doing and how he was handling the client, and what he suggested the client do.

A couple of days later, he was explaining further, but he changed his story. Instead of his suggesting to the client to do things, he said the client suggested to do this. Now, I knew that wasn’t true because the first time he told me that HE suggested it to the client. It was a tiny difference, but it fed his anger and justified more anger.

His carelessness made the story lose some of its credibility, because now the facts were distorted. His emotion was causing the distortion, but even if our words were merely the result of careless thinking, they need swift correction!

If we sincerely claim these attributes (James 3:17-18: first pure, then peaceable, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, unwavering, without hypocrisy…), our actions and words will follow. These are the seeds we plant. These are the heavenly attributes we claim for our hearts.

I heard a story about a quiet brother in Christ. Someone remarked, "You don't say much, do you?" He answered, "That just means I have less to account for." His response reflects the biblical principle that our words matter, and every unnecessary criticism, rumor or careless comment has consequences.

There is such wisdom in that kind of silence!

It is one thing to claim those attributes; now they must be planted and cultivated.

To plant is a clear decision that requires desire, thought, planning and action:

Ephesians 4:30–32: 30 Do not grieve the holy spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. 31 Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander <988> be put away from you, along with all malice. 32 Be kind to one another, tender-hearted, forgiving each other, just as God in Christ also has forgiven you.

There are SO MANY scriptures, and this is just one example, that talk about how much God hates gossip and evil talk. It’s a great homework assignment to find all of those and consider just how serious this is. Today, we need to not only consider, “What am I saying?" but also, "What am I sharing?" Even Christians who would never consider verbally slandering someone might still be tempted to participate in online gossip simply by forwarding, liking, sending a screenshot, reposting or commenting on something untrue, unverified, none of our business or even harmful.

Our intention may not be to harm, but we can cause harm anyway. As representatives of Christ, it is critically important for us to think these things through.

Instead, let us intentionally focus our energy as the Apostle Paul directs:

Philippians 4:8: Finally, brethren, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is right, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is of good repute, if there is any excellence and if anything worthy of praise, dwell on these things.

If we spend our time dwelling on these things, we have no time to repeat those things. We have no time to post, think about, repeat or listen to gossip and slander, because we’re listening to that which is godly through Christ. Let gossip and slander no longer be a part of our daily lives.

So, are gossip and slander part of my social connections?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

Word Study:

Many of our topics are compiled with a Word Study using several concordances and other Bible helps. We see how a particular word is used in both the Old and New Testaments. Understanding how the words are used not only tells us what they mean, but it gives us the nuances of the original Hebrew or Greek when comparing how the writers of the Bible use them in different contexts. We can also learn more by seeing the origins of a particular word, providing a depth of understanding just reading scriptures in English cannot provide. Here we present New Testament words on our topic.
