## Episode 1463 — Are Christians Allowed to Complain and Are There Limits?
Published: 2026-11-16
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1463-are-christians-allowed-to-complain/
Rewind PDF: https://resources.christianquestions.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/06112822/CQ_Rewind_11-02-2026_Are_Christians_Allowed_to_Complain_and_Are_There_Limits.pdf

Philippians 2:14: Do all things without grumbling or disputing.

Let’s face it, we all complain! Whether it’s because our Amazon delivery didn’t show up on time, or the weather forecast was way off AGAIN, or somebody parked too close to our car in a parking lot, or our phone bill had extra charges, or we didn’t get the pay increase at work that we were promised; we all complain! Sometimes complaints are legitimate, and sometimes they’re reactions. Sometimes they’re appropriate and necessary, and sometimes they’re just gripes. Sometimes we don’t say them out loud, and they just run in our minds like a hamster on a wheel, going nowhere and aggravating us along the way. Sometimes they’re announced so that the masses can identify with our gripe. Okay, we all complain, so the BIG question is, when is it appropriate for Christians to complain, and how should those complaints be expressed?

Our theme scripture is simple and to the point:

Philippians 2:14: Do all things without grumbling <1112> or disputing <1261>.

Grumbling: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1112 goggusmos; a grumbling

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) a murmur, murmuring, muttering 1a) a secret debate

1b) a secret displeasure not openly avowed

Disputing: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1261 dialogismos; discussion,

i.e. (internal) consideration (by implication, purpose), or (external) debate

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) the thinking of a man deliberating with himself

2) a deliberating, questioning about what is true 2a) hesitation, doubting 2b) disputing, arguing

The Greek word translated grumbling is goggusmos. Interestingly, the word itself almost sounds like muttering under your breath. It refers to a low murmuring, whispered dissatisfaction or quiet, outward complaining.

The Greek word translated disputing is dialogismos. It is related to our English word “dialogue.” The Strong’s Concordance definition includes, “the thinking man deliberating with himself,” “questioning about what is true.” Grumbling is the outward complaint; disputing is the inward debate behind it, our internal dialogue.

Dialogismos is not inherently negative. Depending on the context, it can refer to reasoning, deliberation, questioning or argumentation. In Philippians 2:14, however, the context clearly points to argumentative reasoning and inward objections.

Scriptural grumbling or complaining is a reaction to circumstances or people that creates internal unrest. It can be silent or communicated. It has the potential to disrupt our peace and distract our focus.

This kind of complaining does not appropriately call attention to trying to right a wrong in the world around us, which is something we should do, as long as we do it by displaying godly grace and wisdom. Instead, it’s a reaction to circumstances or people that affects our view of our experiences.

Let’s look at a prolonged biblical example of what inappropriate complaining looks like in action and see where it leads us:

Israel had just been rescued from generations of slavery in Egypt. They were delivered as a nation through the miraculous parting of the Red Sea, and in Exodus 15 had all sung the “Song of Moses” in praise and thanksgiving to God. They were led in the wilderness for three days without water and came to Marah, but couldn’t drink the water there because it was bitter. In fact, the name Marah means “bitter.”

Here we see the small beginnings of the grumblings of God’s delivered people and God’s response to them:

Exodus 15:24-27: 24 So the people grumbled at Moses, saying, What shall we drink?

This was a legitimate problem—they needed water to survive! Had God made a mistake leading them here?

25 Then he (Moses) cried out to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a tree; and he threw it into the waters, and the waters became sweet.

God easily solved the problem using Moses, and now would also establish a process of loyalty testing: There He made for them a statute and regulation, and there He tested them.

God now gives them a four-part description of what He expects from them. It starts out with “hearing” and moves to “doing.”

26 And He said,

If you will give earnest heed to the voice of the LORD your God,

and do what is right in His sight,

and give ear to His commandments,

and keep all His statutes,

I will put none of the diseases on you which I have put on the Egyptians; for I, the LORD, am your healer.

God had not only miraculously delivered them, He would continue to do so by keeping them healthy—that is, as long as they would TRUST IN HIM.

27 Then they came to Elim where there were twelve springs of water and seventy date palms, and they camped there beside the waters.

God brings them to an almost resort-type place with springs and date palms and beauty after the dry wilderness. They were led to a place of beauty and comfort! God was showing them His care. He did His part. He brought them this far, so why would He stop caring for them now? God was telling them to trust Him because He can take care of them. This was the theme for natural Israel.

Causes for complaining can be justified and are easy to find. With Israel as a delivered nation, God set a standard to handle their complaints that simply said, “Focus on Me as your deliverer and healer, and I will manage all of your justifiable reasons for complaining.” God’s immediate solving of their issue verified His power and presence in their lives.

There was a problem. God brought a solution. The complaint of not having enough water to drink was resolved.

What about us as Christians? Christians are “spiritual Israel.” When we say "spiritual Israel," we aren’t suggesting that God's promises to natural Israel have been transferred to Christians. We simply mean that Scripture uses Israel's experiences as spiritual lessons and parallels for followers of Christ.

In other words, we can see how God led natural Israel physically through the wilderness and subsequent experiences. We can parallel our own spiritual experiences along the same lines.

Our deliverance is not from Egypt, but we have been freed from the “shackles” of sin and death by Jesus’ ransom being applied to us here and now. Those who are true, faithful Christians and have been given God’s spirit are now justified in His sight and have His spirit leading us in our experiences.

Here is what Jesus told us about some of the worries that can bring complaints:

Matthew 6:31-33: 31 Do not worry then, saying, What will we eat? or What will we drink? or What will we wear for clothing? 32 For the Gentiles eagerly seek all these things; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. 33 But seek first His kingdom and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.

Verse 33 has been the theme text of my life, reminding me for decades and decades that if I am truly looking to follow in God’s righteousness, He will take care of

everything else. It doesn’t mean He is going to miraculously pave the road, but I can put everything else into His hands.

Jesus is telling us we are cared for so completely that we should work on not only putting away complaining and disputing, but also on reducing the worry and anxiety that often fuels them. These attitudes tend to rise up within us and stay there. Jesus reminds us we do not need to let that grow, because our heavenly Father knows what we need.

Like the ancient Israelites, if we are a “delivered people,” we don’t want our internal dialogue to be so loud that we can’t hear God’s direction.

Here’s a simple phrase to remember throughout this episode:

Every challenge presents a choice. If we tend to complain, maybe we put this reminder on our refrigerator where we can see it to help us remember. These are powerful biblical lessons.

So far, we have only one example of complaining in Scripture, and already we can see a new perspective on how to handle it.

God allowed Israel to have a chance to complain so they could appreciate His care. Is it really that simple?

Actually, the principle really IS that simple. However, the real-life application of that principle is far more complex. As we shall see, complaining, murmuring, debating and doubting the basics of our lives can come up again and again and again. The key is learning a new and higher response pattern so we can stay firmly rooted in our faith when life’s experiences become frenzied and we get stuck in the experience.

Let’s go back to the newly-delivered nation of Israel.

Exodus 16 begins after their stay in Elim. They are back to journeying:

Exodus 16:1-3: 1 Then they set out from Elim, and all the congregation of the sons of Israel came to the Wilderness of Sin (this name isn’t our modern-day word for “sin.” It’s the name of a region related to the name Sinai) which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after their departure from the land of Egypt. 2 The whole congregation of the sons of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness. 3 The sons of Israel said to them, Would that we had died by the LORD'S hand in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the pots of meat, when we ate bread to the full; for you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger.

That’s a pretty big complaint! They were very hungry. This was another VERY legitimate concern, this time about food. The question is, was their complaint stated as a legitimate concern, or was it stated as an accusation? This is an important question.

How are my complaints being stated?

At Marah, the complaint was, "What will we drink?" Now it has escalated to, "You brought us out here to kill us!" They are no longer just expressing a need; they're assigning motives to God! Comparing slavery to their present condition by saying, when we sat by the pots of meat, when we ate bread to the full, is not good. It sounds as though they have forgotten all about the oasis at Elim, let alone the miraculous deliverance from slavery in Egypt. That was then, this is now. What have you done for us lately? This is how we end up complaining.

You have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger. How would God react to these accusations against Moses, Aaron and God Himself?

God’s answer was patient AND miraculous! It also was a reminder of their need to TRUST Him:

Exodus 16:4: Then the LORD said to Moses, Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you; and the people shall go out and gather a day's portion every day, that I may test them, whether or not they will walk in My instruction.

He brings up the test again. Now it will be with manna from heaven, given on a daily basis except on the Sabbath.

Now manna from heaven would clearly answer the need for food. Meat would follow as well. God was not done blessing them in spite of the harshness of their complaint:

Exodus 16:6-8: 6 So Moses and Aaron said to all the sons of Israel, At evening you will know that the LORD has brought you out of the land of Egypt; 7 and in the morning you will see the glory of the LORD, for He hears your grumblings against the LORD; and what are we, that you grumble against us? 8 Moses said, This will happen when the LORD gives you meat to eat in the evening, and bread to the full in the morning; for the LORD hears your grumblings which you grumble against Him. And what are we? Your grumblings are not against us but against the LORD.

Moses is saying, “You Israelites can complain to me, but you are also grumbling against the Lord, and He hears it!”

Even though they accused God of careless neglect, He responded with compassion and rescue. He gave them the manna which would be a staple for them throughout their whole wilderness experience. He would also give them meat because He was compassionate towards them.

Why was He so compassionate when they were so angry? Because He was teaching them trust. It is a great lesson of God’s compassion as we go through these experiences with Israel as well as our own.

When we are privileged to be watched over by God and to be clearly cared for by Him, we need to truly embrace His patience and compassion. Even when we lose our way regarding complaining and grumbling, He is compassionate while reminding us of our responsibilities to trust Him implicitly!

When we fall down over and over again and keep getting up, He understands. His compassion is a beautiful thing. The experiences of Israel show us God’s great compassion and power.

Our Christian responsibilities towards avoiding grumbling and complaining echo this lesson:

1 Timothy 6:6-8: 6 But godliness actually is a means of great gain when accompanied by contentment. 7 For we have brought nothing into the world, so we cannot take anything out of it either. 8 If we have food and covering, with these we shall be content.

Godliness with contentment is great gain. The contentment is what diffuses the complaining. If we have food and covering, the basics, we need to find contentment in those things.

Do I comply wherever that providence leads me?

Continuing with one more example in Israel’s journey:

Exodus 17:1-4: 1 Then all the congregation of the sons of Israel journeyed by stages from the wilderness of Sin, according to the command of the LORD, and camped at Rephidim, and there was no water for the people to drink. 2 Therefore the people quarreled with Moses and said, Give us water that we may drink. And Moses said to them, Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test the LORD? 3 But the people thirsted there for water; and they grumbled against Moses and said, Why, now, have you brought us up from Egypt, to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst? 4 So Moses cried out to the LORD, saying, What shall I do to this people? A little more and they will stone me.

They are complaining against Moses, making him responsible because he is their spokesman. This is the same legitimate issue, but now they choose a different target for their accusations. This is how complaining often works. In spite of God’s repeated mercy and care, their complaints are refocused only on Moses.

God is still merciful, and He will clearly put Moses in a position of authority as God solves the issue:

Exodus 17:6-7: 6 Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb; and you shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it, that the people may drink. And Moses did so in the sight of the elders of Israel. 7 He named the place Massah and Meribah because of the quarrel of the sons of Israel, and because they tested the LORD, saying, Is the LORD among us, or not?

- At Marah, they complained about water.
- In the Wilderness of Sin, their complaint escalated into an accusation of God bringing them into the wilderness just to die.
- Now, here at Rephidim, they go even further by questioning God's very presence: Is the LORD among us, or not?

They were essentially saying that God could not be trusted to provide for them where He had led them.

An interesting side note is that the names Moses gave this location reinforce the seriousness of what happened there:

Massah = "testing" Meribah = "quarreling" or "contention"

This place wasn’t named to commemorate God's miracle of providing water from the rock. Instead, it was named to memorialize Israel's failure to trust Him. Massah reminded future generations that they tested God, and Meribah reminded them that they argued with His servant.

The crisis was a lack of water, but the real issue was a lack of trust.

Do we want our experiences to be named after God’s deliverance or after our complaints?

It's often easier to blame someone than to address the real issue. Moses didn't create the lack of water, but he became the target of Israel's frustration. We do the same thing when we direct our complaints at our spouse, coworker, church member and so on. Sometimes the person we're criticizing isn't the real problem at all. They're simply the easiest target. The real issue may be that we are struggling to trust God’s overruling in our circumstances.

Complaining can be insidious. If an issue or circumstance is having a dramatic effect on our emotions, we can easily give in to it as the only optional reaction. (“I have no other choice but to…”) It’s at times like these that we need to remember what God told Israel:

If you will give earnest heed to the voice of the LORD your God,

and do what is right in His sight,

and give ear to His commandments,

and keep all His statutes,

This is a comprehensive view of how to maintain trust. By maintaining trust, we diffuse complaining.

For Christians, we need to deeply focus on our truest and most powerful source of strength, no matter what circumstances we face:

Philippians 4:11-13: 11 Not that I (the Apostle Paul) speak from want, for I have learned to be content in whatever circumstances I am. 12 I know how to get along with humble means, and I also know how to live in prosperity (King James Version: I know how to be abased, and I know how to abound); in any and every circumstance I have learned the secret of being filled and going hungry, both of having abundance and suffering need. 13 I can do all things through him (Christ) who strengthens me.

Like the ancient Israelites, we too can begin with a problem and spiral until we end up questioning God’s care.

Grumbling is a memory problem.

We forget what God has done.

We turn off the memory of God’s providence, guidance, care, grace, strength and power. Are we overwhelmed in the moment of emotion rather than living in the overall experience, following God’s providence? Israel had a tough time doing this.

All I have seen teaches me to trust the Creator for all I have not seen. —Ralph Waldo Emerson

The challenges Israel faced in the wilderness were massive. While their complaints were significant, God’s solutions were ALWAYS enough!

With the foundation for handling our complaining so firmly established by God

dealing with Israel, how do we practically apply it to Christianity?

Obviously, our practical application needs to have its foundation built upon Jesus. A concise way to do this is to go into the context of our theme verse, Do all things without grumbling or disputing. In this context, we will find how Jesus fulfilled the very commands God had given to Israel on their journey as a delivered people.

We know Jesus left the heavenly realm to pay the price required to buy Adam and his race back from sin. Jesus fulfilled the four commands God had given Israel in Exodus 15:26. This overview of his journey is the foundation upon which all Christians follow his attitude, actions and choices.

give earnest heed to the voice of the LORD your God

Prophetically, Isaiah here represents Jesus:

Isaiah 6:8: Then I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for Us? Then I said, Here am I. Send me!

Isaiah’s (representing Jesus’) answer was giving earnest heed to the voice of the Lord your God. In Jesus’ pre-human, spiritual existence, Jesus showed his compliance with that first command God gave to Israel.

We will next look at the scriptures in Philippians 2 leading up to our theme text to see how Jesus fulfilled the other three commands to the Israelites in Exodus 15.

do what is right in His sight

For Jesus, the right thing—the only thing—was freely choosing humble submission. No complaint, just positive action:

Philippians 2:5-6: 5 Have this attitude in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, 6 who, although he existed in the form of God, did not regard equality with God a thing to be grasped,

Jesus, though in a spiritual form like God, did not consider he was equal to God. Instead, he was willing to do what was right in His sight and be sent to earth to fulfill God’s will. He heeded the voice of God, Here am I, send me, and he was willing to be humbled in stature to a human because that was what God required.

give ear to His commandments

For Jesus, the right thing—the only thing—was freely choosing mere and lowly human mortality. No complaint, just positive action:

Philippians 2:7: …but emptied himself, taking the form of a bond-servant, and being made in the likeness of men.

He emptied himself, by taking the lower form of a man. That’s what God commanded, so that’s exactly what he did.

keep all His statutes

For Jesus to be the ransom for Adam, God’s justice required a life for a life. God’s wisdom gave Jesus’ suffering value, but he had to suffer and die.

Jesus complied, no complaint, just positive action:

Philippians 2:8-11: 8 Being found in appearance as a man (Weymouth translation: And being recognized as truly human), he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.

Keep all His statutes means to keep the details. Jesus had to follow through all the way to the end. Jesus followed these four commands completely in the process of becoming the ransom for all.

For Israel, following these four commands would have brought them health, healing and protection.

For Jesus, his overwhelming compliance to God’s will brought him exaltation beyond measure: 9 For this reason also, God highly exalted him, and bestowed on him the name which is above every name, 10 so that at the name of Jesus EVERY KNEE WILL BOW, of those who are in heaven and on earth and under the earth, 11 and that every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

God exalts Jesus by bestowing on him the name which is above every name! He exalts him higher than ever before. This is the end result of pure compliance with no complaining to the holy sacred will and word of God.

This summer, my husband and I took a special anniversary trip to Norway. One part of the trip was advertised as "the most scenic train ride in the world," so this was to be a highlight of the vacation. The reality didn't match my expectations. The train was old, the seats weren't great, our view was limited, one of the bathrooms wasn’t working and the ride was much longer than I expected. I became fixated on everything that was wrong. In fact, I was so worked up that I barely slept the night before because I was worried about where we'd be sitting!

Looking back, I was absolutely grumbling and disputing. I was rehearsing every disappointment and convincing myself how justified I was in feeling frustrated. After several hours, I took a deep breath and suddenly saw things differently. I was on an amazing trip with my husband. We were healthy. We were getting along wonderfully. We had more than enough to eat. What I was focusing on were tiny inconveniences compared to the many blessings God had given me, I felt ashamed at how quickly I had spiraled.

Then a sentence came into my mind, fully formed: "The Lord will always take care of me."

At that exact moment, I looked out the window and saw two sheep standing alone on a rock. During the entire eight-hour trip, these were the only animals we saw, not a squirrel, not a fox, not a bird—nothing! I immediately thought of how the Lord is my Shepherd.

The train hadn't changed. My circumstances hadn't changed. What changed was my perspective. I spent much of that day apologizing to God for letting a few momentary disappointments blind me to so many blessings. What a lesson for me!

It wasn’t a good reaction initially, but the end result was! We might all get stuck in our complaining, but the point is that by moving our hearts and minds into a different direction, we learn to become unstuck. Nothing on the train ride had changed, but Julie recognized her complaining and changed her mind and heart to thankfulness. At that moment, she saw the two sheep out there. It was like the Lord was giving her assurance that, just like He was shepherding these two little sheep in the wilds of Norway, He was also loving and taking care of her.

With this perfect example of Jesus (and that of Julie’s example) learning to do God’s will without grumbling or complaining, it’s now our turn:

Philippians 2:12-13: 12 So then, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your salvation with fear and trembling; 13 for it is God who is at work in you, both to will and to work for His good pleasure.

No complaint, no grumbling, no hesitation—just positive action. Our “default” setting cannot be complaining! If we fall into complaint as a default, we are falling into what the Jewish nation did. The end result was they ended up having to wander for 40 years because they weren’t trusting. We don’t want to be wandering; we want to be following.

Paul continues and now introduces what a complaining-free and disputing-free character produces:

Philippians 2:14-16: Here’s our theme text: 14 Do all things without grumbling or disputing; 15 so that you will prove yourselves to be blameless and innocent, children of God above reproach in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you appear as lights in the world, 16 holding fast the word of life, so that in the day of Christ I will have reason to glory because I did not run in vain nor toil in vain.

It occurred to us that the four results in these verses correspond to the four commands God gave Israel, but in backwards order!

This is how we overcome complaining!

Our theme text is Philippians 2:14, Do all things without grumbling or disputing. We might not even grumble out loud with “low muttering,” but we might do a lot of disputing to justify how we feel. We mentally rehearse the problem, replay conversations in our mind (I woulda, shoulda, coulda…), argue our case and convince ourselves why our discontent is totally justified.

It’s not fair.

Why would God allow this? Does He even care?

I want things to go back to the way they were!

I don’t see why I have to deal with this.

We CAN question and bring it to the Lord in prayer. Reasoning is healthy when it leads us toward God's perspective. It becomes disputing when it leads us away from trusting Him.

Look at Israel—the accusations and complaining brought them further away from trusting the One who was actually delivering them.

Remember, Jesus told us to not be anxious. Peter now reminds us of what to do with our anxiety:

1 Peter 5:6-9: 6 Therefore humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that He may exalt you at the proper time, 7 casting all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you. 8 Be of sober spirit, be on the alert. Your adversary, the devil, prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. 9 But resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same experiences of suffering are being accomplished by your brethren who are in the world.

Truly casting our cares fully upon the Lord diffuses our emotional reactions that feed complaining. That’s what Julie did on her trip. She diffused the emotional reactions so she could reset the default to something that was God-glorifying instead of just being miserable. Big difference!

It’s important to see that being anxious is often a foundation for grumbling and complaining. Anxiousness belongs in the hands of God. Casting all our anxiety on Him, because He cares for you. The Greek word for casting means to throw the weight of something onto another. We deliberately transfer our anxiety to God’s care instead of hanging on to it.

Someone might be thinking, Wait a minute. Didn't David complain throughout the Psalms? Not exactly. There's an important difference between complaining and lamenting.

Complaint focuses on the problem, and as we have seen, can drift into questioning God's goodness or accusing Him of neglect. Lament, on the other hand, brings the problem to God while the lamenter continues to trust Him. In Psalm 13, David cries out, How long, O LORD? He honestly expresses his anguish. Yet, by the end of the psalm he says, I have trusted in Your lovingkindness. This isn’t grumbling. David is bringing his pain to God, not his accusations against God.

This is what Israel should have done. This is what we should be doing.

It’s okay to lament, to bring our pain to God. But we can’t inflame that honest feeling with accusations and emotional baggage. We can dilute the value of sharing our pain with God if we pile complaining and disputing onto the pain.

With this example of Jesus before us, it is much easier to see that complaining because we don’t like the way things are is simply counterproductive. His heart and actions were clearly focused on accomplishing God’s will first and foremost. When we are faced with challenging people and circumstances, let us lean into following his example!

Will I comply no matter where it brings me?

Our Christian lives are to be clearly focused on higher things. When I complain, am I thinking about that higher pathway?

Earlier we talked about “appropriate” complaints. Where do those fit in the context

of all of the anti-complaining lessons we are learning?

This is a really important question as it rounds out our understanding of appropriate Christian complaining. Appropriate complaining DOES have a place in our lives, but as we

will see, it is a specific place that is not driven by emotions or even necessarily by disappointments.

We need to start with an “appropriate complaining” reminder.

The Apostle Paul is telling the Corinthians to learn from the inappropriate reactions and responses of Israel when they were delivered from Egypt:

1 Corinthians 10:10-13: 10 Nor grumble, as some of them did… 11 Now these things happened to them as an example, and they were written for our instruction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. (From this we know we can use these examples of the Israelites for ourselves) 12 Therefore let him who thinks he stands take heed that he does not fall. 13 No temptation has overtaken you but such as is common to man; and God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will provide the way of escape also, so that you will be able to endure it.

The promise at the end follows nor grumble, as some of them did—Israel was the example. Remember the trouble they had in the wilderness. No temptation has overtaken you but such as is common to man; and God is faithful! All of our behavior needs to be Christlike, and we are PROMISED deliverance through any and all experiences. Does that sound familiar? That is the parallel to what happened to Israel.

Our lives are on a spiritual level as followers of Christ. We need to rise to that level and put complaints where they belong.

What about appropriate complaints? Two things need to be present for appropriate complaints: attitude and perspective.

Attitude:

Ephesians 4:15: But speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in all aspects into him who is the head, even Christ.

Speaking the truth, not the exaggeration, not our feelings, but the truth in love. We then grow up in all aspects into him… even Christ. Based on this attitude, our “complaining” should look VERY different from others’ complaining. Whatever emotion, desire, disappointment or challenge is involved, it should be tempered by love.

If speaking the truth in love is our standard, what should our complaints sound like? We shouldn’t exaggerate, which we tend to do when we’re upset or emotional. We should address the issue, not attack someone's motives.

There are times I'm so frustrated that I tell my husband or my sister, "Look, I just need to vent. Sit down and just let me unload this." I need a safe place to express all those big feelings. More than anything, I'm looking for an unemotional, trusted sounding board who can help me sort through my thoughts and get me back on the right path with a godly perspective.

I’m not looking for them to pile on even more complaints or automatically agree with me. I need to get back to the right attitude. Often, as I'm talking it through, I realize I've magnified its importance far beyond what the issue deserves.

Similarly, I do that with my wife Trish. There is a lot of stress and tension in my life, and sometimes it’s overwhelming. I’ll talk to her and say, I’m not complaining; I just need to express the situation and try to figure it out.

She is really good at letting me get it out—not jumping on board with my perspective—but just calmly letting me express myself so I can deal with the emotions. That’s the point of the exercise.

In counseling others, I’ve had experiences where there are two individuals very much at odds with one another. Sometimes, I can’t even talk to the two of them together because of the tension. I’ve had this one experience where I’m talking to one and then the other. Each of them independently said to me, “I don’t want you to be on my side.” I said, “Well, that’s good because I’m not going to be on your side.” But what they were really saying was, “I don’t want to gang up on the other person; I want to figure out how to diffuse the situation.” Each of their intentions was for the conversation to get to a healthier place. That is a legitimate approach and is the attitude we need to have.

Perspective: We will next read about Jesus praying in the Garden of Gethsemane the night before his crucifixion, all alone. He has something on his heart and mind that is overwhelming and is essentially “complaining” to God.

Listen to how he did it:

Matthew 26:39: And he went a little beyond them, and fell on his face and prayed, saying, My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will, but as You will.

There was a part of this experience Jesus did not want to have to deal with. We aren’t told what that exactly was, but we understand the cup was the experience of being crucified as a blasphemer of God. From the prophecies, Jesus would have understood the impending crucifixion and what it entailed. He accepted this. But to be labeled as one who stood directly against his Father would have seemed unbearable. So he asks if the cup could pass from him; if that part could just be taken away.

Here is what happened:

Matthew 26:42-44: 42 He went away again a second time and prayed, saying, My Father, if this cannot pass away unless I drink it, Your will be done. 43 Again he came and found them sleeping, (his apostles) for their eyes were heavy. 44 And he left them again, and went away and prayed a third time, saying the same thing once more.

Jesus is deeply troubled. He didn’t ask once or even twice. He asked three times, similar to how Paul would later pray three times to have his thorn in the flesh removed.

There is nothing wrong in telling God about something that troubles you—even more than once.

Jesus’ desire here was pure and God-centered. His “complaint” (we hesitate to use that word here) was made with God’s will first and foremost in his heart and mind. His complaint had godly purpose and was handled in a godly way. God’s reply was no; Jesus had to go through even that experience. Jesus’ reply was, Yet not as I will, but as You will. This is an appropriate complaint and response. He embraced a challenge God knew had to be done. Similarly with us, if God’s answer is no, He cannot remove the trial, then we need to acquiesce and embrace the challenge God sees we need to deal with.

At the heart of many of our complaints is us expecting that things should be going according to OUR plan; that’s a sense of entitlement. Jesus demonstrated the opposite attitude: Not my will, but Yours.

Will we complain or comply? His example helps us stretch ourselves towards a higher standard of managing our own complaints.

Let’s look at Jesus through slightly different eyes as we look at his overall experience and how it affects us:

Hebrews 4:15-16: 15 For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who has been tempted in all things as we are, yet without sin. 16 Therefore let us draw near with confidence to the throne of grace, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.

This is encouraging because this doesn’t mean we can never be upset or can never express the pain or hurt or disappointment of what we are going through. God created us with a wide range of emotions, and we are allowed to talk to Him through Jesus.

We are encouraged to come boldly with those things because we have seen all through this how God is compassionate, understanding and wise. His providence will prevail. We just have to learn to be able to turn our minds and hearts into that rather than our own complaining attitude.

Sometimes putting ourselves out may be challenging, but it doesn’t mean we need to complain:

1 Peter 4:8-10: 8 Above all, keep fervent in your love for one another, because love covers a multitude of sins. 9 Be hospitable to one another without complaint. 10 As each one has received a special gift, employ it in serving one another as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.

This short phrase, Be hospitable to one another without complaint almost gets lost here. We need to go out of our way for each other and not complain. Yes, it might be inconvenient or even a little costly, but these are God’s people. Be hospitable. Do it for the love of God, His will and His people.

Sometimes we have issues with our brotherhood, but it doesn’t mean we need to complain:

James 5:9: Do not complain, brethren, against one another, so that you yourselves may not be judged; behold, the Judge is standing right at the door.

When we complain against one another we end up putting ourselves in a place of judgment to be judged. We are not to be inappropriate judges of each other. We can start getting into slander and gossip and bad feelings towards our brethren which eventually creates spiritual destruction.

Instead of complaining and disputing, let’s walk where Jesus walked and do what he did:

Colossians 3:12-13: 12 So, as those who have been chosen of God, holy and beloved, put on a heart of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience; 13 bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, whoever has a complaint against anyone; just as the Lord forgave you, so also should you.

What a great example. If we have a complaint against anyone; just as the Lord forgave you, so also should you. Just look up and remember—have I been forgiven? Then what should I do, if I have been given that new lease on life? Surely, I can find it in my heart to have that response toward others.

The end result is remarkable:

Philippians 4:19-20: 19 And my God will supply all your needs according to His riches in glory in Christ Jesus. 20 Now to our God and Father be the glory forever and ever. Amen.

In the wilderness, God told the Israelites He would take care of all of their needs. They just needed to trust Him. Here the Apostle Paul assures us He will supply all your needs according to His riches in glory in Christ Jesus. Same message; different context, as ours is a spiritual fulfillment. We just need to see things from the context of the higher life Jesus showed us. And complaining just doesn’t cut it. It doesn’t fit.

The final conclusion is not “Don’t complain.” Instead, we ask what transforms an honest concern into sinful complaining? A legitimate problem becomes sinful complaining when it causes us to distrust God's care.

Let us put every aspect of our complaining attitude behind us.

God’s promise to Israel remains true:

give earnest heed to the voice of the LORD your God

do what is right in His sight

give ear to His commandments

keep all His statutes

We also have Jesus’ own example of living this blessing as proof of its power.

These four pieces echo again and again as a recipe Jesus followed, and that we need to follow to remove complaining in our lives.

We make our choice based upon what we see in Scripture and the beauty and value of God’s providence no matter what it may bring. Complaining is a waste of time.

Let us glorify God instead!

So, are Christians allowed to complain and are there limits?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions…

…Think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.

Word Study:

Many of our topics are compiled with a Word Study using several concordances and other Bible helps. We see how a particular word is used in both the Old and New Testaments. Understanding how the words are used not only tells us what they mean, but it also gives us the nuances of the original Hebrew or Greek when comparing how the writers of the Bible use them in different contexts. We can also learn more by seeing the origins of a particular word, providing a depth of understanding just reading scriptures in English cannot provide. Here we present New Testament words on our topic.

Murmuring: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1112 goggusmos; from #1111, a grumbling

The King James Version translates this as “murmuring” 3 times, and “grudging” 1 time

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) a murmur, murmuring, muttering

1a) a secret debate 1b) a secret displeasure not openly avowed

All uses in the King James Version:

John 7:12: And there was much murmuring <1112> among the people concerning him: for some said, He is a good man: others said, Nay; but he deceiveth the people.

Acts 6:1: And in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplied, there arose a murmuring <1112> of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration.

Philippians 2:14: Do all things without murmurings <1112> and disputings:

1 Peter 4:9: Use hospitality one to another without grudging <1112>.

Murmur: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1111 gogguzo; of uncertain derivation; to grumble

The King James Version translates this as “murmur” 8 times

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to murmur, mutter, grumble, say anything against in a low tone

1a) of the cooing of doves 1b) of those who confer secretly together

1c) of those who discontentedly complain

All uses in the King James Version:

Matthew 20:11: And when they had received it, they murmured <1111> against the goodman of the house.

Luke 5:30: But their scribes and Pharisees murmured <1111> against his disciples, saying, Why do ye eat and drink with publicans and sinners?

John 6:41: The Jews then murmured <1111> at him, because he said, I am the bread which came down from heaven.

John 6:43: Jesus therefore answered and said unto them, Murmur <1111> not among yourselves.

John 6:61: When Jesus knew in himself that his disciples murmured <1111> at it, he said unto them, Doth this offend you?

John 7:32: The Pharisees heard that the people murmured <1111> such things concerning him; and the Pharisees and the chief priests sent officers to take him.

1 Corinthians 10:10: Neither murmur ye <1111>, as some of them also murmured <1111>, and were destroyed of the destroyer.

Thoughts: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1261 dialogismos; from 1260; discussion, i.e. (internal)

consideration (by implication, purpose), or (external) debate

The King James Version translates this as “thought” 9 times, “reasoning” 1 time, “imagination”

1 time, “doubtful” 1 time, “disputing” 1 time, and “doubting” 1 time

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) the thinking of a man deliberating with himself 1a) a thought,

inward reasoning 1b) purpose, design 2) a deliberating, questioning about what is true

2a) hesitation, doubting 2b) disputing, arguing

Matthew 15:19: For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts <1261>, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies.

Mark 7:21: For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts <1261>, adulteries, fornications, murders…

Luke 2:35: (Yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also,) that the thoughts <1261> of many hearts may be revealed.

Luke 5:22: But when Jesus perceived their thoughts <1261>, he answering said unto them, What reason ye in your hearts?

Luke 6:8: But he knew their thoughts <1261>, and said to the man which had the withered hand, Rise up, and stand forth in the midst. And he arose and stood forth.

Luke 9:46-47: Then there arose a reasoning <1261> among them, which of them should be greatest. And Jesus, perceiving the thought <1261> of their heart, took a child, and set him by him…

Luke 24:38: And he said unto them, Why are ye troubled? and why do thoughts <1261> arise in your hearts?

Romans 1:21: Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations <1261>, and their foolish heart was darkened.

Romans 14:1: Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful <1261> disputations.

1 Corinthians 3:20: And again, The Lord knoweth the thoughts <1261> of the wise, that they are vain.

Philippians 2:14: Do all things without murmurings and disputings <1261>.

1 Timothy 2:8: I will therefore that men pray every where, lifting up holy hands, without wrath and doubting <1261>.

James 2:4: Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts <1261>?

thoroughly, i.e. (genitive case) to deliberate (by reflection or discussion)

The King James Version translates this as “reason” 11 times, “dispute” 1 time, “cast in the mind” 1

time, “muse” 1 time, “think” 1 time, and “consider” 1 time

Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1) to bring together different reasons, to reckon up the reasons, to

reason, revolve in one’s mind, deliberate

Mark 2:6: But there were certain of the scribes sitting there, and reasoning <1260> in their hearts.

### Study Questions

https://christianquestions.com/character/1463-are-christians-allowed-to-complain/

1.

What is the distinction between “grumbling” and “disputing” based on the Greek definitions of goggusmos and dialogismos? How might each of these attitudes reveal a lack of trust in God's providence? (Philippians 2:4)

2. Was the Israelites’ concern upon arriving at Marah legitimate? What four commands did God gave Israel at

Marah, and what promise accompanied those commands? (Exodus 15:24-27)

3. How did the concern over water at Marah change into complaints in the Wilderness of Sin? Who were the

Israelites complaining against? What had they lost sight of? (Exodus 16:1-8)

4. Why did Moses rename Rephidim, the location where God provided water from the rock, Massah and

Meribah? In what way did this memorialize Israel’s behaviors? What was their real problem? (Exodus 17:1-7)

5. Looking at the experiences of Marah, the Wilderness of Sin and Rephidim, what evidence shows that Israel's

real problem was trust rather than water or food? How can the same thing happen in our own lives?

6. When you get frustrated, do you simply bring your concerns to God looking for His guidance, or do you allow

your thoughts to develop into grumbling, disputing, accusations or questions on God’s care? What must you NOT lose sight of? How is grumbling a “memory problem?”

7. What does the Apostle Paul mean by “godliness accompanied by contentment is great gain”? How did he find

the secret of contentment in his life of troubles? (1 Timothy 6:6-8, Philippians 4:11-13)

8. Compare the four commands God gave Israel in Exodus 15:26 with the way Jesus fulfilled them in Isaiah 6:8

and Philippians 2:5-11. What can we learn about overcoming complaining through Jesus' example of obedience?

9. Discuss the differences between reasoning, disputing and lamenting. How can we prevent our internal dialog

from becoming destructive disputing? Why is lament a healthy biblical response to pain while disputing can lead us away from trust? (Philippians 2:14, Psalm 13)

10. Explain the roles of attitude and perspective in an appropriate Christian complaint. How were Jesus and Paul

examples for us in this? (Ephesians 4:15, Matthew 26:39, 42-44)

11. How should we respond to anxiety, difficult people and other trials? Discuss practical ways to overcome and

diffuse complaining and disputing. (Hebrews 4:15-16, 1 Peter 5:6-9, 4:8-10, James 5:9, Colossians 3:12-13)

12. What does it mean to choose God’s providence over our own expectations and to glorify Him rather than

remain focused on our complaints? (1 Corinthians 10:10-13, Philippians 2:14-16, 4:19-20) Describe a time when your circumstances did not change, but your perspective did. How did gratitude, trust or a renewed focus on God's providence affect your attitude?
